09/18/2026
’Once an alcoholic, always an alcoholic is outdated. Here’s why’
This one is going to ruffle a lot of feathers.
From page 31 of the Alcoholics Anonymous Big Book:
We are like men who have lost their legs; they never grow new ones. Neither does there appear to be any kind of treatment which will make alcoholics of our kind like other men. We have tried every imaginable remedy. In some instances there has been brief recovery, followed always by still worse relapse. Physicians who are familiar with alcoholism agree there is no such thing as making a normal drinker out of an alcoholic. Science may one day accomplish this, but it evidently hasn’t done so yet.
You might rightfully have read this and wondered, “so how do we know science has accomplished this?”
Abstinence-centric programs like Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) and related 12-step offshoots have historically been reluctant, if not hostile, towards the idea of using medication-based approaches towards reducing substance use. It’s not uncommon at all to hear those undergoing Medication for Opioid Use Disorder (MOUD) or Medication-Assisted Treatment (MAT) report stigma from those in 12-step programs, usually under the claim that they’re not truly sober if they’re still dependent on a chemical to manage their lives. Naltrexone as a harm-reduction approach to limit drinking instead of manage cravings during abstinence is another approach that you might never hear about or only hear negative things about in recovery groups. William Wilson (Bill W.) himself explored hallucinogens like LSD to prompt spiritual awakenings and high-dose Vitamin B supplements to address stubborn phases of depression, which others within the AA umbrella were strongly against discussing in AA literature. AA was founded in 1935, so its foundations are very distant from the findings of modern neuroscience. The analogy of the brain being a cucumber that’s turned into a pickle which can never go back doesn’t exactly hold up to scientific consensus.
We know now that our brain is an incredibly versatile muscle that is constantly changing throughout our whole lives, just like every other aspect of our body. Contrary to popular conception, antidepressants don’t work by correcting a chemical imbalance but by increasing neuroplasticity, allowing the brain to grow, repair, and reinforce neural circuits that regulate moods. The reason Behavioral Activation (BA) as a therapeutic intervention works alongside antidepressants is because it provides a structured set of tasks you can complete while your brain is better able to process the rewards from their completion. It stands to reason that if we can design a pharmacological-behavioral intervention that helps change people’s brains to the point that they no longer meet the criteria for clinical depression, we might keep an open mind towards a possible intervention into substance use patterns. The goal of interventions into depression isn’t to eliminate the experience of negative emotions or negative outlooks (i.e. abstaining from the symptoms of depression) but to help someone regulate the symptoms of depression as they come up so they can still pursue a life aligned with their long-term values. The medical and academic community has largely acknowledged this in their concept of “recovery,” acknowledging the benefits of any reduction in harmful behavioral patterns that makes someone’s life more manageable.
The CNN article describes several notable studies that identified individuals who returned to low or moderate drinking patterns in their recovery beyond just Brad Pitt. Some studies suggest that as many as 1 in 5 people who met the criteria for alcohol use disorder were able to do so. In my experience, you will almost never hear this side of research presented in recovery programs or professional treatment facilities, which almost universally are focused solely on abstinence.
On a personal note, I would virtually never recommend to someone who has at one point met the criteria for a substance use disorder of any kind to attempt moderation. It’s impossible to know if any particular individual can manage a return to low-risk drinking or recreational use of a substance before they attempt it, and the odds and consequences of failure are high. There haven’t been many studies examining the risk profiles of those who can or can’t return to moderate drinking, but even a risk factors analysis will only give probabilities instead of guarantees. I could not in good conscience recommend someone attempt that if abstinence is on the table. All alcohol consumption is toxic, after all.
That all being said, I also believe individuals should have access to all the information they can to make the decisions that are best for them, and I believe anyone who does manage to moderate their substance use should be celebrated for their achievements in reducing harm to themselves and others. You should know about programs like SMART Recovery that explicitly make room for those seeking to moderate their substance use. You should know about Buprenorphine (Suboxone) as a partial opioid agonist, Methadone as a full opioid agonist, and Naltrexone as an opioid antagonist. These are evidence-based approaches that improve health and quality of life outcomes for individuals struggling to manage their substance use.
Understandably, an organization that identifies itself as providing abstinence for a discrete group of “alcoholics” may experience a conflict of interest on the topic of whether people can stop identifying as “alcoholics” at some point in their lives. AA has fundamentally Protestant roots that adopts the psychology of moral surveillance into its perspective on alcohol and addiction, likening them to the temptation to sin associated with Satan or the Devil, or at least contrary to the Higher Power that’s almost always a stand-in for a personal, interventionist Biblical God. If that’s your framing of the world, then harm-reduction towards moderating substance use is comparable to only occasionally consorting with the Devil, and leaning on medications to manage a disorder implies that leaning on one’s Higher Power has been insufficient. There’s a built-in resistance to working alongside scientific breakthroughs within this moral-psychology framework.
09/15/2026
Help - is it just me ? How to get out ?
The fact that you have sober periods where you enjoy the normal things in life is really encouraging. A lot of people don’t seek help until their life is unmanageable, like being unable to get out of bed in the mornings without using or burning their professional and personal relationships. If they do achieve a continuous stint of sobriety, they report feeling chronically depressed and anxious. I was in that category and I wish I had the desire and opportunity to get help sooner. You also have a well of financial stability it seems, and you’re starting therapy soon with an awareness of the traumas that might be relevant to your lifestyle as it is. I’d be very optimistic for you to have the capacity, means, and willpower to change if you’re able to commit to it.
How to prevent an addict from self-isolating?
For all the criticism I direct at 12 Step programs, one of the best features of it is instant access to a bunch of people in recovery who have experienced relapse patterns and can attempt to intervene in each others’ lives without necessarily alerting others in your social network who don’t have experience with addiction.
However, I don’t know your friend, and some people react to the suggestion of attending a recovery meeting as if you’re accusing them of being too broken to participate in everyday life with you and in need of containment. If that’s the case, the most you might be able to do is lend a non-judgmental ear to them, and perhaps remind them that if they do need help in an emergency, you care about being there for them and won’t be upset. If you live close by, just offer to hang out and be a no-pressure distraction.
Guilt, shame, and hopelessness are some of the biggest drivers of self-isolation, and self-isolation by definition makes any other intervention or desire to get help much harder. I can’t count how many times I’ve been saved from dark thoughts by someone who had a funny story about their own day and gave me an hour of their time to have normal human conversation. The benefit of recovery groups is that you can have access to that almost any time and anywhere. Telehealth since COVID has helped a lot, and many people in recovery will try to pick up a call anytime and check-in at your place if you go even a day without responding to them. That’s too intense for a lot of people, but you can replicate a fraction of that through your friendship rather than a fellowship.
The relentless pressure to ‘be positive’ in recovery
I think there’s a general inclination towards toxic positivity in modern culture that’s driven in large part by a desire to sweep problems under the rug until they become so unsustainable that they can’t be ignored before then blaming individuals for just not trying hard enough. I’ve heard a lot of people in 12 Step circles come to believe that some emotions are just unhealthy to experience at all, including grief, anger, and sadness. In my opinion, this comes out of an expectation that a spiritual awakening puts someone past these emotions, which are framed necessarily as byproducts of an individual ego that has not been subdued to the will of a Higher Power that would remedy one’s character defects if sought. To be fair, it could also be an overcorrection from a well-intentioned impulse towards the constant guilt and shame that individuals in recovery and active addiction impose on themselves, since those aren’t conducive to healthy living either, but the goal of never experiencing guilt and shame is distinct from the goal of learning to manage appropriate levels of guilt and shame. Moving onto the future means accepting the past, but not forgetting it, or else we’re doomed to repeat the patterns we’re trying to change. I like the saying in Recovery Dharma circles that pain does not erase goodness but informs it. Exploring the depths and nuances of “negative” emotions is still an aspect of exploring our human selves, and that in turn gives us a more complete picture of how we and others experience life.
09/14/2026
Missing the rush?
My timeline matches up with yours pretty closely. I know what you mean, there’s a part of me that romanticizes all the self-destructive (and externally destructive) tendencies I used to have. And they did accomplish things that, on some level, satisfied the impulses I had even when I was stone cold sober. My brain still bundles together cues and triggers with memories that remind me how intense the feelings used to be. I like to reference Frank Cotton from Hellraiser: “The doors to the pleasures of Heaven or Hell, I didn’t care which.” I wanted the relief of a catharsis that was intense enough to match how angry and hopeless I felt about my life and the world it was put into. I wanted to break something as much as I felt broken to make sense of things. I felt that I couldn’t even feel anything without using or comprehend anything beyond a tragic ending for myself. A lot of contradictions that couldn’t work themselves out within me poured out of me.
But I remind myself that my values, goals, and actions now make me a different person. When I struggle to separate a feeling from the memory of a feeling, I know I can draw a clean line at the point of my decisions from now onwards. The pain I’ve felt and caused now inform my goodness instead of erasing it. I have empathy for others, including you, who struggle in that cycle of hurt people hurting people. I know from looking at children who openly take and share love that cold-heartedness is not an inevitable fact of the human condition, but a response to a traumatizing world, more often manmade than not now. I think there’s plenty of pride to be had in even the effort of trying to choose a better response. If there’s something I appreciate most about addicts in recovery, it’s that we become intimately acquainted with the monster we can become, and we walk around sober to live in spite of it. Many people walk around rationalizing all the monstrous things they do without ever taking a hard look at the trail of destruction they cause. I’d rather wear my guilt to keep me grounded than be blissfully ignorant, and I feel an instant camaraderie with anyone who makes that decision.
Would it be easier one day?
You don’t sound crazy at all. The acute withdrawal symptoms you mention like chills will definitely stop soon, but the longer consequences of substance use can continue for a while, even years.
But, it also generally gets easier each day as your brain heals and retrains itself to enjoy things that fill the boredom. With alcohol for instance, your brain gets used to cutting down receptors for the neurotransmitters that calm you down while flooding itself with the ones that excite your nervous system, which is why you might get very anxious and have shakes for a while after. At the same time, it’s harder to feel rewards or pleasure from activities that feel good to others.
Our brains are crazy good at regulating themselves back to something functional and close to the baseline before substance use. The key is consistency in a positive direction. You’re not doomed, you’re just recovering from a condition your brain has been adjusting to for ten years. It’s going to take time to change that trajectory, and it won’t be easy, but most of those who have done it will swear it was worth.
I’m terrified to quit
In active addiction, it’s really easy to forget that you have a brain that’s naturally curious and looking to engage people, start hobbies, and create things. It takes a while for that personality to come back and develop, but it does happen.
09/13/2026
Help to rebuilt life after deaddiction
Addiction and depression will do a lot to damage not just the act of participating in hobbies but interest in anything at all. I think it’s absolutely true that, for every mental health condition, someone needs to have something they value that can be an incentive or a goal to target. Emptiness leads to boredom, isolation, and hopelessness, all of which are standard threats to sobriety and will worsen symptoms of depression. I would say your intuition is absolutely on the mark.
But, he got sober, so he must value something, and that something is a good starting place to develop interest and passion again. Even if it’s just valuing the simple act of not dying or being in pain, it’s possible to turn healthy living and wellness activities into an interest that engages someone into a community of those with a similar mindset. It’s not going to replace or extinguish the pain of what’s already been lost, and I personally think it’s risky to build someone’s expectations about that, but there are things worth going through the pain of staying sober over. Health and wellness are a lot bigger than just eating a balanced diet and exercising. Just trying to rearrange your own room for a change of mental cues can be extended into an interest in decor and deep dives into how some cultures have very elaborate traditions around interior design for mental health. Just adding a plant to spruce up the room can create a sense that one is both responsible for another life and capable of nurturing life.
There’s no one-size-fits-all solution, but anything that brings someone into a social network or group of some kind would be very helpful. In early sobriety and clinical depression, the brain struggles to process rewards from the basic activities and hobbies that it would normally treat as meaningful and pleasurable activities. Beginning with small steps and a peer group that can empathize with the struggle of emptiness while providing external motivators to act can go a long way. Medication and a therapist could too, if your brother is not already seeing one.
Fix addiction to fix mental health or vice versa
In medical settings, addiction is called substance use disorder because, well, it’s considered a psychiatric disorder. It appears in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders because it’s a mental health issue. It doesn’t actually make much sense to separate those, even though many rehabs will, for some reason, treat them as entirely separate things. If depression makes you feel hopeless and incapable of things ever getting better, you’re more likely to use substances to feel better and are less likely to weigh substance use against the delayed gratification of sobriety, because you’re certain you’re not going to feel good anyways. It’s all connected.
You have one brain. The same pathways that are blunted or atrophied as a result of clinical depression are also impacted by chronic substance use. Behavioral interventions like Behavioral Activation for depression or Contingency Management for stimulant use disorders aim at the same pathways and often rely on the same conceptual mechanisms of retraining the brain’s concepts of reward. At least half of those with a substance use disorder have a co-occurring disorder, like depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress, etc. Symptoms of anxiety and panic disorders are common as triggers for substance use, which is where the idea of the self-medication hypothesis comes up. A lot of facilities and providers are pivoting towards “dual diagnosis” frameworks in recognition of this. Some recent studies suggest that addressing trauma and substance use at the same time is more effective than waiting for someone to stabilize their sobriety before doing meaningful trauma work, while many standard cognitive therapies that work best on simpler cases are less effective during this period; there has to be more specialized and nuanced care that looks at overall mental health and recovery capital.
In other words, addiction is a mental health issue, even if it feels like compulsions to use are physical or bodily cravings, or that nutritional deficiencies resulting from chronic substance use are just diet and exercise issues. It’s very bizarre to me that rehabs and healthcare policymakers are resistant to recognizing how holistic heath is. But as far as we as individuals navigating the system go, we should be aware that it’s not either/or. Every mental health analysis should include the degree to which substances are a part of the attempt to regulate our overall moods and status.
Recovery and Dharma
I’d say it’s more common than not, based on my experience in both peer recovery groups and treatment facilities. Colloquially they’re just called “using dreams,” and for some it leads to cravings when they wake up, so it’s a good idea to have some kind of plan in case that happens. Personally, using dreams have always been nightmares where I wake up panicked, expecting myself to have the old shakes and heart palpitations while figuring out how long it’ll take for the 7/11 to open from whatever unholy hour I awoke at. It’s a huge fucking relief when that’s not the case and I actually have a day of things planned that don’t involve digging my life into a deeper trench than it was last night.
Do not call crisis hotlines
I run some online recovery resources and have grappled with whether or not I should be listing helplines. My own experiences tell me a strong NO. It has never been a helpful experience, and sometimes actively made situations worse. I have almost never heard of someone having a good experience with them.
When I asked others managing content in the online space how they felt about it, including those who chose to list emergency lines, the consensus seemed to be that they thought it reduced liability for them in case anyone ever argued their website was a trigger for a suicidal or self-harm episode. Even more cynically, some said it just made their content seem more official by association with an emergency tool backed by governments and nonprofits.
At that point I just determined that helplines and emergency services exist to make a problem invisible so that everyone else can continue with their day, such that someone deciding to off themselves because they refuse to seek help through terrible, traumatizing services is an acceptable outcome to most people. I’m no doctor, but “First, Do No Harm” comes to mind as a good principle here. I’m also no fan of Twelve-Step Groups, but I would rather direct someone to Suicide Anonymous than institutions that are first and foremost out for their own self-preservation.
Wanting to be chosen over the substance - partner of an addict
One of the defining features of addiction is that what the brain values diverges intensely from what the brain likes. Someone can be completely honest when they say they love their partner more than anything else in the world, including drugs, but the brain refuses to translate that value system articulated consciously into plans and goals that they feel rewarded for acting on. It’s why we call it a disorder instead of an issue of willpower or morality.
That all being said, is your partner trying but failing to stay sober? Or are they rationalizing away the fact that they have a problem? Denial isn’t actually a step everyone with an addiction goes through. Many are perfectly aware they have a spiraling life that’s getting worse but might struggle with depression or trauma in a way that makes change feel hopeless. In my opinion, that’s very different than continuing to use substances in a way that hurts those around you while denying there’s even a problem to address, particularly loved ones who have chosen to stay with someone through their active addiction. At that point, they’re dismissing the harms they cause others. If your partner is in denial and refuses to seek help, whether that means therapy, medication, or inpatient rehab, there’s no reason to think the current situation would get better. I think it’s more than fair to expect a partner to value you enough to at least be honest, even if they’re using. The compulsions to lie and steal to fuel an addiction are not, in and of themselves, a biological necessity of having addiction. They’re often the result of guilt and shame, which are emotions that can be responded to in different ways, some of which are going to be less destructive than others.
Also, it might be helpful to consider your own part here in potentially enabling her. Sending money to someone you know is likely to relapse or in active addiction is giving them the means to continue using. It shields them from the financial consequences that can serve as barriers to use and relapse, or even encourage them to seek treatment. Not that I’m saying you should blame yourself or you should feel responsible for her addiction in any way, but it is true that placing guardrails or boundaries around money might help both you and her.
09/12/2026
9K people recovering from addiction trained in vocational skills over 8 months
Did you know there are countries that aren’t America? I forget that all the time.
Much like other countries in the 20th century, Egypt’s approaches in the 1900s approached substance use through criminalization and incarceration. The Anti-Narcotics Law No. 182 of 1960 criminalized simple possession of drugs for personal use, including those with a long tradition of use in the region like hashish and opium. Around the 1970s and 1980s, substance use as a public health issue went from manual laborers trying to relieve pain and stress to younger demographics getting hooked on heroin and cocaine as highly addictive and dangerous substances. Over 85% of those who entered hospital detoxificiation programs relapsed, and the failures of incarceration and emergency medical interventions couldn’t be ignored by state officials and policymakers. Law No. 122 of 1989 amended the 1960 law, with Article 37 offering a diversion program where courts could place individuals into medical internment for up to 3 years as an alternative to prison. Presidential Decree No. 46 set up the Fund for Combating and Treating Addiction and Substance Abuse (FDCTA) in 1991 while working alongside civil institutions like the Coptic Church.
Since then, Egypt has taken many more steps towards addressing substance use as a health issue requiring treatment and destigmatization. This story covering 9,000 individuals in recovery completing vocational training is the result of funding from the FDCTA, which led to specialized rehabilitation facilities called Al-Azima (Determination) Centers. They host technical workshops run by a combination of professional educators and behavioral specialists and tailor their trainings to market demands, like “Mobile Phone Maintenance and Repair,” so that they’re employable after treatment in something stable and gainful. There’s also another state program called Bi-Aydina, or “With Our Hands,” in which those who take vocational trainings in furniture manufacturing can design and build furniture for new FDCTA centers. A really interesting facet of these programs is that completion of a vocational training program unlocks special low-interest micro-loans to open independent workshops and small businesses, which works around corporate hiring barriers and stigma.
I have spoken about, and will continue to speak about, Contingency Management (CM) as one of the strongest approaches to addressing problems in recovery treatment that both directly offers a competing reward to the compulsions to use while also setting someone up with an expansion of their overall recovery capital after clinical treatment ends. In America, CM programs are decentralized and heavily limited by federal Medicaid guidelines. The Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) allocates billions of dollars for State Opioid Response (SOR) and Tribal Opioid Response (TOR) grants, but they limit “patient rewards” by an annual incentive cap that maxes out at 750 and must be given as non-cash gift cards or vouchers. State-level CM interventions, like California's CalAIM initiative, requires a Section 1115 Demonstration Waiver to be filed to bypass federal restrictions on "prizes" or "rewards." Under CalAIM, dozens of counties can pay out escalating e-gift cards up to 599 over 24 weeks for drug-free urine samples.
Egypt has been, comparatively speaking, more aggressive about creating a macro-level infrastructure to build an actual reintegration program for those with substance use disorders that stretches across healthcare, education, and financial sectors. In America, CM and other behavioral interventions relying on incentives are highly decentralized, separate silo from education and financial policies. For all the touted benefits of private sector facilities offering choice, competition, and innovation, people often ignore the holistic nature of health and social integration. Getting someone sober is not the end goal of meaningful recovery programs; building a sustainable, stable life that strongly incentivizes sustained sobriety is. You could just lock someone in a box until they’ve undergone withdrawals and coach them into regurgitating coping skills to accomplish the former… which is what a lot of treatment boils down to. Hell, we can’t even address the problem of therapists giving advice in complete contradiction of facility-mandated 12-step group attendance. But hey, at least you get the choice of deciding which of these facilities based on the Minnesota Model prints out the same few CBT/DBT worksheets for you while you argue with your insurance provider.
09/11/2026
I’m addicted to ordering drugs just to throw them away, what can I do
To add on, studies show that brains with addictions experience relief at the moment that the decision to use again is made, before consuming a substance. We have distinct mechanisms for anticipation, wanting, and liking, such that our brains can understand relief is on its way and respond by reducing the anxiety that comes with the conflict of resisting something that’s ingrained as highly rewarding.
09/10/2026
My boyfriend of two years is leaving me because I can’t get clean
A core aspect of addiction is that the brain’s sense of what’s rewarding and what’s pleasurable diverge, so that you can really want to be better because addiction is a painful condition but your brain doesn’t translate that into a series of goals that take you there. That’s not something that can reliably be overcome by willpower alone. I’d say to treat addiction like the actual psychiatric disorder it is and seek treatments like a stint in rehab where you’re around a bunch of people who are in the same situation as you, and you can focus intensively on both coping skills and addressing the underlying mechanisms of addiction. The sense of obligation you feel towards being a good parent for your daughter is a powerful anchor. Not everyone entering treatment can identify something they value like that.
Can someone who’s addicted to a substance ever get to that point where they can use their drug of choice recreationally with control (and not be addicted to it?)
Strictly speaking, studies do show that a sizable minority of people who meet the criteria for alcohol use disorder do return to a moderate or low-risk usage.
The caveat is that you can’t reliably know if you’re one of those people before you attempt to use again, and if you’re someone who has entered recovery communities and rehabs in search of a solution because first-line individual care like therapy within your old environment didn’t work for you, you’re definitely not among the likely candidates for whom resuming usage is safe. At least half of those diagnosed with a substance use disorder have a co-occurring mental health disorder, and it’s hard enough to manage the symptoms of just one condition in ideal conditions.
So whether or not some people can moderate, attempting to resume moderate usage is virtually never a good idea. I certainly wouldn’t recommend it to anyone, and I would be very cautious about anyone who does moderate as taking a substantial risk of relapsing into their previous patterns in active addiction.
How do you avoid replacing one addiction with another?
Addiction is more than just the cravings and compulsions to use when you don’t want to. Your brain’s pathways have been damaged in a way that will take time to heal, which could mean anywhere from months to years before it processes rewards and pleasure from those rewards in a comparable way to the baseline prior to chronic substance use.
One of the biggest reasons people get involved in recovery groups instead of doing it on their own is for the structure of peers who have felt the way you’re feeling now and can keep you engaged in activities that slowly promote healing alongside a sense of external accountability. Sobriety is effectively an exercise in retraining the brain to adjust its baselines and expectations of reward. Some therapeutic interventions for depression like Behavioral Activation work along the same lines of getting the brain to process dopamine and feel rewards even when there isn’t the instant gratification that addiction gets the brain to expect. Trying to find substitutions for addictive compulsions is harm reduction at best; it’s better to eat candy or spicy foods than relapse, but that doesn’t really address the mechanisms of addiction.
I would seriously consider therapy and medication if you aren’t seeking those right now and have the ability to afford it. A good therapist can help you structure some routines or schedule some events that are calibrated to your current levels of motivation and energy while also identifying any triggers, cues, and/or trauma at work behind your compulsions to use. Medication like antidepressants can go a long way to promoting neuroplasticity that makes it easier for your brain to begin changing its pathways.
Natural defense: Unlocking the brain’s hidden ability to suppress addiction
Researchers at the University of Texas at San Antonio (UTSA) have made significant breakthroughs in their focus on using midbrain astrocytes as a natural mechanism for the brain to suppress addictive compulsions. Matthew Wanat, a professor and co-principal investigator (PI) of a grant provided by the National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA), has led a project titled “Targeting the midbrain astrocyte epigenome to regulate drug-dependent behavior.”
Astrocytes are cells in the central nervous system (CNS) that support and protect neurons, and they help control the molecules that move across the blood-brain barrier. While they were initially assumed to only play a supportive role in maintaining the health and structure of neurons, newer paradigms study astrocytes as having direct relevance to neuronal activity. Specifically, Wanat’s team has focused on the way astrocytes interact with neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) of the midbrain that house the primary mechanisms for releasing dopamine impacted by the conditioning of chronic substance use. In brains that haven’t been exposed to habitual drug use, promoting astrocyte activity is associated with a stronger reward-seeking drives, but they do the opposite in drug-experienced brains by turning down the excitability of neurons that produce dopamine. Activating the Gq G-protein coupled receptor signaling pathway through epigenetic changes can release a steady stream of GABA and adenosine that dampen the mechanisms that produce intense cravings preceding a relapse.
Traditional neuropsychiatric drugs in substance use disorder treatments target neuronal receptors directly, which can lead to severe side effects or even transferring a chemical dependence to the drug itself. Medications that attempt to blunt the sensitivity of dopamine pathways and intense cravings can produce anhedonia and lower the rewards or pleasure experienced from any activity one engages in. Through collaboration with the Oklahoma Medical Research Foundation (OMRF) and Astrocyte Pharmaceuticals, Wanat’s team is exploring the potential of a drug referred to as AST-004, which works as an agonist of adenosine receptors on the surface of astrocytes. This mimics a distress signal that triggers a defensive response from an astrocyte cell’s mitochondria and produces a metabolic boost through increased ATP production, which in turn triggers a series of supportive functions like cleaning up toxic levels of neurotransmitters and counteracting edema from the bodily stresses of substance use. The cumulative effect is in stabilizing neural pathways that suppress the compulsions to relapse that occur when astrocytes are drained of energy from substances that forced neurons to overwork.
Although AST-004 is undergoing active preclinical evaluation as a treatment for substance use disorders, it’s already been approved for clinical research in other neurological conditions like Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI) and Acute Ischemic Stroke (AIS). Overall, this work signals a departure from the common assumption that addiction is first and foremost a dysfunction of the neurons themselves, such that pharmacological interventions must either promote neuronal connections or substitute for the mechanisms of a particular exogenous substance on which an individual is dependent. Working through astrocytes is almost like having access to a new organ that can address addictive compulsions across the board rather than studying the particular mechanisms of drug-specific dependencies. Both stimulants like cocaine and opioids like fentanyl could be addressed through focusing on the astrocyte-neuron interactions of pathways shared across addictive substances.
Northwest researchers develop vaccines to prevent opioid overdose and support addiction recovery
The Pravetoni Research Group at the University of Washington (UW) have made breakthroughs in developing a fentanyl vaccine that could teach the body’s natural immune system to not only block the effects of fentanyl and close analogs like carfentanil but reduce the intensity and likelihood of cravings, dependency, and overdoses.
Normally, fentanyl molecules are haptens, or molecules too small for the immune system to recognize. The vaccine works by attaching a molecule structurally similar to fentanyl to a carrier protein, roughly 500 times larger, that forces the immune system’s B-cells to activate and find a configuration capable of interacting with the shape of fentanyl. Later, when real fentanyl molecules enter the bloodstream, the B-cells produce antibodies capable of trapping them inside a much larger moleculer cluster that neutralizes their potential to interact with the brain. Due to the drug’s potency (studies indicate fentanyl might be 50 to 100 times stronger than heroin and morphine), the vaccine is administered alongside immune boosters and cutting-edge nanoparticle delivery systems. The kidney and liver safely break down the antibody-fentanyl clusters and toss them out through urine.
Although the idea of using pharmacokinetic immunological responses isn’t new, this breakthrough is the first opioid vaccine to ever reach Phase I human clinical trials in the United States. Unlike naloxone (Narcan) which wears off within an hour or two and leaves open the potential for re-narcotization, the vaccines last for days at full effectiveness and may even work up to a year. If it passes trials and is rolled out as a treatment protocol, it would be aimed at providing extra voluntary security for those actively trying to quit, since the vaccine would interrupt the high from a potential relapse and overdose.
Vaccines to limit the influence of other substances are actively being researched as well. A breakthrough for methamphetamine or cocaine would be especially significant since there are no FDA-approved medications to alleviate the symptoms of dependence on those substances. Unfortunately, it’s unlikely we would ever see one developed for alcohol since ethanol, the molecule that actually produces the psychoactive effects in alcoholic products, is too small for even a highly-boosted immune system to detect as a distinct marker and manufacture antibodies for.
09/09/2026
What role does society play in making recovery from addiction harder, and how can we shift this to be more supportive?
Within recovery spaces and academic circles, there’s ongoing intense debate about how many social factors are at play in substance use disorders.
For instance, it’s incredibly common for those with substance use disorders to also have another co-occurring health issue. Studies have found that as many as 60% of those with a substance use disorder experience another mental health condition; that number rises to 80% when looking at adolescent demographics. Only 50% of adults with mental health conditions of any kind receive treatment. These numbers get worse when looking at communities of color where healthcare access is underdeveloped, strong cultural stigma against psychiatric care exists, and/or intergenerational trauma makes members reluctant to trust medical institutions. The trend towards dual diagnosis healthcare programs in recent years reflects a growing acknowledgment of this co-occurrence of mental health disorders.
If we accept the core premise of the self-medication hypothesis, that people try to choose substances that regulate some underlying issue rather than becoming dependent on whatever’s randomly available, we might interpret this data as suggesting that we as a society are systemically failing to address health issues in a majority of our population, and some people will attempt to deal with that by self-medicating with substances. Even when people do receive care, it takes an incredibly long time to adapt evidence-based modalities into institutions, especially where it concerns the insurance industry. The emphasis on CBT and derived approaches in recovery programs is in no small part attributable to incentives that insurance companies have towards manualized approaches that can be easily standardized and operationalized. Interventions with comparable or higher effectiveness like combinations of Contingency Management, MOUD, and Housing First policies) require allocating much more capital to treatments and specialists that insurance companies find difficult to calculate profit margins for covering. Yet, we live in a time when states like Minnesota have just closed 3 of their 5 CARE network facilities which were dedicated to people presenting with complex cases of substance use disorder and co-occurring disorders, due to budget considerations.
Basically, we need a lot more money to train a lot more people to try many more interventions that research has found effective, and that means we need to have the political will to overhaul major aspects of our healthcare system that put barriers in the way of connecting people who need help to solutions that work. Unfortunately, far too many people still believe that punitive measures must be the center of addiction policies, and almost no culture in the world tends to value those with illnesses as much as those who are healthy. I wish I had more optimism to share about the prospect of change, but the more I’ve looked into this problem, the more I’m convinced some type of crisis point that breaks the system will have to happen before there’s political will and public appetite for major changes.
Sponsorship without any (or at least without strict) adherence to the 12 steps
I have a strong preference for Recovery Dharma (or Refuge Recovery) meetings that still have a structure to support mentorship, which can mean either a one-on-one relationship or a circle of mentors. It’s very common for RD attendees to also attend AA meetings, so you might have a way of using an RD mentor in the place of a pure AA sponsor, who has flexible alternatives to the traditional AA approaches but still can walk you through the Steps. The main issue you might run into is that AA is far more widespread than RD, so you may not have in-person access depending on where you live.
09/08/2026
The Minnesota Star Tribune - Minnesota closed three addiction centers, leaving dwindling treatment choices
The Community Addiction Recovery Enterprise (CARE) network is managed by the Minnesota Department of Human Services (DHS) that used to maintain five 16-bed inpatient facilities for those requiring more specialized care for more complex care than other programs might provide, especially private sector programs.
Why 16? Because the Social Security Amendments of 1965, which signed Medicaid into law, excluded institutions for mental disease (IMD) from receiving federal funds for serving patients between 21 and 65. The idea was to disincentivize institutionalizing mass numbers of people into asylums that provided poor care while simply taking unwell people out of public view while forcing states to finance their own healthcare rather than shifting operational costs onto the federal government.
Whatever the merits of this argument at the time, there is widespread criticism of this policy in the present. Recovery treatment has advanced substantially since the 1960s and includes all kinds of evidence-backed therapeutic modalities and technologies that never existed before. State officials, whose local tax dollars are insufficient to implement the most effective interventions, are caught between a rock and a hard place when deciding where bottlenecks for psychiatric care should exist. The closure of CARE facilities was framed as a necessary step towards consolidating services in regional state facilities for all types of urgent high-acuity psychiatric care, where shortages also exist, but this means more individuals with specialized dual-diagnosis needs will bounce between emergency rooms and local jails since no private sector option exists for them.
Unions like the Minnesota Association of Professional Employees (MAPE) and AFSCME Council 5 launched public campaigns to argue against the disclosure, pointing out that they were given assurances from DHS management that the facilities would be expanding their staffing and improving their quality. Their resistance preserved the Carlton faciltity that was originally planned for closure would stay open, as it was the only all-women facility among the CARE network centers. (Source) Still, after the closures and flooding that sliced one facility’s available beds in half, the capacity of the CARE network went from 80 to just 24 for the entire state. As of writing this, there are 53 people on the waitlist for the two remaining facilities. Studies cited by American Addiction Centers claim that 45% of those on waitlists end up not seeking treatment because the wait was too long and that the likelihood of someone attending rehab after having to wait before admittance is less than 50%. (source). The number of those admitted into a CARE program in 2022 were 333, which fell to 194 last year. In fairness, part of this may be due to a decline in overall cases of civil commitment for someone struggle with chemical dependence or a substance use disorder, but there was also an increase within the last year of recommitted patients. Either way, it’s not safe to declare a long-term falling demand for the services the CARE network provides.
Carolyn D. Gorman, a fellow at the Manhattan Institute, presents a report arguing for the reform, if not repeal, of the IMD exclusion:
“Analysis of hospital data and prior reforms suggests that further modest modifications of the IMD exclusion will not suffice to increase bed supply. Full repeal would be ideal, but if that’s not politically feasible, IMDs should, at a minimum, be defined as facilities with more than 108 beds (up from the current 16 beds). This would allow as many as 332 existing psychiatric hospitals (with more than 20,000 beds) to receive Medicaid reimbursement for their services.” (Source)
Quel Health launches telehealth platform for addiction treatment using GLP-1s
Quel Health, a New Mexico-based startup, announced the “the first national telehealth company built specifically around the use of GLP-1 receptor agonists for addiction,” with the nonprofit Caron Treatment Centers as a Founding Strategic Partner. The platform is available in 41 states and the District of Columbia right now with plans to expand nationally by the end of the year. Marlene C. Lira, the CEO and Co-Founder of Quel Health explains the premise of the platform:
“We live in a society in which our dopamine networks are sold to the highest bidder… We’ve built entire industries on the deliberate exploitation of the reward system, and then we treat the resulting conditions as separate diseases in separate clinics with separate specialists. Quel exists because we think that framing is incomplete, and because the science is finally filling in the gaps.”
GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1), the most popular version of which is Ozempic, has only been approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for Type 2 diabetes and chronic weight management, or obesity. Quel acknowledges that using GLP-1 for substance use disorders is an off-label practice, but also that it’s common to prescribed drugs off-label for substance use disorders given the complexity of these cases. Plus, there is evidence to suggest GLP-1s modulate dopamine release in a way that acts directly on the “hijacked” dopamine pathways that result from chronic substance use. A 2026 study of 600,000 veterans across three years published in the British Medical Journal (the BMJ) and authored by researchers at Washington University in St. Louis found that GLP-1 users had a reduced risk of developing substance use disorders of any kind. There was a 14% reduction in risk across the board, with 14% for cannabis, 18% for alcohol, 20% for cocaine, 20% for nicotine, and 25% for opioids. This also led to 25% fewer hospitalizations, 30% fewer visits to an emergency room, 40% fewer overdoses, and 50% fewer drug-related deaths. Overall, this is a very exciting finding that opens the door to directly addressing the “hijacked” pathways of dopamine networks that facilitate all kinds of addictive and compulsive behaviors, and GLP-1s are inherently non-addictive without causing physical dependence that substitutes for an existing one. Over 50 large-scale Phase III trials are registered with ClinicalTrials.gov specifically examining GLP-1s for addiction, and smaller randomized controlled trials have already tested low-dose semaglitude for a decrease in cravings for alcohol with those diagnosed with Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD).
That being said, delivering drugs off-label in a telehealth format can understandably raise eyebrows. Quel seems to require more manual interventions than other platforms that can use automated questionnaires to quickly screen and prescribe GLP-1s to patients, but experts still raise reasonable concerns that telehealth programs aren’t capable of the continuous monitoring and testing capabilities of in-person clinics. Personally, I think telehealth can solve a lot of problems with healthcare access that we struggle to establish with in-person clinics (especially when the article mentioned just above shows the finicky nature of funding and staffing) but I imagine this works best as a supplement than a substitute. The nature of private sector operations is that they compete with other services for the sake of profit, which means that a private sector healthcare provider has incentives to market themselves towards patients who would be better serviced by an in-person provider. As with most things, this means that the most complex cases among the most vulnerable populations might not find the care that’s truly best suited to their needs.
Why is it that even professionals like doctors and lawyers struggle to seek help for addiction, and what can be done to change this stigma?
The occurrence of substance use disorders (SUD) among the physician population is about 10–15%, which is about the same rate as the general population. About 50% of adults with any mental health condition receive treatment of any kind, while only 13 to 36% of physicians seek out treatment for mental health disorders, including SUD.
Part of this disparity has to do with the cultural perception that medical providers should be free of health conditions themselves in order to help others be free of them, despite many cultural traditions of the “wounded healer” who uses their own experience battling a disease or illness to teach others how to manage them. This creates both external pressures to present the picture of perfect health and internalized pressures that lead one to believe that one is less effective a physician if they have chronic health issues. Substance use disorders carry even more stigma than mental health disorders like anxiety and depression, as it’s easier to imagine that there’s some kind of “broken brain” leading to an inability to experience pleasure or motivation than it is to imagine the reward system breakdown between what we want and what we like that accompanies addiction. For doctors, who are expected to have developed extraordinary self-mastery after the grueling gauntlet of medical training, admitting to substance use disorders can feel like admitting to have failed in a core tenet of their education.
It doesn’t help that many state regulatory boards interrogate clinicians about their history of mental health conditions, which leads to professionals worrying that disclosing their conditions or seeking treatment could seriously impact their careers. Massachusetts and other states are beginning to dial back these probes into clinical history to only ask about present mental and physical health conditions that might affect their work.
In my opinion, recovery communities have always thrived on peer support away from the judgment of institutions, so one of the best ways to reach people is to provide non-judgmental resources delivered by anonymous peer-led formats, particularly for Physician Health Programs (PHPs) that give confidential support. Anything that avoids labels and institutional records will go a long way to working around stigma. As for addressing the stigma itself, mental health activists and advocates have historically leveraged media to tell stories about addicts that humanize them and promote empathy for the context of their struggles. I imagine we’ll just have to wait for more of those to move the needle on stigma.

rants/aa-is-religious.title: AA is Religious and That's Okay
rants/aa-is-religious.content:
AA is Religious and That’s Okay
Seriously, this isn’t bashing A.A. I think religious programs are a valid option and even an optimal one depending on the person. I think Buddhists would have a great time at Recovery Dharma meetings, and I think Christians would have a great time at A.A. meetings. I come from a Hindu background, which is kind of like saying “I come from a Western background” in terms of how little it conveys if we don’t default to common stereotypes. At different times for different reasons, A.A., Recovery Dharma, and SMART meetings all resonated in different ways.
But A.A. does rise to the level of religious content, not just an endorsement of spirituality. Much like fish in water, it can be difficult to see the distinctive qualities of something you take for granted as a structural aspect of reality. I will come across as snarky and biased on the arguments that it’s not religious beyond non-denominational, because I think it’s a matter of rigorous honesty.
Before I go into my own thoughts, I’m going to bring up the findings and analysis from actual court cases that made it through the American legal system. That way, you can rest assured that this perspective has been argued by more credible sources than me.
Warner v. Orange County (1996)
In Warner v. Orange County (1996), the 2nd Circuit Court ruled that even if it was possible for every person to substitute God with a Higher Power consistent with their own beliefs, holding hands in a prayer circle to recite a passage from the New Testament attributed to Jesus Christ unquestionably made it a Christian program. Standing silently in the circle is still considered a form of coercion into a fellowship that does not align with someone’s sincerely held beliefs, even if they’re an atheist who considers the prayer inconsequential. That sounds silly until we remember similar arguments being made against school prayer because everyone notices the person who doesn’t participate, and it’s human nature to think of them as fundamentally outsiders.
Interestingly, there was a dissent in a remand in 1999 that claimed attendance of a few meetings waives one’s right to object to it. If it was truly religious, then a genuine objector would refuse to participate until they were just emotionally dissatisfied. The majority disagreed that AA was forthcoming enough about its religious nature for someone to provide informed consent that quickly.
Griffin v. Coughlin (1999)
In Griffin v. Coughlin (1999), the specific argument about replacing God with a Higher Power, or that AA is spiritual but not religious, is addressed:
Pointing to A.A. literature, respondents averred that the references to God actually mean some “higher power as the individual may understand such higher power,” not as the concept would be known by “organized religions.” Thus, respondents claimed that the A.A. component of the ASAT Program “does not make specific references to God as an institutional religion would wherein the individual is required to worship, praise, give thanks or petition to a Creator” (Affidavit of Lorraine Cohen, Senior Correctional Counselor for ASAT, N.Y. St. Dept. of Correctional Servs).
The argument being made by those who say AA is not religious is that references to God should be seen as a personal Higher Power or personal Creator, not a reference to a concept from an organized religion. I would argue that almost no one uses “religion” just to mean an organized method of worship associated with particular institutions.
As previously noted, the Appellate Division relied upon the A.A. Big Book and the A.A. Twelve Steps/Twelve Traditions texts to find that, despite the repeated references to “God” in the Twelve Steps and Twelve Traditions, A.A. does not ” ‘demand’ ” adherence to any particular faith but to ” ‘spirituality’ ” and ” ‘open mindedness’ ” (id., at 190, 626 N.Y.S.2d 1011 [quoting the A.A. Big Book and A.A. Twelve Steps/Twelve Traditions] ). The Court also found quite significant that A.A. allows participants to select their own conception of God, as shown by the reference in Step 3 to “God as we understood Him.”
This is something you will still hear in recovery circles, but it’s really not malicious. There is a genuine belief that the concept of a Higher Power in the program is neutral or universal, and that submitting to one is a critical humbling of the self before recovery can fully happen in order to leave some egoistic past version of oneself behind. You will be told that you can use anything as a Higher Power, but I really doubt you can do the Steps in a meaningful way if you’re asking your pet rock to cure you of your “character defects.” If you understand God to be an impersonal substrate for existence, you might be able to treat your pet rock as an emergent part of that substrate, but you would still be unable to meaningfully engage with it in the way the Steps ask. If you have to communicate with the Higher Power, you’re implicitly being asked to pick a real entity with agency outside of yourself that you can have dialogue with to ask for things you cannot achieve on your own, otherwise you’re kind of playing pretend.
In our view, the Appellate Division erred in rejecting the petition in this case by applying too narrow a concept of religion or religious activity for Establishment Clause analysis and disregarding the compulsion used to induce petitioner to attend and participate in A.A. meetings heavily laced with at least general religious content.
As pointed out above, to many, “religion” refers to organized methodologies surrounding an institutionalized canon of works and “spirituality” refers to the parts concerning physical, emotional, and/or mental regulation for an individual or a group. This isn’t wrong per se; this distinction can be very functional for everyday life to signal that you’re not trying to invoke an established denomination with its own authorities and canons to explain a ritual or practice. A spiritual practice can seem like a supplement to a religious practice rather than a replacement, which means programs like AA can claim they’re a spiritual wrapper for any religion. However, separating religion from spirituality and philosophy is not as easily done as you might think.
In America, the First Amendment means defining Religion is necessary to enforce protections of civil rights, Philosophy is a department at universities experimenting with technical approaches to niche abstract problems, and Spirituality can be a catch-all for anything mystical, exotic, immaterial, and/or esoteric without a hierarchical social organization. These categories can feel natural if you’ve grown up with them, but it’s not a distinction that universally makes much sense. Many belief systems begin with a metaphysical framework.
Certain Shaivist sects argue that all of reality and existence is of one infinite consciousness that we are born out of. Buddhists argue that all things are impermanent, so an infinite consciousness that exists in some permanent sense outside of reality isn’t possible. That might influence whether your practice includes developing an awareness of nothingness, purifying yourself of pollutants, exploring yourself without inhibitions to see what comes out, performing rituals to work with forces outside yourself, inquiry and contemplation of the relation between things, praying, studying texts, making a pilgrimage, or sitting in a group where you feel good vibes whether it’s a place of worship or not. How do we decide which of these is religious and which of these is spiritual in a way that would have consensus among the practitioners?
The court here is aware of this subjectivity around the interpretation of “religion” but concludes that the version being used was far too narrow. The phrase “at least general religious content” helps to clarify that things can be considered religious without referring to a specific belief system. Simply, non-denominational is different than non-religious.
Moreover, even if we were to agree with the Appellate Division’s holding that the governing principles and practices of A.A., as incorporated in the ASAT Program, do not necessarily require an atheist participant to accept the existence of God in the religious sense, or to engage in religious activity, we would, nonetheless, find that the mandatory and exclusive incorporation of A.A. doctrine and practices in the ASAT program violates Establishment Clause principles requiring governmental neutrality with respect to religion.
The Court mentions that even if they bought into the argument that no one is required to accept the existence of God to participate in AA, the requirement to attend without alternatives still represents an institutional bias towards general religious programming.
Concededly, there are passages in A.A. literature, relied upon heavily by respondents, the Appellate Division and the dissent here, which, in stressing the openness and inclusiveness of the A.A. movement, eschew any intent to impose a particular sectarian set of beliefs or a particular concept of God upon participants.
However, a fair reading of the fundamental A.A. doctrinal writings discloses that their dominant theme is unequivocally religious, certainly in the broad definitional sense as “manifesting faithful devotion to an acknowledged ultimate reality or deity” (Webster’s 9th New Collegiate Dictionary 995 [9th ed 1990]). Indeed, the A.A. basic literature most reasonably would be characterized as reflecting the traditional elements common to most theistic religions.
The Court doesn’t seem to think that the AA passages about neutrality check out with the “unequivocally religious” nature of the rest of the literature. There is nothing that really stops someone from saying “I believe in a personal God but I am not a religious Christian, even though I attend a Christian Church where we read the Bible, recite prayers in circles, proclaim our love for Jesus Christ, and confess sins as determined by Biblical morality and ethics.” The Oxford Group’s literature actually does do that, as we’ll see later.
To do a CTRL+F and replace “God” with “Higher Power” while throwing in some disclaimers doesn’t really make it neutral. A well-meaning person once suggested to me that the meetings taking place in Christian churches was just because the churches were friendly to the AA community and had long-lasting relationships from its inception. I wasn’t quite sure how to say this, but it seemed to me that is exactly the point. If a particular type of religious institution is consistently finding that a certain program is worth hosting within their halls, that may be because they find their religion to be very compatible with that belief system.  If other religious institutions aren’t as open, that may suggest less compatibility.
Thus, God is named or referred to in five of the 12 steps. “Working” the 12 steps includes confessing to God the “nature of our wrongs” (Step 5), appealing to God “to remove our shortcomings” (Step 7) and seeking “through prayer and meditation” to make “contact” with God and achieve “knowledge of His Will” (Step 11 [emphasis supplied]). The 12 Traditions include a profession of belief that “there is one ultimate authority — a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience.”
In my opinion, you could go further and say The Big Book is an analogy to the Bible (which is itself a term for books from an Ancient Greek root), and the 12 steps and traditions arguably seem inspired by the 10 commandments and 12 apostles. I dislike this pattern of argumentation though. I feel too much like a conspiracy theorist throwing numbers into a calculator until 9.11 pops out.
the writings demonstrably express an aspiration that each member of the 682 682 movement will ultimately commit to a belief in the existence of a Supreme Being of independent higher reality than humankind. Thus, in the A.A. Big Book — the basic text of A.A. — chapter l, “Bill’s Story,” describes the spiritual transformation of one of the cofounders of A.A., in which he finally achieved salvation from his alcoholism: by “enter[ing] upon a new relationship with my Creator * * * [i]t meant destruction of self-centeredness. I must turn in all things to the Father of Light who presides over us all” (A.A. Big Book, at 13-14).
Creator, Father of Light, salvation, “spiritual transformation”, “presiding over”, and Supreme Being are all loaded with implications related to religious discourse. But the phrase that actually cements this as a very particular type of religious and spiritual framework is “independent higher reality than humankind.” This is explicitly asserting dualism which numerous religious belief systems explicitly reject . Many religions argue that there is only one infinite reality that we observe with our finite measurements, and there is no external entity who resides in another reality.
In chapter 4, entitled “We Agnostics” the theme is unambiguously proselytizing: “As soon as we admitted the possible existence of a Creative Intelligence, a Spirit of the Universe underlying the totality of things, we began to be possessed of a new sense of power and direction, provided we took other simple steps. We found that God does not make too hard terms with those who seek Him” (id., at 46). “Instead of regarding ourselves as intelligent agents, spearheads of God’s ever advancing Creation, we agnostics and atheists chose to believe that our human intelligence was the last word, the alpha and the omega, the beginning and end of all. Rather vain of us, wasn’t it? “We, who have traveled this dubious path, beg you to lay aside prejudice, even against organized religion. We have learned that whatever the human frailties of various faiths may be, those faiths have given purpose and direction to millions. People of faith have a logical idea of what life is all about” (id., at 49).
A passage about how it is vain to not seek God in a chapter about agnostic perspectives really strains the “spiritual, not religious” label. You cannot say you are neutral in spirituality while characterizing those who aren’t part of the dominant interpretation as having moralized “character defects.”
The foregoing demonstrates beyond peradventure that doctrinally and as actually practiced in the 12 step methodology, adherence to the A.A. fellowship entails engagement in religious activity and religious proselytization. Followers are urged to accept the existence of God as a Supreme Being, Creator, Father of Light and Spirit of the Universe. In “working” the 12 steps, participants become actively involved in seeking such a God through prayer, confessing wrongs and asking for removal of shortcomings. These expressions and practices constitute, as a matter of law, religious exercise for Establishment Clause purposes, no less than the nondenominational prayer in Engel v Vitale (370 US 421), that is, “a solemn avowal of divine faith and supplication for the blessings of the Almighty. The nature of such a prayer has always been religious” (id., at 424-425 [emphasis supplied]; see also, Lee v Weisman, 505 US 577, 603-604 [Blackmun, J., concurring]).
The “God as we understand Him” part becomes a lot narrower when the Higher Power is likened to a Supreme Being, Creator, Father of Light, and Spirit of the Universe. You are not just being asked to agree to God, you’re being asked to participate in dialogue with a personal God.
The dissent’s thesis that there was an historical evolution of A.A. doctrine and therapeutic/rehabilitative methodology from the initial, more religious A.A. Big Book to the later, essentially secular, Twelve Traditions (see, dissenting opn, at 699-700, 702-703), is refuted by the writings themselves. Thus, the 1952 A.A. Twelve Steps/Twelve Traditions volume itself states unequivocally in its Foreword that “[t]he book `Alcoholics Anonymous’ [the 1939 A.A. Big Book] became the basic text of the Fellowship, and it still is” (A.A. Twelve Steps/Twelve Traditions, at 17 [emphasis supplied]). The Foreword to the 685 685 1952 volume also explains the differing roles of the Twelve Steps and the Twelve Traditions. “A.A.’s Twelve Steps are a group of principles, spiritual in nature, which, if practiced as a way of life, can expel the obsession to drink and enable the sufferer to become happily and usefully whole” (A.A. Twelve Steps/Twelve Traditions, at 15 [emphasis supplied]). “[T]he spiritual ideas of the Society were codified for the first time in the Twelve Steps” (id., at 17 [emphasis supplied]).
And this should answer those who say AA used to be religious but secularized as it spread.
You can read the whole case here: aaagnostica.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/Griffin-v.-Coughlin-1996.pdf. It’s very thorough in examining the evidence from AA literature.
Now let’s take a look at excerpts from the dissent:
Many people may believe that A.A. is an entity of spiritual essence or experience. Referenced incorporation of its literature into ASAT to forge a religious alchemy that implicates the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment by some foreboding compulsion feature, however, is not justified or proven. Greater quantum and quality should be required to cross that constitutionally blurred barrier. Indeed, the repeated evocation of a generalized deity figure and symbol or some nondenominational, secular alternative “Higher Power” fails to support this profound absorption of A.A. and ASAT into the territory of a compulsory, constitutionally forbidden religious encounter. We reiterate, in summary, the cogent resolution of this case by the unanimous Appellate Division:
So the problem is fundamentally one of ignorance, willful or not. “Generalized deity figure” and “alternative ‘Higher Power’” are obviously religious concepts. I cannot imagine anyone could say this if they were aware of non-Abrahamic religions, particularly from non-Westernized cultures.
“[I]t is our conclusion that petitioner has failed to 715 715 make an adequate record to state a claim for an Establishment Clause violation. The petition cites nothing of a religious nature about this particular ASAT program or its practices other than the fact that it is modeled after the principles of AA which make references to ‘God’ and a ‘Higher Power’.
Kerr v. Farrey (1996)
We can hop over to Kerr v. Farrey (1996) from the 7th Circuit Court for some explicit discussion about theological premises:
When Kerr first attended the NA meeting, he objected to dragging God’s name into “this messy business of addictions,” and he expressed his disagreement with the view of God that was propounded at the meeting.   Kerr regarded NA’s deterministic view of God to be in conflict with his own belief about free will;  more generally, he found it offensive to his personal religious beliefs.
Note that here, we don’t have an atheist or an agnostic or someone from a non-monotheistic belief system, but someone who believes in God but from a different monotheistic perspective. If we accept that addiction is a disease, then bringing religious engagement into a treatment protocol is not necessarily an obvious step.
Warden Farrey confirmed in her affidavit that inmates were required to “observe” the NA meetings, although she stated that they were not required to “participate.”   She also conceded that “Narcotics Anonymous does use the concept of a ‘higher being’ in their treatment approach.”   This concept, she went on to say, was viewed as a very personal matter and could range from a religious concept of God to the non-religious concept of individual willpower.
One of the most commonly noted frustrations with attempting to generalize the concepts from AA is the way specific rituals are required but the justification to do them is left for you to fill in. You’ll be told that the Higher Power can be an inanimate object, but when it turns out your pet rock isn’t granting you the wisdom to know the difference between things you can and can’t change, you’re just going to have to find a new Higher Power. But you know, God is a very convenient one that will always be there for you if you tire of praying to your pet rock:
The district court thought that the NA program escaped the “religious” label because the twelve steps used phrases like “God, as we understood Him,” and because the warden indicated that the concept of God could include the non-religious idea of willpower within the individual.   We are unable to agree with this interpretation.   A straightforward reading of the twelve steps shows clearly that the steps are based on the monotheistic idea of a single God or Supreme Being.
I like to imagine there’s a bit of exasperation behind “We are unable to agree with this” followed by “A straightforward reading… show clearly that the steps are based on the monotheistic idea of a single God or Supreme Being.”   
True, that God might be known as Allah to some, or YHWH to others, or the Holy Trinity to still others, but the twelve steps consistently refer to “God, as we understood Him.” Even if we expanded the steps to include polytheistic ideals, or animistic philosophies, they are still fundamentally based on a religious concept of a Higher Power. Kerr alleged, furthermore, that the meetings were permeated with explicit religious content. This was therefore not a case (again, on the present record) where the only religious note was struck by the insertion of the words “under God” in the Pledge of Allegiance, or other incidental references that the courts have upheld.   See, e.g., Sherman v. Wheeling School District, 980 F.2d 437 (7th Cir.1992).
The very concept of a Higher Power is fundamentally religious. You just can’t do a program based on the premise of having a theistic idea of a Higher Power in a dualistic reality without that theistic premise being part of the bottom line. The 12 steps run through a cycle of sin, confession, repentance, divine grace, spiritual awakening, and proselytization. That’s a feature of the program and why it can work for those who follow certain faiths, and also why it can be deeply alienating to others. Kerr didn’t really develop the free will argument much further, but we can at least see that there are reasons even those following a monotheistic faith might feel alienated by the premises of AA.
Keswick Tent Revivalism
I was being a little generous by leading with court case excerpts that examined the literature and practices at face value. If we look at the history, it’s very hard to figure out when exactly in the development of this program it became spiritual rather than religious.
Jessie Penn-Lewis was born in 1861 South Wales to a Calvinist Methodist family. Her grandfather was a minister, and her mother worked in the temperance movement. At 19, she married William Penn-Lewis, who claimed a lineage to the William Penn who founded Pennsylvania as a Quaker. She had a leadership position in a temperance movement chapter and the Young Women’s Christian Association (YWCA) in Richmond through the Holy Trinity Church.
That’s where she was exposed to vicar Evan H. Hopkins of the Keswick tent revival movement, also referred to as the Higher Life movement after a book called Higher Christian Life. The movement’s core premise is that there are actually two categories of Christians: those who accept Christ on Earth and count as carnal Christians, and then those who have surrendered to a second conversion that elevates them into spiritual Christians. The phrase “Let Go and Let God” was about this notion of surrendering so that Christ can work through you rather than pursuing spirituality with your own will.
Frank Buchman and The Oxford Group
In 1908, following a surge of depression after a financial dispute over a hospice for young men that led to his resignation, the Lutheran minister Frank Buchman traveled to the Keswick convention in the hopes of discussing his problems with a Quaker-influenced Baptist pastor named Frederick Brotherton Meyer. Meyer wasn’t there, so Buchman listened to Penn-Lewis preaching to a small group of less than two dozen people instead. Without getting into the specifics of Penn-Lewis’ theological propositions just yet, we can see that her warning about centering one’s own righteousness rather than the Cross or Holy Spirit would be a thread in the inspired groups going forward. Buchman began to feel that his hatred and rage towards the board over the hospice was actually egoistic pride that his way was righteous because his cause was helping children:
I sat there and realized how my sin, my pride, my selfishness, and my ill-will had eclipsed me from God… I was the center of my own life. Not Him. That big ‘I’ had to be crossed out. I saw my resentments against those men standing out like tombstones in my heart.
He took a moral inventory, confessed his sins, and tried to make amends. So began Buchman’s explicit journey to replace his ego with Spirit. When he finally met Meyer later, Meyer asked him: “Do you let the Holy Spirit guide you in all that you are doing… Do you give God enough uninterrupted time really to tell you what to do?” From here comes the notion of meditation to improve conscious contact with God. As Buchman grew a following through the YMCA at Pennsylvania State University, and eventually a global reputation, he settled into a practice based around personal evangelism in intimate circles. A harsh analysis of Buchman might conclude that he grew very skeptical of institutions despite his external emphasis on forgiveness, humility, and avoiding self-righteousness.
He first had a nervous breakdown after his quarrel over funding with the board members of his hospice. At Hartford, he began holding private personal evangelism groups in parallel to the academic theology of the university, and he refused to comply with university demands to actually adhere to a schedule and curriculum instead of traveling whenever God’s will told him to leave. He eventually wrote “The seminary today is an expensive luxury for propagating theology which is oftentimes wholly divorced from life.” In 1920, John D. Rockefeller was impressed by Buchman and offered to finance a global evangelist movement based on his works. Buchman rejected the offer with skepticism towards developing an administrative apparatus run by a corporation that would prioritize its own survival as an institution. The Ministerium of Pennsylvania that served as Buchman’s Lutheran synod was routinely upset that he ignored financial reporting requirements, geographical boundaries, and theological guidelines. Large anonymous donors tend to raise concerns. A few years later at Princeton, followers of Buchman penetrated the Philadelphian Society to practice “soul surgery,” which really meant forming small groups to confess their sexual activities and anxieties. The Princeton president John Grier ordered an investigation after numerous complaints which led to Buchman and his followers being banned from campus. At one point, he had traveled to China as a missionary, but was asked to leave the country after complaints about his attitude towards other missionaries created conflict.
