wiki/active-addiction.title: Active Addiction
wiki/active-addiction.content:
Overview
“Active addiction” refers to a phase of Substance Use Disorders (SUDs) in which someone is in a cycle of actively using and seeking substances. This is distinct from someone who identifies with having an addiction but has sustained abstinence in spite of cravings.

wiki/actor-network-theory.title: Actor-Network Theory (ANT)
wiki/actor-network-theory.content:
Overview
Actor-Network Theory (ANT) is a social theory that posits that social phenomena are the result of a network relationships between interacting entities rather than dividing the world into a material reality and a social reality.
For instance, a conventional biomedical perspective of addiction might frame the problem as beginning with exposure to substances, escalating to chronic use that changes brain chemistry and tolerance levels, developing into a dependence or addiction, and leading to drug-seeking behavior with its associated consequences.
A more ANT-centric perspective steps back from a linear cause-and-effect chain to instead examine the network of relationships from which a substance use disorder emerges. We might end up with a non-linear list:


a pharmaceutical company oriented towards profitability as a result of shareholder, managerial, and worker interests manufactures and markets an addictive substance after a series of clinical trials, regulatory approval processes, and patent applications


a public policy agenda supports private insurance companies as a way to fund healthcare protocols that involve processing prescriptions to the products of a pharmaceutial company


an insurance company decides which substances it will pay for and under which conditions through a combination of risk-analysis algorithms trained on healthcare data, documentation from Electronic Health Records, and contractual policies involving prior authorization


a treatment facility or clinic hires from a competitive marketplace of medical professionals who have varying educational credentials and memberships with professional organizations whose outputs are regularly cited in private and public standards


medical education institutes train physicians according to regulatory guidelines from accreditation organizations that examine the state of academia and research to derive guidelines and consolidate core materials for physician education


a physician prescribes this addictive substance to patients according to diagnostic criteria and protocols, including pain scale assessments that negotiate between a patient’s expression of pain and a physician’s interpretation of pain


a patient’s family has a history of health issues and substance use disorders, which a physician evaluates through their engagement with risk-related discourse and genetic research


a patient suffers from major trauma that leads to a clinical encounter with a physician whose interpretation of the patient’s expression of pain leads to a prescription to an addictive substance


a patient lacks culturally or religious compatible support networks around them, leading to increased isolation and the substance as their primary means to alleviate pain or suffering


a patient’s neurochemistry changes to produce cravings and dependence that lead to job performance issues and unemployment at the discretion of an employer that might or might not be understanding of substance use disorders


public intoxication laws criminalize the dependence for homeless individuals with substance use disorder, further marginalizing them while adding the traumas associated with the abuses of incarceration and increasing potential exposure to illicit addictive substances or those who can provide them


political coalitions formed by middle and upper class communities reject proposals to fund social services through systemic reforms out of concern for their tax burdens and property values


So on and so forth. In a system like this, we can’t really isolate any single thing as the cause or even cleanly carve out a discrete set of causes. In fact, we can keep unpacking each phenomenon as the product of an even more granular network, like pointing out that the political coalitions are comprised of local politicians and property owners navigating the forces of housing and labor markets through digital media as information exchange platforms.
Each actor or agent influences how other actors and agent’s have the capacity and incentives to act. When we consider this model of social phenomena, it becomes increasingly hard to see addiction or substance use disorder as solely a health issue within an individual’s mind-body duality. I would argue that this guides us away from hyperindividualized, radically materialist perspectives of lived reality and towards concepts like interconnectedness and impermanence, which are found very commonly in the “Eastern” traditions” before being crudely adapted into “Western spirituality.”

wiki/acute-stress-disorder-asd.title: Acute Stress Disorder (ASD)
wiki/acute-stress-disorder-asd.content:
Overview
Acute Stress Disorder (ASD) is a short-term mental health condition that generally develops in the first month after experiencing or learning about a traumatic event. Symptoms include anxiety, intrusive thoughts, avoidance, and dissociative symptoms that interfere with the activities of daily life.

wiki/ada-halbeirch.content:
Overview
Ada Halbeirch established the We Humanists secular Alcoholics Anonymous meetings on the East Coast in 1986, which was highly influential in driving other secular 12-step groups like We Agnostics and Freethinkers. Her co-founders included John Yablon and David L.

wiki/adaptive-coping.title: Adaptive Coping
wiki/adaptive-coping.content:
Overview
“Adaptive coping” refers to the pattern of choosing methods to manage suffering or problems that are better than the alternatives. Someone who feels mild anxiety in social settings might have a drink to loosen up at a networking event, which could be considered adaptive in an environment where extroverted behavior is the expectation and drinking is the norm. If that same person continues drinking after work to deal with any anxiety they have about their career and future, we might begin categorizing that as a “maladaptive behavior” instead.
History and Etymology
In 1990, Bruce K. Alexander published “The Empirical and Theoretical Bases for an Adaptive Model of Addiction” that argued addiction itself can be an adaptive mechanism to certain psychosocial circumstances. Virtually by definition, addiction is considered a pattern of substance or process use that an individual feels compelled to continue even after observing the consequences and wishing to stop. It seems logical at face value to consider it maladaptive by definition, but Alexander’s paper asks us to consider what the development of an addiction might be an adaptation to.
Recall that “adaptive” doesn’t mean healthy or normal, but just a choice that appears to be the best in a particular circumstance. Someone who experiences uncontrollable panic attacks might adapt by drinking often, which might increase baseline anxiety and irritability but decrease the occurrence of these attacks. Someone who lives in cycles of poverty without a clear way out might adapt through substance use, which provides extremely reliable pleasure and relief in a community where no other kind might be available, particularly if the individual is struggling with other health issues like Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) and lacks access to adequate interventions. Someone trapped in an abusive and traumatizing environment might similarly use substances as the only method to feel in control of their own experiences.
With this framework, we can consider more options both prevention and treatment than assuming the problem lies solely in a brain that learned the “wrong” lessons.

wiki/adaptive-treatment-strategy.title: Adaptive Treatment Strategy
wiki/adaptive-treatment-strategy.content:
Overview
An adaptive treatment strategy (ATS) involves tuning treatment plans based on a patient’s history of responses to previous treatments. Chronic diseases and health conditions that require ongoing management and long-term coordination implicitly follow an ATS, but some patients may also have an explicitly specified ATS.
Links

pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2739674/

wiki/adderall.title: Adderall
wiki/adderall.content:
Overview
Adderall is a central nervous system (CNS) stimulant that uses mixed amphetamine salts to increase dopamine and norepinephrine levels in the brain. It’s most commonly used to treat attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and narcolepsy, usually through improving focus and impulse control. In the United States, adderall is classified as a Schedule II drug as it has high potential for becoming part of a substance use disorder, so it requires a prescription for controlled doses that stabilize chemistry rather than producing a high. Even if taken exactly as prescribed, over a long period of time, the body can adapt to it so that sudden cessation leads to withdrawal symptoms like fatigue and depression.

wiki/addicere.title: Addicere
wiki/addicere.content:
Overview
From classical Latin, addicere meant roughly “to be given over” and was used in the context of someone being given over to a creditor as a slave to pay off their debts. It also was used in the context of divination to reveal the will of gods as a means of describing the strong devotion it took to perfom augury rituals. In its simplest uses, it could just mean to have a strong preference towards something.
History and Etymology
John Frith (1503-1533) is the first author we’ve found to use “addict”:
“Be not partially addict to the one or the other, But judge them by the scripture”
In this case, he uses “addict” in a way we might consider interchangeable with “biased”. As the word caught on amidst an early Protestant wave that sought new terms for concepts to describe their theology, it was seen as an action rather than a force. You could “addict” yourself to something, rather than “addiction” seizing control of you. In doing so, it occupied a space between an irresistible compulsion and a freely voluntary choice.

wiki/addiction-depictions.content:
Overview
Stories
Berks Opera Company’s ‘Faust’ focuses on addiction (2015)

Article Link

A take on Faust that has the titular character selling his soul to heroin rather than the Devil as a 21st century temptation. Whether intentional or not, this evokes the description of Faust as being “addicted” in The English Faust Book published in 1592, when “addict” was a newer term referring to the paradoxical choice of giving up one’s choice continually to something else, like sin.

Overview
Hosted by the National Association of Addiction Treatment Providers (NAATP), the Addiction Leadership Conference (ALC) focuses on gathering executives, owners, marketers, and directors to discuss national substance use disorder treatment standards.
In the late 1970s, California program directors were discussing the lack of public and political representation for nonprofit treatment programs in the private sector. In 1978, this led to a formal proposal to establish the National Association for Alcoholism Treatment Programs (NAATP), which has hosted the Addiction Leadership Conference almost every year since.

The Addiction Prevention Coalition (APC) is a non-profit dedicated to addressing substance use in the Birmingham area of Central Alabama. wiki/addiction-recovery-arts-network-con.content:

They enable the sharing of lived experience either directly, through autobiographical work, or indirectly, through exploring themes relating to addiction, wellbeing and recovery. wiki/addiction-technology-transfer-cente.title: Addiction Technology Transfer Center (ATTC) Network
wiki/addiction-technology-transfer-cente.content:
The Addiction Technology Transfer Center (ATTC) Network emerged as a federally-funded network of 11 regional centers coordinating with a National Office in order to help community-based treatment programs adopt the latest treatments.
That originally came in the form of funding more professionals, facilitating training courses, building partnerships with education and research institutions, and developing cross-discipline curriculums. Like many organizations and projects in this era, it sought to work across disciplines that interacted with addiction, like nursing, criminal justice, social work, and psychology.
Over time, the network also began focusing on supporting change in systems and organizations rather than just educating clinicians on the latest tools and protocols. A recurring theme in information-sharing projects is that simply presenting information doesn’t actually lead to long-term changes in practice. Producing change in organizations is a field unto itself called Implementation Science that grew in popularity through the 90s.
Wait, Mank, isn’t your website just presenting information? That was already presented?
Shut up. This is different. Shut up. Moving on.
On average, it takes an average of 17 years to integrate a new medical intervention into standard healthcare practice. That lines up with what a professor once gave me as a rule of thumb: assume that American protocols are 5-10 years behind the international standards and assume the international standards are 5-10 years behind the research consensus for state-of-the-art approaches. Some of the evidence-based interventions included motivational interviewing, contingency management, and buprenorphine treatment. CM is among my favorite proposals to address addiction as both social policy and individual assistance.
The ATTC Network remains one of the longest running public efforts to translate evidence from research into clinical practice.

pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4454479/

wiki/addiction.title: Addiction
wiki/addiction.content:
History and Etymology
“One of the defining features of addiction is an impairment of self-control: addicts are people who (to all appearance) find it especially difficult to bring their behavior into line with their best judgments. Addicts often report a loss of control, and theorists have often used the language of loss of control to describe addiction.” - Neil Levy, Addiction and Self-Control: Perspectives from Philosophy, Psychology, and Neuroscience

wiki/addictive-personality.title: Addictive Personality
wiki/addictive-personality.content:
Overview
An “addictive personality” is an informal collection of traits that are considered to place someone at a high risk of developing an addiction. These might include a strong preference for novelty-seeking and risk-taking behaviors, high emotional sensitivity that can compel a desire for immediate relief, or alignment with high-stress roles in professional and personal lives.
It should be noted that there is no clinical term or diagnosis for an “addictive personality.” It emerged primarily out of pop-psychology through memoirs and armchair theorizing about the kinds of persistent psychological mechanisms that raise someone’s risk of developing an addiction. There is no single profile or personality type that has been empirically validated so that it can be described as an “addictive personality,” even if researchers find that certain traits are associated with a higher risk of addiction.

wiki/addictology.title: Addictology (formerly Adiktologie)
wiki/addictology.content:
Overview
In the 1990s, Czech researchers like Tomas Zabransky, Michal Mivosky, and Viktor Mravick argued that addiction research was too divided between psychiatry, criminology, social work, and other disciplines. The concept of “addictology” was conceived as a specialized interdisciplinary effort to approach addiction. Charles University in Prague developed a unique “addictology” program across bachelor’s, master’s, and doctoral levels. In 2001, Adiktologie launched as an interdisciplinary journal about addiction research. Zabransky was the founding editor of the journal, and it’s now published through the Department of Addictology, First Faculty of Medicine, Charles University.
Notable Papers

wiki/adela-gjuricova.title: Adela Gjuricova
wiki/adela-gjuricova.content:
Overview
Adela Gjuricova is a historian and researcher whose scholarship focuses on socialist politics and cultures under communism in the context of late 20th century Central Europe, including psychiatric institutions and psychological treatment of alcohol use disorder (AUD) (often called alcohol addiction in her works). Her work investigates Jaroslav Skala, a Czech psychiatrist whose approach to addiction treatment included detoxification units and group therapy models that include families. Her exploration of the intersection of treatment for Substance Use Disorders (SUDs) and socialist ideals involves the design of therapeutic practices across an individualist-collectivist spectrum.

wiki/adela-maria-isvoranu.title: Adela-Maria Isvoranu
wiki/adela-maria-isvoranu.content:
Overview
Adela-Maria Isvoranu is a clinical psychologist who uses network psychometrics to study how alcohol, cannabis, and stimulants impact symptoms of mental health like the effects of trauma and psychosis. Her research has connected substance use to clusters of symptoms mediated by anxiety and depression, as well as psychosocial difficulties like impulsivity, stress, and adverse childhood experiences (ACEs). Isvoranu’s work has helped establish statistical standards used to model DSM-5 Substance Use Disorder (SUD) criteria and treat the disorder as behaviors that loop into each other rather than latent underlying conditions.

wiki/adenosine.title: Adenosine
wiki/adenosine.content:
Overview
Adenosine is one of the four components of RNA and forms adenosine triphosphate (ATP) as the main source of energy in human cells. It directly interacts with dopamine pathways and reward circuits in our brains, which can be disrupted through chronic substance use. Adenosine can function as a kind of “brake” for excessive dopamine signaling, so if it depletes in the course of a dopamine surge from a substance or process, its receptors become desensitized as well. Once dopamine flows without breaks from adenosine, the brain reduces overall dopamine receptors to protect itself, which then lowers the brain’s baseline dopamine production. This leads to dampened rewards experienced from daily life while fueling cravings for more of the addictive substance or process.
Caffeine directly blocks adenosine receptors, so the brain’s natural dopamine prduction flows more freely. The brain responds by building more adenosine receptors, which is how tolerance for caffeine builds over time and fatigue headaches set in when suddenly stopping. On the other hand, alcohol floods the brain with adenosine by blocking a protein, called the ENT1 transporter, that would remove extra adenosine. This explains how caffeine and alcohol can both be addictive to the brain and interfere with dopamine pathways while also producing the exact opposite effects in terms of alertness and sedation.
Links

wiki/adi-jaffe.title: Adi Jaffe
wiki/adi-jaffe.content:
Overview
Adi Jaffe is a psychologist in recovery who founded IGNTD, an online recovery platform. His own history involves struggling with Substance Use Disorders (SUDs) with methamphetamine and alcohol before earning degrees in psychology from the University of California, Los Angeles while researching addiction. Jaffe argues against the prevalence of shame and abstinence-only models in treatment, as addiction is often a maladaptive coping mechanism or attempt at self-medicating another problem.

University of California, Los Angeles: earned bachelor’s degree and doctorate in psychology before lecturing for a decade while researching the mechanisms of addiction and its social stigma

wiki/adjustment-disorder.title: Adjustment Disorder
wiki/adjustment-disorder.content:
Overview
Adjustment disorders refer to a pattern of atypical strong reactions to changes or events that usually involve intense stress. Someone might find that they begin to feel depressed or act unusually reckless. Separation anxiety is one way that adjustment disorders can manifest, particularly in children.
Links

www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/adjustment-disorders/symptoms-causes/syc-20355224
my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/21760-adjustment-disorder

wiki/adolescence.title: Adolescence
wiki/adolescence.content:
Overview
“Adolescence” refers to a transitional stage of development between childhood and adulthood, suggesting that a process of “maturing” has started. The World Health Organization formally defines the age range for adolescence as between 10 to 19 years old, but studies show that the brain continues significant development that impacts independence and judgment into the 20s.
History and Etymology
The stage of adolescence comes with a lot of new impulses that are difficult to regulate with a brain still developing the mechanisms associated with stable judgment and long-term thinking. Many cultures have acknowledged that this liminality between childhood and adulthood is a sort of crossroads for a growing human in which their impulses can meet dangerous temptations that they struggle to resist. This can include substance use and risky behavior, though the idea of what constitutes risky behavior is of course subject to cultural influences. In 19th century Western medical institutions, masturbation was treated as a psychological problem relating to a lack of self-control that should be developed in adolescence. Repeated indulgence was thought to form unhealthy habits, similar to gambling and drinking alcohol.

wiki/adolescent-brain-cognitive-developm.title: Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study
wiki/adolescent-brain-cognitive-developm.content:
Overview
The Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study is a longitudinal project tracking brain development and health in children throughout the United States.
Addiction Context
The ABCD Study has identified biomarkers associated with a genetic vulnerability to developing a substance use disorder (SUD).

wiki/adverse-childhood-experience.title: Adverse Childhood Experience (ACE)
wiki/adverse-childhood-experience.content:
Overview
Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs) are events or situations experienced by minors that could potentially have caused trauma or other lingering effects that impact one’s health and wellbeing.
The 10 core types of ACEs currently used are physical abuse, emotional abuse, sexual abuse, physical neglect, emotional neglect, intimate partner violence, household substance misuse, household mental illness, parental separation or divorce, and incarcerated household member.
History and Etymology
While the concept of childhood trauma is an old one, the exact term “Adverse Childhood Experience” was coined by a CDC-Kaiser study in 1998 that surveyed over 17,000 adults found that nearly two-thirds had at least one ACE, which dramatically changed the assumption among many medical practitioners that trauma with lasting health impacts was rare. The idea to measure ACEs started in 1985 at a Kaiser Permanente obesity clinic where Dr. Vincent Felitti observed that the majority of patients who rapidly regained the weight they dropped had experiences severe childhood abuse, suggesting that eating habits were linked to coping mechanisms that provided safety, comfort, and/or relief. Studies have since showed that an increase in ACE scores is correlated with a drastic increase in the risk of developing chronic disease as an adult.
The 10 ACE types above are directly lifted from the CDC-Kaiser study from 1998, so some modern frameworks have tried to expand ACEs to include systemic issues and community trauma, like racism, bullying, and economic hardship. The original 17,000 adults surveyed were mostly middle-class Americans with education and health insurance.
Links

pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11522112/

wiki/advocates-for-opioid-recovery.title: Advocates for Opioid Recovery
wiki/advocates-for-opioid-recovery.content:
Overview
Advocates for Opioid Recovery (AOR) is a non-profit founded in 2016 as a bipartisan effort to advance evidence-based treatments for Opioid Use Disorder (OUD), launched by Patrick J. Kennedy, Newt Gingrich, and Van Jones.

wiki/aerosol.title: Aerosol
wiki/aerosol.content:
Overview
A mixture of either liquid or solid particles suspended in a gas.
Many substances are consumed through aerosols, such as e-cigarettes and cannabis, but also traditional medications like some metered-dose inhalers (MDIs) used for asthma. Compared to digestion or other forms of consumption, aerosolized delivery of a substance goes to the bloodstream faster through the lungs. The specifics of the compounds determine what part of the ear-nose-throat system they land in for absorption. As a result, studying the impact of aerosolized substance use requires studying the effects that aerosolization itself has on substances prior to entering the body. It’s also hypothesized that the rapid delivery of the substance into the bloodstream plays a role in reinforcing substance use patterns with stronger behavioral reinforcement.

wiki/affect.title: Affect
wiki/affect.content:
Overview
In the context of psychology, “affect” refers to the observable external expressions of someone’s internal emotional and mental state. That can mean facial expressions, body language, tone of voice, etc.
Types of affects used in the Mental Status Examination (MSE) for clinical purposes include:


Broad/Normal Affect


Restricted/Constricted Affect


Blunted Affect


Flat Affect


Labile Affect


Inappropriate Affect


Congruent Affect


Incongruent Affect


Commentary

wiki/affective-world.title: Affective World
wiki/affective-world.content:
Overview
“Affective world” (also referred to as “affective landscape”, “affective environment”, and “Umwelt”) describes the subjective emotional filter through which every piece of reality is interpreted.
For instance, “I am safe” might be a subconscious baseline in an affective world in which trauma is absent or managed well, whereas “I am under constant danger” might be the baseline for someone who has unresolved negative impacts from past trauma. In the first person’s affective world, well-intentioned criticism might only lead to fleeting irritation. In the second person’s affective world, the criticism might be seen as preceding a threat of abandonment or discipline. Another example is social anxiety. To the first person, a crowded room might be seen as energizing with many opportunities to socialize. To the second person, the room might seem like a place where threats could come from any direction, so they might scan for exit routes or more secluded spaces.

wiki/against-the-stream.title: Against the Stream - Buddhist Meditation Society
wiki/against-the-stream.content:
Overview
Against the Stream is an American Buddhist movement founded by Noah Levine in 2007 that blends Theravada Buddhist foundations with Gen-X rebellious attitudes. Levine claims Buddhist meditation practices saved him from a life of addiction and crime as a form of subverting social standards that worked against the normalization of greed, hatred, delusion, and identification with ego. 1

wiki/agape.title: Agape
wiki/agape.content:
Overview
Agape is a Greek word that refers to an ultimate form of love that’s unconditional and self-sacrificial. Within Christian scriptures and philosophical literature, agape is used to describe God’s unconditional love for humanity that humans should aspire to practice for each other.
History and Etymology
Ancient Greek had several different words for “love” depending on the context and relation. “Eros” refers to romantic passionate love, while “philia” refers to brotherly love or friendship.

wiki/ageism.title: Ageism
wiki/ageism.content:
Overview
Ageism refers to prejudices or biases against older adults that can lead to discrimination. Unlike most other prejudices around immutable characteristics, all healthy adults eventually experience some degree of ageism over time.
Ageism can be a barrier to accurate diagnoses in older adults, since some of the symptoms of chronic substance use can align with stereotypical expectations for older adults or symptoms of dementia, such as memory loss and frequent falls. Public health campaigns discussing the dangers of substance use or pathways to treatment are focused on younger people and prevention.
Discrimination can work the other way as well. A distinct set of organizations (Young People in Alcoholics Anonymous, or YPAA) formed to support younger people in Alcoholics Anonymous as the traditional demographics skewed towards older people, and there was often a sentiment that younger alcoholics had not experienced enough consequences, or hit “rock bottom,” to be ready for reform. While younger people may not have the extensive history of drinking, they can definitely have had the trauma and rapid-onset of substance use disorders to benefit from treatment and peer support.

wiki/agency-for-healthcare-research-and-.title: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality

wiki/agency.title: Agency
wiki/agency.content:
Overview
“Agency” refers to the capacity to act. In everyday terms, we might use agency to describe an individual’s autonomy.
To imprison someone is to deprive them of the agency to freely move and participate in society. As children grow, they feel a stronger sense of agency over the environment around them through both experience and brain development. Medical euthanasia gives people with terminal health conditions the agency to decide a more peaceful or pleasant end to their life.
Because action is central to our human understanding of change in the world, agency and its related concepts (such as free will) are central to practically every metaphysical framework that’s applicable to human experiences. We can find discussions about thoughts, intentions, actions, and agency in the works of Aristotle.
Philosophers tend to break down agency into types including:


intentional agency


unintentional agency


mental agency


shared agency


collective agency


relational agency


artificial agency


Commentary
Agency is potentially the thorniest aspect of discussing the ethics and metaphysics of addiction.
Consider that we might label an instance of someone having sex with someone who passed out drunk as sexual assault, but we would pursue criminal charges against someone who passed out drunk behind a wheel. In both cases, someone clearly has impaired agency, but we might feel very differently about how that connects to responsibility and accountability. Susan Dimock addresses this issue in 2012 by noting that we can expand our concept of agency beyond someone’s choices in the present moment. If someone goes to a bar while intending to drive themselves home after, it seems fair to hold them responsible for the consequences after that even if their agency later was impaired. If someone goes to a bar and gets blackout drunk, they didn’t preemptively consent to having sex with anyone, so we can still examine it as sexual assault that violates consent.
Addiction by its modern definition involves compulsions that are thought to impair agency by interfering with standard reward pathways and compulsions. We might not want to say someone planned to develop a substance use disorder, but neither can we say that someone has no agency in addressing the way the deal with their substance use patterns, which can include denial of more severe usage and association with consequences. In many Alcoholics Anonymous groups and related literature, addiction is described as a “disease of the will” that has to be remedied with embracing the will of a Higher Power. The Serenity Prayer is often recited at the end of the meetings precisely to define the limitations of individual human agency in the universal order.
Links

plato.stanford.edu/entries/agency/

wiki/agitation.title: Agitation
wiki/agitation.content:
Overview
“Agitation” in everyday use refers to a state of restlessness, tension, and nervousness or excitement. However, the term has clinical significance as well that can feel much stronger than the casual use of it you might be more familiar with.
A 2024 paper posits that “Agitated individuals can be dangerous to themselves and others, making agitation an emergency. Acute presentations of agitation can include restlessness, inability to stay calm, paranoia, suspiciousness, irritability, hostility, confusion, disorientation, inability to communicate, changes in vital signs, and violent behavior.”
The DSM-5-TR defines agitation as “Excessive motor activity associated with a feeling of inner tension. The activity is usually nonproductive and repetitious and consists of behaviors such as pacing, fidgeting, wringing of the hands, pulling of clothes, and an inability to sit still.”
The federal Food and Drug Administration has borrowed the International Psychogeriatric Association’s definition of agitation for dementia that includes pacing, rocking, restlessness, yelling, profanity, grabbing, shoving, throwing objects, hitting self or others, repetitive mannerisms, etc.
The International Experts’ Meeting on Agitation in 2016 acknowledges the lack of consensus around a definition for agitation, though they did provide a working description as “a state where patients cannot remain still or calm, characterized by internal features such as hyperresponsiveness, racing thoughts, and emotional tension; and external ones, mainly motor and verbal hyperactivity, and communication impairment.”
Agitation is also distinct from, but related to, aggression. In fact, aggression is sometimes defined as “behavioral expression of severe agitation with the potential to cause harm to oneself or others.”
If you’re using agitation in an everyday context, you might not mean anything as serious as clinicians and researchers do when discussing the agitation associated with a health condition. It’s good to be mindful of that distinction when reading literature.
Links

www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK493153/

wiki/agonist.title: Agonist
wiki/agonist.content:
Overview
An agonist is a molecule that mimics the behavior of a bodily compound as it binds to cell receptors and triggers a biological response.
A full agonist produces as much response as possible from the cell. A partial agonist produces a weaker response. An inverse agonist produces the opposite response of a regular agonist once it binds to the same receptors. A co-agonist activates the receptors in conjunction with another molecule.
Methadone, a full opioid agonist, and buprenorphine, a partial opioid agonist, are highly effective Medication-Assisted Treatments (MATs) for those with Opioid Use Disorder (OUD).
Vareniciline is a partial nicotinic agonist that can ease withdrawal symptoms while making smoking less rewarding, while standard Nicotine Replacement Therapy (NRT) products like patches, gums, and lozenges are full nicotinic agonists.
Benzodiazepines are GABA agonists prescribed for panic disorders and acute withdrawal symptoms.
Buspirone is a partial serotonin arguments commonly used to treat Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) since it’s non-addictive and doesn’t form physical dependence.

wiki/ahimsa.title: Ahimsa
wiki/ahimsa.content:
Overview
Ahimsa comes from Sanskrit and means “non-harming” and is commonly translated as “nonviolence,” though it refers to forms of harm beyond just physical violence.
History and Etymology
The Early Vedic religious practices were developed around 1500-800 BCE, and many  included animal sacrifices, or “yajna.” This didn’t mean violence in general was permissible, but rather that the permissiveness was extremely context-specific. The ritual, the victim, the presence of experts to monitor the procedures, the mantras, and the intended purpose all changed the religious status of the sacrificial killing. It might be understood as a necessary but dangerous act that required care and expertise to carry out successfully. The Brahmanas detail discussions of sacrificial killings leading to potential injury, pollution, and spiritual contamination. Arguably, there was already an anxious ambivalence surrounding any kind of killing within Vedic communities, so ritualizing it allowed a way for killing to be contained by elaborate methods that took it out of the context of daily life. I think it’s important to keep that anxiety over killing in mind, given how we have a tendency to see humans of the past as more crude and violent than our purportedly advanced selves today.
The Upanishads of the Late Vedic period contain some of the earliest occurrences of “ahimsa” as an ethical concept as part of a relocation of sacrifical rituals into the internal world of the self. Rather than sacrificing physical objects into a literal fire, living life by virtues was seen as a sacrifice itself. Namely, these virtues are tapas (austerity), dana (generosity), arjava (sincerity), ahimsa (non-harming), and satya (truth). This is also the period where a spectrum of religious traditions emerge from ritualistic householding to ascetic renunciation.
In the Jain tradition, ahimsa is developed as a foundational systemic principle to minimize injury to all living beings, which can lead to a very extensive set of rules based on a broad concept of what “living” means. Buddhism takes a less consequentialist approach by asking about the intentions behind harmful actions. Brahmanical yogic traditions consider ahimsa not just part of a doctrine of virtue ethics but part of a disciplined practice to achieve personal transormation. Accordingly, the goal is not just have a compassionate disposition to others and oneself, but to cultivate a mode of being that is no longer organized around harm, possession, or disturbance. Many Hindu schools of the Advaita Vedanta tradition argue that harm stems from the ignorance of misidentifying oneself with a limited ego instead of part of a greater ultimate reality, as it is simply illogical to cause harm to the same ultimate existence one is a part of.
Links

thesobercurator.com/exploring-yoga-philosophy-understanding-ahimsa-and-its-role-in-sobriety-and-personal-growth/
pascal-francis.inist.fr/vibad/index.php

wiki/aian-american-indians-and-alaska-na.title: American Indians and Alaska Natives (AIAN)
wiki/aian-american-indians-and-alaska-na.content:
Overview
“American Indians and Alaska Natives” (AIAN) is a demographic category defined by U.S. federal government standards as ” having origins in any of the original peoples of North and South America (including Central America), and who maintains tribal affiliation or community attachment.”
History and Etymology
In 1977, the United States Office of Management and Budget (OMB) adopted the Standards for Maintaining, Collecting, and Presenting Federal Data on Race and Ethnicity for consistency in demographic data across government. This established four categories for race: American Indian or Alaskan Native, Asian or Pacific Islander, Black, and White. It also established Hispanic and Not of Hispanic Origin as the two ethnicites. If you feel that this is not necessarily the most thorough classification system for grouping people of similar backgrounds and identities together, you are not alone.
Officials and agencies were free to allow or provide more specificity, so many who fell under the American Indian or Alaskan Native category would provide specific tribal affiliations as forms would permit. As of 2026, there are 575 federally recognized tribes, but the term can be used by anyone who self-identifies with indigenous tribal heritage regardless of federal recognition.
“American Indian” has a legal legacy as a term used in federal treaties and statutes, and it remains in usage for the sake of continuity and consistency despite the frequent confusion with the term “Indian American.” The term “Alaskan Native” (changed later to “Alaska Native”) was appended because the indigenous communities of Alaska have a distinct cultural and legal history than indigenous nations of the continental United States, though the two groups have shared a unique sociopolitical status with claims to ancestral lands occupied by the U.S. government and its citizens.
Some revisions and changes have been made since, notably in 1997.
Links

civilrights.org/blog/the-decades-long-fight-for-accurate-race-and-ethnicity-data/

wiki/akathisia.title: Akathisia
wiki/akathisia.content:
Overview
Akathisia refers to a severe restlessness that produces an uncontrollable urge to move around, such as pacing, rocking, fidgeting, or constant shifting.
Within substance use disorders, it can be both a risk factor and a complication of withdrawal. Medications that block dopamine receptors like antipsychotics or alter serotonin levels like SSRIs can trigger akathisia. It’s also possible for withdrawals from opioids, alcohol, benzodiazepines, and stimulants to provoke akathisia as one’s neurochemistry undergoes rapid changes. At the same time, someone who experiences akathisia might end up self-medicating with those very substances to alleviate the physical and mental discomfort, which can quickly become a rapid spiral of using substances to avoid the symptoms caused by using the substances. It’s unfortunately possible for akathisia to be mistaken for worsening psychiatric symptoms, which can lead doctors to increase the dose of medications that trigger it.

wiki/akira-hashimoto.title: Akira Hashimoto
wiki/akira-hashimoto.content:
Overview
Akira Hashimoto is a Japanese medical historian and professor at Aichi Prefectural University with a focus on the history of psychiatry and mental health policies, including welfare sciences and substance use programs. His recent projects include comparing the development of drug treatment and harm-reduction frameworks across Australia, Switzerland, and Germany in comparison to Japan’s abstinence-focused policies.
Works

Mental Patients and Home Custody (2011)

Chapters

Alcoholism, Family and Society in Post-WWII Japan (2022)

Papers

wiki/akira-kurosawa.title: Akira Kurosawa
wiki/akira-kurosawa.content:
Overview
Akira Kurosawa was a Japanese filmmaker who created contemporary dramas in the aftermath of WWII, where addiction was a characteristic of postwar trauma and social oppression. Kurosawa was known to be a heavy drinker and chain smoker, but it was his collaborator Toshiro Mifune who was known to struggle with severe dependency that impacted his behavior and health. Reportedly, Kurosawa once drank heavily with Andrei Tarkovsky in Moscow after a screening of Solaris.
Works
Films


Drunken Angel (1948)


High and Low (1963)


Dodes’ka-den (1970)

wiki/akrasia.title: Akrasia
wiki/akrasia.content:
Overview
Akrasia is sometimes translated as a lack of self-control, but it specifically is used in a situation where one intentionally acts against their own judgment. In active addiction, for example, someone may have complete understanding of all the consequences of using a substance again and have a sincere desire not to, but a craving might be so overwhelming that they give in.
Those like Socrates via Plato argued that people acting against their own interest is the result of ignorance as they necessarily choose whatever feels like the best choice. Aristotle instead believed internal conflict in people could explain seemingly contradictory facts, like knowing something is bad for you but doing it anyways.

wiki/al-anon.title: Al-Anon
wiki/al-anon.content:
Overview
Al-Anon is an anonymous support group for those who have been impacted by someone else’s drinking and substance use patterns.
Although the term isn’t originally from the program’s literature, “Q” for “Qualifier” has been used to describe a person whose drinking patterns are an ongoing factor in someone’s life.

al-anon.org/

wiki/alabama-alliance-for-recovery-resid.title: Alabama Alliance for Recovery Residences (AAAR)
wiki/alabama-alliance-for-recovery-resid.content:
Overview
The Alabama Alliance for Recovery Residences (AARR) is a nonprofit that certifies sober living homes and recovery housing for the state of Alabama. It serves as a state affiliate of the National Alliance for Recovery Residences (NARR) and partners with the Alabama Department of Mental Health (ADMH). They publish a directory of certified homes, conduct workshops to teach housing operators about best practices, and advocates for supporting recovery infrastructure to policymakers and politicians.

alrad.info/aarr

wiki/alabama-community-college-system-in.title: Alabama Community College System (ACCS) Innovation Center
wiki/alabama-community-college-system-in.content:
Overview
The Alabama Community College System (ACCS) Innovation Center provides specialized workforce training tailored to high-demand industries in the state of Alabama. Their work on substance use includes partnering with the Alabama Alliance for Recovery Residences (AARR) for Alabama Recovery Advocacy Day, hosting the “Recovery Is Here” Campaign, and workforce training for individuals recovering from Substance Use Disorder (SUD) or transitioning out of correctional facilities. They also provide training and certification for frontline mental and community health workers.

wiki/alabama-drug-use-central-data-repos.title: Alabama Drug Use Central Data Repository (DrugUse-CDR)
wiki/alabama-drug-use-central-data-repos.content:
Overview
The Alabama Drug Use Central Data Repository (DrugUse-CDR) tracks substance use in Alabama with a particular focus on the opioid crisis. Some of their focus areas include deploying first responders to overdose out breaks, measuring the effectiveness of community initiatives, and providing the public with interactive dashboards. It was established in 2018 through the University of Alabama’s Institute of Data and Analytics.

opioidcdr.ua.edu/

wiki/alabama-recovery-advocacy-day.title: Alabama Recovery Advocacy Day
wiki/alabama-recovery-advocacy-day.content:
Overview
Established in 2023 by the Alabama Alliance for Recovery Residents (AARR) in partnership with the Alabama Bureau of Pardons and Paroles (ABPP), the Alabama Recovery Advocacy Day facilitates engagement between leaders of the recovery community and state officials that implement addiction-related policies. The event was initially hosted on the Alabama State House steps as a kind of rally, but the success and growth quickly led to using major venues like the Multiplex at Cramton Bowl to host larger exhibitions and audience capacity.

wiki/alabama-summit-on-addiction-and-pai.title: Alabama Summit on Addiction and Pain (ASAP)
wiki/alabama-summit-on-addiction-and-pai.content:
Overview
The Alabama Summit on Addiction and Pain (ASAP) began in 2024 while sponsored by the Center for Addiction and Pain Prevention and Intervention (CAPPI) to address the intersection of chronic pain and Substance Use Disorders (SUDs). This includes looking at the physiological mechanisms of pain signaling and experiencing, non-addictive treatments like non-hallucinogenic derivatives of ibogaine and psilocybin, and pain care as a fundamental human right.

wiki/alan-i-leshner.title: Alan I. Leshner
wiki/alan-i-leshner.content:
Overview
Alan Leshner is a psychologist who served as director of the National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA) and the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH).
Education

wiki/alcohol-clinical-and-experimental-r.title: Alcohol - Clinical, and Experimental Research (ACER)
wiki/alcohol-clinical-and-experimental-r.content:
Overview
In 1977, the National Council on Alcoholism (now called the National Council on Alcoholism and Drug Dependence, NCADD) established a journal called Alcohol: Clinical and Experiment Research (ACER). It followed a major expansion in alcohol research in 1970 through the creation of the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA). Biomedical, clinical, and behavioral studies were all growing in volume, so ACER was proposed as a specialized outlet for addiction research across these domains. The name reflects the growing emphasis on synthesizing clinical experiences and laboratory experiments.
The NCADD was originally a project founded by Marty Mann, who was the first woman to maintain sobriety through AA. Its focus was advocacy and education rather than scientific research, so it became the official journal of the newly formed Research Society on Alcoholism (RSA). To simplify, this kind of partnership isn’t unusual in the academic space. A publishing entity might have the means and mission to distribute scientific literature, but a dedicated scientific society can determine the academic direction. Today, the partnership involves Wiley as the commercial publisher, RSA for scientific governance, and the International Society for Biomedical Research on Alcoholism (ISBRA) which uses ACER as an official outlet for international research since 1990.
In 2014, the journal ended its regular print publication and became exclusively available online.
In 2023, the journal swapped “Alcoholism” for “Alcohol” in its name, reflecting the way that “alcoholism” as a term had phased out of the vocabulary of scientific literature in place of “alcohol use disorder.” Plus, alcohol was increasingly being studied for its impacts outside of addiction, like metabolism and fetal alcohol spectrum disorders.
Links

researchsocietyonalcohol.org/acer-journal/
onlinelibrary.wiley.com/journal/29937175

wiki/alcohol-dependence-provisional-desc.title: Alcohol dependence - provisional description of a clinical syndrome
wiki/alcohol-dependence-provisional-desc.content:
“Anyone concerned with treating drinking problems must find that his patients often tell him more than is in the textbooks. Each tells a different story, but there are also repeated patterns. Much of the varied experience that is recounted can be interpreted as the patient’s astute observation of the alcohol dependence syndrome - a condition certainly far better described by the average alcoholic than in any book.”
“Routine clinical questions may impose a pattern on patients’ accounts, and patients may themselves organize their uncertain recall of events in terms of expectations given to them.”

pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/773501/

wiki/alcohol-drugs-and-the-family-resear.title: Alcohol, Drugs, and the Family research interest group
wiki/alcohol-drugs-and-the-family-resear.content:
Overview
Led by James Orford, this group from the University of Birmingham developed the stress-strain-coping-support model for addiction-affected family members (AFMs) and the 5-Step Method (5SM).

wiki/alcohol-myopia.title: Alcohol Myopia Model (AMM)
wiki/alcohol-myopia.content:
Overview
The Alcohol Myopia Model (AMM) is a theory about the way substance use influences decision-making processes. In the same way that myopia (nearsightedness) represents a limitation around one’s perspective, AMM describes a limitation on the brain’s processing capacity to weigh the trade-offs around decisions or control reactive impulses. If intoxication impairs attention, someone might only be able to engage with the immediate cues in some activity front of them, which could boost self-esteem and block negative self-evaluations. At the same time, intoxication would interfere with long-term planning and short-term inhibitions, which can lead someone to act with much more impulsive confidence.

wiki/alcohol-research-center.title: Alcohol Research Center (ARC)
wiki/alcohol-research-center.content:
Overview
The Alcohol Research Center (ARC) at the University of Connecticut’s health campus is both a research and a clinical institution that conducts trials and studies. Its programs include Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy, Individualized Assessment and Treatment Programs (IATP), Contingency Management (CM), case management, Medication-Assisted Treatment (MAT), and routine clinical procedures.
The ARC is also known for developing screening tools for Substance Use Disorders (SUDs): Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test (AUDIT) and Alcohol, Smoking and Substance Involvement Screening Test (ASSIST).
Links

health.uconn.edu/psychiatry/research/alcohol-research-center/

wiki/alcohol-research-lab.title: Alcohol Research Lab
wiki/alcohol-research-lab.content:
Overview
The Alcohol Research Lab at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (UIUC) is a specialized research group focused on the effects of alcohol consumption and the progression into Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD). Their studies include electroencephalogram (EEG) studies, biosensor tracking, automated text processing (Natural Language Processing), and other measurements that monitor brain activity to see the effects of social anxiety.
Links

www.alcoholresearchlab.com/

wiki/alcohol-tobacco-and-other-drugs-ato.title: Alcohol, Tobacco, and Other Drugs (ATOD)
wiki/alcohol-tobacco-and-other-drugs-ato.content:
Overview
Alcohol, Tobacco, and Other Drugs (ATOD) was a designation that emerged in the 1980s to capture emerging trends in neuroscientific studies that showed alcohol, nicotine, and other substances shared biological mechanisms that impacted the brain’s reward system. In 1985, the American Public Health Association (APHA) officially created an Alcohol, Tobacco, and Other Drugs Section that repeated terms like “chemical dependency” and “substance abuse.” The phrase was intentionally crafted to explicitly categorize alcohol and tobacco as drugs and tackle the assumption that legal and illicit substances were inherently different.
In 1989, the United States Congress passed The Drug-Free Schools and Communities Act (DFSCA)  which requires all educational institutions receiving federal funding to create prevention programs for substance use. One vendor for these Drug and Alcohol Abuse Prevention Programs (DAAPPs) was D.A.R.E, or Drug Abuse Resistance Education. D.A.R.E. adopted the ATOD framework guide three categories of responses, usually through an umbrella narrative that alcohol and tobacco were “gateway drugs” to illicit substances.

wiki/alcohol-use-disorder.title: Alcohol Use Disorder
wiki/alcohol-use-disorder.content:
Overview
Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD) is a type of Substance Use Disorder (SUD) that applies when alcohol is the substance of choice, generally referring to ethanol.

wiki/alcohol.title: Alcohol
wiki/alcohol.content:
Overview
Alcohol in general conversation refers to ethanol, which is added to food or beverages as one of the world’s most common recreational substances. Excessive drinking habits have gained a myriad of terms across the world across thousands of years of traditional rituals, recreational activities, and trauma followed by maladaptive coping mechanisms. These include alcoholism, habitual drunkenness, inebriety, and Alcohol Use Disorder.
In the context of chemistry, alcohol actually refers to a class of chemicals that includes ethanol and methanol.

wiki/alcoholics-anonymous-agnostica.title: Alcoholics Anonymous Agnostica
wiki/alcoholics-anonymous-agnostica.content:
Summary
AA Agnostica was founded in 2011 by Roger Couvrette, an atheist AA member from the Greater Toronto Area.
The inspiration came from a controversy where We Agnostics and Beyond Belief, two secular AA groups, were removed from the GTA Intergroup’s meeting directory after the groups began using an alternative version of the Twelve Steps and Traditions. While documenting these events and the history of secularism in AA, Couvrette realized there was far more than he expected for an initial investigation. So came about the website. Generally, “agnostic” as a term is used to signal that you at least accept that no belief in God is required to work the Twelve Steps, without asserting a claim about God in general.
In 2015, Couvrette published Do Tell! Stories by Atheists and Agnostics in AA which documented stories from 15 men and women each about their gratitude for AA Agnostica. In 2017, Couvrette published A History of Agnostics in AA that compiled the research collected over the years.
Note: In April 2026, AA Agnostica announced they would no longer post new articles to their site after 14 years and 777 articles, though it remains up and accessible. The site had seemed to cease publishing new content in an early announcement in 2022 with 742 articles, but they seem to have restarted at some point before stopping again.
I would be doing a disservice if I did not credit this website for being an invaluable inspiration for what an independent knowledge base about recovery can look like.
Links

aaagnostica.org/
aaagnostica.org/the-last-post-on-aa-agnostica-eleven-years-old/
aaagnostica.org/the-very-last-post-on-aa-agnostica-more-than-14-1-2-years-old/

wiki/alcoholics-anonymous-fascimile-firs.content:
For those who aren’t in the book collectors niche, a “fascimile edition” is an exact reproduction of the first edition a book was printed in.

wiki/alcoholics-anonymous.title: Alcoholics Anonymous - The Big Book
wiki/alcoholics-anonymous.content:
A Mutual Aid Success Story
I can sound very critical about A.A., but it’s only in response to the tone set by the How It Works section that’s read at the beginning of every meeting. If any enthusiastic newcomer is taken aback by the language about people being born too naturally dishonest to work the program, I want them to know there are people promoting other paths to recovery. They don’t have to decide between active addiction and alcoholics anonymous.
If I set aside my own reservations about the program, I have to honestly admire that AA is perhaps one of the biggest success stories for what a mutual aid network can accomplish if its people are sufficiently motivated. After every social institution has proved to have a disastrous handling of substance abuse and mental health, an explicitly non-professional society with religious overtones started with collectives across the world. In theory, anyone can walk into an AA meeting and find fellow addicts trying to recover or maintain sobriety together.
It’s not just emotional support either. Tangible resources are shared in recovery meetings. I’ve seen jobs reserved for people in recovery, first-month rental assistance, transportation arrangements, food and basic essentials especially when partnering with churches that hold donation drives. It’s more than I’ve seen out of grassroots political movements for sure
The Big Disclaimer
I can sometimes take a somewhat critical stance around A.A. literature and the official A.A. nonprofit organization. I try to contextualize my tone as a contrast to the specific parts of A.A.’s philosophy that can be harsh towards those it may not be the best fit for, especially when religion and spirituality are used interchangeably.
Despite showing up as a newcomer with a lot of enthusiasm to begin managing an unmanageable life, I was taken aback when I saw the terms “unfortunates” and “constitutionally incapable” applied to those who search of an “easier, softer way” as if alternative recovery options didn’t exist. I generally have a strong aversion to the idea that immoral or amoral lifestyles are the result of being “born that way” since that can be a slippery slope to associating poor character with genetic predestination. I was confused for a while about how a loving, caring, all-powerful Higher Power from a “higher independent reality” that is prayed to as “God”, “Creator”, and “Father” under the justification of convenience isn’t actually just God.
If we wanted to talk about general spiritual principles, well the concepts of “self-will run riot” and “misidentification with an impermanent ego through attachment” from various Buddhist and Hindu traditions are quite similar. There could be something to finding common ground rooted in empirically verifiable psychology, like framing the results of excessive self-will or egoistic attachment as irrational distortions to be challenged. That common ground can fall apart when introducing a Higher Power as a causal independent agent in recovery, yet the Steps aren’t possible to do without it.
These can certainly have a discouraging effect on newcomers to recovery or even those simply curious about a desire to stop drinking - not because they don’t believe in God or a Higher Power that would be compatible with the Steps, but because it’s unexpected and heavy-handed for people who are shopping around a recovery marketplace. My tone is intended to convey to these newcomers that no, you are not crazy for experiencing doubts about the spiritual vs religious nature of the program. It is general religious content, not just general spiritual principles. I’m not even sure those can be split up and defined separately.
But the same applies to my own content. It can be discouraging to see someone only express criticism about the most widely available free community to meet others struggling with one of the most complex yet stigmatized diseases to exist. My desire to share alternatives to A.A. should not be read as a condemnation of A.A., and by no means does being religious mean that A.A. is any less effective or worthy as a solution for recovery. I have no problem believing the claim from A.A. that over 2 million alcoholics have improved their sustained abstinence through the program and the Steps.
By nature I am an anarchic contrarian, so my M.O. always involves poking holes in the common narratives promoted by institutions out of a suspicion of power. I am rarely motivated to discuss anything because of A.A. members or meetings on the whole, which are filled with lovely supportive people and decades of wisdom in recovery. It’s the way A.A. has become institutionally embedded as a manualized suggestion or protocol in standard recovery treatment, partially because of the literature and public relations media put out by an official organization, that catches my suspicion. After all, A.A.’s philosophy itself highlights the non-professional, non-hierarchical network with no opinion on outside issues as critical to its success.
I make a point not to do a blanket endorsement or condemnation of any program as long as it’s not advocating for sacrificing babies for adrenochrome under a mountain on a remote island or doing massive amounts of untested hallucinogenics in a haunted cave. It would be entirely against the spirit of this site if someone who might only have access to A.A. meetings in their area ends up isolating and continuing to experience a life becoming increasingly unmanageable by substance use.
So, despite not being someone who intends on working the Steps, I’m going to cover the ideas behind A.A. in the most charitable way I can while honoring the many Christian philosophers who laid the foundation for the program. I will resist the temptation to cite Reinhold Niebuhr. That way, even if we end up at disagreement about The Big Book of Alcoholics Anonymous itself or the character defects of William Wilson (Bill W.), we can step back and still engage with the ideas through other means.
The only exception is going to be scientific claims. If there is a reliable body of evidence that substantially impacts the merits of a claim about addiction and recovery, I will bring it up so that you can separate the principles of recovery from the dynamics of the disease.

wiki/alcoholics-victorious.title: Alcoholics Victorious
wiki/alcoholics-victorious.content:
Alcoholics Victorious (AV) is one of the “Christian AA” groups that considers AA to be secular and prefers a more overtly Christian approach to recovery. As their website states, “there is a ‘spiritual’ element in addiction that must be addressed through the true GOD.” Non-Christians or non-believers can attend, provided they “feel compelled to search out the true ‘higher power’ Jesus Christ, attempting to identify Him, to come to know Him, and then to trust Him for healing power.”
AV is an official program of Christians in Recovery, which is a ministry of TechMission, which is a nonprofit organization that operates City Vision College. AV chapters are required to annually renew their charters with the official organization, including forms and fees. Meetings can involve Bible teachings but are not intended to be Bible study groups.
History
Alcoholics Victorious was founded in 1948.
The “True Higher Power”
“Those who have not yet placed their faith in Christ have an opportunity to come to know the true “Higher Power” spoken of in AA, finding an atmosphere of accepting Christian love in which to form a personal relationship with the Lord.”
The premise of the group isn’t necessarily a meeting space for those who have chosen Jesus as their Higher Power for the Twelve Steps, but those who believe that the Higher Power of AA is Jesus. The term “true higher power” appears multiple times on the site.
“Founded in 1948, Alcoholics Victorious support groups offer a safe environment for people recovering from the effects of alcoholism or drug addiction. We recognize Jesus Christ as our “Higher Power” and gather together to share our experience, faith, strength and hope. AV meetings use the 12 Steps, the Bible and the Alcoholics Victorious Creed.
CBD Offer
June 2019 News: Royal CBD is offering 30% off to all Alcoholics Victorious chapter members on their 250mg and 500mg CBD oils using code AV30.”
That text about the CBD oil is on the front page of Alcoholics Victorious. Since it’s from June 2019, it’s probably not an active offer and it’s safe to share without enticing anyone.
From this article written in July 2019, the very next month, there was a company called the Christian Book Distributors that went by the acronym CBD and held the domain www.cbd.com whose owner described a common confusion with the chemical:
““I was driving my mum down the road recently,” he told the New York Times. “She saw a sign that said ‘CBD sold here.’ I was like, ‘No, mum. That’s not us.’””
Major advertising networks like Google Ads banned cannabis-related ads, which means companies like Royal CBD are far more dependent on search engine optimization (SEO) to appear higher in Google search results. One approach to SEO is to place links to your website on niche high-authority websites. Alcoholics Victorious is a niche community, so the official home page has high authority on the topic. The website owners may have thought that the CBD making them an offer to be paid for a backlink was somehow related to the Christian Book Distributors, especially if the latter or an agency they hired was sneaky about the pitch. It’s plausible that someone not familiar with marijuana might interpret “CBD oils” as some kind of accessory wellness product sold alongside spiritual wellness literature.
Either that, or this is a really, really flexible group.
There’s other things about the website that are strange too. If you’re compulsive about numbers, you may have realized that if AV was founded in 1948, then to be serving needs for 66 years brings us to 2014.
Unfortunately I couldn’t find much material about Alcoholics Victorious out there. It seems to have always remained a niche but enduring group for Christians whose spirituality might come entirely from Biblical teachings.

wiki/alcoholism.title: Alcoholism
wiki/alcoholism.content:
Overview
Alcoholism refers to the compulsive and habitual consumption of alcohol in spite of worsening consequences, health or social.
The history of terms used to describe compulsive and habitual substance use are as varied as presentations of substance use disorders themselves. “Alcoholism” and “alcoholic” have a lot of baggage that produces a lot of stigma, though some groups, particularly Alcoholics Anonymous (A.A.), embrace the term as one that can bring unity among their fellowship. Sharing at a meeting usually begins by announcing “my name is… and I’m an alcoholic/addict.” SMART Recovery, Recovery Dharma, Refuge Recovery, and other groups either forego this tradition or discourage its usage to create distance from the stigma. “Alcohol use disorder” is more commonly used in clinical contexts. For the purposes of this site, “alcoholism” is often used for brevity and interchangeably used with “alcohol use disorder” or “substance use disorder” in hopes of diluting the stigma.
History and Etymology
Magnus Huss termed habitual drunkenness as “Alcoholismus Chronicus”, from which we get the term “alcoholism.”

wiki/alexander-hamilton.title: Alexander Hamilton
wiki/alexander-hamilton.content:
Overview
Alexander Hamilton was the first Secretary of the Treasury of the United States.
Hamilton wrote extensively about the threat “ardent spirits” (or hard liquor as concentrated forms of alcohol) posed to public health and the national moral character of the US, especially for soldiers and militias. In Federalist No. 12, he discusses the virtues of taxing liquor with the added benefit of bringing in significant revenue for the state:
The single article of ardent spirits, under federal regulation, might be made to furnish a considerable revenue… That article would well bear this rate of duty; and if it should tend to diminish the consumption of it, such an effect would be equally favorable to the agriculture, to the economy, to the morals, and to the health of the society. There is, perhaps, nothing so much a subject of national extravagance as these spirits.
He believed that beer and cider were healthy alternatives to the hard liquor that was associated with “habitual drunkenness”, so he believed in moderation rather than abstinence as many early temperance advocates did. In 1790, he submitted a report to Congress advocating for the Whiskey Excise Act and attributed excessive drinking habits to the affordability of spirits.
There is no evidence to suggest Hamilton participated in substance use or drinking alcohol to a problematic extent, although some scholars and authors have argued that Hamilton did suffer from hypomanic episodes or bipolar disorder exacerbated by extreme stress and trauma. In the day following his fatal duel with Aaron Burr, he was given laudanum to manage the pain of being shot as a standard medicine administered by physicians in the early 1800s.

wiki/alexander-the-great.title: Alexander the Great
wiki/alexander-the-great.content:

He held a drinking contest in honor of Kalanos, an Indian Brahmin philosopher and sage who was at one point Alexander’s teacher. The winner, along with 40 other participants, drank themselves to death.

wiki/alexithymia.title: Alexithymia
wiki/alexithymia.content:
Overview
Alexithymia literally translates from Greek as “a lack of words for emotions,” coined in 1973 by the Greek-American psychiatrist Peter Sifneos. A similar description of a phenomenon had been created by earlier French clinical psychoanalysts like Pierre Marty who noticed some patients presented with physical illnesses but couldn’t articulate their internal emotional reactions to it, instead speaking almost entirely in literal operational terms (“pensée opératoire”). Sifneos similarly observed that some patients struggled immensely with traditional psychotherapy that came to a standstill if emotions couldn’t be identified and processed.
Just two years later in 1975, Henry Krystal formally discussed alexithymia in his research into the internal world of people with substance use disorders, arguing that they tended to experience emotions as chaotic physical states rather than psychological feelings. Under this framework, drugs were a physical chemical shield that substituted for the cognitive mechanisms responsible for managing intense emotional experiences.
This led Edward Khantzian to propose the oft-cited Self-Medical Hypothesis in 1985, which has worked its way into general public discourse through “self-medicating.” Khantzian used Krystal’s connections from alexithymia to substance use as evidence that addiction is generally a self-regulation disorder where individuals learn that substances are predictable solutions to coping with unmanageable internal states. How often do we hear someone say “I need a drink” after a stressful day at work? That’s arguably a mild form of self-medication that addresses stress with an external substance.
In the 1980s, Graeme Taylor, Michael Bagby, and James Parker proposed the Toronto Alexithymia Scale (TAS) as a tool to empirically measure degrees of alexithymia. Early surveys shows that it presents in about 5-10% of the general population, but up to 78% of people seeking treatment for substance use disorders. Since then, modern neuroimaging through fMRIs have shown that presenting with high alexithymia scores correlates with reduced activity in the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), which is responsible for connecting bodily states with emotional awareness.

wiki/alignment.title: Alignment
wiki/alignment.content:
Overview
“Alignment” as a concept has wide applicability in psychology, self-help, spirituality and religion, and recovery circles. In general, it refers to bringing different components of an overall system into coordinated functionality. Some examples include alignment of mind-body-soul, of internal values with external behaviors, and of oneself with one’s environment.
History and Etymology
One of the earliest concepts of misalignment in modern clinical psychology comes out of cognitive dissonance theory, advanced by Leon Festinger in 1957, which posits that when people’s behavior contradicts their internal beliefs, they experience psychological distress. Though it doesn’t explicitly use the concept of alignment, we can easily see how the language of misalignment can be applied to the mismatch between internal and external realities.
In 2011, Mary Leamy and a team of researchers who proposed the CHIME Framework after a meta-analysis of 97 papers from 13 countries led them to identify five core components of recovery processes:


Connectedness: a sense of belonging fueled by supportive relationships, community participation, and social inclusion


Hope and optimism: a belief that change and recovery are possible, which often involves role models and aspirations


Identity: a sense of self based around one’s positive attributes that challenge external and internalized stigma


Meaning: a pursuit of purposeful existence guided by personal values, principles, and philosophies


Empowerment: a sense of agency, autonomy, and authority over one’s life that allows decision-making according to one’s strengths and values


“Alignment” as a term is used explicitly when referring to the mapping between daily actions and the CHIME components, especially for Identity and Meaning.

wiki/all-california-young-people-in-alco.content:
Overview
All California Young People in Alcoholics Anonymous (ACYPAA) was established in 1973 after decades of Young People’s groups had formed in cities like Los Angeles to reach new demographics, since most AA members at the time were older white middle-class men who had histories with alcohol longer than some of the younger members had even been alive. The organization’s Advisory Council was established as the administrative body to keep growing the network between the annual conferences. Namely, the Advisory Council manages a bidding system where young people’s committees from across California cities compete to be chosen to host the annual Roundup- a process which involves a skit, a Q&A interview, and financial and logistical reviews.

Overview
The Alliance for Recovery Centered Organization (ARCO) is a national program under the Faces & Voices of Recovery that serves as a network for Recovery Community Organizations (RCOs) across the United States. This includes peer support services, public campaigns against social stigma, advocacy for improved funding and supportive recovery legislation, professional trainings, and supporting community infrastructure like sober living environments (SLEs). They also host the Recovery Leadership Summit every year as a national conference for policymakers, regulators, advocates, and practitioners to meet and discuss issues in recovery spaces.
