wiki/assay.title: Assay
wiki/assay.content:
Overview
An assay refers to a laboratory test used to measure the presence of some target, such as a drug, protein, or cell.
Qualitative assays are generally binary, reporting either the presence or absence of a target. Quantitative assays measure the relative concentration or absolute amount of a target.
In the context of addiction, assays are used as tests to detect specific drugs or their metabolites (the compounds that a drug breaks down into once it has been processed, or metabolized). They’re a standard part of initial clinical assessments to confirm which substances might be in a patient’s system as well as the relative concentration. Illicit substances, and even legal substances from companies that don’t comply with safety regulations, often have dangerous additives that the patient may not be aware of. Fentanyl is among the riskiest of these additives. Treatment providers use the results of these assays to calculate the initial detoxification plans and the medication dosages that are most appropriate for the patient’s condition. It also allows providers to check if patients are taking their medications as prescribed. In the case of multiple substances that might cross-react in ways that complicate assay results, advanced assays may be necessary.
Assays are also valuable from a legal perspective, as child custody cases, professional licensing boards, and probation all use assays to help determine if someone has been compliant with the requirements.
Just the act of random drug testing with assays can be a reliable psychological deterrant against use.

wiki/assemblage.title: Assemblage
wiki/assemblage.content:
Overview
Recent work in anthropology treats addiction as an assemblage, or a network of human bodies, chemicals, syringes and pipes, laws and police, urban infrastructure, and affective states

wiki/assertive-communication.title: Assertive Communication
wiki/assertive-communication.content:
Overview
Assertive communication refers to expressing yourself clearly without passively downplaying your boundaries or aggressively imposing your needs on others.

wiki/association-for-multidisciplinary-e.title: Association for Multidisciplinary Education and Research in Substance Use and Addiction (AMERSA)

wiki/ataraxia.title: Ataraxia
wiki/ataraxia.content:
Overview
“Ataraxia” is an ancient Greek term that translates roughly to “lack of disturbance,” so “tranquility” and “equanimity” are often used as the translations. Different Greek philosophies interpreted ataraxia differently, with Stoic philosophers like Seneca often using it interchangeably with “apathaeia” though Epicurean philosophers would challenge that.

wiki/athens-medical-society.title: Athens Medical Society
wiki/athens-medical-society.content: Established in 1835 shortly after Greece as a modern nation-state, it is the oldest medical scientific society in the country. It organizes the Panhellenic Medical Congress annually.

wiki/atman.title: Atman
wiki/atman.content:
Overview
Atman is a Sanskrit word referring to a true inner core of a living being upon which temporary aspects of existence like body, mind, and ego are constructed. Within most Hindu theology and cosmology, the atman is immortal and is reborn into cycles of living, usually until the realization of one’s true nature liberates oneself into unity with Brahman, or the ultimate reality.
This is also one of the biggest points of divergence between Hinduism and Buddhism as belief systems heavily reliant on impermanence and interconnectedness. Buddhism rejects that there is a permanent soul-like aspect to our existence in the first place, instead using the concept of anatta or anatman to refer to a “not-self.”

wiki/atomoxetine.title: Atomoxetine
wiki/atomoxetine.content:
Overview
Atomoxetine is a prescription medication used for Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) as a selective norephinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI) that blocks the norephinephrine transporter (NET) from clearing norepinephrine and dopamine out of the space between nerves in the brain’s prefrontal cortex to stop their signaling.
Unlike other ADHD medications, atomoxetine is not a stimulant and lacks the same potential for dependency that stimulant medications have, so it’s not a controlled substance either. If someone has a history of struggling with substance use disorders or associated symptoms, professional prescribers may opt to try atomoxetine before other medications that cause dopamine spikes in the brain’s reward pathways. A 2017 study published in The American Journal of Psychiatry found that atomoxetine is associated with reducing the risk of consequences related to substance use:
In adjusted within-individual comparisons, relative to periods in which patients did not receive ADHD medication, male patients had 35% lower odds of concurrent substance-related events when receiving medication (odds ratio=0.65, 95% CI=0.64–0.67), and female patients had 31% lower odds of concurrent substance-related events (odds ratio=0.69, 95% CI=0.67–0.71).
Moreover, male patients had 19% lower odds of substance-related events 2 years after medication periods (odds ratio=0.81, 95% CI=0.78–0.85), and female patients had 14% lower odds of substance-related events 2 years after medication periods (odds ratio=0.86, 95% CI= 0.82–0.91). Sensitivity analyses supported most findings but were less consistent for long-term associations among women.
Commentary
This one made me meaner and eliminated my pangs of guilt around considering doing and saying mean things. It’s a strange feeling.
Links

wiki/attachment-theory.title: Attachment Theory
wiki/attachment-theory.content:
Overview
Attachment theory refers to a framework of understanding the way our development influences our attachments within relationships. While the conventional formulation of attachment theory tends to separate styles into secure, anxious, avoidant, and anxious-avoidant with a strong emphasis on childhood development, modern researchers tend to see anxiety and avoidance as continuous spectrums subject to neuroplasticity. That means healthy relationships and positive experiences can help adults achieve “earned security” in their connections with others. Modern psychologists have also moved away from centering the relationship between infants and mothers to include all family members, community caregivers, peer groups, and early romantic engagements as having influence over the dimensions to attachment.

wiki/attapulgite.title: Attapulgite
wiki/attapulgite.content:
Overview
Attapulgite is a magnesium-aluminum silicate clay mineral that’s often used as to treat diarrhea and stomach distress. It binds to bacteria and toxins in the digestive tract to harden loose stool and soothe gastrointestinal linings. It can also be found in some industrial drilling sites as a thickening agent and litter boxes for its high liquid absorption.
For a while, Donnagel was one of the more popular forms of it available over-the-counter, though medicines like Pepto-Bismol outperformed it after.

wiki/attention-deficit-hyperactivity-dis.title: Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
wiki/attention-deficit-hyperactivity-dis.content:
Overview
Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is widely defined as a neurodevelopment disorder that impacts executive function and makes it difficult to sustain attention, regulate emotions, and manage impulsivity. In most cases, ADHD is genetic with a heritability rate of 80%, thought it has sometimes been observed to occur in adults who experience traumatic brain injuries (TBIs). Diagnosing ADHD can be difficult since many other disorders can be responsible for symptoms that include impulsivity and difficulty maintaining focus.
As of the DSM-V, ADHD comes in three primary presentations:


Predominantly Inattentive: overlooks details, makes careless mistakes, has difficulty focusing on a single task, losing focus when spoken to without competing distractions, fails to complete tasks or follow instructions as written, struggles with organization and deadlines, expresses reluctance to start tasks that might require long periods of focus, losing track of essential items for life or work, easily distracted by external stimuli or internal thoughts, forgets to complete daily activities for living


Hyperactivity-Impulsivity: fidgeting and squirming while sitting in place, trouble sitting still during occasions where remaining seated is expected, pervasive restlessness, appearing uncomfortable when not in motion, talking excessively, interrupting people to finish sentences or answer a question, struggling to wait in a queue, impulsively uses other people’s things without asking


Combined: criteria for Inattentive and Hyperactive-Impulsive are both met with neither having a clear predominance


ADHD and substance use disorders both are characterized in part by a shortage of neurotransmitters along reward pathways. Specifically, brains with ADHD struggle to produce and transport dopamine and norepinephrine, which address our ability to focus, retain motivation, and experience the sensation of a reward for completing a task. The prefrontal cortex then struggles with impulse control, future planning, and emotional regulation. Consequently, those with ADHD are at a higher risk of developing substance use disorders both because of an increased impulsivity to experiment with substances and to bridge the natural deficiency in dopamine. It’s common to find that those with both disorders had been using substances to self-medicate, whether it’s stimulants to provide an artificial boost to clear brain fog or depressants to mute the brain’s hyperactivity and anxiety. Some studies show that as many as 25% of people in substance use disorder treatment also have ADHD.
Commentary
Anecdotally, it’s extremely common for people to only find out in treatment that they had been dealing with ADHD, among other disorders, their whole lives. The failure to screen for these disorders in childhood and provide children with adequate treatment is obviously one of the most glaring flaws in our approach to addressing mental health. We save a lot of time, money, resources, heartache, and suffering when we address health concerns at the earliest possible moment instead of leaving someone to self-medicate in far costlier and more dangerous ways.

wiki/attention.title: Attention
wiki/attention.content:
Overview
“Attention” is one of those terms that suffers from being used so often that it has numerous definitions put forward by different institutions.
From Lindsay, 2020:
“Attention is the important ability to flexibly control limited computational resources. It has been studies in conjunction with many other topics in neuroscience and psychology including awareness, vigilance, saliency, executive control, and learning.”
From Krauzlis et. al, 2023:
“We define attention as ‘the set of evolved brain processes that leads to adaptive and effective behavioral selection.’ Our emphasis is on understanding the biological and neural echanisms that make the behavioral properties of attention possible.”
Links


 Attention in Psychology, Neuroscience, and Machine Learning (Lindsay, 2020)


 What is attention? (Krauzlis et. al, 2023)

wiki/attributability.title: Attributability
wiki/attributability.content:
Overview
With addiction, the debate around attributability centers on whether chronic substance use as a disease impairs judgment enough for addictive behaviors to no longer be attributable to someone’s core character, comparable to a brain injury or dementia. Most with a substance use disorder genuinely want to quit and live a sober life, but they struggle with cravings and withdrawals intensely enough that they also struggle to align their behaviors and intentions. A few may not have any desire to quit or have any regard for the consequences of using, even if it affects others or could lead to their own death.
Those with an addiction are also generally able to articulate their reasoning for using which satisfies the answerability pillar of moral responsibility. However, we can also see that cravings and withdrawals can operate as strong forms of pressure, similar to how someone who feels like they’re starving or dying of thirst might commit acts of violence in order to get food and water. They can answer questions about their justification for the actions, and they might be able to do so without being hypocritical; “I only wanted to use it one last time before quitting” might be a flawed idea, but it can seem quite logical under the pressure of cravings that feel intolerable.

wiki/auguste-henri-forel.title: Auguste-Henri Forel
wiki/auguste-henri-forel.content:
Overview
Auguste-Henri Forel was a professor of psychiatry at the University of Zurich and co-formulated the neuron theory in 1887. He served as the director of the university’s Burgholzli asylum from 1879 to 1898 and researched the potential applications of hypnotism. He also researched ants and published works like The Social Life of Ants.
In 1889, he partnered with Jakob Bosshard to open a specialized treatment facility for substance use disorders (SUDs) in Ellikon an der Thur, which now operates as the Forel Clinic. Although Forel opposed alcohol on the basis of it being a neurotoxin that damaged brain tissue and examined alcohol use as a medical issue rather than a moral failing, he also adopted eugenics perspectives that argued alcohol consumption directly passed on harm to one’s future generations. He campaigned against alcohol use through lecturing and organizing with temperance movements across North America and Europe, connecting it to mental illness, poverty, crime, and domestic violence.
Forel was a close associate of Emil Kraepelin, with whom he founded the Association of Abstinent Doctors in 1896 under the belief that psychiatrists ought to be fully abstinent, since any amount of alcohol consumption has harms and moderate use was argued to be an illusion.

wiki/avoidance.title: Avoidance
wiki/avoidance.content:
Overview
Avoidance in a psychological context is a coping mechanism where someone either acts or fails to act in a way that evades an unwanted experience. In the short-term, this serves as a coping mechanism that provides immediate relief in response to a distressing encounter, but in the long-term, this can end up reinforcing avoidance as a reaction instead of addressing the roots of triggers.

wiki/avoidant-attachment.title: Avoidant Attachment
wiki/avoidant-attachment.content:
Overview
Avoidant attachment refers to a style of attachment that’s characterized by hyper-independence when encountering stress or the prospect of emotional intimacy. Historically, under conventional attachment theory frameworks, the avoidant attachment style is thought to emerge from a pattern of neglect or rejection from caregivers in response to a child’s needs, leading the child to believe they must handle their difficulties themselves in order to maintain a relationship.

wiki/axiom.title: Axiom
wiki/axiom.content:
Overview
An axiom is a proposition that serves as a starting premise for a line of reasoning or argumentation.
Commentary
Kurt Godel’s Incompleteness Theorem is thrown around a lot in lay debate contexts, which I myself am guilty of, and I don’t have strong foundations in the philosophy of math to comment too heavily on it, but the high-level consequences of it are very relevant to the limitations of logical reasoning.
In short, Godel proved that a formal system cannot prove its own consistency, so any set of axioms we propose as a logical system cannot end up proving its own validity. At some point, we are forced to rely on some concept akin to intuition or faith in order to arrive at our axioms from which we can then construct a system that we vet for consistency and completeness. I found this revelation to be impactful on a personal level.
Rebecca Goldstein, a philosopher who wrote the biography Incompleteness: The Proof and Paradox of Kurt Godel, noted that Godel himself hated a mechanistic view of the world that distilled everything into rational algorithmic processes. Human intuition was often approached as either random noise or an evolutionary development, stemming from a combination of genetic predispositions and environmental conditioning to approximate rationality. My own background skews heavily towards the computations of intelligence; to me, this intuition is fundamentally what separates a machine from a sentient organism. A computer can only detect the logical blind spots that its programmed axioms permit it to explore, whereas a human can use intuition to detect a failing in logic even before they can articulate the logical proof or rationale for exploring it.
Alan Watts, a philosopher who occupies a space in popular counter-cultural movements that sought to reconcile New Age spiritual mysticism with Western scientific revelations, has frequently invoked and consequently popularized Godel’s Incompleteness Theorem in public discourse. Watts criticizes the “Western” impulse to “define and conquer” the world by placing new concepts within the bounds of a familiar hyperrationalist system that neutralizes intuition, mysticism, and subjective expression as immeasurable byproducts of a messy organic brain. I’ve made many of the same criticisms myself. It leads to reductionism that deflates the nuances of new ideas.
For instance, Western cultures are highly predicated on the moral-psychology of Abrahamic religions that affirm strong dualistic binaries, such as Heaven against Hell, sacred against profane, good against evil, etc. When we examine Eastern belief systems like those of Hindu sects through this lens, the notion of devas and asuras collapses into “angels” and “demons,” which is radically different. Within Hindu cosmology, devas and asuras are born of the same father and different mothers, with the former representing a transcendental presence of harmony through unity and the latter representing a materialist presence of chaos through division. The moral-psychology of sorting the world into good and bad is itself an ideology associated with the asuras. Yet, both are required to continue the motion of the cycles that sustain the universe as it exists.
In axiomatic terms, Abrahamic moral-psychology posits the existence of a definite good and definite evil locked in a moral war. Hindu moral-psychology posits order and chaos as inherent parts of the universe and the self, such that destruction of the agents of chaos is a destruction of the self, so self-discipline and evolution are necessary to navigate these conflicting forces. The goal is not thus to kill off one’s ego the way one would want to kill off the compulsion to “sin,” but to understand the ego’s purpose in driving one’s actions while ensuring it adheres to a higher purpose than its own satisfaction. This sounds abstract, but it directly influences how we see concepts like punishment, justice, retribution, change, repression, and other threads that compose our daily moral fabrics.

wiki/ayn-rand.title: Ayn Rand
wiki/ayn-rand.content: Ayn Rand is technically a writer, so I guess she belongs here.

wiki/bad-boys.title: Bad Boys
wiki/bad-boys.content:
Overview
Bad Boys is a 1995 buddy-cop action-comedy film that features Will Smith as a cop who routinely breaks the law in the process of enforcing it while pursuing violent criminals and drug dealers, following the theft of $100 million worth of heroin from the police department’s evidence lockers.
Commentary
Copaganda
The heroin is a MacGuffin to give our protagonists an excuse to play the role of aggressive, sarcastic cops who flout the rules and norms in the name of the greater good. Crime entertainment from the 1990s framed drug enforcement as a heroic, masculine role whose aggression and violence are an inevitable result of fighting the dangers of organized crime in the drug trade. Those who lie to conceal their connection to the drug use or the drug trade are built up as villainous thugs while the cops who lie are just getting into wacky shenanigans as a result of their human flaws. To quote one of the punchlines as a witness in protection is handcuffed to a steering wheel inside a car: “Is this even legal? I don’t think this is legal.” Meanwhile, the drug dealers that the cops investigate are literally set up at a place called Club Hell. “Bad Boys” is meant to have a kind of charming rogueishness to it, like “Mad Men.”
Glamorizing
The movie has been accused of glamorizing the nightlife associated with drugs through aesthetics that involve flashy displays of wealth, gloss and glamour, and a reference to sexual thrills or taboos. Michael Bay is known for including these aesthetics in the films he directs. However, there are plenty of grimy environments that the movie shows as well, especially around manufacturing and low-level distribution. If anything, the main lifestyle glamorized is that of Will Smith’s character Mike Lowrey, who lives the life of a wealthy bachelor thanks to his inheritance. His partner Marcus Burnett, a family man with three kids who feels dissatisfied with his sex life in his marriage, is regularly jealous of Lowrey. The drug dealers are depicted in a range between stereotypical bosses in suits and low-level informants who still work physical jobs, absent of any “rags-to-riches” storyline or “thieves with honor” characters.
Black Masculinity
One of the reasons that the buddy-cop formula is popular is because it naturally forces confrontations between two people who represent a dynamic of opposing pairs yet have to protect each other in dangerous situations. Sometimes that means a good cop/bad cop pairing to present a carrot/stick approach and how the state needs to use both in the process of law enforcement.
In this case, Lowrey and Burnett are both the stick who abuse their authority and disregard norms, but since the aggression is constantly leading to banter and slapstick comedy that furthers the plot, it becomes entertaining rather than threatening to an audience imagining this world. The contrast between Lowrey as a privileged bachelor and Burnett as a working family man give two different but valid representations of masculinity in black men, who are even accepted for their rule-breaking violence by a system of law enforcement so long as it furthers the agenda of apprehending criminals. It’s also noteworthy that the main leader of the cartel is a wealthy European, Fouchet, which means that the strength of these black men is directed towards foreigners rather than a domestic system of crime or racialized politics around US drug policing.
In sum, the film signals that black men can retain their masculinity while navigating different lifestyles and roles in society, and even indulge in the excesses of toxic masculinity that lead to violence and abuse of power, so long as their actions ultimately align with the greater good of taking down the villains of the state. Specifically these include international organized crime syndicates whose operations reach the lowest level of working Joe looking for a quick and dirty side hustle. Various scholars who study the evolution of black archetypes in comedy, which includes the infamous Jim Crow, have examined the buddy-cop formula in the 1980s and 1990s as a way for black celebrities to play vigilante-like roles that superficially break ordinary norms while serving the main interests of a criminal justice system built on politics from the War on Drugs. Ed Guerrero has described this pattern of adopting the aesthetics of violent black resistance to vigilante or anti-hero policing as “contain and commodify.”

wiki/bad-habits-drinking-smoking-taking-.title: Bad Habits - Drinking, Smoking, Taking Drugs, Gambling, Sexual Misbehavior, and Swearing in American History by John Chynoweth Burnham (1992)

wiki/barbara-ehrenreich.title: Barbara Ehrenreich
wiki/barbara-ehrenreich.content:
Favorite Quotes
“Breast cancer, I can now report, did not make me prettier or stronger, more feminine or spiritual. What it gave me, if you want to call this a ‘gift,’ was a very personal, agonizing encounter with an ideological force in American culture that I had not been aware of before- one that encourages us to deny reality, submit cheerfully to misfortune, and blame only ourselves for our fate.”
I can now report, the institutions of recovery and mental health function the same way.
“The question is why one should be so inwardly preoccupied at all. Why not reach out to others in love and solidarity or peer into the natural world for some glimmer of understanding? Why retreat into anxious introspection when, as Emerson might have said, there is a vast world outside to explore? Why spend so much time working on oneself when there is so much real work to be done?”
I’m a huge fan of Barbara Ehrenreich. Although she doesn’t explicitly spell this out, her work is a robust argument for a perspective about the self that resonates more with me, perhaps through an indirect connection with “Eastern” thought.
Ralph Waldo Emerson and other American transcendentalists, oft-described as the nation’s first homegrown philosophical movement, drew heavily on romantic appropriation of “Oriental” cultures. It was, and arguably remains, a common fashion in the West to project onto the East the qualities it considers foreign to itself. The materialist industrialist West moves forward through rationality and individualism; the spiritual nature-centric East preserves the past through tradition and collectivism. His reworkings of Eastern concepts inspired those like Helena Blavatsky and the Theosophical Society, who was among the first to popularize the concept of a superior Aryan race meant to hegemonize the world, and you can figure out what that inspired in the first half of the 1900s on your own.
Despite his hierarchical views about Western supremacy, Emerson did manage to capture a genuine notion of the self that still feels foreign to America through a succinct metaphor: the transparent eyeball. Seeing everything while occupying nothing. Free oneself to explore freely.
Emerson certainly encouraged people to lean on their own potential rather than seeking the instruction or refuge of institutions that would inevitably corrupt the individual with systemic prerogatives. But the outcome of such an endeavor would be to then experience the universe through this newly freed self, not obsess over the self as if it were the sole determinant of reality. The intention was to facilitate liberative action through disconnecting the self from the machines of society, not disconnecting the self from reality to preserve a bubble of self-care routines or happiness rituals. As he said:
“Action is with the scholar subordinate, but it is essential. Without it he is not yet man. Without it thought can never ripen into truth.”
Henry David Thoreau, a friend of Emerson, did exactly that. He moved to a cabin he built and minimized his demands of the world to his basic needs. He acted, and he built a new life away from society where he achieved an intellectual and spiritual freedom he could not find within the rat-race facilitated by institutions. Thoreau believed that you have a moral obligation to actively break unjust laws as “friction to stop the machine.”
In no way can Emerson or Thoreau be said to have withdrawn from the external world into themselves to cultivate positive thinking. Instead, they took radical responsibility for their engagement with the world to free themselves from the control of institutional standards. Changing the individual was supposed to lead to changes in the environment around individual. That’s aligned very well with the takeaway I have from the Gita. Everyone has a role to play in the universe, and you have to discover what that is for yourself, or you might die realizing you never lived.
It is with this consideration that Barbara Ehrenreich critiques the modern happiness industry by invoking Emerson’s name. By turning the ideas behind liberation from social standards into commodified self-help and spiritual guides that becomes the new social standards, the movement defeats itself while turning a pretty penny for any guru who finds their niche of miserable people to shepherd through shallow material befitting an AI chatbot.
Ehrenreich has far surpassed both Emerson and Thoreau in both action and thought, at least to me.
“Like a perpetually flashing neon sign in the background, like an inescapable jingle, the injunction to be positive is so ubiquitous that it’s impossible to identify a single source. Oprah routinely trumpets the triumph of attitude over circumstance… you’ll find a smorgasboard of workshops on how to succeed in life by overcoming pessimism, accessing your inner powers, and harnessing the power of thought.”
“A whole coaching industry has grown up since the mid-1990s, heavily marketed on the Internet, to help people improve their attitudes and hence, supposedly, their lives. For a fee on a par with what a therapist might receive, an unlicensed career or life coach help you defeat the ‘negative self-talk’ - that is, pessimistic thoughts - that impedes your progress… It has its ideologues, spokespeople, preachers, and salespersons - authors of self-help books, motivational speakers, coaches, and trainers… It was New Age meets middle-American business culture.”
Those familiar with my attitude towards The Four Agreements have likely heard me point out that the book was popularized by Ellen and Oprah. It is an insane book that says things like no one can abuse you more than you abuse yourself, so it’s really your fault for agreeing to lower your self-worth into accepting abuse. It is a masterpiece in blurring the lines between empowerment and blame.
That aside, the last sentence in that excerpt is almost exactly what I’ve said before. The contemporary American spiritual wellness movement seems to be some intersection of New Age appropriation of colonized cultures and outdated pseudopsychology embedded in the collective consciousness of institutional managers. If I had to distill our challenges with institutions into a single problem statement, it would be that institutions change their environment faster than they can change themselves. The arrogance of individuality in assuming that a system can be circumvented or ignored, whether by an anarchist outsider or a sufficiently Great Man as a leader, with the proper cultivation of inner traits is fatal. It is, literally, a superhero fantasy.
I suppose that’s the point, isn’t it? In a world where no one is coming to save you, be your own superhero. All it takes is buying a book or doing a course or hiring a coach, all of which give some variation of the advice “don’t do the thing associated with negative moods, and do the thing associated with positive moods, like spending less time watching the news and more time in nature.” In other words, despite living in a liberal democracy that was explicitly predicated on having an enlightened citizenry that would compete through debates in a marketplace of ideas, we are never to look at actually using those mechanisms to produce systemic changes. As Ehrenreich says,
“This retreat from the real drama and tragedy of human events is suggestive of a deep helplessness at the core of positive thinking. Why not follow the news? Because, as my informant at the NSA meeting told me, ‘You can’t do anything about it…’ The possibilities of contributing to relief funds, joining an antiwar movement, or lobbying for more humane government policies are not even considered. But at the very least there seems to be an acknowledgement here that no amount of attitude adjustment can make good news out of headlines beginning with ‘Civilian casualties mount…’ or ‘Famine spreads…‘”
One thing I appreciate about AA is that it wears its philosophy on its sleeve. It commits to the notion that the individual is powerless to facilitate a surrender to a Higher Power which, for all intents and purposes, is based on the Protestant concept of God. The thesis behind suffering is that the individual’s self-will has run riot and produced an unmanageable life, so only by seeking something outside of oneself for an alternative will can one find an anchor point of sanity. This is actually a far more coherent perspective than the positive thinking that becomes magical thinking, because at least God or a Higher Power is a mechanism through which meditation and prayer can lead to observable changes in the world. You can call AA a cult if you want, and I do call it religious rather than spiritual, but it’s the easiest cult in the world to leave if you don’t like it.
The happiness industry around positive thinking has no such coherence, and in fact invites you to be the God of your own life. The Four Agreements, a text referenced in psychoeducation classes in treatment centers that insurance companies pay for, says this explicitly. You’re God, I’m God, all things are God, and you have complete control of the reality that is your life once you awaken to the dream you’re in. It’s a book that makes a claim, and I’m not exaggerating in any way here, that if you tell someone their face looks like one belonging to someone with cancer, they will develop cancer within a year. It is a book that takes every critique made of the happiness industry’s absurd reliance on the power of willpower and responds with “Yes.” The entire first chapter of this book is a scathing rebuttal of such flippant claims made by New Age profit-seekers as we see Ehrenreich’s firsthand experience with breast cancer and the attitude cures. Much less a negative attitude, she suspects that years of hormone treatments at the recommendations of previous professionals increased her risk of developing cancer.
A rather heartbreaking account in the book comes from a woman writing to Deepak Chopra, who positively reviewed The Four Agreements since they used the same New Age publisher:
“Even though I follow the treatments, have come a long way in unburdening myself of toxic feelings, have forgiven everyone, changed my lifestyle to include meditation, prayer, proper diet, exercise, and supplements, the cancer keeps coming back. Am I missing a lesson here that it keeps reoccurring? I am positive that I am going to beat it, yet it does get harder with each diagnosis to keep a positive attitude.”
Chopra replies,
“As far as I can tell, you are doing all the right things to recover. You just have to continue doing them until the cancer is gone for good. I know it is discouraging to make great progress only to have it come back again, but sometimes cancer is simply very pernicious and requires the utmost diligence and persistence to eventually overcome it.”
I have a hard time not immediately thinking of televangelists and YouTube gurus who solicit money in exchange for reassurance from desperate and lost people. That money could go towards actual treatments, improving their quality of life, or simply savings for their family to use. Any of those sound better than the false hope of magical thinking disguised as a trajectory of positive thinking. And because you can’t measure a positive attitude or negative vibes, the whole theory of positive thinking is unfalsifiable:
“without question there is a problem when positive thinking ‘fails’ and the cancer spreads or eludes treatment. Then the patient can only blame herself: she is not being positive enough; possible it was her negative attitude that brought on the disease in the first place. At this point, the exhortation to think positively is ‘an additional burden to an already devastated patient,’ as an oncology nurse Cynthia Rittenburg has written.”
If you replace “cancer” with “addiction”, “depression”, or “cravings,” you get a very close approximation of the core of the American recovery philosophy. Suffering is not a condition produced relationally between an individual misaligned with an environment, but instead a dysfunction of the individual that is somewhere between personal ignorance, irrationality, and immorality. To have ended up in a position to suffer, one must have one of these vices. To escape suffering, one must remedy these vices and see their illness as some type of opportunity for an awakening. In doing so, those in suffering suffer again from these standards, whether imposed or internalized.
It’s not Just Injustice
“Clearly, the failure to think positively can weigh on a cancer patient like a second disease. I, at least, was saved from this additional burden by my persistent anger.”
Fun fact, studies show that witnessing unfair behavior actively raises our stress levels with measurable heart rate spikes, even when they don’t happen to us. Sharing it with other people, or gossipping if you want to be righteous about it, actually lowers our stress. We are built to observe something like injustice, be angry about it, and try to change it.
For America, it’s been two and a half centuries since it won independence. It’s been about eight decades since it became a world superpower and over a century since it’s been the largest economic in the world. American history talks of “The Civil Rights Movement” as a singular wave across the 1950s and 1960s that restored civil rights. The optimists thought 2008 proved America was mostly over racism by electing a black President, and 2015 showed through the legalization of gay marriage that only the most marginal groups were left out of the umbrella of egalitarianism. A reality check is sorely needed.
South Sudan was recognized as an independent state in 2011. From 1955 to 2026, only 27 years have not involved a major civil war.
Timor-Leste became an independent sovereign nation in 2002, though it wasn’t until 2012 that the United Nations ended its peacekeeping mission to facilitate democratic elections amidst refugee crises affecting hundreds of thousands of people.
Croatia, Bosnia, and Slovenia fought wars to maintain independence amidst widespread ethnic conflicts from 1991-1995 in what we call the Yugoslav Wars. Notably, Melania Trump and Luka Doncic are from Slovenia.
South Africa had its first fully democratic elections open to all races in 1994, leading to the election of Nelson Mandela and marking a pivot from apartheid policies.
Eritrea won independence in 1991 after a 30-year war with Ethiopia. Namibia, 1990 after a guerilla conflict with South Africa’s apartheid regime.
Bangladesh seceded from Pakistan in 1971, which became an international conflict involving India.
Zimbabwe underwent The Rhodesian Civil War from 1964 to 1979 as a conflict that ended white minority rule and implemented universal sufferage, with independent sovereignty established in 1980.
I’ll draw on my own heritage here.
India celebrates 1947 as the year of independence because that’s when the British decided to leave. That’s not when the French and Portuguese decided to leave though. In 1954, local Indian socialist and nationalist groups launched a violent uprising against the French encalve on the Malabar Coast. The French administrators were physically driven out ahead of an official treaty to surrender the territory. The Portuguese in Goa, which had occupied India for 451 years, was expelled within 36 hours of a 1961 military operation, after years of attempts to negotiate diplomatically and unarmed protests that were met with fatal violence. My grandparents were alive to see that. Portugal did not acknowledge the sovereignty of India until 1974, which was after my parents were born.
So, you can hopefully understand how viscerally upsetting this happiness industry is to me when it carves up our traditions into commodities for Western institutions on the receiving end of historic exploitation without reparations. The aesthetics are all too easy to adopt: vague notions of aligining yourself with the vibrations of the universe through breathing exercises, planting positive intentions for karmic appraisal, detachment from the environment coupled to increasing attachment to the ego, rearranging furniture to balance your chakras, go on a walk through nature while thanking the sun and the trees, lighting incense while making herbal teas for a lunch break, so on and so forth.
It is within the living memory of my family that things do not get better until you roll up your sleeves to lock arms in a covenant of collective action. I cannot imagine a single piece of advice from this industry I’ve heard that could be useful to anyone who has answered the human call to be angry about injustice. After all, Reinhold Niehbur, author of the Serenity Prayer, was a pro-union socialist who believed that ruling classes must be forced to concede power as they would never do so of their own volition.

wiki/barbiturate.title: Barbiturate
wiki/barbiturate.content:
Overview
Barbitutares are a class of nervous system depressants that have a sedative-hypnotic effect inducing relaxation and drowsiness. They were commonly used in the past to address anxiety disorders and insomnia but have since been replaced with safer alternatives like benzodiazepines. Barbiturates are considered to have a high risk of addiction, severe withdrawal if stopped suddenly, and overdose. Phenobarbital is the example that’s usually most familiar to people as a medication to address seizures. Pentobarbital is sometimes used in veterinary medicine.

wiki/barry-seal.title: Barry Seal
wiki/barry-seal.content:
Overview
Barry Seal was an American airline pilot who smuggled drugs for the Medellin Cartel until he became an informant for the United States Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA).

wiki/bath-salts.title: Bath Salts
wiki/bath-salts.content:
Overview
“Bath salts” actually have nothing to do with baths. They refer to a class of stimulants called synthetic cathinones derived from the khat shrub that grows in East Africa and southern Arabia. Manfacturers that were intending to evade drug enforcement laws disingenuously marketed their products as “bath salts” so that they could argue they were never intended for consumption. Some cathinones have been approved as medication, such as bupropion which you might recognize as Wellbutrin, which can treat Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) and nicotine cravings. Ongoing research is attempting to see if bupropion can address stimulant use disorder too.

wiki/bayer-corporation.content: In 1898, the company manufactured and distributed heroin commercially as a safe alternative to morphine.

wiki/bed-sores.title: Bed Sores
wiki/bed-sores.content:
Overview
Bed sores are injuries to the skin and underlying tissue that result from being stationary in a single position for a long period of time. The constant weight applied to a single area can constrict blood flow, and certain postures can lead to skin and bones being slid in opposite directions. In extreme cases, it can lead to deep sores and wounds that expose muscle, tendons, and/or bone. This can be seen in some people with substance use disorders as heavy intoxication or compulsive processes like gaming lead to fixed positions for hours or even days. Other conditions like severe depressive withdrawal can also lead to someone lying in bed for similar lengths of time. Malnutrition and substances that constrict blood vessels can increase the risk of developing sores as well.

wiki/bedside-manner.title: Bedside Manner
wiki/bedside-manner.content:
Overview
“Bedside manner” refers to empathetic communication skills that clinicians exercise to build trust with patients. Historically, the stigma around substance use disorders has led to an assumption that punitive measures must be taken to correct someone’s behavior. Recent studies show that labeling substance use as “substance abuse” is still associated with less empathy and more punitive attitudes in a clinical setting. Despite what the latest research has shown, a prevalent prejudice is that pain and suffering are just par for substance use and even a component of successful recovery. This can be completely counterproductive as people with substance use disorders and co-occurring conditions face enormous stigma that discourages seeking treatment or efforts to recover. Patients fearing stigma can underreport symptoms or avoid seeking care out of fear of judgment or punitive medical practices.

wiki/behavioral-activation.title: Behavioral Activation
wiki/behavioral-activation.content:
Overview
Behavioral Activation (BA) is an approach to addressing depression that considers it a response to an environment that lacks positive reinforcement through meaningful rewards and remedies it by building a plan to engage in behaviors that would naturally lift one’s mood.
Under a radical behaviorist perspective, depression is the result of an initial drop in mood and motivation that spirals into a cycle of withdrawing from pleasurable activities and experiencing worsening moods and motivation levels. Eventually, chronic neuroinflammation and the products of stress hormones like cortisol blunt dopamine signaling pathways in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and nucleus accumbens. When someone attempts to perform an activity that once brought them pleasure, the brain realizes that it took effort to attempt an activity that underdelivered on the expected dopamine spike. This reward prediction error is then associated with the memory of the activity, and over time, someone might be reasonably convinced that there’s no point to spending an already-diminished level of energy on something that has repeatedly failed to feel rewarding. This also leads to a drop in Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor (BDNF), a protein that drives neuroplasticity, so the neural pathways in the brain’s hippocampus and prefrontal cortex being to atrophy. These are distinct physical changes in the brain that make it more rigid and difficult to change thought and behavioral patterns.
The goal of BA is to get the brain’s reward mechanisms to reactivate by scheduling activities that would ordinarily be rewarding even when the motivation to act is lacking. This outside-in approach attempts to stimulate the production of BDNF by structuring small tasks in one’s life that are easily completed with minimal effort while still engaging the body physically in ways that reduce inflammation and force the brain to parse sensory rewards. With an increase in BDNF comes an increase in neuroplasticity, which allows pleasure and reward pathways in the brain to be rebuilt.
Note that this is not the same as saying “do pleasurable things” to someone whose brain is struggling to experience pleasure. Cliches from toxic positivity circles about simply persevering through uncomfortable states of mind or feelings through willpower are not justified with this explanation. The core elements of a successful BA intervention include incrementally replacing avoidance patterns with alternative coping mechanisms that are aligned with one’s long-term values and substantial accomplishments that reduce chronic stress, not just impulsive pleasure-seeking. Hedonism is not a solution to the problem of anhedonia.
For instance, someone with depression may have a messy house. Rather than simply telling them to clean their house so they can feel the pleasure of a tidier and less stressful space, a clinician or therapist might first frame the project as aligned with their values of having an organized environment to operate in and then break it down into steps over a period of time, with regular calibration based on the individual’s capacities. The first level might be as basic as folding a handful of clothes from a laundry pile on a room’s chair, allowing the use of the chair again. The second level, scheduled for the next day, might involve putting all the dirty clothes on the floor into a laundry hamper and experiencing the convenience of walking around without trudging through them. The third level might involve doing dirty dishes that allows someone to eat with clean silverware and plates.
Studies have shown that BA is just as effective at addressing the symptoms of depression as Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (CBT) that incorporates BA into a larger paradigm of combing through thought patterns for distortions and opportunities to reframe a mental schema towards different outcomes. In other words, directly addressing irrational or unhelpful thinking patterns may not actually do much to improve symptoms of conditions like depression.
Contingency Management (CM) is a behavioral intervention for substance use disorders that is heavily rooted in similar ideas as BA about retraining the brain’s decision-making and thought patterns through direct rewards rather than first challenging one’s mental frameworks.
Commentary
I’m a fan of behaviorist interventions, not necessarily because I think cognitive or psychodynamic approaches are inherently ineffective or harmful, but because any institutional implementation of a modality that privileges a professional as the ultimate determinant of a client’s successful participation is subject to a plethora of biases, prejudices, misinterpretations, and miscommunications that can significantly impact the fidelity of treatment. BA and CM track outcomes that are far easier to measure, like a binary evaluation of the completion of a task, and minimize the role of the professional in interpreting a client’s cognitive state compared to symptoms of depression.

wiki/behavioral-and-substance-addiction-.title: Behavioral & Substance Addiction Clinic
wiki/behavioral-and-substance-addiction-.content:
Overview
The University of Chicago Medicine Behavioral & Substance Addiction Clinic operates under the Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Neuroscience as a clinical recovery program. Their offerings include confidential screenings, medication-assisted therapy (MAT), managing co-occurring conditions like depression and anxiety, and individual and group therapy sessions often rooted in Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (CBT).

wiki/behavioral-economics.title: Behavioral Economics
wiki/behavioral-economics.content:
Overview
“Behavioral economics” is a field that incorporates psychology into economic theories and models instead of assuming humans are purely rational actors. It accepts as a constraint the fact that humans have limited time, information, and resources to make decisions, so they often settle for what seems “good enough” rather than finding the optimal choice. Even when we try to optimize, we might arrive at a “good enough” assumption of the optimal path. We also have a litany of biases at work, such as loss aversion that treats negative experiences as more impactful than positive ones or cognitive shortcuts like stereotypes.
Addiction has posed a big challenge for traditional economics since it cannot possibly seem rational to acknowledge that a substance or process could ruin your life and present no long-term gains but choose it anyways. Behavioral economics attempts to model addiction through additional concepts, such as delay discounting that argues people weigh immediate rewards heavily over future ones. The immediate physical relief that a substance or process provides is heavily favored over the abstract delayed benefits of sustained sobriety. Another useful concept is bounded self-control which describes the limits people have to resist temptations as stress, fatigue, and external pressures can wear down their decision to abstain.
At the same time, some really impactful treatment designs have come out of the emphasis on behavioral interventions. Behavioral Activation (BA) is one of the most effective ways to help people not just struggling with substance use disorders but depression as well, and it begins by guiding patients into making small but achievable steps towards establishing a positive reinforcement cycle from pleasurable and sober choices. Contingency Management (CM) is one of my favorite concepts for addressing addiction as it simply provides an immediate tangible reward for clean drug tests and participation in treatment, which appeals to the same bias for short-term rewards that substances provide.
Both BA and CM show either comparable or higher effectiveness to cognitive therapies that locate the sources of a patient’s distress within their worldview rather than the incentives in their actual world. In fact, some studies show that trying to combine Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (CBT) with CM actually leads to worse outcomes, splitting the patient’s focus between cognitive self-assessments and the behavioral rewards that might change cognition. It helps to see CM as a competing economy or choice framework to a patient’s previous framework that made substance or process use seem compelling, which is especially helpful for people whose material problems cannot be reduced to cognitive distortions. “I won’t have enough money to afford food” is addressed immediately when a CM reward provides a grocery voucher while CBT negotiates it as “catastrophizing” or “future-tripping” that can be addressed with coping skills until things somehow work out.

wiki/behavioral-neurology.title: Behavioral Neurology
wiki/behavioral-neurology.content:
Overview
Behavioral neurology is a field concerned with the impacts of physical brain changes on memory, thinking patterns, emotional processing, and external behavior. Dementias like Alzheimer’s disease are among the most common conditions addressed by behavioral neurologists, though they deal with all kinds of incidents ranging from strokes to traumatic brain injuries (TBIs) to diseases responsible for sudden personality changes.
The behavioral neurological perspective on addiction concieves it as a chronic brain disorder resulting from structural changes in neural circuits as a result of prolonged substance or process use. Compulsive behaviors emerge as a result of changes in the pathways that govern reward, memory, and self-control. When using a substance, the ventral tegmental area and nucleus accumbens are flooded with dopamine.

wiki/behaviorism.title: Behaviorism
wiki/behaviorism.content:
Overview
“Behaviorism” within psychological circles generally refers to an approach to understanding humans through an examination of their behavioral outcomes.
For empiricists who embrace behaviorist perspectives, assessing a state of mind is impossible except for the end results that can be empirically observed. If someone says they hate ice cream but eats it every day, there is nothing we can conclude about their beliefs that differs from someone who says they love ice cream and eats it everyday. B.F. Skinner is perhaps the most famous foundational behaviorist, who described his philosophy as “radical behaviorism.” Staunch behaviorists might be entirely uninterested in neuroscienctific and psychological models, or see them as theoretical exercises comparable to fictional worldbuilding where a system of logic is clearly at work but only applicable to the real-wold insofar as it is observed. Others might acknowledge them as useful for explaining the mechanisms through which behavior occurs, but not a useful way to explore the independent sources of behavior.
Cognitive scientists and neuroscientists usually reject radical behaviorism, arguing that treating humans like black boxes won’t provide a complete enough explanation to model our attitudes and actions. Humans generally seek explanations preceding behavioral change that work with our mental model of reality.
Commentary
I’m a big fan of behavioral interventions like Contingency Management (CM) and Behavioral Activation (BA), and I’ve expressed criticism of cognitive therapies, but I wouldn’t classify my thoughts as anything resembling radical behaviorism. I really enjoy exploring psychological and neurological models, not just for the sake of intellectual completeness but also because I find it intuitively uncomfortable to treat our internal worlds as black boxes.

wiki/bender.content:
Overview
“Bender” is colloquially used to refer to an extended period of substance use in which someone is almost perpetually under the influence. For chronic substance users, benders can last from days to weeks to months.

wiki/benjamin-rush.title: Benjamin Rush
wiki/benjamin-rush.content:
No Rush to Judgment
Benjamin Rush is one of those influential people who happened to be around a bunch of famous and influential people, so he fades into the background easily but also pops up a lot once you start noticing him.
He attended Princeton University and the University of Edinburgh. He later taught at the University of Pennsylvania as a professor of chemistry and published one of the first American textbooks on chemistry. He signed the Declaration of Independence and was at Pennsylvania’s Constitutional Convention, briefly serving as a surgeon-general for the Continental Army during the Revolutionary War. Thomas Paine, John Adams, Thomas Jefferson, Benjamin Franklin, and a littany of physicians and chemists ran in the same influential circles as Rush. We have access to a lot of his correspondence that we can look at when examining medicine in the colonial and post-independence era. He taught both future-President William Henry Harrison and Meriwether Lewis of the (in)famous Lewis & Clarke expedition at the instructions of President Jefferson.
Rush was active in social justice in a way that shows decency was always possible, regardless of the time period and social norms. He strongly opposed slavery as “so foreign to the human mind, that the moral faculties, as well as those of the understanding are debased, and rendered torpid by it.” He thought there was no reasonable interpretation of scientific evidence that would suggest there was any natural inferiority by race, though he also thought being black was a hereditary yet curable skin disease after meeting someone with vitiligo, which warranted policies against interracial mixing. On criminal justice, he opposed public punishments, solitary confinement, slavery or forced labor, and the death penalty. Although he had prejudices against women learning advanced sciences, he proposed education plans for the women of wealthier families and helped found one of the first higher education institutions for women in America. He set up a medicinal dispensary for the poorest workers and advised various public health projects that led to a reduction in disease outbreaks. While he did subscribe to the notion that indigenous nations were “primitive” rather than “civilized,” he took a genuine interest in health disparities between indigenous nations and colonial settlers.

wiki/benzedrine.title: Benzedrine
wiki/benzedrine.content:
Overview
Benzedrine was the brand name for the first commercially successful synthetic stimulant in the world.
History
In 1927, Gordon Alles injected himself with a synthetic amphetamine in the course of investigating an alternative to ephedrine to address asthma. He published clinical results in 1929 and was granted a U.S. patent for oral amphetamine salts by 1932. The same year, the pharmaceutical company Smith, Kline, & French (SKF) patented a volatile base form of the same chemical before launching an over-the-counter (OTC) version called a Benzedrine Inhaler. In 1935, SKF purchased Alles’s patent and monopolized the manufacturing and distribution of Benzedrine. They released Benzedrine Sulfate as tablets to address depression, narcolepsy, fatigue, and weight loss. The Allies in WWII experimented with Benzedrine rations as a tool to boost the endurance of their soldiers.
In 1951, the United States Congress passed the Durham-Humphrey Amendment which made Benzedrine tablets prescription-only, although the inhalers were still available OTC. Recreational users would open the inhalers to swallow the internal strips, which contained the equivalent of the dosage of dozens of tablets. Jack Kerouac (in)famously relied on Benzedrine and coffee for a three-week nonstop writing marathon to complete his novel On the Road, a stream-of-consciousness inspired by his road trips printed onto a 120-foot long scroll. The Beat Generation cultural movement adopted Benzedrine and amphetamines generally to invoke these altered states of mind.
Unfortunately, amphetamines were quite destructive to the body, and after observing a spike in cardiovascular events related to usage of the Benzedrine inhaler, the FDA banned it in 1965. After Congress passed the Comprehensive Drug Abuse Prevention and Control Act of 1970, the Bureau of Narcotics and Dangerous Drugs classified all amphetamines as Schedule II controlled substances, which took it out of recreational usage and firmly into the territory of regulated prescription substances. Benzedrine is no longer manufactured today as the brand name drug, but the generic active ingredient amphetamine sulfate are still used in medications to address ADHD, narcolepsy, and obesity. Adderall is probably the most commonly known modern variant of it.
Benzedrine should not be confused with Benzedrex, which are nasal decongestant inhalers that are far less likely to be used dangerously for recreational purposes.

wiki/benzodiazepines.title: Benzodiazepines
wiki/benzodiazepines.content:
Overview
Benzodiazepines (benzos) are a class of sedative-hypnotic central nervous system (CNS) depressants. Depending on the variation and its half-life, it might be used for medical sedation, insomnia, panic attacks, chronic anxiety, seizure, and alcohol detoxification. They work by attaching to GABA receptors and make them more sensitive, with GABA as the brain’s primary calming neurotransmitter.
Benzos and alcohol are the two substances known for particularly dangerous withdrawals that can be life-threatening. I am not a doctor and nothing I say is medical advice, but you really should not attempt to quit either of those cold turkey on your own. Seeking medical professionals for assistance in managing withdrawals is not just potentially life-saving but a massively more comfortable way to process the hellish symptoms of them.

wiki/betel-nut.title: Betel Nut
wiki/betel-nut.content:
Overview
Betel nuts are seeds of a palm tree species called Areca catechu that are chewed as a recreational stimulant. It’s the fourth most commonly used substance associated with addiction in the world after alcohol, nicotine, and caffeine. That might be surprising to many in cultures driven by Western trends, but it’s used with relative regularity in South Asian nations and the Pacific islands, particularly for special occasions and local traditions. The market for it is localized and decentralized unlike tobacco, which has massive multinational conglomerates lobbying against regulations.
The World Health Organization (WHO) categorizes betel nuts, through the alkaloid called arecoline, as a Group 1 carcinogen right next to alcohol and tobacco. It’s a leading cause of oral and esophageal cancers among other health issues like tooth decay and painful stiffness in the jaw. The United States outright bans the importation of betel nuts.

wiki/bf-skinner.title: B.F. Skinner
wiki/bf-skinner.content: When Milton’s Satan falls from heaven, he ends in hell. And what does he say to reassure himself? ‘Here, at least, we shall be free.’ And that, I think, is the fate of the old-fashioned liberal. He’s going to be free, but he’s going to find himself in hell.

wiki/big-tobacco.title: Big Tobacco
wiki/big-tobacco.content:
Overview
“Big Tobacco” is a term for the largest companies from the tobacco industry: Philip Morris International (PMI), British American Tobacco (BAT), Japan Tobacco International (JTI), Imperial Brands, China Tobacco, and Altria Group.
Big Tobacco is known for funding a variety of groups that sound harmless or benevolent at a superficial level, like the Global Action to End Smoking (GAES) organization funded by PMI who neither the World Health Organization nor major universities will work with because of their conflicts of interest. Despite sounding like the group wants to end smoking, they actually promote alternatives to traditional cigarettes, like e-cigarettes which the company also happens to sell. They argue that doing so is harm reduction, which is arguably true, but it’s still motivated by selling addictive substances for profit.

wiki/bigotry-of-low-expectations.title: Bigotry of Low Expectations
wiki/bigotry-of-low-expectations.content:
Overview
The “bigotry of low expectations” is an oft-repeated phrase that argues that having different expectations for minority groups who have been historically discriminated against is itself a form of discrimination that assumes they are bound to perform worse than their peers. It’s heavily politically charged, with many arguing that it’s used in bad faith against diversity initiatives that factor the skills developed under socioeconomic hardship into someone’s evaluation.

wiki/binge-drinking.title: Binge Drinking
wiki/binge-drinking.content:
Overview
Binge drinking is used casually to refer to a period of heavy drinking, but the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) defines it specifically as drinking enough alcohol to raise blood alcohol concentration (BAC) to 0.08% or higher. That’s also the standard legal limit for driving in the United States. For the average person, this means consuming 4-5 standard drinks in the span of roughly two hours. Anecdotally, a lot of people I’ve met who actively drink overestimate the amount needed before it’s considered binge drinking, or only use the term “binge drinking” in the context of “problem drinking” rather than the “weekend warrior” routine.

wiki/biohacking.title: Biohacking
wiki/biohacking.content:
Overview
“Biohacking” is a marketing term that refers to commercialized health trends which repackage health and wellness paradigms with the aesthetics of sophisticated technical optimization.
One of the problems with health and wellness fields is that the ultimate arbiter for the success of any particular practice is the human whose mind-body is being evaluated. If someone is absolutely convinced that a cold water plunge makes them feel better, it becomes true through the strength of the belief alone. After all, they might become quite distressed if they aren’t able to keep up that routine. The mind-body system is also incredibly complex with a lot of reasonable disagreement over the interpretation of different measurements, so it’s possible to find some type of evidence for almost any claim provided you’re willing to look far enough and back enough. It’s very easy to promote correlations between different biometrics as a causal connection, and there’s ample incentive for media institutions to lean into sensationalism over scientific literacy.

wiki/biopsychosocial-models.title: Biopsychosocial Models (BPSM)
wiki/biopsychosocial-models.content:
Overview
Biopsychosocial models emerged as health models that consider the connection of biological, psychological, and social dimensions to someone’s lived experiences. It was first advocated for within modern medicine by George Engel in 1977, and it has steadily grown in interest and adoption since. In comparison to the biomedical model that preceded it which prefers mechanistic physiology as the mode of analysis for health, the biopsychosocial model is a more holistic iteration that emphasizes the connection between different angles to life. It’s especially beneficial when managing chronic health issues or conditions that are difficult to precisely define like substances use disorders that can impact multiple areas of life without standard discrete solutions.

wiki/bitter-pills-inside-the-hazardous-w.title: Bitter Pills: Inside the Hazardous World of Legal Drugs

wiki/black-and-white-thinking.title: Black-and-White Thinking
wiki/black-and-white-thinking.content:
Overview
In clinical settings, black-and-white thinking refers to a type of cognitive distortion where someone thinks in extremes or polar opposites. For example, they might define success on an exam by achieving 100% and anything less to be a failure, or they might go between wanting to break up with a significant other to putting them on a pedestal.
In the context of substance use disorders, black-and-white thinking can manifest as an Abstinence Violation Effect (AVE) which can lead someone who deviates from their standards of abstinence to spiral much harder. “I messed up, so fuck it, I give up” is a very common thought preceding one of these relapses, whereas sometimes people can recognize that they don’t have to let a night of drinking become a whole bender.

wiki/black-jack-and-other-temperance-tal.title: Black Jack and Other Temperance Tales for Boys and Girls
wiki/black-jack-and-other-temperance-tal.content:
Overview
This book is a collection of fictional tales warning young readers about alcohol, which was somewhat typical for temperance movements of the 19th and 20th centuries. It was published in London by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge (SPCK) and pushed the framework at the time that alcohol was itself inherently dangerous in its consumption of personal agency and moral sensibilities. To be honest, this is not at the top of my reading list.

wiki/black-market.title: Black Market
wiki/black-market.content:
Overview
Black markets are exchanges for products and services that have been outlawed by a state entity.
Historically, government efforts to ban substances like alcohol or addictive processes like gambling tend to shift economic activity into black markets. Localized crime rings or organized crime syndicates often recognize that laws do not remove people’s incentives to pursue illicit activities or contrabrand, so they build alternative economies that take advantage of the limitations of a system to surveil itself. Even the most totalitarian regimes in countries like North Korea fail to successfully crackdown on contraband, although, the price of illicit goods and services can go up to skirt regulations just as they do when complying with regulations.
The United States had a famously disastrous Prohibition of alcohol that led to a constitutional amendment banning alcohol. In practice, bootleg operations filled the gap with poorer quality products that led to an increase in public health issues. Wealthy individuals were still able to procure alcohol for lavish parties while working-class drinkers visited black market sellers. It was enormously profitable for organized crime syndicates that considerably marked up both.
