wiki/blackout.title: Blackout
wiki/blackout.content:
Overview
A blackout is a period of time in which someone might appear to be functional but is failing to transfer any short-term experiences into their long-term memories, so they have no recollection of what happened during the blackout.

wiki/blaues-kreuz.title: Blaues Kreuz
wiki/blaues-kreuz.content:
Overview
Blaues Kreuz (Blue Cross) is an international Christian non-governmental organization (NGO) focused on addiction prevention and treatment. It was founded in Switzerland in 1877 and grew to over touch over 40 to 50 countries under the International Blue Cross (IBC) umbrella organization. Their programs include interactive workshops at schools, alcohol-free cocktail bars, workplace health consultations to help employees struggling with dependence, outpatient clinics, counseling sessions, rehabilitation centers, peer support groups, sober recreation and retreats. As a whole, the organization aims at encouraging people to achieve abstinence.

wiki/block-grant.title: Block Grant
wiki/block-grant.content:
Overview
“Block grants” in the United States refers to a form of federal funding for programs that delivers money to state governments rather than directly to individual citizens. In theory, this means each state can use the funds to design a program for their unique needs instead of hoping a federal program can manage to fit everyone’s needs. In practice, this can lead to an extremely uneven distribution of services as each block grant then has to go through each state’s own political bureaucracies before reaching the taxpayer at the end.

wiki/blood-alcohol-concentration.title: Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC)
wiki/blood-alcohol-concentration.content:
Overview
Blood alcohol concentration (BAC) measures the amount of alcohol someone has consumed by testing the weight-to-volume ratio within their body’s bloodstream. 0.08 grams per 100 milliliters, or 0.08%, is generally the legal limit for driving in the United States, which is reached on average after 4 standard drinks defined as 14 grams of pure alcohol, though of course this varies enormously by each individual’s unique body composition. Body mass can make a huge difference, as well as biological sex since women generally have lower levels of enzymes to process alcohol than men of similar body mass.

wiki/bloodborne.title: Bloodborne
wiki/bloodborne.content:
Introduction
“In Yharnam, they produce more blood than alcohol, as the former is more intoxicating.”
Bloodborne is not shy about embracing addiction themes as part of its eldritch Lovecraftian vibes. The “Old Blood” is explicitly said to be more intoxicating than alcohol, and the citizens of Yharnam pursue blood despite the insanity and gruesome decay it brings. The Old Blood as a substance and the Hunt as the chase for it form a good allegory on their own, but, to me, the really compelling aspect is in how heavily the game explores the notion of transcendence given how central that concept is to what we seek from the world outside our finite human selves.
Lovecraft
Like many prolific writers who suffered from a particularly severe case of bigotry, Lovecraft attempted to reconcile his deeply held contradictions through his work but becomes more interesting as an artifact of study himself.
Lovecraft was deeply passionate about science though he held no formal qualifications himself. Both his parents had experienced violent episodes that led to institutionalization in a psychiatric hospital, and he himself experienced a litany of both physical and mental health ailments while living through extreme poverty. These were debilitating enough that he never completed high school or attended college, but he still wrote to publish work about scientific topics in local newspapers. At one point he published his own independent periodical that reviewed astronomy while maintaining a home chemistry lab and telescope setup. His works sometimes go into great authentic detail when describing these labs, no doubt a reflection of his enthusiasm for actual laboratory work and analysis.
Unfortunately, a passion for science does not translate to anything resembling an approach free of predetermined biases and prejudices. Consider the following excerpt:
“…could not by any stretch of the imagination be call’d human. They were monstrous and nebulous adumbrations of the pithecanthropoid and amoebal; vaguely moulded from some stinking viscous slime of earth’s corruption, and slithering and oozing in and on the filthy streets or in and out of doorways in a fashion suggestive of nothing but infesting worms or deep-sea unnamabilities.”
He’s not describing any creature out of his stories here. This is how he chose to describe Syrian and Italian immigrants he observed in New York. As for Chinatown,
“You can’t imagine the horror of being engulfed in a maelstrom of repulsive Orientals whose aberrant physiognomies & rat-like temperaments grate more & more on the sensibilities of an aesthetically impressionable person.”
And he did head-to-head comparisons too:
“There is here a grave and mighty problem beside which the negro problem is a jest—for in this case we have to deal not with childlike half-gorillas, but with yellow, soulless enemies whose repulsive carcasses house dangerous mental machines warped culturelessly in the single direction of material gain at any cost.”
Lovecraft’s revulsion here is pure in its irrationality. He simply does not like non-Anglo-Saxon people as an axiom of his worldview, so much so that even when he did like a non-Anglo-Saxon person, he would bend his reasoning in very unscientific ways. He was actually married to a Ukrainian-Jewish businesswoman and immigrant, Sonia Greene, for a brief two years, which he rationalized as an exception that proves the rule.
He would say Greene had shown assimilation to a superior Western culture was possible for lesser races that could sever a connection to their inferior heritage, even though Lovecraft was the one struggling financially, physically, mentally, and professionally. Greene was seven years older than him (he was 33 and had never been with a woman before) and almost took a maternal caretaking position to support him, which Lovecraft might have appreciated given how early he lost both his parents. After an economic downturn ruined Sonia’s fashion business, Lovecraft looked for work on the streets of New York, but he would regularly launch into racist tirades upon seeing immigrants on the street. He was not exactly a team player. Greene could no longer look past this prejudice and bitterness, and she left him.
So, despite Lovecraft’s love for science, absolute atheism, and strict materialism, he struggled immensely with intense emotions rooted in irrational aversions, and he tortured almost every instance of diversity into confirmation for his biases.
The “cosmic horror” he writes about is derived from the Others he was horrified about in his own life, directly provoking his imagination of what an otherworldy (literally, Other-worldly) entity behind the forces of change might look like. The protagonist of his story is often an educated and radical skeptic who leans on scientific processes and rationality to feel an order to the universe. The secondary antagonists are often a conspiratorial cult or secluded society who represent the agents of primitive degeneration walking on Earth. He was not subtle about using minorities, immigrants, and indigenous nations as inspiration for these agents.
It’s also noteworthy that Lovecraft strongly despised the Theosophist Society as one such pseudoscientific occult subculture, yet loved their mythology for world-building and borrowed heavily from their concepts. He wrote in letters that he too was building a mythological pantheon, but without the pretense of trying to start a religion. The opposite, in fact. He wanted to illustrate that the universe was indifferent to humans, that the “primitive” peoples worshipped the indifferent materialist forces while scientific skepticism reveals the harsh truth. Recall above that Lovecraft characterized Asians, and in particular Chinese ethnic groups, as ruthlessly efficient towards material pursuits as a result of lacking soul and culture. Totally unrelated to rationalizations about his own financial instability and reliance on a Jewish immigrant as a sugar mommy. After all, to him, he was just a temporarily embarrassed aristocrat who appreciated art and culture as human achievements, while the classless immigrants and minorities were ruining the community by pooling together capital earned from low-wage jobs to start businesses especially in underserved markets and communities. That script might sound a little painfully familiar.
Retrospectively, it’s a little amusing to see two different types of racist pseudosciences interact with each other. Lovecraft attempted to make self-aware and critical references to the Theosophists as a pseudoscientific occult group. Meanwhile, the Theosophists, particularly after his death, believed that Lovecraft was genuinely a medium receiving some kind of spiritual insight that his personal resistance and lack of training prevented him from interpreting correctly.
Transcendence
The core framework of transcending is nothing new. We can go back to Hesiod and the Dionysian Mysteries to see examples of this in Ancient Greece. Some of the oldest branches of Hinduism build on the premise that turning inwards and looking past the ego leads to a recognition of oneness with the world. The American transcendentalist movement with Thoreau and Emerson is often considered the first philosophical movement to have grown from American soil, and it’s no coincidence that it emerged out of dissatisfaction with “Western” industrialization and exoticism of the “Oriental” cultures. You can find a lot of interconnectedness and impermanence repeated in modern DBT techniques and Buddhist-inspired spiritual programs. Jungian psychoanalysts examine the archetypes surrounding transcendental experiences and operators. I certainly reference the concepts a lot in my ranting.
My notes about Talk to Me draws heavily on what Jung’s successors have said about substance use in youth subcultures that are driven by a desire for transcendental experiences to develop both their own identity and connections to a community. We know there must be more within this infinite universe than our finite sense show us, or at least our imagination can process the concept of infinity as something we lack. Yet, we are bound only to what our bodies allow in their limited form. To escape it and transcend or connect with something outside of ourselves, perhaps even greater than ourselves. Then, we want to share that transcendental experience in the hopes of deepening or heightening it through our connections with others.
Lovecraft’s work deals with a corruption of this concept of transcendence. As his protagonists seek to grow their insight into the truths of the world, their own sanity and ability to handle the universe are questioned. The creatures worshipped as gods in his stories come closer to an alien species that have incomprehensible rules and experiences of consciousness. Yet,he still ends up articulating a WASP (White, Anglo-Saxon, Protestant) moral psychology featuring original sin, predestination, indifference to prayer, nature as a corrupt foil to pure civilization, and suspicion of curiosity as temptation for forbidden knowledge. These are just expressed in terms of cosmic horror and incomprehensible entities that engage with us in our profane world rather than a philosophy of sacred divinity that set a universe in motion.
In stories like The Shadow over Innsmouth or The Rats in the Walls, original sin manifests through ancestral connections. In the former, a captain meets a mysterious tribe that maintains relations with an amphibious alien race and brings these aliens back for intermarriages under the promise of abundant wealth and immortality. Lovecraft is not just critical of a decline due to exchanges with exotic cultures, but also capitalism as a driving force behind the exchanges as a result of prioritizing profit over everything else, including cultural and racial purity maintained through strict segregation.
The second story is where many of Lovecraft’s contradictions come to a clash. The protagonist in this case is a stereotypical refined scholar and gentleman whose family curse reveals an original sin that tainted their descendants. He wrote the story just a couple years after his mother died in the same pyschiatric asylum his father also died in. I mentioned this contradiction earlier in the context of his marriage: despite claiming to be from a superior pinnacle of “Aryan” evolution, Lovecraft was experiencing the downfall of an old-money family in a rapidly changing community with new people and practices he didn’t recognize. We can see how this leaks into the protagonist’s journey as he explores an ancestral home revealing a history of imprisoning humans for perverse rituals that included cannabalism. A common notion in Lovecraft’s day was to project the qualities of individual organisms onto social organizations like family, ethnicites, and countries. In the same way an organism is born, matures, and dies, family bloodlines might have at one point peaked before degenerating into insanity and ill health as time went on. Perhaps Lovecraft thought it was good to be in something from the ground floor, but he came too late for that, at the end, when the best is over. His father’s commitment to a psychiatric institution was the result of neurosyphilis, which was highly stigmatized and assumed to cause degeneration in offspring. Lovecraft no doubt saw his own health issues as a type of original sin haunting his bloodline. Many scholars have argued that this also allowed him to deflect from taking accountability for himself if he was biologically predetermined to be more degenerate.
It’s also in this notion of original sin and ancestral decay that we see how Lovecraft, despite his atheism and materialism, craved something akin to transcendence, at least psychologically. He was an avid traveler even as he lacked funds, with a special appreciation for old colonial architecture. From the perspective of cosmic proportions nurtured by his passion for astronomy, he could see his own life’s tragedies and supposed degeneration as ultimately insignificant. In his imagination, this meant the freedom to explore the pantheon of eldritch entities and symbols he created for his stories. Engaging with cosmic insignificance and the awe of a mechanistic universe across literature and astronomy allowed him to experience something akin to the transcendence of the ego without a core religious or spiritual framework.
I’m reminded of a phrase from Hellraiser here: “the doors to the pleasures of Heaven or Hell, I didn’t care which.” Frank Cotton, the movie and source novel’s antagonist, finds that totally submitting to extreme hedonism has left him with nothing on Earth to pursue for fulfillment anymore. At some point he’s so desperate for a new experience to chase that he ends up unlocking an eternal torture from otherworldly beings who obliterate the distinction between pain and pleasure that parametrize the limits of human experience. Clive Barker, the creator, explicitly connects this mindset to addiction and consumerism. The Cenobites who answer Frank’s call mention that they are “demons to some, angels to others.” Recall how Lovecraft said that his eldritch creatures appeared as gods to the “primitive” humans, while others could see them as extra-terrestrial beings with frightening indifference to human affairs at best, and malicious sadism for personal amusement at worst.
Trickle-Down Economics
Bloodborne consistently weaves threads of ambivalence and ambiguity into the story beats surrounding transcendence, but notably inverts Lovecraft’s perspective as an elitist repulsed by those suffering in the lowest classes of society. The institutions of Yharnam are to blame in this story for the hubris of chasing transcendence through an appeal to eldritch entities. The residents who follow these institutions, be it from fear or faith, are led into a tragic nightmare in an arguably literal sense. The Victorian aesthetics of Yharnam invites comparisons to the historical intersections of healing, science, and religion through apothecaries, colleges, and churches.
From Software, the studio that made the game, uses environmental storytelling with extremely minimal narration, so rather than going through the game’s events, we might look at the lore chronologically.
The Great Ones are the eldritch entities of Bloodborne’s universe who mostly lived in a network of caverns underground. Millions of years before the city of Yharnam was built, an ancient civilization called the Pthumerians built a sophisticated civilization carved into these caverns. They resembled humans, but are a distinct species in the fashion of Theosophic Root Races. When the Pthumerians discovered the Great Ones slumbering in these caves, they started collecting what we later call the “Old Blood” from the bodies and secretions of these entities. Consuming it unlocked supernatural powers and conscious awareness of higher dimensions that could not have been ordinarily perceived through the finite limits of a mortal organic body.
The Old Blood became a critical part of the structure of Pthumerian civilization. A hierarchical caste system formed around the distribution of Old Blood, with the final ruler being Queen Yharnam after who the city we play in is named. Other layers of the caste involved ritual keepers who dedicated themselves to the collection, processing, and allocation of the Old Blood. There were also guardians for the Great Ones as they slept, which the player encounters should they go exploring in these underground ruins.
The Great Ones are not a monolith, however. They have complex motives and agendas that are far deeper than the typical Lovecraftian indifference to humans. And that’s actually more horrifying than apathy might be. It’s said that “Every Great One loses its child, and yearns for a surrogate.” In other words, the Great Ones are conscious and sympathetic to the humans who venerate them. Since the Great Ones are incapable of reproducing, they form relationships with humans to bear cosmic children. Oedon, a formless Great One who is known only through sound and presence of blood, chooses Queen Yharnam to bear his, named Mergo. This stands out starkly with Lovecraft’s framing of mating with alien races as a secret degeneration of the race under the surface of civilization; it is the aspiration of this advanced civilization to merge with otherworldly aliens. The Pthumerians celebrated the fusion of a royal bloodline with a cosmic one as a form of ascension. Unfortunately for the Pthumerians, mass consumption of the Old Blood did not actually lead to mass ascension but mass mutation. Rather than Lovecraft’s emphasis on original sin that haunts bloodlines, individual destinies were shaped by their contemporary relation to the Old Blood.
The guardians and enforcers who consumed massive amounts of blood gained immortality but still decayed, so the players fights them as emaciated skeletal figures. In particularly brutal instance, Pthumerians surgically altered giant guardians to replace their limbs with weapons, including cannons bolted into their spines. Others that sought pyromancy powers appear charred and ashen, as if slowly burned alive. Some seem to have succumbed to bloodlust, which leads to a beastly transformation that resembles something between a satyr and minotaur, and other Pthumerian creatures attack them in the dungeons. The ruling castes seem to have grown obese and doughy, working in tight groups to continue their blood-drunk euphoria.
Flora and fauna were impacted by exposure to the Old Blood too. Rats that ate rotting Pthumerian corpses grew giant and sprouted multiple eyes. Plants that sprouted from soil tainted with the Old Blood grew into sentient centipede-like creatures capable of channeling cosmic energy. Their giant watchdogs also transformed with flesh crystallizing into armor and blood boiling to the point of fire.
Blood also wasn’t the only thing driving madness and transformations. Another avenue to asenscion is found in Insight, representing the “eyes” spiritually and mentally within someone, though sometimes also displayed through the growth or implantation of physical eyes.
An enemy called “Labyrinth Sages” are Pthumerians whose pursuit of Insight rather than the Old Blood produces a different kind of madness. One might almost liken them to different addictive substances. They were part of an elite caste of religious scholars whose purpose was to discover and preserve the intellectual traditions of the Old Blood and Great Ones. Through excessive Insight, the Sages attempted to internalize information too overwhelming for a finite limited brain to process, and so they seem to have lost their senses except to continue attacking any threats. Some Sages wield the bodies of other Pthumerians as weapons, possibly as holy relics as in the case of a saint’s corpse, although some of them are still alive. These Sages appear to be constantly twitching, hyperaggressive, and
Surrogacy
The servants of Queen Yharnam become enemies called “Shadows of Yharnam”, and the Blood Rapture Rune that they drop has a description that reads:
“‘Blood Rapture’ is the raw euphoria of the warmth of blood. Restores HP with visceral attacks, one of the darker hunter techniques. This rune resonates with servants of the Queen, carrier of the Child of Blood, who yearn for their Queen’s blood with little hope of requitement. For them, they find solace in ‘Blood Rapture,’ that serves as a surrogate for their desires.”
The word “surrogate” appears again here, which is no coincidence. A recurring theme in the game is how often people are seeking a substitute for something they cannot have or do themselves.
The Great Ones seek human surrogates since they are doomed to lose any child after conception. The leaders of both the Pthumerians and Yharmanites seek the Old Blood for an evolution they cannot induce within themselves. There’s a symbiotic surrogacy in their dynamic as Great Ones grant surrogate pregnancies in exchange for the transformation seen as ascension. The Moon Presence, having lost a child before, treats Gehrman as a surrogate child which gives the main hub the appearance of a serene nursery with dolls, flowers, and books. The Great One named Kos loses her child as well, so she chooses a human scholar Rom to transform into a mindless premature Great One. Oedon is formless yet is still able to choose Queen Yharnam as a surrogate.
The servants of Queen Yharnam, as well as the later servants of another Queen Annalise, derive their purpose and connection through service to their ruler’s apparently divine and royal bloodline; in its absence, they seek euphoric sensations of blood to fill that lost purpose. The hunter Gehrman was once in love with his pupil Lady Maria, whose guilt for her actions as a hunter lead to her committing suicide, so he crafts a doll in her likeness that becomes animated by a Great One (referred to as The Moon Presence) as his caretaker.
Master Willem and his then-student Laurence, the leader of Byrgenwerth College and later-First Vicar of the Healing Church respectively, used to have a surrogate father-son dynamic. Willem believed insight through eyes was needed to perceive the true nature of reality, while Laurence believed ingesting the Old Blood was the way to understand it. Their split is characterized by Willem as a betrayal, as if Laurence was in line to succeed Willem and the philosophy of insight.
We know there must be more within this infinite universe than our finite sense show us, or at least our imagination can process the concept of infinity as something we lack. Yet, we are bound only to what our bodies allow in their limited form. To escape it and transcend or connect with something outside of ourselves, perhaps even greater than ourselves. Then, we want to share that transcendental experience in the hopes of furthering it through our connections with others.

wiki/bobby-mukkamala.title: Bobby Mukkamala
wiki/bobby-mukkamala.content: A long time member of the American Medical Association (AMA), Bobby Mukkamala served a tenure as AMA President until June 2026. He now leads the AMA’s substance use task force.

wiki/bodhi.title: Bodhi
wiki/bodhi.content:
Overview
“Bodhi” is a Sanskrit term that roughly means “enlightenment.” Buddhist traditions generally conceive of bodhi as a state free of suffering and endless cycles of rebirth through achieving an enlightened understanding of an impermanent reality and one’s self, or not-self, within it. The Buddha is said to have attained bodhi when meditating and contemplating reality under a fig tree. It is also used as a first name as an auspicious appeal to the wisdom gained from enlightenment.

wiki/bodhicitta.title: Bodhicitta
wiki/bodhicitta.content:
Overview
Bodhicitta is a Sanskrit word composed of bodhi, meaning “enlightenment,” and citta, roughly referring to “heart-mind” or “consciousness,” so combined, it means “the heart-mind of enlightenment.” While attaining bodhi as an awakening to the reality of non-duality is the goal of many Buddhist traditions, bodhicitta is the mindset to cultivate in the process which breeds compassion for the suffering of all sentient beings.

wiki/bodhisattva.title: Bodhisattva
wiki/bodhisattva.content:
Overview
A Bodhisattva is a Buddhist practitioner who has taken a commitment to delay their own liberation through enlightenment into Nirvana until every other living being has also been able to achieve this liberation. This generally involves taking a vow to demonstrate that one has cultivated bodhicitta, or the heart-mind of an enlightened being.
Mahayana and Zen Buddhism put forward four vows for Bodhisattvas to take:


Beings are numberless. I vow to save them.


Delusions are inexhaustible. I vow to end them.


Dharma gates are boundless. I vow to enter them.


The Buddha’s way in unsurpassable. I vow to attain it.

wiki/boredom.title: Boredom
wiki/boredom.content:
Overview
Despite boredom being a universal experience that extends even beyond humans to other species, researchers and clinicians have historically neglected to create a consensus around its definition. In 2012, John Eastwood was part of a team that proposed a framework in a journal called Perspectives on Psychological Science:
“…boredom is best described in terms of attention. A bored person doesn’t just have nothing to do. He or she wants to be stimulated, but is unable, for whatever reason, to connect with his or her environment - a state Eastwood describes as an ‘unengaged mind.‘”
The American Psychological Association references this paper in its online coverage of boredom as a concept [^0].
Links

Never A Dull Moment [^0]

wiki/born-in-synanon.title: Born in Synanon (2023)
wiki/born-in-synanon.content: To everyone who says Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) is a cult, you have not yet seen Synanon.

wiki/borrachos.title: Borrachos
wiki/borrachos.content:
Overview
“Borrachos” translates to “drunkards” in Spanish, referring either to a group of people who are actively drunk a group of people who are generally heavy drinkers.
History and Etymology
In 1629, Diego Velazquez completed a Baroque painting for King Philip V that was officially called The Triumph of Bacchus as a depiction of the god of wine Bacchus, the Roman interpretation of the Greek Dionysus, placing a crown on working-class peasants as a symbol of wine providing relief to the grief and misery of daily life. However, to much of the Spanish public, what stood out most were the peasants who seemed to be inviting the viewer to have a drink with them. The painting was referred to widely as [[los-borrachos|Los Borrachos]] instead as a representation of celebratory drinking rituals that was strongly embedded and institutionalized in many Latin American communities.

wiki/boundaries.title: Boundaries
wiki/boundaries.content:
Overview
“Boundaries” generally refer to someone’s stated preferences for social conduct and interpersonal engagement that respects their autonomy and integrity.
There are lots of context-specific frameworks and definitions for boundaries. The American Psychological Association (APA) maintains the APA Dictionary of Psychology which articulates two definitions. The casual one reads:
“a psychological demarcation that protects the integrity of an individual or group or that helps the person or group set realistic limits on participation in a relationship or activity.” [^0]
Common boundaries people put forward include privacy around personal details, a limit on the topics one feels comfortable discussing, foregoing physical touch as a form of intimacy, and establishing space to have time to recharge. In healthy relationships, all parties feel comfortable expressing their boundaries with the confidence that they will be respected, and any violations will be identified and corrected.
In unhealthy relationships, where enmeshment and codependency might be present, someone’s boundaries, self-worth, and sense of safety and security can become contingent on someone else’s determination. This can be observed in children who are afraid to express an opinion their caretakers haven’t approved of including desires for physical space, partners in a relationship who routinely violate each other’s privacy like going through their phone when in the bathroom, and employers who ask their employees to do personal tasks unrelated to the job description or success of the workplace environment. Particularly extreme cases can involve stalking, manipulation, and domestic violence and abuse.
Medical professionals, from therapists to physicians to nurses, have an especially delicate appreciation for boundaries since their work requires them to earn the trust of a patient to gain consent for procedures and treatments. There’s a long, unpleasant history of medical institutions condoning boundary violations when a moral framework or personal bias is attached to the condition or person being treated. Recent studies show that simply referring to someone as a “substance abuser” rather than someone with “substances use disorder” can change the way trained professionals view the justification for punitive measures [^1].
To that end, the APA’s dictionary provides a second definition:
“in psychotherapy, an important limit that is usually set by the therapist as part of the ground rules in treatment. Boundaries may involve areas of discussion (e.g., the therapist’s personal life is off limits) or physical limits (e.g., rules about touching), which are guided by ethical codes and standards. Respect for boundaries by both the therapist and client is an important concept in the therapeutic relationship.” [^0]
A more abstract definition of “boundaries” in the context of professional conduct for medical workers from the Indian Journal of Psychological Medicine reads:
“A boundary may be defined as the ‘edge’ of appropriate professional behavior, transgression of which involves the therapist stepping out of the clinical role or breaching the clinical role. Boundaries define the expected and accepted psychological and social distance between practitioners and patients. Boundaries are derived from ethical treatise, cultural morality, and jurisprudence. Sometimes, it is difficult to clearly define the perimeter of these boundaries and the integrity of the relationship.” [^2]
Boundaries come up very commonly in recovery circles as substance use is often a coping mechanism for managing violated boundaries, and it can lead to behaviors that violate the boundaries of others. A typical story of an addiction trajectory might involve someone growing up in an abusive household that regularly ignored their physical and emotional boundaries, so they used substances to cope with the distress, and then they end up stealing from others around them in order to sustain their substance use. A less overtly harmful pattern is simply texting or calling people at late hours for company under the influence after the bedtime they’ve indicated they’re trying to maintain.
The Society for the Advancement of Psychotherapy, Division 29 of the APA, discusses some of the specifics of boundaries within the context of clinical psychotherapy:
“Boundaries provide:


“A therapeutic frame which defines a set of roles for the participants in the therapeutic process” (Smith and Fitzpatrick, 1995, p. 499)


“a foundation for this relationship by fostering a sense of safety and the belief that the clinician will always act in the client’s best interest (Smith & Fitzpatrick, 1995, p. 500)


a “distinction between the expectations and interactions that would be considered appropriate within the relationship and those that would be considered inappropriate within the relationship” (R. Sommers-Flanagan, Elliot, & J. Sommers-Flanagn, 1998, p. 38).


They also break down the types of boundaries in psychotherapeutic contexts into touch, time, space, location, gifts, and self-disclosure. A recurring theme in [[the-sopranos|The Sopranos]] is the frustration experienced by opening up to a therapist in a way that feels intimate but having to adhere to professional codes of conduct that limit what can be done with that exposed vulnerability. Within the show, Tony regularly tests his own therapist’s boundaries across all of these dimensions, and though she herself is tempted to often cross them, she acts as a rare beacon in the show’s corruption and abandonment of ethical codes. Something as innocuous as bringing a cup of coffee to a session to share with a therapist can be seen as a form of gift-giving that opens the door to the complexities of interpreting material exchanges between patient and practitioner. We perhaps can’t expect perfect adherence to boundaries in any context, even among highly trained and ethically-grounded professionals, because human relationships are inherently messy with missteps and mistakes. For better or worse, professionals are human too.
Links
[^0] APA Dictionary of Psychology
[^1] Does it matter how we refer to individuals with substance-related conditions? A randomized study of two commonly used terms (Kelly, 2009)
[^2] Boundary Crossings and Violations in Clinical Settings (Aravind et. al, 2012)
[^3] Boundaries and Multiple Relationships in Psychotherapy

wiki/brahman.title: Brahman
wiki/brahman.content:
Overview
“Brahman” is a Sanskrit term which has many meanings in Vedic, Hindu, and other belief systems with South Asian roots, but generally can be seen as referring to an ultimate reality that’s at the source of the existence of all things.
In the Vedas, the oldest religious texts from the South Asian subcontinent, Brahman was an evolving and fluid concept that invoked the idea of a truth underneath apparent differences. The Upanishads took steps towards consolidating some of these ideas into a fundamental reality that creates and contains the universe. With that came a personification of this reality as a divine being or deity, the contemplation and understanding of which produces liberation.

wiki/brain-fog.title: Brain Fog
wiki/brain-fog.content:
Overview
“Brain fog” is a term commonly used to describe some combination of confusion, difficulty thinking, and lack of ability to focus. The term gained fresh momentum in the wake of COVID-19, when it was both a highly publicized symptom of long COVID and discussed alongside a spike in substance use disorder cases defined by a dysregulated state of altered consciousness. Since then, there has been a renewed wave of interest in examining brain fog as one of many symptoms impacting someone’s quality of life that can persist after someone has supposedly been cured of a conventional disease like the flu.
The National Center for Biotechnology Information defines it as
“a type of transient cognitive dysfunction that comprises a constellation of symptoms that impair intellectual functioning to a level that interferes with daily activities, commonly including forgetfulness, mental slowness, difficulty thinking or focusing, a perceived slowing of mental processing speed, inability to find the right words, a sensation that the mind went blank or is “cloudy”. Brain fog tends to recur and may be triggered by factors such as physical fatigue, lack of sleep, and prolonged standing or may appear to occur spontaneously.” [^0]
The International Classification of Diseases for Mortality and Morbidity Statistics (ICD-11) defines a related term through “clouding of consciousness,” which means
“An impairment in the clarity of consciousness characterised by impaired ability to comprehend aspects of the environment or the self in relation to the environment, inattention, and abnormalities in thought processes, comprehension. It is typically accompanied by subjective experience of mental clouding described as feeling ‘foggy’. Clouding of consciousness is a common form of cognitive disturbance in Delirium, but it is not synonymous with Delirium because Delirium includes additional diagnostic requirements.” [^1]
For those with substance use disorders, brain fog is extremely common in early recovery, not just from chronic substance use but as a side effect of prescribed medications. Drugs that alter the brain’s dopamine pathways and reward mechanisms directly impact one’s capacity for motivation and concentration, the lack of which can feel like brain fog. Disorders and conditions that commonly co-occur with substance like chronic pain are also associated with brain fog.
Brain fog should not be confused with depersonalization, which can involve the persistent feeling that one is in a dream, or with drowsiness and fatigue, though attempting to work through brain fog can certainly produce exhaustion. Someone with brain fog can be quite awake and physically energized, but struggle to summon the focus needed to chain together a complex train of thought or retrieve memories required for daily tasks.
History and Etymology
Georg Greiner was among the first to connect the concept of a “clouding of consciousness”, or Verdunkelung des Bewussteins in German, to the condition of delirium. It wasn’t uncommon then to see the term associated with severe disturbances like entering a coma.
Links
[^0] Brain fog (Concept Id: C0015676) - MedGen - NCBI
[^1] MB20.2 Clouding of consciousness

wiki/brave-new-world.title: Brave New World by Aldous Huxley
wiki/brave-new-world.content: I’ve often thought of Aldous Huxley as the bastard child of H.P. Lovecraft and Carl Jung, conceived in a pile of experimental psychedelics. You can find a lot of Huxley’s anxieties about a changing world  reflected in Brave New World, from the commercial commodification of art and culture as a form of mental dissociation through consumption to the concerns about European genetic pools “deterioriating” over time, at least in his early life.

wiki/breathalyzer.title: Breathalyzer
wiki/breathalyzer.content:
Overview
A breathalyzer is, as the name suggests, a tool that analyzes one’s breath to estimate blood alcohol concentration (BAC).
History and Etymology
The idea that something about alcohol lingers on the breath after drinking is as old as drinking itself. I mean, it’s hard to ignore the odors of a drunk person thinking they’re whispering secrets into your ears. It was generally assumed though that alcohol was still coating someone’s mouth and throat. Francis Anstie discovered in 1847 that alcohol is actively excreted by the lungs as vapor after traveling to the bloodstream, meaning it was a byproduct of respiration rather than just residually present in the mouth. In the 1910s, Francis Gano Benedict found quantitative evidence for a direct relationship between BAC and the concentration of alcohol vapor in air from lungs. Emil Bogen linked breath samples themselves to BAC in 1927.
Various entrepreneurs have attempted to leverage these discoveries to test someone’s intoxication levels. In 1931, Rolla N. Harger invented a device called the “Drunkometer” which captured one’s breath in a balloon and measured intoxication through color changes in a purple chemical solution. Robert F. Borkenstein, an Indiana State Police captain, patented the Breathalyzer in 1954 to help law enforcement agents estimate BAC in the field. Through the latter half of the 20th century, breathalyzers began incorporating technology that replaced color reactions with infrared spectroscopy, gas chromatography, fuel cell sensors with electric currents, and micro-sensors linked to smartphones and vehicle ignitions.
Breathalyzers are a standard protocol in treatment facilities to monitor the sobriety of patients. It’s also a great way for you to monitor how out of shape you are and how much your lungs hate you for inhaling drugs. It’s good to be aware though that you can set off the breathalyzer with drinks like kombucha that aren’t always labeled as containing alcohol, and you probably have no way of proving either that you didn’t intend on consuming enough to be intoxicated or that you didn’t sneak in a real drink with it. It’s best to exercise a lot of caution when it comes to fermented fruits. After all, lots of animals have a history of getting loaded that way.

wiki/breathwork.title: Breathwork
wiki/breathwork.content:
Overview
“Breathwork” refers to breathing techniques that can help reduce stress and anxiety, decrease blood pressure and heart rate, strengthen respiratory muscles, and facilitate emotional processing.
Most breathwork discussed in a recovery context is about activating the parasympathetic nervous system and soothing the vagus nerve in order to lower stress, reduce anxiety, improve focus, and prepare for sleep:


4-7-8 Breathing: inhale through the nose for 4 seconds, hold for 7 seconds, exhale through the mouth for 8 seconds


Cyclic Sighing: take one deep inhale through the nose, then take one sharp inhale, then release a long slow exhale through the mouth


Box Breathing: inhale for 4 seconds, hold for 4 seconds, exhale for 4 seconds, hold empty for 4 seconds


Resonant Breathing: breathe 5 seconds in and 5 seconds out


Alternate Nostril Breathing (Nadi Shodhana): using the thumb and ring finger, close one nostril, inhale through the open nostril, alternate the nostril that’s closed, and exhale through the newly open nostril.


Diaphragmatic Breathing (Belly Breathing): place one hand on your chest and one on your belly, and breathe only so that the belly rises and falls


Humming Bee Breath (Bhramari): inhale deeply, close your ears and eyes with your fingers, and make a long drawn-out humming sound as you exhale

wiki/brian-p-akers.title: Brian P. Akers
wiki/brian-p-akers.content:
Overview
Brian Akers is an ethnomycologist who studies psychoactive mushrooms and their depiction in prehistoric art, like the Selva Pascuala mural in Spain and the Tassili mushroom figures in Algeria.
Works
Books

wiki/brief-alcohol-screening-and-interve.title: Brief Alcohol Screening and Intervention for College Students (BASICS)
wiki/brief-alcohol-screening-and-interve.content:
Overview
The Brief Alcohol Screening and Intervention for College Students (BASICS) was first trialed in 1990 at the University of Washington for college students around 18 to 24 years old. Within trials, it has repeatedly shown to be an effective way to screen for alcohol use disorders and suggest interventions, but institutions vary widely in how they deliver it, including through groups, telehealth, written feedback, and electronic portals. It’s considered a form of Brief Motivational Intervention (BMI) [^0]
In 2021, researchers at the University of Washington iterated on BASICS with the Brief Alcohol Screening and Intervention for Community College Students (BASICCS), recognizing that the needs of community college students differ from 4-year students living on university campuses, yet the scientific literature around BASICS and public health focused substantially on the latter. Almost 40% of undergraduate students in the United States attend community colleges that have large commuter populations and less physical infrastructure like student health clinics. Jason R. Kilmer, who worked on the original BASICS model, was involved with the project led by Christine M. Lee. BASICCS adopts a digital-first approach that embraces remote accessibility and mobile integrations like a text notification component to substitute for the reinforcement provided by in-person peers. The trial showed that, at the three months mark, there was about a 29% reduction in alcoholic drinks consumed weekly compared to control groups.
History and Etymology
BASCIS has its origins in the individualized intervention portion of another proposal called the Alcohol Skills Training Program (ASTP), which combined CBT-style cognitive behavioral skills with group facilitation. While the content is largely shared, BASICS allows for personalized approaches to discuss an individual’s alcohol consumption patterns. Historically, programs addressing alcohol use disorder on college campuses was rooted in abstinence-only education, but BASICS represents a step towards evidence-backed harm reduction philosophy instead. [^0]
Links
[^0] Thirty Years of BASICS: Dissemination and Implementation Progress and Challenges
[^1] Brief Alcohol Screening and Intervention for Community College Students (BASICCS): Feasibility and Preliminary Efficacy of Web-Conferencing BASICCS and Supporting Automated Text Messages

wiki/brief-motivational-intervention.title: Brief Motivational Intervention (BMI)
wiki/brief-motivational-intervention.content:
Overview
Brief motivational interventions (BMIs) are an individualized method to address substance use patterns with personalized feedback from facilitators applying motivational interviewing techniques.
The National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) mentions that
“BMI combines a brief intervention with motivational interviewing. BMI emphasizes personal responsibility and self-efficacy of participants, offering them personalized feedback on their alcohol use, risks, expectancies, perceptions of social norms, and options for reducing problems and consequences. Discussions are guided by a trained facilitator. Goals for behavioral change are set by participants.” [^0]
The Brief Alcohol Screening and Intervention for College Students (BASICS) is one of the most common forms of BMI that involves a trained facilitator reviewing personalized feedback with an individual who directs their own goal. Studies since 1990 have found that it effectively helps students identify risky patterns in their consumption of alcohol and make lifestyle adjustments to meet goals to cut back.

wiki/brownout.title: Brownout
wiki/brownout.content:
Overview
A brownout is similar to a blackout where, as a result of drinking to excess, someone loses part of their memory or has hazy recall of it. A blackout is when someone experiences complete memory loss because the brain didn’t transfer anything from short-term to long-term memory. Both are distinct from passing out, which is losing consciousness altogether rather than just losing memory. In terms of mechanisms, the difference between brownouts and blackouts is the extent to which a higher BAC leads to disruption in the brain’s hippocampus region. There’s an argument to be made that the real value of the distinction is social, since making two categories lessens the apparent severity of drinking to the point of brain disruption or damage. Yet, it’s entirely possible to meet the criteria for substance or alcohol use disorder without blacking out once.

wiki/bulimia-nervosa.title: Bulimia Nervosa
wiki/bulimia-nervosa.content:
Overview
Bulimia nervosa is an eating disorder in which someone cycles between binge eating and a behavior like vomiting, fasting, or excessive exercise in an attempt to offset the amount eaten.
History and Etymology
The pattern of purging as a potential mechanism to improve health goes back to ancient civilizations where physicians often attributed diseases to having eaten something toxic, and we have ample evidence of zealous partygoers across the world who deliberately purge so they can keep eating. While this can’t be declared healthy behavior, it also doesn’t show the same kind of body image distortion and weight monitoring that produces distress and urges we associate with a consistent psychiatric disorder. Once eating disorders were acknowledged by psychiatrists, the pattern of binge eating and purging were assumed to be a dysfunction related to anorexia nervosa or obesity rather than a distinct phenomenon. In 1979, Gerald Russell identified 30 patients he met who maintained a healthy weight but still presented with a cycle of binge eating and purging and published Bulimia nervosa: an ominous variant of anorexia nervosa. The DSM-III came out in 1980 and introduced bulimia nervosa as its own diagnostic category. [^0]
Links
[^0] Emergence of bulimia nervosa as a separate diagnostic entity: review of the literature from 1960 to 1979 (Vandereycken, 1994)

wiki/bundling-bias.title: Bundling Bias
wiki/bundling-bias.content:
Overview
Bundling bias refers to a pattern where people who buy a bundle of items are less likely to use each one than if they had bought the items individually.
The concept emerges out of the intersection of psychology and behavioral economics. Our brains tend to seek shortcuts to estimate the value of a transaction, so when we see a bundle, we look past the cost of each individual item to a general sense of the bundle’s benefit. This in turn makes us less likely to feel compelled to use each item in order to ensure our benefits outpace our costs.
Within the context of coping skills developed for substance use disorders, bundling can be a mental exercise that discourages future use. Many will be familiar with a rationalization that sounds something like “I really need relief, so one dose of the substance is all I’ll take and then I’ll be straightened out.” By definition, to struggle with substance use to the point of it being classified a disorder means to be unable to control one’s impulsives and compulsions to do just that. As a result, reframing the decision as “if I take one dose, I’m actually committing to taking a dose every day for weeks or months and the consequences of that” can be an easier way to conceptualize the totality of that choice. In recovery circles, this is often summarized through the adage “play the tape forward,” which effectively bundles consequences of the future. Credit where it’s due, sometimes conventional cliches work before we have fancy explanations for them.
Links

journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1509/jmkr.38.1.30.18828

wiki/buprenorphine.title: Buprenorphine
wiki/buprenorphine.content:
Overview
Buprenorphine is a partial opioid agonist that relieves cravings and withdrawal symptoms from Opioid Use Disorder (OUD) without causing euphoria. It can be prescribed for Medication for Opioid Use Disorder (MOUD) in the United States by any clinician licensed by the Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA). Brand names include Suboxone, Sublocade, and Brixadi.

wiki/burnout.title: Burnout
wiki/burnout.content:
Overview
Burnout in its most casual sense means running out of the energy or capacity to keep up some level of activity.
The International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11) states
““Burn-out is a syndrome conceptualized as resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed. It is characterized by three dimensions:

feelings of energy depletion or exhaustion;
increased mental distance from one’s job, or feelings of negativism or cynicism related to one’s job; and
reduced professional efficacy.

Burn-out refers specifically to phenomena in the occupational context and should not be applied to describe experiences in other areas of life.”” [^0]
This narrowly interprets burnout, at least in a clinical context, to a work-related state of mind. It’s not considered a medical condition in itself, but it is still explicitly signaled as something that has to be addressed from the intersection between public health and psychology. This isn’t necessarily dismissive as much as a precaution to ensure that symptoms described under the umbrella of burnout aren’t indicative of another health condition. From the Center of Disease Control:
“Take for instance the idea that both depression and burnout can leave someone too tired to do their work. These are similar symptoms that could come up in both measures, even if they have some differences.”
“It is not always clear how burnout differs from depression, anxiety, and other mental health conditions. Burnout is typically caused by chronic demand overload at work, while mental health conditions can have a variety of underlying causes.”
The CDC goes on to identify “similar yet different strain conditions to distinguish from burnout” that include fatigue, boredom, loneliness, engagement, moral distress, moral injury, and compassion fatigue. [^1]
History and Etymology
The term “burnout” in the context of psychology was coined by Herbert Freudenberger in 1974 while identifying fatigue that persisted beyond normal exhaustion and systemically occurred in organizations.
Links
[^0] Burn-out an “occupational phenomenon”: International Classification of Diseases
[^1] Module 2 Outline: What burnout is and is not

wiki/c-ptsd.title: C-PTSD
wiki/c-ptsd.content:
Overview
C-PTSD, or Complex Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder, is a mental health condition that can present with symptoms similar to PTSD, but usually as the result of prolonged recurrring trauma rather than isolated events. It’s also sometimes denoted as CPTSD or cPTSD.
The current Diagnostic Statistical Manual (DSM-5) does not include C-PTSD as a diagnosis, but the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11) does, meaning that the diagnosis can’t be obtained United States for any insurance or medical billing purposes. Instead, American clinicians might diagnose a patient with PTSD and some combination of Borderline Personality Disorder, Major Depressive Disorder, or Other Specifc Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorder, even if they might communicate that C-PTSD is a better label for the constellation of symptoms they observe.
History and Etymology
In 1988, Judith Herman officially proposed an argument for a separated C-PTSD diagnosis apart from PTSD to better emphasize the unique experiences of chronic trauma from childhood abuse compared to the PTSD of an accident or violent assault. The DSM committee within the American Psychiatric Association argues that PTSD, depression, and personality disorders already capture the presentation of C-PTSD and another label might add to confusion rather than precision.

wiki/caffeine.title: Caffeine
wiki/caffeine.content:
Overview
Caffeine is the most commonly used drug in the world with as much as 90% of the global adult population consuming some version of it daily. On average, adults consume 200mg of caffeine per day, which is more than would be found in two 6-oz cups of coffee. Studies that attempt to measure the prevalence of dependence find that 8% to 20% of regular caffeine users meet the criteria of caffeine use disorder (CUD). 1
Commentary
I like caffeine.

wiki/california-sober.title: California Sober
wiki/california-sober.content:
Overview
“California sober” was a term popularized around 2019 to describe a pattern of substance use that foregoes alcohol and “hard” drugs while allowing for the use of cannabis, psychedelics, caffeine, and other “soft” drugs. Rather than the conventional total abstinence model used by many peer recovery groups, especially 12-step programs, the concept of “California sober” is a shift towards harm reduction principles that acknowledges the increased quality of life from any reduction of use in substances. The term has no fixed meaning, so one person may limit themselves to cannabis while another person might include psychedelics in their definition. The association with California stems from the state’s generally lenient and progressive orientation towards decriminalizing substance use and alternative wellness approaches.
The research on the sustainability of California sobriety is mixed.
A study from Brown University that was published in the American Journal of Psychiatry, the first randomized controlled trial (RCT) on the subject, found that subjects who smoked THC joints just before visiting a bar drank 19% to 27% less alcohol than the control group given a placebo. Higher THC concentrations correlated with a greater reduction in drinking. 1 A 2025 University of Colorado study found that participants who bought cannabis from a dispensary to use at home chose to drink about 25% less alcohol and experienced far fewer cravings. Researchers from the University at Buffalo published a paper in the Journal of Psychoactive Drugs that showed that nearly 2/3 adults who used cannabis-infused beverages reduced their alcohol consumption by half or completely stopped drinking alcohol.
On the other hand, a 2024 study published in the Journal of Substance Use and Addiction Treatment looked at sober living homes (SLHs) specifically and found that almost one-fifth of residents had reported using cannabis in the past six months, which correlated with an increase in alcohol use and drug problems in general. 2 That being said, it’s also true that someone who can’t abstain when living in an SLH with an abstinence-only policy might have a significantly different profile than someone who abstains in an SLH and begins to use cannabis only after moving to a house that permits it.
Anecdotally, I’m inclined to think there is, as I’ve observed a huge holistic difference between people whose substance use emerges as a consequence of problems in their old environments and lifestyle compared to people who struggle to maintain sobriety when in a treatment facility. I’ll also qualify that by saying the people I know who have been able to moderate cannabis usage who have at one point met the criteria for substance use disorder did not approach their treatment with plans to resume using cannabis. Those who did relapsed into other substances quite soon. I would argue that someone set on being able to maintain complete abstinence for at least some period of time is on a different place in the spectrum of compulsive and impulsive behaviors associated with addiction than someone who does not perceive sober life to be tolerable at all.
Links
Footnotes


As ‘California sober’ catches on, study suggests cannabis use reduces short-term alcohol consumption ↩


The Exploration of Cannabis Beverage Substitution for Alcohol: A Novel Harm Reduction Strategy (Kruger et. al, 2025) ↩

wiki/cambridge-health-alliance.title: Cambridge Health Alliance
wiki/cambridge-health-alliance.content:
Overview
The Cambridge Health Alliance (CHA) is a medical provider and health system for over 140,000 residents, with an official affiliation with Harvard University. They operate the CHA Bridge Clinic as a walk-in outpatient center that does not require insurance and provides harm reduction, counseling, wound care, recovery coaching, detoxification, and buprenorphine and naltrexone as Medication-Assisted Treatment (MAT). Within the Department of Psychiatry is the Division on Addiction and Center for Mindfulness and Compassion, which have conducted clinical trials and training programs on Substance Use Disorders (SUDs).
Links

www.divisiononaddiction.org/

wiki/canadian-centre-on-substance-use-an.title: Canadian Centre on Substance Use and Addiction (CCSA)
wiki/canadian-centre-on-substance-use-an.content:
Overview
The Canadian Centre on Substance Use and Addiction (CCSA) is an independent non-government organization created in 1988 through an Act of Parliament. The CCSA conducts and analyzes scientific research to give evidence-based recommendations to policymakers and decision-makers, ideally remaining as neutral and objective as possible for a government-created institution subject to political approval. Most recently, the CCSA has been working on the Small Cities Playbook for Action, the Canadian Community Epidemiology Network on Drug Use (CCENDU), and National Guidance for Youth Substance Use Health.
Links

www.ccsa.ca/

wiki/cannabinoids.title: Cannabinoids
wiki/cannabinoids.content:
Overview
Cannabinoids are a group of chemical compounds that interact with the body’s endocannabinoid system, which is involved in the regulation of mood, sleep, and appetite. Phytocannabinoids are derived from the cannabis plant and include the psychoactive THC responsible for producing a high when consumed and CBD which is not considered intoxicating. Endocannabinoids are made naturally by the body. Synthetic cannabinoids can be manufactured in labs to interact with the endocannabinoid system in ways that might strengthen or weaken its influence, or produce unpredictable side effects as any manufactured drug might.
The cannabis plant itself remains illegal at the federal level in the United States, but the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved a few prescription drugs that are derived from cannabinoids. Epidiolex is based in CBD, Cannabidiol, which is extracted from the plant and can treat serious disorders known to cause seizures. Marinol and Syndros are synthetic cannabinoids using THC that can treat nausea and appetite loss found in patients undergoing chemotherapy or managing AIDS. Cesamet is a synthetic cannabinoid similar to THC in structure that can also be used for nausea and vomiting caused by chemotherapy. Over-the-counter cannabinoid products are still illegal, and they lack the same regulatory oversight and testing regimes applied to prescription cannabinoids.

wiki/cannabis.title: Cannabis
wiki/cannabis.content:
Overview
Cannabis refers to a psychoactive substance derived from Cannabis plants, which contains more than 100 compounds called cannabinoids that interact with the body’s endocannabinoid system. It can be consumed through smoking, vaping, edibles, pills, tablets, and lotions to produce feelings of euphoria and relaxation. The main component responsible for the “high” is tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), while cannabidiol (CBD) doesn’t cause a “high” while still having therapeutic properties.

wiki/capsaicin.title: Capsaicin
wiki/capsaicin.content:
Overview
Capsaicin is a natural compound found in chili peppers that creates the sensation of spice and heat by interacting with receptors in our tongue’s nerves designed to detect temperature. The brain interprets this as a physical burn and releases endorphins and dopamine to counteract the perceived discomfort, which can create a “natural high.” Much like substances, regularly eating foods high in capsaicin desensitizes the pain receptors, spicier foods are required to achieve the same sensations and release of endorphins and dopamine. The craving for this type of sensation is associated with thrill-seeking and sometimes referred to as “benign masochism.” Fortunately though, capsaicin doesn’t alter the dopamine-associated reward pathways in the brain that produce the cravings and compulsions associated with substance use disorder. Also, within a single sitting, consuming too much capsaicin can lead to vomiting and intense burning that stop intake and offset the pleasure, and there are no physical withdrawals associated with suddenly stopping.

wiki/carcinogen.title: Carcinogen
wiki/carcinogen.content:
Overview
A carcinogen refers to anything that can increase the risk of developing cancer, whether it’s a substance, an organism, or radiation exposure.
The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) groups carcinogens into four categories based on hazard, defined as whether the carcinogen can cause cancer under any circumstances, rather than risk, defined as the likelihood of the carcinogen causes cancer in typical exposure.


Group 1: Carcinogenic to humans. Examples include tobacco, alcohol, processed meats, radiation exposure, asbestos.


Group 2A: Probably carcinogenic to humans. Examples include red meat, graveyard shifts, extremely hot beverages, byproducts of frying foods.


Group 2B: Possibly carcinogenic to humans. Examples include aloe vera extracts, engine exhausts, pickled vegetables.


Group 3: Not classifiable as carcinogenic. Coffee, tea, fluorescent lighting, chlorinated drinking water.


Yes, I also found it weird that they use 2A, 2B, 3 rather than just 2, 3, and 4.
As for meats, there’s an increasingly popular argument that the disparities in colon cancer and gastrointestinal issues between Western nations and Eastern nations can be tracked to red meat consumption patterns. South Asian countries like India and Bangladesh maintain lower baseline rates of colon cancer, which is often attributed to cultural principles and socioeconomic systems that emphasize plant-centric diets with fiber rather than red or processed meats. In Asian communities that have begun to rapidly industrialize and shifted toward processed foods, GI cancer rates seem to be increasing as well. The exact mechanisms are still being studied, but some theories suggest that red meat diets encourage the growth of inflammatory carcinogenic gut bacteria while plant-based diets promote the growth of fiber-loving bacteria that fortify intestinal linings.

wiki/caregiving.title: Caregiving
wiki/caregiving.content:
Overview
Caregiving is the act or role of providing support to someone who struggles to manage their own lives due to age, illness, disability, or other ailment that makes independent survival difficult or impossible.
People who have substance use disorders are likely to need more caregiving from the community and network around them, but also might have developed a pattern of substance use in response to their own caregiving duties and burnout. Caring for someone in your household who is focusing on their recovery can mean picking up the daily routines and financial obligations they once handled while also dealing with the their own trauma experienced in the course of engaging with a loved one’s active addiction. That itself can lead to substance use to cope, with alcohol being a common way to unwind and induce sleep when the stress of caregiving leads to constant anxiety or insomnia. If a caregiver is managing someone’s pain medication, this gives them direct access to controlled substances; it’s not unheard of for parents to use their children’s prescriptions either. Caregiving is also inherently isolating as it pulls someone away from their usual networks and activities to be dedicated to another’s well-being.
Commentary
Caregiver burnout is implied to be a part of Jesse Pinkman’s story of drug use in Breaking Bad. He grew close to his Aunt Ginny who died of lung cancer seven months after her diagnosis in contrast to parents who are implied to be controlling and abusive. Anecdotally, young people burning out in the course of caregiving for older members of their community, especially family, is a more common story in recovery circles than I had thought. On a related note, one of the most predictive population-level correlates with youth substance use and overdoses is declining socioeconomic mobility. I’d argue this means that the prospect of a bleak future is an incredibly strong driver in self-destructive coping skills.

wiki/cars-peer-recovery-organizations.title: CARS Peer Recovery Organizations
wiki/cars-peer-recovery-organizations.content:
Overview
peer-recovery organizations generally refer to independent centers that address mental health and substance use without a clinical or medical intervention. They provide services such as coaching, support groups, resource navigation for housing and employment, social events, etc. They’re more involved in everyday life than a treatment center, which delivers government-regulated and approved healthcare services.
The Center for Addiction Recovery Support (CARS) is a program run by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, a U.S. government federal agency. The directory they maintain contains, as of August 2026, centers across the country, including some territories like Guam. There is both an interactive search tool available on their website that allows filtering by organization type and location, as well as a PDF containing a spreadsheet with similar information.

wiki/case-management.title: Case Management
wiki/case-management.content:
Overview
Case management is a process in many social work fields that involves a trained case manager evaluating a client and facilitating their connection to health, social, and legal services.
In treatment centers, it’s typical for a patient to be assigned a therapist, a psychiatrist, and a case manager as three independent members of their care team. While therapists can deliver cognitive behavioral interventions and psychiatrists can deliver medications, case managers can help individuals address needs like housing, documentation, employment, peer support, and other aspects of recovery capital.

wiki/catatonia.title: Catatonia
wiki/catatonia.content:
Overview
Catatonia is a syndrome common in mood disorders like major depressive disorders that involves a severely withdrawn affect and difficulty processing information, sometimes appearing to be motionless or repeating certain movements.
The ICD-11 and DSM-5 both recognized catatonia based on a list of criteria, three of which must be met:


Agitation: restlessness or excessive movements


Echolalia: repeating another person’s verbal speech patterns


Echopraxia: repeating another person’s physical movements


Grimacing: holding facial expressions that are disconnected from normal or appropriate emotions in their environment


Stupor: appearing to be immobile and unresponsive


Catalepsy: holding a posture or gesture despite gravity


Waxy flexibility: slight resistance to adjustments to movements


mutism: lack of verbal responsiveness despite appearing to be alert


negativism: resistance or unresponsiveness to instructions or external stimulus


posturing: voluntarily adopting unusual posture


mannerism: exaggerated movements


stereotypy: repetitive movements or gestures that don’t serve any purpose

wiki/category-error.title: Category Error
wiki/category-error.content:
Overview
A category error is a logical error in which some phenomenon is labeled as part of one category when it belongs to another. Children make category errors constantly when learning about the world, which can lead to nonsensical questions like “what color is the number 6?” or “why is the sky angry?” when observing a storm.
History and Etymology
The term was specifically popularized by Gilbert Ryle in The Concept of Mind (1949) as a challenge to Rene Descartes mind-body duality that assumed the mind was a type of invisible formless substance that was independent of the empirically-observable substance that composed the body. Instead, Ryle argued that the mind was not a separate entity from the body at all. What we call the “mind” is simply the cumulative observations that a human body has abilities and states that something like a plant body does not. Thus, Ryle argued that Cartesian dualists were wrong in treating the mind as a category of object rather than a category of behavior that stems from the body.
Within the world of psychology, this disagreement about category errors is the foundational distinction between behaviorists who prioritize the empirically observable and psychodynamic cognitive scientists who propose internal models for the human mind. Behaviorists might argue that cognitive scientists make a category error in assuming the mind has a separate set of processes through which behavior can be redirected. Instead, they might argue that what we call the mind is a construct produced through observing behaviors, so we should measure the behvaior directly rather than speculate about the model and state of mind.

wiki/catharsis.title: Catharsis
wiki/catharsis.content:
Overview
Catharsis in common usage refers to a feeling of intense satisfaction, usually in reference to some kind of repressed emotion, thought, or fantasy being expressed.
History and Etymology
The word is derived from the Ancient Greek term katharsis which was used in the context of spiritual purification. Aristotle used it in Poetics in reference to the way audiences react to tragedies in theaters. By drawing out unpleasant feelings like pity, fear, and grief, the theater can serve to cleanse the audience of these emotions. We might say the modern equivalent is watching a sad movie to help release and work through sadness within us, which we might call a cathartic experience.
In the 19th century, psychologists like Sigmund Freud and Josef Breuer began using the term “catharsis” to describe the release of repressed emotions and trauma lingering in one’s unconscious or subconscious.

wiki/cathinones.title: Cathinones
wiki/cathinones.content:
Overview
Cathinones are a class of stimulants derived from the compounds of the khat plant (Catha edulis). In East Africa and other regions where the khat shrub is found, there are traditions around chewing the leaves for a mild stimulant effect.  “Bath salts” refer to synthetic cathinones, which are called that purely as a marketing gimmick to get around regulations for stimulant drugs. When consumed, they have an effect comparable to amphetamines, cocaine, or MDMA. Bupropion is a synthetic cathinone that also functions as a legally prescribed antidepressant, but makes gradual adjustments to the brain’s dopamine and glutamate pathways rather than mimicking the sudden spikes associated with recreational synthetic cathinone use that leads to addiction.

wiki/catnip.title: Catnip
wiki/catnip.content:
Overview
Catnip (Nepeta cataria), sometimes called catmint, is an herb of the mint family that contains nepetalactone, a terpene that repels insects, causes euphoria in many cats, and has sedative properties when used in herbal teas.
As the name suggests, the herb is strongly associated with its influence on feline species because of its mimicry of familiar pheromones that release endorphines. While many catnip-laced products are freely available on the market for domestic pets, leopards, cougars, lions, and tigers have all been observed reacting to it. About one-third of cats are immune to catnip; whether or not a cat can be influenced by catnip appears to be hereditary.

wiki/ccar-recovery-coach-academy.title: Recovery Coach Academy (RCA)
wiki/ccar-recovery-coach-academy.content:

Although it’s not a license or state certification program itself, its curriculum can satisfy the educational hour requirements of formal credentials for positions like a Certified Peer Recovery Specialist (CPRS) or a Certified Recovery Coach (CRC).

wiki/cesare-lombroso.title: Cesare Lombroso
wiki/cesare-lombroso.content:
Cesare Lombroso is both considered a founder of modern criminology and one of the most prolific eugenicists we’ve seen. Rather than seeing crimes and sin as part of human nature, he believed some people were born with a criminal aptitude, which he theorized was indicative of some reversion of humanity to primitive primates. He thought these natural-born criminals could be identified through physical features, and even the types of crimes they would commit could be determined. He also coined the term “criminaloid” to refer to those who conceal a “criminal personality” underneath a projection of respectability.
Lombroso’s theories ran into empirical problems even his day, but he stubbornly held fast to them. For instance, he believed men were superior to women, but this didn’t square with women being involved in crime far less than men. He actually managed a mental institution himself and became the first professor to specialize in mental health at the University of Pavia. Italian universities did not remove his school of thought from the curriculums until after WWII, because predictably, fascist movements thrived on the aesthetics of scientific legitimacy he provided.
This had nuanced implications for legal systems and policies. Lombroso and his school of biological determinists actually argued that criminality should be understood in the context of biological predisposition to crime, and he advocated for socialist ideas that expressed sympathy for the lower classes suffering from the stigma of poverty. In a way, by arguing that certain people were biologically limited from full participation in society, he was advocating for more lenience than the classical schools of his predecessors. The classical schools of thought that believed
As far as addiction goes, he thought left-handedness led to disabilities like alcoholism.
As as aside, I was watching The Gambler just before writing this, and I’m reminded of the monologue Mark Wahlberg’s character gives about the rage we experience at the unequal distribution of human talent. Someone with every privilege possible can end up completely mediocre in everything they try, while someone born with every disadvantage can be outright prodigious in a way that can be observed at the age of two. That kind of stochasticity is upsetting to people, even those who benefit from the luck of the draw. It’s a different kind of unfairness to realize that you can give your child every advantage possible as a result of your work ethic and judgment, but you can’t do anything about whether your child is predisposed to a talent you could guide or nurture. It’s also similarly uncomfortable to realize that you have access to a talent or perspective no one else does for no discernible reason. You’re different and you don’t know why, and you’re probably going to experience the world differently. That can be lonely and ostracizing in its own way. Even really bad pseudoscience can become a strongly internalized rationalization to fill the gaps.
