wiki/charles-fain-lehman.title: Charles Fain Lehman
wiki/charles-fain-lehman.content:
Links

manhattan.institute/person/charles-fain-lehman

Articles
Harm Reduction
Summary

www.cbsnews.com/news/nyc-drug-addiction-onpoint-harm-reduction/

“‘There is a lot of evidence that interventions of this type generally do not have an appreciable effect on overdose deaths,’ Lehman told CBS News. ‘There’s a fixed pool of resources available for helping people who are dealing with substance use disorder. If you’re spending the dollars on an intervention that doesn’t work, like supervised consumption sites … you’re not spending dollars on [addiction medication] and evidence-based treatment.‘
Commentary
Lehman is wrong. We do have evidence that supervised consumption facilities (SCFs), also referred to as overdose prevention centers (OPCs) or overdose prevention sites (OPSs), have appreciable effects on overdose deaths.
From Kennedy et. al (2017):
“Consistent evidence demonstrates that SCFs mitigate overdose-related harms and unsafe drug use behaviours, as well as facilitate uptake of addiction treatment and other health services among people who use drugs (PWUD). Further, SCFs have been associated with improvements in public order without increasing drug-related crime. SCFs have also been shown to be cost-effective. This systematic review suggests that SCFs are effectively meeting their primary public health and order objectives and therefore supports their role within a continuum of services for PWUD.”
From Levengood et. al (2021):
“Supervised injection facilities in the included studies (n=number of studies per outcome category) were mostly associated with significant reductions in opioid overdose morbidity and mortality (n=5), significant improvements in injection behaviors and harm reduction (n=7), significant improvements in access to addiction treatment programs (n=7), and no increase or reductions in crime and public nuisance (n=7).”
From Potier et. al (2014):
“Seventy-five relevant articles were found. All studies converged to find that SISs were efficacious in attracting the most marginalized PWID, promoting safer injection conditions, enhancing access to primary health care, and reducing the overdose frequency. SISs were not found to increase drug injecting, drug trafficking or crime in the surrounding environments. SISs were found to be associated with reduced levels of public drug injections and dropped syringes. Of the articles, 85% originated from Vancouver or Sydney. Conclusion: SISs have largely fulfilled their initial objectives without enhancing drug use or drug trafficking.”
What is true is that we don’t have enough studies that test whether these sites lower population-level overdose mortality rates, as the evidence we do have is limited and inconsistent. But the goal of these sites is not just to save lives, which we know it does on-site even if the users experience a fatal overdose at a later point in life. It also serves as an access point to the very medical services Lehman is suggesting we spend money on, and it draws users away from public locations towards a designated place with supervision. Studies show it succeeds at these, which is not something we can say for prohibition, mass incarceration, or the War on Drugs. As time goes on, we might find that they can reduce overdose death rates for the population as well. We do know that there is no observable increase in crime or trafficking as a result of these sites, so the fears about drug dealers using these sites as a base to find more customers is unfounded.

wiki/chemical-imbalance.title: Chemical Imbalance
wiki/chemical-imbalance.content:
Overview
The framework of a “chemical imbalance” is a popular one used to conceptualize neurobiological changes that provide the physiological basis for disorders like Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) or Substance Use Disorder (SUD), but the scientific community generally considers it to be an oversimplified model that overlooks neural connectivity and neuroplasticity.
History and Etymology
As with many models of health and anatomy that become embedded in the public consciousness, the notion of a chemical imbalance as the root cause of mental health disorders was fueled by marketing campaigns. From the 1950s to the 1960s, clinicians who prescribed medications to address infections like tuberculosis or chronic conditions like high blood pressure noticed that they also improved patients’ moods. Joseph Schildkraut formally proposed a framework for depression in 1965 that claimed a deficiency in monoamine neurotransmitters (such as norepinephrine and serotonin) was a cause for depression. After all, it seemed pretty straightforward and logical to conclude that if a medication raised the level of a neurotransmitter while improving mood, then a deficiency of that neurotransmitter was related to the low mood. When Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs) like Prozac, Zoloft, and Paxil were created, pharmaceutical companies rolled out marketing campaigns that used the model of a chemical imbalance to explain their mechanisms. The model was also used by public health advocates to address the stigma of mental health conditions being problems of morality or character without a physiological basis. However, by the early 2000s, the scientific community had accumulated ample evidence that people with depression did not actually have a measurable chemimcal deficiency in the brain. Antidepressants appeared to work by promoting other factors in the brain involved with repair and growth through flooding the brain with neurotransmitters.

wiki/child-abuse.title: Child Abuse
wiki/child-abuse.content:
Overview
“Child abuse” refers to any act or neglect from a caregiver that leads to harm or risk of harm to someone under the age of 18.
Children who undergo severe mistreatment and abuse for a prolonged period of time are two to four times more likely to develop a substance use disorder than children without a history of abuse. Individuals who score 4 or higher on standard Adverse Childhood Experience (ACE) assessments are eight times more likely to develop alcohol use disorder. Surveys of adults in treatment for substance use show that 60-80% of patients reported significant abuse during childhood. Multi-decade studies that follow children who suffered abuse into adulthood tends to validate these elevated risk ratios.
Commentary
As with all public health issues, screenings and counseling to intervene as early as possible is paramount in the effort to improve quality of life and reduce lifelong treatment costs.

wiki/chinatown.title: Chinatown
wiki/chinatown.content:
Overview
A “Chinatown” refers to a neighborhood where immigrants or cultural establishments from China are concentrated.
History and Etymology
The term “Chinatown” emerged from the California Gold Rush around the 1850s amidst anti-immigrant hysteria as labor groups blamed Chinese workers for taking jobs rather than poor speculative decisions from investors in a railroad bubble. Xenophobia and anti-drug hysteria often go hand-in-hand with both assigned the quality of an exotic Other that disrupts the order of the status quo. When Chinatown communities set up opium dens that took the customers that bars in white neighborhoods frequented, the local governments passed restrictions on opium to give law enforcement cover to disrupt all networks with Chinese immigrants, not just the drug users in Chinatown.

wiki/chloroform.title: Chloroform
wiki/chloroform.content:
Overview
Chloroform, or trichloromethane, is a compound used in research labs and the manufacturing of plastics like Teflon, though it was briefly used as an anesthetic in the mid-19th century before the potential for severe toxicity was acknowledged. There was a period of time in the late-19th century when some European elites, particularly in Paris, experimented with it for recreational use alongside ether and opium. However, compared to other substances, the window in which someone can experience euphoric effects is very small while the risk of fatal respiratory paralysis and organ toxicity is incredibly high.

wiki/chronic-alcoholism-in-the-first-hal.title: Chronic Alcoholism in the First Half of the 19th Century by William F. Bynum (1968)

wiki/chronic-disease.title: Chronic Disease
wiki/chronic-disease.content:
Overview
The American Center for Disease Control (CDC) defines chronic diseases as “conditions that last 1 year or more and require ongoing medical attention or limit activities of daily living or both.” The most common chronic diseases in the United States are heart disease, cancer, and diabetes, which are considered preventable to various extents. The vast majority of adults in America have at least one chronic health condition, with more than half having two or more. This isn’t skewed much by older demographics; 60% of adults between the ages of 18 and 34 have at least one chronic condition.
Many of these health issues can increase the vulnerability to other issues. The global cases of chronic kidney disease (CKD) has more than doubled since 1990, and about 15% of adults in the United States developed it. The risk for CKD increases through diabetes, high blood pressure, and obesity. Up to 90% of people with early-stage CKD are unaware they have it or appear asymptomatic until severe damage triggers emergency visits, though basic blood tests and urine assays can screen for it early. Their chronic impact on lifespan and quality of life is comparable to major respiratory and cardiovascular diseases. Stress, anxiety, and depression elevates hormones like cortisol and increases systemic inflammation, which produces a higher baseline risk for heart disease, stroke, and dementia.
The global prevalence of mental health conditions have increased by 95.5% since 1990, with depression and anxiety contributing the most. More than 1 in 8 Americans have met the diagnostic criteria for clinical depression. That number is even higher among adolescents, as the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) finds that almost 1 in 5 adolescents screened positive for depression. The CDC’s Youth Risk Behavior Survey (YRBS) finds that almost 1 in 3 adolescents will meet the criteria for an anxiety disorder before turning 18 and 1 in 5 high schoolers have had serious suicidal ideation in the 12 months before the survey.
Asian, Black, and Hispanic students experiencing targeted racial discrimination have more than twice the risk of developing suicidal ideation or attempting suicide. The vast majority of adolescents regardless of ethnicity do not receive the required prescription medications for their diagnosis. Only 17% of white teens, 10% of Hispanic teens, 8% of Black teens, and 4% of Asian teens are able to access appropriate medication for themselves.
Asian-American teens are the least likely to receive any form of mental health services, and when they do, it’s usually after the condition has become severe and begun to produce acute crises. Even after that, 55% report difficulties finding a provider who understands their cultural backgrounds and lived experiences. There are nuances that emerge across gender: Asian-American girls are more likely to report suicidal ideation and depression while 70% of suicide mortalities among Asian-American youth are male. It’s hardly a wonder that many of these teens turn to substance use to self-medicate, and some fraction of those develop a dependence or substance use disorder in the attempts to regulate themselves.

wiki/chronic-pain.title: Chronic Pain
wiki/chronic-pain.content:
Overview
Chronic pain is generally defined as pain that continues for over three months even after an injury has healed or illness has subsided. Often, it results from modifications to the nervous system that causes the brain to continuously perceive pain. The same neuroplasticity that the brain uses to learn and heal from mental health conditions also allows for the brain to misinterpret harmless input or mild discomfort as extreme pain. Unfortunately, the brain can also end up interpreting this pain as a stressor that triggers chronic fight-or-flight modes, so that the problems of chronic pain are closely interwoven with the problems of chronic stress. The prefrontal cortex, responsible for decision-making and self-control, can produce brain fog.
Many who suffer from chronic pain turn to substance use to self-medicate and seek relief, which can quickly become a vicious cycle as the additional pains and brain changes of chronic substance use or dependence exacerbate the initial symptoms of distress. Opioids that are prescribed for chronic pain can increase sensitivity to it, called hyperalgesia, through inflammation and changes to the spinal cord’s chemistry. Naturally this might cause someone to consume even more opioids to manage that which then further increases sensitivity. Recent research shows that individuals with a genetic predisposition to developing substance use disorders also have genetic variations that can predispose them to chronic pain.

wiki/cigarettes.title: Cigarettes
wiki/cigarettes.content:
Overview
Cigarettes are rolls of paper containing finely cut tobacco that are lit with a flame on one end so that smoke can be inhaled from the other end. They are considered tobacco containing tobacco products (TCTP), likely the first one that comes to mind for most people.
Modern cigarettes include about 600 additives to raw tobacco leaf. Freebase nicotine: ammonia is added to nicotine so that it vaporizes more efficiently and crosses the blood-brain barrier faster. Sensory modifiers like sugars, cocoa, and menthol are added to ease the naturally harsh character of burning tobacco.
Upon being lit, cigarettes produce a mixture of over 7000 chemicals like monoxide, formaldehyde, arsenic, and at least 69 carcinogens. Cigarette smoke is recognized as a leading cause of disease and death since it damages nearly every organ system.

wiki/cinchona.title: Cinchona
wiki/cinchona.content:
Overview
“Cinchona” describes a genus of plants within the coffee family whose bark is a source of quinine and quinidine, which have historically been used to treat treatment-resistant strains of malaria, heart arrhythmias, and nocturnal leg muscle cramping.
Some commercial products like tonic water contain small amounts of quinine that is known to add a bitter taste. However, in high quantities, often found in unregulated supplements, it’s toxic enough to produce a syndrome called cinchonism, characterized by:


tinnitus, or a persistent ringing in the ears


headaches


dizziness


altered vision


nausea


heart block


fatal arrhythmias


hearing loss


thrombocytopenia, or a drop in blood platelets


miscarriage


History and Etymology
By 1944, the technology to develop synthetic quinine led to a decline in large-scale cultivation of the plant, though it remains significant culturally (e.g. as the national tree of Peru.)

wiki/circular-inference.title: Circular Inference
wiki/circular-inference.content:
Overview
Circular inference, not to be confused with circular reasoning, is a mathematical model of information-processing defects in the brain where internal predictions are processed as external sensory evidence instead of balancing each other. The concept is used often in interpreting the neurological basis of disordered thinking patterns found in conditions like schizophrenia.
In a typical brain, bottom-up sensory information is gathered and passed on as raw data to be interpreted by regions responsible for holding a model of the world based on memory and context, like the prefrontal cortext. If we step outside after a long day and our senses tell us that the sky is dark and the air is chilly, our higher-level models of the world inform us that this is because it’s nighttime and the sun has set.
Conditions like schizophrenia lead to a breakdown in this process as the neurons responsible for inhibiting a message after its processing fail to function correctly. Excitatory pathways that amplify messages and signals continue to pass input around. If someone steps outside and expects the sun to be up because they believe it should still be daytime, the brain interprets this as a fact rather than an expectation from an internal model, so that person might be more likely to think that something has gone wrong with the sun or passage of time itself. As a less extreme example, someone who feels anxious in a room might generate expectations to locate the source of the stimulus creating anxiety, like the suspicion that someone across the room taking notes is actually logging their movements. Rather than being evaluated against context in the way cognitive therapies encourage challenging irrational distortions, this message loops repeatedly through the brain and registers as empirical evidence each time. This can produce a very strong and sincerely held belief as the brain struggles to distinguish thoughts generated through its internal models from sensory perceptions.
History and Etymology
The term was formally defined by Renaud Jardri and Sophie Denève in a 2013 paper published in the journal Brain called Circular Inferences in Schizophrenia.

wiki/circular-reasoning.title: Circular Reasoning
wiki/circular-reasoning.content:
Overview
Circular reasoning is a common logical fallacy in which an argument’s conclusion is used as evidence for the argument.
Examples:


“We should support this candidate because they are the only electable choice.” In politics, electability arguments often suffer from circular reasoning; they are electable because people would vote for them, and people would vote for them because they are electable.


“Decriminalizing marijuana would be condoning illegal behavior.” There is an implicit idea that something being illegal makes it immoral, so something illegal must stay illegal because it is illegal. It is the law that makes it illegal to begin with.


“Everyone pays attention to them because they’re always doing something newsworthy.” Calling something “newsworthy” is already implying that it’s the type of thing people will attention to, so reporting on something because it’s arbitrarily deemed newsworthy becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. People pay attention to what is reported on, which is what makes something newsworthy to begin with.


“The patient is suffering from maladaptive behaviors because of cognitive distortions, and we know that they’re having distorted thoughts because they keep choosing maladaptive behaviors.” Some Cognitive-Behavioral Theory (CBT) applications can fall into the trap of setting up frameworks in which irrationality is necessarily the problem behind every issue. A clinician might assume that a patient presents with depression because they mention irrational thoughts or patterns that are self-deprecating as symptoms, but those irrational thoughts or patterns are also seen as a cause of the depressed state of mind that prevents rational perceptions that should change their experience of reality.


“The patient is resistant to treatment because they’re not applying the coping skills we taught them, and we know they’re not applying the coping skills because the treatment has not been improving their symptoms.” If a patient tries every CBT coping skill but fails, a clinician can interpret that as the patient being resistant or failing to apply the skills properly. It’s difficult to argue that the coping skills were applied appropriately but just weren’t that effective, or that depression or anxiety are actually rational reactions to certain circumstances. This circular reasoning always leads to the patient being resistant.

wiki/clergy-recovery-groups-from-the-ame.title: Clergy Recovery Groups from the American Anglican Council

wiki/clinical-decision-support-system.title: Clinical Decision Support System
wiki/clinical-decision-support-system.content:
Overview
A clinical decision support system (CDSS) is a tool that helps a doctor collect data and make decisions about patient care.
History and Etymology
The term was coined by Gerald A. Goertzel in 1969, who envisioned a system that would eliminate messy guessing and documentation in favor of a standard structured codes that computers could then analyze. Despite the recent hype around Artificial Intelligence, designs for automated systems to support experts go back to the mid-20th century, as soon as it became clear that computers would be more commonplace in institutions and eventually homes. Goertzel treated every entity in the patient’s record as a node in a network where relationships were mapped as edges between them. However, implementing these systems required doctors to translate their notes into codes that the computer would interpret, which they despised doing. Natural language processing (NLP) techniques that could parse handwritten notes or record human speech didn’t exist back then.

wiki/clinical-trial.title: Clinical Trial
wiki/clinical-trial.content:
Overview
A clinical trial is a research experiment that tests medical or behavioral procedures in humans to measure effectiveness and detect risks.
Clinical trials in modern scientific institutions generally follow four phases:


An investigation in a small group of people, typically less than 100, to scope out the ranges for safe dosages and document side effects to look at.


A larger trial on 100-300 people to begin tracking treatment effectiveness.


A trial with hundreds or thousands of patients to obtain coverage across multiple regions and monitor side effects in a diverse selection of people


Monitoring long-term safety and effects across a population after approval has been granted

wiki/cluster-b-personality-traits.title: Cluster B Personality Traits
wiki/cluster-b-personality-traits.content:
Overview
Cluster B personality traits makes it difficult for someone to control their emotions and maintain stable, healthy relationships. There are four personality disorders recognized by the DSM-5:


Antisocial Personality Disorder, characterized by a pattern of disregard for the rights of others and a lack of empathy after manipulation


Borderline Personality Disorder, involving intense mood swings surrounding a fear of abandonment and feelings of emptiness


Histrionic Personality Disorder, defined by a strong need to be the center of attention through overly dramatic actions or their physical appearance


Narcissistic Personality Disorder, in which someone has an inflated sense of self-importance with a desire for attention and praise that disregards the feelings of others

wiki/co-occurring-disorders.title: Co-Occurring Disorders
wiki/co-occurring-disorders.content:
Overview
A co-occurring disorder refers to someone having a mental health condition at the same time as substance use disorder. Sometimes, this is also referred to as a “dual diagnosis” or “comorbidity.” Increasingly, mental health professionals and facilities have begun to recognize that treating substance use disorders only leaves other disorders intact that may have been a source of self-medication. Studies show that addressing trauma at the same time as substance use is more effective than prior assumptions that stability through sobriety was needed before deeper work on trauma could be done.

wiki/co-regulation.title: Co-Regulation
wiki/co-regulation.content:
Overview
Co-regulation describes the process through which two nervous systems influence each other’s state and activities. It includes both internal physiology, such as shared changes in stress and bonding hormone levels, as well as external behaviors mimicking each other.
One of the most common examples of co-regulation involves the parent-child dynamic. A child being joyful can lower cortisol and raise oxytocin in a parent, which indicates to the parent that the child is not under any kind of threat. On the other hand, a child crying can cause a spike in a parent’s adrenaline which prompts them to assess for threats. The parent, if they find none, can then attempt to calm the child by presenting a calm presence for them to emulate. If a parent reacts to a child’s distress with their own distress, this can end up spiraling into co-dysregulation. In many cases, the child’s nervous system attempts to regulate the parents back, which can lead to the child applying survival mode thinking to the parents’ reactions to avoid abandonment or punishment.
Commentary
Midsommar
Midsommar is an excellent representation of co-regulation, though I don’t mean at all that it’s healthy or worthy of being emulated.

wiki/coalition-for-cannabinoid-policy-ed.title: Coalition for Cannabinoid Policy, Education, and Regulation (CPEAR)
wiki/coalition-for-cannabinoid-policy-ed.content:
Overview
The Coalition for Cannabinoid Policy, Education, and Regulation (CPEAR) is a non-profit dedicated to advocating for a science-driven regulatory framework for cannabis and cannabinoids. It brings together industry representatives, academia, think tanks, public safety officials, medical professionals, financial services firms, and social justice organizations. 1
Links



Footnotes


Home - Coalition for Cannabinoid Policy, Education, and Regulation (CPEAR) ↩

wiki/coalition-for-whole-health.title: Coalition for Whole Health
wiki/coalition-for-whole-health.content:
Overview
The Coalition for Whole Health is a national coalition of over 150 organizations with the goal of ensuring federal health care laws fully fund and include mental health disorders, including substance use prevention, treatment, and recovery. It’s managed under the Legal Action Center (LAC), a non-profit for law and policies concerning mental health.

wiki/coalition-on-physician-education-in.title: Coalition on Physician Education in Substance Use Disorders (COPE)

wiki/coast-mental-health-foundation.title: Coast Mental Health Foundation
wiki/coast-mental-health-foundation.content:
Overview
Coast Mental Health Foundation is the fundraising and public awareness arm of Coast Mental Health, a Canadian non-profit with the mission of supporting recovery, housing, employment, education, and other social programs for people with mental health conditions. 1
Links



Footnotes


Home - Coast Mental Health ↩

wiki/coca.title: Coca
wiki/coca.content:
Overview
Coca is a plant native to South America known for containing the alkaloid used in cocaine.
Fun fact, the United States has authorized exactly one commercial organization to import and process coca leaves called the Stepan Company with a facility in Maywood, New Jersey. The coca extract, free of cocaine, is sold to The Coca-Cola Company as an ingredient for soda while the filtered cocaine itself is sold to Mallinckrodt as a topical anesthetic for surgeries. Even though the coca leaf extract can be replaced with a synthetically-manufactured substitute, it allows the Coca Cola company to justify keeping Coca in the brand name. This means that the United States government effectively has state-backed monopolies for coca and cocaine within the beverage and pharmaceutical industries.

wiki/cocaine.title: Cocaine
wiki/cocaine.content:
Overview
Cocaine is an alkaloid derived from coca plants (primarily Erythroxylum coca) in South America that serves as a stimulant by causing a buildup of dopamine, serotonin, and norepinephrine.

wiki/codependence.title: Codependence
wiki/codependence.content:
Overview
Codependence refers to a relationship dynamic characterized by unhealthy reliance on each other. Even when one person might appear to be entirely dependent on another, financially, socially, interpersonally, etc., the other person may have a need to feel like they’re rescuing someone in order to feel secure. This doesn’t apply just to romantic or family dynamics either; friendships and professional relationships can also be characterized by codependence.
Codependence and substance use disorders have a bidirectional relationship. Someone with a substance use disorder can quickly become dependent on someone else to manage daily life as the consequences of chronic substance use interferes with their functioning. At the same time, someone in a codependent relationship who regularly experiences violations in their boundaries can end up using substances to cope.

wiki/codependent-no-more.title: Codependent No More
wiki/codependent-no-more.content:
This book was one of the first to bring the term “codependency” out of academic jargon and into the public vernacular through the self-help format. By explicitly applying the 12 step process to codependency, Melody Beattie directly inspired the formation of Codependents Anonymous (CoDA). However, modern psychologists have been critical of the book’s conceptualization of co-dependency.
Links

wiki/cognitive-behavioral-therapy.title: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT)
wiki/cognitive-behavioral-therapy.content:
Overview
Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) refers to a set of therapeutic modalities that focus on the connection between thoughts, feelings, and actions with the goal of questioning and reframing thought patterns to promote shifts in behavioral patterns.
Commentary
So, CBT is controversial. Perspectives on CBT are also controversial. There is no way to talk about CBT without making someone upset. But there are ways to talk about CBT that are at least somewhat anchored in the efficacy explored by research.
I’ll be upfront: I’ve soured on CBT after my experiences with its mass operationalization through manualized worksheets and exercises in group settings, which is the dominant form of psychoeducation or group therapy in most rehabilitation facilities. I fully acknowledge that the biases resulting from my bad experiences colors the way I approach the theory of CBT, not just the flawed implementations of it in practice. I’m still grouchy though.

wiki/cognitive-capacity.title: Cognitive Capacity
wiki/cognitive-capacity.content:
Overview
Cognitive capacity generally refers to the mental abilities and functions involved in language processing, memory and attention spans, sensory perception, decision-making, and ability to learn. As a concept, it isn’t a discrete property that’s easy to measure, so definitions and assessments vary a lot. Adjacent phrases that refer to similar concepts include “mental bandwidth”, “brainpower,” and “mental real estate.”

wiki/cognitive-distortion.title: Cognitive Distortion
wiki/cognitive-distortion.content:
Overview
Cognitive distortions in the context of psychology are irrational thought patterns that can worsen symptoms of depression or anxiety. Common distortions include:


All-or-Nothing Thinking


Catastrophizing


Overgeneralization


Mental Filtering


Disqualifying the Positive


Mind Reading


Fortune Telling


Emotional Reasoning


“Should” Statements


Personalization


A major goal of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) is identifying and then reframing these patterns within oneself to reduce unhelpful experiences.
History and Etymology
Cognitive distortions were popularized within psychotherapy by Aaron Beck in the 1960s as part of the movement towards CBT.
Commentary
My thoughts on CBT and the concept of cognitive distortions have changed a lot over time. Initially, I really liked the idea of being able to prune my mind of irrational and dysfunctional ideas to have a better mental toolkit at my disposal. Over time though, I ended up highly skeptical of putting the idea of cognitive distortions into practice.
As a general rule, I dislike the idea of institutions shaping reality for individuals. Power dynamics inherently corrupt the exchange of knowledge in my view as it is impossible for someone subject to another’s power to not alter their conduct based on the fact of that power alone, almost by the definition of what power is as a capacity to change aspects of reality. I argue that, within the context of Eurocentric “Western” nations, spiritual and mental healing is heavily modeled after the moral-psychology of the institution of confession, where an expert backed by an institution is given the power to elicit and define someone’s true essence so that they conform to the social expectations that define functionality.
Cognitive distortions and irrationality are concepts that take for granted that some objective reality exists and that someone’s interpretation of reality can be determined to be out of alignment with the objective version based on their emotional distress. Consider that people aren’t assigned to CBT because they’ve demonstrated a pattern of irrational thinking or logical errors, but because they’ve experienced emotional distress that has risen to the level of a pathologized health condition, and it is believed that improving the client’s rational or logical thinking can improve their symptoms of distress. The Cognitive Errors Rating Scale (CERS) is a measure of 15 cognitive errors that trained evaluators can apply to the transcripts of therapy sessions, and studies that examine its correlation to other scales like the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI) find that there generally isn’t much observable difference in depression symptoms between those with high and low cognitive distortions. In fact, most clients processed the data they were considering quite logically, and where they actually struggled most was in considering all available data before applying their logic.
For instance, a client whose boss reprimands them for being late one day might experience distress and believe that they’re being seen as a failing employee. The issue here isn’t that the client is processing the feedback illogically, as it follows logically that if someone is being fairly reprimanded then they failed to meet some expectation, but that the client is overlooking all the positive feedback they’re received to assign more weight to the negative feedback. This isn’t a logic or rationality issue as much as an attunement to potential threats as a survival mechanism. Someone who grew up in an environment where authority figures were quick to deliver harsh consequences for minor failures is not being irrational in placing much more weight on negative feedback than positive feedback. No amount of positive feedback guarantees job security, but any negative feedback can become a reason to be fired or laid off. The client might spiral into all-or-nothing thinking if they feel “I can’t do anything right,” but “I won’t have security no matter how many things I do right” is a distinct and very realistic premise. A therapist can’t step into the client’s life and understand it through their lived experiences to make a comparable judgment either. Consequently, studies have repeatedly found that CBT practitioners lack consensus around the use of cognitive distortion categories and consistently blur the lines between formal logic problems and differences in a client’s personal values. One study found 567 distinct variations of what a cognitive distortion is across clinical literature.
Links


Three Problems with the Theory of Cognitive Therapy


Cognitive Errors in Cognitive Behavioral Therapy: A Survey of Researchers and Practitioners and an Assessment of the Face Validity of the Cognitive Error Rating Scale (Milman & Drapeau, 2012)


Cognitive Distortion: Propositions and Possible Worlds

wiki/cognitive-load.title: Cognitive Load
wiki/cognitive-load.content:
Overview
Cognitive load refers to the strain or burden put onto someone’s working memory.
History and Etymology
The idea of humans having limited mental bandwidth has been observed for a long time. Modern cognitive psychology has been interested in measuring the limits and mechanisms of that bandwidth and related capacities. In 1956, George Miller published a study that found our short-term memory is generally limited to holding about five to nine items at a time. In 1968, Richard Atkinson and Richard Shiffrin proposed a model of information flow through sensory memory, working memory, and long-term memory. Herbert Simon and William Chase published a 1973 study that examined the patterns of Chess Grandmasters to conclude that they organized blocks of pieces into chunks, or “schemas”, rather than looking at each piece individually. Educational psychologists were particularly interested in exploring the way models of the world are created, updated, and applied. Richard Anderson used the concept of schemas to show that reading comprehension is heavily driven by prior context about the world a reader has developed. David Rumelhart furthered the idea of using schemas to navigate the world in 1980 by proposing a theory that schemas are fundamental building blocks of intelligent cognition which allows minds to navigate the world without becoming overwhelmed by sensory input and information.
Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) was developed into a formal framework in 1988 by John Sweller. While studying the way students approached math and science problems, he noticed that the trial-and-error approach of problem-solving that worked when navigating daily life consumed massive amouts of mental energy, so students often didn’t have the capacity left to internalize an abstract concept after completing a problem. He and other researchers delineated a few categories of cognitive load:


Intrinsic Load: how difficult a topic is to learn on its own. College-level math courses will almost certainly register as inherently difficult for most people relative to the abstractions and operations needed for their daily lives.


Extraneous Load: how difficult the environment makes it to learn the topic. If you have an apathetic teacher, obnoxious classmates, or a hungry stomach, you have a variety of factors that can make it difficult to learn topics that have a low intrinsic load


Germane Load: how much effort it takes to build long-term schemas by building relationships between past knowledge and new information. A topic might be easy to learn and a stellar learning environment may be accessible for a student, but if the material is only presented through extremely dense texts or complicated software, the student has to expend extra effort to allocate attention to the medium of the information itself. They might have to remember how to use the software at the same time that they’re trying to connect the material presented within it.


In practice, these forms of cognitive load are considered to be interconnected with significant overlap in their mechanisms.

wiki/cognitive-reframing.title: Cognitive Reframing
wiki/cognitive-reframing.content:
Overview
Cognitive reframing in modern psychology refers to a shift in mindset that can change the perspective interpreted from a situation. Within Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), cognitive reframing is considered a valuable coping skill to diffuse distressing emotions by finding an equally valid interpretation of the same facts of a situation, generally to shift away from catastrophizing or black-and-white thinking. Here are some basic examples of how cognitive reframing works in practice:


You notice that some of your friends go to a party without you. An instinctive, unhelpful thought born out of a fear of abandonment might be “my friends didn’t want me to come with them because they’re souring on me.” A reframed thought might be “my friends have relationships and interests outside of me, so it makes sense that they won’t invite me to every single thing they do.”


You’re texting someone you have a romantic interest in, but they don’t reply to your texts as quickly as you reply to theirs. The unhelpful thought might be “they’re losing interest in me because they don’t like talking to me.” A reframed thought might be “they have a busy life outside of me and they want to reply to me thoughtfully from a position of comfortable focus.”


Your boss gives you feedback about what you could be doing better on your first day of work. The impulse to catastrophize might lead to thinking “I’m not a good fit for this role and it’s only a matter of time that they find out I’m a fraud.” A smoother reframing might be “my boss probably didn’t expect a new hire to do things perfectly on their first day, and they’re spending time and energy giving me feedback because they intend to keep me on the job.”


You forget to pay a phone bill in time. An inner critic might say “I’m so irresponsible, I can’t do anything right.” A helpful reframing might be “everyone makes mistakes, so I’m just normal, and I might be able to set reminders next time so it doesn’t happen again.”


You experience a headache. The tendency to worry (paired with a search on WebMD or consultation with Dr. Google) can lead to the thought “I have brain cancer.” A reframing that can ground someone from this state of mind is “headaches are normal and happen all the time because of simple things like dehydration, stress, or lack of rest.”


Cognitive reframing, when done right, isn’t about gaslighting yourself away from realistic problems through toxic positivity, though certainly a lot of implementations of cognitive reframing exercises lend themselves to that. Ideally, it’s about neutralizing black-and-white thinking, catastrophizing, and analysis paralysis by remembering that the worst-case interpretation of a scenario isn’t necessarily true. There are other interpretations and possibilities than what our preexisting schemas might set up for us.

wiki/cold-intimacies.title: Cold Intimacies
wiki/cold-intimacies.content:
Overview
“Cold intimacies” is a concept proposed by Eva Illouz that refers to the way interpersonal connections are mapped onto transactional frameworks and intangible aspects of lived human experience are treated as commodities. Illouz posits that cold intimacies are a byproduct of the intersection between industrialized bureaucracies, institutions of psychological management, and socioeconomic conditions under capitalism.
If this sounds abstract, think about the last time that a boss or manager referred to the company as a supportive family and extolled the virtues of workplace productivity as a source of existential fulfillment. These only superficially cover the contractual arrangement underlying the labor agreements of the workplace for the sake of promoting a sense of psychological wellbeing. Nothing about the emotional and empathetic expressions we observe from others in the workplace provides security against a contract that allows you to be fired from the family if the cost of supporting you no longer justifies itself.
Commentary
Severance
Severance tackles the absurdity of cold intimacies taken to the extreme, where a company fully takes on the role of a guardian that defines the parameters of the world and relationships individuals experience.

wiki/cold-turkey.title: Cold Turkey
wiki/cold-turkey.content:
Overview
“Cold turkey” is an informal phrase that references attempts to quit substance use suddenly at once rather than gradually reducing usage over time.
With some substances like alcohol and benzodiazepines, this can be fatal, so it’s almost never a good idea to quit cold turkey. It really is gambling with your life, and most medically-managed detoxification protocols will make your experience vastly more comfortable than quitting at once. If quitting at home or on one’s own, a better idea is to gradually taper off drinking patterns, with a rule of thumb being to decrease the total amount of drinks consumed per day by 2. That being said, I am not a doctor and have no medical training, so I cannot give medical advice and nothing on this page or site should be construed as such.
Even outside of alcohol and benzos, quitting cold turkey can be a miserable experience. Modern medicine has come up with some really helpful solutions to managing some of the symptoms of withdrawal, and I highly encourage you to take advantage of them instead of trying to tough it out. There are no extra credit points given for getting sober on your own without help.

wiki/collegiate-recovery-and-interventio.title: Collegiate Recovery and Intervention Services (CRIS)
wiki/collegiate-recovery-and-interventio.content:
Overview
The Collegiate Recovery and Intervention Services (CRIS) under the Collegiate Recovery Community (CRC) at the University of Alabama offers both clinical interventions and an abstinence-based recovery community. Their services include:


First Steps Program: early intervention for students experiencing low or moderate negative consequences from their substance use


Insight Program: individualized clinical intervention and strategies for navigating campus life


University Community Program (UCP): an intensive outpatient intervention designed for students who need structure and external accountability


Community Campus Drug Court Program: an intensive drug court diversion program for students facing offenses related to substance use


Specialized Clinical Care: screenings, counseling, and other direct support for students struggling with SUDs, eating disorders, or problem gambling

wiki/collegiate-recovery-community.title: Collegiate Recovery Community
wiki/collegiate-recovery-community.content:
Overview
The Michigan State University Collegiate Recovery community (CRC) offers a campus environment for students seeking recovery from Substance Use Disorders (SUDs). Their services include recovery-focused housing, peer support meetings, 24/7 student lounge, administering the Jamie Daniels Memorial Scholarship, Recovery Ally Training, sober recreational activities, and harm reduction through overdose prevention training and Naloxone (Narcan) distribution. Data from the MSU National College Health Assessment Survey shows that 3.2% (1600) of campus members identify as being in recovery.

wiki/communities-mobilizing-for-change-o.title: Communities Mobilizing for Change on Alcohol (CMCA)
wiki/communities-mobilizing-for-change-o.content:
Overview
Communities Mobilizing for Change on Alcohol (CMCA) describes a community-level public health intervention aimed at reducing underage drinking by shaping institutional practices and local social norms. Some of these include:


Mandatory Retail Compliance Checks: law enforcement agents might regularly send undercover decoys who look underage to see if clerks ask for valid ID at establishments that sell alcohol. Sometimes this is reinforced through rewards for refusing sale to a minor and legal warnings for those who fail to do so. Consequences can escalate from fines to suspensions of liquor licenses.


Mandatory Responsible Beverage Service (RBS) Training: local laws might require all workers at establishments that sell liquor to undergo certified training to check IDs and spot potential fakes.


Keg Registration: laws might require that every keg of beer have a traceable tag attached with a unique ID that allows it to be tracked to the adult who purchased it in case it appears in the possession of underage drinkers. Some laws might go as far as to hold the property owner where underage drinking occurs liable under civil or criminal laws.


Zoning Restrictions: these might limit the number of liquor licenses that can be issued in commercial or residential areas, or they might mandate that liquor stores be a minimum distance from public zones and child-centered areas like schools or playgrounds.


Sobriety Checkpoints: Law enforcement agents might increase these roadside checkpoints to address drinking under the influence generally, although advertising these checkpoints in media, especially online, can be a deterrent for underage drinkers.


CMCA acknowledges that programs like DARE focused on individual education will still fail to land with lots of teens (with many studies questioning claims about DARE’s basic effectiveness), so CMCA instead targets the adults in the environment who might provide alcohol or be responsible for monitoring minors for alcohol use. This gives CMCA an edge on influencing young adults over 18 with increased independence.

wiki/community-based-participatory-actio.title: Community-Based Participatory Action Research (CBPAR)
wiki/community-based-participatory-actio.content:
Overview
Community-Based Participatory Action Research (CBPAR) is a research approach that treats the participants being observed as equal partners in the study as the experts conducting the experiment with the goal of more closely integrating their findings with real-world environments.

wiki/community-mental-health-centers-act.title: Community Mental Health Centers Act of 1963

wiki/community-trials.title: Community Trials (CT)
wiki/community-trials.content:
Overview
“Community trial” sounds self-explanatory as studies that collect data from communities, but this type of collection usually requires paying special attention to the structure of communities beyond just a population-level bucket of relationships. Communities are grounded in physical geographical spaces that sustain institutions and cultures with unique histories understood differently by diverse perspectives.

wiki/comorbidities.title: Comorbidities
wiki/comorbidities.content:
Overview
A comorbidity is a medical condition that occurs alongside another condition. For instance, diabetes and hypertension are common comorbidities, as are depression and anxiety. Sometimes the conditions directly related through the mechanisms they operate through, where one is caused by the other or they share underlying dysfunctions. It’s also possible for them to just have shared risk factors like poor diet with high cholesterol or smoking. Sometimes they’re called co-occurring disorders instead.

wiki/comprehensive-center-for-pain-and-a.title: Comprehensive Center for Pain and Addiction (CCPA)
wiki/comprehensive-center-for-pain-and-a.content:
Overview
The Comprehensive Center for Pain & Addiction (CCPA) at the University of Arizona was founded in 2020 as a research and clinical hub to address the intersection between chronic pain and substance use, particularly in the wake of the opioid crisis and the demand for non-addictive medications to manage pain. Their services include workforce training like a minor degree in Substance Use Disorder (SUD), harm-reduction advocacy for treatments like buprenorphine, and facilitation of clinical trials like direct transcranial stimulation.

wiki/compulsion.title: Compulsion
wiki/compulsion.content:
Overview
Compulsions are reptitive behaviors someone feels they have to do in order to alleviate the anxiety called by persistent thoughts.
Common compulsions include handwashing, showering, checking if the stove is off or doors are locked, silently or mentally counting repetitively, or arranged items in a specific order or pattern.

wiki/computational-psychiatry.title: Computational Psychiatry
wiki/computational-psychiatry.content:
Overview
Computational psychiatry refers to a field of applying computational methods to interpret data from brain activity and human behavior to drive clinical treatments of mental health conditions. This includes both optimizing health outcomes for individual patients and driving theoretical models forward with data and, more recently, machine learning.

wiki/concentration.title: Concentration
wiki/concentration.content:
Overview
The American Psychological Association provides a definition for “focus”, though not “concentration” itself, but we can consider the two synonymous: ""the concentration or centering of attention on a stimulus

wiki/confession.title: Confession
wiki/confession.content:
Overview
The concept of a confession is much deeper than just sharing a secret with someone, which is how we commonly speak of it.
Etymology and History
The New Testament was originally written in Ancient Greek, where the term “homologeo” was used in the place of “confession”. “Homo” means “same” and “logos” means “word”, so from “same words” we actually arrive at the idea of agreeing by saying the same things.
When the Romans were translating this to Latin, they use the word “confiteri”, with “con”/“com” meaning “together” and “fateri” meaning “to acknowledge.” So, the verb “confiteri” meant roughly “to acknowledge together”, and the noun “confessio” meant something like “total acknowledgement.” St. Augustine wrote his “Confessions” in the 4th century right as arguments about translations were happening. He uses it to mean both acknowledging the sins of his past and declaring his love and faith in God.
In Old French, the word “confession” adopted a more specific meaning under the Catholic Church as part of a sacrament to disclose one’s sins to a priest. It’s at this point that we can see how the concept of confession has implications for the way institutions assert control. The schism between Catholicism and Protestantism led the Catholic Church to alter the nature of confessions as a method of tightening control by preserving stricter, more distinct identity of what Catholicism required against Protestantism. The confessional booth was invented by Charles Borromeo to incorporate anonymity and isolation into the act.
By the 16th century, “confession” replaced terms in Old English like “andetnes” (acknowledgment) and was adopted by legal systems to mean a formal admission of legal guilt. European monarchies had begun surveilling their citizens’ participation in church confessions, sometimes requiring written “Confessions of Faith” to be signed. To avoid attending a church confession or signing a written confession would raise suspicions that you could be politically rebellious or traitorous. Criminal statutes inherited this value on confessions, so Eurocentric judicial systems placed a lot of value on being able to get a criminal to issue a confession as the gold standard for evidence or proof. This confession of guilt was literal; the criminals were expected to explain the psychology that drove their actions, not just the mechanisms through which they broke a law.
Those like Michel Foucault argue that in the 19th century, Western institutions secularized confession while preserving its structure as a tool to extract repressed desires and pathologize them. Confessing a “sin” to a priest in a confessional booth was replaced with confessing “perversions” and “sickness” to a professional in a clinical setting. The priest saves your soul from sins, the professional saves your mind-body from symptoms.
As much credit as Freud gets for emphasizing the importance of subconscious processes in psychology, Foucault argues the opposite: psychoanalysis introduced a scientific dimension to a culture obsessed with self-surveillance to inspect oneself for deviations that lead to damnation. Rather than being sexually repressed because we couldn’t confess our desires, we become even more repressed by the incitement to confess these desires in spaces where institutions can monitor and regulate it while also engaging in a public discourse that shapes cultural norms. It’s arguably even more controlling than the confessional, where you at least have the agency in identifying sins as discrete actions connected to higher principles. Within the premises of psychoanalysis is the notion that your subconscious or unconscious mind has the truth that your conscious thoughts are hiding, and you must seek a credentialed analyst to construct truth out of their interpretations or inferences about your mind.
The most recent evolution of confession emerged in the post-WWII mass media space that feuled the growth of the attention economy. Daytime television as a business model is effectively the turning of confessions into content for consumption. In fact, generating attention from confessions actually meant someone’s social capital increases from performing a successful confession. Consider Oprah. The studio assumes the role of a sacred space that was once occupied by a church or temple. Oprah is the recognizable spiritual leader who guides an audience seated in rows resembling pews. Guests coming to confess state the trauma they experienced (or caused), display their true inner feelings as a result of reflection, and then are absolved when Oprah and the crowd cheer for their growth. It’s not even a joke to say that Oprah occupies the same space in many people’s lives as a high priestess would. She herself has referred to her own platform as a “ministry,” and her personal background involved Southern Baptist traditions alongside New Age spiritual philosophy.
Fast forward to 2026, and we see AI-boosted algorithmic analysis and delivery of confession as content to be measured for engagement costs and return-on-investment.
Interpretations
Confessional Technologies
“Confessional technologies” is a term coined by Michel Foucault.
Commentary
Bojack and Ben Affleck
I’m sympathetic to Ben Affleck as a celebrity whose struggles with alcoholism made him a poster boy he didn’t ask to be. My analysis of The Way Back is built on the premise of the movie being a form of confession for him in a format he’s most familiar and expressive with as an actor. It’s not a very remarkable movie if taken at face value, but seeing it as Affleck working through his history with drinking and recovery, as well as the impacts it had on his career and relationships, elevates it quite a bit.
Bojack Horseman is not a show I’m actually very interested in unpacking. While I’m very partial to media criticism and Southern California, I don’t think the show says too much about mental health or addiction that isn’t readily available at face value. There are some slices of it that are helpful to pull out in the context of other discussions, and this is one of those instances. In the first season, Bojack is looking to inject fresh life into his career by publishing a book, though his lack of work ethic and chronic substance use leads to him relying on a ghost writer, Diane. Contrary to his expectations of a glowing PR piece, she writes a deeply flawed portrayal of him through his trauma and bad decisions. Contrary to making him look bad, it’s met with great acclaim by the public who feel a sense of vindication themselves from seeing him as more relatable through his flaws.
The contrast between Ben Affleck, whose project inspires catharsis, and Bojack, whose project still leaves him dissatisfied as to the question of whether he can be a good person, is noteworthy. Confession can still have the catharsis that promotes real healing for an individual, but it can just as easily be a form of trying to raise social capital from a history of developing a portfolio with toxic assets.
Wouldn’t I be a hypocrite if I said managing this site wasn’t doing the same for me?

wiki/confidentiality.title: Confidentiality
wiki/confidentiality.content:
Overview
According to the American Sociological Association (ASA), “confidentally generally means that private information about an individual will not be shared without his or her consent.”
Commentary
Honestly, I don’t really believe that any policy about confidentiality can really be trusted to be confidential.
Alcoholics Anonymous is explicit that communication in groups is not legally privileged in any way and relies on the trust of the fellowship, many of which resemble high school cliques in terms of gossip and drama.
A survey of 500 psychologists conducted by Kenneth Pope showed that 62% of admitted to breaching patient confidentiality at least once accidentally, with 50% believing that confidentiality is the easiest ethical rule to accidentally violate. 8% of therapists admitted that they talked about their clients by name to outsiders. The American Psychological Association reports that 15% of the complaints tracked by the Ethics Committee concerned confidentiality issues. The Association of Marital and Family Therapy Regulatory Boards (AMFTRB) publishes state licensing board data that reveals confidentiality violates and failure to maintain records as the most common reasons therapists face official repercussions for their conduct.

wiki/confirmation-bias.title: Confirmation Bias
wiki/confirmation-bias.content:
Overview
“Confirmation bias” refers to the tendency for people to prefer interpretations of evidence that confirm their prior models and assumptions of reality.

wiki/connecticut-community-for-addiction.title: Connecticut Community for Addiction Recovery (CCAR)
wiki/connecticut-community-for-addiction.content:
Overview
The Connecticut Community for Addiction Recovery (CCAR) is a centralized resource for addressing substance use disorders and is formed as a non-profit Recovery Community Organization (RCO). It has financial backing and oversight from the Connecticut Department of Mental Health and Addiction Services (DMHAS). They support physical Recovery Community Centers (RCCs), deploy recovery coaches to emergency rooms in hospitals, appoint coaches to prison and parole offices, provide statewide professional training, and operate community-based peer recovery coaching for youth ages 12-17 with mental health conditions.
Links

ccar.us/about-ccar/

wiki/conscientization.title: Conscientization
wiki/conscientization.content:
Overview
Conscientization is the process through which individuals develop the critical consciousness required to participate in shaping the social, political, economic systems that power dynamics exist in.
History and Etymology
The modern usage of the term was popularized by Paulo Freire in Pedagogy of the Oppressed (1970) which discussed the ways that individuals facing oppressive systems that marginalize them moved from passive dispositions or learned helplessness to become actively self-empowered within the systems they live in.

wiki/consciousness.title: Consciousness
wiki/consciousness.content:
Overview
Defining consciousness leads to some of the most abstract debates in philosophical discourse. For convenience, we can define consciousness as the quality of being aware of one’s subjective experiences.
Major neuroscientific schools of thought around consciousness include Global Neuronal Workspace Theory (GNW), Integrated Information Theory (IIT), and Attention Schema Theory. The philosophical problems include the Hard Problem, coined by David Chalmers to ask why first-person experience emerges from the brain at all, and the mind-body problem about how mental states and physical matter are related.

wiki/consent.title: Consent
wiki/consent.content:
Overview
Consent in its most basic sense means an agreement to something, but the devil here is in the details, particularly when we have to make legal judgments. Not every human interaction has a contract or paper trail of evidence we can examine to locate an unambiguous, indisuptable affirmative statement of consent. The role of “enthusiastic consent” becomes particularly important in these cases.

wiki/consumerism.title: Consumerism
wiki/consumerism.content:
Overview
Consumerism is broadly a set of beliefs or practices in which individuals are framed as consumers in a marketplace who can change their quality of life based on their consumption patterns. It’s related but distinct from materialism, as not every good or service necessarily requires material transfers or transformations.

wiki/contaminant.title: Contaminant
wiki/contaminant.content:
Overview
Contaminant loosely refers to an undesirable or unexpected presence of some substance. Depending on the environmental or legal context, the definition may be more narrow.
From the United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA):
The Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) defines “contaminant” as any physical, chemical, biological or radiological substance or matter in water. Drinking water may reasonably be expected to contain at least small amounts of some contaminants. Some contaminants may be harmful if consumed at certain levels in drinking water. The presence of contaminants does not necessarily indicate that the water poses a health risk. 1
Note that this definition explicitly indicates that contaminant has a technical meaning that differs from the connotation of a toxic or harmful pollutant. The EPA maintains Candidate Contaminant Lists that are reviewed and updated every few years, covering each kind of the contaminants mentioned. 2

wiki/contingency-management.title: Contingency Management
wiki/contingency-management.content:
Overview
Over three decades of research into contingency management interventions has shown that it routinely outperforms Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy and 12-step facilitation models. It is the gold standard for stimulant use disorders, which have no FDA-approved medications. Adding CM to Medication for Opioid Use Disorder (MOUD) protocols substantially improves cigarette use, medication adherence, illicit opioid use, polysubstance use, and therapy attendance. Even after the external rewards stop, those who completed a contingency management program were significantly more likely to maintain long-term abstinence.
Types
By Reinforcement
Voucher-Based Reinforcement
Stephen Higgins pioneeered this model by awarding points or vouchers for passing drug tests, with each voucher having monetary value that can be used to buy groceries or other goods.
Prize-Based CM (Fishbowl Method)
Nancy Petry designed a stochastic method of contingency mangement that could lower costs: instead of a guaranteed voucher for a set amount, participants who pass a drug test can draw a slip from a bowl that contains anything from encouraging words to a substantial prize (up to $100).
Financial Incentives
These methods cut to the chase and directly exchange money for clean drug tests without constraints on how it’s used.
Clinical Privileges
Found largely in Opioid Treatment Programs (OTPs) where medications like buprenorphine and methadone exist, these systems give patients more liberty for consistent behavior like doses to take-home as a sign of trust and convenience.
Therapeutic Workplace
Developed by Kenneth Silverman at John Hopkins University, therapeutic workplace programs are evidence-based interventions that provide training and employment as an incentive to maintain sobriety.
Yes, people will literally stay sober if you promise to guide them into a job. Just like people will commit fewer crimes if they have stable employment and housing. Just like people will report a higher quality of life when they don’t have chronic stress building from financial instability.
This is one of the only interventions I’ve found that have incredibly strong empirical support for long-term sobriety and quality of life improvements that addresses the psychosocial causes of substance use, which is alarming since we claim to now work through a biopsychosocial model of health yet completely overlook this in favor of expanding manualized therapies that are less effective.
I’ll put it this way: I have been in psychoeducation classes that consisted entirely of YouTube videos featuring TedTalks and sound bowl ASMR, with facilitators saying, quote, “I get paid either way” if clients say don’t see it as valuable or if one client derails an entire session. We’re not talking minimum wage jobs either; they have proudly quoted $35/hr with free daily meals. This is the same formula as a substitute teacher turning on Bill Nye the Science Guy and turning a blind eye to everyone being on their smartphones. This class might then be followed by one about projection, so that if you did have any feedback about the process, you can learn about how the real problem is you being judgmental to deflect from your own insecurities. Or it might be a class about taking responsibility, though not if it leads you to feeling responsible enough for your recovery that you would try to adjust the treatment you’re receiving. If you really keep pushing as I once did, you’ll get told that you should leave it to professionals since your own judgment got you to where you are, which completely tosses out our biopsychosocial premises in favor of a Puritan moral-psychology that elevates obedience and confession to authority over humanist ideas of treating people as the center their own lived realities.
That exact same hourly wage could have been allocated to helping some of these clients with their career goals. Many have expressed a desire to become peer counselors who can use their own trauma and recovery as experience to guide others, which seems to me far preferable to paying babysitters who will literally use an ASMR stream to get paid while napping.
By Target Behavior
Abstinence-Based
Most contingency management programs aim to test sustained abstinence with urine testing or breathalyzer screenings.
Attendance/Adherence-Based
Some models experiment with rewarding patients for participating in treatment, such as showing up for therapy sessions and taking medications as prescribed, regardless of their drug use.
Goal-Directed CM
Because every individual has their own goals from not just recovery but life in general, these models set up rewards or incentives for completing long-term goals tailored to someone’s specific circumstances, like building a resume or submitting applications for housing.
By Format
Digital CM
Modern devices make it much easier to deliver contingency management programs without requiring visits to a clinic. Remote testing devices and digital cards mean that we can both instantly validate someone’s drug or treatment status and instantly reward them upon completion.
Variable Ratio Schedules
Variable scheduling changes some aspect of reward delivery with respect to time. For instance, if someone has maintained a streak of hitting their goals, the value of the reward might increase as well. If the streak is broken, the reward schedule might reset to square one.

wiki/continuum-of-care.title: Continuum of Care
wiki/continuum-of-care.content:
Overview
A Continuum of Care (CoC) refers to a local agency or organization that manages the coordination plan of social services for homeless members of a community. It is formally defined by the United States Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) as
“the group organized to carry out the responsibilities prescribed in the CoC Program Interim Rule for a defined geographic area. A CoC should be composed of representatives of organizations including: nonprofit homeless providers, victim service providers, faith-based organizations, governments, businesses, advocates, public housing agencies, school districts, social service providers, mental health agencies, hospitals, universities, affordable housing developers, law enforcement, organizations that serve homeless and formerly homeless veterans, and homeless and formerly homeless persons.” 1
History and Etymology
HUD introduced the CoC model in 1994 in response to fragmentation in the requests for funding from local organizations. A community might have many organizations apply for funding without coordination, leading to duplicate services or a lack of services depending on the overlap in their functions. Individuals might need assistance from multiple organizations at once but end up with the burden of overseeing the transfer of their data between them, which would be a hard task even if they weren’t struggling with homelessness. 2
In 2009, the United States Congress codified and consolidated the CoC process into federal statutes through the Homeless Emergency Assistance and Rapid Transition to Housing (HEARTH) Act. Healthcare professionals also began to adopt the term in reference to an integrated system that could track patients over time through preventative care, emergency services, rehabilitation, and long-term management for chronic health conditions.3

wiki/convulsions.title: Convulsions
wiki/convulsions.content:
Overview
The National Cancer Institute (NCI) defines convulsions as:
“A condition in which muscles contract and relax quickly and cause uncontrolled shaking of the body. Head injuries, high fevers, some medical disorders, and certain drugs can cause convulsions. They may also occur during seizures caused by epilepsy.” 1
The distinction between convulsions and seizures pertains to brain activity, with the latter being the result of electrical disturbances. The stereotypical depiction of seizures in media almost always involves convulsions, but absence seizures involve lapses in consciousness that can just appear as a frozen blank expression. Convulsions can happen as a result of the sudden drop in blood pressure associated with fainting, which can temporarily deprive the brain of oxygen and consequently trigger convulsions.

Footnotes
