wiki/core-beliefs.title: Core Beliefs
wiki/core-beliefs.content:
Overview
Within the context of psychology, “core beliefs” often refer to “self-related core beliefs” for which the American Psychological Association cites a 2025 study for a definition:
“Self-related core beliefs describe what individuals think about themselves. They usually develop due to experiences individuals make while striving for goals or interacting with their environment. In this study, a structural model was developed that describes what kind of core beliefs individuals hold. It can be used to measures self-related core believes, give feedback, or change core beliefs, for example in coaching.” 1
That sounds simple enough, but the actual identification and taxonomic categorization of these beliefs proves to be extremely complex tasks:
“The present research started with a thorough review of the literature, identifying nearly 800 self-related core beliefs that were described in the literature. In a two-step process, using natural language processing and empirical data, these beliefs were analyzed and integrated in a hierarchical model.” 1
History and Etymology
The ideas behind the significance self-related core beliefs are at least as old as Sigmund Freud, whose focus on the unconscious aspects of human existence as a source of base drives attempted to identify internalized scripts from childhood dynamics that we replay. Alfred Adler, a peer of Freud who shared a deterministic perspective of the human mind where behaviors could be mapped to unconscious mental structures, coined the term “Basic Mistakes” in reference to the flawed foundations a person might hold that produces phenomena like an inferiority complex. Schema theory in the mid-20th century was further developed by Sir Frederic Bartlett, who coined the term “schema” for the templates that brains use to facilitate efficient interpretation of external input from the world, and Jean Piaget, who began applying schemas into developmental and child psychology. In 1955, Albert Ellis proposed Rational Emotive Behavioral Therapy, which argued that emotional suffering isn’t produced by experiences themselves but from flawed frameworks that are applied to the interpretation of those experiences.
Aaron T. Beck developed Cognitive Behavioral Therapy as a response to experiments he led in the 1960s that contradicted many assumptions common to Freud-inspired psychoanalysis that assumed negative thoughts within patients were the result of masochistic self-directed hostility. Instead, Beck grew to believe that depressive symptoms were the result of a disorder of information processing in which patients were engaging in conscious dialogue with themselves (what we might sometimes call the “internal monologue”) that featured negative automatic thoughts. It’s no coincidence that this was a period in which computer science and psychology were moving towards a model of the world’s entities as information-processing systems rather than black boxes containing a whirlwind of unconscious drives. Within this framework, Beck postulated that these internal dialogues were rooted in a patient’s schemas about the world, which then became known as “core beliefs.” A child could form the core belief that “I always have to be proving that I am worth loving,” which in adulthood could manifest as a strong bias against accepting unconditional love while seeking conditional or transactional relationships. That adult might then dismiss affection from their partners or believe setting up any boundaries at all would risk abandonment.
Commentary
I’m inclined to feel towards Beck what many feel towards Freud, that he was undoubtedly influential in moving the fields of clinical psychotherapy and philosophy of the mind forward, but many of his core ideas are worthy of intense scrutiny from both theoretical standpoints and empirical studies.
In 1991, a study published in Psychology Bulletin found evidence that depressive thinking was associated with increased negative self-perception, hopelessness, themes of loss, and mood incongruence, but depressive thinking was not especially illogical or irrational. It was more likely that people expressing depressive system had a realistic, even if harsh or negative, evaluation of their lives and environment rather than irrational core beliefs. They stop short of condemning the theoretical foundations of cognitive therapies outright, however:
“We thus find little convincing support for causal hypotheses of cognitive theory, but at the same time it would be premature to abandon them. For example, the idea that dysfunctional beliefs are stable rests uneasily beside the findings from research on remitted depressives, and longitudinal research has generally not supported the onset hypothesis. Given that most of these studies have not used procedures suitable for printing latent beliefs, though, the hypotheses remain viable. Similarly, initial studies have yielded inconsistent results concerning hypothesized interactions between personality modes and specific stressors in predicting depression recurrence.”
This is one of the reasons I remain highly skeptical of positive psychology and New Age spirituality that attributes an almost magical power to optimistic mindsets that allegedly manifest outcomes through intentionality alone. While a patient might still be able to make better or healthier choices as a result of therapeutic discussions,
In 1995, Michael Mahoney published Cognitive and Constructive Psychotherapies: Theory, Research, and Practice, in which he took issue with the theoretical foundations of CBT as reducing humans with “crude computationalism” into flowcharts of thoughts and emotions instead of adopting a fluid, holistic perspective of how humans assemble experiences into schemas. One of Beck’s students Jeffrey Young argued that the concept of “core beliefs” was an intellectualized oversimplification of what he termed Early Maladaptive Schemas (EMS), which were too ingrained to be addressed through pointing out logical errors or irrationality.
More recently, trauma-informed critiques from those like Bessel van der Kolk, author of The Body Keeps the Score, argue that core beliefs stem from deeply ingrained memories of experiences that have been reinforced through the nervous system each time it was reconsolidated.
Links
Footnotes


The structure of self-related core beliefs. ↩ ↩2

wiki/corporate-induced-disorder.title: Corporate-induced Disorder (CID)
wiki/corporate-induced-disorder.content:
Overview
“Corporate-induced disorder” is a slang phrase that emerged to describe anxiety, depression, and burnout that results in part from exposure to unhealthy workplace environments commonly found in 21st century bureaucratic corporations. Other related terms include “Corporate Traumatic Stress Disorder” (CTSD) and “Corporate Stockholm Syndrome,” which earned an article in Psychology Today. 1
Links
Footnotes


Corporate Stockholm Syndrome | Psychology Today ↩

wiki/corporate-political-activities.title: Corporate Political Activities (CPAs)
wiki/corporate-political-activities.content:
Overview
Corporate Political Activities (CPAs) refer to strategies that companies use to shape the political, legal, and social environment that are considered outside the scope of market strategies or business decisions. This can include:


Lobbying: meeting with policymakers, lawmakers, and/or decision-makers to influence the way regulations are created or enforced


Campaign contributions: donating money or resources directly to political actors or initiatives


Political Action Committees (PACs): pools of money coalesced by those employed by a company that allocate funds to political candidates


Trade Associations: groups or networks that pool money for shared interests across the industry


Industries wrapped around substance use have always been heavily politically active.
The alcohol and tobacco industries have famously lobbied against regulations on marketing and warning-labels. In fact, they even lobby against media that featured cautionary themes about substance use, like The Lost Weekend (1945). Allied Liquor Industries, a trade association for the alcoholic beverage industry, led an influence campaign against Paramount Pictures’ distribution of the movie that claimed the film’s messages would reignite a Prohibition movement. Mad Men references the tobacco industry’s pattern of funding science and research that muddies the water of real policy discourses.
Pharmaceutical companies, medical trade associations, and healthcare providers are incredibly influential through their CPAs. The specialized nature of their fields leaves most lawmakers without any firsthand experience in the process of scientific research or even the latest findings about basic human biology. Policymakers in regulatory agencies who do have credentials often cut their teeth through these groups. Nora Volkow is a prolific researcher whose brain imaging studies with Positron Emission Tomography (PET) were instrumental in establishing that chronic substance use produced physiological changes in neurobiology that elevated addiction into a health issue from a moral one. She also has been involved as an elected member of the National Academy of Medicine, American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and Association of American Physicians. She’s also won awards and recognition from the American Psychiatric Association, the American College of Psychiatrists, the Society of Biological Psychiatry, and Children and Adults with ADHD. These organizations certainly offer research infrastructure and industry guidelines that aren’t solely rooted in the political bureaucracies of the state, but mainly by decentralizing political bureaucracies into what arguably amounts to an extension of academic alumni networks.

wiki/corporate-social-responsibility.title: Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR)
wiki/corporate-social-responsibility.content:
Overview
Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) is a term that describes the arguments that large corporations have become one of the dominant structures of social organization and so they are obligated to be aligned with the social values of the communities they operate in.
Employee Assistance Programs (EAPs) can be argued to be a form of CSR. Although employers benefit from retaining a productive employee who might struggle with their substance use, including EAPs and addiction treatment within health insurance plans also goes a long way to legitimizing substance use disorders as a health issue within public perception.
History and Etymology
The idea of philanthropy or paternalism from powerful leaders is nothing new; whether assumed under a mantle of stewardship or PR for a personal legacy, those like Carnegie and Rockefeller have stamped their names across countless projects, including the Oxford Group that laid the theoretical and philosophical foundations of AA. CSR was coined by Howard Bowen in 1953 in Social Responsibilities of the Businessman as an argument that

wiki/cosmology.title: Cosmology
wiki/cosmology.content:
Overview
A “cosmology” is a study or body of work exploring the origin and structure of the universe as reality.
Commentary
Recovery programs like Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) and Recovery Dharma are inspired by religious systems while those like SMART Recovery are rooted in the guidelines of scientific institutions, but each group has its own cosmological foundations. I would argue that a strong portion of one’s affinity for a group stems from alignment in cosmological preferences.
To relay an anecdote, Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and AA both initially appealed to some of my own intuitive feelings about the universe. Towards CBT, I enjoy the expressive value of pattern-recognition and computational or algorithmic thinking, as I have a tendency to map interactions between different phenomena as information exchanges, so the notion of pruning a model of reality of irrational distortions that defy the body of propositions vetted through my epistemological foundations is very appealing. It’s perhaps no coincidence that my undergraduate degree is in Computer Science and that CBT emerged in a late 20th century paradigm shift away from the modes of psychoanalysis that view the self as an emergent property of chaotic base drives, sometimes termed the Cognitive Revolution. The earliest theoretical foundations for Artificial Intelligence as we practice it today emerged from close collaboration between cognitive scientists and computer scientists, though the focus on scaling through data and computation has occasionally spurred on estrangements that sideline direct interpretations of reality in favor of industrialized instrumentalism that mechanistically explores connections for predictive value. Where I began to take issue with the cosmology of CBT is perhaps the same place I might begin to take issue with constructions of world ontologies from older neurosymbolic paradigms, which is the subjectivity each individual loads into their axiomatic premises of the world, shaped by both the biases of their unique lived experiences and epistemic injustice afforded by their institutionalized positions of authority. Predictive power certainly provides a remedy for that, and one can look to both Hindu and Buddhist traditions of logic and epistemology to find elaborate defenses of instrumental perspective before modern industrialization and the scientific management mythos. But if we then look at the overall efficacy of CBT, we don’t find meaningfully different outcomes than most other forms of therapy, and in fact, we don’t find even consensus about interpreting cognitive distortions between practitioners. It becomes very difficult for me to then see humans as information-processing rational machines whose suffering is intrinsically related to dysfunctional irrationality, as if the changes in our species and societies has ever been predicated on anything approximating a priority for demonstrably objective rationality. I feel that there’s a momentum to this perspective that emerges out of Enlightenment-era Cartesian dualism that places the mind as an immaterial substance independently, and often above, the body as a material substance, and then supposing that the ordering of the mind will produce ordering in the material nervous system. That ordering of the mind is itself a modernist objectivist concept which supposes that a grand design can be crafted through the perfection of an initial set of axioms and their applications, akin to a software-hardware dichotomy that privileges the creative possibilities of mathematical designs over the fundamental limitations of hardware-based calculation.
New waves of CBT counteract these impulses by inquiring about the core beliefs and inferences people make within the context of their own life, not unlike attempts within the field of AI to construct localized ontologies within symbolic reasoning systems that eschew the grand narrative of universal ontological principles. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) is implicitly a recognition that the cosmological foundations of conventional manualized CBT fail to account for the constraints that our minds operate within that shape our experiences. For instance, our minds are not capable of deleting memories or modifying an algorithmic information-processing protocol the way that mechanistic models of memory found in computational devices can, and our memories are themselves constantly reconsolidated artifacts of the present. The notion of rational linearity that updates itself as per some Bayesian inference analogue echoes the notion of linear evolution in cultures and civilization that form the Enlightenment teleology of modernism.
Towards AA, my initial impression was that its cosmological premises invite us to sublimate the dominance of the individual self in favor of transcendental relations of meaning. It’s common enough for most religious and spiritual systems to counsel against rigid evaluations of the self through connections with material, worldly configurations, or at least that’s what tends to appeal to me about those frameworks. I might have been a smidge too eager to project impermanence and Jungian archetypes from a collective unconscious onto the “surrendering” of one’s ego, as AA literature asks us to seek a “Higher Power” from an independent, higher reality. After all, Carl Jung wrote to William Wilson (Bill W.), the founder of AA, describing the need for some kind of wholeness of the self that an ego cannot rationally construct for itself, nor can medical science provide a physiological reparation of, necessitating something of a spiritual awakening through religion or collective comraderie. Addiction itself is not the result of occasional failures in a system otherwise using rational impulses to navigate reality but an intolerance for the experience of reality. AA cosmology leans into the contradictions of dualism like an elaborate koan: one surrenders to the powers of a higher reality to gain freedom in this reality. For Enlightenment ideals based in a mind-body dualism, the exhaustion of intellectual and rational approaches is celebrated as a rite of passage. This spiritual awakening represents the collapse of the ego’s resistance to accepting conscious contact with a Higher Power. Yet, the very schema of the AA program as a series of Steps and Traditions risks the development of a dogmatic set of institutions that maintain a new system of rationality. Rather than honoring Jung’s appreciation for Rudolf Otto’s articulation of the numinous that we can consciously contact through archetypes of the collective unconscious, the Protestant roots of AA can drive a fierce moral surveillance that becomes an end in and of itself, dragging one away from the direct experiences with the numinous and individual self-discovery with a dependence on the group consciousness.
I’m most biased towards Recovery Dharma (RD) as having roots in something “vaguely Eastern.” It stems from a cosmology that views suffering as a structural part of the human condition rather than a deviation from the prescriptions of a Higher Power or universal order. Our self-awareness of our finite impermanent selves causes us to seek something infinite and permanent, even if only through temporary participation in a meaningful project that lasts longer than our lives. I’m often reminded of Albert Camus’ discussion of the absurd condition we find ourselves in when we ask for answers about meaning and purpose from an uncaring universe and the suffering that accompanies that existential isolation of an independent embodied reality. However, the resulting prescriptions are entirely different: Camus advocates for living in rebellion of absurd meaninglessness by choosing to embrace the passions of the moment, while Buddhist philosophy advocates for the cessation of craving and attachments in favor of mindful acceptance.
I split the difference, I suppose, in my preference for Kashmir Shaivist traditions that accept an infinite scope of the universe as the sole principle of permanence within which all other things are impermanent, interconnected, interdependent finite contractions. The suffering and the yearning that stem from our inability to achieve permanence are ends to themselves, for the creativity and curiosity to comprehend the breadth of experience are apathetic to pleasure or lack thereof. Nietzsche’s use of [[amor-fati|amor fati]] comes close to this perspective in which suffering is as irreducible a component of experience as pleasure, and so to appreciate the full breadth of experiences that lead to wholeness is to appreciate even the suffering of the condition of addiction on its own terms. To feel an utterly irrational need for something we don’t even want can be revelatory.
Consequently, though I find the cosmology within Recovery Dharma’s interpretation of Buddhism the most palatable to my own convictions, I couldn’t honestly say that I attend with the purposes of deepening my engagement with Buddhist principles. Hindu and Buddhist sects have engaged in plenty of ideological and cultural exchange over the centuries, so it feels easier to find common metaphysical and ontological vocabulary in RD than AA for me. Still, I would be thrilled to find a peer group that approaches recovery with a radical appreciation for existence rather than the cultivation of the principles of non-self or a surrender to a Higher Power through faith, rather than a curiosity towards what one’s intuition creates.

wiki/cost-benefit-analysis.title: Cost-Benefit Analysis (CBA)
wiki/cost-benefit-analysis.content:
Overview
A cost-benefit analysis (CBA) is a decision-making tool that finds the difference between what is gained and what is lost in a decision. If you’ve ever made a pros and cons list, you’ve done a basic cost-benefit analysis before. It’s considered a basic tool within Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (CBT).
In policymaking and financial analysis contexts, the costs and benefits are both measured monetarily, with net present value (NPV) or benefit-cost ratios (3 returned for each 1 invested) being the metrics observed to compare decisions or make projections about future resource flows.

wiki/cost-effectiveness-analysis.title: Cost-Effectiveness Analysis (CEA)
wiki/cost-effectiveness-analysis.content:
Overview
A cost-effectiveness analysis is a tool to judge the impact of a policy or decision relative to the costs incurred in enacting it. Specifically, it tends to evaluate the costs monetarily and the effectiveness through a standard non-monetary unit.
For example, the Incremental Cost-Effectiveness Ratio (ICER) metric of a medical intervention that costs 40,000 to extend someone's lifespan by 4 years would be 10,000/life-year. This works well when comparing decisions or options that are aimed at influencing the same ends, such as two interventions aimed at expanding someone’s lifespan, but it doesn’t help us compare decisions that aim for different things. Say another medical intervention costs 40,000 to rectify a disability someone experiences for 4 years rather than extending their life by 4 years. In this case, we end up comparing 10,000 per additional life-year to $10,000 per disability-free life-year. The value of a disability-free life-year compared to an additional life-year will depend on each individual’s subjective evaluations of whether they would prefer being free of a health condition to living longer while coping with it.

wiki/counseling-and-mental-health-servic.title: Counseling and Mental Health Services (CAMHS)
wiki/counseling-and-mental-health-servic.content:
Overview
The Counseling and Mental Health Services (CAMHS) under Harvard University Health Services (HUHS) was established in 2018. Their initial services include consultations through Care Coordinators to connect with clinicians that specialize in Substance Use Disorders (SUDs) and co-occurring disorders like anxiety and depression.

wiki/counseling.title: Counseling
wiki/counseling.content:
Overview
According to the American Psychological Association, counseling refers to:
“professional assistance in coping with personal problems, including emotional, behavioral, vocational, marital, educational, rehabilitation, and life-stage (e.g., retirement) problems. The counselor makes use of such techniques as active listening, guidance, advice, discussion, clarification, and the administration of tests.”1
The American Counseling Association offers the definition:
“a professional relationship that empowers diverse individuals, families, and groups to accomplish mental health, wellness, education, and career goals.”
Wex, a legal encyclopedia supported by the Legal Information Institute at Cornell Law School, also covers a definition of counsel:
“To counsel is to provide legal advice or guidance to someone on specific subject matter. Counsel is also a lawyer giving advice about a legal matter and representing clients in court. ” 2
So generally, “counseling” has the implication of advice given by a trained professional who can come from various specialities or fields. In informal usage, we might say that a friend counsels you with good suggestions, but it heavily suggests that the person giving counsel or being a counselor has some degree of credentials or qualification that provides legitimacy to their authority or expertise.

wiki/crack-baby.title: Crack Baby
wiki/crack-baby.content:
Overview
The term “crack baby” is a derogatory reference to babies who were exposed to cocaine as fetuses, which emerged as part of the general hysteria over the crack epidemic in the United States during the 1980s onward. Some studies then had suggested that those exposed to cocain in the womb would develop severe, permanent disabilities that would compromise their quality of life and become a burden for social services. Later studies contradicted the strength of the claims in these earlier studies, many of which were methodologically flawed and failed to separate a mother’s usage of cocaine from other health complications and managed small sample sizes. Nevertheless, as with many narratives rooted in moral panics that served sociopolitical agendas divorced from the realities of good scientific practices and evidentiary standards, particularly from the peak of the War on Drugs era, the misconceptions were embedded into the public consciousness.

wiki/crack-cocaine.title: Crack Cocaine
wiki/crack-cocaine.content:
Overview
“Crack cocaine” refers to a version of cocaine that’s vaporized and smoked by heating up “rocks,” as opposed to chewing coca leaves as South American peoples had for thousands of years or snorting powder cocaine.
History and Etymology
While powder cocaine was treated as a medical solution in the late 19th century and emerged as a “classy” luxury drug in the late 20th century, crack cocaine was associated with communities of color in impoverished city districts as a distinct threat within the context of the War on Drugs. In reality, any variant of cocaine is highly addictive and dangerous, and the disparities found in criminal justice systems were motivated by sociopolitical agendas that capitalized on public hysteria. The “crack” in “crack cocaine” comes from the crackling sound heard when heating the rocks before smoking the substance for a high.

wiki/crank.title: Crank
wiki/crank.content:
Overview
“Crank” is slang for methamphetamine, usually with the implication that it’s impure and cheaply manufactured. In other words, the opposite of what Walter White produces.
History and Etymology
The slang comes out of the 1960s when motorcycle gangs were known to carry methamphetamine inside a bike’s crankcase.

wiki/craving.title: Craving
wiki/craving.content:
Overview
In casual usage, “craving” refers to a preoccupying desire for something. Within the context of Substance Use Disorders (SUDs), cravings refer to urges to use substances that can happen throughout the phases of both active addiction and abstinence.

wiki/criminology.title: Criminology
wiki/criminology.content:
Overview
Criminology refers to the study of crime and the psychology behind behaviors considered criminal.

wiki/crisis-centers.title: Crisis Centers
wiki/crisis-centers.content:
Overview
Crisis centers in the context of substance use generally refer to Crisis Stabilization Units (CSUs) and Behavioral Health Urgent Care Centers (BHUCCs), which are designed to address individuals experiencing psychological or physical distress as a result of substance use or other mental health disorders. They tend to be a response to the failures of a system that only provides Emergency Rooms (ERs) and incarceration as pathways for someone whose substance use requires urgent intervention. Instead, crisis centers operate from a “No Wrong Door” mindset that specialize in triage for mental and behavioral health crises. While modern science and clinical practice has come a long way towards seeing substance use disorders as a legitimate health issue with evidence-backed interventions available, that doesn’t always translate to effective implementations, whether because of stigma, lack of resources, or outdated training. Crisis centers dedicated to providing these interventions can bridge critical care gaps in communities. For alcohol, which is commonly available and presents one of the highest risks of fatal withdrawals, and opioids, for which highly effective pharmacological interventions exist, these centers can be literal life-savers that are far more cost-effective than ER visits or engagement with the criminal justice system.

wiki/croonian-medal-and-lecture.title: Croonian Medal and Lecture
wiki/croonian-medal-and-lecture.content:
Overview
The Croonian Medal and Lecture is awarded by the Royal Society and Royal College of Physicians, both based in the United Kingdom. Named after the 17th century Fellow William Croone, the award includes a medal, a cash prize, and an invitation to give a lecture to the Society.
History
The 2021 Croonian Lecture was given by Professor Barry Everitt, who discussed his research into the neurological mechanisms behind motivation and their application to Substance Use Disorders (SUDs).

wiki/cross-reaction.title: Cross-Reaction
wiki/cross-reaction.content:
Overview
Cross-reactions refer to unexpected reactions as a result of a chemical that interacts with something outside the intended target or reaction.
When cross-reactions between substances lead to a medical event, we might use the term combined drug intoxication (CDI). Mixing either alcohol or benzodiazepines with opioids, including pharmaceutical ones like vicodin or oxycodone, can lead to a compounding suppression of the nervous systems regulation of breathing that’s greater than the sum of its parts. Mixing depressants like alcohol with stimulants like cocaine places contradictory demands on the cardiovascular system, so rather than neutralizing each other, they add extra stress on the heart and lungs which can cause cardiac arrest or strokes.

wiki/crosstalk.title: Crosstalk
wiki/crosstalk.content:
Overview
Crosstalk, in the context of group therapy or recovery meetings, means directly commenting on the experiences someone shares.
Some groups openly allow crosstalk or indicate that a speaker who shares can individually grant permission for others to provide input, while others ban it entirely. Many of these groups are generally intended to be safe spaces to share how one feels without judgment, and crosstalk, even if it’s just positive affirmations, still means that a speaker will undergo judgment. In AA, in my experience, crosstalk is generally discouraged and exceptions come from members who have known each other for a long time and can confidently read each other’s body language and mannerisms to judge when a comment is likely be received well. On the other hand, SMART Recovery actively encourages crosstalk as an interactive problem-solving forum to critically examine each other’s issues. I’ve seen this go really well before with members appreciating the advice to use CBT tools and even being called out on excuses or rationalizations, and I’ve seen this go really poorly where a facilitator feels uncomfortable stepping in to cool a heated discussion. And I mean REALLY poorly, as in threats of violence. I have yet to see hands actually be thrown but I don’t doubt that the day will come where I do.

wiki/cylinder-seal-of-queen-puabi.title: Cylinder Seal of Queen Puabi
wiki/cylinder-seal-of-queen-puabi.content:
Overview
The Cylinder Seal of Queen Puabi is an lapis lazuli seal that was found in the Royal Cemetery at Ur in the queen’s tomb with her body in 1928. It holds a cuneiform inscription of her name without any mention of male family members, which would be uncommon for female royalty of that era. It also depicts an upper register featuring Puabi raising a cup alongside two male guests while being served by attendants and a lower register with two groups facing each other across a table piled with food as attendants pour drinks.
Queen Puabi ruled Early Dynastic Sumer, where drinking at royal banquets had social and religious significance in enhancing ritual feasts, cementing diplomatic alliances, and demonstrating the luxury of noble classes. Sumerian religion includes the goddess Ninkasi, associated with beer and alcohol, and it was thought that drinking alcohol lowered the barrier between oneself and sacred planes. Brewing alcohol and running taverns were considered female professions (sabitu), so the association between alcohol and women’s roles was strong. Puabi’s depiction in the seal thus commemorates her as an intersection between spirituality and femininity, facilitating both the creation and serving of alcohol through her royal influence.

wiki/daily-reprieve.title: Daily Reprieve
wiki/daily-reprieve.content:
Overview
“Daily reprieve” is a phrase found on page 85 of the Big Book of Alcoholics Anonymous and refers to the idea that sobriety is a temporary pause from a progressive disease that’s only maintained through daily “maintenance of our spiritual condition.”
Specifically, page 85 reads:
“It is easy to let up on the spiritual program of action and rest on our laurels. We are headed for trouble if we do, for alcohol is a subtle foe. We are not cured of alcoholism. What we really have is a daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition. Every day is a day when we must carry the vision of God’s will into all of our activities. “How can I best serve Thee - Thy will (not mine) be done.” These are thoughts which must go with us constantly. We can exercise our will power along this line all we wish. It is the proper use of the will.”
Commentary
The concept of a “daily reprieve” is heavily rooted in Protestant and Calvinist theological premises that the human condition is one of fundamental sin and flawed depravity. Only by throwing oneself into the mercy of God’s guidance and grace can one hope to achieve a transformation of the self. Otherwise, the temptations that surround one in daily life can easily lead to wandering astray from divine sanctity and sanctuary. AA heavily adopts this paradigm in which alcohol, described as “cunning, baffling, powerful,” adopts the role of the Devil and alcoholism is interpreted through the human predilection to sin. The only way in which the Devil’s temptations can be warded off is through regular conscious contact with one’s Higher Power, or God, and integration with a fellowship of like-minded members. In this sense, one can never be cured of the disease of alcoholism any more than human nature can be cured of the proclivity to sin. Some have argued that this idea drives much of AA’s stickiness with individuals, who, rightly or wrongly, believe that daily engagement with AA and incorporation of its principles “in all our affairs” is a requirement to gain this reprieve. In doing so, the Higher Power, or God, can provide some degree of personal intervention.

wiki/daniel-anderson.title: Daniel Anderson
wiki/daniel-anderson.content:
Daniel Anderson joined the army from 1942 to 1945 as a radarman in the Pacific, after which he used the GI Bill to pursue higher education. He had a poor academic record (he and his friends literally made a game out of trying to get low scores in the past since they hated school), but the College of St. Thomas accepted him despite the missing courses anyways. He enrolled in 1946 and began working at the Hastings State Hospital in 1947, which inspired him to pursue psychology. Dr. Nelson Bradley was the superintendent of Hastings when Anderson met him, and the two hit it off so that Anderson followed Bradely to Willmar State Mental Hospital in 1950.
Anderson pursued a master’s degree in clinical psychology from Loyola University, a private Jesuit college, because he disliked the idea of secular psychology divorced from religious beliefs. Jean Joseph Rossi, who joined Willmar, recommended that Anderson complete a dissertation at the University of Ottawa which replaced Sigmund Freud with St. Thomas Aquinas. He abandoned his master’s thesis, An Exploratory Investigation of Anxiety in Alcoholics, but finished a doctoral dissertation in 1966: Personality Correlates of Complex Instrumental Avoidance Learning.
In the early 1960s, the Alcoholic Addiction Project had published papers about the outcomes of the Willmar model for recovery, and it wasn’t great. Only a third of patients were described as “improved” in 1957, and only 7% were described as maintaining “continuous abstinence” in 1963. By this point, Anderson had left to accept a leadership position at the Hazelden Institute, where the Hill Family Foundation sponsored an applied research program. He would serve both as Vice-President and CEO. Unfortunately, this is also where Anderson began playing fast and loose with science.
In 1976, David J. Armor, J. Michael Polich, and Harriet B. Stambull were commissioned by the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) to study thousands of alcoholics across dozens of federally-funded centers:
“Client characteristics that may be of prognostic significance in alcoholism, such as social background, ethnicity, marital status, employment, and previous drinking, are examined in detail. Using a definition of remission that includes both abstention and drinking behavior within a range specified as normal, the study finds that 70 percent of those treated are in remission at 6 and at 18 months following entry. These remission rates are quite similar regardless of the type of treatment given.”
The findings would prove to be controversial, as the authors were well-aware:
“The authors are aware that some of the findings of the present study-particularly the finding that some alcoholics appear to return to and maintain patterns of normal drinking-may be controversial in some quarters. To remove any possible misunderstanding, the authors wish to emphasize that this study makes no recommendation about treatment goals for alcoholics, and in particular does not recommend or suggest that any alcoholic should resume drinking.”
Let me echo that too: no part of anything I say should be construed as permission, justification, rationalization, recommendation, or suggestion about anyone drinking.
Nevertheless, this finding posed some challenges for what had become conventions within the culture of addiction treatment. If the data shows that some alcoholics do return to drinking in a pattern that’s typical of those never diagnosed as alcoholics, that suggests some problems about the “powerless over alcohol” or “pickles can’t go back to cucumbers” lines. Abstinence-only programs could no longer say that their way was the only possible way to address addiction or chemical dependence meaningfully. That’s a problem for organizations that have spent a lot of time marketing themselves that way.
The backlash from Anderson, Hazelden, and sympathetic allies on the National Council of Alcoholism (NCA) was strong and swift. They scheduled a press conference on the same day the report was released to claim the information about remission rates would cause alcoholics to resume drinking and relapse. In terms of methodology, they argued the 18-month tracking window of the NIAAA-backed Rand study was too short for a chronic disease that lasted a lifetime. The Rand authors countered that an 18-months window was standard across federal programs. They argued it was also possible that alcoholics who internalized the “powerlessness” narratives would turn a slip at a social event into a fatal spiral over the idea of being doomed after a sip. The heightened stress and anxiety from that alone could be a driver in a relapse, or make a relapse worse.
Hazelden had its own press and publication infrastructure, which meant that information they distributed about programs and outcomes didn’t have to go through a peer-review process from the scientific community. Until 1978, Sister Mary Leo Kammeier had been in charge of the program and was consistently publishing in peer-reviewed journals. After her death, it seems everything started going through Hazelden’s own press without scientific scrutiny. In 1982, a consultant named Clark Laundergan for Hazelden published Easy Does It: Alcoholism Treatment Outcomes, Hazelden and the Minnesota Model. He claimed that 54% of patients from their program stayed abstinent while 18% reported improvement. 72% of patients benefitting from addiction treatment is certainly substantial.
In response to the counter-arguments from Anderson and Hazelden, the Rand authors did what researchers do when they encounter criticism: more experiments. They designed a 4-year follow-up study of the same cohort they had assessed before, and they found that 46% were still in active remission. 28% stayed completely abstinent but 18% no longer met the criteria for problem drinking. 1 in 5 patients admitted to programs for alcoholism resumed non-problem drinking.
Andersen’s takeaway from the study was that those who attempted non-problem drinking increased their chances of relapsing by 16% compared to those who maintained total abstinence among a subgroup that presented with high physical dependence, which he used to argue that controlled drinking was statistically so unlikely that it should be discounted. The authors pointed out that Andersen conveniently ignored those who presented with low physical dependence who attempted total abstinence actually had a higher relapse rate than those just aiming to no longer be problem drinkers.
Meanwhile, Christopher C.H. Cook analyzed the Hazelden data in 1988 and discovered that Laundergan threw out the data for over 2000 patients who had been readmitted or given extended care. He really analyzed just 1200 of the patients who seemed like clean cases that completed the program as intended. When considering all 3638 patients, 37.8% were abstinent, 9.2% showed improvement, and a shocking 53.1% reported no improvement.
This is not a minor issue in interpreting data or statistical methodology. A program that claimed to benefit a supermajority of its patients was actually a failure for most of them. Not only that, the proponents of this program sought to convince the public and policymakers to stop funding research into treatment models that conflicted with theirs. The fear they spread led to media and political backlash, including wealthy donors and philanthropists threatening to pull funding for anything other than abstinence-only guidelines.

wiki/daniel-defoe.title: Daniel Defoe
wiki/daniel-defoe.content: The author of Robinson Crusoe once defended gin and other distilled spirits out of a nationalist desire to keep wealth in the country and promote British liquor over foreign dinks. It’s also worth mentioning that his published defenses were funded by distillery companies, effectively making him paid propaganda to sell liquor while blaming the character of individuals for the sins and crimes committed while intoxicated. He condemned low-quality gin but eventually reversed course once he saw the effects that mass drinking was having in communities.

wiki/daniel-patrick-moynihan.title: Daniel Patrick Moynihan
wiki/daniel-patrick-moynihan.content:
Most known for the Moynihan Report, a 1965 report that studied poverty in African-American communities and concluded that, rather than structural or systemic momentum from an explicit racial hierarchy, the primary reasons for continued cycles of poverty could be attributed to problems with “ghetto culture.”
William J. Ryan responded to the report with a major rebuttal in his 1971 book Blaming the Victim, where is where the term “victim blaming” was coined in reference to a fallacy that confused cause-and-effect, assuming that culture affected the cycles of poverty instead of poverty affecting the culture of a community. This included observations like single-mother households and births out of wedlock.
Specifically, Ryan responded that the report “seduces the reader into believing that it is not racism and discrimination but the weaknesses and defects of the Negro himself that account for the present status of inequality between Negro and white.”

wiki/danshukai.title: Danshukai
wiki/danshukai.content:
Overview
Danshukai is the largest self-help and mutual-aid organization in Japan for those struggling with alcohol use disorder or dependence.
Unlike 12-step groups that prioritize individual recovery journeys and anonymity to make a bubble away from daily life, Danshukai actively encourages family members to participate in meetings and recovery alongside the person struggling with alcohol use, since Japanese perspectives of alcoholism traditionally see it as a family issue requiring group healing. Participants use their real names and might even have membership pins. The core idea of Danshukai is “one-day abstinence,” or focusing on daily commitments towards social reintegration while avoiding alcohol and pursuing shinsei, or a “New Life” model. There isn’t the same emphasis on personal surrender in recognition of powerlessness to a Higher Power’s will that is found in AA. Danshukai also keeps a centralized body with formal localized chapters while AA chapters can be formed anywhere while using The Big Book text as a guide.
Historical Context
The term literally translates as dan = “stop”, shu = “liquor”, and kai (“society”): “stop liquor society.” It was founded in 1953 after Nihon Kinshu Domei (“Japanese Temperance Union”) brought Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) to Japan, but Japanese recovery communities felt it had to be adopted to their culture.

wiki/dark-paradise-a-history-of-opiate-a.title: Dark Paradise - A History of Opiate Addiction in America (2001)

wiki/data-breaches.title: Data Breaches
wiki/data-breaches.content:
Overview
I love data, but I am highly skeptical of centralized databases of any kind. I don’t like it when groups of people make lists of other people they want to monitor. I don’t like it when private corporations do it, I don’t like it when rogue militias do it, I don’t like it when state agencies do it. Yet, it’s in the nature of institutions and systems that they only exist insofar as they can draw boundaries between themselves and the outside world to be defined, modeled, and controlled. Data and surveillance are key ingredients for institutions seeking to construct a predictive model that enhances their ability to monitor their influence and control.
On a personal level, I am constantly torn between the desire to collect data to detect patterns and the desire to preserve privacy and anonymity for maximal freedoms. I don’t include any tracking mechanisms on this site to collect your data aside from what Cloudflare tells me as the hosting service for these pages. I can see unique visitors, total page requests, geographic distribution, and some other adjacent surface metrics, but nothing that gives me a clue about who you actually are or what you do once you leave my site. Some people think that’s excessive paranoia, and they might be right, but on the other hand, most of us aren’t aware of most security issues that exist in the technology we use. I record the ones I’m aware of here.
Also, many of these breaches involve class action lawsuits, so get that bread, friends.
Incidents
National Association on Drug Abuse Programs (2026)

Notice of Data Security Incident

American Addiction Centers (2024)


American Addiction Centers reaches $2.75M settlement for ransomware breach


American Addiction Centers Data Breach Investigation


Drug and Alcohol Treatment Services (2024)

$594K Drug and Alcohol Treatment Services Settlement Resolves Class Action Lawsuit Over October 2024 Data Breach
