wiki/drug-consumption-room.title: Drug Consumption Room (DCR)
wiki/drug-consumption-room.content:
Overview
Drug Consumption Rooms (DCRs), also referred to as a supervised injection site or overdose prevention center (OPC), are facilities where someone can use substances they’ve obtained while under medical supervision as part of harm reduction policies. This allows the immediate administration of medications like naloxone (narcan) for opioid overdoses, access to social services like peer counseling and entry points into treatment programs, and amenities that those without hosuing lack like showers and refreshments. Some estimates show that 100 to 140 of these facilities are legally approved around the world. There is a solid body of evidence indicating that DCRs reduce public substance use, connect individuals to health and social services, and prevent drug overdoses, all without increasing local crime rates.

wiki/drug-court.title: Drug Court
wiki/drug-court.content:
Overview
Drug courts, or treatment courts, are specialized court programs to handle cases involving those struggling with Substance Use Disorders (SUDs), usually with alternative diversions that involve mandatory rehabilitation or SUD treatment. The National Treatment Court Resource Center (NTCRC) has set out guidelines stating that ideally, drug courts function collaboratively with a multidisciplinary team that includes a judge, prosecutor, defense counsel, treatment provides, and probation officers who review a person’s progress. There are specific types too: Adult Drug Courts, Juvenile Drug Courts, Family Treatment Courts, Veterans Treatment Courts, DUI Courts, etc. Studies show that individuals who go through drug court are significantly less likely to reoffend compared to traditional criminal justice channels, reduce the costs of incarceration and emergency healthcare services, and lower costs for the individual.

wiki/drug-enforcement-agency.title: Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA)
wiki/drug-enforcement-agency.content:
Overview
The Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) is a law enforcement agency of the United States Department of Justice tasked with enforcing the Controlled Substances Act and similar policies regulating substances.
It operates 241 domestic offices and 93 foreign offices across 110 countries to target drug trafficking organizations with raids against money launderers, organized criminal gangs, and narco-terrorists with a Special Operations Division (SOD) that works alongside global intelligence agencies. It also establishes strict quotes for how much of a controlled substance can be legally manufactured in the United States to reduce the potential supply for recreational use and make the existing supply easier to monitor. The agency’s forensic laboratories test seized materials to analyze their chemical structures, including emerging synthetic drugs like nitazenes and trace their origins through black markets geographically.

wiki/drug-of-choice.title: Drug of Choice
wiki/drug-of-choice.content:
Overview
“Drug of choice” (DOC) refers to someone’s primary preference for a recreational substance. Many of those who struggle with Substance Use Disorders (SUDs) often struggle with one primary substance the most, even if they use other substances. The most common example is typically someone who says that they use weed or shrooms, but alcohol is what’s actively ruining their life or driving the worst of the destruction. For those with a history of polysubstance use, there may not be a clear DOC to pick, so many will often choose their first substance that served as a gateway into the others.

wiki/drug-policy-alliance.title: Drug Policy Alliance
wiki/drug-policy-alliance.content:
Overview
The Drug Policy Alliance (DPA) is a national non-profit heardquartered in New York City, New York with the goal of ending the war on drugs and advocating for evidence-based policies instead, like harm reduction. Their advocacy has included:


unifying a network of syringe service programs (SSPs)


leading a campaign for marijuana decriminalization, especially calling attention to racial disparities in arrests


supporting the expansion of Overdose Prevention Centers (OPCs)


lobbying against the Rockefeller Drug Laws that implemented strict mandatory minimum sentencing guidelines in 1973

Nevertheless, it is clear that the conception of addiction, like the concept of drug abuse, has long been approached in an unscientific or pseudoscientific way.”
“One reason for the prevalence of definitions of drug abuse that are neither logical nor scientific is the strength of Puritan moralism in American culture, which frowns on the pleasure and reaction provided by intoxicants… Our Puritan heritage is so deeply ingrained that even drinking is attended by a deep-seated ambivalence… The idea that pleasure, or at least the kind of pleasure that leads to escape and euphoria, is potentially dangerous and must be rationed in imprinted in the American consciousness… as my study has revealed, even very moderate drug users also reflect Puritan attitudes and values by feeling guilty about their use.”

wiki/drug-users-unions.title: Drug Users Unions
wiki/drug-users-unions.content:
Overview
Drug user unions are peer-led groups that advocate for those who either use substances actively or used to struggle with substance use disorders to improve access to healthcare, overall quality of life, and civil and human rights.
History and Etymology
One of the first formal drug user union was Junkiebond in Rotterdam, Netherlands as a response in 1977 to the spread of infectious diseases like hepatitis and police harassment among substance users. In 1981, they launched the world’s first official peer-led syringe exchange program.
In 1997, the Vancouver Area Network of Drug Users (VANDU) was launched and became a template for organizing supervised injection sites in 2003 through InSite, North America’s first. This was quickly followed by Landesverband der Junkie-Selbsthilfen (National Junkie Union) in 1998 in Germany.
In America, the National Survivors Union (NSU) and the San Francisco Drug Users Union advocate for clinical reforms and safe consumption sites. Many modern unions have advocated for a regulate supply of pharmaceutical-grade substances to reduce the overdoses caused by drugs from illicit manufacturing which may have contaminants that users aren’t aware of. These “safe supply” laws are obviously controversial, although many studies have suggested they could be a valuable part of harm reduction packages.
A common slogan these unions adopt is “Nothing About Us Without Us,” which addresses the objectification of those with a history or pattern of substance use into “addicts” who must be evaluated, monitored, and regulated by institutional authorities. Instead, they argue that substance users and their lived experiences should be at the forefront of public health policy interventions.

wiki/drugs-addiction-and-the-brain.title: Drugs, Addiction, and the Brain
wiki/drugs-addiction-and-the-brain.content:
Summary
“The cost to society of drug abuse and drug addiction is prodigious in terms of both the direct costs and indirect costs associated with secondary medical events, social problems, and loss of productivity. In the United States alone, illicit drug use and addiction cost society 161 billion per year in 2011. Alcoholism cost society 223 billion per year in 2012, and nicotine addiction costs society $155 billion. In terms of health burden, alcohol and tobacco use are in the top 10 greatest risk factors for loss of years to disease and disability.”
Although these are older numbers, I appreciate a textbook that begins with the scope of substance abuse and addiction as a public health issue. Time after time, one of the biggest takeaways from the history of substance abuse policies is that it is extremely preventable and treatable. In most drugs and most people, the time between someone’s first use as a maladaptive coping mechanism and the point of compulsive use is very far. It’s why it’s so frustrating to see institutions hack away at highly effective programs for short-term spending cuts in exchange for long-term crisis spending.
“Sound arguments have been made to support the hypothesis that addictions are similar to other chronic relapsing disorders, such as diabetes, asthma, and hypertension, in their chronic relapsing nature and treatment efficacy.”
Medications and therapeutic interventions can be effective at targeting symptoms and increasing sustained abstinence, but we have nothing we could call a cure or a strong equivalent to insulin for diabetes or an inhaled corticosteroids for asthma.

wiki/dual-diagnosis.title: Dual Diagnosis
wiki/dual-diagnosis.content:
Overview
Dual diagnosis treatment programs are iterations of substance use and mental health programs that acknowledge the co-occurrence of multiple mental health conditions and disorders alongside substance us.
The relationship is bidirectional: the self-medication hypothesis claims that people use substances as a way of addressing underlying health issues that could be a source of emotional or mental dysregulation, and substance use disorders can be a factor in exacerbating depression and anxiety. Contrary to historical assumptions in the treatment community, rather than stabilizing patients in sobriety prior to addressing trauma, recent studies show that addressing the trauma at the same time as coping skills for substance use is most effective, as trauma is often an underlying issue in substance use disorders to begin with.

wiki/dwight-anderson.title: Dwight Anderson
wiki/dwight-anderson.content: A PR professional hired by the Research Council on Problems of Alcohol, who was himself a recovering alcoholic, to promote the view that addiction was a disease that could be treated through medicine.

wiki/dysmorphia.title: Dysmorphia
wiki/dysmorphia.content:
Overview
Body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), often called dysmorphia as a shorthand, is a mental health condition in which someone is obsessively preoccupied with an apparent flaw that might be minor or nonexistent. These can include skin anomalies like acne or blemishes, hair conditions, nose shape, and overall bodily proportions, which someone might be excessively or compulsively checking. Repetitive actions, camouflaging, social avoidance, and heavy cosmetic investments like plastic surgery can all be symptoms of dysmorphia.

wiki/dysphoria.title: Dysphoria
wiki/dysphoria.content:
Overview
Dysphoria refers to a state of strong mental discomfort or distress, the opposite of euphoria. It’s not necessarily considered a mental illness itself, but it often accompanies mental health conditions like depression, anxiety, chronic stress, hormonal shifts, bipolar disorder, borderline personality disorder, and withdrawal symptoms. The ICD-11 includes dysphoria as a distinct diagnosis under “Mental or behavioural symptoms, signs or clinical findings,” where it’s defined as:
“An unpleasant mood state, which can include feelings of depression, anxiety, discontent, irritability, and unhappiness.”
“Gender dysphoria” is the clinical term to describe the distress experienced when someone’s gender identity feels misaligned with their sex or gender assignment at birth, leading to participation in gender presentations or roles that feel incongruent with someone’s true self. The DSM-5 uses the term “gender dysphoria” in place of “gender identity disorder” from previous editions.

wiki/dysregulation.title: Dysregulation
wiki/dysregulation.content:
Overview
The exact definitions and parameters of dysregulation depends on the context, but generally it means deviations from some expected normal regulatory functions.
Emotional dysregulation refers to difficulty controlling or adjusting one’s emotional state.

wiki/e-cigarette.title: E-cigarette
wiki/e-cigarette.content:
Overview
An e-cigarette is a battery-powered device that heats liquids to produce aerosols, so the user inhales vapor containing nicotine rather than smoke from traditional cigarettes.

wiki/early-career-addiction-science-show.title: Early Career Addiction Science Showcase (ECASS)
wiki/early-career-addiction-science-show.content:
Overview
The University of Southern California’s Institute for Addiction Science hosts the Early Career Addiction Science Showcase, an annual symposium for undergraduate students, graduate students, and junior faculty to demonstrate addiction research before its publication.

wiki/early-maladaptive-schema.title: Early Maladaptive Schema (EMS)
wiki/early-maladaptive-schema.content:
Overview
Under the Schema Therapy model advanced by Jeffrey Young, an early maladaptive schema (EMS) is a recurring pattern or core belief that develops in childhood or adolescence that serves as a source of dysfunction throughout one’s life. Generally, these schemas are rooted in formative experiences or trauma and are strongly held in a way that shapes new information to reinforce them.
Following the Young Schema Questionnaire-Revised (YSQ-R), clinicians generally acknowledge 20 schemas:


Abandonment or Instability


Mistrust or Abuse


Emotional Deprivation


Defectiveness or Shame


Social Isolation or Alienation


Dependence or Incompetence


Vulnerability to Harm or Illness


Enmeshment or Underdeveloped Self


Failure


Entitlement or Grandiosity


Insufficient Self-Control or Self-Discipline


Subjugation


Self-Sacrifice


Approval-Seeking or Recognition-Seeking


Negativity or Pessimism


Emotional Constriction


Fear of Losing Control


Unrelenting Standards or Hypercriticalness


Punitive-Self


Punitiveness-Others

Abstract

(2005) based their pie chart on the idea that, if 50% of variance in well-being is explained by genetic factors and 10% by circumstances, this “leaves as much as 40% of the variance for intentional activity” (p. 116). While these authors’ arithmetic cannot be faulted, it is not clear that the rest of their reasoning is as impeccable.”

wiki/eating-disorder.title: Eating Disorder (ED)
wiki/eating-disorder.content:
Overview
Eating disorders are patterns of consumption that are based in an unhealthy level of concern about caloric intake, weight gain, body image, or relationship to food. The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5-TR) acknowledges the following conditions under “Feeding and Eating Disorders”:


Anorexia Nervosa: restriction of food intake driven by excessive concerns about weight gain, often accompanied by a distorted body image and a dangerously low body weight. Anorexia is further split into the restricting subtype that uses excessive diet and exercise to reduce weight while the binge-eating/purging subtype involves, as the name suggests, bingeing and purging.


Bulimia Nervosa: cycles of eating that involve bingeing large amounts of good followed by purging to reduce caloric intake and prevent weight gain, which is usually done through vomiting, laxatives, fasting, or extreme exercising.


Binge-Eating Disorder (BED): episodes of bingeing large quantities of food past the point of pleasure or comfort in a way that feels like a loss of self-control without the purging of bulimia.


Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (ARFID): limitations in the amount or types of food someone consumes to the point of health consequences, such as a general disinterest in eating, discomfort with certain textures or colors, or fear of choking or vomiting.


Pica: repeatedly eating non-food substances without nutritional value, such as clay, paper, hair, etc.


Rumination Disorder: repeatedly and involuntarily regurgitating food to be re-chewed and re-swallowed without another medical condition explaining the struggle to keep down food.


Other Specified Feeding or Eating Disorder (OSFED): this diagnosis is used for serious disordered eating patterns that don’t necessarily meet the criteria for other diagnoses but can still be addressed with similar approaches and understanding of etiologies. This can include atypical anorexia nervosa, purging disorder, night eating syndrome, subthreshold bulimia, and subthreshold BED.


Unspecified Feeding or Eating Disorder (UFED): this diagnosis is used when someone has a serious disordered eating pattern but there isn’t enough information to make a more specific diagnosis. This might be used in emergency rooms when taking someone’s history or observing them over a period of time isn’t possible, but all the hallmarks of an eating disorder are present.


While the DSM-5-TR doesn’t mention the following disorders, medical professionals still often recognize them:


Orthorexia Nervosa: an obsession with eating foods that are “pure” or “perfect” in some way to the point of malnutrition or distress


Diabulimia (ED-DMT1): for those with Type 1 diabetes who skip or restrict required amounts of insulin to spur on weight loss, which is highly dangerous.

wiki/echo-valley.title: Echo Valley
wiki/echo-valley.content:
Overview
Commentary
Echo Valley is about enabling. Kate enables her daughter’s addiction, Richard enables his ex-wife’s failing business, and Les enables her best friend’s emotional decision-making.
Richard chastises Kate for giving money to Claire despite her obvious motive to keep using drugs, yet Richard is indirectly financing Claire by writing thousands of dollars to Kate when unexpected costs hit her farm that he never thought was a good idea. Kate then provides Claire with a home and money as needed.
When Kate is clearly distraught after Claire’s violent outburst and threats to steal the family dog as ransom for money, Les provides a night of good company as Kate drinks, dances, and drinks into a hangover the next morning. We don’t see Kate struggle with drinking in a way we might call dependence, so perhaps we get this scene to understand the degrees of enabling and self-destructive tendencies. It’s not unlike Breaking Bad with Marie’s kleptomania. She undoubtedly leans on alcohol periodically to cope with stress and loneliness, but she doesn’t struggle with cravings as much as tremendous grief and regrettable decisions when drunk. Both Kate and Claire express at various points that they feel their entire life is a complete failure. When Kate gets drunk, she ends up confessing that she dumped a body in a lake to protect her daughter.
Also, it’s a little on-the-nose that her lesbian friend is named Les. I’m not saying there aren’t lesbians named Leslie who use the Les pun all the time, but I am saying that when it’s a movie, you can choose any name you want for whatever reason you want.

wiki/edibles.title: Edibles
wiki/edibles.content:
Overview
Most commonly, “edibles” reference cannabis products that can be consumed the same as any food or drink item. The most popular edibles tend to be candies like gummies, baked goods like cookies and brownies, and other products that are based in fats like butter and oils in order to bind to the THC that produces psychoactive effects.
History and Etymology
Some forms of edibles have been around for thousands of years. Bhang is a traditional drink in India used for spiritual festivals like Holi that mixes ground cannabis paste, milk, ghee, and spices.
Anecdotally, a grand-aunt of mine in India was once heading to the market on Holi to pick up groceries and accidentally (no, seriously, this was a reserved temple lady very orthodox conservative environment) picked up Bhang instead of normal milk on the way back. She drank some and didn’t notice that it was spiked, so she went about her day in preparation for the evening’s ceremonies. It’s normal for Hindu homes to have a mini-temple or shrine set up to pray to deities and ancestors, and a family’s elderly women would often have the ritual responsibility of organizing the religious events and prayers. When she sat down in front of the shrine to pray with clasped hands, no one thought anything of it. Then an hour passed, and another hour passed, and she was still seated in front of the shrine. The family at first thought she was simply feeling very devotional that particular Holi, but they grew concerned after the second hour passed, and they tapped her on the shoulder to make sure she was alright. She replied with fear and wonder in her eyes: “I can’t pull my hands apart.”

wiki/ego.title: Ego
wiki/ego.content:
Overview
In philosophical and psychological contexts, “ego” doesn’t have the connotation of a negative byproduct of arrogance or narcissism; instead, it refers to an aspect of our identity that we construct as the “I.” Unconscious or subconscious feelings are generally considered outside of the ego’s scope.
In casual usage, we might say something like “you have such a huge ego, you’re impossible to talk to” when we mean that someone is fixated only on their own goals and desires without compromise or trust in others. We might also say “you have a healthy ego” when we mean that someone has an appropriate amount of self-esteem and self-awareness.
History and Etymology
In Ancient Greek and Latin, “ego” was synonymous with “I”. For instance, “ego cogito, ergo sum” is Latin for “I think, therefore I am,” which was coined by Rene Descartes. Rather than an “ego” located inside one’s self or mind, writers and philosophers discussed concepts like anima as a soul or intellectus as intellectual capacity. As Enlightenment thinkers began to discuss rationality and knowledge within oneself, which led to questions about what the “ego” really referred to. Immanuel Kant split the concept of the ego into the empirical ego, or the observable aspects of our personality and memories, and the transcendental ego, or the underlying consciousness that organizes sensory data into experiences that we observe.
Arthur Schopenhauer was among the first Western philosophers to pioneer a reconciliation between the Upanishads and ideas about the ego through maya, which gets roughly translated as “illusion” in a deceptive sense, though I would argue it’s closer to something like “constructed perception” in the way that a statue is constructed out of a marble slab without the statue being either “true” or “false” in a conventional sense. William James
Sigmund Freud is perhaps associated with the most well-known definition proposed about ego, though Freud himself wrote in German when discussing the id (“das Es”), ego (“dash Ich”), and superego (“das Uber-ich”). In a literal translation, they would mean “the it”, “the I”, and “the Over-I”, which is understandably clunky in English, so James Strachey translated Freud’s terms into id, ego, and superego.
William James, with his strong interest in Buddhist psychology and pluralistic systems, proposed a split in the self between a worldly “me” and an “I” of pure awareness that observes the “me.”
Carl Jung was heavily influenced by Eastern traditions from Tibetan belief systems, Buddhism, and Hinduism.
Post-structuralist philosophers like Michel Foucault argued that the ego is not objective or physiological fact, but a socially-constructed tool that allows institutions to reduce humans to a manageable model.

wiki/elder-abuse.title: Elder Abuse
wiki/elder-abuse.content:
Overview
Elder abuse refers to intentional acts or intentional failure to act that causes harm to older adults, generally 60 or older, though this varies by legal jurisdictions.
For elders who aren’t necessarily capable of taking care of themselves and have caregivers, being intentionally over- or under-medicated can be classified as elder abuse. Seniors who have struggled with substance abuse in the past can be vulnerable for financial exploitation.
Commentary
Anecdotally, I’ve heard multiple stories of elders in treatment whose children become controlling over their finances and affairs while they’re aware. I won’t say this necessarily rises to the level of elder abuse, especially since the elders in question themselves don’t use that term to describe their frustrations, but it’s not hard to see how easily it could happen to someone.

wiki/electroconvulsive-therapy.title: Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT)
wiki/electroconvulsive-therapy.content:
Overview
Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is a medical procedure that runs electrical currents to the brain and triggers seizures for mental health conditions that are otherwise treatment-resistant. This stimulates a kind of reset in the brain that can break toxic patterns without needing weeks or months like antidepressants and therapeutic interventions.
Commentary
I was honestly surprised that ECT was still a real thing and not just known as a meme from One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest that was as archaic and pseudoscientific as icepick lobotomies. Not only is it a real thing actually, but it has an incredibly strong base of evidence as an acute intervention.

wiki/electroencephalogram.title: Electroencephalogram (EEG)
wiki/electroencephalogram.content:
Overview
Electroencephalograms (EEGs) are tests to measure the electrical activity in the brain.
EEG Neurofeedback (EEG-NF) is a medical intervention that retrains the brain’s electrical patterns that connect to subconscious cues for cravings and impulsive behavior. Someone might be hooked up to a brainwave monitoring system through EEG sensors and told to achieve some rewarding tasks solely through bringing their state of mind to emit particular brainwaves. For instance, if you begin to slip into a stressful state that can induce cravings, the task might issue a penalty, like dimming the light of a screen with an interesting movie or slowing down a character’s movement in a video game. If you are able to bring your brain into a calmer state, the reward is restored or increased, like improving picture quality or character speeds. Not only does this train the brain to reach stable emotional states through immediate rewards for the behavior, it also improves the brain’s capacity to remain stable while processing trauma and triggers.

wiki/electronic-drug-delivery-devices.title: Electronic Drug Delivery Device (EDDD)
wiki/electronic-drug-delivery-devices.content:
Overview
Electronic drug delivery devices (EDDDs) are medical instruments that release medications into the body. These can include:


Insulin Pumps that continuously monitor glucose levels to release insulin


Connected Inhalers that use sensors to track adherence to medication schedules and log usage on devices like smartphones


Iontophoretic Devices are systems that use electrical currents to push drugs through the skin


Implantable Smart Systems include microchips and wireless reservoirs to manage chronic conditions with targeted, long-term release medications and therapies


For substance use disorders, EDDDs include:


Electronic neurostimulation devices like the NSS-2 Bridge or NET Device as battery-powered processors placed behind ears to apply electrical currents and stimulate the vagus and trigeminal nerves to block distress from withdrawal symptoms such as nausea, anxiety, and tremors.


Smart Implantable Pumps controlled by microchips are placed under the skin with a reservoir of medications such as buprenorphine to release precise doses into the bloodstream to eliminate cravings


Wearable Biosensors such as wristbands and patches continuously track vitals to detect biometric signatures associated with cravings or stressors that precede a potential relapse. These can also alert clinicians or begin an automated inteventions like an exercise out of Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (CBT). Recent advances in machine learning have opened the door to tracking all kinds of biometrics for latent patterns that clinicians and patients may not consciously think to monitor.

wiki/electronic-health-records.title: Electronic Health Records (EHRs)
wiki/electronic-health-records.content:
Overview
Electronic health records (EHRs) are a major part of the technical infrastructure in our healthcare system.
Commentary
When I worked on healthcare AI problems, parsing and interpreting EHRs was a common task, and it’s not as straightforward as it sounds. The proliferation of software vendors in the healthcare space often means that there are significant hurdles to clean and efficient communication of EHR data between clinics and researchers. In fact, one of the major healthcare policy goals of the Obama administration was to improve the interoperability of EHR records, which unfortunately did not succeed.

wiki/emergency-medicine.title: Emergency Medicine
wiki/emergency-medicine.content:
Overview
Emergency medicine is the field of medicine concerned with diagnosing and treating health issues that require immediate care to avoid long-lasting harm or fatalities.
Many who struggle with substance use disorders don’t seek or receive treatment until the disorder leads to a crisis point, whether that involves external harm addressed by a criminal justice system or a health crises that could result in permanent disabilities or death. Naloxone (narcan) is one of the most commonly known emergency interventions in response to opioid overdoses, especially as fentanyl-related overdoses have become a concerning epidemic in recent years in America. Addressing the delirium tremens (DTs) of alcohol withdrawal or complications of benzodiazepine withdrawals, both of which can be particularly fatal through their ability to cause seizures. For drug users who practice injections, infections like skin abscesses and endocarditis can require urgent treatment as well. And of course, substance use can always be a factor in physical trauma such as those from car crashes that involve Driving Under Influence (DUI).
Historically, emergency rooms (ERs) focused on stabilizing substance users who suffered from an overdose or required oversight for managing withdrawal before discharging them with contact information for long-term treatment facilities like rehabilitation centers. This has since changed through ED-Bridge Programs that inititate long-term treatment within ERs, such as Medication for Opioid Use Disorder (MOUD) protocols involving buprenorphine (also called Suboxone). Substance use navigators (SUNs) are dedicated peer counselors or social workers who guide patients into clinics or rehabs for long-term management and treatment. Many ERs also embrace harm-reduction policies that distribute take-home naloxone (narcan) kits and fentanyl test strips that can address fatal overdoses without requiring a risky and costly trip to the ER.

wiki/emotional-flashback.title: Emotional Flashback
wiki/emotional-flashback.content:
Overview
The term “emotional flashback” was popularized by Pete Walker in 2005:
“Emotional flashbacks are sudden and often prolonged regressions (‘amygdala hijackings’) to the frightening circumstances of childhood. They are typically experienced as intense and confusing episodes of fear and/or despair - or as sorrowful and/or enraged reactions to this fear and despair. Emotional flashbacks are especially painful because the inner critic typically overlays them with toxic shame, inhibiting the individual from seeking comfort and support, isolating him in an overwhelming and humiliating sense of defectiveness.”
Notably, “emotional flashback” has not been incorporated into official medical guidelines or classification systems. There are related terms, such as affect dysregulation, somatic re-experiencing, affective re-experiencing, state-dependent memory, implicit memory activation, etc., but “emotional flashback” itself isn’t a term you’d find often in academic or scientific literature. Walker doesn’t pretend otherwise; his writings repeatedly refer to the clinical experiences he has had that, in his perspective, validate the concept:
“Numerous clients tell me that the concept of an emotional flashback brings them a great sense of relief. They report that for the first time they are able to make some sense of their extremely troubled lives. Some get that their addictions are misguided attempts to self-medicate. Some understand the inefficacy of the myriad psychological and spiritual answers they pursued, and are in turn feel liberated from a shaming plethora of misdiagnoses. Some can now frame their extreme episodes of risk taking and self-destructiveness as desperate attempts to distract themselves from their pain. Many experience hope that they can rid themselves of the habit of amassing evidence of defectiveness or craziness. Many report a budding recognition that they can challenge the self-hate and self-disgust that typically thwarts their progress in therapy.”
The term “emotional flashback” evidently invites comparisons to the “flashbacks” of PTSD. A quick browse through Reddit forums about trauma and CPTSD reveals extremely strong support for the concept, as well as the exact type of catharsis at having the vocabulary to discuss the intense emotional experiences that Walker discussed seeing in his clients. Walker’s website lists steps for managing these flashbacks:


Say to yourself: “I am having a flashback”


Remind yourself: “I feel afraid but I am not in danger! I am safe now, here in the present.”


Own your right/need to have boundaries.


Speak reassuringly to the Inner Child


Deconstruct eternity thinking.


Remind yourself that you are in an adult body with allies, skills and resources to protect you that you never had as a child.


Ease back into your body through progressive muscle relaxation, breathwork, and safe spaces.


Resist the Inner Critic’s Drasticizing and Catastrophizing


Allow yourself to grieve.


Cultivate safe relationships and seek support.


Learn to identify the types of triggers that lead to flashbacks.


Figure out what you are flashing back to.


Be patient with a slow recovery process: it takes time in the present to become un-adrenalized


Links

wiki/emotional-sobriety.title: Emotional Sobriety
wiki/emotional-sobriety.content:
Overview
“Emotional sobriety” is a term from 12-step programs that refers to maintaining emotional, mental, and spiritual conditions conducive to a healthy and sober lifestyle.
History and Etymology
The term comes from a January 1958 issue of the AA Grapevine magazine where William Wilson (known as Bill W. in AA circles) published an article, based on an old personal letter, titled “The Next Frontier: Emotional Sobriety”:
“I think that many oldsters who have put our AA “booze cure” to severe but successful tests still find they often lack emotional sobriety. Perhaps they will be the spearhead for the next major development in AA — the development of much more real maturity and balance (which is to say, humility) in our relations with ourselves, with our fellows, and with God.”
“Those adolescent urges that so many of us have for top approval, perfect security, and perfect romance — urges quite appropriate to age seventeen — prove to be an impossible way of life when we are at age forty-seven or fifty-seven.”
“Since AA began, I’ve taken immense wallops in all these areas because of my failure to grow up, emotionally and spiritually. My God, how painful it is to keep demanding the impossible, and how very painful to discover finally, that all along we have had the cart before the horse! Then comes the final agony of seeing how awfully wrong we have been, but still finding ourselves unable to get off the emotional merry-go-round.”
“How to translate a right mental conviction into a right emotional result, and so into easy, happy, and good living — well, that’s not only the neurotic’s problem, it’s the problem of life itself for all of us who have got to the point of real willingness to hew to right principles in all our affairs.” 1
Commentary
In my experience, the term has been sufficiently used outside of the context of AA and 12-Step programs enough so that it can to refer to any attempt to address unhealthy aspects of one’s life that are associated with active addiction or the potential for relapse, especially if increasing one’s capacity for emotional regulation, consistent self-care routines, and protective boundaries. Many of these habits and capacities are the result of therapeutic interventions that at least attempt to root their practices in empirical approaches and modifying theories of the mind.
Still, if the term is being used in the context of AA circles, it can carry all the connotations of engagement with Protestant spirituality and religion that characterizes AA philosophy. That includes monitoring for character defects and emotions that accompany them, such as anger, self-pity, and fear. In theory, it might sound obvious that those negative emotions might be associated with producing intolerable states that precede a relapse, but in practice, this can veer into suppression and gaslighting that labels those emotions as unhealthy entirely. For instance, if someone is spreading untrue and hurtful rumors about you, experiencing anger, betrayal, and insecurity are themselves considered threats to emotional sobriety. To care about what others might think of you is considered a relic of pride and ego that must be uprooted, usually with a recitation of the Serenity Prayer that declares that what others think of you and do about it is out of your control and none of your business. In fact, you might be told to focus on your part in that situation, like what you may have done that incentivized someone to spread rumors about you. If you struggle to internalize that framework, you become in-need of a spiritual awakening that brings you closer to acting through the will of your Higher Power instead of your own. As Wilson wrote:
I kept asking myself, “Why can’t the Twelve Steps work to release depression?” By the hour, I stared at the St. Francis Prayer…”It’s better to comfort than to be the comforted.” Here was the formula, all right. But why didn’t it work? Suddenly I realized what the matter was. My basic flaw had always been dependence — almost absolute dependence – on people or circumstances to supply me with prestige, security, and the like. Failing to get these things according to my perfectionist dreams and specifications, I had fought for them. And when defeat came, so did my depression
Bluntly, this is delusionally naive.
Depression is a distinct experience from the situational disappointment and grief that comes from mourning a loss of material attachments or an angst driven by a perfectionism unrequited with reality. Study after study into the neurological and biological mechanisms through which depression is experienced demonstrate that there are physiological foundations for its executive dysfunction. The argument that one need only release their dependency and expectations of the world around them to look inward amounts to a mind-over-matter, mindset-is-everything proclamation of radical Cartesian mind-body dualism. It’s steeped in the Protestant moral-psychology that posits an ultimate soul endowed by a Creator as a Higher Power that can be strengthened spiritually to conquer the material sins, weaknesses, and flaws of the flesh.
Imagine if someone were to recommend “walking it off” in response to a broken leg. We would reasonably call this person stupid. They’ve extrapolated walking as a healthy exercise into an infinitely healing activity, and then they’ve decided someone who cannot do it can be healed if only they chose to do it. If they fail, they simply didn’t choose hard enough and should seek a Higher Power’s will to do what they themselves cannot. If they succeed by powering through, which would inevitably worsen a broken leg into a bleeding one, this is seen as proof that the solution works regardless of the worsening situation at-hand. Similarly, calls for someone who experiences depression to simply not do things that make them sadder and to do things that make them happier are also flawed. The individual’s exact capacity to experience reward from dopaminergistic pathways rather than be stuck in a state of anhedonia is broken. You cannot use a broken tool to fix itself. Depression is a disorder precisely because it leads to a distinct phenomenological engagement with the world that changes one’s perception of rewards, risks, time, agency, intentionality, sensory information, intersubjectivity, communication, etc.
Wilson himself was a proponent of using psychedelics to induce spiritual awakenings, as he had undergone one himself in a hospital while being administered belladonna and was close friends with an even bigger drugs enthusiast in Aldous Huxley, with whom he shared a doctor named Humphry Osmond who literally coined the term “psychedelic.” Later in life, in part through his discussions with Osmond that brought somewhat more grounded biological and therapeutic concepts to the forefront of his worldview, Wilson embraced biochemical interventions that the AA General Service Board was furiously opposed to and censored from AA communication channels. Aside from LSD, Wilson had also explored high doses of Niacin (Vitamin B3) to counter his depression through a doctor named Abram Hoffer, and Wilson reportedly felt enormous improvements in his symptoms after.
I bring all this up primarily because of two incidents where, in a more neutral recovery setting, an AA diehard attempted to impose a perspective of emotional sobriety that was completely incongruent with their experiences, which only led to friction. In one case, someone expressed frustration that there is no 12 steps for a depression that left them without intrinsic motivation to live their own life, articulating almost exactly some of the sentiments that Wilson does in his letter, only to be recommended a Codependents Anonymous (CODA) meeting: “sometimes we need someone to give us a kick to get started.” This is one of the reasons I take a critical focus towards AA in my commentary, because elevating something into a gold standard also turns it into a hammer that treats every problem like a nail. Our brains naturally seek shortcuts, so echo chambers that encourage a reliance on a gold standard, even as a first-stop, run the risk of discouraging critical reasoning that actually addresses the roots of someone’s problem. In the second case, someone was attempting to express that they didn’t automatically see certain emotions as unhealthy, even if they have negative implications like anger or grief that might be ordinary parts of the human experience. This same person had undergone months of counseling about managing emotions that could get out of hand by seeing their feelings as information to act on rather than an enemy to suppress or endure. The facilitator in this setting shut it down simply with “I don’t have time for that shit” while repeating the framework that certain emotions are unhealthy. This strikes me as a natural consequence of the notion of emotional sobriety that Wilson developed. After all, if physical sobriety referred to abstinence that views substances or disorders as enemies to personify and combat as if they’re agents of the Devil lying in wait that must be warded off through constant moral surveillance, then emotional sobriety is naturally going to have echoes of that thinking by framing certain emotions as comparable to substances.
Links
Footnotes


“The Next Frontier: Emotional Sobriety” by Bill Wilson ↩

wiki/empathy.title: Empathy
wiki/empathy.content:
Overview
In its most basic sense, empathy describes the ability to understand how others feel, think, or believe things.
The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (SEP) describes the complexity of defining and measuring the concept:
“…since researchers in different disciplines have focused their investigations on very specific aspects of the broad range of empathy-related phenomena, one should probably not be surprised by a certain amount of conceptual confusion and a multiplicity of definitions associated with the empathy concept in a number of different scientific and non-scientific discourses” 1
The DSM-5-TR defines “Empathy” as a part of the Self when considering stable characteristics of personality functions:
“Empathy: Comprehension and appreciation of others’ experiences and motivations; tolerance of differing perspectives; understanding of the effects of one’s own behavior on others.”
For instance, one of the proposed diagnostic criteria for antisocial personality disorder under Empathy is
“Lack of concern for feelings, needs, or suffering of others; lack of remorse after hurting or mistreating another.”
And for avoidant personality disorder:
Preoccupation with, and sensitivity to, criticism or rejection, associated with distorted inference of others’ perspectives as negative.
Some attempts by researchers to measure empathy include the Multifaceted Empathy Test (MET), Empathy Quotient (EQ), Interpersonal Reactivity Index (IRI),
Links
Footnotes


Empathy ↩

wiki/empiricism.title: Empiricism
wiki/empiricism.content:
Overview
Empiricism refers to the beliefs and practices that emphasize the value of data that can be observed in forming models of the world. This contrasts with rationalists or idealists who argue that logical principles should come first as a lens to interpret empirical data. For instance, if we conduct some experiment that suggests 2 + 2 = 5, an empiricist might argue that we have to revise the logical principles that made us think 2 + 2 = 4, while an idealist might argue that the experiment should be examined more closely for another factor producing 5. In practice, most people are not radical empiricists or radical idealists.

wiki/employee-assistance-program.title: Employee Assistance Program (EAP)
wiki/employee-assistance-program.content:
Overview
An Employee Assistance Program (EAP) is defined by the U.S. Office of Personnel Management as:
“a voluntary, work-based program that offers free and confidential assessments, short-term counseling, referrals, and follow-up services to employees who have personal and/or work-related problems.  EAPs address a broad and complex body of issues affecting mental and emotional well-being, such as alcohol and other substance abuse, stress, grief, family problems, and psychological disorders.  EAP counselors also work in a consultative role with managers and supervisors to address employee and organizational challenges and needs.  Many EAPs are active in helping organizations prevent and cope with workplace violence, trauma, and other emergency response situations.” 1
EAPs for substance use disorders and other mental health conditions have been an instrumental part in shifting the perception of these conditions as mere issues of morality and willpower into legitimate health issues that are worthy of treatment. They are sometimes considered a form of Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) that aims to rehabilitate and treat employees who have the disorder rather than immediately terminating them, although it does obviously provide benefit to a company to be able to retain a productive employee after they seek treatment rather than gamble on the overhead costs of replacing them with a new employee.
Links
Footnotes


What is an Employee Assistance Program (EAP)? - OPM.gov ↩

wiki/enabling.title: Enabling
wiki/enabling.content:
Overview
The American Psychological Association (APA) offers two contexts to define enabling through:


“a process whereby someone (i.e., the enabler) contributes to continued maladaptive or pathological behavior (e.g., child abuse, substance abuse) in another person. The enabler is typically an intimate partner or good friend who passively permits or unwittingly encourages this behavior in the other person; often, the enabler is aware of the destructiveness of the person’s behavior but feels powerless to prevent it.”


“the process of encouraging or allowing individuals to meet their own needs and achieve desired ends. A therapist attempts to enable clients to believe in themselves, have the confidence to act on their desires, and affirm their ability to achieve.”


For substance use disorders, enabling refers to support provided for someone to continue their pattern of substance use. This can be material, emotional, financial, or other forms of support.
Commentary
Echo Valley
[[echo-valley|Echo Valley (2025)]] is a movie that I praise for two things: not leaning on Sydney Sweeney’s cleavage to bring in an audience, and for putting the concept of enabling at the core of a story whose events are driven by addiction rather than focusing on the spiral of addiction with enablers at the periphery as collateral damage. While the movie is certainly driven by the consequences of each character’s actions, it also doesn’t resort to a morality play, instead taking us through the many grey areas between different types of relationship dynamics in which we might enable each other, intentionally or unintentionally.
Kate Garrett owns a farm called Echo Valley in which she tends to horses and teaches a list of clients to ride and train them. Kate was once married to Richard and had a daughter Claire who has struggled repeatedly with substance use. At the start of the movie, we see that Kate’s business is not particularly sustainable; when she struggles to afford the repairs to the roof of her barn, she visits her ex-husband and wealthy lawyer Richard to ask for a check. Richard voices what appear to be old concerns, reminding Kate that he never thought the farm was a good idea, that they aren’t married anymore, and that the advice of a counselor they had visited was to stop giving money to Claire that went towards sustaining her addiction. After losing Patty, Kate begins cancelling lessons to self-isolate and attempt to cope with her grief, which doesn’t help improve the financial viability of the business. Yet, Richard still cuts the check, indicating that despite his awareness that the family dynamics are built around enabling, he still struggles to just say no.
We also learn that Kate had married a woman named Patty after splitting with Richard and that Patty died tragically in a horse-riding accident. The persistent crack in the ceiling above Kate’s bed symbolizes the persistence of her grief, as one of the last messages Patty left her was a promise to fix that crack. Her refusal to sell the farm despite the financial losses appears tied to the way she clings to the objects that remind her of Patty, even down to Patty’s death. We also hear Patty say in one message, “I just wanted to say sorry about last night. I was just drunk and being insensitive. Anyways, I’m back home in half an hour and I’m going to shower you with kisses until you forgive me.” Evidently, Kate struggles with letting go of the people and things she’s become attached to or setting boundaries, even to her own detriment. Patty’s message foreshadows this pattern in the movie where Kate’s willingness to forgive those she loves for the promise of affection and appreciation later proves to be a source of suffering.
Claire inevitably shows up at Kate’s farm with a story about a recent fight she just had with her boyfriend Ryan and declares her intentions to leave and start over. Kate’s parental affection dominates their interactions as she tries to coax Claire into returning to school as part of a fresh start, although, in perhaps one of the few genuine moments Claire gives us when she isn’t in active addiction, Claire echoes a self-defeating sentiment that Kate herself does later: “I guess it was a failure, just like the rest of my life.” My interpretation of Kate’s character is that she isn’t particularly introspective, not out of a lack of ability, but a lack of desire. She looks for reasons to validate a narrative in which her enabling or excuses for others are a sign of her commitment, which saves her from setting boundaries that could risk a loss of the intimacy she holds onto. If you squint hard enough, being manipulated looks like being wanted. The movie takes this to a radical extent when Kate gets roped into covering for a murder and burning her barn down to pay back a dealer because Claire ropes her into her schemes.
There are more subtle versions of enabling in the show too. Kate’s best friend Les, in trying to help Kate let loose from the tragedies and trauma of her life, seems to be liberal with using alcohol as a means of dancing off or venting emotions. We don’t see dependence comparable to Claire’s addiction, but we do get the sense that Les, understandably, aims to help her friend feel comfortable rather than work through some of the obstacles and grievances in her life.
Links

wiki/end-addiction-bham-walk.title: End Addiction BHAM Walk
wiki/end-addiction-bham-walk.content:
Overview
The End Addiction BHAM Walk was organized by the Addiction Prevention Coalition (APC) in Birmingham, Alabama for the first time in 2017. Originally, it was named the “End Heroin Birmingham Walk” before being renamed for all substance use disorders. It gathered 3000-4000 attendees and 75 community organizations before its final year in 2026. The organizers and participants are now pivoting to new community outreach initiatives.
Links

endaddictionbham.swell.gives/

wiki/endocannabinoids.title: Endocannabinoids
wiki/endocannabinoids.content:
Overview
Endocannabinoids, or endogenous cannabinoids, are molecules naturally made by the body that maintain the body’s internal homeostatic balance through regulating mood, appetite, sleep, pain, memory, and the movement of other molecules like dopamine and serotonin.
A chapter from Neurobiology and Physiology of the Endocannabinoid System (2023) describes endocannabinoids as:
“a class of small signaling lipids consisting of amides, esters, and ethers of long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids derived naturally from lipid precursors in plasma membranes of animal organisms (Burstein, 2014) and can be found throughout the human body. Endocannabinoids are part of the endocannabinoid system consisting of endocannabinoids, their metabolic enzymes for biosynthesis and biodegradation, the cannabinoid type 1 (CB1) and type 2 (CB2) receptors, and the endocannabinoid membrane transporter (De Petrocellis & Di Marzo, 2009).”
“The endocannabinoid system operates as a homeostatic regulator in essentially all organ systems of physiological processes such as neurodevelopment and cell fate, synaptic transmission, learning and memory, nociception, stress and emotions, immunomodulation, hormone secretion, food intake and energy balance, digestive tract motility and secretion, bone mass, and reproduction, among others (Almeida et al., 2021; Maccarrone et al., 2015; Mechoulam & Parker, 2013).”
“Aside from the physiological roles, elements of the endocannabinoid system may serve as potential therapeutic targets in various pathological conditions (Aizpurua-Olaizola et al., 2017). Indeed, pharmacological manipulation of the endocannabinoid system has yielded antinociceptive, anticonvulsive, anxiolytic, antiinflammatory, antiemetic, and orexigenic outcomes, alleviating the symptoms or slowing the progression of different diseases (Fraguas-Sánchez & Torres-Suárez, 2018; Reddy et al., 2020).”
In the context of cannabis, the plant’s cannabinoids, or phytocannabinoids, mimic the natural endocannabinoids produced by the body.Tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) binds strongly to CB1 and CB2 receptors, while cannabidiol (CBD) does not bind as strongly, which is why THC is associated with psychoactive effects that produce a “high” while CBD is associated with anti-inflammation, pain relief, and anxiety reduction.
Links

wiki/endogenous.title: Endogenous
wiki/endogenous.content:
Overview
“Endogenous” in the context of chemicals and biology refers to something produced from within a system.
For instance, the tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) and cannabidiol (CBD) present in cannabis mimic the endogenous cannabinoids, or endocannabinoids manufactured naturally by the body’s system.
Many of the substances and medications that we use, illicitly or otherwise, function by emulating endogenous chemicals, especially Designer drugs that often modify a chemically found naturally:


Opiates and Opioids like heroin, morphone, oxycodone, and fentanyl mimic endogenous endorphins and enkephalins


Cannabis mimics endocannabinoids like anandamide which bind to CB1 receptors


Alcohol, benzodiazepines, and barbiturates bind to Gamma-Aminobutyric Acid (GABA) receptors


Nicotine mimics acetylcholine


Psychedelics like LSD, psilocybin, and DMT hyper-activate 5-HT2A serotonin receptors


Caffeine mimics adenosine


Stimulants like cocaine and amphetamines don’t mimic endogenous chemicals, but instead provoke the body into releasing its own dopamine and norepinephrine in excess amounts to produce the pleasure of a high.

wiki/enmeshment.title: Enmeshment
wiki/enmeshment.content:
Overview
Enmeshment is defined by the American Psychological Association as
“a condition in which two or more people, typically family members, are involved in each other’s activities and personal relationships to an excessive degree, thus limiting or precluding healthy interaction and compromising individual autonomy and identity.”
It’s one of the signs of codependence in relationships, where someone becomes reliant on a person or an interpersonal dynamic to such an extreme degree that it harms them but they feel they cannot separate from it.
That being said, enmeshment is not a culturally neutral concept. “Western” ideas of a nuclear family with parents and children in a single unit until adulthood when the children acquire homes of their own are not universal. Cultures in Asia, South America, the Middle East, and Africa have long traditions of collective identity and strong interdependent dynamics between family and community structures. Some studies have shown that high interdependence actually correlates with better psychological and socioeconomic outcomes, particularly in immigrant communities that might experience marginalization. Co-regulation between nervous systems is a real phenomenon, and the scope creep of enmeshment, particularly in pop psychology and self-help, can lead to framing critical supportive networks as unhealthy enmeshments. In these cases, dysfunction might be better addressed by treating the family or network as a unit that has difficulty accommodating a member’s independent preferences rather than prioritizing the individual as a unit that must set boundaries or create distance from their community. That way, rather than pathologizing a structure of relationships that people might have long traditions surviving and thriving through, the focus of therapeutic work can be the reactions of members within those dynamics.
Links

wiki/entheos.title: Entheos
wiki/entheos.content:
Overview
In Ancient Greek, entheos is formed out of en (within) and theos (god), forming the phrase “the god within.” It was used to describe people who appeared so passionate or talented that they seemed possessed by some kind of divinity. The word “enthusiasm” comes out of “entheos” and originally referred to operating with something that seems like a divine inner spark.

wiki/entitlement.title: Entitlement
wiki/entitlement.content:
Overview
“Entitlement” has at least two distinct uses depending on the context.
For healthcare providers and insurance, “entitlement” refers to a legal right to receive healthcare benefits or coverage once an individual meets criteria.
Within psychology and psychiatry, entitlement can be interpreted as a personality trait or a cognitive distortion that presents with personality disorders:


Narcissistic Personality Disorder (NPD): entitlement can be seen in an individual’s constant need for admiration, validation, and/or rewards from others


Antisocial Personality Disorder (ASPD): entitlement can be a factor in one’s belief that they can violate the rights of others or break the rules for personal gain


Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD): during emotional crises, people with BPD might feel entitled to ask for reassurance or support that breaks boundaries in response to intense fears surrounding the possibility of abandonment or rejection

wiki/epidemiology.title: Epidemiology
wiki/epidemiology.content:
Overview
Epidemiology is the field that concerns the spread of health determinants and distributions across populations, generally with the goal of influencing public health policy. This extends beyond infectious diseases and environmental contamination to trends in obesity and stress. Studies show that weight gain actually spreads across populations, implying that even something as fundamental as diet has psychosocial dimensions independent of individual factors or socioeconomic circumstances.
Commentary
Personally, I love epidemiology as a field. I don’t have much exposure to it aside from my undergraduate education and some MIT hackathons around the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic, but, for me, it combines the social impacts of public health policy with the theoretical models of network science and graph theory.

wiki/epigenetics.title: Epigenetics
wiki/epigenetics.content:
Overview
Epigenetics is the field of studying how behavioral functions and environmental factors influence how genes and DNA operate. The term “epigenome” is used to describe the chemical tags that collectively attach to DNA that turn certain genes on or off.
With chronic substance use, the “hijacking” of neural pathways associated with reward and self-control are directly rooted in epigenetic mechanisms. For instance, cocaine and alcohol stimulate enzymes that activate genes increasing neuroplasticity and the production of dendritic spines, which is how the brain can become more sensitive to cues associated with substance use.

wiki/essay-on-drunkenness-by-thomas-trot.title: An Essay, Medical, Philosophical, and Chemical on Drunkenness and Its Effects on the Human Body by Thomas Trotter (1804)

wiki/ethanol.title: Ethanol
wiki/ethanol.content:
Overview
“Ethanol” is the name for the type of alcohol that goes into alcoholic beverages.
In the context of chemistry, “alcohol” refers to a group of compounds that contain a hydroxl group bound to a carbon atom. What we call “alcohol” in a casual context to refer to beverages is specifically ethanol. For the rest of this page, I’ll use “alcohol” in its chemical context and “ethanol” when referring to drinks.
Ethanol is a product of fermentation, a metabolic process that transfers electrons between organic molecules. When consumed by humans, it serves as a psychoactive depressant for the central nervous system (CNS). The liver and stomach are the primary organs that metabolize ethanol through enzymes that produce acetaldehyde as an intermediate, which is listed as a Group 1 carcinogen by the International Agency for Research on Cancer. Many of the consequences associated with consuming beverages containing ethanol actually stem from an association with acetaldehyde. The so-called “Asian glow” or “Asian flush”, where people of East Asian descent seem to turn red quickly after drinking, can be attributed to genetic mutations that hamper the enzymes responsible for processing acetaldehyde while improving the process by which ethanol produces acetaldehyde.
The history of ethanol is an incredibly long and varied one, as almost every part of the world in almost every civilization that has existed has at some point experimented with ethanol. Because it can be produced as the result of naturally-occurring fermented fruits, even animals learn and adapt to the effects of alcohol. It has been observed being used as a sedative, anesthetic, antidote, and antiseptic aside from just a recreational substance. Since the early 20th century, ethanol has been explored as a fuel source.

wiki/etheridge-foundation.title: Etheridge Foundation
wiki/etheridge-foundation.content:
Melissa Etheridge founded this organization after the loss of her son from an overdose at 21 after he started using pankillers for an accident at 17.
Links
www.etheridgefoundation.org/

wiki/etiology.title: Etiology
wiki/etiology.content:
Overview
“Etiology” is a term for the study of causes, which historically has meant a combination of medical, biological, political, and theological analyses into understanding why someone might be suffering.
Suppose we look at someone who experienced a car crash. We can obviously trace the physical injuries resulting from it to the traumatic experience itself, but it may not be sufficient to explain why the car accident happened or why someone continues to suffer after it passed. They might report an increase in symptoms of depression not as a direct result of the car accident but as a result of lacking trauma-informed support from their surrounding network that leads to feelings of isolation about their experience. They might also ask why they specifically were in a car accident compared to someone else, which might involve referencing one’s religion or spiritual frameworks. It might be true that a car accident is caused by someone Driving Under Influence (DUI), but someone might believe that the reason they specifically ended up in an accident had to do with divine punishment or karmic justice. They might try to find some moral lesson in their accident, which involves exploring distinct etiologies than the physiological mechanisms that biomedical physicians and clinicians deal in.

wiki/eugenics.title: Eugenics
wiki/eugenics.content:
Overview
Eugenics refers to the application of selective reproduction towards creating a human population with particular genetic characteristics.
It is widely considered one of the most horrific set of beliefs that humans have ever proposed and put into practice. Not only has it relied heavily on pseudoscientific essentialist frameworks that are widely refuted through empirical analyses, but it has attracted some of the worst personalities and dehumanizing impulses available to humanity. Eugenicists have attempted to address every social, physical, and spiritual ill of humanity through genetic explanations, with stopping a certain group’s reproduction as the part of every solution. Everything from “criminality” to intelligence to mental illness to poverty has been a problem hat eugenics has attempted to tackle with barbaric solutions like forced sterilization or mass exermination. That includes substance use disorders; the idea of sterilizing those struggling with SUDs to prevent the transmission of genes with a predisposition for addictive behaviors.
History and Etymology
The United States has been a prolific incubator of eugenics, so much so that Nazi Germany was inspired by the eugenics movements and laws of the US. In Buck v. Bell (1927), Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes of the Supreme Court wrote “three generations of imbeciles are enough” as an endorsement of forced sterilization programs against over 60,000 people in the United States. The case has never been formally overturned.
Commentary
The line between elitism and eugenics is paper thin. Eugenics provides those suffering from elitism an etiology to rationalize and justify their position and rewards within a system larger than them. After all, the alternative involves either admititng that one’s position has largely been determined by factors out of their control or adding even more rationalizations to explain the dissonance between themselves and everyone else who expresses the same virtues without the same rewards.

wiki/european-union-drugs-agency.title: European Union Drugs Agency
wiki/european-union-drugs-agency.content:
Overview
The European Union Drugs Agency (EUDA) is the official agency of the European Union in charge of providing information about illicit drugs across the continent. It was originally called the European Monitoring Centre for Drugs and Drug Addiction (EMCDDA), but in 2024, it transitioned into EUDA as part of a shift into being a service-oriented organization rather than just an information hub. Their model is “anticipate, alert, respond, and learn.”
Their recent projects include:


European Drug Alert System: a 24/7 early warning framework to coordinate forensic lab data and deliver security alerts when synthetic drugs, new psychoactive substances (NPS), hazardous contaminants, and precursor manufacturing trends are identified


EUDA4Peru: an operation to integrate European intelligence with South American law enforcement near the origin points of cocaine trafficking routes to prevent commercial container shipping hubs from being exploited by cartels


European Drug Report: an annual publication issued by EUDA as a definitive reference for the illicit drug market in Europe and its influence on public health outcomes


Links

wiki/evaluative-beliefs-scale.title: Evaluative Beliefs Scale (EBS)
wiki/evaluative-beliefs-scale.content:
Overview
The Evaluative Beliefs Scale (EBS) is a psychological assessment in the form of a questionnaire that is designed to evaluate beliefs associated with negative affects, cognitions, and emotional disturbances such as anxiety and depression.

wiki/evidence-based-intervention.title: Evidence-Based Intervention (EBI)
wiki/evidence-based-intervention.content:
Overview
Evidence-based interventions (EBIs) are treatments and programs whose results have been validated through scientific research.
These can include therapies like:


Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (CBT)


Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT)


Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy (MBCT)


Emotion-Focused Therapy (EFT)


Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT)


Relational-Cultural Therapy (RCT)


Rational Emotive Behavior Therapy (REBT)


Behavior Activation (BA)


Functional Analytic Psychotherapy (FAP)


Compassion-Focused Therapy (CFT)


Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR)


Prolonged Exposure Therapy (PE)


Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT)


Somatosensory Psychotherapy


Narrative Exposure Therapy (NET)


Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP)


Habit Reversal Training (HRT)


Parent-Child Interaction Therapy (PCIT)


Multisystemic Therapy (MST)


Functional Family Therapy (FFT)


Positive Parenting Program (Triple P)


Motivational Interviewing (MI)


Contingency Management (CM)


Community Reinforcement Approach (CRA)


Relapse Prevention Therapy (RPT)


These can also include programs and partnerships that operate within a community:


Housing First


Critical Time Intervention (CTI)


Nurse-Family Partnership (NFT)


Syringe Services Programs (SSPs)

wiki/evive-summit.title: Evive Summit
wiki/evive-summit.content:
Overview
The Evive Summit is a specialized conference for business development and networking among owners and executives of treatment centers, especially with B2B vendors. Organized by Powwow Events, it tends to be scheduled alongside EDGE, a similar summit that focuses on Applied Behavioral Analysis (ABA) for children and adolescents. This makes it easier for executives and owners to

wiki/excoriation-disorder.title: Excoriation Disorder (Dermatillomania)
wiki/excoriation-disorder.content:
Overview
Often referred to as skin-picking, excoriation disorder is considered a form of Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) in which someone feels compulsions to pick at their skin or lips, even to the point of leaving scars that bleed. One of the most effective interventions for excoriation disorder is exposure and response prevention therapy (ERP), a type of Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (CBT) that builds tolerance and comfort in avoiding compulsive behaviors.

wiki/executive-dysfunction.title: Executive Dysfunction
wiki/executive-dysfunction.content:
Overview
Executive dysfunction is a symptom that presents as disruption to the brain’s ability to manage information, create plans, and regulate emotions. It’s unfortunately all-too-common for executive dysfunction to be framed as a “character defect” like laziness, flakiness and inconsistency, or poor time management skills. Underlying disorders or conditions that might be present when observing executive dysfunction include:


Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)


Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD)


Depression


Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI)


Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD)


Anxiety Disorders


Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD)


Neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, Huntingon’s, and frontotemporal dementia


Chronic stress


Substance use, including Post-Acut Withdrawal Symptoms (PAWS)


Nutritional deficiencies

wiki/existentialism.title: Existentialism
wiki/existentialism.content:
Overview
Existentialism refers to branches of philosophy that question the nature, value, and modalities of existence.
Within Western philosophy, existentialism is often broken down into a few schools:


Humanism: those like Sartre argue that human experience is the center of reality and that we are free to construct our own meanings rather than pursue an objective answer from outside of us


Nihilism: those like Schopenhauer argue that meaning doesn’t exist in any shape or form, and that humans are animalistic in their pursuit of pleasure and avoidance of pain


Absurdism: those like Camus argue that the gap between our desire for existential answers and the lack of answers from the universe cannot be bridged, but that we should respond to that by living our life rebelliously as if to spite that gap

wiki/exogenous.title: Exogenous
wiki/exogenous.content:
Overview
“Exogenous” refers to biochemical factors that originate or operate outside of a given system, in contrast to endogenous factors. Bacteria, drugs, and radiation are all considered examples of exogenous factors to the human body that can act to change its state and relative health. In the world of designer-drugs, the goal is often to produce a product that, despite being exogenous to the body, operates like endogenous compounds. For instance, the phytocannabinoids of cannabis are exogenous to the human body but function like endogenous cannabinoids, or endocannabinoids, in order to deliver feelings of pleasure and eliminate feelings of anxiety.

wiki/expected-value.title: Expected Value
wiki/expected-value.content:
Overview
“Expected value” is a statistical construct that estimates the value of something by multiplying it by the probability of it happening.
For example, if you want to buy a pack of random Pokemon cards where the chance of getting a card worth 50 is 2% and rest are worthless, the expected value of the card pack is 50 * 0.02 = 1. If you're being charged 10 for it, you can reason that it’s not worth the price. You would need a 20% chance of pulling a 50 card in order to reach an expected value of 10 and have it be worth your while.
Expected value allows us to factor risk and uncertainty into our calculations about costs and benefits.

wiki/experience-strength-and-hope-award.title: Experience, Strength and Hope Award
wiki/experience-strength-and-hope-award.content:
Overview
In 2008, the nonprofit Writers in Treatment was founded by Leonard Lee Buschel and Robert Downey Sr. to help workers in the entertainment industry gain access for alcohol and drug addiction. In 2010, the organization established and presented the Experience, Strength, and Hope Award to Christopher Kennedy Lawford of the Kennedy family. The annual award ceremony is traditionally hosted in Los Angeles at the Skirball Cultural Center.
