wiki/explication.title: Explication
wiki/explication.content:
Overview
In the philosophy of science, explication refers to the process of creating precise and logically consistent definitions for fluid and ambiguous concepts.
In Logical Foundations of Probability (1950), Rudolf Carnap proposed four principles for explication:


Similarity: new definitions or formulations for a concept should map onto similar old ones


Exactness: definitions should have strict logical or mathematical expressions


Fruitfulness: new definitions and concepts should be useful in ways that old ones are not


Simplicity: between competing concepts or definitions that satisfy the other criteria, choose the simplest option


A basic example of explication is the concept of “temperature.” We might say something is warm and cold to create prescriptions for daily life, like “drink warm water in the mornings to clear your sinuses” or “take cold showers to boost your metabolism,” but we can’t test the validity of these recommendations until we properly define what “warm” and “cold” mean. “Temperature” as a concept allows us to directly reference the kinetic energy of a group of particles and compare it to another, so we can set thresholds for what’s considered “warm” vs “cold.” We can go back as far as Aristotle’s breakdown of the physical world to see the observation that many binary scales are actually measuring a single property rather than two different ones, such as cold being the absence of heat or lightness being a lack of weight. Explicating these concepts into something like “temperature” which can be approaches through standardized measurements is a relatively recent practice. Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit introduced the mercury thermometer and a standardized scale for using it in 1724, followed by Anders Celsius proposing another scale in 1742.
Substance use disorders (SUDs) have always been particularly tricky to explicate. Even the term SUD is subject to one day being replaced with another that might step away from the implications of the word “disorder,” which necessarily involves some concept of ordered or moderated use.

wiki/expungement.title: Expungement
wiki/expungement.content:
Overview
“Expungement” refers to a legal process of sealing or destroying a criminal record so that it no longer appears on background checks or public reviews. The criteria for expungement varies based on the legal jurisdiction, and especially serious crimes are often excluded from the possibility of expungement entirely.

wiki/externalizing-spectrum.title: Externalizing Spectrum
wiki/externalizing-spectrum.content:
Overview
The externalizing spectrumi is a psychological framework that groups impulsive and rule-breaking behaviors together because of shared predispositions in vulnerabilities and deficiencies in impulse control. This includes:


Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)


Oppositional Defiant Disorder (ODD)


Conduct Disorder (CD)


Antisocial Personality Disorder (ASPD)


Substance use disorder (SUD)


Researchers have found that common sub-factors like “disruptive-dissocial” and “impulsive-hostile” can be found as part of the externalizing spectrum’s dimensions. The Externalizing Spectrum Inventory (ESI) is a psychological assessment based on self-reporting traits tied to callous-aggression, substance use, and lack of inhibition.

wiki/extraversion.title: extraversion
wiki/extraversion.content:
Overview
Extraversion, also spelled extroversion, is a personality or character trait that psychometric instruments aim to measure around orientation towards stimulation from the external world like social interactions. Low extraversion is also called introversion, which is to say that there’s a spectrum of extroversion than a simple introvert vs. extrovert dichotomy.
High extraversion has been associated with an increased likelihood for substance use, in part because individuals with it are more likely to encounter them by seeking constant social interaction, but also because extraversion has been associated with increased novelty-seeking and risk-taking behaviors. They might also have more sensitivity around rewards and positive reinforcement. Still, other traits like high neuroticism or low conscientiousness tend to be stronger predictors of developing substance use disorders or addictive compulsions.

wiki/faces-and-voices-of-recovery.title: Faces & Voices of Recovery
wiki/faces-and-voices-of-recovery.content:
Overview
Faces & Voices of Recovery is a national non-profit that mobilizes a network of Recovery Community Organizations (RCOs). Their projects include advocacy with lawmakers and public institutions, certification through the Council on Accreditation of Peer Recovery Support Services (CAPRSS), peer-run education, training and technical assistance (TTA), and public messaging campaigns like “The Anonymous People.”

wiki/facing-addiction.title: Facing Addiction
wiki/facing-addiction.content:
Overview
Facing Addiction was a nonprofit founded by Greg D. Williams before it merged with the National Council on Alcoholism and Drug Dependence (NCADD).

wiki/fallen-angels-dance-theatre.title: Fallen Angels Dance Theatre
wiki/fallen-angels-dance-theatre.content:
Overview
Founded in 2011 by Paul Bayes Kitcher and Claire Morris, Fallen Angels Dance Theatre is a dance company in the United Kingdom dedicated to promoting creative expression among dancers in recovery. According to their website, they are the only company in the UK with their mission. Their regular sessions involve grounding techniques, breathwork, and improvisation to release feelings of fear, ego inflation, and isolation.
Links

fallenangelsdt.org/

wiki/falsifiable.title: Falsifiable
wiki/falsifiable.content:
Overview
Falsifiable refers to the ability for a proposition to be tested and shown to be false.
For instance, page 58 of the Alcoholics Anonymous Big Book states “Rarely have we seen a person fail who has thoroughly followed our path,” which is also part of the conventional preamble before meetings. This is unfalsifiable: if someone has remained sober while working the program, it’s proof of the success, but if someone continues drinking, it means they didn’t work the program thoroughly enough. Under this unfalsifiable statement, the program’s effectiveness cannot be challenged through empirical evidence.
History and Etymology
Commentary
A big problem in recovery is that repetition of unfalsifiable cliches or paradigms that lead to continual self-blame rather than practical reforms. Some of these include:


“Your best thinking got you here.” Well, duh, you can’t use anyone else’s thinking except your own. You can take suggestions, but it’s your own thinking that will decide to take them or not. This phrase is generally used as a response to challenges


“It’s not a drinking problem, it’s a thinking problem.”


It can be both, or both can be part of a bigger overarching problem. If we use the widely accepted biopsychosocial model of individual health, there are structural changes caused to the brain from chronic substance use that you cannot reverse simply by following different thought patterns. That’s why behavioral interventions like Behavioral Activation (BA) and Contingency Management (CM) are so effective compared to Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (CBT) which focuses on challenging cognitive distortions and irrational thinking.

“It’s not a religious program, it’s spiritual.”

This is one of those statements that might make sense if you come from a background with a hierarchical religious organization, as many Christian families do. It makes less sense if you come from a background with a decentralized syncretic belief system, as many Hindu and Buddhist families do. Devout Hindus do not necessarily have the same mandates to attend organized practices or rituals, and where it does happen, it’s often for the sake of community integration rather than personal belief systems. Also, even within the American legal system, courts have ruled consistently that AA at least includes “general religious content” such that it cannot be mandated as part of a legal punishment without violating the Establishment Clause of the U.S. Constitution.

“You have a case of terminal uniqueness.”

If you claim there’s something unique about your situation that isn’t being factored into a discussion, you can get hit with this dismissal. Arguably, this is in the interest of uniformity and solidarity, but in the same way that every shape can fit into a square peg once you cut enough of it off. It begins with a conclusion and dismisses details that challenge its fundamentals, rather than considering all the details and drawing a conclusion that’s consistent with those details.
Also, while the U.S. Census Bureau estimates that 60% of the population is white, AA’s internal tracking shows that it consistently hovers around 88% white. 86% identify as Christian, with 84% saying they had a pre-existing belief in God beforehand, and the vast majority explicitly use God or Jesus Christ as their Higher Power. The average age of an AA member is 50, with 74% of the organization being over the age of 40. 62% of the members identify as men. 26% have a Bachelor’s degree or higher compared to 35% of the general public. To be blunt, or rather, rigorously honest, this is not a diverse organization. Its culture is rooted in the mid-20th century social networks of white middle or upper class Christian professional men who became skeptical of corporate bureaucracy, medical institutions, and the government. They worked on Wall Street, had surgical practices, led high-powered sales careers, etc. These were people who had immense privilege and opportunity but squandered it in the course of their drinking, not people who had struggled their whole lives against systemic barriers that have nothing to do with their individual conduct.
I’ll simplify my point: the vast majority of people who use this phrase about “terminal uniqueness” cannot describe at a basic level Hinduism, Buddhism, Taoism, Shintoism, or any of the belief systems practiced by billions of people across the ocean. I don’t think you can claim people are all fundamentally the same when you don’t actually understand people who didn’t grow up in the same culture and community as you.

“Once an alcoholic, always an alcoholic. This disease is doing push-ups in the parking lot.”

Substance use disorders are generally considered chronic health conditions that are progressive if left untreated. However, a significant number of people who once met the criteria for a substance use disorder eventually don’t, whether it’s the result of abstinence or low-risk moderation. If someone in that category relapses after 30 years, this adage is used to argue that the disease of addiction was always building in the background, and the only way to ward it off is constant hypervigilance that weaves the rituals of AA into daily life. A lot of Americans may not realize how rooted in Protestant theology that is. Early American Puritanism framed the Devil as a constant threat lying in wait behind every daily temptation. To combat this threat, people needed to be engaged in constant spiritual warfare against the “cunning, baffling, powerful” enemy.
“Everything happens for a reason.”
This one is easy to see as unfalsifiable. Either you can find a reason that fits into your worldview, or you can assume one exists but you haven’t found it yet. There’s no way to prove that something happened for no reason.
As humans, we really want to believe this, because the notion of a random universe that is indifferent to our experiences can be scary. It’s much more comforting to imagine there’s a plan or a reason we just aren’t aware of, and some entity with more knowledge and power than us, who cares about us, is administering it. I’m not attempting to discourage religious belief with this, as I do think there are religious philosophers who have a more consistent and coherent worldview than me and I couldn’t claim to refute theirs.  I’m just focusing on the way this is thrown around in isolation as a cliche that essentially dismisses the very genuine and valid feelings someone has who believes in a random or indifferent universe.
Lest you think I’m singling out A.A. or Abrahamic religious systems, here are some from contemporary traditions in psychology and psychiatiry:

“You’re being defensive and resisting the process.”

This can come up in the context of Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (CBT), where therapists often deliver worksheets or curriculums from manualized intervention protocols intended to develop coping skills. If these don’t align with the patient’s experience, there is no way to falsify the effectiveness of the tool. If the patient agrees with the therapist’s assessment, the intervention works. If the patient is reporting that the coping skills either don’t work or aren’t making sense, the therapist can interpret this as resistance or defensiveness, which is just proof that there’s a deeper truth the patient is avoiding but the therapist must elucidate.

“If you claim to have tried Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy and don’t think it works, tell me about the cognitive distortions and core beliefs you’ve challenged before with the tools.”

I’m unsure how someone is supposed to report their own cognitive distortions, because if you recognize something is a distortion, you don’t really have the distortion anymore. If you’ve challenged your core beliefs, you’ve likely reevaluated them into new or modified versions of the core belief. And if neither of those were really your problem to begin with, you simply have nothing to report, which is then seen as proof you didn’t really do CBT correctly. The premise behind this line of argument is that the professional therapist is guaranteed to find distortions or dysfunctional core beliefs if they look hard enough, so a lack of distortions is only proof of a lack of CBT.
It becomes very difficult for anyone to express that CBT isn’t addressing their problems or aligns well with them, especially since general psychoeducation classes are often just rehashed CBT modules with a group-discussion component. If you complete every worksheet and assignment provided by a CBT practice, but still remain depressed or chronically stressed, the only lever CBT provides is that you haven’t adequately challenged enough distortions to uncover the true core beliefs at the root of your suffering. In this way, we essentially have recreated the Christian confessional model of counseling. If you’re suffering, it is because of some sin or flawed core belief that has not been confessed, and the role of the authoritative expert is in eliciting this confession and sorting it into a narrative to change the individual’s conduct. To challenge the ideological underpinnings of CBT in this situation is akin to questioning the existence of God in a confessional booth.
Even if you succeeded in presenting the argument and gained a concession, what have you actually accomplished except upsetting someone with significant control over labeling you as non-compliant? In moments when I’ve completely rationally explained my situation, my reaction, my past distortions and beliefs and how I’ve changed, I’ve literally been asked by a therapist: “so what’s the problem? Why are things going wrong?” Buddy, that’s what I’m fucking paying you to figure out.
Thankfully, I did encounter another therapist who, at the very first session, broke down the difference between insight and capacity, noticed I didn’t struggle with insight into myself but executive dysfunction from co-occurring disorders, and quickly facilitated further evaluation.

“You need to accept that sometimes in life we are going to be overwhelmed and distressed, but we shouldn’t catastrophize about them or try fortune-telling.”

This one is profoundly condescending. A therapist has an extremely limited ability to assess a patient’s life outside of the short hour-long sessions in which they try to communicate their perspective from their lived experiences. Dismissing a patient’s reasonable concerns about a potential catastrophe as low distress-tolerance and rational capacity to assess future risk is incredibly damaging.
In my own case, I’ve had a therapist condescendingly retort that I don’t understand the job market because “you’re 25” when I was referring to a type of job I’ve done for over a decade - longer than they said they had been a therapist. They also thought that I was in too much of a rush to apply for jobs that I knew could take weeks to arrange, reflecting a fundamental out-of-touch perspective that they reiterated often with derogatory remarks about “young people these days” lacking in work ethic. There was no way for me to falsify any of their positions. If I argued that my concerns about sustainable employment in the face of managing new health conditions and a volatile job market were justified, the therapist would read that as resistance to having my cognitive distortions challenged. As I said above, there is no lever that says “your disturbance in response to the circumstances of your life are completely rational and systemic reform is necessary to change those circumstances.”
I credit that experience with helping me feel vindicated in critiquing therapeutic modalities and institutions. The heavy emphasis on individual therapists to determine someone else’s rationality or cognitive distortions invites subjectivity that can be deeply harmful.

wiki/family-based-treatment.title: Family-Based Treatment (FBT)
wiki/family-based-treatment.content:
Overview
In the context of eating disorders, Family-Based Treatment (FBT) is an outpatient therapeutic intervention in which a trained clinician provides parents with guidance in supporting the healthy eating habits of their adolescent children.

wiki/family-smoking-prevention-and-tobac.title: Family Smoking Prevention and Tobacco Control Act (2009)

wiki/fascism.title: Fascism
wiki/fascism.content:
Overview
Fascism refers to a totalitarian movement or ideology that rejects individual rights and pluralistic societies in favor of a collectivized nationalist or ethnic identity maintained through strict crackdowns on expressive liberties and political opposition.
In the aftermath of WWII, researchers became interested in potentially identifying markers of a “fascist personality” and even designed some psychometric assessments along those lines.

wiki/fatigue.title: Fatigue
wiki/fatigue.content:
Overview
The International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11) defines MG22 Fatigue as:
“A feeling of exhaustion, lethargy, or decreased energy, usually experienced as a weakening or depletion of one’s physical or mental resource and characterised by a decreased capacity for work and reduced efficiency in responding to stimuli. Fatigue is normal following a period of exertion, mental or physical, but sometimes may occur in the absence of such exertion as a symptom of health conditions.”
In an everyday context, “fatigue” has a much more casual usage. One might say, “after Breath of the Wild and Elden Ring, I have open-world fatigue” to mean that someone is “tired” of something in the sense of being bored or burnt out, or one might say, “I feel fatigued after a party” to just mean they’re extremely tired. These aren’t wrong uses of the term per se, but clinicians are interested in fatigue that’s persistent and interferes with daily life such that it may be associated with underlying health conditions:


Hypothyroidism: an underactive thyroid leads to slow metabolic function that’s slow to process energy


Hyperthyroidism: an overactive thyroid leads to higher metabolic function that burns through energy reserves quickly


Diabetes Mellitus: an inefficient rate of processing glucose means cells are continuously starved for energy


Addison’s Disease: Low cortisol production leads to poor management of stress and metabolic processes


Hypopituitarism: dysfunction in the pituitary gland can cause multiple hormone disruptions


Anemia: severe iron deficiency can lead to a lack of red blood cells that transport oxygen throughout the body


Vitamin B12 Deficiency: a lack of B12 can hamper nerve function and the production of red blood cells


Dehydration: the disruption of balance to fluids and electrical conduction between the nerves can lead to exhaustion


Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA): apnea presents as sudden pauses in breathing when sleeping that can disrupt the quality of rest and levels of oxygen in the blood

wiki/federation-of-state-medical-boards.title: Federation of State Medical Boards (FSMB)
wiki/federation-of-state-medical-boards.content:
Overview
The Federation of State Medical Boards (FSMB) is a non-profit founded in 1912 that represents the over 70 medical regulatory boards across the United States that manage physician credentialing.
They work closely with the Federation of State Physician Health Programs (FSPHP). Physician Health Programs (PHPs) are confidential programs where a physician can seek treatment for substance use disorders without fear of punishment or disciplinary consequences. The FSMB House of Delegates maintains that licensees should abstain from using marijuana while practicing medicine because the cognitive impairments are difficult to measure.
They also update a framework for physicians managing controlled substances called the “Model Policy for the Use of Opioid Analgesics in the Treatment of Chronic Pain.” 1

wiki/feighner-criteria.title: Feighner Criteria
wiki/feighner-criteria.content:
Overview
In 1972, researchers at Washington University led by John Feighner proposed a set of diagnostic rules to be operationalized for psychologists and psychiatrists:


Primary Affective Disorders, divided into depression and mania


Seconday Affective Disorders, like depression resulting from another disorder or condition


Schizophrenia


Anxiety Neurosis


Obsessive-Compulsive Neurosis


Phobic Neurosis


Hysteria


Antisocial Personality Disorder


Alcoholism


Drug Dependence


Mental Retardation


Anorexia Nervosa


Homosexuality


Undiagnosed Psychiatric Illness, for when the other categories fail to describe someone’s condition or they don’t strictly meet the explicated criteria

wiki/fellowship.title: Fellowship
wiki/fellowship.content:
Overview
A fellowship is any association of people bound by common interests, friendship, or shared values. It can also refer to a financial grant or title bestowed to someone by an organization, usually in the context of research and education. In the context of peer recovery circles, a “fellowship” means a group of sober peers who regularly meet to discuss their struggles and provide mutual aid support.

wiki/fentanyl-test-strips.title: Fentanyl Test Strip (FTS)
wiki/fentanyl-test-strips.content:
Overview
A fentanyl test strip (FTS) is a cheap, portable assays that can detect the presence of fentanyl in powders, pills, and injectable substances.
History and Etymology
FTS were originally manufactured for clinical settings to test human urine for fentanyl, but harm reduction activists like Tino Fuentes realized they could be used off-label to test for fentanyl prior to consumption. Syringe service programs (SSPs) and grassroots networks like drug user unions began to buy and distribute them to prevent the accidental consumption of fentanyl in contaminated street drugs. Under the Controlled Substances Act of 1970 and laws based on the 1979 Model Drug Paraphernalia Act, FTS were actually classified as drug paraphernalia despite the clear use to save lives and improve the safety of substance use. Rhode Island was the first US state to decriminalize FTS in just 2018. In 2021, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) of the federal government announced that federal funding could be used to purchase FTS, which cleared the way for health departments and nonprofit organizations to begin distributing them.

wiki/fentanyl.title: Fentanyl
wiki/fentanyl.content:
Overview
Fentanyl is a synthetic opioid that can be prescribed for severe pain after surgery or as a result of advanced cancer, and pharmaceutical versions come in patches, lozenges, injections, and nasal sprays. It’s considered to be 50 to 100 times stronger than morphine and heroin.
History and Etymology
The precursor chemicals for fentanyl are manufactured primarily by industrial chemical and pharmaceutical companies in China and India. This means that, through either active complicity or willful ignorance, these companies are doing business with illicit brokers and manufacturers who will turn the legitimate precursors into the final product we call fentanyl. I hesitate to cite fiction for something this complicated, but Breaking Bad does a decent job showing how street level substance use is downstream of the incentives of bigger players at the scale of international trade networks. The global commerce industry is too large and fast for any regulatory regime at customs and ports to fully manage, and cartels can easily exploit blindspots when enforcement mechanisms can only inspect a tiny fraction of overall trade. I hesitate to cite fiction again, but The Wire also does a good job tying the street level economics of dealing drugs to port management and international trade networks, including an interesting intersection of automation replacing human workers and potentially interfering with cartel networks as a result. Machines can’t be bribed, intimidated, or incentivized to turn a blind eye. To cite one last work of fiction, The Sopranos has a scene where Tony works himself up after seeing a news segment that showed how easy it would be for terrorists to smuggle illicit goods or plant explosives, and it pushes him to begin cooperating with the FBI under a loose concept of nationalist unification. Media in the early 2000s seemed ripe for commentary on the international drug trade amidst the idea that global corporatism was coming to swallow up “the little guy.”

wiki/fermentation.title: Fermentation
wiki/fermentation.content:
Overview
Fermentation is a metabolic process that breaks down sugars to create acids, gases, and alcohols:


Lactic acid fermentation: bacteria turn sugars into lactic acid, which is how we get yogurt, sauerkraut, kimchi, and pickles


Alcoholic fermentation: yeast breaks down sugars into alcohol and carbon dioxide, which is how we produce beer, wine, and rising dough for bread


Acetic acid fermentation: bacteria turns alcohol into acetic acid to create vinegar


Fermentation occurs naturally all the time; when fruits fall around trees and microorganisms begin to break it down, animals who consume it are often capable of also becoming intoxicated off the generated alcohol.

wiki/fidelity.title: Fidelity
wiki/fidelity.content:
Overview
Fidelity is the quality of being faithful or loyal to something, sometimes with an implication of accurately reflecting something else. For instance, when examining the treatment fidelity of a therapeutic intervention, we might look at how closely the therapist follows a manualized outline to implement the intervention. Every therapist is only human after all, and each client has their own unique needs and experiences, so no intervention can be implemented with complete fidelity to theoretical ideals.

wiki/fiend-a-novel-2013.title: Fiend - A Novel (2013) by Peter Stenson

wiki/fiend.title: Fiend
wiki/fiend.content:
Overview
“Fiend” is slang for someone who uses drugs compulsively, so it amounts to a more derogatory version of calling someone an “addict.” Someone that’s “fiending” is expressing strong cravings to either relapse or continue a bender.
History and Etymology
“Fiend” from Old English originally meant “enemy” or Satan as the enemy of mankind. Around the late 19th century, American media was using “fiend” to imply someone with an excess or uncontrollable urges, such as “autograph fiends” referencing people who hounded celebrities for autographs. Eventually, the term “dope fiend” arose in reference to those who habitually and compulsively sought out liquid opium from dens.

wiki/fight-flight-freeze-fawn.title: Fight, Flight, Freeze, Fawn
wiki/fight-flight-freeze-fawn.content:
Overview
The 4 Fs represent four general buckets of reactions to potential threats:


Fight: react aggressively towards the threat


Flight: run from the threat


Freeze: minimize attention from the threat


Fawn: try to appease the threat through flattery or negotiation


History and Etmyology
It used to be common for this threat response framework to just be “fight or flight,” but since then we’ve come to acknowledge freeze and fawn as responses as well.

wiki/find-treatment-gov.title: FindTreatment.gov
wiki/find-treatment-gov.content:
Overview
Under the authorization provided by the 21st Century Cures Act, the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) launched FindTreatment.gov as a centralized source for finding substance use and mental health treatment. As of a 2023 audit, they had 22,106 facilities listed.
History
While SAMHSA itself has procedures to update the directory when information changes or inaccuracies are reported, these are largely reliant on voluntary survey responses and cooperation with Single State Agencies. The Office of Inspector General (OIG) audited the directory and found that approximately two-thirds of sampled facilities contained some inaccurate information, including addresses or treatment approaches offered. For every 100 sampled facilities, 66 contained inaccurate information with 14 containing inaccurate contact information and 62 containing inaccurate services information. The latter is a lot more concerning than the former. From the audit report:
“SAMHSA officials said that after contact and services information is reported on FindTreatment.gov, SAMHSA and the Contractor do not reach out to a facility to verify its information until the following year’s Survey starts or until being informed of changes by the facility, a Single State Agency, or a consumer.”
Dr. Cara Poland, an assistant professor at Michigan State University, told CNN in 2022: “It’s being treated as a gold-standard tool, but it’s not.” Jonathan Stoltman, directory of the Opioid Policy Institute in Michigan, remarked “we need FindTreatment.gov to be better… it’s crucial to get this right.” Some private and independent alternative directories shut down because they trusted FindTreatment.gov to do what they used to do.
This site emerged in part because gaps don’t just exist in navigating the world of mental health, but are arguably increasing alongside a doubling of the world’s population living with a mental health condition since 1990. The need to step back and comprehensively rebuild recovery perspectives is paramount in addressing substance use and mental health disorders.

wiki/firewater-myths.title: Firewater Myths
wiki/firewater-myths.content:
Overview
The firewater myth is the disproven myth that those with indigenous American heritage (including Alaskan Native tribes) have a unique genetic vulnerability to alcohol and addiction. Critical scholarship argues that it arose as a way to deflect blame from the traumas caused by colonization and genocide that disrupted communities and their ways of life. Studies have failed to find evidence to support the idea that the populations of these communities have unique genetic predispositions that explain the elevated rates of substance use following European colonization. In fact, there’s evidence that suggests the myth becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy; those with tribal affiliations or indigenous heritage can end up believing that they’re genetically doomed to addiction and avoid seeking help.

wiki/first-pass-metabolism.title: First-pass Metabolism
wiki/first-pass-metabolism.content:
Overview
First-pass metabolism refers to the way that human bodies first metabolize compounds and substances through the digestive system before it reaches the cells to be processed again. Prescription medications often take this into consideration when designing their structure so that certain compounds are released when the dose is moving through the digestive tract while other interactions occur only after compounds reach the bloodstream.

wiki/flashback.title: Flashback
wiki/flashback.content:
Overview
A flashback, as defined by the American Psychological Association (APA) in their online Dictionary of Psychology, has two definitions:
the reliving of a traumatic event after at least some initial adjustment to the trauma appears to have been made. Memories may be triggered by words, sounds, smells, or scenes that are reminiscent of the original trauma (as in a backfiring car triggering a flashback to being in combat). Flashbacks may be associated with posttraumatic stress disorder.
and,
the spontaneous recurrence of the perceptual distortions and disorientation to time and place experienced during a previous period of hallucinogen intoxication. Flashbacks may occur months or even years after the last use of the drug and are associated particularly with LSD.
History and Etymology
The observation that people could re-experience events of the past is incredibly old. Tablets from the Assyrian Dynasty of ancient Mesopotamia mention soldiers who seemed to see and hear the spirits of enemies they had killed in combat. Many Assyrians believed that this was a supernatural disease that was the natural outcome of war. Plutarch, an ancient Greek historian, described in The Life of Marius a Roman general who suffered from night terrors and what sound like flashbacks to previous battles. Ancient Sanskrit texts describe “Smaranajanya Manovikar” which can be literally translated as “memory-born mental affliction” in which someone repeatedly disturbed by memories of the past. In the Hindu epic Ramayana, the rakshasa (demon) Maricha was shot by an arrow fired by Rama, which he survived but was permanently traumatized by until he renounced his ways and moved to a secluded forest. Maricha describes seeing Rama everywhere, even in the shadows of the trees that resembled the bow he was shot with, and hearing any word that started with “Ra” triggered paralyzing fear in him as his mind went to “Rama.”
The roots of modern psychology’s explication of this notion of being “haunted by the past” can be traced to Pierre Janet and Sigmund Freud, both of whom observed something like “re-enacting” or “reminiscences” in people who had experienced trauma and could not recount a straightforward narrative about it. Army doctors in WWI and WWII often framed these as hallucinations or psychotic breaks rather than a distinct experience connected to trauma. Around the same time, the term “flashback” was being used in technical manuals describing an engine failure where fuel gases travel in reverse and flame is shot backward. In 1915, D.W. Griffith used the term “flashback” to describe a narrative device in his films that interrupted a sequence of events to suddenly shift backward in time to depict past events. The term picked up in the world of art criticism alongside the film industry’s growth, where it was then applied to plays and novels. Around the 1960s, it became slang that referred to recurring hallucinations that continued days or weeks after a trip on psychedelics.
By the time the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-III) was written, “flashback” was codified as a symptom of Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD).
Commentary
I’ve sometimes remarked that the plight of someone experiencing frequent flashbacks in which memory and agency are both compromised is not too different than that of a chronic substance user who experiences benders. I’m not necessarily sure how appropriate or accurate the comparison is, but my own experiences reveal a degree of empathy to be found in the “episodes” that each may have.

wiki/florida-center-for-prevention-resea.title: Florida Center for Prevention Research (FCPR)
wiki/florida-center-for-prevention-resea.content:
Overview
The Florida Center for Prevention Research (FCPR) is an applied research center at Florida State University founded in 1998, initially to evaluate the Florida Tobacco Pilot Program. Since then, it has provided data analytics for the FLORENCE Project to reduce fatal overdoses, measured the prevalence of Opioid Use Disorder (OUD), coordinated local substance prevention programs like the Wakulla Drug-Free Communities Initiative, and hosted family and marital stabilization workshops.

wiki/folk-psychology.title: Folk Psychology
wiki/folk-psychology.content:
Overview
Folk psychology, which stands apart from armchair psychology and pop psychology, refers to the common explanations used by lay people to explain concepts and predict human behavior.
The moral model of addiction, which posits that individuals who compulsively use substances are simply suffering from a weak will or moral foundation, and the rational actor model, which assumes that people make decisions based on a rational analysis of their capacities and incentives, are common ones that folk psychology can arrive at. Note that these aren’t wholly irrational or internally inconsistent frameworks, since holding most people to the expectations derived from (at least what appears within the context of one’s culture to be) moral and rational standards is a fairly effective way to navigate the world for predicting people’s behavior and implementing a system of accountability. However, these models do face serious challenges when modern empirical evidence enters the equation and complicates ideas about agency, self-control, and long-term decision-making.

About
“This irrational relation with happiness and well-being does not only apply to individuals, but also to society as a whole. In the end, a state has the purpose of protecting the security, quality of life and well-being of its people. In the US, the right to the pursuit of happiness is even guaranteed at the basis of the Declaration of Independence. And yet, states, like individuals, take so much illogical and even harmful actions.”
“We want to help our countries and our people achieve a state of happiness.”
“How? Not with vague blah blah – there are enough sites for that. Not by telling people how to find their inner selfs – there are enough self-help books and therapists who do that. We want to discover the state of happiness by exploring the vast body of research related to happiness and well-being.”

wiki/formaldehyde.title: Formaldehyde
wiki/formaldehyde.content:
Overview
Formaldehyde is a flammable gas used in industrial manufacturing and can be dissolved in water as a way to preserve organic samples or specimens in laboratories.
In underground labs, substances like tobacco and marijuana might be combined with embalming fluid, which is a mixture of formaldehyde and methanol. This has the effect of both slowing the burn rate of cigarettes and joints while causing distinct dissociative and psychoactive influences, leading users to believe that they were getting longer and more intense highs. Ivan Spector was among the first researchers to document clinical cases of AMP in 1985, where someone had arrived at a clinic with acute toxicity as a result of soaking marijuana in embalming fluid.

wiki/franklin-evans-by-walt-whitman-1842.title: Franklin Evans
wiki/franklin-evans-by-walt-whitman-1842.content:
Overview
There are various anecdotes floating around about Walt Whitman writing this temperance novel while heavily drinking himself, which does explain why critics have called it “an incoherent and often aesthetically dissatisfying text.” The historian David Reynolds biographical accounts of Whitman include a claim that he wrote the novel in three days while drinking heavily. However, there seems to be some dispute about the veracity of this report. Whitman himself generally saw temperance virtues and movements favorably based on his written works as a journalist. It’s possible that the rumors or jokes persist as an explanation for the work being regarded as far worse than other writings from Whitman; perhaps Whitman himself found the explanation convenient. Some scholars interpret the work as a historical artifact rather than a literary work that represented Whitman’s own racism and bigotry despite a reputation among readers suggesting otherwise.

wiki/free-energy-principle.title: Free Energy Principle
wiki/free-energy-principle.content:
Overview
Proposed in 2005 by Karl Friston, the free energy principle states that any self-organizing biological or mechanical system maintains existence by minimizing internal surprisal and uncertainty through adaptations to the environment. This means that the self-organizing system must maintain some set of internal states distinct from the outside world but also have boundaries that allow information to pass through. Since the initial proposal, Friston and his colleagues put forward a unified theory that centers the free energy principle as an organizing principle for all self-organizing systems.
History and Etymology
The free energy principle has a long history that spans across the fields psychoanalysis, statistical machine learning, and neuroscience.

wiki/free-will.title: Free Will
wiki/free-will.content:
Overview
“Free will” refers to the philosophical concept that living things have the ability to make decisions based on independent agency.
One of the most common neuroethical controversies surrounding Substance Use Disorder (SUD) is over the extent to which an individual’s agency is compromised both by the influence of substances in active addiction and intense cravings even when sober.

wiki/freebasing.title: Freebasing
wiki/freebasing.content:
Overview
A free base is a neutral, non-salt form of a compound, especially an alkaloid like cocaine, nicotine, and morphine. Many chemicals are manufactured in a salt form for the convenience of dissolving in water and remaining stable. Pharmaceutical companies manufacture different versions of drugs depending on the ideal consumption method.
In recreational substance use, “freebasing” refers to converting a salt form of a drug into a base form, which means it can be vaporized and smoked for a rapid high. Studies suggest that faster penetration of the blood-brain barrier increases the risk of addiction and overdose.

wiki/functional-magnetic-resonance-imagi.title: Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI)
wiki/functional-magnetic-resonance-imagi.content:
Overview
Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) is a brain scan that monitors blood flow to map brain activity. Parts of the brain that are more active consume more oxygen, driven by the blood-oxygen-level dependent (BOLD) response.
fMRI scans were instrumental in determining substance use disorders to be more than moral failings by demonstrating that parts of the brain functioned differently in response to chronic substance use. When presenting someone with a clinical diagnosis of SUD cues associated with their past use, the fMRI can capture increased blood flow to the limbic system and prefrontal cortex that coincide with cravings or urges to use. These individuals may also show reduced brain activation in brain networks associated with impulse control and inhibition. Recent studies show that we can even predict the risk of relapse or completing treatment from cue-exposure scanning based on activity in the insula and cingulate cortex. The same types of scans can also show that the hot spots that light up as a reaction to cues dampen over time as the brain heals.
Real-time fMRI neurofeedback (rtfMRI-nf) is a new technology that allows patients to see a representation of their own brain while practicing techniques that dampen the hot spots, giving them visual feedback as they gain experience in the practice of self-regulation.

wiki/future-tripping.title: Future Tripping
wiki/future-tripping.content:
Overview
“Future tripping” is a popular casual term for the concept of anticipatory anxiety, which is a form of anxiety about potential negative outcomes from an event before it happens. This can manifest as constant rumination over “what-if” worst-case scenarios and the standard physical symptoms of anxiety like muscle tensions, elevated heart rate, tension headaches, stomach discomfort, and difficulty sleeping. The term was adopted heavily in recovery circles, particularly Alcoholics Anonymous literature in the 1970s and 1980s, to discuss the importance of taking life “one day at a time,” since future-tripping could become a trigger for drinking.
History and Etymology
The use of the word “trip” to describe the experience of substance use emerges out of the 1960s, alluding to substance use as a kind of journey. This led to “-tripping” as a suffix for all kinds of terms, like Maya Angelou’s use of “ego-tripping” and political journalism featuring “power-tripping.” In 1978, AA literature begins to use “future-tripping” to describe the escalating thought spirals that can lead someone to losing hope in their sobriety. It’s very easy to go from “what if I relapse in the future anyways?” to “might as well relapse now,” which becomes something of a self-fulfilling prophecy.
Commentary
I have mixed feelings about this concept. Like with almost every term or concept that arises from folk psychology or pop psychology, there are some solid foundations that are very, very easily twisted into counterproductive uses. It’s just not easy or even possible to determine that a particular anxiety about the future is unjustified.
As humans, we generally try to create worldviews that minimize the risk of being caught by surprise. From Hermann von Helmholtz discussing the concept of “unconscious inference” in the 1860s to Richard Feynman popularizing variational free energy as a method to approximate intractable problems in the 1980s to Geoffrey Hinton applying variational free energy to neural networks in the 1990s to Karl Friston introducing the free energy principle of all biological systems, researchers have consistently approached the problems of biology and information science through an analysis of uncertainty. Simply put, our brains are actively making inferences about the world in order to reduce the chances of being surprised. It’s plainly not possible to live entirely in the moment without a thought about the future unless you’re experiencing severe executive dysfunction or possibly a manic episode.
At the same time, it’s also possible for someone’s projections or inferences about the future to be wildly dysfunctional themselves. Someone who thinks about whether a meteor will hit the Earth and cause a mass extinction event, similar to one that took out the dinosaurs, is not necessarily wrong to consider that possibility, but a chronic fixation on it is actually more paralyzing than it is helpful. We would hope to find some middle ground between “what if everyone dies tomorrow?” and “what if I get fired from my job and can’t pay rent?” One is commonly called catastrophizing as a cognitive distortion under Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy frameworks, while the other is a reasonable worry directly tied to survival needs that might have actionable pathways as a response. Mitigating risk is generally a good thing. This grey area between the two is where gaslighting and denial can creep in, especially since it’s extremely easy to parrot an adage like “one day at a time” when someone is trying to plan out their future in ways they can prepare for. After all, how can you know what you can do about the future until you actually allow yourself to brainstorm and process the emotions along with it? Making peace with the possibility of certain outcomes is healthy, and it’s not achievable without undergoing some of the distress of considering those possibilities. I’ve seen this play out just enough in real recovery circle conversations that I feel a warning is warranted. You’re not future-tripping if you’re just walking yourself through actions you can take in response to problems of the future or you’re trying to make peace with the worst-case scenario. You might be future-tripping if you find yourself unable to make peace with an outcome and ruminate over it to the detriment of the present.

wiki/gamblers-fallacy.title: Gambler's Fallacy
wiki/gamblers-fallacy.content:
Overview
The gambler’s fallacy is the belief that random outcomes of the past affect the probability of future outcomes. For example, if you’re flipping a coin and it lands on 5 heads in a row, the fallacy would be in assuming that a tail is due imminently because a 50-50 chance of tails should balance out in the long-run. In reality, the coin always has a 50-50 chance of landing on heads or tails, so there’s no reason to expect a tails is more likely than a heads the next time you flip the coin. The coin does not contain any memory of past flips.
That doesn’t mean betting on 5 heads in a row before a single coin has been flipped has a 50-50 chance though, since that would be a bet placed on 5 events with a 50% chance each all happening is 3.135% (1 in 32).
For many with a process addiction to gambling, the gambler’s fallacy can be a tempting rationalization to keep gambling, especially with an appeal to some kind of superstitious counter that runs differently.

wiki/gambling-disorder.title: Gambling Disorder
wiki/gambling-disorder.content:
Overview
“Gambling disorder” is the term used by the DSM-5 in reference to persistent gambling compulsions. Specifically, it’s defined as:
“Persistent and recurrent problematic gambling behavior leading to clinically significant impairment or distress, as indicated by the individual exhibiting four (or more) of the following in a 12-month period:”


“needs to gamble with increasing amounts of money in order to achieve the desired excitement”


“is restless or irritable when attempting to cut down or stop gambling”


“Has made repeated unsuccessful efforts to control, cut back, or stop gambling.”


“Is often preoccupied with gambling”


“Often gambles when feeling distressed”


“After losing money gambling, often returns another day to get even”


“Lies to conceal the extent of involvement with gambling”


“Has jeopardized or lost a significant relationship, job, or educational or career opportunity because of gambling”


“Relies on others to provide money to relieve desperate financial situations caused by gambling”


History and Etymlogy
The DSM-IV instead used the term “Pathological Gambling” that was put under “Impulse-Control Disorders Not Classified Elsewhere” as a Disorder Class rather than the “Substance-Related and Addictive Disorders” under the DSM-5.

wiki/gangrene.title: Gangrene
wiki/gangrene.content:
Overview
Gangrene refers to the death of body tissue as a result of lost blood supply, which can be a downstream consequence of the complications of many different conditions. It should be seen as a life-threatening emergency that warrants immediate care and surgical interventions.
Within the umbrella of substance use, gangrene can begin as a result of injecting drugs into arteries instead of veins which cuts off blood flow to tissues, vasospams as a result of stimulants like cocaine, infections and abscesses from unclean injections, and a generally weakened immune system that becomes more susceptible to other infections.

wiki/ganja.title: Ganja
wiki/ganja.content:
Overview
Ganja, also spelled ganjah, is a traditional Sanskrit term for cannabis in the form of dried flowers and leaves, which spread to the Caribbean in the 19th century and integrated into Jamaican culture and the Rastafari movement.

wiki/garcia-de-orta.title: Garcia de Orta
wiki/garcia-de-orta.content:
“The Portuguese, who navigate over a greater part of the world only procure a knowledge of how best to dispose of that merchandise of what they bring here and what they shall take back. They are not desirous of knowing anything about the things in the countries they visit. If they know a product they do not learn from what tree it comes, and if they see it they do not compare it with one of our Indian trees, nor ask about its fruit or what it is like.”
From the whimsical era of European medical practitioners encountering new ingredients and materials for the first time as they began traveling the world to conquer other peoples. De Orta specifically noted that many in India would use opium to calm mental troubles, not just physical ones as the Europeans had.

wiki/gateway-drug.title: Gateway Drug
wiki/gateway-drug.content:
Overview
The idea of “gateway drugs” is that someone who uses substances like alcohol, nicotine, and cannabis will be automatically triggered into seeking out harder substances.
However, there isn’t much evidence to support the idea of gateway drugs. The idea stems from an interpretation of data that shows a correlation between those who use harder substances like meth or heroin and those who used “softer” substances like alcohol or weed, where it’s assumed that the softer substances cause the use of “harder” substances later in life. However, most people who use “softer” substances never end up using “harder” substances, which suggests that the “softer” substances aren’t a cause but an early stage of a chronic condition that afflicts a minority of people, namely Substance Use Disorder (SUD).
Gateway drugs go hand-in-hand with prohibitionist and abstinence-only approaches to substance use that advocate against any experimentation with looking to substances for relief, though caffeine is still a notable exception in most cases.

wiki/geneva.title: Geneva
wiki/geneva.content:
Overview
Geneva is an older British English term for gin from the Netherlands and Belgium called jenever. You’ve likely noticed that Geneva is also the name of a city in Switzerland, but there’s actually no connection between the city and the drink. English speakers who brought the drink home after fighting alongside the Dutch in the Eighty Years’ War (1568-1648) mistakenly called it Geneva instead of jenever. It was eventually shortened into Gin from Geneva, especially during the Gin Craze when it became widely used among everyday drinkers.

wiki/george-pettey.title: George Pettey
wiki/george-pettey.content:
Overview
A physician likely born around 1850-1860, Pettey was controversial in his time for criticizing substances like heroin and opium in all its forms as addictive, regardless of the method of ingestion. He also proposed a now-discarded theory of addiction that relied on toxins and internal medicine over psychology or neurology.
Pettey’s motivations were personal and social. From his 1913 book, The Narcotic Drug Diseases and Allied Ailments: Pathology, Pathogenesis, and Treatment, he writes:
“The author had, recently, under his care a Harvard graduate who, with a class of four others, became addicted to morphone during the last year of their medical course, they having the assurance of one of the faculty that the use of morphine hypodermically would not produce addiction. Four of this quintet died prematurely, two committing suicide, while the fifth after thirty-seven years of enslavement was finally released by treatment. These fallacious teachings did much to increase the number of habitual users of opium, but aside from these influences the discovery of morphine and the perfection of the hypodermic syringe have been the greatest factors in extending the use of narcotics.”
Pettey’s decision to skip over the general history of substance use to relate a tragedy he personally observed comes remarkably close to the way books are still written about addiction, treatment, and recovery. Both medical practitioners and lay writers covering the topic of addiction begin by explaining the grief and hope that motivate their work:
“It has only been during the last quarter of a century, however, that narcotic addiction has grown to such proportions as to attract much attention. The evil is now recognized as alarmingly extensive and rapdily spreading. It is hardly profitable, therefore, at this time to consider farther the origin and growth of the addiction. This has been sufficiently done by others.”

wiki/geritol.title: Geritol
wiki/geritol.content:
Overview
Geritol is a brand of supplements that are high in B-vitamins and iron among other minerals.
For those in recovery from chronic substance use, especially alcohol, they may need to correct severe nutritional deficiencies such as a depletion of Thiamine (Vitamin B1). Geritol Liquid is sometimes used to help restore baseline levels of these nutrients. At the same time, using the supplement without medical supervision is dangerou since high-iron supplements can overload the liver’s capacity to process iron, which is impacted by chronic drinking, and consequently trigger hepatotoxicity. Geritol Liquid also contains a small amount of alcohol as a solvent that stabilizes its ingredients, which should be taken into consideration if an individual is intending to maintain strict abstinence and might be triggered into an abstinence violation effect from even trace amounts.

wiki/getting-over-it.title: Getting Over It
wiki/getting-over-it.content:
You either don’t know this game or wish you didn’t know this game. It’s not so dissimilar to addiction in that way, which is no coincidence. Bennett Foddy, the designer of the game, is one of the few people who can claim to have both studied the philosophy behind gaming and addiction as well as developed them with those principles in mind:
“You’re shooting for benign, minor addiction that the person will break free of eventually… I want them to play intently for a while and then get over it.”

Gia Marie Carangi was an American supermodel who died at the age of 26 from AIDS-related complications acquired after developing a Substance Use Disorder (SUD) around heroin.

wiki/gift-of-desperation.title: Gift of Desperation
wiki/gift-of-desperation.content:
Overview
The “gift of desperation” is a term coined in Alcoholics Anonymous circles to describe a desire to change after an alcoholic hit a bottom in which they lost, or were about to lose, something important enough as to inspire intense desperation. The premise of the term is that most alcoholics are unable to change until they experience consequences so severe that the resulting hopelessness tears at one’s self-will and ego, forcing open the possibility of following the AA Steps to surrender to a Higher Power. It’s not a coincidence that the acronym for “gift of desperation” is GOD. The gift of desperation is often believed to precede a spiritual awakening that allows a Higher Power’s will to operate through an individual.
History and Etymology
According to the AA Book Club, the term “gift of desperation” was born out of language from the official AA literature, namely Twelve Steps and Twelve Traditions (often called the 12&12). The book doesn’t use the phrase, but the AA Book Club credits it with the roots that prompted the phrase to emerge from meetings and conventions:
“The sponsor explicitly details the inadequacies of will power in fighting this disease. In describing the progression of his own drinking history, he may be able to convince a relatively high-bottom person that the latter’s habits show some of the same traits. Seeing the hopelessness of our situation, we are said to become “openminded to conviction and as willing to listen as the dying can be.” Thus was born the now-common phrase “gift of desperation”, and the path to Step Two made clear.” 1
From the Step One chapter of the book:
“We know that little good can come to any alcoholic who joins A.A. unless he has first accepted his devastating weakness and all its consequences. Until he so humbles himself, his sobriety—if any—will be precarious. Of real happiness he will find none at all. Proved beyond doubt by an immense experience, this is one of the facts of A.A. life”
It’s hopefully easy to see how, with a framing like this that emphasizes the necessity of rock bottom, the idea of a gift of desperation as the mechanism of bouncing back can take rot.
Commentary
Insofar as the “gift of desperation” is a version of “playing the tape” backwards and forwards, I think there’s a lot of merit to the idea. Bundling together a reminder of a horrific event or powerfully shameful feeling with the compulsion to use can make it easier to give oneself the motivation to abstain. It might even serve as an inciting incident for Behavioral Activation

wiki/gin-craze.title: Gin Craze
wiki/gin-craze.content:
Overview
The Gin Craze described several decades of a trend of “rotgut gin” being consumed in increasingly large quantities by the English populace. From Carl Erik Fisher’s book The Urge: Our History of Addiction (2022), gin consumption doubled from 1700 to 1720 and then again by 1729. 1743 had six times the levels of 1700. The term “gin” was popularized during this period as a shorthand for “geneva”, which was, contrary to the name suggests, a Dutch drink soldiers used before battle. The British English speakers botched it in translation; it was originally “jenever” but they mistook it for “Geneva”, as in the city in Switzerland.

wiki/global-health-advocacy-incubator.title: Global Health Advocacy Incubator
wiki/global-health-advocacy-incubator.content:
Overview
The Global Health Advocacy Incubator (GHAI) is a non-profit with civil society organizations (CSOs) in over 40 countries, with its core financial backing from Bloomberg Philanthropies.
GHAI manages an Overdose Prevention Initiative to reduce barriers between individuals and care, particularly in bureaucratic environments. They were part of the coalition that advocated for the passage of the Mainstreaming Addiction Treatment (MAT) Act which increased the number of clinicians who can prescribe buprenorphine for Opioid Use Disorder (OUD). They also worked to secure the reauthorization of the SUPPORT Act, which funded opioid recovery centers, peer support training, residential treatment for pregnant women, and loan repayments for treatment providers. In partnership with the National Safety Council, they pushed OSHA to issue official workplace guidance about stocking Naloxone (Narcan) to reverse an opioid overdose. Lastly, they push the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) to protect the access to healthcare coverage from those with Substance Use Disorders (SUDs).

wiki/global-north-global-south.title: Global North, Global South
wiki/global-north-global-south.content:
Overview
The dichotomy of the Global North and Global South describes a split in the world between nations considered forward-looking and progressive versus those considered backwards-looking and regressive.
History and Etymology
An early version of this concept can be found in the works of Hans Singer and Raul Prebisch, who argued against the idea that trade between developing and developed nations would naturally lift all social classes of all nations out of poverty over time. Instead, they claimed that, as the price of primarity commodities fell in comparison to the price of manufactured goods, developing nations that focused on extracting and managing raw materials would actually suffer a decrease in their ability to industrialize. More raw materials would have to be exported from a developing nation per piece of manufactured good or industrial equipment imported from a developed nation.
Consider a nation like Colombia that’s well-suited to produce lots of coffee and a nation like Germany that has the capital to produce tractors efficiently. Let’s say Colombia has to export 100 bags of coffee to import 1 tractor. This might make it easier for Colombia to produce more coffee, so say they double the production of coffee over the next few years. However, this doesn’t mean the German population will necessarily consume twice as much coffee to match the production from Colombia. At the same time, Germany might be innovating to produce more advanced tractors, and German laborers might negotiate better wages and working conditions for themselves. So the cost of producing and acquiring a tractor rises while there’s no significant change in the demand for coffee. Colombia might need to trade 400 bags of coffee to import the same tractor they previously acquired for 100 bags of coffee. This dynamic, which has found increasing empirical validation from economic studies since it was proposed, means that wealth is steadily transferred from Colombia to Germany even as both nations advance their industrialization.
Various terms have been suggested when explicating this inequality between nations. The works of Singer and Prebisch suggest a “Core-Periphery” model where nations on the “Periphery” are forever bound to be exploited by the “Core” nations. Franz Fanon describes a compartmentalization between colonialist powers and colonized peoples. Carl Oglesby is credited with using the term “Global South” when arguing against the Vietnam War in his “Briefing on Vietnam” (1969) published in the magazine Liberation.

wiki/gold-standard.title: Gold Standard
wiki/gold-standard.content:
Overview
A “gold standard” refers to the best possible practice, method, or benchmark available within a field or discipline.
There are a handful of practices that are often considered a gold standard in treatment for substance use disorders, though it should be noted that gold standards are highly subject to change as more research is conducted and more evidence is aggregated:


Medication-Assisted Treatment (MAT): also referred to as Medication for Opioid Use Disorder (MOUD), treatment schedules involving Buprenorphine (Suboxone) and Methadone have been shown in studies to cut overdose mortality rates in half


Naltrexone or Acamprosate: these medications block the pleasant psychoactive effects from and cravings for alcohol


Contingency Management (CM): there are no FDA-approved medications for stimulant use disorders, so CM steps in as a behavioral intervention that delivers tangible rewards for passing drug tests and participating in other treatments like therapy or counseling sessions


Motivational Interviewing (MI): every type of substance use disorder, or any health condition for that matter, can leave individuals ambivalent about their perspective and desires to attempt behavioral changes. MI is a style of delivering therapeutic interventions that works alongside a patient’s goals and values rather than attempting to persuade or impose changes.


Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy has often been treated as a gold standard. In my own experience, there’s an almost perverse delight some practitioners and clinicians have taken in their stacks of worksheets and manuals. There’s substantial mounting evidence indicating that CBT does not consistently outperform other evidence-based therapeutic interventions like psychodynamic therapy, which researchers have called the Dodo bird verdict. In fact, the cognitive elements of CBT that involve challenging cognitive distortions may not be a significant factor in the outcomes of CBT, as Behavioral Activation alone provides comparable benefits. Much of the prevalence of CBT comes from its manualization that enables its operationalization, which means that it’s easier to provide mass training for CBT to practitioners and easier to calculate the costs of delivering CBT for insurance companies and healthcare services. Jonathan Shedler is one of the most vocal critics of CBT:
“Even ardent CBT advocates have acknowledged that manualized CBT offers lasting help to few. Writing in Psychological Science in the Public Interest, eminent CBT researcher Steven Hollon noted ‘Only about half of all patients respond to any given intervention,and only about a third eventually meet the criteria for remission…Moreover most patients will not stay well once they get better unless they receive ongoing treatment.’ Ironically, this was written by the same researcher who declared other forms of psychotherapy ‘inadequate.’ Sadly such information reaches few clinicians and fewer patients. I wonder what the public and policy makes would think if they knew these are the same treatments described publicly as ‘evidence-based,’ ‘scientifically proven,’ and ‘the gold standard.‘”

wiki/gout.title: Gout
wiki/gout.content:
Overview
Gout is a type of inflammatory arthritis resulting from uric acid crystals surrounding the body’s joints after eating certain foods that contain purines.
Alcohol consumption and diuretic medications both increase the concentration of uric acid in the body. Beer is actually more likely to trigger a gout flare than wine or hard liquor because it contains high levels of purines, though hard liquor has still been found to raise the risk of gout flares by a factor two or three.

wiki/gratification.title: Gratification
wiki/gratification.content:
Overview
Gratification is defined in the American Psychological Association’s Dictionary of Psychology as:
“the state of satisfaction following the fulfillment of a desire or the meeting of a need.” 1
There are several dimensions of gratification:


Instant/Immediate Gratification vs. Delayed Gratification, with the former driven by the limbic system chased dopamine and the latter managed by a prefrontal cortex with high executive function


Intrinsic Gratification vs. Extrinsic Gratification, determined by whether the satisfaction is the result of performing an action because it aligns with personal values or growth or the result of achieving some external benefit or validation, including avoidance of a negative outcome. Intrinsic gratification engages the parts of the brain involved in self-schema while extrinsic gratification involves the reward pathways in the ventral tegmental area (VTA)


Sensory Gratification vs. Social Gratification, which depends on whether the satisfaction is tied to physiological/physical urges or positive feedback from another human or social structure. Vicarious gratification is closely related to social gratification, except that it comes from witnessing or knowing that someone else is experiencing gratification, like a parent feeling happy about their child’s success. Social gratification involves oxytocin and dopamine pathways.


Note that “gratification” is not strictly synonymous with “pleasure.” While pleasure is a state of feeling good, gratification is the satisfaction following the fulfillment of a desire or action. This distinction is observed at a neurobiological level, with endogenous opioids and serotonin being responsible for what we explicate as pleasure and dopamine being associated with gratification. For many chronic substance users, the brain begins to separate “liking” and “wanting” along these lines; even if using a substance no longer delivers the experience of pleasure, the brain still experiences gratification from acting on the compulsion that signals an intense reward.
In SMART Recovery, the Problem of Instant Gratification describes the urges, cravings, and/or compulsions to engage in harmful behavior and is appropriately abbreviated as the PIG. A common saying you might hear is “don’t feed the PIG, starve it” as a reference to slowly and incrementally training the brain away from chasing gratification based on instant impulses and towards exercising delayed gratification that triggers ordinary pleasure.
Within behavioral economics and its intersection with psychiatry, we can frame the loss of delayed gratification capacity as a form of hyperbolic discounting in which the brain perceives the immediate reward of substance use to be preferable to the goals of sobriety. One of the reasons that Contingency Management (CM) is so effective as a behavioral intervention is that it seeks to directly substitute for the short-term gratification of substance use.
