wiki/grey-rock-method.title: Grey Rock Method
wiki/grey-rock-method.content:
Overview
Grey rocking, or the grey rock method, is the practice of making oneself as non-response and non-reactive as possible in order to avoid giving manipulative individuals the reactions or attention they’re looking for. This can look like:


One- or two-word answers like “yes,” “no,” and “okay” that try to end the conversation as soon as possible


Limiting emotional expressions like keeping a neutral or stiff facial expression, avoiding eye contact, and keeping a flat affect in one’s voice


Limiting personal discussions that include your private life and future plans


Avoid taking the bait, which includes refusing to defend yourself in an argument from accusations or insults


History and Etymology
The term was coined in a blog called 180 Rule, authored by someone who went only by Skylar, which is no longer a live site but can still be browsed through archives:
“When dealing with malignant narcissists, psychopaths, sociopaths, borderlines, drama queens, stalkers and other emotional vampires, it’s commonly advised that no response is the best response to unwanted attention. This is often true and No Contact (the avoidance of all communication) should be used whenever possible.”
“There are some situations however, when No Contact is not feasible, as in when you share child custody with a psychopath. As another example, if you are being stalked by an ex, a restraining order can infuriate the unwanted suitor, and refusing to respond to him or her is seen as an insult. They might become convinced that they can MAKE you respond and in that way satiate their need for power over you.”
“For all these situations, we have the Gray Rock Method.”
I don’t necessarily like the terminology used to describe those that grey rocking might be useful for, but the advice is solid. In particular, “borderlines” is a dehumanizing way to refer to people who have Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD), which is very distinct from the stereotypes of “psychopaths” or “sociopaths.” People who struggle with BPD deal with emotional dysregulation and strong fears of abandonment, not a lack of empathy or remorse that can lead to predatory or manipulative behaviors. That doesn’t necessarily mean the advice can’t work when it comes to protecting oneself from dynamics that aren’t healthy for them, but dehumanizing the other party isn’t a prerequisite to developing those coping mechanisms.
Links

wiki/grog.title: Grog
wiki/grog.content:
Overview
Grog is a synonym for alcohol. It used to refer to a specific drink made from rum, lime, and sugar as a precursor to modern hard seltzers. Over time, it became slang for any type of liquor, and “groggy” became a common term for feeling fatigued, disoriented, or dazed.

wiki/grounding.title: Grounding
wiki/grounding.content:
Overview
“Grounding” in a psychological context refers to coping mechanisms and techniques that can disrupt dissociative episodes, oncoming flashbacks, hypervigilance and hyperarousal, and anxiety or panic attacks by interrupting these symptoms to redirect awareness towards the present. These include:


The 5-4-3-2-1 Method: Name 5 things you can see, 4 things you can feel, 3 things you can hear, 2 things you can smell, and 1 thing you can taste. This addresses each of the senses with a new sensation to focus on.


Temperature Shock: Splash cold water on your face, hold ice cubs in your hand, or run warm water over your hands and wrist to shock the nervous system into processing a new sensation.


Axial Foot Pressing: Sit down and press both feet into the floor while focusing on the sesnsations of pressure between the bottom of your feet and the floor.


The 4-7-8 Breathing Method: Inhale through the nose for 4 seconds, hold your breath for 7 seconds, and exhale through the mouth for 8 seconds. There’s a common warning given with this one as being potentially risky for those who struggle with sudden changes in blood pressure.


Texture Tracking: Run your fingers over some object near you while describing physical properties about it the best you can, like texture, weight, and temperature


Progressive Muscle Relaxation: Slowly clench, flex, or tense parts of your body for a few seconds each and release the tension, focusing on physical stress leaving the body as muscles relax.


Anchoring Statements: Repeat facts about the present out loud, like “My name is Mank, and I am safely resting in my room while surrounded by people who care in the year 2026.”


Mathematical Disruption: Repeat some kind of formula or pattern in your head like counting backward from 100 by 7s, calculating the Fibonacci sequence, or repeating multiplication tables.


Alphabetical Categorization: Choose a category of things and name one item for each letter in the alphabet in sorted order.


Spatial Inventory: Examine the room or environment you’re in while counting each object of a particular color or shape.


Spelling Reversal: Spell long words backwards out loud as fast as you can.

wiki/growth-vs-fixed-mindset.title: Growth vs Fixed Mindset
wiki/growth-vs-fixed-mindset.content:
Overview
“Fixed mindset” is a term that refers to mindsets that viewed people and their traits as rigid and static entities. In other words, the fixed mindset is characterized by the idea that you either had talent or you didn’t, and nothing you do could change that fact.
It’s often framed as a contrast to a “growth mindset,” which views people and their traits as malleable and capable of predictable influence. A student with a growth mindset views test scores as feedback for where they currently are rather than a determination of their innate talent.
There is also a distinct term from the growth mindset called a “mutable mindset.” The “fixed vs growth” dichotomy can suggest that change either doesn’t happen or happens in a positive direction, but this can lead students with a growth mindset to become deeply demotivated if, for any reason, their performance declines against their expectations of growth. “Mutable” suggests a more neutral fluidity, such that a student is prepared for the possibility of declining scores as part of an ebb and flow in the circumstances around their performance.
Commentary
The concepts of growth and fixed mindsets have become staples of the culture of (pseudo)scientific management that conveniently provides an aesthetically-pleasing vocabulary to simply blame individuals for not trying hard enough within broken systems. Anyone who feels that they’re struggling with finding solutions or coping with impossible situations can just be told to adopt a growth mindset that encourages change rather than dwelling on a fixed mindset that concludes failure is certain. The idea of overcoming the impossible certainly lends itself to inspirational quotes and optimistic projections, but reality has a way of defying projections. After all, the difference between landing on the moon and landing on the sun is not the difference between a fixed mindset and a growth mindset.
In defense of Carol Dweck, who popularized the framework in 2006 with empirical evidence that has since come under intense scrutiny, she didn’t advocate that changing one’s mindset alone was adequate to improve the capacity for people to learn and grow. She identified that a growth mindset was associated with better performance, not that individuals who simply chose a growth mindset would perform better:
Prodding students to increase effort alone, telling them they would have done better if they had tried harder, isn’t enough, Dweck said. Without suggesting learning strategies when students are stymied and judiciously offering help at the right time, a student may feel more incompetent if more effort doesn’t work. Telling students to “keep trying and you’ll get it” does not instill a growth mindset, Dweck said. “I call it nagging.”
Teachers who heap encouragement on students may assume they have adopted a growth mindset. But, Dweck said, “growth mindset is about closing the achievement gap, not about making low-achieving kids feel good in the moment but not learn in the long run.” 1
That being said, even if fixed mindsets are associated with lower performance, evidence for an association between the two doesn’t necessarily mean we have evidence that changing a student’s mindset will lead to changes in performance. It’s plausible that a student who is able to develop a growth mindset has fundamentally different factors in their social environment and personal experiences than a student who remains in a fixed mindset, such as a home environment with parents who attained college degrees and can reinforce educational practices everyday. A student who notices that learning study skills pays off through the reward of improved performance may show all the hallmarks of a growth mindset. It’s also possible that growth mindset interventions don’t succeed at cultivating a growth mindset, even if having one plays a role in one’s performance, so the growth mindset theory might be absolutely true yet lack actionable proposals for testing and implementation. An interesting discussion between academics Russell Warne and David Yaeger over the interpretation of the evidence around growth mindset theory can be found here, in which Warne argues that evidence for growth mindset theory is overblown and Dweck’s research is influenced by her own career ambitions while Yaeger argues that the evidence is too nuanced to discard growth mindset theory and interventions, especially if certain subgroups and at-risk student populations benefit in ways that average metrics may not yield statistically significant results for.
In my own opinion, I certainly think there are merits to cultivating stronger growth mindsets as part of a student’s educational journey. It’s practically a prerequisite to learning that you reject the idea that your knowledge and skills are fixed. In that sense, mindsets aren’t discrete. You’re not either in a fixed mindset or in a growth mindset; you might believe that certain aspects of yourself are fixed while others can change, and you might have very reasonable evidence you use to arrive at those conclusions. If you fail every math test after trying your hardest, even if the problem lies in instruction or resources, you might reasonably begin to think math isn’t your strong suit and invest your attention and energy elsewhere. We might call that a fixed mindset in regards to math, but it would take a lot more than restoring the positive attitude of a growth mindset for someone to feel comfortable with math. In my tutoring experience, I find it necessary to build bridges between areas a student feels capable of growth in to areas where they feel fixed, which can require meeting them halfway on their personal interests before broaching academic subjects.
Regardless of the future consensus about growth mindset theory or your opinion about it now, we can be reasonably certain that the evidence base for workplace “growth mindset” positivity interventions is incredibly weak. Satya Nadella, the CEO of Microsoft as of 2014, branded his attempts to overhaul Microsoft’s purportedly toxic work culture with Dweck’s theories about growth mindsets. It’s telling then that in 2016, Dweck, much like William Edwards Deming and Peter Drucker, felt the need to speak out shortly after observing the widespread corporate adoption (read: bastardization) of her work:
“Scholars are deeply gratified when their ideas catch on. And they are even more gratified when their ideas make a difference — improving motivation, innovation, or productivity, for example. But popularity has a price: People sometimes distort ideas and therefore fail to reap their benefits. This has started to happen with my research on ‘growth’ versus ‘fixed’ mindsets among individuals and within organizations…’Growth mindset’ has become a buzzword in many major companies, even working its way into their mission statements. But when I probe, I often discover that people have a limited understanding of the idea.” 2
She links to another Harvard Business Review article that espoused the value of her work when implemented at the CME Group:
“We hired Carol to speak with senior leadership and then with all employees. We recorded the sessions, and all new employees watch the video. Gill emphasizes the idea of highlighting the growth mindset. Instead of focusing on output, which can be seen as the result of talent (and emblematic of a fixed mindset), we think about effort. Instead of celebrating employee achievements, we say, ‘Thank you for your effort…’ We’ve adopted behavioral interviewing techniques using mindset-focused questions. For example, ‘Describe a time you confronted a challenge. How did you work through it to overcome your doubts?‘… It’s too early to say it’s a huge success. But it has allowed us to formalize and institutionalize our innovation process and innovate more quickly.” 3
If you have the same hate for Ted Talks that I do, then this description possibly induced some twitching around the eyes. It’s hard enough to see what kinds of students could benefit from a growth mindset intervention when it’s a popular topic in the research community. Bringing in an expert to give employees a brief management-approved recorded talk that preaches a reductive version of nuanced research is the entire basis of my disdain for Ted Talks. I distinctly remember wanting to pull out my hair when I first heard a manager recommend that I look into a “fixed mindset” after describing a personal rut I was in, as if I hadn’t been bombarded with pseudoscientific management psychology since middle school, but had not once undergone a meaningful mental health screening. It turns out that it can be much easier to have a growth mindset with the right antidepressants if you have clinical depression. By all accounts, this was a smart guy who had bootstrapped a significant portion of his career, and I’m sure he followed what he preached. Back to Dweck’s article:
“People often confuse a growth mindset with being flexible or open-minded or having a positive outlook — qualities they believe they’ve always had. My colleagues and I call this a false growth mindset. Everyone is actually a mixture of fixed and growth mindsets, and that mixture continually evolves with experience. A pure growth mindset doesn’t exist, which we must acknowledge to attain the benefits we seek.” 2
This idea of “false growth mindset” has been acknowledged by researchers for years. From a 2019 paper published in the journal Research in Organizational Behavior:
“In addition to the false dichotomy, one of the most common misunderstandings that constitutes part of the false growth mindset is that growth mindset is just about effort. However, we know that when people struggle, if they simply apply rote effort and do the same thing over and over again in the same way, they are not necessarily more likely to succeed. Instead, a true growth mindset involves trying new strategies and seeking help when one is stuck. Sheer effort alone will not enhance learning and development. Another dimension of false growth mindset is praising effort when that effort is not really effective. If a worker does not try hard on a task, for example, and their supervisor nonetheless praises their effort, the supervisor has communicated that they don’t really understand what the job entailed. It is important to praise effort when something has been effortful – and when that effort actually leads to learning. A third dimension of false growth mindset is believing that people have a growth mindset about everything all of the time. Research in fact reveals that mindsets about different characteristics (e.g., intellectual ability, personality, sports ability) are not necessarily correlated with each other (Dweck, 2000; Scott & Ghinea, 2013) and the situational nature of mindset suggests that the same person can have fixed or growth mindset beliefs depending on the situation (e.g., Hoyt, Burnette, & Innella, 2012; Kray & Haselhuhn, 2007). Dweck notes that it is important to legitimize the fixed mindset and acknowledge that we all have both sets of beliefs within us. “If we ‘ban’ the fixed mindset, we will surely create false growth mindsets”, Dweck wrote (2015).”
I was initially primed to view the concept of “false growth mindset” as a No True Scotsman fallacy in which failed interventions or implementations under the “growth mindset” would simply be sweeped under the “false growth mindset” label, but Dweck and other researchers have been  consistent about defining the specific mechanisms that distinguish it from a real “growth mindset.”

wiki/grue-paradox.title: Grue Paradox
wiki/grue-paradox.content:
Overview
Nelson Goodman proposed the Grue Paradox, also called the Grue Problem or the New Riddle of Induction, to discuss a problem within the philosophy of science where categories constructed from present evidence can fail to predict future cases.
Simply put, let’s say we can observe that objects in a bucket are either green or blue today. However, after 10 years, we observe that some green objects turn blue. We might call these “grue” to distinguish them from permanently green and blue items. In the present though, we have no way of distinguishing green from grue.

wiki/guardianship.title: Guardianship
wiki/guardianship.content:
Overview
Guardianship in a legal context refers to a relationship in which a designated guardian is given the authority to make decisions for a ward whose ability to safely and rationally make decisions for themselves is compromised.
Courts can grant various levels of guardianship as a result of substance use:


Emergency or Temporary Guardianship: this often lasts 30 to 90 days in crisis situations like overdose risks or medical neglect in order to guide someone into treatment facilities, sometimes coercively


Limited Guardianship: this might allow a guardian to have control over some areas of life like medical decisions while allowing the ward to keep independence in all other areas of life


Plenary Guardianship: this givens the guardian complete legal authority to manage all areas of someone’s life, including residential and medical decisions


Conservatorship: this is often given alongside guardianship, with the distinction being that a conservator can be allowed to manage someone’s finances to prevent them from spending their resources on substances


If someone struggles with chronic substance use is able to enter treatment and maintain sobriety, the orders concerning guardianship can be petitioned for removal or dissolution. The details of how this works varies enormously by regional legal jurisdictions.

wiki/guilt.title: Guilt
wiki/guilt.content:
Overview
The American Psychology Association’s (APA) Dictionary of Psychology:
“a self-conscious emotion characterized by a painful appraisal of having done (or thought) something that is wrong and often by a readiness to take action designed to undo or mitigate this wrong. It is distinct from shame, in which there is the additional strong fear of one’s deeds being publicly exposed to judgment or ridicule.”
Commentary
The distinction between guilt and shame that the APA points out is an extremely common theme in recovery circles, though that doesn’t mean there’s a consensus about the difference. The APA definition adds a social dimension to shame as a type of anticipatory fear of backlash from the environment.
I find that in ideas of shame within recovery circles, the fear of being perceived as fundamentally flawed is conflated with the fear of being fundamentally flawed. A common framing is that “guilt” translates to “I did something bad” while “shame” translates to “I am fundamentally bad.” Personally, I always engaged with the distinction as one between a personal feeling and a social mechanism, rather than the distinction between an action and a fundamental trait. When we say “you should be ashamed of yourself,” I assume we mean that someone should feel bad about violating social standards, not that someone should see themselves as fundamentally bad.
If we do separate “guilt” and “shame” on the basis of an action vs a trait, we see arguments emerge to challenge whether either is ever good. Many people in recovery will say guilt is part of their gift-of-desperation that anchors them to sobriety. Others will say that the feeling of being ashamed of who one becomes in active addiction keeps them clean. Alcoholics Anonymous and other 12-step groups that discuss moral inventories and making amends necessarily run into the emotion of guilt, and while it may not be explicitly considered healthy to put oneself into a position of guilt, it’s still expected that guilt emerges as a motivation during the Steps that is resolved through their completion.

wiki/guttempler.title: Guttempler
wiki/guttempler.content:
Overview
The Guttempler, known before as the Good Templars or the Independent Order of Good Templars (IOGT), are the German branch of a global organization to address alcoholism. The original organization was founded in 1850 by Daniel Cady in Utica, New York and called the Knights of Jericho. It was renamed and reshaped, and it grew to arrive in Germany by 1889. With around 500 local groups, they form the largest religiously independent addiction self-help association in all of Germany. 1

wiki/h-westley-clark-award-for-distingui.title: H. Westley Clark Award for Distinguished Service | NAADAC
wiki/h-westley-clark-award-for-distingui.content:
Overview
The H. Westley Clark Award for Distinguished Service was established in 2024 in honor of Dr. H Westley Clark.
Clark served as the Director of the Center for Substance Abuse Treatment (CSAT) under the U.S. federal government’s Substance Use and Mental Health Administration (SAMHSA), before which he also served as chief of the Associated Substance Abuse Programs at the U.S. Department of Veteras Affairs Medical Center in San Francisco. His public service record is extension across over 40 years of public service work in addiction and recovery. He also held a B.A. in Chemistry, a Master’s in Public Health, a Medical Degree, and a Law Degree, and he drew from all of these fields in his career.
To be eligible for the award, one must have ten years of addiction counseling or service experience across prevention, research, public policy, administration, education, law, social advocacy, and/or treatment methodologies. Membership with the NAADAC is not required.
Past Winners

Cynthia Moreno Tuohy, Executive Director of NAADAC and founder of the Critical Issues in the Black Community committee (2025)

wiki/habit-forming.title: Habit-Forming
wiki/habit-forming.content:
Overview
“Habit-forming” is a legal definition, not a medical one, that refers to substances with a risk of introducing chemical dependence. Medical organizations like the World Heath Organization (WHO) have explicitly mentioned that “habit-forming” introduces confusion when we’re also considering the nuances of the definitions of “dependence” and “addiction.” Still, it persists in legal codes as a way to designate the potential risks of using certain drugs on their warning labels. To illustrate how contingent this label is on legal and political mechanisms, we can look at guidelines from the federal Food and Drug Administration (FDA) which explicitly state that habit-formings drugs:
are chemical derivatives of substances specified in section 502(d) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.
Links

wiki/habitual-drunkenness.title: Habitual Drunkenness
wiki/habitual-drunkenness.content:
Overview
Habitual drunkenness, much like habit forming and other terms associated with “habit”, is an outdated reference to some constant use of alcohol that might today be described as “alcoholic dependence”, “alcoholism”, or “alcohol use disorder.”
History and Context
“Habitual drunkenness” is a term we can trace at least as far back as Benjamin Rush, a prominent physician who was alive to sign the Declaration of Independence and who advocated for treating “habitual drunkenness” as a disease that should be approached with compassion rather than purely a moral failing.
A 1942 review paper titled “Habitual Drunkenness”: Meaning in Divorce and Criminal Law Statutes by Anthony Frank discusses the way “habitual drunkenness” is used in the paper’s contemporary legal contexts:
Plaintiff sued for a divorce on the grounds of cruel and inhuman treatment and habitual drunkenness. The parties were married in 1918, and the present divorce action was commenced in September, 1939, and was the fourth upon these grounds, the other three having been dismissed after reconciliations.
Defendant had been drinking for a number of years, and to great excess since 1931. He had been arrested five times for drunkenness. Defendant’s desire for liquor reached its highest intensity during the last year. For the plaintiff, the testimony was that the defendant was drunk anywhere from “one-third to one-half” of the time. He had been seen “laid out” or to “crawl up the stairs many times.” Frequently he was so intoxicated that he did not “know what he was doing.” Defendant’s own witness, upon being asked as between sobriety and intoxication for the defendant’s condition replied, “Well, I guess it would be about half and half.”
Defendant’s routine was not daily or regular. He would be drunk for five days or a week at a time, and then perhaps he would be sober for two or three weeks again, and he would start over again. All the witnesses agreed that the defendant’s hours of intoxication were longer and oftener during the preceding summer. During these periods of drunkenness, the defendant was an abusive, molesting and boisterous person.
This is an incredibly common pattern with those experiencing substance use disorders, and in particular, alcohol use disorder. It’s also a reason that many who drink resist seeking help and treatment, as the periods of sobriety that one achieves become evidence for the notion that one can successfully moderate and control their compulsions to drink, even if their intoxicated states are highly destructive and dangerous, even if only to oneself. I’d also infer that it’s harder to treat something as habitual if someone can demonstrate weeks of abstinence from that habit; it might be easier to conceive the drinker as maintaining habitual sobriety, with occasional drunkenness, under this framework.
Defendant contended that his drunkenness was only occasional and not habitual, and that these occasional periods of drunkenness were caused by plaintiff’s criticism and nagging.
I can only imagine that this exchange went something like “can you stop drinking our entire tavern out of its inventory and beating me when you’re upset?” followed by “Do you never shut up? I need another drink to cope with this.” Based on my recent watch of Reefer Madness, that seems perfectly plausible.
Under the divorce statute, the “habitual drunkenness” complained of must have been “for one year immediately preceding the commencement of the action.” Plaintiff was denied a divorce; she appealed from an order denying amended findings or a new trial.
An habitual drunkard within the divorce statutes is one who, by frequent, periodic indulgence in liquor to excess, has lost the power or desire to resist alcoholic opportunity with the result that intoxication becomes habitual rather than occasional.
This is interesting. The plaintiff, or the wife, seems to be appealing to a specific set of rules around the justifiable grounds for divorce that stipulates that the condition of “habitual drunkenness” must have been present for at least a full year before the divorce would be processed. The terms “habitual” and “occasional” are used without necessarily a strict line to determine how much drinking constitutes being a “drunkard” or how often something has to happen for it to be considered habitual rather than occasional. Based on the testimony provided by witnesses and the plaintiff, it seems like they settle for asking lay witnesses how often the drinker in question appears to be drunk. Today, we might examine whether an individual meets the official guidelines for alcohol use disorder as it is laid out in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM), which might be assessed by a clinician or someone else capable of being an expert witness. The DSM-5-TR guidelines are far more focused on the individual’s capacity to resist cravings and compulsions to use rather than external observations of episodic binge drinking.

wiki/hadacol.title: Hadacol
wiki/hadacol.content:
Overview
Hadacol was a vitamin and mineral supplement mixed in a 12% alcohol solution.
Commentary
The story of Hadacol is one of the many that can make someone in 2026 wonder if everyone was just always wasted on something in the 20th century.
Hadacol was a backyard laboratory concoction made by Louisiana State Senator Dudley J. LeBlanc, who had no medical training and was trying to reverse-engineer a painkiller his doctor gave him by buying medical textbooks that listed the benefits of different minerals like calcium and magnesium. He reportedly mixed his first batch in a wash tub in his backyard and stirred it with an old wooden boat oar. The purported purpose of ethyl alcohol was as a “preservative,” though conveniently this meant it could get around the bans on liquor in “dry” counties across the American South.
When asked about the name, he would joke “Well, I hadda call it something!”
LeBlanc eventually opened the LeBlanc Corporation to build manufacturing plants for Hadacol, including a massive facility in Burbank, California. He made over 20 million in sales by 1950, which is the equivalent of 200 million USD today. He even chartered a customized multi-car train called the “Hadacol Special” as part of his supply chain. In 1951, the American Medical Association (AMA) condemned it for both a lack of evidence of its efficacy and dangers of its use of hydrochloric acid, and the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) began investigating the company for false advertising, after which LeBlanc finally sold it.
So much for free market innovation and pulling yourself up by your bootstraps.

wiki/half-life.title: Half-life
wiki/half-life.content:
Overview
“Half-life” is the period of time it takes for the amount of some substance to reduce by half.
You might be wondering why we use “half-life” to measure the duration of a drug instead of its total lifetime or an hourly rate, which might be more intuitive.
In many chemical reactions, the concentration of substances follows exponential decay closely, which means that it disappears quickly at first, but the rate of reactions slows down over time. Imagine a room filled with 100 balls that are constantly bouncing around. Let’s say each collision between any two balls results in the balls disappearing. At first, we might imagine a lot of balls would disappear because there are a ton of balls bouncing in every direction. It only takes 5 collisions to go from 100 to 90. However, we can hopefully imagine that it would take a lot longer for 10 balls to go to 0 since collisions are way less likely to happen as more space clears for balls to bounce without collisions. We couldn’t reliably issue a metric like “10 balls will be gone every hour” because of this dynamic. What we typically can say instead if “half the balls disappear every hour.”
Replace these balls with drug molecules, and you arrive at the rationale for describing the duration of the effects of drugs through a half-life.
As an example, you might’ve heard of reports about re-narcotization, in which someone suffering from a fentanyl overdose is given naloxone (Narcan) to reverse the drug’s effects. However, naloxone’s half-life is substantially shorter than fentanyl’s, which means that someone can still overdose as a result of the existing fentanyl in their system that persists after the naloxone is processed. It’s still a life-saver, but it’s not a silver bullet.

wiki/hallucinogenic.title: Hallucinogenic
wiki/hallucinogenic.content:
Overview
Hallucinogens are defined in the American Psychological Association’s Dictionary of Psychology as:
“a substance capable of producing a sensory effect (visual, auditory, olfactory, gustatory, or tactile) in the absence of an actual stimulus. Because they produce alterations in perception, cognition, and mood, hallucinogens are also called psychedelic drugs or psychedelics (from the Greek, meaning “mind-manifesting”). They are a group of heterogeneous compounds, many of which are naturally occurring; others are produced synthetically. Many hallucinogens are structurally similar to one of several neurotransmitters, which may be used as a mechanism of categorization.” 1
The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5-TR) describes many disorders and symptoms related to hallucinogens, though emphasizes that the dynamics and mechanisms of their chemistry are substantially different from each other:
Hallucinogens comprise a diverse group of substances that despite having different chemical structures and possibly involving different molecular mechanisms, produce similar alterations of perception, mood, and cognition in users. Hallucinogens included are phenylalkylamines (e.g., mescaline, DOM [2 5-dimethoxy-4-methylamphetamine], and MDMA [3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine; also called “ecstasy” or “molly”]); the indoleamines, including psilocybin (and its metabolite psilocin, the compound primarily responsible for the psychedelic effects of hallucinogenic mushrooms) and dimethyltryptamine (DMT); and the ergolines, such as LSD (lysergic acid diethylamide) and morning glory seeds. In addition, miscellaneous other ethnobotanical compounds are classified as hallucinogens, of which Salvia divinorum and jimsonweed are two examples.
To emphasize this distinction between hallucinogens and substances with hallucinogenic effects, the DSM-5-TR explicitly indicates that cannabis is not in and of itself a hallucinogen:
Excluded from the hallucinogen group are cannabis and its active compound, delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) (see the section “Cannabis-Related Disorders”). These substances can have hallucinogenic effects but are diagnosed separately because of significant differences in their psychological and behavioral effects.

wiki/hangover.title: Hangover
wiki/hangover.content:
Overview
Hangovers refer to the unpleasant feelings and physical symptoms that start shortly after the levels of the substance in the body return to almost zero, most commonly in reference to alcohol, where the symptoms include:


Headaches, thirst, and dry mouth: alcohol blocks the release of vasopressin, an antidiuretic hormone that inhibits the reabsorption of water by the kidneys (which is why you feel the need to urinate so much when drinking) which leads to dehydration that shrinks the brain volume and puts tension on the membranes that connect the brain to the skull. This also produces the effects of dehydration throughout the body.


Muscle aches: alcohol causes the body to release cytokines that provoke inflammation throughout the body which adds pressure directly to the peripheral nervous system and produces muscle aches comparable to ones found from having the flu


Extreme fatigue and weakness: The liver prioritizes metabolizing alcohol by consuming a vital coenzyme called NAD+, which stops the production of new glucose and leads to low blood sugar that starves the body’s muscles of their primary energy mechanisms. Alcohol is also known to be damaging to the mitochondria, affectionately known as the “powerhouse of the cell” that synthesizes ATP for energy.


Dizziness: Alcohol changes the properties of the fluid within the canals of your inner ear, and it takes time for these to rebalance even after alcohol has left your system, which confuses the tiny hair cells responsible for spatial orientation and can cause you to feel dizzy despite being perfectly still. Plus, with the dehydration, your body has less blood overall, which means your heart struggles to pump enough to the brain. This causes a drop in blood pressure, which also leads to dizziness.


Nausea, vomiting, and stomachaches: Ethanol irritates the lining of the stomach, which causes an overproduction of gastric hydrochloric acid that destroys the layers of protective mucous. Further, ethanol is broken down by the liver into acetaldehyde, which is considered up to 30 times more toxic to the human body than ethyl alcohol and can trigger the brain’s receptors for nausea and vomiting.


Anxiety and irritability: Alcohol mimics GABA, the brain’s primary neurotransmitter for calming the nervous system, while blocking glutamate, the brain’s primary neurotransmitter for exciting the nervous system. The brain compensates by weakening its GABA receptors and flooding itself with glutamate, which then produces anxiety, panic, and irritability.


Shakiness, sweating, and rapid heartbeat: As noted above, glutamate floods the brain while drinking, which can feel psychologically like anxiety and irritability, but physically it also leads to tremors and shakiness. It’s very common to hear about those with alcohol use disorder who have “shaky hands” in the morning until they have a “hair of the dog.” Alongside glutamate, the body floods itself with stress hormones like cortisol and epinephrine, or adrenaline, that’s responsible for the fight-or-flight response from the sympathetic nervous system.


Sensitivity to light and sound: flooding the nervous system with glutamate also makes it difficult for the sensory cortex of the brain to filter for important signals among background noise, so even small sounds and lights are interpreted as overwhelming inputs.


Difficulty concentrating: Alcohol blocks Rapid Eye Movement (REM) sleep during which the brain achieves actual rest

wiki/harcourt-assessment.title: Harcourt Assessment
wiki/harcourt-assessment.content:
Overview
Before merging into Pearson in 2008, the Harcourt Assessment was a company that sold educational and assessment resources for psychological and therapeutic purposes.
History
In 1919, Af

wiki/hard-drugs.title: Hard Drugs
wiki/hard-drugs.content:
Overview
“Hard drugs” is a term that loosely refers to substances that have powerful effects, a high risk of forming dependence or habits, and a higher chance of irreversible or fatal consequences like an overdose. Examples of typical hard drugs include heroin, cocaine, fentanyl and methamphetamine.
As a general rule of thumb, if it’s not alcohol, caffeine, cannabis, over-the-counter (OTC), or a naturally-occurring psychoactive herb like kratom and kava, it can potentially be considered a “hard drug.”

wiki/harm-reduction-hysteria.title: Harm-Reduction Hysteria
wiki/harm-reduction-hysteria.content:
Overview
Stories
The Atlantic
The Cities That Said Yes to Drugs (07/30/2026)
Article Link
“Seattle, like a striking number of other liberal American cities, has embraced a radical form of “harm reduction,” which is more a philosophy about treating addiction than a scientific approach to it.”
No. This is false.
Harm reduction is absolutely an evidence-backed scientific paradigm towards, as the name says, reducing the harms caused by substance use. There is nothing about harm reduction that prevents us from offering programs and treatments geared towards abstinence. It is not an alternative philosophy to abstinence-based policies. It is not the product of some bleeding-heart ruinous empathy from a nanny state, or whatever the terms are now for anything other than the most punitive policy option.
The fact is that not everyone is going to choose abstinence-based treatment, so we should reduce the harms of that choice. People who use clean needles provided by a center instead of dirty needles that have been in a dozen other veins are less likely to develop health issues that require emergency interventions, which are far more expensive and scarce as resources than mass-manufactured supplies.
We have decades of research that show harm reduction interventions prevent overdoses, lower rates of infectious diseases like HIV, and become bridges towards long-term recovery by supporting incremental but lasting change. Some evidence indicates that those who use harm reduction services are five times more likely to enter treatment than those who don’t.
Powell also cites the New York Department of Health’s page to define harm reduction as a “social movement” to “building leadership” among drug users. The more complete sentence he butchers actually reads:
“It is a belief in and respect for the rights of people who use drugs and strategies that include building leadership among people who use drugs and supporting communities in reducing the negative consequences associated with drug use and the harms associated with the context of drug use such as racism, homelessness, violence, and poverty.”
You know who else believes in building leadership among people who use drugs and supporting communities in reducing the negative consequences?
Alcoholics Anonymous.
As well as every other recovery group out there: Crystal Meth Anonymous, Narcotics Anonymous, Recovery Dharma, Refuge Recovery, SMART Recovery, Lifering Secular Recovery, etc. All of these groups very explicitly state their philosophy revolves around peer support rather than professional or institutional mechanisms. Harm reduction interventions lean into the fact that it often takes someone who has experience with substance use to reach others still struggling with it. It works with these networks rather than cracking down and disrupting them.
Powell makes it sound like they’re giving leadership courses to drug dealers to better organize crack houses, like a cartoonish version of Stinger Bell.
“in some rare cases they’ve created dedicated spaces for addicts to shoot up. Meanwhile, police departments struggling with staffing shortages and budget cuts have stopped devoting resources to sweeping users and dealers off the streets or out of parks and playgrounds.”
It’s almost as if creating dedicated spaces for people to use substances under medical supervision reduces the need for law enforcement to sweep them out of other public spaces…
I’ll comment on the rest of this article, but I feel confident in condemning it as poorly researched at worst and bad faith at best, and sensationalist either way.
Also, I for one do not want to live in a society where a government’s agents, rather than trained healthcare professionals, can label someone as having a health condition requiring institutionalization. I would rather pay fewer taxes while affording more freedoms for myself and a higher quality of life for those in active addiction, than pay more taxes to expand a surveillance state into nabbing anyone off the streets and into a box.

wiki/harm-reduction-peers.title: Harm Reduction Peers (HaRPs)
wiki/harm-reduction-peers.content:
Overview
The Harm Reduction Peers (HaRPs) are a cohort of peer volunteers who perform outreach and education. That includes overdose-reversal workshops, Naloxone (Narcan) distribution, and pop-ups about myths surrounding substance use.
Links

counselingcenter.illinois.edu/get-involved/harm-reduction-peers

wiki/harm-reduction.title: Harm Reduction
wiki/harm-reduction.content:
Overview
Harm reduction is an approach to substance use policy and treatment that views any reduction in substance use to be a victory, in contrast to viewing anything except total abstinence as a defeat. These policies include:


Syringe Services Programs (SSPs)


Naloxone Distribution Policies


Overdose Prevention Centers (OPCs)


Opioid Agonist Therapy (OAT)


Fentanyl Test Strips (FTS)


Managed Alcohol Programs (MAPs)


Safer Supply Programs


Decriminalization of Possession


Housing-First

wiki/harold-hughes.content: An AA member openly in recovery, Harold Hughes was elected to the Senate and helped Marty Mann and William Wilson (Bill W.) testify before Congress.

wiki/harrison-narcotics-tax-act-of-1914.title: Harrison Narcotics Tax Act of 1914
wiki/harrison-narcotics-tax-act-of-1914.content: Before 1914, it was federally legal for practically anyone to manufacture and sell opium, morphine, cocaine, and other drugs that are highly regulated today. There were a patchwork of local, state, and tribal regulations, but without the ability to regulate interstate commerce, it was easy enough to just order drugs through the mail from another state’s pharmacy to skirt those regulations.

wiki/harvard-undergraduate-psychedelics-.title: Harvard Undergraduate Psychedelics Club (HUPC)
wiki/harvard-undergraduate-psychedelics-.content:
Overview
The Harvard Undergraduate Psychedelics Club (HUPC) is a student-run organization that explores and advocates for the usage of psychedelics, including cultural and spiritual growth. Their initiatives include the “Psychedelic Week at Harvard” that presents scientific research and harm-reduction protocols to the public.

wiki/harvard-university-health-services.content:
Overview
The Harvard University Health Services has roots going back to institutions from 1899, but its modern consolidation was completed in 1961. For substance use, their services include:


Office of Alcohol & Other Drug Services, operated by the HUHS Center for Wellness and Health Promotion

clinician-led, abstinence-based support groups

wiki/hashish.title: Hashish
wiki/hashish.content:
Overview
Hashish is a cannabis concentrate made by compressing the plant’s resin glands, called trichomes, which contain high levels of cannabinoids like THC that produce intense psychoactive effects.

wiki/hazardous-medicinal-products.title: Hazardous Medicinal Products
wiki/hazardous-medicinal-products.content:
Overview
Hazardous medicinal products (HMPs) are pharmaceutical substances that can have adverse health consequences or present health risks to both the healthcare workers managing them and the patients ingesting them. There is no single definition that’s universal, as different regulatory agencies use different processes to arrive at the label. Even within the United States alone, NIOSH, OSHA, the EPA, and the DOT all have varying definitions of “hazardous.”

wiki/hazelden-foundation.title: Hazelden Foundation
wiki/hazelden-foundation.content:
Alumni
The Hazelden alumni is expansive.
Spin-offs from Hazelden’s early single-modality program include Chit-Chat Farms (Caron), established in 1959 in Wernersville, Pennsylvania, Cumberland Heights, established in Nashville, Tennessee in 1969, Lynnville Treatment Center, established in Jordan, Minnesota in 1969, and Carrollton Treatment Center, established in Cedar Rapids, Iowa in 1973.
Direct spin-offs from Hazelden’s multimodality program include Northwestern Hospital in Minneapolis (1970), Edgewood Treatment Center in St. Louis, Missouri (1971), St. John’s Hospital in St. Paul, Minnesota (1971), Nebraska Methodist Hospital in Omaha (1971), St. Joseph Community Hospital in Vancouver, Washington (1973), St. Vincent Hospital in Sioux City, Iowa (1974), Clifton Springs Hospital and Clinic in Clifton Springs, New York (1976), Mississippi Baptist Hospital in Jackson, Mississippi (1976), and Mercy Hospital at Council Bluffs, Iowa (1977). All of these were established by former Hazelden staff.
Finally, there was the Parkside chain of alcoholism treatment hospitals spawned by Nelson Bradley’s program at Lutheran General Hospital in Park Ridge, Illinois. By 1989, Parkside delivered addiction treatment at nearly 100 sites. The Parkside chain collapsed in the mid-1990s.
Hazelden also became the country’s biggest publisher of addiction treatment materials in the 1970s, publishing countless video and audio tapes of their lectures.
Links

wiki/heal-ohio.title: HEAL Ohio
wiki/heal-ohio.content:
Overview
HEAL Ohio is an organization that builds networks between mental health and substance use initiatives in the state that advocate for harm reduction, education, and improved care. Their projects include distributing naloxone (Narcan) through Project DAWN, providing syringe service programs (SSPs), and maintaining harm reduction vending machines that supply test strips for fentanyl.
Links

wiki/heat-not-burn.title: Heat-not-burn (HNB)
wiki/heat-not-burn.content:
Overview
Heat-not-burn (HnB) devices heat tobacco leaves just enough to create an aerosolized version of a nicotine vapor instead of burning tobacco completely like in traditional cigarettes. This still exposes users and those around them to toxins and carcinogens, but less than traditional cigarette smoke. The United States Food and Drug Administration does not consider it an aid in quitting tobacco or cigarettes, since it still sustains nicotine addictions.
Commentary
It’s actually really easy to become addicted to nicotine in rehab facilities. It’s almost as easy to get vapes or cigarettes as candy. Quitting nicotine seems like a “nice-to-have.”

wiki/hedonism.title: Hedonism
wiki/hedonism.content:
Overview
Hedonism is a philosophy that places pleasure as the highest goal of life.
Psychological hedonism is a descriptive theory that posits humans are driven by the desire to maximize pleasure while minimizing pain, similar to Freud’s idea of the pleasure principle.
Ethical hedonism is a prescriptive theory that people should place pleasure as their highest goal in life and that pleasure is inherently valuable.

wiki/hellraiser.title: Hellraiser
wiki/hellraiser.content:
Overview
“The doors to the pleasure of Heaven or Hell. I didn’t care which… I thought I’d gone to the limits. I hadn’t. The Cenobites gave me an experience beyond limits… pain and pleasure, indivisible.”
The original Hellraiser movie is comfortably a contender for one of my favorite movies of all time. The sequels have been not as good, to say the least, including at least one movie clearly made just to extend the IP rights. In the 2022 sequel, the protagonist is overtly struggling with addiction as part of the plot, but I still feel the original was far better at tapping into the raw themes underlying addiction.
One of the most confusing aspects of addiction to people who have never abused substances or struggled with compulsions is how someone can keep using despite the pain outweighing the pleasure. It’s actually confusing for most addicts who attempt recovery too, which often leads to the conclusion that one must simply be incapable of valuing anything over the addictive stimulus. The quotes above from Frank Cotton, the real antagonist driving the events of the film, reveal some of this thinking when taken to the extreme in a visual narrative that’s helpful to dissect.
The neurobiological explanation of addictive compulsions first requires dispelling the common myth that dopamine is a pleasure molecule. In reality, it’s a reward chemical that builds the associations between cues and the potential for desirable outcomes. You can absolutely hate the experience of something but want it anyways because your brain has coded it as rewarding before you even experience it. The lines of pain and pleasure blur as the lines between wanting and liking diverge.
Clive Barker
“I think one of the things that fantastic writing does is that it joins up the places of power. It actually says to the reader: ‘This thing that you remember from your childhood, this moment of epiphany you know from your childhood, is actually connected up with this piece of physics, and this piece of physics is actually connected with the theory of magic, and the theory of magic is actually connected to your ideas about sex and your ideas about sex are actually connected to your ideas about love, which, in turn, are connected to your ideas about death which are, in turn, connected with higher physics’… We live in such strictly decompartmentalised times, when it’s all about specialisation.”
I just really like this quote from Barker. I’d argue that the specialized, decompartmentalized times he speaks about is one of the reasons traditional institutional authorities are less compelling to us and face existential challenges to their credibility. A diversified global economy necessarily relies on increasingly specialized sets of skills who operate through standards that eliminate the need to understand the nuances of the network one interacts within. This works to optimize processes along the metrics that those standards can reflect, but it also sidelines the holistic individual human as a body and a being. Consider education. We can create a set of standards and use grades as a metric to evaluate the process of education, and we can create specialized pathways for students to pursue so they can work cutting-edge problems, but this also stratifies the life experiences each student has, with each topical specialty becoming its own social niche as well. Drawing connections across niches requires one to occupy a position whose incentives are not driven along any single hierarchical institution, and so writers who take a step back from their niches to look at the bigger picture necessarily gravitate towards living in the social margins between niches. It’s from those margins that one can identify the constellation of interwoven relationships and epiphanies that Barker speaks about.
The Hellbound Heart
The movie is a loose adaptation of The Hellbound Heart which had the great fortune of involving the author in its production. I’m going to avoid referencing too much of the book here, but I find it hard not to analyze the book and movie at the same time, seeing both as the result of the same perspectives on escapism and hedonism.
Frank
Frank is shown to be a hedonistic thrill-seeker who has no regard for norms or rules. He travels the world in search of taboo pleasures beyond what everyday life could provide, obviously including drugs and sex. He has an affair with his brother Larry’s wife, Julia, which introduces the elements of Frank’s debauchery into the family. Kirsty, Larry’s daughter, is our primary protagonist as a typical coming-of-age woman seeking to carve out an independent life for herself.
In the book version, Frank’s hedonism burns through the capacity for normal life, and he becomes jealous of Larry’s ability to be fulfilled in his routine ordinary life with a family. We can conclude then that Frank was born into a mental or neurological state that predisposed him to seeking more risks to fill a low baseline of the ability to experience pleasure, rather than experiencing a traumatic upbringing or inflicting some curse on himself. Pop psychology has always been fascinated by personality constructs like the addictive personality, psychopathy, or Cluster B Personality Traits. I wouldn’t go as far as to be an armchair doctor and label Frank with any of these in particular, but it tracks that Frank’s baseline personality traits emerge from a related disturbance or disorder.
In the movie version, we see Frank put on Larry’s skin after a murder as a disguise, but the context from the book adds another dimension to Frank becoming Larry and having an affair with Larry’s wife. He wants to be his brother, and he horrifically attempts to literally enact the substitution.
I’m going to avoid referencing too much of the book here, but the written description of the experience of using the Configuration within the opening of the novella is very close to a bad trip. Frank’s backstory, which is mostly dropped in the movie, features waves of depression, suicidality, and nihilism that persisted since his adolescence. Larry, or Rory in the book, turns out to be a very vanilla man who finds the routine of ordinary life to be engaging and overreacts to mild disturbances. From this perspective, the addiction analogy seems natural. When Frank says he doesn’t care whether he found heaven or hell, he’s reached the point that many addicts do where nothing on Earth seems to satisfy the desire for instant intense gratification.
By the time he gets to the Configuration: “this new addiction quickly cured him of dope and drink. Perhaps there were other ways to bend the world to suit the shape of his dreams.” So the book is explicit about the box being a reference to addiction. There are some really good passages I’d love to keep referencing, but I’ll save it for the page about the book.
The Lament Configuration that he finds on his travels to Morocco has the same promise of exotic transcendentalism that give substances their allure. Talk To Me plays with a similar concept by treating its cursed hand as something ancient that has traveled all around the world while remaining esoteric. The Lament Configuration is a puzzle box which someone must activate intentionally before knowing what the outcome can be, mimicking the ritual preparation that goes into using substances alongside the risk of something horrible happening after. The way Frank brings the box back to the old home Larry, Julia, and their daughter Kirsty move into isn’t very different than the way drugs can cross borders to end up in the hands of everyday people.
Kirsty is the protagonist of the film, a teenager on the threshold of exploring adulthood. She’s beginning to explore sexuality with her boyfriend at the same time that she encounters Frank and the Lament Configuration, which we can read as experimenting with drugs she stumbled upon. No peer pressure, no crazy partying, just the all-too-common story of kids  finding an adult’s stash and applying their basic human curiosity. Even though she was absentmindedly playing with the Configuration, she still activates it to summon the Cenobites. Rather than dragging her away though, she has the presence of mind to cut a deal that would lead the Cenobites to Frank, their escapee.
The Cenobites are a great concept that stands out in an era were villains like Freddy Krueger and Jason Vorhees became breakout icons of the horror genre. Fun fact, Clive Barker was inspired by his visits to underground BDSM clubs for the movie’s costuming choices, so if your instinct upon seeing them was to scream “BDSM DEMONS”, you’re definitely not alone. Well, as the iconic Cenobite Pinhead says: “Demons to some, angels to others.”

wiki/hepatitis-c-virus.title: Hepatitis C Virus
wiki/hepatitis-c-virus.content:
Overview
The Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is an infection that attaches to liver cells and causes inflammation and liver damage. White blood cells that attempt to destroy the virus end up killing healthy liver cells. The virus clears up in 30% of people within six months without treatment, and many people in this stage may not appear sick or show symptoms that can be attributed to other conditions. 70% of people develop chronic hepatitis, which can result in cirrhosis, liver failure, and liver cancer. If detected early and treated with direct-acting antiviral (DAA) pills, over 95% of people are able to be fully cured. HCV is considered to be 10 times more infectious than HIV, as it can survive on surfaces or syringes for weeks.
Up to 80% of cases are the result of sharing needles, cookers, or water containers between injection drug users. One of the biggest touted benefits of syringe service programs (SSPs) is cutting down on the transmission of HCV while providing an entry point to testing and treatment for those concerned about exposure.

wiki/hepatotoxicity.title: Hepatotoxicity
wiki/hepatotoxicity.content:
Overview
Hepatotoxicity literally means liver toxicity. Specifically, it refers to the liver damage that might be caused by prescription medications, substance use, herbal supplements, and exposure to toxins. For the most common substances in disorders:


Cocaine overdoses can cut off oxygen and blood flow to cause sudden cell death in the liver


MDMA and methamphetamine can cause extremely high body temperatures and oxidative stress that injure the liver


Opioids rarely causes liver failure on their own, even if chronic use is related to cirrhosis in the long run, but injection drug use in general has a high chance of spreading viral infections that do directly attack the liver like Hepatitis C when needles or equipment are shared

wiki/heroin.title: Heroin
wiki/heroin.content:
Overview
Heroin, or diacetylmorphine, is a synthetically manufactured substance that uses natural morphine as a base before being altered with chemical groups to dissolve more effectively in lipids and penetrate the blood-brain barrier. It metabolizes back into morphine inside the central nervous system, but the rapid and concentrated delivery presents more intense impacts and a higher risk of dependency or death from respiratory depression.

wiki/higher-power.title: Higher Power
wiki/higher-power.content:
Overview
“Higher Power” refers to a religious deity, spiritual force, or other entity that has a role or power over one’s life.
The 12 steps of Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) explicitly call on individuals to submit to or engage with some kind of Higher Power in Steps Two, Three, Five, Six, Seven, and Eleven.
History and Context
The language of “Higher Power” was used in the place of “God” in AA in an attempt to make the program more accessible to those of all faiths or no faith at all. I would argue this attempt has failed for the most part, and that the steps are straightforwardly religious in a way that is difficult to adhere to faithfully without accepting something of a personal, interventionist deity that’s rooted in Protestant moral-psychology.
A 2020 survey published in The American Journal of Drug and Alcohol Abuse found that 98% of participants in Narcotics Anonymous (BA) explicitly believe in God or another higher power, which is 9% higher than the baseline American population. 67% believe that God plays a direct role in shaping the events of their life, and 78% report hearing God talk to them in their minds. AA does help people stay sober, but it seems that it does so by bringing people into a religious fellowship that provides a sober network of resources to increase individual and community recovery capital. 1
Links
Footnotes


Full article: An empirical study on the construct of “God” in the Twelve Step process ↩

wiki/hippocampus.title: Hippocampus
wiki/hippocampus.content:
Overview
The hippocampus is a part of the brain’s limbic system that handles the formation of long-term memories, processing of spatial information, and association of emotions to experiences.
With chronic substance use, the hippocampus stores the people, places, and things as cues associated with the high of using substances. The processes of long-term potentiation (LTP), in which the connections between neurons are strengthened as part of learning, and neurogenesis, in which new brain cells in the hippocampus are developed, are both stunted. The hippocampus is physically smaller in people who use substances constantly, which heavily impacts memory, spatial orientation, and new cell growth as part of healing or learning.

wiki/hippocratic-oath.title: Hippocratic Oath
wiki/hippocratic-oath.content:
Overview
The Hippocratic Oath is an ethical commitment that medical professionals take in the interests of building confidence that their actions will be solely for the benefit of the patient’s health.
The Traditional Hippocratic Oath
The traditional Hippocratic Oath, as printed by Johns Hopkins Press in a publication by Ludwing Edelstein in 1943, reads,
I swear by Apollo Physician and Asciepius and Hygieia and Panaceia and all the gods and goddesses, making them my witnesses, that I will fulfill according to my ability and judgment this oath and this covenant:
To hold him who has taught me this art as equal to my parents and to live my life in partnership with him, and if he is in need of money to give him a share of mine, and to regard his offspring as equal to my brothers in male lineage and to teach them this art—if they desire to learn it—without fee and covenant; to give a share of precepts and oral instruction and all the other learning to my sons and to the sons of him who has instructed me and to pupils who have signed the covenant and have taken an oath according to the medical law, but to no one else.
I will apply dietetic measures for the benefit of the sick according to my ability and judgment; I will keep them from harm and injustice.
I will neither give a deadly drug to anybody if asked for it, nor will I make a suggestion to this effect. Similarly I will not give to a woman an abortive remedy. In purity and holiness I will guard my life and my art.
I will not use the knife, not even on sufferers from stone, but will withdraw in favor of such men as are engaged in this work.
Whatever houses I may visit, I will come for the benefit of the sick, remaining free of all intentional injustice, of all mischief and in particular of sexual relations with both female and male persons, be they free or slaves.
What I may see or hear in the course of the treatment or even outside of the treatment in regard to the life of men, which on no account one must spread abroad, I will keep to myself holding such things shameful to be spoken about.
If I fulfill this oath and do not violate it, may it be granted to me to enjoy life and art, being honored with fame among all men for all time to come; if I transgress it and swear falsely, may the opposite of all this be my lot.
The Modern Hippocratic Oath
The modern version was written in 1964 by the Dean of the School of Medicine of Tufts University, Louis Lasagna, and it reads:
I swear to fulfill, to the best of my ability and judgment, this covenant
I will respect the hard-won scientific gains of those physicians in whose steps I walk, and gladly share such knowledge as is mine with those who are to follow
I will apply, for the benefit of the sick, all measures are required, avoiding those twin traps of overtreatment and therapeutic nihilism
I will remember that there is art to medicine as well as science, and that warmth, sympathy, and understanding may outweigh the surgeon’s knife or the chemist’s drug
I will not be ashamed to say “I know not,” nor will I fail to call in my colleagues when the skills of another are needed for a patient’s recovery
I will respect the privacy of my patients, for their problems are not disclosed to me that the world may know. Most especially must I tread with care in matters of life and death. If it is given me to save a life, all thanks. But it may also be within my power to take a life; this awesome responsibility must be faced with great humbleness and awareness of my own frailty. Above all, I must not play at God
I will remember that I do not treat a fever chart, a cancerous growth, but a sick human being, whose illness may affect the person’s family and economic stability. My responsibility includes these related problems, if I am to care adequately for the sick
I will prevent disease whenever I can, for prevention is preferable to cure
I will protect the environment which sustains us, in the knowledge that the continuing health of ourselves and our societies is dependent on a healthy planet
I will remember that I remain a member of society, with special obligations to all my fellow human beings, those sound of mind and body as well as the infirm
If I do not violate this oath, may I enjoy life and art, respected while I live and remembered with affection thereafter. May I always act so as to preserve the finest traditions of my calling and may I long experience the joy of healing those who seek my help.

wiki/hitsman-lab.title: Hitsman Lab
wiki/hitsman-lab.content:
Overview
The Hitsman Lab at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine studies nicotine dependence, tobacco cessation in underserved populations, and the health impacts of quitting smoking.
Links

www.preventivemedicine.northwestern.edu/divisions/behavioral-medicine/hitsman-lab.html

wiki/holding-space.title: Holding Space
wiki/holding-space.content:
Overview
“Holding space” is a pop psychology term that refers to listening and witnessing someone’s emotions without attempting to judge their solutions or provide one yourself. It differs from the idea of being a good listener in that holding space focuses on allowing someone to express their emotions without judgment while good listening often involves active participation in a conversation.
History and Etymology
The concept of creating a safe environment for someone to process their emotions has been present in psychoanalytic practice and research for decades, but the phrase “holding space” is largely associated with Heather Plett’s blog. 1
Links
Footnotes


What it means to “hold space” for people, plus eight tips on how to do it well - Heather Plett ↩

wiki/holistic.title: Holistic
wiki/holistic.content:
Overview
“Holistic” means a consideration of all aspects of a situation or circumstance. In college applications, “holistic review” refers to an admissions review process that considers every aspect of a student’s profile like extracurricular activities and personal struggles rather than just their test scores and GPA. In healthcare, “holistic care” refers to an approach that considers every aspect of someone’s health (often through biopsychosocial approaches), so that something like clinical depression is addressed through a consideration of diet, exercise, medication, social networks, financial stability, purposeful living, and other dimensions that influence health. Recovery capital frameworks take a holistic perspective when addressing substance use disorders to monitor whether someone has access to community support beyond whatever coping skills they might learn in a long-term treatment or rehabilitation program. Although “holistic” isn’t a specific medical or legal term, the medical community acknowledges “integrative medicine” which essentially covers the same concepts.
At the same time, “holistic” can very easily be used as a marketing buzzword in the alternative health and wellness industry, especially when marketing products or services that lack evidence. The argument from these sellers tends to be that “Western” biomedical institutions only study surgical and pharmaceutical interventions that are profitable for parties in the private sector, so there’s no incentive to study other “holistic” approaches. I certainly think there’s a lot of merit to this argument, and an entire field called metascience exists to critically exmaine the way science is done, but that doesn’t automatically mean a particular product should be trusted.

wiki/homeostasis.title: Homeostasis
wiki/homeostasis.content:
Overview
Homeostasis is the process through which an organism’s body attempts to regulate itself to some baseline of stable balance, essentially forming a negative feedback process in response to either internal or external changes. This contrasts with allostasis, in which the body predicts that a change will happen and proactively adjusts itself in anticipation to preserve some kind of baseline equilibrium. Examples of homeostasis include:


Thermoregulation: The hypothalamus of the brain will respond to rising temperatures by signaling the sweat glands to release moisture and blood vessels to dilate (vasodilation). When body temperatures fall, the hypothalamus signals the body’s muscles to shiver and create heat while narrowing blood vessels (vasoconstriction).


Blood Glucose Regulation: When glucose levels rise after eating food, the pancreas releases insulin, which signals to the liver that it should absorb glucose out of the blood. When fasting, exercising, or avoiding eating for any other reason, the pancrease releases glucagon instead, which signals to the liver that it should released stored glucose into the blood.


Osmoregulation: If you become dehydrated, the brain releases antidiuretic hormone (ADH), which tells the kidneys to reabsorb water. That causes urine to become more concentrated and appear darker. When drinking more water than your body needs to maintain a balance with its dissolved salts, the brain decreases the ADH it releases so that the kidney pushes out water, and urine becomes clearer through dilution.

wiki/hospital-anxiety-and-depression-sca.title: Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS)
wiki/hospital-anxiety-and-depression-sca.content:
Overview
The Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) is a self-report questionnaire that serves as a screening for anxiety and depression.
The fourteen items, each ranked somewhere between 0 and 3 depending on frequency or intensity, are split between Anxiety and Depression.
For Anxiety:


I feel tense or ‘wound up’


I get a sort of frightened feeling as if something awful is about to happen


Worrying thoughts go through my mind


I can sit at ease and feel relaxed


I get a sort of frightened feeling like ‘butterflies’ in the stomach


I feel restless as I have to be on the move


I get sudden feelings of panic


For Depression:


I still enjoy the things I used to enjoy


I can laugh and see the funny side of things


I feel cheerful


I feel as if I am slowed down


I have lost interest in my appearance


I look forward with enjoyment to things


I can enjoy a good book or radio or TV program


History and Context
HADS was published by Anthony S. Zigmond and R. Philip Snaith in 1983 in the journal Acta Psychiatrica Scandinavica:
“A self-assessment scale has been developed and found to be a reliable instrument for detecting states of depression and anxiety in the setting of an hospital medical outpatient clinic. The anxiety and depressive subscales are also valid measures of severity of the emotional disorder. It is suggested that the introduction of the scales into general hospital practice would facilitate the large task of detection and management of emotional disorder in patients under investigation and treatment in medical and surgical departments.” 1
