wiki/housing-first.title: Housing First
wiki/housing-first.content:
Overview
“Housing First” refers to a policy framework that addresses homelessness by directly providing housing options without requiring sobriety or treatment for any potential health conditions, including substance use disorder.
As the National Alliance to End Homelessness states,
Housing First is an approach that prioritizes providing permanent housing to people experiencing homelessness, thus ending their homelessness and serving as a platform from which they can pursue personal goals and improve their quality of life. This approach is guided by the belief that people need basic necessities like food and a place to live before attending to anything less critical, such as getting a job, budgeting properly, or attending to substance use issues. Additionally, Housing First is based on the belief that client choice is valuable in housing selection and supportive service participation; exercising that choice is likely to make a client more successful in remaining housed and improving their life. Housing First programs remove barriers faced by households trying to attain permanent housing, and do not require prerequisites to access housing support beyond what is required in a tenant’s lease.
Housing First Fact Sheet
The Overwhelming Evidence in Favor of Housing First as a Solution to Homelessness (with a quirky visual aid)
Commentary
Recovery Requires Capital
The science of recovery and addiction treatment has moved away from focusing on total abstinence and CBT individualist therapies as a “gold standard,” and instead towards a holistic view of the way recovery capital influences quality of life for both an individual and their community.
Recovery Capital refers to the internal and external resources that an individual can access to begin and sustain recovery from addiction or mental health conditions. These resources span personal strengths, social networks, and community or cultural supports. Originally introduced by researchers Cloud and Granfield in 1999, Recovery Capital highlights that recovery success depends not only on individual willpower and abstinence but also on the broader social and environmental context. Unlike traditional abstinence-focused measures, recovery capital through the Recovery Capital Index evaluates the holistic components of wellbeing, enabling a person-centered approach to recovery.
If we accept that addiction is a complex biopsychosocial disorder with roots in personal trauma and genetic predisposition that cause physiological changes in the brain’s reward mechanisms after sustained exposure to a particular material environment, it makes sense to move beyond discussions about knowledge gaps and into capital gaps. All the diet, exercise, and spiritual changes in the world will not change the fact that people with diabetes need insulin, people who struggle to walk need wheelchairs, people who are deaf need hearing aids or sign language, people who are blind need Braille, and people who are suffering from multiple complex mental health disorders need a safe place with professionals, a bed, and running water to work through the instability of their lives.
Recovery Capital is generally split into three types, though this is more for convenience than an implication that these are independent categories:


Personal: Physical/Mental/Emotional Wellbeing, Balanced Nutrition, Employment Status, Job Satisfaction, Workplace Support, Formal Education, Growth Opportunities, Financial Stability and Stressors, Stable and Safe Housing, Transportation Accessibility, Clothing Availability


Social: Emotional and Practical Family Assistance, Relationship Support from a Significant Other, Friendships, Comfort and Aid Networks, Professional and Personal Mobility, Wellness Activities, Support Groups, Access to Healthcare, Community Safety


Cultural: Alignment and Respect for Beliefs, Clarity and Strength of Principles, Integration of Spiritual Practices, Meaning & Purpose, Culturally Appropriate Support Groups, Feelings of Community Belonging


Although called “recovery” capital, the many dimensions to one’s health that are discovered in the process of recovery are applicable to practically anyone. We can see how complex of an issue addiction is when there’s so much overlap and intersection from the types of capital above. This isn’t a new idea either; this was identified as a model in 1999. Its lack of adoption has a lot to do with the shape of our institutions rather than scientific justifications.
In the 1980s, American medical institutions that practiced psychology and psychiatry began seeking operationalizable methods that could fit into manuals and be readily tested with experiments. If you had a method that was 80% effective but took 3 years to do, you’re not going to get far compared to a treatment that’s 25% effective but can be tested in 3 weeks. A lot of comparative studies in therapy will do something like compare a standardized CBT regimen with worksheets to psychoanalytic therapy delivered by graduate students who had a couple days of rushed training from researchers who are biased by a prior body of work favoring CBT. Jonathan Shelder has a great set of criticisms that are really specific about the methodologies of these papers in promoting CBT as a “gold standard” modality. I had my own peek into the research world when I was in college, and I don’t have trouble believing much from the things he’s pointed out. The WEIRD problem feels especially salient.
One finding from recovery capital studies is that an individual’s recovery capital is not as strong in predicting sustained abstinence as social recovery capital. The difference between someone with a highly supportive relationship and without one tends to be larger than the difference between two individuals’ personality traits. Changes in social networks actually tend to precede changes observed in personal functioning. Someone can present in treatment with high motivation, confidence, and awareness, but they will still struggle to maintain abstinence if they lack consistent transportation, safe housing, sober friend groups, and employment opportunities. Someone with modest confidence in their ability to maintain abstinence can do better than someone with high confidence if they have access to a more supportive network.
Recovery capital is also a better predictor of overall quality of life than sustained abstinence, meaning someone with high recovery capital might relapse but not suffer from the same lowered quality of life as someone who relapsed with less recovery capital. Some people can spiral faster than others on this basis. By the same token though, recovery capital is capital; it tends to work like an investment where even a few months of stable living can dramatically improve someone’s ability to generate recovery capital.
How someone’s recovery capital changes during treatment is a better predictor for how they’ll do than the baseline recovery capital they start with. Someone who enters treatment and experiences a negative social environent might experience a net decrease in recovery capital that has more influence on sustained abstinence than the therapeutic and medication interventions. Because of diminishing marginal returns on any particular form of capital within recovery capital, those who have really low capital, who might feel the most desperate and hopeless, can actually make much more progress than those with high recovery capital at baseline. Some argue that treatment is effective because it helps increase recovery capital rather than directly addressing the compulsion to use or maintenance of abstinence.

wiki/human-immunodeficiency-virus.title: Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV)
wiki/human-immunodeficiency-virus.content:
Overview
Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is a chronic infection that destroys the body’s immune system and spreads through the transfer of bodily fluids, including blood, semen, vaginal and rectal fluids, and even breast milk. It can be dormant or present with mild flu-like symptoms for years before progressing into chronic fevers from frequent infections and extreme fatigue. The final stage of HIV is known as Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS), though AIDS can be reversed into HIV-only through treatments like Antiretroviral Therapy (ART).
Substance use can increase the risk of indulging behaviors through which someone might be contract HIV, like sharing needles or engaging in unprotected sex.

wiki/hungry-angry-lonely-tired-halt.title: HALT: Hungry, Angry, Lonely, Tired
wiki/hungry-angry-lonely-tired-halt.content:
Overview
The HALT acronym points to four emotional states that make one more vulnerable to impulsive decision-making. It originated in 12-step programs as a way to stave off the triggers or cravings for a potential relapse.


Hungry: low blood sugar can be a source of irritability and anxiety


Angry: many people within recovery spaces will stand by the claim that resentment is the number one trigger of relapses


Lonely: isolation, boredom, and rumination all make room for triggers and cravings to resurface


Tired: our brains are finite organs, and they have a finite amount of energy to spend on self-control, patience, and willpower; being tired will make it harder to regulate yourself

wiki/hymn-to-ninkasi.title: Hymn to Ninkasi
wiki/hymn-to-ninkasi.content:
Overview
The Hymn to Ninkasi is a prayer song that was sung by Sumerian farmers to the goddess of beer Ninkasi, and it is also considered the oldest beer recipe in the world for which evidence currently exists. The hymn was found preserved on cuneiform tablets from the Old Babylonian period, though it functioned as a mnemonic guide for brewers to remember and share the steps of fermentation without written instructions. It also recommends the use of straws since early Sumerian beers were unfiltered, so they contained yeast sediment and bread crumbs that reed or metal straws would filter out through strainers. Examples of this can be seen in works like the cylinder-seal-of-queen-puabi, in which a royal banquet shows a Sumerian queen serving drinks to guests. Also, significantly, brewing and managing taverns that served liquor was conventionally a role women played.

wiki/hyperarousal.title: Hyperarousal
wiki/hyperarousal.content:
Overview
Hyperarousal refers to a physical state that the body enters as a response from the nervous system to continuous stress. This includes hypervigilance, and it contrasts withhypoarousal.
In a typical stress response, the amygdala sends signals to the adrenal glands to flood the bloodstream with adrenaline and norepinephrine and trigger a potential fight-or-flight response while increasing your heart rate, constricting muscles, dilating pupiles, and making breathing more shallow. It also releases the stress hormone cortisol to flood your blood with glucose for energy, sharpen your focus on stimuli around you, and slow down processes like digestion and reproduction that aren’t needed in an emergency. The prefrontal cortex simultaneously processes the actual information that triggered the amygdala and can mute the stress response if there’s no real threat, like realizing that the loud sound you just heard was a car backfiring and not a gunshot. The brain has dedicated receptors to monitor the amount of cortisol in the blood and stop producing it past a certain point, with the premise that the threat has likely been dealt with.
In hyperarousal, the amygdala is constantly firing signals to produce stress hormones, and the brain’s receptors become desensitized to the levels of cortisol in the blood. This is literally toxic; the hippocampus region of the brain atrophies in response to cortisol which makes it harder to add context to the memory of threats. Instead of being able to process a subsided threat as something in the past, the threat appears continually present to the brain, so the amygdala keeps firing. The loop is incredibly damaging to the brain, which is why chronic stress is such a big deal and takes more than a shift in mindset.

wiki/hypernormalisation.title: Hypernormalisation
wiki/hypernormalisation.content:
Adam Curtis’ basic thesis behind the documentary is that the world became too complex for the institutions of power to actually manage, so they instead turned to managing the simpler narratives that set the parameters for reality, namely the feelings and mindsets at the atomized individual level. Hypernormalisation refers to the way everyone can clearly see reality is broken, but changing the world seems either overwhelming or outright impossible in comparison to changing personal feelings about it. He draws a constellation with this pattern through social media as a tool to control information flows, pharmaceuticals to remedy social conditions that precipitate mental illnesses, a wellness industry worth multi-trilliong-dollars, recycling and carbon footprint campaigns, and liberal counterculture that grew cynical about changing systems when retreating into self-expressive activities was easier.
If we take this thesis as plausible,

wiki/hypervigilance.title: Hypervigilance
wiki/hypervigilance.content:
Overview
Hypervigilance is a part of hyperarousal, in which the nervous system’s “fight-or-flight” stress response is continually excited. Specifically, hypervigilance refers to the component of hyperarousal in which someone is constantly diverting their attention to scanning the environment for threats. Hypervigilance can manifest as:


Analyzing micro-expressions, like reading subtle changes in someone’s tone of voice, posture, pauses when speaking, changes in vocabulary, and facial expressions


People-pleasing, such as apologizing unnecessarily, instinctively choosing to inconvenience oneself for others past boundaries, and proactively trying to ensure that everyone around feels calm and happy


Defensive hostility, in which statements that are neutral or vague are interpreted as a personal attack, insult, or threat leading to disproportionate reactions


Positioning rituals, including never sitting with the back to the door in a room if avoidable (often in a corner to keep a wide field of vision) or keeping a clear path to the exit in mind when choosing a spot in a room


Tracking, so that one keeps a mental map of where everyone in a building or location is or noting the way people walk to identify them with

wiki/hypoarousal.title: Hypoarousal
wiki/hypoarousal.content:
Overview
Hypoarousal is a state in which the nervous system shuts down to conserve energy in response to prolonged or intense stress and trauma. This is in contrast to hyperarousal, though notably, a stressed nervous system may swing abruptly from one to the other. Signs of hypoarousal include:


Emotional numbness


Low energy or chronic fatigue


Brain fog or trouble concentrating


Dissociation

wiki/hypochondria.title: Hypochondria
wiki/hypochondria.content:
Overview
Hypochondria, or Illness Anxiety Disorder (IAD) as of the publication of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5) in 2013, refers to a condition in which someone experiences constant and intense fear of having a serious illness. The term “hypochondriac” is weighed down by a lot of social stigma, much like “addict,” so the American Psychiatric Association (APA) began explicitly reframing the condition as a disorder. Symptoms include:


Constant anxiety about personal health and normal functions like heart rate (although Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder also has this as a symptom, the two are distinct)


Persistent concerns despite medical testing that detect nothing wrong


Misinterpreting minor symptoms like a cough for a severe illness


Many people turn to substance use in an attempt to self-medicate the distress caused by IAD, which can significantly worsen the anxiety experienced while adding a new constellation of sensations and symptoms to worry about.

wiki/hypomania.title: Hypomania
wiki/hypomania.content:
Overview
Hypomania is a short-lived form of mania in which someone experiences increased energy and elevated or irritable moods. Someone must be experiencing symptoms for four days consecutively that are not considered characteristic of someone’s personality outside of the symptomatic episodes. More specifically, these symptoms include:


Grandiosity


Decreased desire for sleep


Speaking fast or as if under pressure


Racing thoughts


Lack of attention or focus


Spikes in productive activities toward goals and projects


Risky behavior

wiki/hysteria.title: Hysteria
wiki/hysteria.content:
Overview
Hysteria in a casual everyday sense refers to some kind of extreme excitement or overwhelming emotion. I use it often in the context of anti-drug or anti-immigrant hysteria, in which people are so frightened over something unfamiliar that they jump to radical or pseudoscientific solutions. However, “hysteria” used to describe a now-defunct disorder that framed an excess of emotion as a pathology that requires treatment, and it was usually assigned to women.

wiki/i-statements.title: I-statements
wiki/i-statements.content:
Overview
I-statements are expressions that avoid generalizing by focusing on personal experiences. For instance, rather than saying “a good parent is always attentive to their kids’ needs”, an I-statement might reframe the sentiment as “I feel like a good parent when I’m attentive to my kids’ needs.”
Commentary
No one ever actually does this anywhere. I don’t even consistently do it on this site. In fact, I’m about to break that principle right now: we as people have a strong tendency to want to share our information and experiences, which requires some degree of generalization that assumes we and another person are, to some extent, interchageable.

wiki/impairment.title: Impairment
wiki/impairment.content:
Overview
The National Cancer Institute defines “impairment” as:
A loss of part or all of a physical or mental ability, such as the ability to see, walk, or learn. 1
Taber’s Medical Dictionary provides a somewhat more specific definition that explicitly invokes a biopsychosocial perspective:
Any loss or abnormality of psychological, physiological, or anatomical structure or function. Impairments represent a deviation from generally accepted benchmarks in biomedical or psychosocial functioning. 2
Substance use is almost always going to involve impairment in some way as they interact with the nervous system.


Depressants like alcohol and benzodiazepines enhances the activity of GABA while blocking glutamate, which leads to slower central nervous system activity and the disorientation associated with drinking, like delayed reaction time, loss of motor coordination, slurred speech, blurry vision, and lack of inhibition and judgment.


Opioids like heroin, fentanyl, and oxycodone mimic natural endorphins while heavily suppressing brainstem activity, leading to lethargy, drowsiness, falling into unresponsive stupors, lack of awareness of the external world, and respiratory depression that might stop breathing.


Stimulants like cocaine and methamphetamine prevent the reuptake of dopamine, so the nervous system is forced into hyperarousal with racing thoughts, hyperfixation, a sense of invincibility, paranoia, agitation, and extreme impulsivity.

wiki/impermanence.title: Impermanence
wiki/impermanence.content:
Overview
Impermanence is a central organizing principle of many non-Western religions that posit that everything in the universe is in a constant state of change. Western religions are heavily based around Abrahamic moral-psychology that posits definite good and evil, and often an objective arbiter to judge that good and evil (i.e. God). Hindu cosmology generally holds that time is cyclical, so even cosmic forces like devas and asuras have beginnings and endings; the only permanent thing is Brahman as the ultimate reality that serves as the substrate for all things. Buddhism practices a radical version of impermanence in which nothing, not the self nor the universe, can be safely treated as a permanent fixture of the universe. In both cases, the construct of an ego is assumed to be an impermanent illusion constructed to interface with the universe, in contrast to say, a discrete permanent soul that carries a single identity with it.
The principles of impermanence are a central part of Recovery Dharma and Refuge Recovery, which are Buddhist-derived peer recovery groups. Many participants report feeling a sense of comfort of knowing that if all things are impermanent, that includes their suffering and the harms they may feel responsible for in the past. Being attached to the past is a form of permanence in which one contracts one’s self by defining it through an image that no longer exists. Even our memories are actively reconstructed and reconsolidated each time we access them, so our real attachment is to the image that results rather than an objective recollection of the past.

wiki/imposter-syndrome.title: Imposter Syndrome
wiki/imposter-syndrome.content:
Overview
Imposter syndrome is not an official medical diagnosis, but it was coined by clinical psychologists to describe the specific anxieties where people continually doubt themselves and feel like a fraud even when experiencing undeniable success. This can manifest as low self-esteem or self-worth, rationalizations that success was the result of luck, worrying about how others perceive one’s competence, and perfectionism that sets up impossible standards.

wiki/impulsivity.title: Impulsivity
wiki/impulsivity.content:

describing or displaying behavior characterized by little or no forethought, reflection, or consideration of the consequences of an action, particularly one that involves taking risks. 1

wiki/inebriety.title: Inebriety
wiki/inebriety.content:
Overview
Inebriety refers to the state of being drunk, normally from alcohol.
History and Etymology
While the term “inebriate” can be found in the 15th century in the context of being “inebriate in the love of God” in reference to feeling overwhelmed with religious zeal and spirit, it was used as a euphemism for being drunk for centuries until the late 1800s. Physicians began using the term when addressing addiction, such as the American Association for the Study and Cure of Inebriety in 1870 or The Journal of Inebriety (1876-1914). Patients were often sent to dedicated “inebriate asylums.” Now, the term is considered outdated, first replaced by “alcoholism” and “addiction”, which in turn were replaced with “substance use disorder” or “alcohol use disorder.”

wiki/inflammation.title: Inflammation
wiki/inflammation.content:
Overview
Inflammation is typically a response from an immune system that increases blood flow, heat, and fluid build up towards some area of the body that might be injured, infected, or irritated.
In the short-term, in cases such as a cut or a cold, inflammation is a healing process that helped deliver immune cells and healing factors to an affected region of the body. In the long-term, chronic inflammation can damage healthy tissues and increase the risk of developing heart disease and diabetes.

wiki/inner-child.title: Inner Child
wiki/inner-child.content:
Overview
The “inner child” is a metaphor that refers to some collection of schemas and emotions rooted in childhood experiences or perspectives.
Commentary
The “inner child” is not a rigid scientific or clinical concept. It has origins in analytical psychology dating back to Carl Jung’s archetypes of a “Divine Child” and “wounded child”, but the concept isn’t defined in ways we can measure for empirical testing. That doesn’t mean the concept is necessarily pseudoscience or therapeutically useless, but it does mean that we should be cautious about making claims around it. Some therapeutic approaches like Internal Family Systems (IFS) rely on the concept of an inner child to guide healing while addressing the formative traumas someone may have undergone in their childhood.

wiki/inner-city.title: Inner City
wiki/inner-city.content:
Overview
The term “inner city” has been used as a euphemism for low-income predominantly minority neighborhoods in urban environments, which came to the forefront of sociopolitical discourse through media coverage of the crack cocaine epidemic in the 1980s and 1990s under the banner of the War on Drugs.

wiki/inner-work.title: Inner Work
wiki/inner-work.content:
Overview
“Inner work” is a term that’s widely used in pop psychology, though it’s rooted in ideas going back to Carl Jung about reflecting on one’s psyche as an internal world that interacts with the external world.
If you’ve encountered phrases like “healing your inner child,” “doing shadow work,” or “protecting your peace” as general concepts divorced from specific therapeutic modalities or treatment protocols, you’re likely dealing with pop psych literature or content that heavily draws on clinical buzzwords without the rigor of the scientific process and peer review. This doesn’t mean it’s outright bunk or pure marketing, but it does mean that a lot of “inner work” that’s commonly discussed in public discourse covers for the intuition of armchair folk psychologists running social media accounts based on mental health.

wiki/inpatient.title: Inpatient
wiki/inpatient.content:
Overview
Inpatient programs involve staying in a treatment facility continuously in order to receive care.
Inpatient rehabs, also sometimes called residential treatment, are considered the most intensive level of care for substance use disorders, as well as other mental health disorders as appropriate. Bringing someone out of their old environment that’s laden with cues and routines related to their substance use is often critical in disrupting destructive spirals. This usually involves 24/7 medical supervision, regular appointments with therapists and psychiatrists, and group sessions involving other clients with the goal of building support networks between them.

wiki/insanity.title: Insanity
wiki/insanity.content:
Overview
Insanity is not a term used in the medical field due to its social stigma and lack of precision. Instead, it has legal weight by labeling a person as being in a state of mind in which they are incapable of understanding the consequences of their actions during a crime.
Contrary to popular wisdom, the definition of insanity is not actually doing the same thing over and over while expecting different results. That came out of a Narcotics Anonymous pamphlet in 1981 and has been misattributed to historically significant intellectuals like Albert Einstein, Mark Twain, and Benjamin Franklin.

wiki/insomnia.title: Insomnia
wiki/insomnia.content:
Overview
Insomnia is a disorder that disrupts sleep, either by making it hard to fall asleep or stay asleep. Short-term insomnia can be caused by stress, travel, substance use, or significant life events that lead to a lot of thoughts at night. Long-term insomnia can be related to chronic pain, mental health disorders like anxiety and depression, and the side effects of some medications.
Insomnia and substance use disorders have a bidirectional relationship, meaning that insomnia can be a result of using substances, but insomnia can also be a target of self-medicating with substances. It’s pretty common to hear alcohol described as a sleep aid for troubled nights, although it actually disrupts deep REM sleep and can easily lead to a cycle of drinking more to overcome persistent sleep issues. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I) is typically the recommended first-line intervention to address negative thought patterns about sleep and improve sleep hygiene, like restricting the time spent in bed to the periods you actually feel sleepy so that your brain associates the bed with sleep rather than problem-solving.

wiki/institute-for-addiction-science.title: Institute for Addiction Science
wiki/institute-for-addiction-science.content:
Overview
The University of Southern California’s Institute for Addiction Science (IAS) claims to be the first university-wide transdisciplinary institute for addiction research and education in the United States. They also run an annual Early Career Addiction Science Showcase (ECASS) for undergraduate students, graduate students, and junior faculty to present research before publication.

ias.usc.edu/

wiki/intellectualization.title: Intellectualization
wiki/intellectualization.content:
Overview
“Intellectualization” is considered a defense mechanism against unwanted emotions that draws someone’s focus to abstractions rather than the lived experience of painful feelings. One of the most commonly depicted forms of intellectualization follows the death of a loved one, where someone might throw themselves entirely into the headspace of resolving the logistical problems of a person’s absence, like spending more time working to compensate for the lost income but also to avoid sitting alone with uncomfortable emotions surrounding that loss. In recovery spaces, those who were good at school, myself included, can quickly learn how to give facilitators or therapists the answers they’re looking for by working in jargon like “challenging my black-and-white schemas that were responsible for my self-sabotage around the fears of success”, but also bypass any real emotional experience.

wiki/intelligence.title: Intelligence
wiki/intelligence.content:
Overview
Commentary
My degree says I have a specialization in Intelligent Systems, but I don’t really know how to define intelligence. The closest I can figure is that we use it to refer to some kind of system that is capable of updating its model of the world after receiving feedback from it. That means any observation of basic Bayesian inference is sufficient to label something as intelligent, but with a definition that broad, we might have to call bacteria and viruses intelligent.

wiki/intensive-outpatient-program-iop.title: Intensive Outpatient Program (IOP)
wiki/intensive-outpatient-program-iop.content:
Overview
Intensive Outpatient Programs (IOPs) address substance use disorders and other mental health disorders by structuring about 10-20 hours of therapy a week so that patients can continue to live at home, maintain full-time employment, or take a full-time class schedule at school. Generally, patients step down from a 24/7 inpatient facility or residential center to a Partial Hospitalization Program (PHP) that takes full-time attention, and then they step down again into an IOP. It’s very common for a single entity or center to manage all three or some combination of the two, especially since IOP can just involve the exact same resources as PHP but for shorter periods of time.

wiki/intentionality.title: Intentionality
wiki/intentionality.content:
Overview
Intentionality is broadly the capacity to direct oneself towards something else. If that sounds vague, it’s because intentionality takes on a variety of meanings depending on the specific context.
Philosophers of the mind discuss intentionality as a property that separates the physical world from constructs of the mind. From the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy:
In philosophy, intentionality is the power of minds and mental states to be about, to represent, or to stand for, things, properties and states of affairs. To say of an individual’s mental states that they have intentionality is to say that they are mental representations or that they have contents. 1
The American Psychological Association (APA) defines intentionality as:
a characteristic of an individual’s acts that requires the individual (a) to have goals, desires, and standards; (b) to select behaviors that are in the service of attaining the goal (e.g., means to an end); and (c) to call into conscious awareness a desired future state. Investigators differ as to whether (a) alone, (a) and (b) but not (c), or (a), (b), and (c) are required for intentionality to be attributable to an individual. 1
In therapeutic modalities like Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), intentionality is used by clinicians to refer to decision-making rooted in values instead of habits or immediate reactions.

wiki/international-overdose-awareness-da.title: International Overdose Awareness Day
wiki/international-overdose-awareness-da.content:
Overview
International Overdose Awareness Day (IOAD) was established in 2001 by Sally J. Finn and Peter Streker, who were working at The Salvation Army’s needle exchange program in St. Kilda, Melbourne, Australia. The first event, set for August 31st, was held at the needle exchange facility as a community barbecue. Ultimately, 6000 silver ribbons were distributed across Australia and New Zealand in honor of those who had passed from overdoses.
In 2012, the nonprofit Penington Institute began officially managing the campaign in order to handle the scale of a global movement. In 2014, the Penington Institute expanded IOAD’s mission to focus on distributing overdose prevention tools like Naloxone (Narcan) rather than just a day of remembrance.
As of 2026, IOAD boasts more than 1000 localized events across 40+ countries.

wiki/intertemporal-bargaining.title: Intertemporal Bargaining
wiki/intertemporal-bargaining.content:
Overview
Intertemporal bargaining is a behavioral economics concept that refers to a person making a strategic decision that alters the benefits or consequences of their future self. Eating a whole row of Double Stuf Oreos might seem very appealing in the short-term, and the impulse to act on that might cause you to decide that the sugar intake is a problem you’re willing to pass onto your future self.
Links

pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3742964/

wiki/intervention.title: Intervention
wiki/intervention.content:
Overview
“Intervention” in a general medical context has been used to refer to any treatment used to address the natural course of a disease.
In preventative medicine, interventions are generally categorized as:


primary interventions that prevent a disease before it occurs, like a vaccine


secondary interventions that use early detection to address a disease at it’s earliest stages


tertiary interventions that stop or delay the worsening of an established disease


The term “intervention” has also been popularized to refer to a gathering of loved ones who (compassionately) confront an individual about their behaviors in a way that might promote a desire to change.
History and Context
Vernon Johnson, an Episcopal priest in recovery, proposed a model of intervention through his book I’ll Quit Tomorrow in 1973 where friends and family could confront a loved one struggling with substance use to induce something of a controlled crisis that might inspire change. Johnson observed that most people struggling with addiction didn’t attempt to quit until some kind of negative consequence disrupted their patterns, so a gentle confrontation led by loved ones could be called an intervention that addresses the disease of addiction. Around the 1980s, public health researchers introduced the concept of Brief Interventions, in which a medical professional might approach a patient with a brief ~15 minute conversation about their substance use patterns during routine visits or ER trips that flag high-risk behaviors. The Screening, Brief Intervention, and Referral to Treatment model is based on using a standardized assessment, having a brief conversation based on motivational interviewing concepts, and referring to specialized treatment programs.

wiki/intimate-partner-violence-ivp.title: Intimate Partner Violence (IPV)
wiki/intimate-partner-violence-ivp.content:
Overview
Intimate Partner Violence (IPV) refers to instances of physical altercation between partners who are in or used to be in a romantic relationship.
In the general population, 33% of women and 25% of men report being the victim of IPV or domestic violence. Within those seeking treatment for substance use disorders, 1 in 2 women report being the victim of IPV. With men, 30% report having engaged in relationships with mutual physical aggression, while only 1 in 10 identify as victims of IPV. Researchers note that social stigma plays a role in the willingness to report incidents or identify as a victim, so generally it might be reasonable to assume that true rates are higher. Some studies show that between 40 to 60 percent of domestic violence incidents involve substance use as a factor.
It’s not hard to see the connection between substances that amplify intense feelings or inhibited judgment and physical violence as a means of conflict resolution.

wiki/intoxication.title: Intoxication
wiki/intoxication.content:
Overview
“Intoxication” is a term used in both clinical and non-clinical contexts to refer to the state of mind resulting from substance use, normally alcohol.

wiki/intramuscular.title: Intramuscular (IM) Injection
wiki/intramuscular.content:
Overview
Intramuscular (IM) injections are injections that aim to go deeper than intradermal (in the skin), intravenous (in the veins), and subcutaneous (fatty tissue under the skin) injections. Vaccines, hormones, steroids, and antibiotics are generally delivered at this depth which allows for rapid absorption of high quantities of a medication or drug.
With injection drug use, generally the goal is to hit the intravenous (IV) level that puts the entire dose into the vein and to the brain at once without the liver processing it. IM injections have a slower onset than IV injections, so if someone ends up injecting at the IM level, it’s usually because they either missed a vein or have ruined veins that can’t handle the needle. Every type of injection carries the risk of contaminating the body and lead to abscesses or infections.

wiki/intravenous.title: Intravenous (IV)
wiki/intravenous.content:
Overview
Intravenous (IV) translates literally into “within a vein.” It’s most often used in the context of IV injections, which deliver some substance directly into a person’s bloodstream through their veins for rapid circulation. As a medical procedure, it’s commonly done to administer medications that act rapidly without going through the digestive system’s metabolic processes. If a patient has lost blood, become critically malnourished, or severely dehydrated, IV fluids might be used to quickly restore a balance of nutrients and electrolytes rather than waiting for the body to naturally arrive at a balance over a long period of time.
In the context of substance use, IV injections are used to administer a variety of drugs for an instant and more powerful high than oral ingestion that passes through the liver and might weaken the effects of the substance. Some studies also suggest that IV injections can lead to significantly higher risks of developing substance use disorders since the brain experiences the association between the injection and the reward of the high instantly. It also raises the potential of fatal overdoses and the transmission of blood-borne pathogens like HIV, Hepatitis B, and Hepatitis C on top of other infections like endocarditis. Repeated injections also cause physical trauma to veins, which can lead to scarring, collapse, or deep vein thrombosis (blood clots).
Harm reduction policies often include syringe service programs (SSPs) or needle exchange programs that provide IV drug users with clean needles to reduce the transmission of diseases. Studies show that these centers are effective at limiting the spread of diseases, and they can also serve as entry points into pathways to treatment that encourages long-term sobriety.

wiki/intrinsic-motivation.title: Intrinsic Motivation
wiki/intrinsic-motivation.content:
Overview
The concept of intrinsic motivation refers to the tendency to perceive activities as their own reward rather than the means to an external reward.
History and Context
The term first entered scientific literature in 1950 in a paper titled “Learning and satiation of response in intrinsically motivated complex puzzle performance by monkeys.” The psychologist Harry Harlow observed how some monkeys would learn to solve puzzles without food or praise as external rewards to reinforce the behavior, suggesting that some kind of intrinsic motivation was driving the behavior. In 1959, Robert W. White published a paper that observed many organisms engaging in behaviors that exploratory or playful, and he claimed that the intrinsic motivation was driven by a need for competence and effectance to master one’s environment.
The concept was eventually applied to human psychology and behavior as well. Edward L. Deci performed an experiment in 1971 that found that introducing external rewards for an interesting experiment actually decreased the intrinsic motivation. Two groups of humans were given a puzzle called Soma cubes that were supposedly naturally fun to solve. Group A was given money for each puzzle solved. When participants were left alone, Group B continued playing with the cubes while Group A stopped the moment the money was gone. This was challenging for behaviorists to reconcile, or at least radical behaviorists who argued that organisms were conditioned into actions and motivations entirely based on environmental cues and rewards.
In 1985, Deci and Richard Ryan proposed Self-Determination Theory that posits that humans are driven by three core psychological needs: autonomy, competence, and relatedness. Within this framework, intrinsic motivation came to be defined as activities done for their own sake because of inherent satisfaction rather than separable consequences. Still, the effect of intrinsic motivation is to produce movement towards satisfying autonomy, competence, and relatedness as needs.

wiki/intrusive-thoughts.title: Intrusive Thoughts
wiki/intrusive-thoughts.content:
Overview
Intrusive thoughts refer to thoughts that interrupt a flow of thoughts. There are some wordier definitions that sound more technical, but that’s the essence of it. In clinical literature, it’s common to see intrusive thoughts referred to as “obsessions”, “mental intrusions”, or other close synonyms. Everyone has some level of intrusive thoughts that come to mind throughout their day and life, but it can reach a pathological level as symptoms of a disorder that would benefit from medical treatment.
From the American Psychological Association’s Dictionary of Psychology:
mental events that interrupt the flow of task-related thoughts in spite of efforts to avoid them. Minor intrusions are normal and widespread (see mind wandering). Upsetting intrusions are common after trauma and in obsessive-compulsive disorder. 1
The phrase “intrusive thoughts” appears in the DSM-5-TR as a symptom of a myriad of conditions that, as mentioned in the APA definition, include OCD and PTSD, but also dissociative disorders and anxiety disorders. The DSM-5-TR doesn’t provide a definition for intrusive thoughts, though.

wiki/ippei-mizuhara.title: Ippei Mizuhara
wiki/ippei-mizuhara.content: An interpreter for Shohei Ohtani, a Major League Baseball player, Ippei Mizuhara was convicted of bank fraud and tax evasion. Specifically, he admitted to stealing almost $17 million from Ohtani to pay off gambling debts. The bookie, Matthew Bowyer, said he recognized Mizuhara’s compulsive gambling habits. However, E. Martin Estrada, then U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California and prosecutor in Mizuhara’s case, claimed that gambling addiction alone couldn’t explain the extent of his actions and criminal opportunism had to be involved.

wiki/isolation-of-affect.title: Isolation of Affect
wiki/isolation-of-affect.content:
Overview
Isolation of affect is a psychological defense mechanism in which the cognitive and emotional components of an experience are isolated from each other so that an individual can cognitively engage with an idea without being conscious of their emotional associations with it. It’s considered to be the opposite of repression, where the emotional affect is impacting an individual but they don’t consciously recognize the idea.

wiki/it-works-how-and-why.title: It Works; How and Why
wiki/it-works-how-and-why.content:
Does It?

wiki/james-mckeen-cattell.title: James McKeen Cattell
wiki/james-mckeen-cattell.content:
Overview
James McKeen Cattell holds the honorable distinction of being the first psychology professor in the United States. He earned his PhD in Germany under Willhem Wundt, who was the first to distinguish psychology from biology and philosophy while calling himself a psychologist.
Metrics and Eugenics
Together, Wundt and Cattell explored the study of intelligence through psychometrics, though their general worldviews were often radically different. Wundt strictly opposed the biological determinism behind eugenics and the biological reductionism behind treating complex mental processes as simple physical processes to examine in a vacuum without reference to one’s identity within broader society. Cattell had somewhat of an obsession with ranking people against each other in the fashion of American management philosophy, which was undergoing the revolution of Scientific Management driven by those like Frederick Winslow Taylor and American Pragmatism championed by psychologists William James and John Dewey - both of whom were Presidents of the American Psychological Assocation as well. While Wundt and other psychologists saw their work as aimed towards discovering truths scientifically, pragmatists argued that the value of ideas were tied to their immediately measurable applications, usually in industrialized corporate environments.
Industrial-Organizational (I-O) Psychology as a field emerged out of the work of Cattell and his contemporaries, who thought the pragmatic application of psychology and psychometrics was to identify the inherent characteristics of a worker that would determine their worth in an environment. Rather than focusing on changing the workplace or seeing workers as people who could grow with time and resources, the focus became on weeding out those who scored lower on psychometric assessments as the individual culprits behind unoptimal productivity. Labor unions and traditionalist psychologists alike condemned this practice as reducing humans to interchangeable components that punished individuality and independence through conformity disguised as scientific standards. Many pragmatists, including Cattel, responded that the purpose of education in democracy was not actually to improve people’s conditions but to match individuals to the role best suited for their natural limitations.
A Hippie Side
Ever the experimentalist, Cattell continued a brave and amusing tradition of researching drugs through self-administration, though he didn’t publish a manuscript about it like many predecessors did. He experimented with cannabis, opium (legally obtainable as hashish at the time), caffeine, morphine, chocolate, etc., and he often went over the limits he prescribed for himself in the course of experimentation.
In 1917, Cattell was fired from Columbia University for opposing the draft into World War I. He sued the university and used his settlement winnings to create the Psychological Corporation. For the rest of his career, he pursued his interests in publications with applied psychology.
Eugenics
Cattell was unfortunately not immune from the anxieties of social changes that led many otherwise brilliant researchers to pursue pseudoscientific paradigms that justified their success as inherent to their being.

wiki/jonathan-blow.title: Jonathan Blow
wiki/jonathan-blow.content:
Overview
Jonathan Blow has been one of the more vocal developers tackling the value of video gaming as an expressive medium. He likens the loops built by games like World of Warcraft to a type of drug that exploits short-term loops that are little more than a series of tasks towards an end “victory” state. To make a game have artistic value instead of just fast food-esque entertainment value, it has to challenge the player into choices and problems that are fundamentally novel.
Background
Blow is a serious developer, not just a game designer. He’s highly opinionated and dedicated towards software development, driving his own language called Jai and criticizing the over-engineering and over-complexity of modern engineering through a long career of talks, think pieces, and courses.
He’s a pioneer in building a brand around indie games through a public persona. The community of single developers was much smaller than it is now in an era where Steam dumpster diving with friends can be a lot more fun (and makes for better content) than a single playthrough of AAA games. Developers like Blow proved that indie games could not just be made by single people but also distributed through online platforms rather than physical retailers like Walmart. Braid and The Witness.
That all being said, Blow has had a bit of a reputation online for being pretentious and attention-seeking, encapsulated best by the satirical meme: Jonathan Blow Crying in a Dark Room about Soulja Boy misunderstanding Braid www.youtube.com/watch He has a lot of opinions some would consider curmudgeonly, though he’s still regarded as a skilled engineer.
That’s about the kindest this section gets, because Blow became very politically controversial after 2018, to say the least. There’s an all-too-common pattern among skilled engineers who assume that their system design skills within the umbrella of technical domains is cleanly transferable to all systems. Politics and society are especially easy for non-experts to comment on and build a following around, so an echo chamber can quickly lead to unhinged spirals from otherwise talented people. Here are some highlights:
December 2017: “Interest is not the same as ability. I believe it is likely that the sexes have different interests on average, and that biological factors play a large part in this. This is NOT REMOTELY a controversial opinion except on Weird Far Left Twitter 2017.”
October 2021: “There’s a weird disconnect in this vaccine mandate debate: many are still pretending that Covid-19 is of natural origin, which gives such mandates a different feel than they otherwise have. If a state entity does an oopsie in a lab, then forces its citizens to undergo an experimental treatment because of the oopsie, while suppressing news of side effects, and also denying that the oopsie is anyone’s fault… that’s just abusive?”
In response to SpaceX criticism from April 2024: “Reading this, I knew you had pronouns in bio before looking.”
From November 2024: “This is true, the gaming press is super left-wing, but on the other hand they have almost no impact now. I would say that the social pressure keeping ‘indies’ in line mostly comes from them being socially fearful in the normal way. (It doesn’t help that all males currently under the age of 40 were raised to be supercucks).”
In reference to President Trump from February 2025: “Are you kidding? He is the best President we have had in my entire life, by far. It’s a miracle. I just hope it doesn’t abruptly go bad.”

wiki/josh-korda.title: Josh Korda
wiki/josh-korda.content:
Note: The foreword of this book is written by Noah Levine, who has since been involved in sexual misconduct allegations through his leadership role at Against the Stream (ATS) and teaching role with Spirit Rock Meditation Center. ATS later dissolved and Spirit Rock revoked his license to teach. No criminal charges appear to have been filed concerning any of the allegations, and Levine denies any wrongdoing. This page will focus on the contents of the book itself.
Foreword
“The Buddha’s teachings are perfect in all ways and will lead any who thoroughly applies them to a profound transformation.”
Yes, it’s the first sentence but I already have to object. I’ve been critical of AA literature for making strong, sweeping statements about how the program can’t fail you, only you can fail the program. This is the same problem again, and it’s common marketing among a lot of self-help products that don’t ever come under scientific scrutiny. Let’s look at some quotes actually attributed to the Buddha.
From AN 3.65:
“Do not go by oral tradition, by lineage of teaching, by hearsay, by a collection of scriptures, by logical reasoning, by inferential reasoning, by reflection on reasons, by acceptance of a view after pondering it, by the seeming competence of a speaker, or because you think, ‘The ascetic is our teacher.‘”
“When you know for yourselves: ‘These things are unwholesome… these things, when undertaken and practiced, lead to harm and suffering’—then you should abandon them.”
“When you know for yourselves: ‘These things are wholesome… these things, when undertaken and practiced, lead to welfare and happiness’—then you should enter and remain in them.”
From MN 22, Alagaddupama Sutta:
“I have taught the Dhamma compared to a raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping”
From DN 16, Mahaparinibbana Sutta:
“Be islands unto yourselves, be your own refuge, with no other refuge; let the Dhamma be your island, the Dhamma your refuge, with no other refuge.”
Obviously, the Buddha is depicted as having critical awakenings to share, but it’s hard to imagine that someone encouraging a radical skepticism towards himself would also approve of such a blanket endorsement.
“As modern American Buddhists we are in the rare and fortunate position to not only receive the Buddha’s Dharma, but to also receive the dharma of psychology. With his teachings and this wonderful book, Josh joins the emerging trend of integrating the best practices of Western theorists with the highest wisdom of the Buddha.”
This is tripping a lot of red flags I got reading The Four Agreements about unifying theories from different cultures in some kind of perennialist fusion, but I’m going to try set that bias aside and be upfront when I recognize it in myself.
Preface
As I make some final touches to this book in the early days of November 2016, I cannot help but note the storm clouds looming in the background of this endeavor… the United States, never to be dramatically outperformed, always seeking the spotlight of history, elects a bigoted sexual predator as president.
Oh, you poor sorry bastard. Just wait until 2026. I yearn for 2016. Simpler times.
On a serious note, I appreciate someone being upfront about their social and political stances. I’m of the opinion that everything is political, and if you don’t feel that it is, it’s because the status quo political situation is fine by you. Not making a choice is a choice.
Addiction is incredibly political. Study after study shows that the biggest factors in determining an individual’s capacity for sustained abstinence involves their access to recovery capital. The movement of capital will always be a political question. The concept of a worthy life enabled by the society we live in will always be political.
All of us suffer, and by trying to achieve peace of mind and security by trudging down capitalism’s Yellow Brick Road of workaholism, careerism, consumerism, fame seeking, and social-media-reputatioan fixation, we waste what little time we have, and wind up absolutely nowhere, not even treated to a glittering, extravagant spectacle such as Oz. Trying to acquire or achieve security and serenity keeps the economy buzzing, chews up our resources, and turns us into competitors, mistrusting each other, viewing each other as obstacles, fighting over slices of an ever-dwindling cake.
One doesn’t need to be a psychologist to discern that constant busyness is a symptom of avoidance, for when we run out of fuel and idle to a full stop, what do we experience? The voidness of meaning that is simply surviving in this world.
There’s not much I can say about capitalism that hasn’t been said a million times before and a million times better. I’d like to focus on the workaholism angle though, because it is unquestionably true that our society elevates certain addictions while stigmatizing others.
I’m reminded of a controversy back in 2017 when Andrew Ng, Stanford Professor and Coursera founder, opened job postings for software engineers to work 70-90 hours a week. I grew up in the Bay around tech people, so there were plenty of stories about tech CEOs, including some you still see making headlines, throwing temper tantrums because their employees weren’t on the 9am to 9pm grind.
I recall a presentation about study abroad during my time at UC Irvine where a slide was dedicated to the culture shock experienced by American students bragging about sleep deprivation as evidence of their hard work. We were told that students in other countries tend to see that as concerning, indicative of either poor work ethic or poor health.
Workaholism is perhaps the most acceptable addiction there is. We elevate it as a form of self-sacrifice and maximization of inner potential. Someone’s works often becomes their legacy. “Greed is good” is unironically a mantra we use to rationalize profit-seeking as meaning-making.
It follows logically that if we elevate one addictive behavior, and addictive behaviors are commonly interchangeable, then we’re elevating addiction itself as a virtue. Addiction to profit, addiction to consumption, addiction to power, addiction to dissociation, addiction to problem-solving, addiction to conflict, addiction to chaos, addiction to stress, addiction to winning, addiction to risk-taking, so on and so forth. A substance or few is just an addition to the pile.
After all, who works more single-mindedly towards a goal than someone in active addiction chasing the next fix? Eventually we elevate cheating as proof of commitment to prioritizing a goal over rules, ethics, integrity, sustainability, and relationships.
“I would sacrifice my child, negotiate with terrorists, and skirt the Geneva Convention if it raised the share price” is simply honoring one’s fiduciary duty to the shareholders.
“having more only leaves us wanting more… the underlying premise is that the answer is out there, not available to me already”
This definitely captures the core of Buddhism. From the Dhammapada, verse 187:
“Sensual pleasures give little enjoyment and much suffering- knowing this, the wise person finds no delight even in heavenly pleasures.”
From MN 75 Magandiya Sutta:
“Now suppose that there was a leper covered with sores & infections, devoured by worms, picking the scabs off the openings of his wounds with his nails, cauterizing his body over a pit of glowing embers. The more he cauterized his body over the pit of glowing embers, the more disgusting, foul-smelling, & putrid the openings of his wounds would become, and yet he would feel a modicum of enjoyment & satisfaction because of the itchiness of his wounds. In the same way, beings not free from passion for sensual pleasures — devoured by sensual craving, burning with sensual fever — indulge in sensual pleasures. The more they indulge in sensual pleasures, the more their sensual craving increases and the more they burn with sensual fever, and yet they feel a modicum of enjoyment & satisfaction dependent on the five strings of sensuality.”
From core Buddhist principles, one posits that there is no amount of material or worldly pleasures that will finally satiate one’s appetite for them. This doesn’t mean that we can just ignore these needs either, but we can’t expect to find a lasting solution to suffering from satisfying our fleeting desires. That’s the same as scratching a wound for the short-term relief, when it will quickly become itchy again as a deeper wound.
To tie it back to our modern America, the entire premise of advertising as an industry is that people can be convinced that part of their insatiable needs will be addressed through the consumption of some product that has relevant value. Go watch Mad Men, which is explicitly about the way an addict uses his own lack of fulfillment as inspiration for advertisements that resonate with consumers in a world celebrating Ayn Rand’s brand of selfish individualism.
One distinction though is that traditionally, Buddhism was not focused on the internal narratives we hold in the same way that modern “Western” psychology tends to emphasize them. After all, if we accept the impermanence of all things, then how could there be a permanently true self? The self and its cravings are both subject to dependent origination, thus an independently true self in a vacuum doesn’t really make sense.
So, it’s less that the answer to suffering is internally available by simply modifying our internal narrative of the self that’s been socially conditioned, and more that the answer to suffering lies in recognizing the constructs of the mind that produce craving through attachment. That tends to go in the opposite direction of many humanistic Western therapeutic interventions though, which can try to find some authentically true self that has experienced alienation but can achieve self-actualization through a transformation into wholeness.
This distinction will become relevant many times throughout the book. For instance, Korda states:
“All of the versions of Buddhist suttas in this book are my own…I find there’s an unfortunate tendency among some to render the early Buddhist transcripts in stitled phrases and word choices, which obfuscates ideas that can actually be quite accessible.”
More of those red flags from the The Four Agreements are coming back to me. I am generally wary of attempts to simplify the core teachings of a belief system for standalone self-help products. It’s one thing for someone beginning a serious study of a discipline who might need to get their foot in the door somehow, but it’s another to start repackaging a version while claiming you’ve preserved the integrity of the original canon. To Korda’s credit, he explicitly does say that you can “consult the now-standard translations of Thanisaro Bhikkhu, Bhikkhu Nanamoli, or Bhikkhu Bodhi” for deeper study. Even so, within the example he gives, we can observe a problem.
From the original Korda cites:
“Suppose there is no hereafter nor fruit of deeds done well or ill. Yet in this world I keep myself safe and happy, free from hatred and malice…”
From Korda’s translation:
“Look, even if there is no such thing as rebirth—if our experience ends with our death—and no way to feel the results of our actions, it’s still worth- while to act harmlessly, as we’ll feel better about ourselves while we’re still alive.”
First, I don’t think the cited excerpt is so challenging that one “would be hard-pressed to understand the Buddha’s important, though straightforward message.” There aren’t any technical terms being used there at all. I assume the word “hereafter” can be frightening?
As for what’s lost or gained in translation, Korda’s interpretation includes an element of self-evaluation. He writes that we should avoid doing harm because we would experience less suffering with a self-image that doesn’t involve doing harm. That goes back to the idea of actualizing an improved self rather than freeing one’s mind from the attachments involved in harm, like spite and obsession. The excerpt comes out of the Kalama Sutta where the Buddha is describing something akin to Pascal’s Wager, except that if there is no afterlife, you can still reduce suffering and have peace in this life. That’s not the same as feeling better about yourself.
Introduction
“I’ve been through riots, arsons, and blackouts, stood witness to the birth screams of punk and the slow death-by-greed of once-vibrant neighborhoods, run from the batons wielded by thugs operating under the guise of law and order, and mourned legions of beautiful artists, writers, and musicians lost to a disease that the most powerful man on earth couldn’t be bothered to speak about.”
I really thought he was talking about COVID until I remembered this book just referenced November 2016, so he’s actually referring to Ronald Reagan’s record of ignoring AIDS as a public health crisis. Make of that what you will.
Korda then describes experiencing 9/11 in New York and losing a firefighter friend he met in AA when the second tower collapsed. In the subsequent existential crisis, he notes:
“I had to face the fact that I, just like everyone else, was falling through time toward my inevitable death with absolutely nothing to cling to…” And what the fuck was I doing with my life… The truth is the lure of a solid paycheck, dangled before the financially struggling, is powerful. The truth is I sold out.
“And what did the twelve-step programs have to offer? They work for a lot of people, but all I got were patronizing pats on the head offered by smug true believers who, armed with quotes from the AA Big Book, dutifully insisted that my clinical depression was repayment for my atheism and lack of effort.”
I might be more skeptical about the negativity in this account if it weren’t for having seen the open disapproval of non-theistic beliefs myself. I’ve met really swell people who believe in AA but have never pushed their beliefs on me, so I don’t think it’s fair to assume that this is all AA has to offer, but that’s how it goes when we have a decentralized autonomous meetings. There will be immense variation between groups, and the East Coast has lots of traditions that the West Coast doesn’t.
