wiki/junkies.title: Junkies
wiki/junkies.content:
Overview
“Junkie” is a derogatory slang term that refers to people with substance use disorders, typically in relation to narcotic substances that were historically called “junk.”
Historical Context
In 1923, Nels Anderson published The Hobo: The Sociology of the Homeless Man in which he writes:
“The Hop Head is an interesting type. He is usually in a pitiful condition, for he has small chance, living as he does, in the tramp class, to get money to buy ‘dope.’ Frequently he resorts to clever and even desperate means to secure it. One type of dope fiend is the Junkie. He uses a ‘gun’ or needle to inject morphine or heroin. A Sniffer is one who sniffs cocaine.”
This is one of the earliest appearances of the word “junkie” in reference to substance use. It entered the mainstream public lexicon through William S. Burroughs’ semi-autobiographical novel Junky in 1953. As time went on, it became a suffix that generally refers to hardcore enthusiasts, like “news junkie” in reference to people who are always keeping up with headlines or “adrenaline junkie” in reference to people who are risk-seekers and court thrilling adventures.

wiki/junky-by-william-s-burroughs-1953.title: Junky by William S. Burroughs (1953)
wiki/junky-by-william-s-burroughs-1953.content: “The question is frequently asked: Why does a man become a drug addict? The answer is that he usually does not intend to become an addict. You don’t wake up one morning and decide to be a drug addict. It takes at least three months’ shooting twice a day to get any habit at all. And you don’t really know what junk sickness is until you have had several habits. It took me almost six months to get my first habit, and then the withdrawal symptoms were mild. I think it no exaggeration to say it takes about a year and several hundred injections to make an addict.”

wiki/juridical-image.title: Juridical Image
wiki/juridical-image.content:
Overview
In legal philosophy, particularly in the works of Hanna Pickard, “juridical image” can refer to the model of human behavior that a legal system uses in evaluating actions and interpreting laws.
The common traditional juridical image found in most legal systems assumes that an individual is a discrete autonomous unit who makes calculated decisions, such that breaking the law is seen as a choice made of complete free will that merits punishment and blame through the assignment of the label “guilty.” There is some room allotted for those who are considered “insane” and incapable of rational decision-making, but the system still leans on binaries: either you can make rational decisions or you can’t, and either you’re innocent or you’re guilty.
However, modern findings out of research communities significantly complicates these ideas. The biopsychosocial models found in medical settings introduces a wide variety of mechanisms through which someone’s holistic well-being and behaviors can be addressed rather than punitive incarceration or fines that can actually worsen someone’s condition while increasing the chance of reoffending. The introduction of diversion programs has gone a long way to offering treatment through rehabilitation programs rather than jail or prison time, which are often environments in which exposure to drug use is still possible, if not common. Rather than focusing on the extent to which an individual should suffer consequences for their actions by interrogating their rationality and character, public health research is focused on the actual outcomes of interventions that might improve public safety while helping offenders avoid further marginalization.
In other contexts, “juridical image” can also refer to the literal visual imagery surrounding the legal system, including the symbols associated with “criminality.” For instance, emphasizing symbols of policing or courtrooms when discussing addiction encourages people to see addicts as criminals rather than those suffering from an unmanaged, untreated health condition. Changing these images is a step towards reducing the stigma around seeking help for addiction, since people might be deterred from admitting they have a problem if they’re going to be associated with criminality or antisocial personalities.

wiki/just-for-today.title: Just for Today is Religious, and That's Okay
wiki/just-for-today.content:
Just For Today
Just for Today describes itself as a daily meditation book that’s derived from the literature and practices of Narcotics Anonymous, which is derived from Alcoholics Anonymous, which is derived from the Oxford Group, which is derived from Higher Life Theology in English Protestant tent revivalist movements. I argue AA is religious, not just spiritual, and you can find a discussion about that here. And that’s okay.
I’ve said numerous times before that religion is absolutely a valid part of an individual and community’s recovery capital, and there are undoubtedly people who would not have noticed any changes to their sobriety or mental health or quality of life without AA. I have no intentions of talking someone out of a religion or into one. I just think we need to be honest when things are religious so we don’t blame people when they don’t fit into a religious solution that’s presumed to be universal. After all, the AA/NA 12 Step programs recite literature every meeting that says those who don’t stay sober through the program are “constitutionally incapable” of having the prerequisite virtues to do so. If I am ever forceful or critical in my tone, it is solely because I think a claim that strong has to be met with a strong repudiation. It’s one of the reasons I’m extremely critical of The Four Agreements as well, so there’s nothing about AA or Christianity in particular which gives me an axe to grind.
Actually, I’m a big fan of Jesus, especially on the evils of hoarding wealth and marginalizing the outcasts who are already suffering. I have no doubt that Jesus wanted us to embrace homeless addicts alongside lepers and prostitutes. Benjamin Rush, one of the earliest doctors to propose a disease model, wrote that a good Christian would not take those afflicted with chronic drunkenness differently than other sinners who were sick and lost. I’m also a big fan of Reinhold Niebuhr, who wrote the Serenity Prayer and believed strongly in collective justice to improve our lives. Hindu belief systems tend to err on the side of syncretic coexistence with other systems so that it’s very easy to take what works and leave what doesn’t while respecting people for their choices.
So in no way do I think Just For Today is bad or unhelpful. I just think it’s religious, and that’s okay. One of the easiest ways to illustrate this point is by looking at how often the daily meditation ends up being about a personal Higher Power who must be loving, caring, and powerful enough to be the cause of all things from an independent higher reality we strive to make conscious contact with. If we take the suggestion that the Higher Power can really be anything of your choice, then let’s see what happens when we directly substitute a few of those into the text. I’m incrementally working through this book, but in the process, I’ll try substituting a doorknob, the abstract concept of love, an impersonal God who doesn’t intervene in daily life after setting the universe in motion, and Satan. None of those describe my own beliefs to be clear, but they cover the kinds of alternatives people might propose.
January 1
We have a daily reprieve from our addiction as long as we remain vigilant. Each day, we carry the principles of recovery into all we do, and each night, we thank our Higher Power for another day clean.
If we look at the origins of the term “daily reprieve” in the Big Book, we see:
What we really have is a daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition. Every day is a day when we must carry the vision of God’s will into all of our activities.
By definition, a “reprieve” is the act of delaying a punishment, such as a government offering a reprieve in a death penalty case so that it may be considered further. A “daily reprieve” thus means having a daily delay in your punishment. This is a morally loaded proposition obviously. Not everyone’s belief system begins with the idea that a disease, disability, or disorder is punishment. It’s possible to be born with an addiction or develop one as a child because of an adult supplying substances. Nearly half the people diagnosed with a substance use disorder also have another mental disorder which might prompt us to ask how much of the compulsive use is about self-medication.
Consider PTSD. It might be normal, if not always healthy, for an individual to suspect that they specifically suffered from PTSD because of a situation they provoked from the universe like karma or God’s punishment for sin. It would be quite strange though if our baseline protocol for handling PTSD involved telling people who were in a car crash or experienced a gruesome combat injury that they need to pray to a Higher Power everyday to have their punishment of a flashback delayed. We might want to consider that your health is in part a function of your environment, that you don’t have infinite capacity to change your environment, that you don’t even have infinite capacity to change your mind/body/soul or however you model human existence, and so adding a moral component encourages blaming the individual rather than evaluating systems-based and evidence-backed solutions. If an individual would like to view their life’s events through the lens of moral consequences, that’s perfectly fine. General recovery advice probably shouldn’t enter the thicket of morality if we want to be inclusive.
But say we accept the moralization of health issues and want addicts to think in terms of a daily reprieve. How do you thank a doorknob for giving you another day of sobriety? How do you pray to the abstract concept of love, is that like praying to Cupid to be struck by love whenever depressive episodes worsen? How do you ask for a daily reprieve from an impersonal God that doesn’t intervene in daily life? What is the vision of the will of an entity that has no will for intervention? We could charitably say that the form matters rather than the substance here. The act of imagining a Higher Power might be enough to reap the benefits of feeling connected to a bigger picture or having a supportive relationship. Evidence certainly suggests a correlation between believing in a Higher Power and reduced symptoms of anxiety and depression. As we’ll see though, the Higher Power or God you’re asked to pick has very restrictive constraints that will rule out many ideas about spirituality and religion.
January 2
“Take a deep breath and talk to God
“Sometimes when we pray, a remarkable thing happens: We find the means, ways, and energies to perform tasks far beyond our capacities.”
Each time life presents us with another little setback to our daily plans, we can simply take a deep breath and talk to the God of our understanding. Knowing we can draw patience, tolerance, or whatever we need from that Power, we find ourselves coping better and smiling more often.
Just for today: I will take a deep breath and talk to my God whenever I feel frustrated.
This one is even more difficult to imagine doing with a doorknob, an abstract concept, or an impersonal God. You can’t talk to any of those with an expectation that anything in your life will change without entering the world of magical thinking or spiritual bypassing. The doorknob is not going to give you the Power to surpass your finite bandwidth to make decisions in your life. It only makes sense to ask for “means, ways, and energies to perform tasks far beyond our capacities” if you’re implying that God will respond by granting you Power you don’t currently have.
You could refer to Satan as a loving and caring Father, but I’m going to guess 99% of you reading this are feeling a little uncomfortable at that idea, especially if you’ve come to describe alcohol (cunning, baffling, and powerful) as a temptation of the Devil. Carl Jung certainly used that framing, and I’ve lifted that comparison myself. I would think someone who mentioned Satan as their Higher Power in a church might be ruffling feathers substantially, and AA is clear that the group sustains the individuals so the group comes first. I wouldn’t say I’m happy if a Satanist was asked to leave, but I can see the logic. Anecdotally, those in recovery I’ve met with Satanic tattoos, however ironic, are often ostracized by others even if they’re willing to work the rest of the program. I would think it’s a good practical decision for there to be a different 12 Step formulation for someone who considers themselves a Satanist, although many Satanists might argue that the entire premise of their beliefs is a rejection of the hierarchy formed by a Higher Power of an independent higher reality.
January 3
“We eventually redefine our beliefs and understanding to the point where we see that our greatest need is for knowledge of God’s will for us and the strength to carry that out.”
In our God’s will we find freedom from self-will.
I will seek the fulfillment of my greatest need: a vital, guiding connection with the God of my understanding.
This seems like a very particular philosophical and theological position on free will in relation to God. But the doorknob has no will for you. An impersonal God might have a will for you if we accept that God set a universe in motion knowing what would happen after as time goes on, but that still doesn’t mean you’re going to establish anything like a “guiding connection” that would create instructions you need to carry out.
It also might just not be your greatest need. It is possible to be spiritually or religiously fulfilled but lack one of the many, many other factors that go into recovery capital. A devout Christian who spends hours meditating on God’s glory and grace might still be homeless and struggle to get medication and make appointments consistently. Giving that person safe and stable housing would substantially improve their lives and even their ability to pray in the way they so choose. Giving that person a copy of Just For Today or The Big Book, probably less so. They might read the whole book thinking “I’ve done all this, but when do I get off the streets and into a doctor’s office as a result of living according to these spiritual principles?” Unfortunately, there’s no obvious path to convert spiritual conviction into other forms of recovery capital.
January 4
In the company of other addicts, we knew we would not be rejected.
As organizations affiliated with the program say:
AA groups are spiritual entities made up of alcoholics who gather for the sole purpose of staying sober and helping other alcoholics to achieve sobriety. Yet, we are not immune to the difficulties that affect the rest of humanity. Alcoholics Anonymous is a microcosm of the larger society within which we exist. Problems found in the outside world can also make their way into the rooms of AA.
ct-aa.org/safety-in-aa
January 5
I actually like this one as is. It’s just about how internal change is not necessarily obvious to those who have seen you in active addiction for prolonged periods of time. It may take time for them to see you’ve been able to address the disease head-on and that you have plans in case of a relapse so that the spirals of the past are far less likely to happen. I would just add that some relationships will never come back with the same trust and intimacy, and it’s good to be prepared for that scenario so that you don’t put all your sobriety’s eggs in a single basket. The concept of living amends is a powerful one that can keep you feeling connected to someone you can’t make actual amends with anymore. What would they imagine you would be doing if you really changed?
It’s also possible you realize burning some bridges was among the best things to ever happen to you. We are incredibly susceptible to the influence of those around us, so much so that some studies suggest individual characteristics are a poor predictor of sustained abstinence compared to the overall recovery capital in the community that individual is in, or even the presence of a couple highly supportive relationships. We tend not to take the bold risk of leaving a social network or relationship to be single free-floating atoms because humans are social creatures. Isolation and exile are strongly associated with death or at least a high likelihood of harm. At the same time, we may not realize how toxic and limiting certain communities or networks can be to our overall health and potential. This doesn’t mean you won’t mourn or grieve for what should’ve, could’ve, would’ve been. It just means the grass can be greener on the other side, especially if you go at it with intention, awareness, skills, and capital that you didn’t have before. You can redefine yourself in a way that makes you comfortable in your skin and find others who like that version of you. It sucks, but it’s also a harsh truth that people sometimes act like crabs in a bucket if someone makes attempts to improve their life.
One of the greatest credits I can give to the Higher Power 12-step methods is that they do provide a real avenue out of those buckets and into other buckets that think about higher principles and fundamental values.
January 6
They no longer ask “why”; they ask “how.” The value of endless speculation pales in comparison to the experience of addicts who’ve found a way to stay clean and live clean.
This one is more subtle, and I’m going to use it to address an underlying theme that occurs outside of this section, so pardon the length.
St. Augustine wrote crede ut intelligas which translates roughly to “believe to understand,” and Anselm of Canterbury wrote fides quaerens intellectum which maps to “faith seeking understanding.” They argued you first had to take a leap of faith in God in order to engage in reason, because otherwise the faculties of reason would be disordered by sin. There are some very lengthy and engaging arguments to this conclusion that I think are absolutely worth reading and discussing, but my main point is that the process of trusting something works on the basis of another’s testimony to a spiritual awakening without knowing how it works has the residue of a particular faith-based epistemology. It’s not even irrational; it makes a lot of sense that you have to first achieve sanity before you can apply sane reasoning to your life, and if a group of people are telling you that they understood the process after taking that step, it makes a lot of sense to follow them on that path. Someone suffering from a disorder that produces delusions might need medication before they can understand they need medication.
But remember that AA asks you to carry its principles in your daily affairs, so you might hear “trust the process” outside of the context of an AA meeting very often in the recovery space. I personally believe in “trust but verify.” Trust that something is worth trying if it has positive testimony, and verify that the outcomes match the personal criteria for success. I can trust that a new medication prescribed by a professional might help reduce symptoms of a health condition. I can verify it does by taking it, and if it doesn’t, I can return to the professional and we can iterate further. I have trusted that trying the Steps would be a worthwhile endeavor. I verified that the concepts of Powerlessness, surrender, higher independent reality, moralistic etiology, and spiritual awakening aren’t components of my specific religious and spiritual philosophy and practices. They absolutely can work for you though.
That’s partly why some groups like Recovery Dharma embrace the spirit of inquiry:
From the Recovery Dharma text: The Buddha did not ask us to believe his teachings on faith alone. He encouraged us to investigate them through our own experience and We encourage everyone to take what is useful and leave the rest.
From the Kalama Sutta: Do not go by reports, by legends, by traditions, by scripture, by logical conjecture, by inference, by analogies, by agreement through pondering views, by probability, or by the thought, ‘This contemplative is our teacher.
This is decidedly not the tone or approach taken in AA/NA and the accompanying literature. It’s radical in the opposite direction: verify everything through your own inquiry. Lean on your own understanding. It’s even more radical than SMART Recovery, which puts considerable trust in medical and scientific institutions to generate the evidence-backed approaches and thereby has narrower methods within which to contest a finding (and there are plenty of criticisms of “evidence-backed” as a marketing term from researchers inside the field criticizing other researchers; I’ll cover that controversy on another page).
None of these mean that you should refrain from acting until you’ve understood the ideas completely, but it does mean that you shouldn’t wait to ask questions and test ideas. Inquire while you practice. Never stop asking “why”, “how”, and “why” again.
January 7
Many of us suffered severely from physical, sexual, and emotional abuse. Getting high and staying high seemed like the only possible way to cope with such abuse. Others suffered in less noticeable but equally painful ways before addiction took hold. We lacked direction and purpose. We were spiritually empty. We felt isolated, unable to empathize with others. We had none of the things that give life its sense and value.
And we’ve been given the gift of conscious contact with a Power greater than ourselves, providing us with the inner strength and direction we so sorely lacked in the past.
I find it a little concerning that we would attach moral and spiritual qualities onto an archetype of a victim of abuse. We emphasize using “I-statements” in meetings so much that saying something like this in one would probably warrant a chairperson or facilitator cutting you off.
If you’ve been through any trauma, you might feel isolated, detached, and stuck afterwards. If you’ve been through an extended period of trauma or even a lifetime of it, you might really feel those things and more. But “unable to empathize with others… had none of the things that give life its sense and value?” That seems harsh. In my experience, those who have trauma from abuse are more likely to be hypervigilant about how others feel. Those who have been in long-term abusive dynamics can easily end up in more people-pleasing or co-dependent dynamics where their empathy and desire for conflict resolution are taken advantage of. They are often very grateful for small acts of kindness and comfort.
Someone in active addiction can certainly lose access to their empathy and prioritize substance use over other things (that’s definitionally what “substance use disorder” means, the brain thinks a substance is as critical for survival as water in a desert), but I would not go as far as to generalize that to all who have been abused even outside of active addiction. It almost sounds a bit like we worked backwards from the assumption that the reader is Godless/Powerless, so they must necessarily have a weakened will and lack a purposeful direction in life as a result of past trauma. It’s possible to feel a strong sense of purpose and the resilience to process trauma consciously while struggling with all the other biopsychosocial dimensions of your body, mind, and soul.
January 8
Our best measure of growth is our spiritual condition, the basis of our recovery. If we’re still depending on people, places, and things to provide our inner satisfaction, like a child depending on its parents for everything, we do indeed have some growing to do. But if we stand secure on the foundation of our spiritual condition, considering its maintenance our most important responsibility, we can claim maturity.
If you’re promoting spirituality, that’s one thing. If you’re claiming spirituality is a priority to be measured alongside your adherence to principles that stem from a Higher Power’s care and direction and will, you’re straying into a religious perspective.
Note that lots of religions are actually very prescriptive about how you relate to “people, places, and things.” You might have sacred spaces with special significance like churches and temples. You might have obligations that relate to the community and society you’re living in. Consider death rites. In many religions, your spiritual health and passage to the afterlife or next life is contingent on having a community that does certain rituals for you after your death. The community is expected to help your family through the rituals while they go through a mourning process, or act in the place of family if you have no available relatives. It’s a really good incentive to not be an asshole leading up to your death. If you want to be of service, you necessarily need other people to serve, so you need to be in a place to serve them and have things you can serve without expecting something in return.
If you interpreted “depending on people, places, and things” to mean “I will drink unless I get to visit Disneyland this year” or “my entire life is pointless because I didn’t get that promotion so I might as well relapse,” then yes, there might be some growing to do.
Remember, the Buchmanism behind the Oxford Group that William Wilson (Bill W.) credits with the AA principles was intended to convert powerful individuals who already had access to all the material things in existence. Henry Ford might be able to agree that more people, places, and things would just yield diminishing marginal returns for his quality of life. Modern addiction researchers are pretty clear that community recovery capital has more predictive power for an individual’s sustained abstinence than individual recovery capital. You can’t meditate away serious health issues like chronic pain, depression, PTSD, or schizophrenia. Sometimes medication is literally a life-saver so you can stay stable long enough to apply spiritual or religious principles.
In other words, you absolutely need other people, places, and things to achieve security and fellowship. You’re responsible for seeking out those things to the best of your ability, but obviously there is never a guarantee that you’re going to have access to what you need. Your doorknob may not be the consistent provider of your necessities that you would prefer out of a Higher Power. That’s why we have each other.
January 9
My sponsor has cared for me when I couldn’t care for myself. Today, I will do something nice for my sponsor.
While this can certainly be true and it can be an excellent aspect of your recovery, as the recovery capital framework suggests that one or two highly supportive relationships can matter more than any particular individual trait, there are also many ways it can go wrong. This one doesn’t have much to do with religion directly, but there’s still advice that should be shared with newcomers.
Sponsors are, by design, not professionals or trained in any capacity by an institution that we can hold accountable or that publishes standard guidelines to uphold. The advice sponsors give for dealing with trauma, relationships, distress, cravings, spirituality and religion, and anything else that’s part of recovery is not professional advice (not even if they’re a Psych major). The same applies to a mentor from Recovery Dharma or Refuge Recovery, and any recovery program that’s peer and volunteer run. You can fire your sponsor or mentor if you don’t feel it’s a good match for whatever reason.
January 10
Belief in a Higher Power can make all the difference when the going gets tough! When things don’t go our way in recovery, our sponsor may direct us to make a “gratitude list.” When we do, we should include our faith in a Power greater than ourselves on the list. One of the greatest gifts we receive from the Twelve Steps is our belief in a God of our own understanding.
The Twelve Steps gently lead us toward a spiritual awakening.
The steps are our path to a relationship with a God of our understanding. This Higher Power gives us strength when our road gets rough.
Are we grateful for our deepening relationship with a Higher Power? Do we remember to thank God for each day clean, no matter what has happened that day? Do we remember that, no matter how deep our despair or how great our joy, the God of our understanding is with us?  Our recovery is a gift, a gift that we sometimes take for granted. Each day we stay clean, we can rejoice in our Higher Power’s care.  Just for today: I am grateful for my relationship with a Higher Power that cares for me.
Notice that the belief in God is actually a gift from doing the 12 Steps, not an ingredient in doing them. This is not a BYO invitation for Higher Powers. We repeatedly see that the book suggests the 12 Steps is a way to meet a Higher Power and that we must convert our Higher Power into a loving and caring one if they don’t fit the 12 Step structure.
Like, you can’t just add “of our understanding” after the word “God” like a spiritual loophole when you’re proposing a specific understanding. Doorknobs, abstract concepts, and an impersonal God do not necessarily have any kind of care for you.
January 11
“As we develop faith in our daily lives, we find that our Higher Power supplies us with the strength and guidance that we need.”  Basic Text, p. 91
The seed is planted when we ask our Higher Power for help and then acknowledge the source of our help when it comes. We nurture the tiny seed of faith with the sunlight of our prayers each day. Our faith grows, a reward for living life on its own terms. One day we realize our faith has become like a huge spreading tree; it doesn’t stop the storms of life, but we know that we are safe in its shelter. Just for today: I know that faith in my Higher Power will not calm the storms of life, but it will calm my heart. I will let my faith shelter me in times of trouble
We’re very explicitly leaning into the “faith seeking understanding” angle here. This is extremely heavy-handed about faith and “acknowledging the source of our help when it comes” as it upgrades the concept of the Higher Power to also be all-powerful, such that it governs the universe and is the source of all helpful things in your life. I shouldn’t have to mention that doorknobs and abstract concepts don’t meet this requirement. No, not even a “love holds the universe together” Hallmark movie way.
January 12
“Having had a spiritual awakening as a result of these steps…”  Step Twelve
“How will I know when I have had a spiritual awakening?” For many of us, a spiritual awakening comes gradually. Perhaps our first spiritual awareness is as simple as a new appreciation for life. Maybe one day we’ll suddenly discover the sound of birds singing early in the morning. The simple beauty of a flower may remind us that there is a Power greater than ourselves at work around us.
Often, our spiritual awakening is something that grows stronger over time. We can strive for more spiritual awareness simply by living our lives. We can persist in efforts to improve our conscious contact through prayer and meditation on a daily basis. We can listen within for the guidance we need. We can question other addicts about their experiences with spirituality. We can take time to appreciate the world around us.
Just for today: I will reflect on the spiritual awakenings I have experienced. I will strive to be God-conscious. I will take time out in the day to appreciate my Higher Power’s handiwork.
What’s cool about this part is that it actually didn’t answer the question proposed at all. The concepts of mindfulness and gratitude are in there, but you can experience those without a spiritual awakening or being “God-conscious.” This isn’t a new problem either. Buchman’s idea of conscious contact with God would involve things like claiming God told him he could only pay a certain amount for a particular service. He would adjust the instructions others had written during their attempts to pray for conscious contact with God.
Also, “handiwork” indicates that this Higher Power might be synonymous with Creator or Maker.
January 13

wiki/justice-involved-individual.title: Justice-Involved Individual (JII)
wiki/justice-involved-individual.content:
Overview
The term “justice-involved individual” (JII) became widespread across state agencies and healthcare fields as a replacement for “convict”, “criminal”, “felon” or “prisoner” which have negative connotations that imply some level of guilt or wrongdoing. There were earlier attempts to shift the language into person-first and system-focused terms like “person with a criminal record” or “formerly incarcerated person,” but professionals settled on JII as means to discuss anyone who has interacted with any part of the legal justice system without assigning guilt or stereotypes.
As with all updates to language, there are criticisms. Some argue that it’s a politically correct term that only makes those discussing the term feel better while doing little to change material reality, though studies have shown that even trained professionals become more susceptible to projecting biases and stereotypes when the “politically incorrect” terms are used. It’s the same reason “substance use disorder” has been prioritized over “substance abuse,” since the connotation of being abusive impacts how punitive medical professionals feel towards patients. Others argue that “justice-involved” is still too loaded with implications, as it implies that they’re facing justice rather than dealing with the coercion of an unjust system. You can’t make everyone happy, but it’s really not difficult to read the room and figure out which term works to communicate your point.

wiki/kahlert-institute-for-addiction-med.title: Kahlert Institute for Addiction Medicine
wiki/kahlert-institute-for-addiction-med.content:
Overview
The Kahlert Institute for Addiction Medicine at the University of Maryland was founded in 2023. Their programs include:


Maryland Addiction Consultation Service (MACS): providestraining and technical assistance (TTA) to healthcare teams and pharmacists across the state to manage Substance Use Disorders (SUDs) and chronic pain


Research Initiative in Infectious Disease and Substance Use (RIIS): provides care and conducts research into infectious diseases and substance use among disadvantaged and underserved populations


Medication-Assisted Treatment (MAT): provides buprenorphine and methadone as harm-reduction methods for Opioid Use Disorder (OUD)


Peer counselors: provides support for relapse prevention and treatment retention


Community Advisory Board (CAB): convenes individuals experiencing or recovering from SUD, their family members, and local harm-reduction advocates to address barriers to care like stigma


Comorbidity Research: examining the co-occurrence of SUD with other disorders, like anxiety and depression


Members

Marco Venniro, Associate Director

Links

kahlertinstitute.umaryland.edu/

wiki/katzenbach-commission.title: The Katzenbach Commission (President's Commission on Law Enforcement and Administration of Justice)
wiki/katzenbach-commission.content:
Overview
The Katzenbach Commission, formally called the President’s Commission on Law Enforcement and Administration of Justice, was a group of 19 people appointed by U.S. President Lyndon B. Johnson in 1965 to study the criminal justice system in response to soaring crime rates through the 1960s. They delivered the National Crime Survey, later called the National Criminal Victimization Survey.
In 1967, they released a report “The Challenge of Crime in a Free Society,” that showed some empirical data suggesting that victimization far outpaced statistics provided by the police. That suggested people were reluctant to report crimes, much of which was driven by the conditions of poverty and youth disillusionment about institutions managing the future, and that the justice system was too fragmented and obsolete to earn people’s trust. They made 200 recommendations, many of which were adopted and shaped the fundamentals of policing:


9-1-1: the creation of a single national emergency number to streamline police dispatch


Centralizing crime data: standardizing the FBI’s Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) system


Community policing: law enforcement needed to walk in communities and build relations, as well as share the diversity of the neighborhoods they police


Professionalization: mandatory minimum training hours, psychological screenings for officers, and hiring more candidates with college degrees


Federal funding: providing the case for the creation of the Law Enforcement Assistance Administration (LEAA) which gave billions of dollars in training and technical assistance (TTA) until 1982 when its structure was absorbed into the Office of Justice Programs (OJP)


Chapter 8 of their report is dedicated to Narcotics and Drug Abuse. It notably includes a separation of marijuana from heroin in terms of the scientific knowledge available then about the dangers of weed and concerns about harsh criminal sentences for it. That aside, it advocates for viewing addiction as a medical and public health issue rather than a moral failing or the result of a criminal personality, as well as the concept of civil commitment which allows individuals with addiction to be placed in regulated rehabilitation facilities rather than standard criminal justice facilities like state prisons. There’s also an argument about mandatory minimum sentencing being counterproductive and recommended that judges have flexibility in sentencing those with a disease from those who participate in trafficking. As for addressing the root cause of drug issues, the commission pointed at organized crime as the primary engine behind the drug trade and recommended that law enforcement renew their focus on high-level networks rather than low-level users. A problem underlying all of these other issues is that the federal government has lacked data on substance use patterns and the effectiveness of rehab programs, which makes data-driven policymaking difficult.

wiki/kava.title: Kava
wiki/kava.content:
Overview
Kava is a beverage made from the root of the Piper methysticum plant and has traditionally been used in rituals and social gatherings across Polynesia, Micronesia, and Melanesia in the South Pacific. It’s also sold as tea, extracts, and supplemental powders globally. Kava contains kavalactones, which are found in the resin of kava roots and are responsible for its psychoactive effects by serving as central nervous system depressants.
The immediate effects of kava include:


Anxiolysis, or a reduction in anxiety through feelings of relaxation and calm


Mild euphoria


Mental clarity in low-to-moderate doses


Sedation in higher doses or specific strains that make it easier to fall asleep


Oral numbness since kavain, one of the kavalactones, serves as a local anesthetic


Muscle relaxation


Analgesia, or pain relief, particularly in the case of stress-induced headaches or body aches


Motor impairment, usually at very high doses that can cause issues with balance and delay reflexes


Long-term effects include:


Dermopathy, or irritated skin that starts on the palms, soles, or back and becomes dry, scaly, itchy, or yellowed


Gastrointestinal distress, such as nausea, indigestion, or upset stomach, though this can vary by the quality of kava


Lethargy as a persistent fatigue or brain fog that lasts after consumption stops


Hepatotoxicity, or liver toxicity that results because kava binds to enzymes that the liver also would use to filter alcohol, sedatives, and certain medications


Kava is not considered chemically addictive in the same way that substances like alcohol or heroin are, but the risk of liver injury is still noteworthy and doesn’t mean it’s a “safe substance.” Many people who have a history of substance use disorders may attempt to use kava as a safer alternative to drinking alcohol or using other substances, but this can compound stress that the liver might already be under from past substance use. Heavy alcohol use is especially damaging to the liver, and while the liver can heal and recover substantially, kava might interfere with that or come with an increased risk of hepatotoxicity.
Interestingly though, kava actually induces a reverse tolerance effect where the substance becomes more effective over time and requires smaller doses to get the same effect. Researchers are still exploring why, but some theories include kavalactones accumulating in fat instead of clearing the body instantly, GABA receptors increasing rather than decreasing as they do for the sedative effects of alcohol, and liver adaptation that optimizes the way enzymes metabolize kavalactones.

wiki/keith-humphreys.title: Keith Humphreys
wiki/keith-humphreys.content:
Humphreys was a psychologist and senior policy advisor for the Obama administration.
Links

www.npr.org/2017/10/26/560083795/president-trump-may-declare-opioid-epidemic-national-emergency

“Dr. Keith Humphreys, a professor of psychiatry at Stanford University and a former adviser in the Obama administration, calls the Trump administration’s response ‘pathetic,’ saying it mostly repurposes long-existing public health programs. Humphreys notes that aside from the emergency declaration, there is little that was recommended by the White House commission in the president’s plan.”
“This week, a group of Democratic senators introduced a bill that would provide more than $45 billion for opioid abuse prevention, surveillance, and treatment… Humphreys, a former official in the Office of National Drug Control Policy, says that if the president is serious about opioids, he should endorse that bill.”

wiki/ketamine.title: Ketamine
wiki/ketamine.content:
Overview
Ketamine is a dissociative anesthetic used for surgical procedures, treatment-resistant depression, and chronic pain. As an NMDA receptor antagonist, it blocks glutamate, the primary excitatory neurotransmitter in the brain. With depression, this leads to the brain creating new pathways extremely quickly that can guide someone out of negative loops in their thoughts and feelings. It’s also used recreationally, with high doses inducing a state that’s colloquially referred to as a “K-hole” in which someone experiences severe dissociation that temporarily immobilizes them.
Long-term complications of Ketamine include:


Cystitis. When ketamine is broken down and filtered into the urine, its byproducts burn the bladder lining and replaces healthy tissue with thick scar tissue. This fibrosis leads to the bladder’s capacity shrinking as far down as the size of a marble, which can cause pain, bleeding, and frequent urination. In extreme cases, this can cause a backup into the kidneys that causes renal failure.


Cramps. While the exact cause isn’t yet established, researchers are exploring toxicity in the bile ducts and gastrointestinal spasms after taking ketamine.


Cognitive decline. Although we noted above that ketamine can help open up new pathways for treatment-resistant depression, it can also impair short-term memory and executive functioning. It’s also been tied to persistent episodes of depersonalization, paranoia, and psychosis.


The brain is able to build tolerance to ketamine quickly, so while overdoses from ketamine are rare, a high quantity mixed with other depressants can be fatal. For instance, ketamine and alcohol have a compounding effect that can trigger fatal respiratory depression, so someone can simply stop breathing while dissociated or sedated from the mix. When ketamine is mixed with stimulants like cocaine, which someone might try as a means of offsetting the sedation of ketamine, the combination places high strain on the cardiovascular system which leads to elevated heart rates and blood pressure.

wiki/kleptomania.title: Kleptomania
wiki/kleptomania.content:
Overview
Kleptomania is a mental health disorder ni which someone has a recurring urge to steal items without personal gain as a motivator.
While it’s often considered a behavioral addiction along the lines of gambling or sex addictions, the DSM-5-TR technically categorizes it as an impulse-control disorder. The underlying mechanisms for kleptomania are almost all shared with other addictions. Much like gambling leads to a spike in dopamine in the tense anticipation of an outcome that engages the brain’s attention, stealing can also trigger the same spikes due to the tension leading up to the theft and gratification while doing it. The item itself is not the source of the brain’s recognition of reward, the same way that addictive gambling is about the act rather than the money gained. At a neurobiological level, the endogenous opioid system in the brain, which regulates urges and self-control, is thought to suffer from imbalances that make it difficult to resist the temptation to steal. Naltrexone, an opioid antagonist that is used to curb cravings for alcohol and opioid addiction, is also effective at curbing the urges to steal found in kleptomania.
It’s common for people suffering from kleptomania to return or otherwise get rid of the items they stole out of guilt and shame. You may have heard a story, online or from a friend talking about a friend of a friend, about someone going to a party and stealing family photo albums because they’re not replaceable even if they’re financially worthless. That’s the stereotype of an unapologetic kleptomaniac, but it shouldn’t be extrapolated to people who have the disorder in general.
Commentary
I’ve heard some people complain that Marie’s kleptomania arc in Breaking Bad was unnecessary or pointless aside from expanding the world beyond the White household a bit. I actually love it. Not every instance of pathologized compulsion leads to death or cinematic consequences. Sometimes it just interferes with your life and relationship in ways that are still distressing and worthy of addressing with medical help.

wiki/know-your-rights-fact-sheet.title: Know Your Rights Fact Sheet by SAMHSA
wiki/know-your-rights-fact-sheet.content:
Overview
I’ve said a few times that I wished there was something like a pamphlet you got when you entered a treatment center that starts with “Welcome to Addiction! Addiction is a disability, and that means you have rights and programs you can explore dedicated to people with disabilities.” Surely something so critical must have been distilled into an accessible format by now in this world of millions of mental health professionals, paraprofessionals, advocates, activists, and peer support groups.
Apparently, it does exist! The Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) has a neat 4-page pamphlet on their website you can look at that does exactly that with ways to find out more depending on what you need. I’m kind of shocked that this isn’t a standard resource we distribute to people on entry to any program that relates to or can diagnose someone with a disability. It’s almost a Catch-22: under 42 USC Ch. 114 10841 K, you have the “right to be told about your rights described in this document clearly when you first arrive and from time to time after that, in words you can easily understand. This includes knowing your rights according to the laws of your state.” But to know about the right to be told about your rights, you have to know you have that right. Under M, you have the “right to talk privately with any available rights protection program in the setting you are in, to the rights protection service within the state mental health system, and to groups created to protect people with mental health conditions, along with qualified advocates.”
Links

library.samhsa.gov/sites/default/files/know-your-rights-pep24-08-002.pdf

wiki/kombucha.title: Kombucha
wiki/kombucha.content:
Overview
Kombucha is a fermented beverage produced by a Symbiotic Culture of Bacteria and Yeast (SCOBY) that’s added to sweetened teas. Yeast breaks down the sugars into ethanol, and then bacteria consumes that to produce organic acids that are responsible for fizzy, vinegary flavors. In theory, though kombucha will contain trace amounts of alcohol, the concentration in commercially sold kombucha leads it to being nonalcoholic. However, kombucha that isn’t refrigerated can continue to ferment and raise the alcohol content, so it’s a good idea to skip the drink altogether if avoiding alcohol is an important concern of yours. This is especially true for kombucha that’s been made at home without industrial equipment to monitor the concentration of alcohol or maintain the proper temperature storage conditions.

wiki/kraepelinian.title: Kraepelinian
wiki/kraepelinian.content:
Overview
To describe an approach as “Kraepelinian” is to mean that it views mental illnesses as distinct biologically-driven neurological conditions that can be identified through their progression rather than just the current presentation of symptoms. This is in contrast to Freudian psychoanalysis, which located the source of symptoms within someone’s fluid, subconscious emotional conflicts that could not be standardized in manuals or diagnostic guidelines.
History and Context
In the 1960s, Freudian psychoanalysis of the subconscious was the dominant form of psychiatry, but this psychodynamic perspective made it incredibly difficult to produce reliable diagnoses. Different doctors could examine a patient and arrive at entirely different theories about the emotional conflicts responsible for a set of symptoms.
In 1972, the Cross-National Project for the Study of the Diagnosis of Mental Disorders in the United States and the United Kingdom (or the US-UK Diagnostic Project for short) initiative was conducted to compare the diagnostic processes between American and British psychiatrists. A group of each watched the same videotaped clinical interviews and were asked to provide diagnoses independently. The psychiatrists from New York were more than twice as likely to diagnose patients with schizophrenia than their London counterparts, whereas the London doctors diagnoses depressive psychoses or mania twice as often as the New York doctors. This dealt a blow to the legitimacy of psychiatry as a field by highlighting the subjective and arbitrary elements of clinical evaluations under a psychodynamic framework, as it was inferred that American psychiatrists used “schizophrenia” as a catch-all bucket for significant psychological distress that couldn’t be cleanly identified as anything else.
Insurance companies and government healthcare programs like Medicaid and Medicare were not pleased that they were being asked to pay for open-ended talk therapy that targeted fluid subconscious conflicts that were lumped into “schizophrenia.” The rapid breakthroughs in the psychiatric drugs, which were designed to address biological or physiological mechanisms, required more clarity in a patient’s disorder to be properly prescribed. Otherwise, patients with bipolar disorders were being labeled as schizophrenic and being prescribed antipsychotics that were ineffective rather than lithium.
The confluence of these circumstances led to a revival of Kraepelinian ideas about building a taxonomy of disorders as discrete entities with unique progressions and biological mechanisms to replace the notion of fluid subconscious conflicts. In the same year that the US-UK project published its findings, a team of psychiatrists include Eli Robins, Samuel Guze, Robert Woodruff Jr., George Winokur, Rodrigo Munoz, and John Feighner published a paper called “Diagnostic Criteria for Use in Psychiatric Research”, which contained operationalized criteria for 14 psychiatric disorders. These are referred to as the Feigher Criteria after the lead author of the paper, and it served as a major influence for the DSM-III and the ICD-9. Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (CBT) arose alongside this pivot to addressing observable symptoms from current, conscious thoughts and behaviors rather than digging into underlying trauma and personality constructs, which insurance companies readily embraced as well for its predictable, manualized delivery and quantitative metrics to show improvements.
Let’s consider depression as an example.
In the DSM-II, we have the diagnosis “300.4 Depressive neurosis”:
This disorder is manifested by an excessive reaction of depression due to an internal conflict or to an identifiable event such as the loss of a love object or cherished possession. It is to be distinguished from Involutional melancholia (q.v.) and Manic-depressive illness (q.v.). Reactive depressions or Depressive reactions are to be classified here.
“Internal conflict” is not a readily observable phenomenon; it requires a clinician to make a qualitative assessment that a patient is suffering from an internal conflict based on what they say or do. Similarly, the clinician could subjectively or even arbitrarily determine that one of the thousands of life events a patient had was the “identifiable event” in question.
The DSM-III has a lengthy entry titled “Major Depressive Episode” that includes a section title “Diagnostic criteria for major depressive episode”:
A. Dysphoric mood or loss of interest or pleasure in all or almost all usual activities and pastimes. The dysphoric mood is characterized by symptoms such as the following: depressed, sad, blue, hopeless, low, down in the dumps, irritable. the mood disturbance must be prominent and relatively persistent, but not necessarily the most dominant symptom, and does not include momentary shifts from one dysphoric mood to another dysphoric mood, e.g., anxiety to depression to anger, such as are seen in states of acute psychotic turmoil. (For children under six, dysphoric mood may have to be inferred from a persistently said facial expression.)
This still calls on some subjective judgment of whether someone’s mood disturbance is “prominent and relatively persistent”, but a mood is more easily observed through someone’s external affect than an “internal conflict.” Plus, we have at least some quantitative guidelines laid out in the next section:
B. At least four of the following symptoms have each been present nearly every day for a period of at least two weeks (in children under six, at least three of the four).
(1) poor appetite or significant wait loss (when not dieting) or increased appetite or significant weight gain
(2) insomnia or hypersomnia
(3) psychomotor agitation or retardation (but not merely subjective feelings of restlessness or being slowed down)
(4) loss of interest or pleasure in usual activities, or decrease in sexual drive not limited to a period when delusional or hallucinating
(5) loss of energy; fatigue
(6) feelings of worthlessness, self-reproach, or excessive or inappropriate guilt (either may be delusional)
(7) complaints or evidence of diminished ability to think or concentrated, such as slowed thinking, or indecisiveness not associated with marked loosening of associations or incoherence
(8) recurrent thoughts of death, suicidal ideation, wishes to be dead, or suicide attempt
There are more stipulations to the diagnosis after this, but this should suffice to demonstrate the differences between the Kraepelinian approach that laid out consistent diagnostic criteria for distinct illnesses and the Freudian psychodynamic approach that located the sources of distress in unobservable internal conflicts.
This solved the problem of doctors arbitrarily or subjectively giving different diagnoses for the same presentation of symptoms, but it introduced a new problem around whether the diagnoses themselves are actually valid as distinct biological diseases. There are no blood tests, genetic markers, brain scans, or anomalies that can deterministically demonstrate a defined diagnosis, which has led to the criticism that ordinary distress from life becomes pathologized and assigned a diagnosis. Studies find that patients often meet multiple disorders at the same time, with Major Depressive Disorder and Generalized Anxiety Disorder being particularly common as a pairing, which brings into question whether these are truly distinct biological diseases. The threshold system also creates strange outcomes. For instance, if you must meet 5 out of 9 symptoms to be clinically diagnosed with a disorder, then two patients might have the same diagnosis while only having one symptom in common.
One of the efforts to remedy the new problems introduced by Kraepelinian frameworks is the Research Domain Criteria (RDoC) framework led by the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH). The RDoC framework focuses on brain circuits and behavioral dimensions across a continuous spectrum that builds a bottom-up picture of someone’s mental health through empirical neuroscience. In the case of an overlap between say, MDD and GAD, the RDoC framework would explore the shared neural circuity that produces the symptoms of both diagnoses, whereas the Kraepelinian framework would explore both as distinct diseases with distinct progressions.
Psychodynamic therapists haven’t become irrelevant by any means either. Instead, they argue that RDoC is simply revealing the physiological mechanisms through which the unconscious mind operates, but that mental patterns are still necessary to explore to facilitate change within a person’s lived experiences by interpreting the meaning of their inner world and perspectives. For instance, two people can both present with MDD according to the DSM’s Kraepelinian-style checklists, but if one has a personality we might describe as high in narcissistic traits while another has a personality we might describe as high in dependent traits, the delivery of any therapeutic modality will fundamentally be different to address the symptoms in each patient. In fact, there’s an entirely separate Psychodynamic Diagnostic Manual (PDM) from the DSM. Those like Jonathan Shedler are strong critics of CBT being treated as a gold standard treatment, raising the argument that patients who undergo psychodynamic therapy continue to improve after the therapy ends because they’ve made deeper changes to their personality functions while patients who undergo traditional CBT primarily learn to manage symptoms that emerge on the surface as a result of those functions.

wiki/kratom.title: Kratom
wiki/kratom.content:
Overview
Kratom refers to the Mitragyna speciosa tree or its leaves that produce psychoactive effects. It has a biphasic profile because it acts similar to a stimulant in low doses, but it acts closer to a sedative in high doses. The active alkaloids in kratom include mitragynine and 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH), which both bind to the body’s endogenous opioid receptors, but in a different way than well-known exogenous opioids like morphine or heroin, which are full agonists. Kratom alkaloids are partial agonists that don’t bind as strongly to opioid receptors.

wiki/law-and-order.title: Law and Order
wiki/law-and-order.content:
Overview
“Law and order” is not just a show that’s spanned 25 seasons across 36 years as of 2026. It’s also one of the most common political euphemisms used to discuss the brutal enforcement mechanisms behind the War on Drugs. After all, the opposite of “law and order” is “crime and chaos,” and what human being lucky enough to be born with the red, white, and blue running through their blood in the shining city on the hill would be opposed to the enforcement of the United States Constitution?
As it turns out, there’s a circular problem here, and we need to delineate three concepts to understand it: power is the ability to act to shape reality, authority is the position of dictating how power should be used, and legitimacy is the acceptance of the use of power. Someone who breaks into your house is exercising power even though the authority to decide what happens in it rests with you, and since you presumably don’t approve of the break-in, it’s not a legitimate entry into your home.
A similar principle can be applied to indigenous reservations in the United States. European colonialists exerted their power to perpetrate mass genocide and warfare against indigenous nations and created their own systems of authority on top of new societies, but indigenous nations never fully recognized those as legitimate, especially the United States federal government which has regularly broken its treaties. Still, the federal government has assigned itself the authority to ultimately dictate what happens on tribal lands; local tribal authorities are allowed to exist and make decisions with some power, but the federal government uses its own power to ultimately approve or disapprove of their structure and decision-making.
One of the inevitable problems with authority is that its power inherently shapes the information that people use to determine the legitimacy of authority. An authority of a system might declare that some material is unsuitable for publication and distribution using their power over information channels, but that material might contain criticisms of that authority figure which would call into question their legitimacy. Instead, the authoritative entity might shape the distribution of information to provide justifications their own legitimacy. Consider education. If a school board or other regulatory body decides to use textbooks that frame colonial America as a necessary progression towards spreading rational Enlightenment thinking that was being attacked by native tribes who wanted to cling onto inferior or outdated traditions, children might grow up thinking the United States is imperfect but generally aims itself towards progress that betters the world’s living conditions. This might fly in the face of other works by researchers and academics that depicts America as an imperialist nation founded on the idea of corporate freedom to seek profits which co-opts all other systems towards that end, which is closer to the narrative someone might receive if they grew up in a country that has suffered from a history of Western imperialism and occupation. At the same time, authorities in those countries seek to legitimize themselves by propagating narratives about their own nobility and progress being undermined by Western powers, which are then blamed for the flaws observed within that nation.
When it comes to drug hysteria, this intersection of power, authority, and legitimacy leads to the promotion

wiki/law-of-attraction.title: Law of Attraction
wiki/law-of-attraction.content:
Overview
The law of attraction is a spiritual or religious belief that the thoughts or attitude one has invites corresponding events; if one maintains positive thinking, then positive experiences will happen, but if one maintains negative thinking, then negative experiences will happen.
Commentary
Of all the New Age bullshit in what passes for “spirituality” in the modern world, the law of attraction is one of the biggest agitators of my nerves.
First, it’s not a real “law” in any sense of the world. It’s pseudoscience. There is no consistent body of empirical evidence that suggests that believing in your ability to manifest positive outcomes actually leads to positive outcomes.
From a 2023 paper published in Society for Personality and Social Psychology:
We explored the psychology of those who believe in manifestation: the ability to cosmically attract success in life through positive self-talk, visualization, and symbolic actions… Those who scored higher on the scale perceived themselves as more successful, had stronger aspirations for success, and believed they were more likely to achieve future success. They were also more likely to be drawn to risky investments, have experienced bankruptcy, and to believe they could achieve an unlikely level of success more quickly. We discuss the potential positives and negatives of this belief system in the context of growing public desire for success and an industry that capitalizes on these desires.
In other words, people who believe their thoughts could manifest positive outcomes certainly believed they were bound to have more positive outcomes, but in fact were more prone to suffering the consequences of greater risk-taking and loftier ambitions.
Where there is some data to back the idea of “positive thinking” or visualizing what you want to manifest can be found in the distinction between process visualization and outcome visualization. In other words, imagining that you’ll be successful as long as you have a positive attitude doesn’t help, but imagining yourself doing the actual steps required for success does seem to help, likely because you’re priming your brain for the task by retrieving relevant information and preparing a strategy to execute. That’s not the same as changing reality through a positive attitude though.
Second, it really easily lends itself to the suppression and stifling of anything that can be perceived or felt negatively. If someone has complaints about negative events or influences in their life, the law of attraction implies that this person has a negative attitude that’s responsible for their outcomes, which completely reverses the order of events in reality. People who undergo negative experiences are understandably going to have negative expectations of the world as well, or at least a negative bias relative to others who had more positive experiences. Giving them the responsibility of their own pain and suffering can often cascade into victim-blaming.

wiki/learned-helplessness.title: Learned Helplessness
wiki/learned-helplessness.content:
Overview
Learned helplessness is the concept that living entities become more passive if they believe their actions cannot influence outcomes, especially after being subjected to chronic stress or failure. One of the researchers who coined the term, Martin Seligman, popularized the concept as a primary founder of the Positive Psychology movement. As with all pop psych concepts, this has often led to it being distorted for feel-good messages.
Consider how many people readily admit to being “bad at math” and recall feeling that way from a young age after some poor early experiences with math classes. One of the biggest obstacles for instructors and educators to overcome in math education is this type of fixed mindset in which students are convinced they can’t deal with mathematical abstractions well while feeling at home in creative pursuits or the humanities. This strongly suggests that learned helplessness isn’t necessarily a general psychological disposition that impacts someone’s overall performance across subjects or tasks, but a response to feeling that the effort previously put into a pursuit rarely materializes in success. Because math is also taught in order of increasingly complex concepts that build on each other, falling behind necessitates accelerated learning later to catch up, which translates to asking for even more effort from an activity that the brain doesn’t associate with success or rewards. Eventually, students who struggle with math might learn to avoid it and try to compensate by specializing in other disciplines. Here, there’s a real utility to identifying the concept of learned helplessness and even developing metrics for tracking it. Studies show that low self-efficacy about math correlates with more hesitation on routine steps and avoidance of challenging problems.
Since the concept was first proposed in the 1960s, neuroscientists and researchers have found that passivity is generally the default psychological state rather than proactive problem-solving. Organisms are observed as having a freeze response to prolonged stress until realizing there are mechanisms to stop the stressor, after which the brain’s medial prefrontal cortex shuts down the freeze response.
Psychologically, it’s still useful to identify learned helplessness when working with depression, PTSD, and other issues associated with trauma, but the latest research shows that our emphasis on changing internal beliefs about helplessness may not be effective without realistic external solutions for someone to take. I’d argue this lines up with studies that have shown that, within Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy and its associated modalities, the component of Behavioral Activation alone appears to have the same effectiveness as an approach that uses both BA and cognitive components. In other words, we are better at changing once we identify that change is possible through repeated experiences than by challenging internal beliefs for rationality or utility, especially if we’re prone to rationalizing our decisions after we intuitively discern our incentives and desires.
Within Liberation Psychology, learned helplessness is not interpreted in terms of lacking coping skills or suffering from negative core beliefs; instead, the core issue is located in the environment and potentially oppressive structures that can be modified through collective action.
Where learned helplessness becomes used problematically is when it’s deployed as a criticism instead of an acknowledgement of someone’s psychological state after their experiences. Take the case of someone who has survived years of abuse where attempts to leave their enviroment failed, either as a result of being punished for their attempts or simply repeated disappointments. What we might call “learned helplessness” in that situation was a survival adaptation to minimize effort where it seems wasteful or worsens the situation; it often ends up being an obstacle when someone has had a change in their environment that allows their efforts to be rewarded but retains the pattern of avoidance or freezing. This is substantially different than being unwilling to put in any effort to begin with or feeling entitled to something without effort, but, especially in popular psychology material, these can be conflated.

“the acquisition of new information, behaviors, or abilities after practice, observation, or other experiences, as evidenced by change in behavior, knowledge, or brain function. Learning involves attending to relevant aspects of incoming information, organizing the information into a coherent cognitive representation, and integrating it with relevant existing knowledge from long-term memory.” 1

wiki/legal-action-center.title: Legal Action Center (LAC)
wiki/legal-action-center.content:
Overview
The Legal Action Center (LAC) is a non-profit that fights discrimination against those who involved with the criminal justice system, substance use disorders, and HIV/AIDS. They also manage the Coalition for Whole Health. Their services include direct free legal assistance, impact litigation challenging systemic discrimination, and advocacy across drug policy, patient privacy, fair hiring practices, and sealing records.

wiki/legalization.title: Legalization
wiki/legalization.content:
Overview
“Legalization” in the context of drug policies refers to a framework in which some type of substance use is not only decriminalized but also treated as a product that can be bought, sold, and used on markets or other platforms. For instance, alcohol is a legalized drug, though it does come with age restrictions and public intoxication laws. In the United States, some states have legalized marijuana so that it can be purchased and used recreationally without a medical license or prescription from a medical practitioner. Other drugs like cocaine, heroin, and fentanyl remain criminalized.
Proponents of legalization argue that people who use substances chronically are going to pursue their patterns regardless of whether it’s illegal. In fact, we can’t even reliably ensure that prisons and jails are drug-free, much less the general civilian population. This means that when drug laws are enforced, it’s highly selective at the discretion of law enforcement and political agendas rather than fairly implemented as a deterrence. Instead of treating drug use as a criminal issue, legalizing it allows substances to be sold with well-regulated quality that avoids contamination and makes it easier for public health interventions to reach the populations that need it, whether that results in harm reduction or sustained abstinence.

wiki/leon-festinger.title: Leon Festinger
wiki/leon-festinger.content:
Overview
Leon Festinger was a social psychologist most known for articulating cognitive dissonance theory and social comparison theory in modern clinical psychology.

wiki/lester-research-group.title: Lester Research Group
wiki/lester-research-group.content:
Overview
The Lester Research Group, or Lester Lab, is a neuroscience and bioengineering lab focused on addiction to nicotine. Their work includes developing wearable continuous nicotine monitors (CNMs), studying the pharmacokinetics of nicotine, researching the “inside-out” psychoneuropharmacology of the upregulation paradox, and developing neuroimaging tools that use fluorescent biosensors to light up when nicotine is present.

wiki/let-go-and-let-god.title: Let Go and Let God
wiki/let-go-and-let-god.content:
Overview
The phrase “Let go and let God” is commonly used in 12-step-based recovery groups like Alcoholics Anonymous, whose religious and spiritual foundations are rooted in the Higher Life Christianity movement tied to the Keswick Convention of the 1870s. The original meaning as invoked by Higher Life theologists meant surrendering personal will and agency so that divine will via the Holy Spirit, which would manifest as a personal moral clarity free of the impulses of the individual ego, including the idea of building endurance for active works and labor. The Oxford Group, and later, Alcoholics Anonymous, drew on this framework to address the psychological feelings of powerlessness that accompany addiction. With this perspective, an alcoholic or addict would acknowledge they are powerless over the people, places, and things around them but can achieve personal peace that leads to abstinence as a result of seeking God, or an equivalent Higher Power. When something happens outside of one’s control, rather than attempt to retain or fight for control, one ought to “let go and let God” handle it as a power outside of oneself.

wiki/lethargy.title: Lethargy
wiki/lethargy.content:
Overview
The National Cancer Institute defines “lethargy” as:
A condition marked by drowsiness and an unusual lack of energy and mental alertness. It can be caused by many things, including illness, injury, or drugs. 1
I also tend to use this definition when I speak, but it was more commonly used in the past to describes one’s state of consciousness. As the Cleveland Clinic states,
Lethargy is a symptom that involves an unusual decrease in consciousness. It’s different from just being drowsy or sleepy. Decreases in your level of consciousness can involve a change in your mental state. That means you may be confused or have trouble remembering things, too.
Lethargy comes from two Ancient Greek words: “Lethe,” meaning “forgetful,” and “argos,” meaning “idle.” As those two terms describe, someone who’s lethargic moves slowly or is difficult to rouse and has trouble thinking, concentrating or remembering. 2
As with many terms related to consciousness, we might be able to gesture at certain stages relative to others as being more lethargic, but it’s been difficult to create definitions that lead to clear standards, so it’s not found too often in modern literature as a technical term. You’re far more likely to see it used to describe the way someone feels on vacation or after a long night than in a way that intentionally refers to a clinically significant disruption in brain function.

wiki/liberation-psychology.title: Liberation Psychology
wiki/liberation-psychology.content:
Overview
Liberation psychology describes an approach to psychology that involves a critical perspective of the models and institutions of the field, namely through the way they’re rooted in the biases of middle-class American norms that emphasize individualism within capitalist and imperialist structures.
One of the more common patterns in liberation psychology is framing suffering and symptoms as normal adaptations to their conditions rather than maladaptive symptoms tied to personal traumas, which runs in strong contradiction to mainstream tenets of Western modalities. It’s common to hear in both recovery circles and mental health treatment that one only has control over one’s own actions and reactions, which is technically true, but can also have the unintended effect of absolving one of considering their role in their broader environment. For instance, it’s true that no individual can single-handedly determine the outcome of a democratic election, but it’s also true that each individual plays a role in the overall outcome, whether they abstain from voting or campaign for new converts. No single person can make or break an ecosystem, but we might still frown upon an individual who casually litters in public places. There are a variety of valid arguments to be made about the extent of this obligation one might have towards others, ranging from a basic principle to minimize harm onto others to an active mandate to protest sociopolitical injustice. Within liberation psychology frameworks, something like learned helplessness might be addressed through facilitating engagement with community structures or collective group dynamics rather than focusing solely on one’s own coping skills or capacity for emotional regulation.

wiki/libido.title: Libido
wiki/libido.content:
Overview
Libido has several meanings in different contexts, but it generally refers to one’s desires for sex. Some schools of psychology and philosophy use the word to mean the general desire or energy of life which is represented best by the example of reproductive instincts and patterns.
If we analyze libido through a biopsychosocial perspective, we can neatly delineate some of the factors that impact one’s libido:


Biological: hormones are the primary biological determinant behind one’s libido, and drugs (pharmaceutical and otherwise) can influence hormones to either increase or decrease libido


Psychological: stress, moods, and self-image play roles in libido, obviously; the human body tends to deprioritize reproductive functions when under sustained stress, although some people react to stress by using sex as an escape or dopamine distraction.


Social: the intimacy, comfort, and communication between partners, especially in long-term relationships, impacts libido as well
