wiki/liquid-chromatography-mass-spectrom.title: Liquid Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry (LC/MS)
wiki/liquid-chromatography-mass-spectrom.content:
Overview
Liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) is a technique for detecting molecules by their structure and metabolites that’s considered far more reliable than testing with immunoassays, which examine antibodies to identify general chemical families. Its sensitivity means that it can detect very small traces of a chemical in biological samples, which also means it can detect evidence of drug ingestion further back in time.
If you’ve ever heard of over-the-counter medications accidentally triggering a false positive for amphetamines or similar situations, it’s because the immunoassays react to the OTC having similar structures as the substance indicated by the false positive, even if the actual bodily responses are completely different. LC-MS separates compounds by mass with high precision through an analysis of weight and fragmentation patterns. This also gives LC-MS tests the advantage of producing data that can be revisited to scan for a new molecule whereas immunoassays require new, specific antibody tests for each new compound.
Commentary
If you test positive for a substance based on an immunoassay, you should know that these are presumptive screenings and not definitive evidence. If you’re facing any kind of consequence as the result of testing positive, you can try to contest it by having it sent to an outside lab for confirmation through LC-MS/MS or gas chromatograpy-mass spectrometry (GC-MS). For instance, some CBD products may contain trace amounts of THC that trigger false positives for immunoassays, but an LC-MS/MS or GC-MS can identify the THC as below a legal threshold. You may also have heard of cough syrup or other over-the-counter medications triggering false positive for amphetamines.

wiki/lived-experience.title: Lived Experience
wiki/lived-experience.content:
Overview
“Lived experience” is a term that’s been used a lot in online discourse in the debates about the value of evidence between statistics and personal anecdotes. Sometimes it’s used to dismiss evidence provided by statistics when they don’t match someone’s expectations of reality, but it’s also fairly used to describe the failure of statistics to offer a complete model of reality. Philosophers, particularly in phenomenology, approach lived experience with a critical examination over consciousness and interpretations of reality. For researchers in the social sciences, measuring lived experiences requires qualitative methods like constructing ethnographies.

wiki/living-amends.title: Living Amends
wiki/living-amends.content:
Overview
In 12-step recovery circles, “living amends” refers to living life with an attitude of making amends towards the world around you, especially in response to being unable to make personal amends with someone. The Oxford Group from which Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) arose laid out Four Practices: sharing, surrender, restitution, and guidance. When Bill Wilson was adapting the Oxford Group’s spiritual principles for AA, he changed “restitution” to “amends” to emphasize that much of the damage that is done in the struggles of addiction is emotional and mental rather than just loans or property damage that could be paid back. Since it’s impossible to make amends with someone who passed away or may have strict boundaries against contacting them, the idea of “living amends” allows one to work through the guilt by changing their actions and behaviors in a way that honors the amends that one would wish to make.

wiki/lobbying.title: Lobbying
wiki/lobbying.content:
Overview
Lobbying includes activities that attempt to influence policy decisions made by government officials. That can include meeting lawmakers to give a pitch, providing public testimony at hearings, drafting legislation for lawmakers to use, producing research papers and policy briefs, organizing public demonstrations, and purchasing ads to shape public discourse.
Within addiction recovery and treatment, there are many organizations with different agendas:


American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM): representing physicians and clinicians with input on legislation like Modernizing Opioid Treatment Access Act (MOTAA)


National Association of Addiction Treatment Providers (NAATP): representing substance use treatment facilities and maintaining an active Political Action Committee (PAC)


Shatterproof: a national non-profit advocating that mobilizes grassroots support for expanding community harm reduction resources, improving medical training on substance use, and structural parity on healthcare coverage


Hazelden Betty Ford Foundation: one of the oldest non-profits in the United States that provides addiction treatment, and it also lobbies for clinical research, the behavorial health workforce, and advancing treatment models.

wiki/locus-of-control.title: Locus of Control
wiki/locus-of-control.content:
Overview
The locus of control describes where someone locates the causes of the events of their life. An internal locus of control means that someone locates the results of their lives to their own agency, whereas an external locus of control means that someone believes outside factors ultimately determine their fate.
It can be easy to assume a strong internal locus of control is preferable because it implies someone is constantly looking to see what their role in a situation is and seeking opportunities to act, but it can also lead to self-blame and guilt where it may not be constructive. Someone can control how well they do in a job interview, but they can’t change a bias from the interviewer about their background. A strong internal locus of control might lead one to continually improve their performance since they believe the effort can produce a change in their outcomes, but this can also hurt if it leads to negative attitudes about oneself for not being good enough to meet standards that may not even be possible. On the other hand, someone with a strong external locus of control may have an easier time dealing with the disappointment of an interview that wasn’t good enough, but they may not be as driven to find room for improvement in their individual performance. In some cases, a external locus of control can extend into the idea of learned helplessness.
These are all generalizations, of course. In practice, one’s locus of control can vary by task or area of life. You might believe that your body weight is in your control but your height is not. A common critique of the original framework of the locus of control is that people separate whether a cause is internal or external from whether or not it is controllable. For instance, you may believe that your math ability or physical appearance is internal and that no outside entity is in control of that, but you may also believe that those aren’t controllable. If you’re religious and believe God personally intervenes in human affairs, then you might locate God as an external locus of control but still believe the internal action of prayer can help facilitate change.
Frameworks of liberation psychology often start by describing an external locus of control to explore how systemic oppression interacts with individual psychology. An internal locus of control can be reclaimed through a community’s collective action that pools individual power together, and the path to helping an individual do so is one of the goals of liberation psychology.

wiki/longitudinal-study.title: Longitudinal Study
wiki/longitudinal-study.content:
Overview
A longitudinal study tracks variables over a period of time, in contrast to a cross-sectional analysis that collects data about a single point in time. When we want to study cause-and-effect relationships between variables that might influence each other, we need a longitudinal study that observes their changes over time.
Consider the relationship between age and intelligence. A cross-sectional study might look at the population by age bracket, see higher intelligence scores in ages 20-30 than 50-60, and suggest a conclusion that this means intelligence decreases as one’s age increases. However, a longitudinal study that tracks a specific group of people from ages 20 to 50 might find that intelligence scores remain stable or modestly increase on average, which contradicts the finding of the first study. Instead, taken together, we might interpret the studies to suggest that each generation of people tends to have higher base intelligence than the generation of people that came before. This is a real phenomenon observed in IQ scores called the Flynn Effect where the growth of education and nutrition in developing nations throughout the 20th century was improving the foundations for learning and abstract thinking in children.
A similar partial picture is painted in studies about the prevalence of substance use disorders. Cross-sectional studies tend to show that the majority of people who meet the criteria for SUD in their youth recover without treatment, also called spontaneous remission. Addiction rates drop off sharply after the age of 30. However, longitudinal studies show that many of those who struggle with addiction go through periods of abstinence that might include relapses and many die young if they follow an uninterrupted trajectory of increasingly risky substance use patterns. For some, meeting the criteria for SUD can be the result of a phase of life like heavy college drinking or the culture of a job that normalizes heavy drinking after work, which they then age out of as they get older and adjust their lifestyles around family, career, or health circumstances. The population that struggles with substance use to the point of requiring clinical treatment generally experience substance use disorder as a chronic progressive condition that presents with alternating periods of remission into abstinence or moderation between relapses into active addiction.

wiki/looksmaxxing.title: Looksmaxxing
wiki/looksmaxxing.content:
Overview
“Looksmaxxing” is the practice of optimizing one’s physical appearance to be as attractive as possible beyond what healthy diet and exercise regimens would lead to. The online subcultures around looksmaxxing largely emerged out of incel and incel-adjacent forums where users are convinced that their lack of social or dating life is the result of their appearance. Many of these users are minors who struggle with social anxiety or bullying, as well as body dysmorphia. Consider the clinical diagnostic symptoms of Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD):


Preoccupation with Perceived Flaws: looksmaxxers will fixate on very specific measurements of their face like the canthal tilt, which is the angle at which one’s eyes are slanted. Supposedly, a positive canthal tilt (where the outer corner of the eye is somewhat higher than the inner corner) is characteristic of “hunter eyes”, while a negative canthal tilt and large round shapes indicate “prey eyes.” Not only will looksmaxxers obsessively measure these out down to millimeters (and probably doing more trigonometry in the process than they ever do in class), but they will attempt to alter their bone structure through facial massaging and eye pulling routines.


Repetitive Compulsive Checking: looksmaxxers can spend hours every day take selfies in order to measure their anatomical ratios and facial symmetry under a variety of camera lenses, angles, and lighting.


Excessive Grooming & Camouflaging: lookmaxxers are known for mewing, in which one holds their tongue against the roof of their mouth in an attempt to alter their jaw structure. Some may wear shoe lifts in order to “heightmaxx,” or just appear taller. Others have extremely strict skincare and hair-care routines that trigger extreme distress and anxiety if done incorrectly or skipped.


Seeking Reassurance or Validation: There are actually websites and apps that will score your proportions according to the conventions of the looksmaxxing community. The looksmaxxing forums tend to have power users, especially minors who have no other obligations except attending school, who obsessively compare their bodies with each other and seek feedback on their latest procedures.


Muscle & Fat Hyper-Fixation: Looksmaxxers have been known to inject themselves with a lot of controversial or experimental chemicals in an attempt to target fat, especially in their face in an attempt to seem leaner or have more pronounced facial structures. This also includes anabolic steroids and human growth hormones.


Repetitive Seeking of Interventions: Looksmaxxers may pursue intense plastic surgery, like rhinoplasty, genioplasty, jaw implants, or canthoplasty. In a truly dangerous DIY fashion, some will try bonesmashing, which is straight up just hitting your face with hard objects in an attempt to create micro-fractures that would heal back stronger or thicker.


Social Withdrawal & Isolation: It might appear paradoxical that someone would invest so much of their time, energy, and health into looksmaxxing only to end up isolating, but it completely tracks if we locate the incentives around looksmaxxing in anxiety. There’s a reason these communities sprung out of incel forums rather than conventional health and wellness communities. Looksmaxxers usually struggle with intense body dysmorphia and social anxiety that’s distressing, so much so that being observed in any way can trigger spirals about their appearance. When they post themselves on social media platforms, they’ve usually spent hours taking photos, applying filters, and stressing over the combination of pictures to use. Many looksmaxxers actually swear off dating entirely, resigning themselves to a Sisyphean effort of achieving a perfect look so they can reject potential partners who they believe they would’ve fumbled anyways.


In my opinion, the goofiness and absurdity of looksmaxxing procedures and content creators makes it easy to forget that the same companies who knew that they were giving young women eating disorders with their algorithms are also behind propagating the messages that drive the anxiety of young men identifying as looksmaxxers. Ultimately, we’re raising our newest generations to be radical consumers by bombarding them with messages to keep chasing increasingly extreme standards in order to stay relevant. The disposable appearance of being put-together has more value than being secure in yourself and confident in the value you provide.
Or, in other words, we’re algomaxxing every aspect of our lives. I trend, therefore I am.

wiki/los-borrachos.title: Los Borrachos
wiki/los-borrachos.content:
Historical Context
In 1629, Diego Velazquez completed a Baroque painting for King Philip V that was officially called The Triumph of Bacchus as a depiction of the god of wine Bacchus, the Roman interpretation of the Greek Dionysus, placing a crown on working-class peasants as a symbol of wine providing relief to the grief and misery of daily life. However, to much of the Spanish public, what stood out most were the peasants who seemed to be inviting the viewer to have a drink with them. The painting was referred to widely as Los Borrachos instead as a representation of celebratory drinking rituals that was strongly embedded and institutionalized in many Latin American communities.

wiki/lyndon-b-johnson.title: Lyndon B. Johnson
wiki/lyndon-b-johnson.content: LBJ was a member of the Texas National Council on Alcoholism (NCA), which meant he was a valuable connection for Marty Mann.

wiki/macguffin.title: MacGuffin
wiki/macguffin.content:
Overview
A “MacGuffin” describes a plot device that is mostly irrelevant to the actions and events of the story except for giving the characters an initial motivation.
Substances and process addictions alike are often MacGuffins in stories, especially as a result of anti-drug movements that produce lots of substance use depictions in the context of crime and underground subcultures. Some of these tropes include:


drug shipments as a highly valuable item that characters chase or fight over, giving law enforcement and criminal groups reasons to have conflicts with each other


dealing drugs as an easy way of making lots of money for characters who might be otherwise ordinary, setting up characters to be independently wealthy and free from daily obligations


active addiction as a reason that a character might do something irrational or extreme, whether it’s from the desperation to keep affording the addiction or from an altered and excited mental state


overdoses as tragic deaths that allow any number of family members to be killed off while invoking a sense of prolonged struggle or suffering


Examples


Bad Boys (1995): though the movie involves $100 million in stolen heroin, the movie is really about providing the protagonists a reason to engage in buddy-cop tropes involving action scenes and crass banter


Breaking Bad: Walter White’s meth could be changed with almost any other illicit substance and have the same outcome since the show centers on how Walt’s ego interacts with personalities deep in the drug trade and criminal underworld


Dune: Spice is a stand-in for oil and drugs as a substance that various factions use to enhance their power and prosperity, towards which their political games are played

wiki/mad-pride.title: Mad Pride
wiki/mad-pride.content:
Overview
Mad Pride is a movement to reclaim the term “mad” and “madness” as part of a challenge to institutional norms about mental health and celebration of neurological diversity. Generally, those in the Mad Pride movement believe that the lived experiences of those who have undergone psychiatric treatment and institutionalization should be prioritized in models of care. Forcing institutionalization and discriminating against people on the basis of mental differences are seen as human and civil rights issues. Although the centralized movement was mainly active from 1993 to 2012, plenty of groups and communities continue to identify with Mad Pride.

wiki/madya.title: Madya
wiki/madya.content:
Overview
Madya is a Sanskrit term that means “something that intoxicates” in reference to alcoholic beverages. In some texts, it referred more specifically to beverages from natural fermentations of sugarcane juice or fruits in contrast to sura, which were hard liquors distilled from grains.

wiki/magic-mushrooms.title: Magic Mushrooms
wiki/magic-mushrooms.content:
Overview
Magic mushrooms refer to fungi that contain psilocybin, which causes psychoactive effects that alter perception and mood. Shrooms are one of the substances alongside alcohol and marijuana that have had thousands of years of use across cultures. The Aztecs referred to them as teonanacatl, mixing them with wild honey for preservation. Some scholars have argued that the ancient Greek’s Eleusinian Mysteries used ergot as a base for a hallucinogenic drink called kykeon.
The term “magic mushrooms” was introduced to Western pop culture in the 1950s through Gordon Wasson and Allan Richardson, who documented their participation in a ceremony with a Mazatec healer. In 1958, Albert Hofmann, the Swiss chemist who discovered LSD, identified psilocybin and psilocin as the active compounds in mushroom specimens from Mexico. There was a brief period of research and exploration into mushrooms, like the Harvard Psychdelic Project, until President Richard Nixon signed the Controlled Substances Act into law in 1970, which placed psilocybin mushrooms into Schedule I and inhibited future research. In more recent years, there has been some movement in research and medicine towards studying the use of mushrooms in addressing treatment-resistant depression. Some states and cities in the United States have also taken steps to decriminalize mushrooms, like in 2020 with Oregon’s Measure 109 that gave a framework for therapeutic psilocybin use.

wiki/maintenance.title: Maintenance
wiki/maintenance.content:
Overview
Maintenance is the fifth stage of recovery from addiction in the Transtheoretical Model (TTM) in which someone has sustained a change in behavior through work that prevents relapse. In recovery circles, the term is used without normally referencing the TTM, instead referring to the general idea of doing the work required to sustain sobriety.

wiki/maladaptive-overcontrol.title: Maladaptive Overcontrol
wiki/maladaptive-overcontrol.content:
Overview
Maladaptive overcontrol is a coping mechanism marked by suppressing emotions, chronic isolation, hypervigilance, and rigidity in forms like perfectionism.
The standard Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) designed by Marsha Linehan was designed for undercontrolled coping styles that involve emotional impulsivity and externalizing distress, particularly those observed in patients with chronic suicidality and borderline personality disorder (BPD). Thomas Lynch recognized that many clients and patients actually struggled with what he termed “maladaptive overcontrol” instead, though society often praised or accepted their coping style because it can appear to be the result of self-discipline and compliance rather than suppression and cognitive rigidity. Lynch developed Radically Open Dialectical Behavior Therapy (RO DBT) to build openness and social connectedness in those with maladaptive overcontrol.
Commentary
Anecdotally, I’ve found that the bias towards undercontrolling coping styles in treatment settings is enormous. Some of the bias comes from the model of addicts as those who impulsively indulge in instant gratification over long-term consequences as a general pattern in their lives, and so they must be taught to develop coping skills that allow for them to delay impulsive acts. Overcontrolling coping mechanisms often look like strict internal rules and masking affects that are crafted to avoid the vulnerability that comes with impulsively revealing oneself. In these cases, substance use is often an attempt to address the pain of chronic loneliness and the stress of a constant inner critic. Without addressing the root problems around vulnerability, openness, and communication, one might remain isolated even if they can manage their impulses and eventually decide it’s worth seeking substances for relief.

wiki/maladaptive.title: Maladaptive
wiki/maladaptive.content:
Overview
“Maladaptive” means that some pattern of behavior or feelings is poorly aligned with the circumstances surrounding it, leading to undesirable outcomes.
Increasingly, there has been a trend of describing behaviors as “adapative” or “maladaptive” rather than “healthy” or “unhealthy” to emphasize the importance of context in categorizing behaviors. For example, suppressing emotions may have at one point been an adaptive behavior in response to an environment that punished someone for expressing themselves. Once someone is able to leave that environment, suppressing emotions can be an obstacle to social connectedness and clear communication in a new environment that values emotional vulnerability. This specific example is a type of maladaptive overcontrol.

wiki/mandatory-minimums.title: Mandatory Minimum Sentencing
wiki/mandatory-minimums.content:
Overview
Mandatory minimum sentencing requirements are laws that require judges to impose a minimum sentence for certain crimes without considering the specific circumstances of the case. Together with mass incarceration, it forms a core part of the War on Drugs in the United States.
Consider a wealthy defendant who commits corporate fraud that wipes out the retirement savings of thousands of people. They might be able to afford a strong legal team who could find a sympathetic judge and hire public relations firms to improve their presentation in court. They can also use their positions to make trades with prosecutors involving financial data that plays a factor in other cases. It’s also possible for an individual judge to be compromised in some way with a conflict of interest that incentivizes lenient sentencing. A mandatory minimum on fraud over some amount might ensure the defendant can’t use their wealth to mitigate the consequences of their crimes.
Now consider a low-income defendant who took money to deliver illicit drugs and has no prior criminal history, like a college student who wanted easy money or a part-time worker who was behind on rent. Sentencing someone like that to a decade or more of time in prison because of a mandatory minimum on drug trafficking charges can seem disproportionately harsh. However, the judge has no ability to lower the severity of the punishment in response to the specific circumstances of the case.

wiki/manic-depression.title: Manic Depression
wiki/manic-depression.content:
Overview
Manic depression is an outdated term for bipolar disorder, coined initially as “das manisch-depressive Irresein” in German by the psychiatrist Emil Kraepelin, who noticed that some patients cycled between high energy states (mania) and low moods (depression). “Manic-depressive” was a common diagnosis for patients who were admitted into growing psychiatric hospitals in the early 20th century. Eventually, the term was phased out in favor of “bipolar disorder” as a spectrum of cycling between extreme affects and to separate it more distinctly from Major Depressive Disorder, especially since they respond to different pharmaceutical treatments.

wiki/manifestation.title: Manifestation
wiki/manifestation.content:
Overview
“Manifestation” means the act of bringing something into existence.
In spiritual circles that overlap with recovery and wellness circles, the term is used to refer to using one’s beliefs or intentions to shape reality. The law of attraction is one spiritual principle that believes positive thinking and visualization is key to manifesting positive outcomes in reality, whereas negative thinking will manifest in negative outcomes. The idea of changing reality through the mind alone is firmly in the realm of superstition, but there are some studies that show that positive mindsets can improve problem-solving skills and confidence by leading to greater perceived rewards for the application of effort.

wiki/marco-venniro.title: Marco Venniro
wiki/marco-venniro.content:
Marco Venniro is an Associate Professor at the University of Maryland, specifically an Associate Director of Education and Training within the Kahlert Institute for Addiction Medicine.
Links

www.medschool.umaryland.edu/profiles/venniro-marco/

Works

Volitional social interaction prevents drug addiction in rat models (2018)

“Addiction treatment has not been appreciably improved by neuroscientific research. One problem is that mechanistic studies using rodent models do not incorporate volitional social factors, which play a critical role in human addiction. Here, using rats, we introduce an operant model of choice between drugs and social interaction. Independent of sex, drug class, drug dose, training conditions, abstinence duration, social housing, or addiction score in Diagnostic & Statistical Manual IV-based and intermittent access models, operant social reward prevented drug self-administration. ”

wiki/marcus-antonius-mark-antony.content: The guy wrote a whole book defending his drinking habits after he was called out for throwing up repeatedly during official events. Come on.

wiki/marginalization.title: Marginalization
wiki/marginalization.content:
Overview
Marginalization is the act of treating specific groups of people to the margins of society, where they’re treated as less valuable than others and deprived of equal access to resources and opportunities.
In the context of substance use, marginalization occurs both prior to and as a result of it. People are far more likely to use substances to self-medicate when they lack access to medical providers or have a mistrust of medical institutions that may not be inclusive towards different groups. Environments with high stressors like housing instability, job insecurity, community violence, systemic discrimination, and intergenerational trauma are more likely to result in people using substances to get relief and cope with stress. Then, once in active addiction, individuals often burn through their employment, housing, and social support networks while also facing potential incarceration if they broke the law under the influence. This means that sustaining sobriety also requires overcoming the obstacles from marginalization acquired while using.
Part of the motivation behind the design of Alcoholics Anonymous as a peer-led mutual aid network, among other recovery programs, is to remain open to those in society who are too marginalized to get help from mainstream institutions or have experienced active harm from them. These recovery programs often have no requirement for participation and are completely free to join and network through. It’s common to hear announcements at these meetings for jobs and housing assistance dedicated for those in recovery or hear advice about navigating social services and local charities. Some meetings are dedicated safe spaces for certain identities, like LGTBQ+, agnostic, and Spanish-speaking meetings in case general groups don’t make appropriately inclusive efforts or one wants to be part of groups that understand marginalization at the intersection of multiple dimensions of lived experience.

wiki/mark-lundholm.title: Mark Lundholm
wiki/mark-lundholm.content:

From performances inside San Quentin State Prison to performing for President Gerald Ford and President Donald Trump (then just a businessman hosting galas), Mark Lundholm has made a comedy career from the lessons learned through his past struggles with addiction and dysfunctional relationships.

wiki/markus-heilig.title: Markus Heilig
wiki/markus-heilig.content:
Overview
Professor of Psychiatry at Linkoping University at Sweden.
Works


The Thirteenth Step: Addiction in the Age of Brain Science (2015)


Addiction as a brain disease revised: why it still matters, and the need for consilience (2021)


“The view that substance addiction is a brain disease, although widely accepted in the neuroscience community, has become subject to acerbic criticism in recent years. These criticisms state that the brain disease view is deterministic, fails to account for heterogeneity in remission and recovery, places too much emphasis on a compulsive dimension of addiction, and that a specific neural signature of addiction has not been identified. We acknowledge that some of these criticisms have merit, but assert that the foundational premise that addiction has a neurobiological basis is fundamentally sound. We also emphasize that denying that addiction is a brain disease is a harmful standpoint since it contributes to reducing access to healthcare and treatment, the consequences of which are catastrophic.”

wiki/maryknoll-mission.title: Maryknoll Mission
wiki/maryknoll-mission.content:
Overview
The Maryknoll Mission is a Catholic non-profit network founded in the United States in 1911. It consists of four independent but collaborative organization: Maryknoll Fathers & Brothers, Maryknoll Sisters, Maryknoll Lay Missioners, and Maryknoll Affiliates. Local missioners often manage support services for those with addictions, like Megan Hamilton who started the first structured Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) meetings in regional clinics in Mombasa, Kenya. 1 They’re an example of wraparound services whose work supports the treatment provided by medical institutions.

wiki/masking.title: Masking
wiki/masking.content:
Overview
“Masking” refers to concealing one’s natural traits to avoid being treated differently, which can be either conscious or unconscious.
Individuals with autism might suppress stimming or mirror body language to fit in. Those with ADHD might suppress hyperactivity or inattentive patterns to be able to conform to standards. Anyone with depression or anxiety who forces a smile all day at work to appear happy is masking too. These are adaptations to the way society expects people to behave, and they can be an incredible drain on mental and physical health. In fact, there’s a negative feedback loop: those who mask will also likely try to mask the symptoms of masking. This can interfere with mental health diagnoses and accommodations since the individual is used to concealing symptoms under stressful conditions.

wiki/mass-incarceration.title: Mass Incarceration
wiki/mass-incarceration.content:
Overview
Mass incarceration refers to the practice of imprisoning large amounts of people, and the term is generally used in reference to the War on Drugs in United States.
Despite having only 5% of the global population, the United States holds almost 25% of the world’s prisoners. 65% of those in prisons have a substance use disorder, and 47% had a substance use disorder in the year before their entry. Many groups of color are overrepresented in the prison population, with Black Americans making up about 33% despite being 14% of the general US population and having comparable rates of drug use with white populations.
Prisons are not generally equipped to address substance use disorder as a genuine medical condition. Many who are incarcerated are suddenly thrust into withdrawals without adequate medical care to manage them. Rehabilitation requires proper treatment to break a cycle of relapse and recidivism through expensive emergency services.

wiki/maudsley-model-of-anorexia-nervous-.title: Maudsley Model of Anorexia Nervosa Treatment for Adults (MANTRA)
wiki/maudsley-model-of-anorexia-nervous-.content:
Overview
The Maudsley Model of Anorexia Nervosa Treatment for Adults (MANTRA) is an evidence-based psychotherapy used as a first-line treatment for anorexia nervosa (AN) in adults in the United Kingdom. MANTRA is delivered as an individual talk therapy involving workbook exercises and motivational interviewing (MI). It uses the Cognitive-Interpersonal Maintenance Model (CIMM), which argues that a combination of intrapersonal and interpersonal factors are involved in restricting AN:


Perfectionism/Cognitive Rigidity: those with eating disorders also tend to have higher levels of obsessive-compulsive personality traits and anxiety traits


Experiential Avoidance: an avoidant temperament (e.g., restricted emotional expression or struggles with intimacy and identity) is a risk factor for developing and maintaining AN


Pro-Anorectic Beliefs: one of the challenges in treatment for eating disorders is that it’s common for clients to have positive beliefs about them. The ‘Pros and Cons of Anorexia Nervosa’ Questionnaire (P-CAN) administered in 2004 found that the positive beliefs about the benefits of AN included a feeling of safety and stifling emotions.


Response of Close Others: relatives who express high amounts of criticism, hostility, and emotional involvement with the patient with an eating disorder are associated with worse overall outcomes for the patient.


MANTRA is a step-by-step treatment program of workbooks, modules, and therapeutic techniques that address the factors identified by CIMM.

wiki/mcgovern-institute-for-brain-resear.title: McGovern Institute for Brain Research
wiki/mcgovern-institute-for-brain-resear.content:
Overview
The McGovern Institute of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology has dedicated projects for research into Substance Use Disorders (SUDs) from a neurobiological perspective. Other topics include optogenetics, cannabis impact studies, and the neuroscience of cravings.

wiki/mdma.title: MDMA
wiki/mdma.content:
Overview
3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine (also known as MDMA, ecstacy, X, E, molly) is a psychedelic stimulant known to cause euphoria, heightened sensory perceptions, and deep emotional connections. Its immediate side effects include:


Bruxism: involuntary clenching of the jaw or teeth grinding


Hyperthermia: high body temperature


Cardiovascular stress: elevated heart rate and high blood pressure


Dehydration


Hyponatremia: low blood sodium levels caused by drinking too much water too quickly


Chills, sweats, and nausea


Dry Mouth


Blurred Vision


Anxiety, panic, or paranoia


Distorted Time Perception


The “come down” from an ecstacy high is known for involving a day or more of severe depression and anxiety. Long-term, chronic use of ecstacy can play a role in the development or symptom severity of:


Memory deficits


Attention issues


Depression


Sleep disorders


Chronic anxiety


Organ damage

wiki/medicalization.title: Medicalization
wiki/medicalization.content:
Overview
Medicalization is the process in which problems and concepts become defined as medical conditions to be treated, usually involving clinical and research institutions.
The history of policy around drugs and treatment for substance use disorder is loaded with moralization that doesn’t account for the way chronic substance use produces physiological changes in the brain. Although those like Benjamin Rush advocated for treating alcoholism as an “odious disease” as far back as 1784, the medicalization of alcoholism began in earnest in the 20th century. Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) was founded in 1935 and was associated with the “disease like any other” campaigns that framed alcoholism as a kind of allergy. In 1956, the American Medical Association (AMA) officially declared alcoholism as an illness and began shifting the focus of addiction treatment from peer-led spiritual groups to methods pioneered from psychology, psychiatry, and neuroscience.

wiki/medication-for-opioid-use-disorder.title: Medication for Opioid Use Disorder (MOUD)
wiki/medication-for-opioid-use-disorder.content:
Overview
Medication for Opioid Use Disorder (MOUD) involves the use of medications that alleviate the cravings of Opioid Use Disorder (OUD) without providing the same euphoria as actual opioids. The biggest examples include buprenorphine, methadone, and naltrexone.

wiki/meditation.title: Meditation
wiki/meditation.content:
Overview
Meditation is one of the most popular coping skills and self-care exercises in any context, both inside and outside of recovery and wellness spaces. The mindfulness that’s cultivated through meditation can improve impulse control, distress tolerance, and emotional regulation, all of which are common targets in treatment settings. It’s also just a way to calm your body’s nervous system when you’re stressed or tense that anyone can use. Cultures across the world have practiced meditation in some form for thousands of years, so there’s an incredibly rich and diverse set of traditions to explore. Some of the scientific evidence about meditation concludes that it:


reduces intensity of the fight or flight response


calms rumination and mind-wandering from the brain’s Default Mode Network (DMN)


increases cortical thickness and gray matter density in regions related to emotional processing and metacognitive awareness


improvements in selective attention, working memory capacity, and cognitive flexibility


strengthens impulse control and delay triggers or cravings from an automatic behavioral response


reduces blood pressure, inflammation, and physical tension


increases cellular longevity markers

wiki/mediterranean-diet.title: Mediterranean Diet
wiki/mediterranean-diet.content:
Overview
The Mediterranean diet refers to diets inspired by plant-heavy traditions of countries surrounding the Mediterranean Sea. Rather than strict rules, the diet emphasizes vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes, nuts, seeds, and extra virgin olive oil on a day-to-day basis. Fish, poultry, eggs, daily, and cheeses should be eaten in moderate portions weekly. Red meat, refined sugars, and saturated fats like butter are to be strictly limited. The benefits from the perspective of recovery include:


Anti-inflammatory effects: chronic substance use causes more inflammation throughout the whole body that can worsen the cravings and depression that influence unhealthy eating patterns. The Mediterranean diet tends to lead to high omega-3 fatty acids, polyphenols, and fiber which actively reduce inflammation


Improvements to mood: the diet has been linked to a 25% to 35% reduction in the risk of developing depression and anxiety


Gut-Brain Axis: whole foods, legumes, fiber, and fermented foods promote healthy gut bacteria that are linked to the regulation of neurotransmitters like serotonin and dopamine.


Cardiovascular health: the diet is associated with lowering bad cholesterol, managing blood pressure, and reducing the risk of heart attacks and strokes by as much as 30%. It’s also associated with lower instances of type 2 diabetes and other chronic diseases.

wiki/mel-schulstad-professional-of-the-y.title: Mel Schulstad Professional of the Year Award | NAADAC
wiki/mel-schulstad-professional-of-the-y.content:
Overview
Mel Schulstad was one of the founders of NAADAC, then known as the National Association of Alcoholism Counselors (NAAC). He was a WWII bomber pilot who retired in 1966 to volunteer for the Fairfax Hospital alcohol program. In 1973, he was a paid counselor for Arlington County and elected as the first President of the Virginia Association of Alcoholism Counselors (VAAC), which renamed later to the Virginia Association of Addiction Professionals (VAAP). For some context on the frequent renaming of awards and organizations, addiction wasn’t always a unified field of study, so many of the organizations and programs we have now were initially focused just on alcoholism. As their scope expanded, they thought it prudent to rebrand to reflect that.
The award was established in 1979, and Schulstad personally presented the award at NAADAC’s Annual Conferences until 2008, four years before he passed away.
To be eligible for the award, one needs to have a minimum of 20 years of service in addiction counseling, demonstrate a history of commitment to advancing the profession, and be an active NAADAC voting member in compliance with the NAADAC Code of Ethics.

wiki/melancholy.title: Melancholy
wiki/melancholy.content:
Overview
In casual usage, melancholy refers to a deep or prolonged sadness that can involve a sense of introspection or self-reflection.
Historically, melancholia was a term from Ancient Greek that translates literally to “black bile” and traced emotional disturbances from seemingly irrational beliefs to an imbalance of fluids inside someone. Humorism declined through advancements in science during the 18th century, but melancholia continued to be used as a diagnosis for the symptoms that we might now attribute to depression and anxiety. As of the DSM-III, the term “melancholia” no longer served as an independent condition but instead as a specifier for a severe version of Major Depressive Disorder.

wiki/mental-status-examination.title: Mental Status Examination (MSE)
wiki/mental-status-examination.content:
Overview
The Mental Status Examination (MSE) is a long-standing psychiatric assessment that a clinician conducts through semi-structured conversation as a screening for someone’s mental state. The kind of observations a clinician makes generally falls into one of the follow categories:


Appearance: age, weight, appropriate clothing, grooming, unique skin marks or tattoos, posture, balance, eye contact


Behavior: hyperactivity, agitation, catatonia, restlessness, tremors, tics, jaw movement, slowed movement, notable postures, twitches


Speech: speed, fluency, tone, quality, volume, and unusual language


Attitude: cooperative, positive, negative


Mood: client self-rating and self-reporting


Affect: quality, range, stability, appropriateness, congruence, consistency


Cognition: level of consciousness, short-term memory, long-term memory, recall, reasoning, calculation, alertness


Insight: awareness of the problem and symptoms, ability to describe the timeline and causes of the problem, ability to articulate how they’re feeling and functioning


Judgment: level of impulse control, adaptability in decision-making, participation in their own care


Concentration: attentiveness, drowsiness, distraction


Orientation: knowledge of personal identity, where one is, what the date is, etc.


Thought Process: circumstantial, tangential, loose associations, echolalia, disorganization


Thought Content: delusions, suicidal or homicidal thoughts, thoughts of self-harm, obsessions, compulsions, paranoia, magical thinking


Perceptual Disturbances: visual, auditory, or somatic hallucinations, illusions, depersonalization, derealization

wiki/mescaline.title: Mescaline
wiki/mescaline.content:
Overview
Mescaline is a psychedelic found most often in the peyote cactus, and it can be consumed in various ways orally like teas or capsules. Although it’s classified as a Schedule 1 controlled substance in the United States, members of federally-recognized Native American tribes can use and transport peyote for ceremonial purposes.
The short-term effects of using mescaline include:


Nausea, vomiting, and loss of appetite


Heavy sweating and chills


Elevated blood pressure and heart rate


Difficulty with motor coordination, including walking


Anxiety, panic attacks, and paranoia


Impaired decision-making, mood swings, and disorganized thinking


Insomnia, fatigue, and body acahes


The long-term effects include:


Psychological dependence


Hallucinogen Persisting Perception Disorder (HPDD)


Exacerbation of Other Conditions, like triggering psychotic reactions for those with conditions like schizophrenia or bipolar disorder

wiki/mesolimbic-system.title: Mesolimbic System
wiki/mesolimbic-system.content:
Overview
The mesolimbic system, or mesolimbic pathway, is a neural circuit in the brain that regulates reward and motivation, incentive salience, and reinforcement learning. Addictive substances and processes are often described as “hijacking” this pathway with artificial surges in dopamine levels. Dysregulation of this circuit, as in cases of depression, can impact motivation or result in anhedonia.

wiki/metabolism.title: Metabolism
wiki/metabolism.content:
Overview
Metabolism refers to the series of reactions that a body undergoes to turn its inputs like food and water into energy to maintain itself. Any intermediate or end product that results from a metabolic process is called a metabolite.
The way drugs are metabolized in the body determines everything from its intensity to duration to side effects, and that depends both on the nature of the drug itself and the unique biology of each living thing. Genetic differences between people changes the rate that substances are metabolized at. While they’re in the body, substances add a lot of stress on metabolic processes that can cause long-term damage to organs.

wiki/metabolite.title: Metabolite
wiki/metabolite.content:
Overview
A metabolite is any intermediate or end product made as the result of metabolism. They might be categorized in the following ways:


Primary Metabolites directly involved in normal growth and development vs Secondary Metabolites that have important roles that aren’t required to sustain basic life


Active Metabolites that produce biological effects vs Inactive Metabolites that await excretion from the body


Many of the effects caused by substances are actually the result of their metabolites interacting with the body. For instance, consuming cocaine and alcohol together leads to a unique metabolite called cocaethylene which is more potent and toxic to the cardiovascular system than cocaine alone would be. Codeine itself is a weak analgesic, but human liver enzymes convert some of it to morphine as a metabolite to produce the opioid effect. Immunoassays are commonly used to detect drug metabolites in urine samples since detecting the parent drug becomes more difficult as time passes from its usage. Liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) is capable of far more precise detection of molecules in a sample, so it allows us to measure the ratio of a parent drug to its metabolite for more a complete picture of someone’s substance use. It’s also why dropping medication raw into a urine sample to pretend you’re taking it doesn’t work; without passing through the body’s metabolic processes, the test doesn’t have any metabolites to detect.

wiki/metascience.title: Metascience
wiki/metascience.content:
Overview
Metascience can be described simply science of science. Contrary to the expectations that science is inherently an objective pursuit of the truth in contrast to religion and spirituality as intuitive or anecdotal approaches, there are lots of subjective elements in the design of experiments, interpretation of their results, and inclusion of evidence in the development of scientific theories.

wiki/meth-storm.title: Meth Storm
wiki/meth-storm.content:
Overview
Meth Storm (2017) is a documentary about methamphetamine use and trafficking operations in the communities of rural Arkansas.

wiki/methadone.title: Methadone
wiki/methadone.content:
Overview
Methadone is a full opioid agonist used to stop cravings and stabilize brain chemistry without producing any feelings of euphoria in those who struggle with Opioid Use Disorder (OUD). It’s dispensed through Opioid Treatment Programs (OTPs) which generally require in-person clinic attendance everyday when starting out, which makes it more restricted than other drugs used for Medication for Opioid Use Disorder (MOUD) like buprenorphine that can be prescribed by any physician to be taken home.

wiki/methamphetamine.title: Methamphetamine
wiki/methamphetamine.content:
Overview
Methamphetamine is a synthetic stimulant derived from amphetamines with a methyl group added and is classified as a Schedule II controlled substance. The methyl group makes methamphetamine more soluble in fat than standard amphetamine, which also allows it to cross the blood-brain barrier faster. It’s usually consumed as either powder, pills, or rocks in a form called crystal meth. In the short-term, the effects include:


Euphoria, or extreme sensations of pleasure or feelings of confidence


Hyperactivity, as increased physical activity and talkativeness


Cardiovascular stress, such as elevated heart rate and blood pressure


Hyperthermia, a rise in body temperature that can strain organs or lead to organ failure


Appetite suppression


Insomnia


Rapid, shallow breathing


In the long-term, the effects include:


Impaired memory, decision-making, and motor skills


Paranoia, hallucinations, and persistent delusions


Dental decay from dry mouth, poor hygiene, and teeth grinding


Sores or wounds resulting from scratching or picking skin, sometimes resulting in infections


Strokes, heart attacks, and cardiomyopathy


Anhedonia


Malnutrition and muscle wasting

wiki/methanol.title: Methanol
wiki/methanol.content:
Overview
Methanol, or methyl alcohol, is a colorless and flammable liquid used to produce formaldehyde, acetic acid, and other chemicals for plastics and synthetic compounds. It has also been explored as an alternative fuel source that burns clean. Unlike ethanol, or drinking alcohol, methanol is incredibly toxic and can cause permanent blindness, comas, and death. Even skin absorption of small amounts can cause severe damage to the body. A very small level of methanol exists in the human body and fermented beverages, and those with a history of chronic drinking will have higher levels.
Some individuals in active addiction with alcohol might try to use methanol as a substitute for ethanol if they’re feeling extremely desperate, which will initially produce a state of drunkenness similar to ethanol in its depression of the central nervous system. However, methanol is metabolism into formaldehyde and then metabolized again into formicacid, which can cause organ failure and death in small amounts.

wiki/methemoglobinema.title: Methemoglobinema
wiki/methemoglobinema.content:
Overview
Methemoglobinema is a blood disorder in which the iron in hemoglobin becomes oxidized and unable to properly deliver oxygen to boy issues. The most common form is acquired through ingestion of certain chemicals, like benzocaine, dapsone, and nitrites (“poppers”). Sometimes other substances are contaminated with enough of these other chemicals to still trigger the disorder. Less commonly, it can be caused by a genetic deficiency that may cause development delays in infants.

wiki/methocarbamol.title: Methocarbamol
wiki/methocarbamol.content:
Overview
Methocarbamol is used as a muscle relaxant and pain reliever for health conditions that produce painful muscle spasms or cramps. As a central nervous system (CNS) depressant, it slows down nerve activity to provide relief.
Side effects include:


Dizziness and lightheadedness


Drowsiness or fatigue


Headache


Blurred vision


Nausea or upset stomach


Combining it with other substances like alcohol, opioids, or anxiety medications can compound the depressant effect.

wiki/michael-a-bozarth.title: Michael A. Bozarth
wiki/michael-a-bozarth.content: Michael Bozarth, alongside Roy Wise, published the famous 1985 Rat Park study that found 90% of rats who were left for a month in a cage with food, water, and cocaine would eventually choose cocaine to the point of death through exhaustion, starvation, and/or dehydration.

wiki/mindfulness.title: Mindfulness
wiki/mindfulness.content:
Overview
Mindfulness refers to maintaining present awareness of thoughts, feelings, and sensations without judgment. Although it’s something of a marketing term that gets easily conflated with authenticity or focus, it has roots in South Asian traditions and was brought into mainstream Western popular culture through a revival of interest in Buddhism during New Age spiritual movements.
Common mindfulness exercises include:


5-4-3-2-1 Sensory Grounding: Look at 5 things you can see, 4 things you can feel, 3 things you can hear, 2 things you can smell, and 1 thing you can taste


Sequential Body Scan: shift attention from the toes to the top of the head to notice the sensations without trying to change them


Progressive Muscle Relaxation (PMR): tense muscle groups for 5 seconds or so at a time, and then release the tension for 10 seconds or so at a time


Thought Labeling: when a thought or emotion arises, just apply a one-word label to it and let it go rather than ruminating or contemplating it.


Urge Surfing: an approach to handling cravings or impulses by imagining them as waves that will peak before slowing down and visualizing oneself as riding the wave


Box Breathing: inhale through the nose for 4 seconds, hold it for 4 seconds, exhale through the mouth for 4 seconds, hold empty for 4 seconds; repeat


4-7-8 Breathing: inhale through the nose for 4 seconds, hold it for 7 seconds, and exhale through the mouth for 8 seconds; repeat


S.T.O.P Checkpoint: Stop, Take a breath, Observe, Proceed


Sensory Task Immersion: do a mundane task while focusing on the sensory information


Mindfulness is complemented with intentionality; once one is mindful of one’s internal patterns, one can more appropriately set their intentions to maintain or change them.

wiki/minnesota-young-people-in-alcoholic.title: Minnesota Young People in Alcoholics Anonymous (MNYPAA)
wiki/minnesota-young-people-in-alcoholic.content:
Overview
The Minnesota Model is one of the most commonly adopted formats for addiction treatment centers, and its start in Minnesota led to a large surge of youth participants in A.A. To accommodate them, especially in the context of old timers being wary that younger alcoholics had “suffered enough” or “hit rock bottom” in order to begin recovery. Overview
The Minoan “poppy goddess” figurines are terracotta sculptures from Greece that depict a goddess crowned with opium poppy seed capsules.

wiki/mishirabe.title: Mishirabe
wiki/mishirabe.content:
Overview
Mishirabe is a Buddhist practice of meditation through sensory and physical deprivation, originating in the traditions of the Jodo Shinshu (Pure Land) branch of Japanese Buddhism. Practitioners would enter a small isolated space like a dark room or a cave for long periods of time - sometimes more than a week. Driving the body and mind to exhaustion was meant to strip away defense mechanisms and rationalizations to facilitate a realization of the boundless forces sustaining someone in spite of their ego. Because it was such an intense practice, Ishin Yishimoto, a businessman and follower of Jodo Shinshu practices, derived a simpler, non-sectarian method known as Naikan Therapy, which is now widely used across clinical settings in Japan and parts of Europe.

wiki/mobilize-recovery.title: Mobilize Recovery
wiki/mobilize-recovery.content:
Overview
Mobilize Recovery is a national non-profit that drives grassroots solutions to addressing mental health and substance use disorders (SUDs). It focuses on community organizing, political advocacy, and [harm-reduction|harm reduction]. Its programs have included Operation Understanding to honor historical recovery movements against systemic stigma, the Overdose Response Initiative to distribute Naloxone (Narcan), Code Recover to bridge gaps between clinical care and local recovery pathways, Day of Service as an annual campaign to complete volunteer projects, and organizing national summits. 1

wiki/moderation.title: Moderation
wiki/moderation.content:
Overview
Moderation refers to using substances or processes in a way that limits the negative consequences.
In recovery circles, the idea of moderation is very controversial. In 12-step groups like Alcoholics Anonymous or Narcotics Anonymous, there’s a firm rejection of the idea that one can ever go back to “drinking like a gentleman.” Other adages include “a pickle can’t go back to being a cucumber” and “one drink is too much, a thousand is never enough.” Within medical and research communities, any amount of alcohol is generally considered harmful to the body, despite any potential benefits behind the media’s sensationalization of a glass of wine a day, so it’s unlikely for there to ever be a circumstance where a clinician recommends drinking to someone with abstinence.
At the same time, research also shows that 1 in 5 people who at one point qualified for alcohol use disorder diagnosis no longer meet the clinical criteria in their drinking patterns, suggesting that harm reduction or moderation is not completely off the table for those experiencing SUD. Some recovery groups like SMART Recovery explicitly validate moderation as a valid goal to aim for as their program follows the medical paradigm found in harm reduction programs that any improvement in quality of life is meaningful. However, anecdotally, the goal of moderation is respected in these meetings but warnings about it are still common. One of the problems is that the people most interested in moderation are those who struggle the most with the idea of living sober, such that it’s virtually never a good idea to recommend moderation to someone who wants or needs to aim for abstinence. But if you really can moderate, all the power to you if the tradeoff of continuing drinking in moderation is worth it. Medications like naltrexone blunt the effects of alcohol which some people use to stop after a couple drinks to prevent a binge or to practice the Sinclair Method that trains the brain to desire alcohol less.

wiki/monitoring-the-future.title: Monitoring the Future (MTF)
wiki/monitoring-the-future.content:
Overview
Monitoring the Future (MTF) is an ongoing national survey that tracks substance use patterns among Americans. It has been conducted yearly since 1975 through the Survey Research Center at the University of Michigan, funded by the National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA). It started with 12th graders but expanded to include 8th and 10th graders in 1991. The survey follows a randomly chosen sample from each cohort of graduating students throughout their lives by checking in every two years until 30 and then every five years from 35 onward. On top of measuring drug consumption across three intervals (past 30 days, past 12 months, and lifetime usage), it also monitors perceived risks and social disapproval, educational and career aspirations, gender roles and parental influences, attitudes toward religion, political opinions, etc. MTF has often been described as a gold standard for tracking epidemiological changes over time.

wiki/mood-congruence.title: Mood Congruence
wiki/mood-congruence.content:
Overview
Mood congruence refers to the way a person’s present emotional state biases their attention and memory to match it. People in a good mood are more likely to share stories or remember events that are positive. Similarly, feeling sad primes more negative memories of times that felt similarly distressing. For those with depression or anxiety, this process can become a cycle where low moods lead to distressing memories which worsens the mood the further.
In the case of substance use patterns, mood congruence can make it more difficult to resist cravings. If someone encounters a trigger for a negative emotional state, mood congruence means it’s less likely that someone will recall the negative consequences of using substances than recall the relief it provided to change their emotional state. The same applies to positive emotional states; if someone is in a celebratory mood but had a habit of using substances when celebrating in the past, mood congruence means the brain is more likely to assign attention and significance to the memories of celebrating with substances in the past compared to the consequences later.
Therapy modalities like Dialectical Behavioral Therapy (DBT) and Behavioral Activation (BA) attempt to break cycles of mood congruence by focusing taking actions that might contradict the current mood. In DBT, this is called Opposite Action, and it attempts to produce a bottom-up signal to the brain that the urge it’s producing is no longer applicable to the current context. An ideal Opposite Action involves an analysis of whether an urge is unjustified or ineffective, and if so, then to commit to the complete opposite action in a way that aligns internal thoughts and external affect with a new mood.
Mood congruence is in contrast to mood incongruence, which can be a clinical problem as well that can indicate issues in emotional processing, cognitive integration, or reality testing. In the DSM-5, mood congruence or incongruence describe the presentation of certain disorders. For instance, in Major Depressive Disorder, a mood-congruent delusion might be that someone believes they deserve to suffer or not feel pleasure. A mood-incongruent delusion might involve external delusions of grandeur and supremacy while internally feeling empty or suicidal.

wiki/mood-stabilizer.title: Mood Stabilizer
wiki/mood-stabilizer.content:
Overview
Mood stabilizers are medications that address extreme mood swings, as are seen during manic and depressive episodes in bipolar disorder. The most common mood stabilizers include:


Lithium


Anticonvulsants: valproic acid/divalproex, lamotrigine, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine


Atypical Antipsychotics: quetiapine, olanzapine, risperidone


They generally work by calming overactive neural pathways in the brain, including GABA and glutamate, and they take weeks of consistent use to reach clinical effectiveness. They also shouldn’t be stopped suddenly in case of symptoms from withdrawal or relapse.

wiki/mood-swing.title: Mood Swing
wiki/mood-swing.content:
Overview
“Mood swings” are a casual term for rapid shifts in emotional states rather than a specific clinical term.
In clinical and research literature, there isn’t much of a consensus for the definition of related terms like affective instability, which looks at someone’s reactivity in relation to their environment; mood instability, which looks at the tendency to quickly experience distinct moods; and affective lability, which looks at the tendency to express intense shifts in emotional states. They’re often used interchangeably, though the differences help delineate symptoms for distinct diagnoses. For instance, “affective instability” is better at describing the patterns of Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) while “mood instability” is better at describing the patterns of Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD).

wiki/moral-psychology.title: Moral Psychology
wiki/moral-psychology.content:
Overview
Moral psychology describes the psychological frameworks used in moral judgment and reasoning, which involves an intersection of philosophy, psychology, and cognitive science.
Categories
There are several systems for categorizing moral psychologies relative to each other.
Shweder’s Big Three Ethics
Richard Shweder proposed that moral reasoning systems across the globe fell into one of the Big Three frameworks:


The Ethic of Autonomy: individuals are the primary moral agents, so actions are morally wrong if they deprive someone of autonomy. Under this view, someone may have a right to use and sell substances because they have ought to have bodily autonomy and the right to trade property, and they can only have their behavior regulated if it impedes on someone else’s autonomy. However, one could also argue that addictive substances inherently impair someone’s autonomy, so selling them is the morally wrong autonomous act in the situation.


The Ethic of Community: individuals are members of larger groups, so actions are morally wrong if they threaten group cohesion for the sake of individual preferences. Substances that lead individuals to fall out of compliance with their social expectations or society’s norms lead to condemnation from this view since it weakens group cohesion. However, other substances are seen as gifts that improve group morale, like bringing coffee for everyone in the office or bringing wine to a dinner party.


The Ethic of Divinity: individuals are creatures that carry the sacred in them, so actions are considered wrong if they degrade or pollute the sacredness of a person or the divine order. In this perspective, the consumption of certain substances or participation in certain processes is thought to harm the sacred character within an individual, and purification rituals are often required to rid one of the contamination or harm.


Rule-based vs. Role-based Morality
Another axis of comparison involves:


Rule-based morality: moral codes operate based on abstract rules like legal codes or math codes, like “do not lie” or “treat others equally”, such that lying about a murder to protect a family member is considered wrong because one’s moral rules say that killing people is wrong and lying is wrong.


Role-based morality: moral imperatives are dependent on the context of one’s role, such that lying to protect a family member in spite of the rules or fairness is considered an act of loyalty in their role as family. Similarly, a lawyer who helps to obscure or diminish evidence of wrongdoing on behalf of a client is considered professional and disciplined in their role as amoral legal defense.


Haidt’s Moral Foundation Theory
Jonathan Haidt’s Moral Foundation Theory identifies 6 moral foundations that overlap with some of the points discussed above:


Harm/Care


Fairness/Cheating


Loyalty/Betrayal


Authority/Subversion


Sanctity/Degradation


Liberty/Oppression


Haidt’s research indicates that those who identify as politically liberal in the United States tend to highly value the Harm/Care and Fairness/Cheating with less emphasis on the others. Meanwhile, the politically conservative tend to have a more even balance across the others, meaning they emphasize Loyalty/Betrayal, Authority/Subversion, and Sanctity/Degradation more.
Examples
Protestant Moral Psychology
A phrase I use very often on this site and in general that’s applicable to American culture is “Protestant moral psychology.” By this, I mean a constant internalized moral surveillance that looks for the signs someone is one of the few destined for success in their demonstrations of purity, discipline, and work ethic. The abstract moral laws of God apply to everyone, which then leads to lot of emphasis on laws and contracts.
Max Weber argued that the Protestant Reformation led a moral transformation in the significance of work such that it became a moral calling instead of just a material necessity. Weber attributed the foothold of capitalism and industrialism in America and Western societies to this psychological association between self-worth, self-reliance, and productivity, though this perspective has been heavily criticized by scholars and commentators. Marxist scholars argued that Weber got the cause-and-effect backwards so that wealthy property owners adopted the Protestant theology that justified their capital accumulation, and modern historians have access to more data analysis that backs that up. Historians have also pointed out that many of the capitalist structures like banking networks and international joint-stock ventures were already being used as far back as the Renaissance under a Catholic Italy. Plus, Protestant regions like Scotland didn’t reflect anywhere near the same kind of growth that America had. Where Protestant beliefs did encourage more growth was through an emphasis on increasing literacy rates, since Protestant communities wanted every child to be able to read the Bible themselves and set up school systems to train children to do so.
Alcoholics Anonymous and other 12-step groups are heavily rooted in Protestant moral psychology. William Wilson (Bill W.) attributes the spiritual theory of AA to the Oxford Group, which was explicitly a Protestant revivalist movement led by Lutheran minister Frank Buchman. The idea of an individual needing to surrender their ego and accept being powerless through a spiritual awakening in order to let the will of a Higher Power restore and maintain their sanity is profoundly Protestant. Internal self-examination to identify moral wrongs and purify oneself through rituals involving the confession of the conscience so that a Higher Power may act on and through you is a core theme in 12-step groups. The use of the term “alcoholic” or “addict” as an equalizer of identity encourages a perspective that views everyone as uniform individuals following abstract rules rather than necessarily repairing one’s relationship to society outside of the program.

wiki/morphinism.title: Morphinism
wiki/morphinism.content:
Overview
Morphinism is a historical term for what we now would call a Substance Use Disorder (SUD) or Opioid Use Disorder (OUD) where the drug-of-choice is morphine. It’s mostly unused now, but the term is still occasionally found in literature or databases.
Historical Context
“The term ‘morphinism,’ or morphine disease, is used in this work to include all forms of opium disease. In fact, it is intended in most instances to be the equivalent of narcotic disease. While sixteen alkaloids have been isolated from opium, morphine is present in so much larger quantities, and is so much more potent than any of the other alkaloids, that practically all the medicinal or narcotic effects of that drug are due to the alkaloid morphine.” - George Pettey, The Narcotic Drug Diseases and Allied Ailments: Pathology, Pathogenesis, and Treatment (1913)

wiki/mothers-against-drunk-driving.title: Mothers Against Drunk Driving
wiki/mothers-against-drunk-driving.content:
Overview
Mothers Against Drunk Driving (MADD) is America’s largest grassroots non-profit dedicated to the issues of drunk driving and underage drinking. It has lobbied for over 1000 laws across the United States at the local, state, and federal levels, notably setting the legal drinking age to 21 and the permitted Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) limit for driving to 0.08%. Recently, MADD is lobbying for the passage of the HALT Act (Honoring Abbas Family Legacy to Terminate Drunk Driving) which would require impairment detection technology in every new passenger vehicle by 2030. Internal metrics show that MADD’s efforts have cut drunk driving fatalities by up to 51%, which means 500,000 lives have been saved since 1980, and about 1 million victims of crashes with impaired drivers have received legal, financial, or emotional assistance. 1

wiki/motion-picture-production-code.title: Motion Picture Production Code
wiki/motion-picture-production-code.content:
Overview
The Motion Picture Production Code, also called the Hays Code, was a set of guidelines used by Hollywood studios between 1934 to 1968 to ward off censorship from every level of government and boycotts from civic organizations. It wasn’t until Joseph Burstyn, Inc. v. Wilson (1952) that movies were actually considered a medium of communication that was protected by the First Amendment’s free speech protections and put them beyond local censorship boards. The Motion Picture Producers and Distributors of America (MPPDA) created the Production Code Administration (PCA) to enforce the Hays Code against its member studios. Studios would be fined 25,000 (about 615,000 in 2026) and member theaters pledged to never screen motion pictures without a PCA Certificate of Approval.
For substance use, this meant any portrayals were forbidden if they:


Encouraged or justified use


Glamorized effects


Oversimplified recovery


Showed mechanics


Emphasized profits


Involved children


Government officials and politicians would often meet with studios to shape the way substance use was depicted. The name “Hays” comes from Will H. Hays, a former Postmaster General who was hired as a lobbyist for the MPPDA. Agencies like the Federal Bureau of Narcotics (FBN) led by Commissioner Harry J. Anslinger met with studio executives to push for storylines that depicted substance use as dangerous and criminal.
In 1968, the Hays Code was replaced with the modern rating system based on ages: G, M, R, and X.

wiki/motivated-belief.title: Motivated Belief
wiki/motivated-belief.content:
Overview
A motivated belief is a belief that someone holds because they want it to be true rather than because they think the evidence suggests the belief is most likely true. Another term for this phenomenon is “motivated reasoning.”
In psychology, it’s considered a self-defense mechanism since someone’s justification can be logical or rational while still being motivated by a personal reason. This helps someone feel better or more secure in their worldview, but it can also be a way to combat feelings of learned helplessness, where someone might overestimate their chances of success to stay persistent. This is especially interesting given the phenomenon of depressive realism, in which individuals suffering from depression or learned helplessness can be more accurate at judging their lack of control.

wiki/mutual-aid.title: Mutual Aid
wiki/mutual-aid.content:
Overview
Mutual aid describes a system where members of a community voluntarily share resources and support each other.
Common examples of mutual aid include:


Community Fridges and Pantries: public locations where anyone can take or leave food and hygiene products, often without verification.


Community Kitchens and Neighborhood Cookouts: locations that provide free, hot meals on a regular basis


Free Stores and Clothing Swaps: places that collect clothes, household goods, books, baby supplies, and other common items and distribute them for free.


Lending Libraries: community-managed inventories of goods shared among neighbors, ranging from books to medical equipment


Community Gardens: plots cultivated by a community to provide fresh produce for the surrounding households.


Bail Funds: money pooled together by a community to pay bail that individuals can’t afford


Within recovery spaces, mutual aid networks play an incredibly large role. Traditional 12-step fellowships like Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) and Narcotics Anonymous (NA) are some of the most recognizable mutual aid networks worldwide. Other programs in the recovery space that are built around mutual aid include SMART Recovery, LifeRing Secular Recovery, Women for Sobriety, Refuge Recovery, Recovery Dharma, and many others. Peer-led nonprofit or community programs can also facilitate material exchanges, like Syringe Services Programs (SSPs) and Drug User Unions.

wiki/n-acetyl-cysteine.title: N-Acetyl Cysteine
wiki/n-acetyl-cysteine.content:
Overview
N-acetyl cysteine (NAC) is an amino acid supplement that can help raise antioxidants, decongest the lungs, and address acetaminophen overdoses. There is some mixed evidence on whether NAC can also address symptoms of Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD).
Commentary
NAC tastes and smells like straight ass. It is made with sulfur, so opening a bottle of NAC can feel like releasing a mild stink bomb. Seriously, it’s like a whiff of Satan’s armpits and I prepare for the potential to vomit each time.

wiki/naatp-addiction-industry-directory.title: NAATP Addiction Industry Directory
wiki/naatp-addiction-industry-directory.content:
Overview
The National Association of Addiction Treatment Providers (NAATP) is a trade association that started in 1978 for private non-profit addiction programs to advocate for regulatory regimes like uniform insurance coverage. In 2016, they launched the Addiction Industry Directory (AID) as an unsponsored database of members in good standing that pledge to follow the NAATP Code of Ethics.
Provider Members are those licensed to provide treatment services, and Accredited Provider Members are those who specifically achieved accreditation through a body the NAATP recognizes. Supporter Members provide support to treatment services though may not be licensed to deliver services themselves. NAATP Members can login to a listing management system to update their information in real-time, which contrasts with services like FindTreatment.gov which rely on voluntary survey reponses which are issued regularly but not in real-time.
Commentary
It should be noted that the AID has a page dedicated to the benefits of being listed in the directory for its members, in which they report nearly 20,000 page views per month and “prestigious” search engine placement. Many are not aware that the online content space for addiction and recovery services is heavily dominated by search engine optimization (SEO) strategies, which is why almost every time you look something up about addiction or recovery, you’re likely to find a blog or information page hosted by a treatment provider marketing their own services. This doesn’t mean the information you might receive is wrong per se, or that there’s anything particularly suspicious about members listed in the directory, but it does speak to the decentralized nature of information and referrals within recovery spaces. The AID markets itself as a cooperative solution to this:
“Not only does the directory help its members; the members help the directory. Through their inclusion in our archives, distinguished members effectively “vouch for” the credibility of the Addiction Industry Directory and reinforce NAATP’s mission to advance the addiction treatment field. In so doing, they ensure the continued high ranking of the service in search results, pushing other, possibly pseudo directories further down in search results.”
So, there’s a little bit of the ol’ “you scratch my back, and I’ll scratch yours” dynamic here.
One of the motivations I had behind this site is to aggregate information about treatment without selling or promoting treatment services, which minimizes the biases that lead some information to be excluded or outdated.
Links

www.naatp.org/resources/addiction-industry-directory
www.naatp.org/resources/news/new-addiction-industry-directory-aid/jul-11-2016
