wiki/naikan.title: Naikan
wiki/naikan.content:
Overview
Naikan is a Japanese approach to introspection that uses three fundamental questions about each relationship in one’s life to guide a sense of gratitude and agency:


What have I received from this person?


What have I given to this person?


What troubles and difficulties have I caused this person?


Traditional naikan is derived from an extremely ascetic Buddhist meditative practice called mishirabe before it was streamlined. It involves 7 days of isolation with 15 hours a day spent on self-reflection, interrupted every hour by a guide, a Naikan-sha, who listens for a few minutes about what the individual has analyzed. 60% of one’s time is meant to be spent on the third question.
In contrast to Western modalities of therapy and wellness, Naikan adopts a more “Eastern” view of an interdependent self whose identity is inextricably bound into the relationships they maintain with the people and world around them. The Naikan-sha is there primarily as a witness to the individual’s analysis and changes rather than playing the role of a therapist who might interpret elicited information.

wiki/naloxone.title: Naloxone (Narcan)
wiki/naloxone.content:
Overview
Naloxone is the generic name of a medication that reverses opioid overdoses. Narcan is the brand name for the same medication, just prepackaged as a nasal spray available over-the-counter (OTC). It works as an opioid antagonist that attach to opioid receptors in the brain to block the molecules of a substance from reacting with the body, which restores normal breathing in the case of an overdose. It’s also safe to take in the case that someone is given the medication but doesn’t have opioids in their body. Although it’s considered extremely effective at reversing overdoses, the half-life for naloxone is much shorter than that of opioids like fentanyl, which means that someone can slip back into an overdose after it’s been reversed - a process called re-narcotization.

wiki/naltrexone.title: Naltrexone
wiki/naltrexone.content:
Overview
Naltrexone is an opioid antagonist that reduces cravings and blocks feelings of euphoria for both Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD) and Opioid Use Disorder (OUD). It can be taken as a monthly injection called Vivitrol.

wiki/narcissism.title: Narcissism
wiki/narcissism.content:
Overview
Narcissism describes a personality trait characterized by excessive fixation on oneself, a sense of grandiosity, and a reduced capacity for empathy for others, which can manifest in clinically-significant levels through Narcissistic Personality Disorder (NPD). The DSM-5-TR identifies 9 criteria for NPD, 5 of which must be met to receive the diagnosis:


A grandiose sense of self-importance


A preoccupation with fantasies of unlimited success, power, brilliance, beauty, or ideal love


A belief that he or she is special and can only be understood by high-status people


A need for excessive admiration


A sense of entitlement


Interpersonally exploitive behavior


A lack of empathy


Envy of others or a belief that others are envious of him or her


A demonstration of arrogant and haughty behaviors

wiki/narcogenocide.title: Narcogenocide
wiki/narcogenocide.content:
title: Narcogenocide
Overview
The term “narcogenocide” sees use mostly in historical and academic debates about drug policies being used to suppress and control mass populations.
One of the earliest uses of the term came from methadone clinics funded by the United States federal government in the early 1970s to deal with heroin addiction in urban communities. Many activists from civil rights organizations, including the Black Panther Party, argued that the clinics were a form of “narco-genocide” that ignored the roots of addiction while normalizing the chemical pacification of communities of color through synthetic opioids controlled by the government.

wiki/narcoterrorism.title: Narcoterrorism
wiki/narcoterrorism.content:
Overview
Narcoterrorism refers to the bidirectional relationship between drug trafficking and terrorism: traffickers use terrorist tactics to expand and protect their operations, and terrorists participate in trafficking to fund their operations.
The Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) defines it more narrowly in the direction of funding terrorism through some relationship with the illicit drug trade:
“a subset of terrorism, in which terrorist groups, or associated individuals, participate directly or  indirectly in the cultivation, manufacture, transportation, or  distribution of controlled substances and the monies derived from these  activities. Further, narco-terrorism may be characterized by the  participation of groups or associated individuals in taxing, providing  security for, or otherwise aiding or abetting drug trafficking endeavors in an effort to further, or fund, terrorist activities.” 1
Historical Context
The term was first popularized in 1983 by then-President Fernando Belaunde Terry of Peru when describing violence by drug traffickers directed towards anti-narcotics law enforcement.

wiki/narrative-therapy.title: Narrative Therapy
wiki/narrative-therapy.content:
Overview
Narrative therapy is a form of therapy that views identity as a series of narratives rather than a structure that may be defective for biological or psychological reasons, and it frames problems as external forces acting on the client which can be addressed by constructing alternative narratives that feature resilience.
Suppose a client says “I can’t go outside because I get overwhelmed with anxiety.” Asking a question from the traditional model of internalized problems might sound like “What are you anxious about when you go outside and see crowds?” Alternatively, a model of externalized problems might sound like “What does Anxiety tell you when you go outside that makes you feel helpless?” or “Where did Anxiety learn to repeat these thoughts at you?” to explore the sociocultural experiences or rules that influence the individual. Finding solutions for this Anxiety might start with a question like “How did you beat Anxiety in the past?”
Narrative therapy, much like liberation-psychology, emerged in the 1970s and 1980s as a rejection of the Western convention of pathologizing individuals with an internal locus of control rather than organizing against social structures that determine someone’s environment and cues. It was founded by Michael White and David Epston and influenced heavily by Michel Foucault’s arguments that internal feelings of failure are the result of dominant societal expectations subjugating individual identity. A major goal of narrative therapy is deconstructing the societal rules that produce an internal sense of failure.

Overview
The National Alliance for Recovery Residences (NARR) is a non-profit that sets national standards for recovery housing like sober living environments (SLEs) in the United States. Founded in 2011, they merged with the Association of Halfway House Alcoholism Programs (AHAP) in 2013. NARR operates on an affiliate network model, which means that it accredits regional organizations which manage inspections for operators in their regions. State health departments will often require a sober living home to receive a NARR-compliant certification from a regional affiliate in order to gain access to subsidies and referrals.

wiki/national-black-harm-reduction-netwo.content:
Overview
The National Black Harm Reduction Network (HBHRN) is the first Black-led harm-reduction organization in the United States, which formalized a decades-old mutual aid and volunteer collective that conducted syringe exchanges in predominantly Black communities. Its work includes opioid settlement advocacy, “Reclaiming Leadership” to promote diversity in public health leadership, national campaigns like “Black Parents Against Overdose,” Naloxone (Narcan) distribution campaigns like “You Have the Power to Save Lives,” technical assistance (TA) to local organizations that provide harm-reduction services, and argue against systemic disparities in public health policy and drug policing.

wiki/national-center-for-advancing-trans.title: National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences
wiki/national-center-for-advancing-trans.content:
Overview
The National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences (NCATS) is a part of the U.S. National Institutes of Health (NIH) and has the goal of translating scientific discoveries into new treatments to be delivered to patients. Their projects include Clinical and Translational Science Awards (CTSA) Program that supports medical research institutions doing translational research with clinics, provides resources to advocacy groups like the “NCATS Toolkit for Patient-Focused Therapy Development,” hosts an assay guidance manual for early-stage drug discovery, and advances New Approach Methodologies (NAMs).
Unlike other NIH institutes that focus on behavioral therapy as part of the Helping to End Addiction Long-term (HEAL) Initiative, NCATS focuses on anti-addiction and pain management therapies that come out of laboratory research. They’ve designed 3-D human tissue chips to mimic human brain systems since animal testing fails often in predicting how medications might work in the brain, curated the HEAL Target and Compound Library featuring nearly 3000 molecules, and sped up clinical trials through its CTSA Trial Innovation Network.

wiki/national-center-for-state-courts.title: National Center for State Courts (NCSC)
wiki/national-center-for-state-courts.content:
Overview
The National Center for State Courts (NCSC) is a non-partisan non-profit organization that supports state courts around the United States and around the world. It drives the growth of Problem-Solving Courts, like Drug Courts, DUI Courts, and Veterans Treatment Courts, which can use diversion through treatment programs instead of traditional sentencing. The NCSC helps courts move through competency restoration backlogs where mental health issues, possibly substance-induced, impaired a defendant’s legal competency. It also manages the National Treatment Court Resource Center to track treatment court metrics against health and demographic data.

wiki/national-conference-on-addiction-re.title: National Conferece on Addiction Recovery Science (NCARS)
wiki/national-conference-on-addiction-re.content:
Overview
Hosted by the Consortium on Addiction Recovery Science (CoARS) since 2024, the National Conference on Addiction Recovery Science (NCARS) claims to be the only national conference exclusively focused on the science of substance use disorder recovery. It was designed as a virtual-first event to maximize accessibility and input into discussions about measuring recovery capital rather than just abstinence or harm reduction.
Attendees


Nora Volkow, Director of the National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA)


George Koob, Director of the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA)


William White


Tom Coderre, then-Acting Principal Deputy Secretary for the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA)


Tisha Wiley, Chief of the Services Research Branch at NIDA


Laura Kwako, Health Scientist Administrator at NIAAA

wiki/national-council-on-alcoholism-and-.content:
Overview
The National Council on Alcoholism and Drug Dependence was founded by Marty Mann to address alcoholism through campaigns arguing that it was “a disease like any other,” making it the oldest nonprofit advocacy organization for addiction in the United States.

wiki/national-fentanyl-awareness-day.title: National Fentanyl Awareness Day
wiki/national-fentanyl-awareness-day.content:
Overview
The National Fentanyl Awareness Day on April 29th was established in 2022 by a grassroots coalition of families who had lost children to fentanyl overdoses.
The organization Facing Fentanyl established National Fentanyl Prevention and Awareness Day on August 21st.
Both were formally acknowledged by federal agencies like the CDC as well as state governments that passed resolutions to officially incorporate the dates into public health calendars.

wiki/national-health-service.title: National Health Service (NHS)
wiki/national-health-service.content:
Overview
The National Health Service (NHS) is the healthcare system of the United Kingdom, which uses public funds to provide most services for free at the point of use for legal residents.
Most care for Substance Use Disorders (SUDs) comes from Community Drug and Alcohol Teams (CDATs), where a keyworker coordinates detoxification, medications like buprenorphone or methadone for Opioid Use Disorder (OUD), Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (CBT), motivational interviewing, etc. For severe cases, the NHS uses Inpatient Detoxification Units (IPUs), where patients at-risk of fatal withdrawals will be admitted to a hospital ward for 24-hour monitoring. Residential treatment program placement is funded by local councils or charities rather than the NHS.
The NHS also manages harm-reduction initiatives like Needle and Syringe Programmes (NSPs), Naloxone (Narcan) distribution, and rapid testing for Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs).
NHS drug and alcohol services generally accept self-referrals, so a previous appointment with a General Practitioner that leads to a referral isn’t necessary. The NHS Find Local Addiction Services Tool allows users to search for services by postcode to find clinics in a desired location. The NHS-backed Talk to Frank platform provides a 24/7 confidential helpline and database of support services across England.

The National Overdose Awareness Week is an American initiative that coincides with a global International Overdose Awareness Day on August 31st, from August 28th to September 3rd.

wiki/national-prevention-week.title: National Prevention Week
wiki/national-prevention-week.content:
Overview
Led by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), the National Prevention Week (NPW) is an annual substance use prevention campaign held in the second week of May, as studies show a spike in first-time drug use around June and July. The campaign gives educators and community leaders an opportunity to educate students before they go off on summer break.

wiki/national-recovery-month.title: National Recovery Month
wiki/national-recovery-month.content:
Overview
Led by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), the National Recovery Month is held every September. Studies have shown spikes in first-time drug use in students over the summer, so September serves as a chance to reach students who might need help at the start of a new school year. Each year has a new theme to give local advocacy groups a common focus point, such as “Recovery is For Everyone.”

wiki/national-survey-on-drug-use-and-hea.title: National Survey on Drug Use and Health (NSDUH)
wiki/national-survey-on-drug-use-and-hea.content:
Overview
The National Survey on Drug Use and Health (NSDUH) is sponsored by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), and it annually surveys 70,000 members of the American civilian population aged 12 or older in all 50 states and Washington, D.C. It excludes those who are unhoused, active-duty military, or institutionalized in jails or hospitals.
The percentage of Americans experiencing a substance use disorder (SUD) in the past year dropped from 16.8% in 2024 to 15.3% to 2025. Any Mental Illness (AMI) percentages decreased from 23.4% to 20.6%. Only 1 in 6 of those who qualified for clinical SUD treatment were able to receive it.

wiki/native-hawaiian-or-pacific-islander.title: Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islanders (NHOPIs)
wiki/native-hawaiian-or-pacific-islander.content:
Overview
In 1997, the U.S. Office of Management and Budget (OMB) issued a directive that separated the racial group “Asian” from “Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander” (NHPI or NHOPI), which refers to those whose origins are traced to Hawaii, Guam, American Samoa, Polynesia, Micronesia, and Melanesia. The category spans as many as 50 distinct ethnic groups.

wiki/negative-reinforcement.title: Negative Reinforcement
wiki/negative-reinforcement.content:
Overview
Negative reinforcement is the process through which the likelihood of a behavior is influenced through the incentive of avoiding or removing a stimulus. Note that “negative” doesn’t mean bad or unpleasant here; it means removing or negating some effect.
In the context of substance use, positive reinforcement is usually the initial motivation since consuming the substance produces pleasure or a high. Eventually, as someone becomes dependent or addicted to the substance to the point of withdrawals without it, negative reinforcement fuels substance use since one’s baseline state becomes seemingly intolerable and they would use to negate that feeling. One of the focuses of modern addiction treatment involves building coping skills that include distress tolerance which can help interrupt the cycles of negative reinforcement, since cravings and withdrawals are temporary experiences that will go away if tolerated.

wiki/neglect.title: Neglect
wiki/neglect.content:
Overview
Neglect has both medical and legal contexts that are related in that they both describe a caregiver abandoning an obligation to help someone dependent on them.
The DSM-5 has a section called “Other Conditions That May Be a Focus of Clinical Attention” with a subsection “Abuse and Neglect” that includes Child Neglect, Parent-Child Relational Problems, Child Affected by Parental Relationship Distress, and Child Psychological Abuse. These aren’t considered mental disorders, but identifying them can guide treatment plans and add context for complications in how a disorder presents itself.

wiki/nelson-bradley-career-achievement-a.title: Nelson Bradley Career Achievement Award | NAATP
wiki/nelson-bradley-career-achievement-a.content:
Overview
The Nelson Bradley Career Achievement Award was established in 1983 by the National Association of Addiction Treatment Providers (NAATP) as a lifetime achievement award.
Nelson J. Bradley was a psychiatrist who served as the superintendent of Willmar State Hospital in Minnesota, pioneering an approach that incorporated 12-Step principles and peer counselors into treatment facilities, now called the Minnesota Model or Twelve-Step Facilitation (TSF). A 2020 Cochrane Systematic Review analyzed 27 studies of 10,000 participants and found that manualized TSF programs inspired by the Minnesota Model are more effective for sustained long-term abstinence than clinical interventions like Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (CBT).
Bradley was instrumental in the scientific community’s shift to seeing addiction as a chronic brain disease than a moral or willpower problem, though other researchers have argued that the brain disease model has pathologized and medicalized an issue rooted in socioeconomic systems.
Some argue that the main value of the Minnesota Model is peer support, which increases recovery capital by introducing people to mutual aid societies that share emotional support, but tangible support as well. Navigating healthcare, employment, housing, culture, and other aspects of daily life are made significantly easier through supportive community networks, which clinical or therapeutic interventions are not necessarily equipped to provide or substitute for.
Bradley’s influence on the field was substantial, and the Minnesota Model remains the most common base for treatment formats used in the United States. Bradley’s legacy did a lot of work to destigmatize addiction away from the untreatable death sentence that medical professionals assumed it was. We can discuss the flaws of the Minnesota Model as a particular protocol or treatment with the advantage of new evidence and hindsight, but the man himself made major changes in the way addiction was perceived by the scientific and medical communities.

wiki/neurasthenia.title: Neurasthenia
wiki/neurasthenia.content:
Overview
Neurasthenia is a diagnosis of chronic fatigue alongside distressing physical symptoms. In Western psychiatry, the diagnosis has mostly been replaced with the diagnoses of depression or chronic fatigue syndrome. The World Health Organization’s ICD-10 still includes it as some cultures still use it as an alternative to depression. The symptoms include:


persistent fatigue


headaches


sleep disturbances or insomnia


irritability


inability to relax


dizziness


muscle aches


gastrointestinal issues


impaired concentration or memory


Historical Context
The term was popularized by George Miller Beard in 1869, and it was often attributed to living in fast-paced urban environments that exhausted mental energy. Physicians regularly prescribed stimulants like laudanum, morphine, and cocaine tonics to give people a boost, with alcohol as a widely-available depressant to counteract the energized mental state.

wiki/neuroadaptation.title: Neuroadaptation
wiki/neuroadaptation.content:
Overview
Neuroadaptation describes the process through which the brain changes its structure and function in response to internal or external conditions.
Within the context of substance use, the brain’s neuroadaptation is what leads to dependence and cravings. When substances repeatedly cause massive spikes in neurotransmmitters in the nucleus accumbens, which holds the reward center, the brain reduces the number of receptors for those neurotransmitters and slows down their natural production. As applied to dopmaine, the brain’s threshold for feeling the pleasure becomes too high to feel rewarded from ordinary activities like eating or socializing, which then drives cravings to use. Over sustained chronic use, this also leads to greater tolerance for the substance.

wiki/neuroanatomy.title: Neuroanatomy
wiki/neuroanatomy.content:
Overview
Neuroanatomy is the study of the structure of the nervous system, generally organized into three systems: the Central Nervous System (CNS), Peripheral Nervous System, and Autonomic Nervous System.
The CNS includes the brain and spinal cord, which means it’s primarily responsible for processing sensory data and issuing motor commands to the body. The brain is split into four lobes: frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital. It also includes the cerebellum and brainstem.

wiki/neurobehavioral-systems-lab.title: Neurobehavioral Systems Lab (NSL)
wiki/neurobehavioral-systems-lab.content:
Overview
The University of Kentucky’s Neurobehavioral Systems Lab (NSL) focuses on the neural mechanisms of decision-making and the cognitive impairments that result from Substance Use Disorders (SUDs), particularly resulting from cocaine, opioids, and cannabis. For instance, they use neuroimaging techniques to model brain activity computationally and examine how brain circuits are affected by chronic substance use or Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS).

Overview
Neurobiology is the study of the nervous system through the structure and function of neurons and their supporting cells.
Neurons are specialized cells that transmit signals through electrical impulses and neurotransmitters.
Neuroanatomy is a specific aspect of neurobiology that focuses on the physical structures of the the nervous system.

wiki/neurodivergence.title: Neurodivergence
wiki/neurodivergence.content:
Overview
Neurodivergence means having a brain whose mental processes and behaviors differ from the norm in one’s society and culture.
Examples include:


Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD)


Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)


Dyslexia, Dyscalculia, and Dysgraphia

wiki/neuroeconomics.title: Neuroeconomics
wiki/neuroeconomics.content:
Overview
Neuroeconomics is a field that explores the neurological and psychological mechanisms behind economic choices.
Classical economics has generally assumed humans follow rational choice theory, where they act to maximize their self-interest according to the information they have. Neuroeconomics views humans are organisms whose behavior is tied to neural circuits in the brain. The orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) calculates the subject value of options, the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) compares the options to each other, and the striatum (basal ganglia) encodes salience and expected rewards. The value of options are dynamically calculated by checking the difference between expected reward and actual reward, which we call the reward prediction error (RPE). A positive error in which reality exceeds expectations causes a dopamine spike that increases the value of that option in the future. A negative error in which reality fails to meet expectations triggers a lower dopamine spike than expected, so the value of the option is discounted in the future. Choices are made as a result of the interactions of two networks. The first is the affective system, which reacts to immediate rewards and threats. The second is the executive system, which applies abstract rules and plans for the future.
With substance use patterns, the brain’s baseline capacity to experience rewards is lowered as an adaptation to the constant dopamine spikes from using a substance. Cravings involve the brain seeking the extreme rewards of a substance that are guaranteed to produce more immediate dopamine spikes than the abstract reward of long-term goals like stable relationships or financial stability. If someone is a scarce environment that lacks natural rewards, then the relative value of using substances increases compared to the boredom or static suffering of other options. Many substances are also associated with a decrease in brain matter volume, so the executive system may further struggle to push back on the affective system seeking immediate rewards. This is one of the reasons Contingency Management (CM) is successful at helping sustain sobriety for those with stimulant use disorders where no reliably effective anti-craving medication is readily available.
Some scholars like Gene Heyman argue for the choice theory of addiction, which claims that addiction is not defined by involuntary compulsions but by voluntary choices shaped by reinforced preferences, and they respond to costs and benefits just like ordinary consumers do. The behaviors we call addiction are the result of melioration, or the act of choosing something that seems the best right now while isolating it from long-term impacts on future options. If the circuits in the brain responsible for calculating long-term consequences and future planning, like the dorsolateral prefrontal cortext (dlPFC), are compromised through chronic substance use, then the option of continuing substance use will seem like a highly rewarding option isolated from the abstract or long-term options.
The cycle of addicts wanting to quit early in the day but wanting to use by the end of it can be explained by hyperbolic delay discounting rather than dishonesty. When someone’s at work or school, their substance is generally not immediately available for open use, so the idea of using again is more distant and abstract. It becomes easier to compare the consequences of using again to the benefits of sobriety when both are in the future. When someone’s at home or driving past a bar, the idea of using substances feels far more immediately accessible, which can genuinely switch the brain’s preferences towards sustaining sobriety.
Examples
Walter Mischel’s Stanford Marshmallow Experiment
You may have heard of Walter Mischel’s Stanford Marshmallow Experiment where a child is given the choice of eating one marshmallow immediately or getting two marshmallows if they can wait for some period of time, like 15-20 minutes. The experiment tests the way the two networks interact to decide whether it’s worth delaying the first marshmallow for the second one. The return on investment (RoI) is 100% for just 15 minutes, which seems high and obvious. Early follow-up studies have shown that a child’s ability to wait strongly predicts higher SAT scores, lower BMI, and improved financial stability. Later studies found that the predictive power of the marshmallow test largely disappears when controlling for family wealth, parental education, and other environmental factors.
In other words, a child who grows up in an unstable environment, where promises are broken and resources are scarce and irregularly available, is more likely to have adapted to a model of quickly securing immediate rewards when they’re available. A child who grows up in a stable environment with a secure baseline for food has adapted to having the time to invest into long-term planning patterns. Neuroimaging studies have shown that children from the latter high-resource environments have greater volume and functional connectivity in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortext (dlPFC) which tracks abstract rules that suppress immediate impulses, like keeping the high ROI in mind. Children from severely impoverished environments have less grey matter volume within their prefrontal cortex and lower volume in the hippocampus, which means there are fewer cognitive resources available to filter distractions or help delay the impulse for immediate gratification. The brain physically structures itself differently to think less about the future if the environment can’t be trusted, which means prioritizing immediate rewards.

wiki/neuroethics.title: Neuroethics
wiki/neuroethics.content:
Overview
Neuroethics is the field that studies the ethical implications of neuroscientific discoveries.
There’s really two things that we mean by neuroethics. There’s the ethics of neuroscience, which contains a lot of extensions of bioethical dilemmas around human experimentation and treatment protocols, and then there’s the neuroscience of ethics, which explores the neurological mechanisms through which human agency and identity are formed.
Topics
Free Will
Consider the trolley problem, where a trolley is headed down a track that has 5 people tied to it, but you can push 1 person in front of the trolley to stop it. The consequentialist and utilitarian answer that sacrifices one person to save five activates the dorsolateral prefrontal cortext (dlPFC) associated with calculations and working memory. The deontological answer that has a rule or principle against actively causing harm activates the ventromedial prefrontal cortext (vmPFC) and the amygdala, which are associated with emotional processing and value assignment. These types of observations raise questions about free will and the extent to which our sense of ethics is tied to the structures of our brain.
There are three major schools of thought around the role of free will and moral responsibility:


Hard Incompatibilism: If our actions are determined by our brains and no one has agency over the design of their brains, then holding individuals morally accountable for the outcomes of that brain is actually punishing them for something out of their control. This means justice should be oriented around the idea that individuals may have dysfunctional neural architectures that should be addressed through rehabilitation that involves scientific and medical guidance.


Compatibilism: It’s possible for determinism to coexist with moral responsibility so long as a person has the capacity for rational thinking, since the purpose of moral rules is to incentivize certain behaviors between people. If there’s a preference in someone’s brain to break a rule and they fail to exercise their rational thinking to stop themselves, holding them responsible with consequences is part of disincentivizing the behavior by reinforcing consequences to a rational brain. In people who suffer from disorders that involve delusions or psychosis, we can see instances where determinism in terms of brain structure is plainly interfering with the individual’s capacity for rational thinking.


Illusionism/Revisionism: Objective moral responsibility may not exist just as the hard incompatibilists might say, but the framework of moral responsibility is an important societal construct. Illusionism follows the idea that people tend to behave less cooperatively and more aggressively when primed with ideas about free will being an illusion, so the illusion is important to maintain. Revisionism begins with the notion of revising the idea of moral responsibility such that we see the function of praising and blaming people as feedback loops for maintaining better standards of behavior.


Substance Use Disorder
Substance use disorders have historically presented controversial challenges around free will and responsibility.
The medical consensus surrounds the Brain Disease Model of Addiction (BDMA), which argues that chronic substance use alters the mesolimbic dopamine pathway and hijacks the reward center such that the brain becomes less responsive to natural rewards while craving the high of a substance instead. The framing initially received support in part because of its potential to reduce stigma by removing moral weakness from the description of addiction. Unfortunately, this only changed the nature of the stigma; the disease model might have decreased blame towards addicts, but it increased social distance since it inadvertently promoted the idea that addicts were fundamentally and structurally broken as people. Many addicts themselves have internalized that idea of being biologically destined to fail in sobriety as a form of learned helplessness.

wiki/neuroimaging.title: Neuroimaging
wiki/neuroimaging.content:
Overview
Neuroimaging refers to the technology and techniques used to picture or map the brain’s structures and activity. The most commonly used ones include:


Computed Tomography (CT)


Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)


Functional MRI (fMRI)


PET/SPECT (Positron Emission Tomography / Single-Photon Emission Computed Tomography)


Electroencephalography (EEG)


Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy (MRS)


Advancements in neuroimaging have played a substantial role in providing evidence for the disease model of addiction and encouraging a shift towards treatment rather than punitive incarceration.

wiki/neuroinflammation.title: Neuroinflammation
wiki/neuroinflammation.content:
Overview
Neuroinflammation refers to a type of inflammation that occurs in the central nervous system, including the brain and spine, in response to injury or infections.
For those struggling with Substance Use Disorder (SUD), neuroinflammation is a symptom whose presence further increases the risk of cravings and relapsing. Addictive substances bind directly to immune system receptors in the brain and provoke the release of cytokines, whose inflammation can be useful for short-term healing but harmful when chronically present. They damage the prefrontal cortex that’s responsible for decision-making and impulse control while inducing anxiety and anhedonia. These neurological changes make it harder for someone to resist cravings when they occur, but they can also compromise the commitments and routines of daily life in ways that increase the chance of relapse.

wiki/neuron.title: Neuron
wiki/neuron.content:
Overview
Neurons are cells that make up the nervous system and signal information throughout the body.

wiki/neuroplasticity.title: Neuroplasticity
wiki/neuroplasticity.content:
Overview
Neuroplasticity is the brain’s ability to change its neural circuits throughout its life. Structural plasticity refers to the ability of the brain to physically alter its connections, while functional plasticity refers to the ability to move functions to different regions. These mechanisms include:


Long-Term Potentiation (LTP): neural circuits that are used more often become stronger with faster and more efficient signal transmission


Synaptic Pruning: rarely used neural connections weaken and disappear to save energy for other parts of the network


Neurogenesis: new neurons are continually generated throughout one’s life, though the rate of generation slows down as one gets older

wiki/neuropsychology.content:

Neuropsychology is a branch of psychology and neuroscience that studies how the brain and nervous system relate to human cognitive and behavior.

wiki/neuroscience-ethics-and-society.title: NEUROSEC (Neuroscience, Ethics and Society)
wiki/neuroscience-ethics-and-society.content:
Overview
NEUROSEC (Neuroscience, Ethics and Society) is a research group under the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Oxford. Its key initiatives include:


NeurOx Young People’s Advisory Group (YPAG): a cohort aged 14-25 who produce research projects on the intersection of ethical frameworks and youth mental health


Design Bioethics Lab (DBL): an initiative building tools to explore moral attitudes and public concerns about health issues


Oxford Winter Neuroethics School (OWNS): an annual training program for students, professionals, and researchers to explore state-of-the-art neuroethics

wiki/neurotransmitter.title: Neurotransmitter
wiki/neurotransmitter.content:
Overview
Neurotransmitters are molecules used by neurons to transmit signals across gaps called synapses. Researchers have identified hundreds of distinct neurotransmitters. Some of the most common types include:


Glutamate: the most common excitatory neurotransmitter, associated with learning and memory


GABA (Gamma-aminobutyric acid): the common inhibitory neurotransmitter, associated with regulating anxiety and calming brain activity


Dopamine: a monoamine involved in reward, motivation, and motor control


Serotonin: a monoamine involved in regulating mood, sleep, appetite, and digestion


Norepinephrine: a neurotransmitter that drives alertness and attention, especially as part of the body’s stress response


Acetylcholine: an excitatory neurotransmitter responsible for muscle contractions and memory


The reward circuit, or the mesolimbic dopamine pathway, issues small releases of dopamine in response to natural survival activities like eating or socializing, but addictive substances produce big floods of neurotransmitters at once. Stimulants like cocaine and amphetamines block the reuptake of dopamine or force its release. Substances like opioids inhibit the “brakes” on dopamine release by mimicking natural neurotransmitters. The brain responds to these floods in neurotransmitters by reducing its receptors available to bind to them.

wiki/new-york-peer-aids-education-coalit.title: New York Peer AIDS Education Coalition (NYPAEC)

Overview
The New York Peer AIDS Education Coalition (NYPAEC) was an organization that pushed for harm reduction policies from 1989 to 2000. Their operations engaged over 20,000 at-risk clients every year through AIDS educator trainings, syringe exchanges, bleach kits, condoms, etc.

wiki/nhrc-drug-overdose-prevention-and-e.title: Drug Overdose Prevention and Education (DOPE) Project Trainings
wiki/nhrc-drug-overdose-prevention-and-e.content:
Overview
The National Harm Reduction Coalition (NHRC) administers the Drug Overdose Prevention and Education (DOPE) Project, which trains bystanders and community groups in San Francisco to recognize the signs of an opioid overdose and use Naloxone (Narcan). They claim to be the largest citywide naloxone distribution program in the country with over 13,000 people educated on reversing an opioid overdose.

wiki/nick-haslam.title: Nick Haslam
wiki/nick-haslam.content:
Works

Concept Creep and the Mental Health Crisis

“I argue that rising attention to harm, coupled with the pervasive influence of the mental health industry, has led to concepts of mental health and illness becoming increasingly expansive. This process of “concept creep” promotes the adoption of diagnostic identities and a tendency to over-pathologize experience and behavior. These trends not only increase the number of people who are identified as having mental health problems and seek treatment for them but may also worsen mental health through a range of self-fulfilling and iatrogenic processes.”

wiki/nicotime-out.content:

The aim of Nicotime-Out is to assist smokers in overcoming their addiction to cigarettes. By leveraging the power of mobile technology, the application provides various features and tools to support users on their journey towards a smoke-free life.”

wiki/nicotine.title: Nicotine
wiki/nicotine.content:
Overview
Nicotine is a naturally occurring alkaloid found in the leaves of tobacco plants that acts as a stimulant. Although it’s not generally classified as a carcinogen itself, it’s still an addictive substance that keeps people using tobacco products and consuming other substances alongside their nicotine.
The short-term effects of nicotine include elevated heart rate and blood pressure, temporary focus, reduced anxiety, appetite suppression, nausea, lightheadedness, etc. The long-term effects include harming adolescent brain development, raising the risk of heart disease and stroke, and interference with blood sugar regulation which can increase the risk of developing diabetes.
Nicotine is often used as a safer alternative to tobacco, but it’s by no means risk-free. Nicotine is the addictive compound in tobacco, but the toxic chemicals and heavy metals found in the smoke from tobacco is what drives cancer and lung disease. However, the other symptoms like heart disease and insulin resistance still occur when using nicotine alone.

wiki/nihon-kinshu-domei.title: Nihon Kinshu Domei
wiki/nihon-kinshu-domei.content:
Overview
Nihon Kinshu Domei, or the “Japan Temperance Union” in English, is an organization dedicated to preventing alcohol-related health issues and supporting rehabilitation programs for alcoholics.
Historical Context
Established in 1898 and called Nihon Kinshu Domei-kai (“Japan Temperance League”), the organization was founded as a nationwide consolidation of regional temperance groups.
In 1922, after 22 years of lobbying the National Diet, Nihon Kinshu Domei pushed for the passage of the Law Prohibiting Minors from Drinking to address underage drinking.
In the 1950s, Nihon Kinshu Domei introduced Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) to Japan, which was adapted for Japanese culture through the growth of Danshukai groups.

wiki/nimby.title: NIMBY (Not In My Backyard)
wiki/nimby.content:
Overview
NIMBY (Not in My Backyard) refers to the various movements opposed to new development within their neighborhoods, generally out of fear that it would impact property values to have services or properties available to low-income people near them. This includes opposition to treatment centers, methadone clinics, syringe service programs, overdose prevention centers, harm reduction facilities, and sober living homes, among other resources for those struggling with substance use. Studies have generally shown that the presence of these services does not increase crime rates in the local neighborhoods.

wiki/nina-s-studer.title: Nina S. Studer
wiki/nina-s-studer.content:
Nina Studer is a research associate at the University of Geneva with expertise in drinking studies, North Africa, colonialism, and women’s history.
Links

scholar.google.com/citations

wiki/ninkasi.title: Ninkasi
wiki/ninkasi.content:
Overview
Ninkasi is the Sumerian goddess of brewing, beer, and alcoholic beverages. The c. 1800 BCE Hymn to Ninkasi is widely considered the oldest beer recipe in the world, which functioned as both prayer and a mnemonic guide for brewers to remember without a common system of written manuals.

wiki/nitazenes.title: Nitazenes
wiki/nitazenes.content:
Overview
Nitazenes are a class of synthetic opioids that were developed as experimental pain relievers that never made it to market due to the severe risk of overdose. However, since 2019, they’ve been found more often as contaminants in other street drugs as a means of extending the psychoactive effects cheaply. Their molecular structure is significantly different than fentanyl’s, which means they can often get around regulations around manufacturing and testing.

wiki/nitrous-oxide.title: Nitrous Oxide
wiki/nitrous-oxide.content:
Overview
Nitrous oxide, also called laughing gas, is a mild sedative and analgesic used often in medical contexts. It’s also used in aerosol cans, like those used in whipped cream. In recreational substance use, nitrous oxide is used as an inhalant that produces euphoria and dissociation, often called “whippets.”

wiki/nora-d-volkow.title: Nora D. Volkow
wiki/nora-d-volkow.content:
Commentary
Volkow is the great-granddaughter of Leon Trotsky. I’m not shitting you even a little bit. She grew up in the house where he was assassinated with an icepick. Trotsky’s granddaughter now heads an organization under the United States federal government that funds more than 85% of the world’s research of the health consequences of drug abuse and addiction. It’s a small world, isn’t it?
Links

pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27475769/

wiki/norepinephrine.title: Norepinephrine
wiki/norepinephrine.content:
Overview
Norephinephrine is a neurotransmitter that functions as a stress hormone that increases focus, alertness, and memory retrieval. It’s released by the adrenal glands into the bloodstream during the fight-or-flight stress response.
Substances like cocaine and amphetamines block the norephinephrine transporter (NET), which leads it to build up in the synapses of the nervous system and produce a physical rush. Others like alcohol and opioids suppress norephinephrine, which is why they have sedating and calming effects at first. When chronic substance use begins to cause dependence or addictive behaviors, it means the brain reacts to stress and triggers with massive norepinephrine floods that increases alertness and focus on the disturbance, leading to cravings to get immediate relief.

wiki/north-american-syringe-exchange-net.title: North American Syringe Exchange Network (NASEN) directory
wiki/north-american-syringe-exchange-net.content:
Overview
The North American Syringe Exchange Network (NASEN) maintains a searchable directory of syringe services programs (SSPs) and other harm-reduction services. It relies on self-reporting, so programs aren’t listed until they reach out to the directory for inclusion.
Links
nasen.org/

wiki/north-american-syringe-exchange-net.title: North American Syringe Exchange Network (NASEN)
wiki/north-american-syringe-exchange-net.content:
Overview
The North American Syringe Exchange Network (NASEN) is the first and largest distributor of low-cost harm-reduction specialist and supporter of syringe services programs (SSPs) in the United States. It was founded by the Dave Purchase Project in 1992, and it maintains a directory on its website that includes over 590 harm-reduction locations and SSPs. 1
Links



Footnotes


North American Syringe Exchange Network - NASEN: NASEN Directory ↩

wiki/northwest-portland-area-indian-heal.title: Northwest Portland Area Indian Health Board (NPAIHB)
wiki/northwest-portland-area-indian-heal.content:
Overview
The Northwest Portland Area Indian Health Board (NPAIHB) was established in 1972 as a non-profit organization serving 43 federally recognized tribes in Oregon, Washington, and Idaho. Their programs include the Northwest Tribal Epidemiology Center to conduct community health research, adolescent health through We R Native, suicide prevention through THRIVE, substance use programs, dementia care, and specialized training for building clinical capacity for SUD.

wiki/nosology.title: Nosology
wiki/nosology.content:
Overivew
Nosology is the field of medicine that tries to systemically classify diseases with operational definitions and characteristics. There are three general methodologies for classifcation:


Categorical Models: diseases are distinct entities, and patients either meet the criteria for a disease or don’t.


Dimensional Models: health is a spectrum rather than a set of states where someone either has an illness or not.


Prototype Matching Models: diseases follow archetypes with some variation, and clinicians assess how close a patient’s presentation mirrors them.


The most common examples of classification systems include the International Classification of Diseases (ICD), Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM), Medical Subject Headings (MeSH), and Research Domain Criteria (RDoC).

wiki/nostalgia.title: Nostalgia
wiki/nostalgia.content:
Overview
Nostalgia casually means the sentiment of longing for the past. In the past, it used to be a formal diagnosis itself that was documented often in 19th century wars when soldiers appeared to have chronic despair after distance from home. By the time the DSM-5 was published, a clinically significant level of nostalgia might be seen as a sign of an adjustment disorder, prolonged grief disorder, or Major Depressive Disorder (MDD).
Although indulging nostalgia is often interpreted as being resistant to change and stuck in old ways, researchers have found evidence that nostalgia can have some positive psychological benefits. It can improve social connectedness, strengthen one’s sense of a continuous identity, be a source of motivation, and stimulate the release of comforting neurotransmitters like oxytocin. At the same time, nostalgia can become a maladaptive coping mechanism that really does enable someone to avoid dealing with a hopeless or unpleasant present. Trying to recreate an idealized past can also be an unhealthy pattern that interferes with growth and accepting change.

wiki/novel-psychoactive-substances.title: Novel Psychoactive Substances (NPS)
wiki/novel-psychoactive-substances.content:
Overview
Novel psychoactive substances (also called new psychoactive substances) refer to synthetic compounds that are intended to mimic the effects of other substances while dodging existing regulations. The term is often used interchangeably with designer drugs.
The main examples include:


Synthetic cannabinoids


Synthetic cathinones, also called bath salts


Synthetic opioids like nitazenes


Designer benzodiazepines


Synthetic hallucinogens

wiki/novelty-seeking.title: Novelty-Seeking
wiki/novelty-seeking.content:
Overview
In the field of psychology, the term “novelty-seeking” is considered a core personality or character trait that has substantial empirical backing in psychology and biology.
C. Robert Cloninger is a psychiatrist who proposed the Temperament and Character Inventory (TCI), which breaks down novelty-seeking into four subscales:


Exploratory excitability vs. Stoic indifference


Impulsiveness vs. Reflection


Extravagance vs. Reserve


Disorderliness vs. Regimentation


Cloninger argued that novelty-seeking emerged in individuals who have low baseline dopamine activity, which prompts them to experiment more in the outside world to chase rewards. Although the TCI model has faced criticisms for its general efficacy and Cloninger’s attempts to map traits to neurotransmitters has since been found to be oversimplified, clinicians often use it as a tool to assess the potential for certain personality disorders. For instance, having high novelty-seeking traits while also having low harm-avoidance traits helps generate a risk profile for substance use disorders. This is distinct from there being some kind of discrete or distinct addictive personality though.

wiki/nutritionism.title: Nutritionism
wiki/nutritionism.content:
Overview
Nutritionism is not actually the term for the study of nutrients, but a term for a framework that judges the healthiness of food by its independent nutrients. It’s considered a reductive way to look at diets that discards the significance of food as anything other a way to optimize health by calibrating nutrient levels.

wiki/nutritionist.title: Nutritionist
wiki/nutritionist.content:
Overview
A nutritionist is someone who provides advice about food choices and lifestyle towards health and wellness. The term “nutritionist” is not legally protected in America, so anyone can call themselves one. The protected titles are Registered Dietitian (RD), Registered Dietitian Nutritionist (RND), and Certified Nutrition Specialist (CNS), and they require degrees, supervised practice, and passing national exams.
Nutritionists who address recovery from chronic substance use will often focus on restoring neurotransmitters critical for the brain’s reward pathways that have been depleted, like dopamine and serotonin. Eating high amounts of protein will help add the amino acids it takes to build neurotransmitters, regulate mood, and reduce aggressive tendencies. Eating regular meals with complex carbohydrates can smooth out glucose spikes and dips; the brain can interpret low blood sugar as a craving because of an impulse for immediate relief from irritable moods or low energy states. Depending on one’s drugs of choice, there might be different types of nutrient depletions to emphasize. Chronic alcohol use interferes with the absorption of B vitamins like thiamine, folate, and B12. Stimulants can lead to extreme appetite suppresion and electrolyte imbalances. All substance use has the potential to significantly impact the gut microbiome, and since a huge portion of the body’s serotonin is produced in the digestive tract, rebuilding a population of healthy bacteria through fiber and probiotic foods can be both a physical and mental boost.

wiki/obesity.title: Obesity
wiki/obesity.content:
Overview
Obesity is a chronic disease characterized by carrying excessive fat to the point of experiencing health issues.
Much like substance use, overeating foods that are high in fat, sugar, or salt triggers a release of dopamine in the mesolimbic reward pathway. Chronically overeating these foods can build tolerance as well since the brain will reduce its dopamine receptors in response to the spikes from eating. However, in the same way that recreational substance use can be harmful even without a dependence or addiction, obesity can be harmful even if someone doesn’t meet the criteria for a food addiction. Up to 70% of someone’s Body-Mass Index (BMI) is determined by genetics, so it’s possible for many people to develop obesity as the result of a sedentary lifestyle or mild overconsumption if they’re genetically predisposed to it. For many who are in recovery from substance use, high-sugar and high-fat comfort foods can become a new addiction that transfers from their drugs of choice. Research tends to find that BMI and obesity are higher in patients who are in residential alcohol or drug treatment programs than the general population.

wiki/observations-on-the-means-of-preser.title: Observations on the Means of Preserving the Health of Soldiers and Sailors by Edward Cutbush (1808)

wiki/office-for-victims-of-crime.title: Office for Victims of Crime
wiki/office-for-victims-of-crime.content:
Overview
The Office for Victims of Crime (OVC) is an agency under the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) that funds crime victime services across the country. This includes a $3.9 billion crime victims fund supported by criminal fines and forfeited bail bonds, training and technical assistance (TTA) for state-level programs, and support for culturally-specific initiatives for indigenous Native American organizations. Its programs include compensation for Substance Use Disorder (SUD) treatment, with the recognition that substance use is commonly an attempt to self-medicate following the impacts of trauma.

wiki/office-of-addiction-services-and-su.title: Office of Addiction Services and Supports
wiki/office-of-addiction-services-and-su.content:
Overview
The New York State Office of Addiction Services and Supports (OASAS) is the state agency responsible for New York’s addiction prevention, harm reduction, treatment, and recovery services. They run:


12 Addiction Treatment Centers (ATCs) that serve up to 8000 New Yorkers annually


oversight of licensing for 1700 community-based programs and 900 treatment facilities that serve over 680,000 individuals a year


credentialing processes for professionals in the state, such as Certified Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Counselors (CASAC)

wiki/office-of-community-development-and.title: Office of Community Development & Substance Abuse (CDSA)
wiki/office-of-community-development-and.content:
Overview
The MIT Community Development and Substance Abuse Center (CDSA) addresses the university’s campus cultur around substance use. Their services include:


Brief Alcohol Screening and Intervention for College Students (BASICS)


PartySafe Training


Peer Education Alliances: partnerships with student safety groups to embed harm-reduction practices into campus culture


Self-Assessment Tools


Links

orgchart.mit.edu/letters/alcohol-abuse-illegal-drugs-and-our-community

wiki/office-of-national-drug-control-pol.title: Office of National Drug Control Policy Reauthorization Act of 1998
Office of National Drug Control Policy (ONDCP)
wiki/office-of-national-drug-control-pol.content:
Overview
The Office of National Drug Control Policy (ONDCP) is part of the Executive Office of the President of the United States and coordinates drug policy across 19 federal agencies. The Director who leads the agency is often referred to as the “Drug Czar” and directly advises the president.
Historical Context
The Office was established under the Anti-Drug Abuse Act of 1988, and the first director, William Bennett, was appointed in 1989. Initially, it focused heavily on the crack-cocaine epidemic and law enforcement as part of the War on Drugs. Under President Clinton, the agency expanded its focus on High Intensity Drug Trafficking Areas (HIDTA) and Drug-Free Communities (DFC) that gave federal grants to local anti-drug coalitions. After 9/11, the Bush administration looked increasingly at narcoterrorism and its role in funding international terrorist networks. The Obama administration applied a public health-oriented approach that focused on community prevention, expanding Substance Use Disorder (SUD) treatment access, and reforming a criminal justice system that featured mandatory minimums and mass incarceration. The next decades involving Presidents Biden and Trump would oversee overdose spikes as a result of drugs like fentanyl that have collectively been called an “opioid crisis.”

wiki/office-of-substance-use-programs-ed.title: Office of Substance Use Programs Education & Resources (SUPER)
wiki/office-of-substance-use-programs-ed.content:
Overview
The Office of Substance Use Programs Education & Resources (SUPER) at Stanford University’s Vaden Health Services, focused on education, prevention, and harm reduction. That includes providing counseling sessions, fentanyl test strips, Naloxone (Narcan), “SUPER cups” that prevent drinks from being spiked, peer-led workshops and trainings, and peer support networks for those with Substance Use Disorders (SUDs).
Links

super.stanford.edu/

wiki/on-the-preparations-of-the-indian-h.title: On the Preparations of the Indian Hemp, or Gunjah by William Brooke O'Shaughnessy (1839)

wiki/oncology.title: Oncology
wiki/oncology.content:
Overview
Oncology is the branch of medicine that focuses on cancer.
Substance use and cancer have a bidirectional relationship. Many substances increase the rate of developing cancer, cancer treatment can involve medications that are addictive, and someone can have co-occurring substance use disorders that can lead to different recommendations for a course of treatment.
According to the American Cancer Society, 80% of all lung cancer deaths involve tobacco use, and 30% of all cancer deaths involve combined tobacco and alcohol use. Intravenous drug use can increase the risk of contracting Hepatitis B and C, which can cause liver cancer.
Because cancer can cause severe pain, many patients are prescribed opioids like fentanyl and oxycodone, and so they may develop a dependence that resembles but is distinct from what we conventionally consider a substance use disorder. Others really will develop substance use disorders, or relapse if they already struggled with using substances.

wiki/onpoint-nyc.title: Onpoint NYC
wiki/onpoint-nyc.content:
Articles
OnPoint NYC operates one of the first Overdose Prevention Centers (OPCs) in the United States. Over four years of data tracking, they’ve saved almost 2000 lives wthout a statistically significant change in drug-related arrests in surrounding neighborhoods, diverting 50,000 instances of illicit substance use away from public areas and into supervised environments. That also has the benefit of keeping millions of units of hazardous public waste and trash, like used syringes, off the streets.
Links

onpointnyc.org/

wiki/opioid-crisis.title: Opioid Crisis
wiki/opioid-crisis.content:
Overview
The “opioid crisis” in the United States refers to a decades-long epidemic of opioid use and overdoses. About 80,000 people died from overdoses involving opioids in 2023, though fatalities peaked in 2022 and have dropped about 12% year-over-year.
Historical Context
In the 1990s, the over-prescription of painkillers like OxyContin led to a wave of drug-seeking behavior and overdoses. As restrictions tightened on those around 2010, heroin increasingly became a source of overdoses, followed by fentanyl in 2013.
Data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) shows that the peak of the crisis was 2022 with 107,000 overdose deaths per year. As of 2026, that number is 67,000 overdose deaths, showing about 14% drop year-over-year. Deaths that result from stimulants like cocaine and methamphetamine have also declined in the same time period, but the sharp reduction in fentanyl deaths is attributed to the widespread distribution of Naloxone (Narcan), expanded access to Medication for Opioid Use Disorder (MOUD), promotion of harm-reduction programs like syringe service programs (SSPs) and fentanyl test strips, and local recovery programs funded by opioid settlement funds.

wiki/opioid-policy-research-collaborativ.title: Opioid Policy Research Collaborative (OPRC)
wiki/opioid-policy-research-collaborativ.content:
Overview
The Opioid Policy Research Collaborative (OPRC) was founded in 2017 under the Institute for Behavioral Health (IBH) at Brandeis University leads data-driven approaches to making public policy and public health recommendations for the opioid-crisis and other substance use interventions. Their projects include:


Massachusetts Drug Supply Data Stream (MADDS): a community drug testing program that allows researchers to issue public health alerts for dangerous additives


StreetCheck App: a mobile application to standardize sample collection for drug-checking and share results with other groups in a community


Rapid Assessment of Consumer Knowledge (RACK): ethnographic studies that evaluate substance use patterns and barriers to harm-reduction services


Respond to Prevent (R2P): a trial investigating how to support pharmacists on educating individuals on using Naloxone (Narcan)


Pharmacy-Based Methadone Toolkit: a resource helping pharmacies work through regulatory barriers so they can begin to dispense methadone for Opioid Use Disorder (OUD)


News
October 2017
Trump Administration Declares Opioid Crisis A Public Health Emergency

www.npr.org/2017/10/26/560083795/president-trump-may-declare-opioid-epidemic-national-emergency

“Dr. Andrew Kolodny, co-directory of the Opioid Policy Research Collaboration at Brandeis University’s Heller School, calls the announcement ‘very disappointing.’ Without funding for new addiction treatment, he says, declaring a public health emergency isn’t enouhg. ‘This is not a plan,’ he says. ‘The administration still has no plan’ for dealing with opioids, he says.”

wiki/opioid-response-network-orn.title: Opioid Response Network
wiki/opioid-response-network-orn.content:
Overview
The Opioid Response Network is a coalition of over 40 organizations and 1000 professionals that address Substance Use Disorders (SUDs), with an emphasis on Opioid Use Disorder (OUD), at every level from individuals to state governments. It’s led by the American Academy of Addiction Psychiatry (AAAP) and funded by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA).
Links

opioidresponsenetwork.org/

wiki/opioid-treatment-program.title: Opioid Treatment Program (OTP)
wiki/opioid-treatment-program.content:
Overview
Opioid Treatment Programs (OTPs) are licensed medical facilities that provide Medications for Opioid Use Disorder (MOUD), usually with other entry points into health services as well. In the United States, OTPs can dispense methadone, buprenorphine, and naltrexone to eliminate withdrawal symptoms and block cravings when someone is coming off of other opioids. They also generally provide individual therapy, group therapy, counseling services, and peer support services for behavioral health interventions. They might also include toxicology tests, screening for infectious diseases, and distribute naloxone.

wiki/opioid-use-disorder.title: Opioid Use Disorder (OUD)
wiki/opioid-use-disorder.content:
Overview
Opioid Use Disorder (OUD) is a more specific category of Substance Use Disorder (SUD), and there are dedicated Opioid Treatment Programs (OTPs) that are licensed to provide therapy, medication, and peer support. Historically, the term morphinism described essentially the same diagnosis.

wiki/opioid.title: Opioid
wiki/opioid.content:
Overview
Opioids are a class of drugs that bind to opioid receptors in the brain and body, which can block pain signals and cause feelings of euphoria. Common examples include codeine, fentanyl, and heroin. Chronic use increases the risk of higher tolerance, dependence, and Opioid Use Disorder (OUD). Harm-reduction frameworks frequently include Naloxone (Narcan) distribution to reverse opioid overdoses.

wiki/opium-smoking-in-america-and-china-.title: Opium-Smoking in America and China (1882)
wiki/opium-smoking-in-america-and-china-.content:
“Much, too, was gathered from two smokers whom I subsequently had under treatment, and a number of the American smokers, male and female, in this city, and some from California and Nevada, who have kindly come to my house to smoke, thus affording me unusual facilities for studying the effects of the drug, when thus used, on different individuals and upon the various systems, organs, and apparatuses of each.”
“Two of my male nurses very kindly obliged me by smoking the drug a number of times, thus affording me special facilities for study, as they were constantly under my observation, and I was able to note more closely and accurately both the immediate and remote effects upon the novice. Finally, I smoked myself a number of times, both in large and small amounts, and often to decided excess, so that I might be the better able to fully understand subjective symptoms. Otherwise I should have been obligated to depend upon the word of the habitual smoker, which is not always reliable.”
Science used to be wild. You could just smoke opium with your homies in a lab or bring the lab to your home, write down a hundred or two pages of your trips and come downs, and influence federal drug policy for decades. Now that’s research. My guy took the Green Goblin approach and I respect it.
On a serious note, self-experimentation was a much more acceptable method in the past when the infrastructure to set up randomized controlled trials (RCTs) wasn’t available like today. Today, we might consider someone self-experimenting “for the sake of science, bro” to be in need of some form of institutionalization. On the other hand, we still do have an industry based around the idea of performing genetic modifications at home through mass-produced kits, so how far have we really come?
To Kane’s credit, he does make some observations that hold up today.
“The very fact that opium-smoking was a practice forbidden by law seemed to lead many who would not otherwise have indulged to seek out the low dens and patronize them, while the regular smokers found additional pleasure in continuing that about which there was a spice of danger. It seemed to add zest to their enjoyment.”
To make something taboo is to coerce people into repressing any expression of desire for that thing, and that in turn makes it an exotic thrill or relief to indulge it as an escape from repressive conditioning or social norms. At least, that’s what an armchair psychoanalyst might suggest. In modern times, we’ve seen a strange trend of anti-drug education in K-12 schooling actually being associated with an increase in use long-term. One explanation is that students who would have had no interest in trying an illicit substance were now informed about it, and the hysteria around it inadvertently implied it was a common practice to skirt institutional authorities to partake in the subcultures that practiced drug use as a ritual. Kane himself notes that,
“The practice spread rapidly and quietly among this class of gamblers and prostitutes until the latter part of 1875, at which time the authorities became cognizant of the fact, and finding, upon investigation, that many women and young girls, as also young men of respectable family, were being induced to visit the dens… No one can question the fascination of a vice, the strength of a habit that will lead people into such degradation for the gratification of the abnormal appetite.”
While the San Francisco Opium-Smoking Ordinance of 1875 was driven in part fears that Chinese men were corrupting young women by luring them into opium dens and either seducing or trafficking them, depending on which demonization upset the public more, Kane’s work points out that sexual immorality was associated with opium itself. Thus, even white young men using opium became an issue as far as the “protection” of women’s purity from such “abnormal appetites.” From an interview in the July 25, 1881 edition of the San Francisco Chronicle that Kane includes in his book:
“It will rapidly increase. The habit in past years, so far as whites were concerned, was confined to hoodlums and prostitutes mostly. Few decent men or women would care to come into Chinatown and smoke in the filthy dens here. Now that there are scores of places where the habit can be contracted in clean rooms and in respectable portions of the city, the practice will gradually extend up the social grade. Schoolboys and clerks who would never have gone into a Chinese den are already finding out the respectable places and learning to like the habit…”
Prior to modern addiction and drug use terminology, it was common to hear compulsive substance use referred to as “the habit” or “the vice.” We’re lucky enough actually to see a comparison between drinking and opium-smoking made here too:
“You know that there are some men who stand very high in the community who sometimes lose their balance and go on howling drunks. It’s nine chances to ten that if they are men moving in good society, they will wind up in the lowest dives on the Barbary Coast, where they drink the vilest whiskey they can get until they can be safely packed in a carriage and taken in charge by their friends. It’s part of the disease to want to get way down in the mud, and it’s the same with some opium smokers… The anti-opium-smoking ordinance drove the white smokers out of Chinatown, but the vice came along and scattered the smokers, planting them, in fact, in every portion of the city.”
Notably, the officer in this interview does refer to both the habit of drinking and opium-smoking as a “disease” well before a disease model had consensus from scientific institutions or the establishment of a group like Alcoholics Anonymous.
Links

s3.us-west-1.wasabisys.com/luminist/EB/I-J-K/Kane%20-%20Opium%20Smoking.pdf

wiki/opium-wars.title: Opium Wars
wiki/opium-wars.content:
Overview
The Opium Wars were two wars between 1839-1842 and 1856-1860, with the Chinese Qing dynasty on one side and Great Britan and France on the other. Western nations had a high demand for Chinese products like tea and silk, which China demanded payment for in silver instead of trading for Western manufactured goods. The British East India Company made up the deficit by trading opium grown in India to black market merchants in China. This led to an opioid epidemic that was tearing apart daily life in China for millions, so the government cracked down on opium by seizing and destroying stashes when they were found. This included the destruction of the property of British entities, who wanted to retaliate with the goal of forcing China to open its market and abide by Western standards of international trade and law. This eventually escalated into military conflict.
The wars still hold significance today for many in China, or the international diaspora, as a clear marker of the beginning of Western imperialism in East Asia.

wiki/opium.title: Opium
wiki/opium.content:
Overview
Opium is a natural narcotic made from the seeds of the poppy plant, containing morphine, codeine, and thebaine as active alkaloids. It’s the primary source from which other opiates are derived, including heroin.
Historical Context
Some of the earliest records of the poppy plant being cultivated date back to ancient Mesopotamia around 3400 BCE.

wiki/optogenetics.title: Optogenetics
wiki/optogenetics.content:
Overview
Optogenetics is a technique that uses genetic engineering and optics to stimulate cells. Scientists might put genes from bacteria into target cells that produce proteins as a reaction to specific colors of light, allowing them to turn cells on and off with high accuracy. This procedure has been used to mimick drug reinforcement by exciting dopamine neurons in living organisms and study the way cells change during dependence.
