wiki/orbitofrontal-cortex.title: Orbitofrontal Cortex
wiki/orbitofrontal-cortex.content:
Overview
The orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) is a region of the prefrontal cortex (PFC) that’s involved in assigning subjective value to choices, evaluating rewards, adapting when rules or rewards change, processing empathy, and regulating moods. In active addiction, the OFC assigns an inflated value to the substance that puts it above survival needs and fails to unlearn the habit of using substances even after it begins to cause harm. After sustained periods of sobriety, the OFC can slowly recovery gray matter volume and begin to reward one for the activities of daily life again.

wiki/oregon-health-authority.title: Oregon Health Authority
wiki/oregon-health-authority.content:
Overview
The Oregon Health Authority (OHA) was established in 2009 by the Oregon Assembly in House Bill 2116 to centralize the state’s public health programs under a single agency. It addresses Substance Use Disorder (SUD) through funding detox programs, outpatient counseling, medication-assisted treatment (MAT) like methadone and buprenorphine, peer support, housing assistance, Naloxone (Narcan), syringe service programs (SSPs), overdose surveillance, short-term stays in residential treatment facilities, and others.

wiki/oscar-wilde.title: Oscar Fingal O'Fflahertie Wills Wilde
wiki/oscar-wilde.content:
Known simply as Oscar Wilde.
Quotes
“Men and women at such moments lose the freedom of their will. They move to their terrible end as automatons move.”

wiki/over-the-counter.title: Over-The-Counter (OTC)
wiki/over-the-counter.content:
Overview
Referring to items that can be purchased at any store by taking it to the counter rather than requiring a prescription or special approval process.
Historical Context
Over the years, some truly crazy things have been available OTC:


Benzedrine inhalers: amphetamines as a spray made by Smith, Klein & French (SKF)


Mrs. Winslow’s Soothing Syrup: contained morphine and alcohol and was marketed to mothers for use to quiet babies


Vin Mariani: a wine infused with cocaine that was endorsed by Pope Leo XIII, Queen Victoria, and Thomas Edison


Cocaine toothache drops: sold for children to numb dental pain in a small dropper


Asthma cigarettes: a combination of jimsonweed and belladonna that dilated airways while causing severe hallucinations and delirium


Quaaludes


Radithor: water laced with lethal doses of radioactive Radium isotopes and marketed as “A Cure for the Living Dead”


Dr. Rose’s Arsenic Complexion Wafers: edible wafers loaded with arsenic that claimed to create cleaner, paler skin


Tapeworm diet pills

wiki/overdose-prevention-centers.title: Overdose Prevention Center (OPC)
wiki/overdose-prevention-centers.content:
Overview
Overdose Prevention Centers (OPCs), also called Overdose Prevention Sites (OPS) and Safer Drug Consumption Services (SCS), are places where someone can use substances they’ve acquired with professionals on-site to act in case of an overdose. They’re part of evidence-based harm reduction strategies that try to reduce the strain on emergency services by keeping populations who might need it nearby.
Links

onpointnyc.org/

wiki/overdose.title: Overdose
wiki/overdose.content:
Overview
An overdose refers to the idea of taking too much of something, resulting in negative consequences.
However, many overdoses can be caused as the result of using multiple substances at once whose combinded effects compound into negative consequences. For instance, mixing opioids with alcohol can lead to a stronger respiratory depression than one might expect from having used each alone, leading to the same thing as an overdose on just one substance. Substances don’t just add up in their effects, they can multiply to cause a reaction many times stronger than each individual substance might provoke.
Harm reduction practices like Overdose Prevention Sites (OPS) and Opioid Treatment Programs (OTPs) often measure the impact of their success by the number of overdoses prevented or reversed.

wiki/oxford-centre-for-neuroethics.title: Oxford Centre for Neuroethics
wiki/oxford-centre-for-neuroethics.content:
Overview
The Oxford Centre for Neuroethics was established in 2009 at the University of Oxford to explore the ethical, legal, and social impacts of breakthroughs in neuroscience. Their focus areas include the ethics of cognitive enhancement, consciousness, free will, and morality in decision-making.

wiki/painkillers.title: Painkillers
wiki/painkillers.content:
Overview
Painkillers are another term for analgesics, which reduce or relieve pain and discomfort.
Etymology
The widespread adoption of the term can be traced back to 1844 to a product called “Vegetable Pain Killer,” created by Perry Davis. It was a mix of alcohol, opium, camphor, and myrrh, and Davis marketed it as a cure for cholera, coughs, burns, toothaches, ailments of all kinds. It was sold to soldiers during the US Civil War and used by Christian missionaries worldwide, and eventually the product name became the common term for the product class of analgesics: “painkiller.” There has been some scholarly discussion about how the term treats pain as a hostile intruder and medicine as a weapon to fight it.

wiki/palliative-care.title: Palliative Care
wiki/palliative-care.content:
Overview
Palliative care is an approach to medical care that focuses on improving the quality of life for patients and their support network. It’s especially helpful for chronic or life-threatening conditions that create complex needs across the biopsychosocial spectrum, like cancer, heart disease, lung disease, kidney failure, dementia, and others.

wiki/panhellenic-medical-congress.title: Panhellenic Medical Congress
wiki/panhellenic-medical-congress.content:
Overview
The Panhellenic Medical Congress is one of the oldest medical conferences in Greece, established in 1901 by the Athens Medical Society, which was founded in 1835. Events were hosted periodically until 1975, when the military dictatorship fell and the Athens Medical Society restructured themselves for an annual event. In the 1903 conference, the participants drafted a proposal to run a state-controlled monopoly over quinine, which was influential for Greek public health frameworks.
Attendees


Athanasios Exadaktylos, President of the Panhellenic Medical Association


Ioannis Arkadianos, President of the European Lifestyle Medicine Organization (ELMO)


Ioanna Michalopoulou


Antonia Trichopoulou, pioneer of the Mediterranean diet

wiki/paranoia.title: Paranoia
wiki/paranoia.content:
Overview
Paranoia in its casual, everyday sense can refer to an attitude that is suspicious of others and hypervigilant in anticipation of something going wrong. When it’s mentioned in medical literature, it refers more specifically to a state in which someone holds rigid beliefs or delusions from reality that can’t be changed through evidence or logic. In some clinical presentations, it can come through Paranoid Personality Disorder (PPD), or a chronic a pattern of mistrust and inflexibility that interprets benign actions as malicious without full psychotic breaks. What separates paranoia from anxiety is that paranoia involves assigning some kind of malicious intent to forces that intervene in one’s life, rather than simply a worry about negative outcomes.

wiki/paregoric.title: Paregoric
wiki/paregoric.content:
Overview
Paregoric is a medication for severe diarrhea that contains morphine derived from opium that includes ethanol, benzoic acid, camphor, and anise oil. It’s classified as a Schedule III controlled substance in the United States and is considered habit-forming.
Side effects of paregoric include:


Gastrointestinal distress: constipation, stomach pain, nausea, vomiting


Central nervous system (CNS) depression: drowsiness, dizziness, lightheadedness


Cardiovascular shifts: shallow breathing, slowed heart rate, dizziness


Difficulty urinating and increased sweating


Itching or a rash


Because it’s an addictive substance that can lead to increasing levels of dependence and tolerance, the severity of symptoms increases alongside prolonged use.

wiki/parentification.title: Parentification
wiki/parentification.content:
Overview
Parentification refers to the pattern of children being put into roles by their parents or guardians that are meant for adults. Instrumental parentification occurs when a child handles the cooking, cleaning, shopping, bills, raising of younger siblings, and other practical or logistical tasks. Emotional parentification occurs when a child becomes part of a parent’s conflict resolution or emotional regulation strategies, such as asking a child to be a confidant, therapist, mediator, messenger, peacekeeper, etc.
Adults who experience parentification often share some patterns in behaviors and mindsets:


Hyper-independence


People-pleasing


Co-dependence


Difficulty with boundaries


There is no official diagnosis just for parentification, but there are some contextual codes included in disease classification systems. The DSM-5 Contextual Codes allows one to note a Parent-Child Relational Problem that may affect clinical care. The ICD-11 notes a similar Caregiver-Child Relationship Problem. Psychometric researchers have proposed the Parentification Questionnaire (PQ) and the Filial Responsibility Scale (FRS) for measuring the severity of parentification and similar family dysfunction.
In legal systems, parentification may be used to describe the dynamics that fall more broadly under “neglect,” “emotional abuse,” or “failure to protect.”

wiki/partnership-to-end-addiction.title: Partnership to End Addiction
wiki/partnership-to-end-addiction.content:
Overview
The Partnership to End Addiction is a national non-profit dedicated to recovery from substance use for youth and young adults by combining family support with systemic advocacy. The organization was founded as the Partnership for a Drug-Free America in 1985 and became famous for the “This Is Your Brain on Drugs” PSA. The current version of the organization was the result of a merger between the Partnership for Drug-Free Kids and Center on Addiction. Their projects include bilingual specialist helplines, peer-to-peer coaching based on Community Reinforcement and Family Training (CRAFT), lobbying the government for more resources for SUD treatment, campaigns to prevent youth vaping, and a podcast hosted by Elizabeth Vargas about destigmatizing addiction.

wiki/party-girl-a-comic-novel-about-addi.title: Party Girl - A Comic Novel About Addiction and Recovery

wiki/pass-it-on.title: Pass It On - The Story of Bill Wilson and how the AA message reached the world (1953)

wiki/passive-aggressive.title: Passive-Aggressive
wiki/passive-aggressive.content:
Overview
“Passive-aggressive” refers to a communication style in which someone doesn’t explicitly articulate how they feel while still acting or saying things that suggest they have negative opinions or feelings. Critically, the term did not originate from academic or research circles, but instead emerged in the context of compliance to orders in the United States military.
History and Etymology
WWII
During WWII, military psychiatrists were tasked with evaluating soldiers who resisted orders without openly refusing them. They might have expressed dissatisfaction through visible emotions (called “pouting”), stubbornness before complying with a rule, and a lack of instrinsic motivation to improve efficiency. In some cases, this resistance came in the form of outright noncompliance or sabotage akin to civil disobedience. In 1945, the War Department Technical Bulletin, Medical 203 under William C. Menninger, proposed the term “passive-aggressive” to refer to the hostility or resistance engendered in soldiers who want to resist orders. The model of passive-aggressive behaviors contained two parts: the observed behavior and the inferred (sometimes subconscious) motivations. It appeared under a category called “Immaturity Reactions” and was pathologized as a psychiatric disorder resulting from excessive routine stress. Menninger thought passive-aggressiveness was the most common psychiatric disorder in the military.
After WWII ended, several psychiatric centers under the Veterans Administration (VA) approved the adoption of “passive-aggressive personality” as a clinical term. The War Department Bulletin proposal was reprinted in the Journal of Clinical Psychology in 1946 to introduce it to everyday psychiatry. Shortly after, in 1948, the American Psychiatric Association’s Committee on Statistics set out to esablished an authoritative taxonomic classification of known disorders and diseases. George Raines, who led neuropsychiatry at the Navy Department Bureau of Medicine, argued that the classification system should take in a wide variety of evidence and sources, but it seems the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM), the DSM-I, was still largely influenced by Medical 203 and related literature from the War Department. Even the International Classification of Diseases (ICD) adopted by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 1948 drew heavily from the War Department.
DSM-I
The DSM-I description of “passive-aggressive personality” split its reactions into three interchangeable subtypes based on the underlying response to frustration or stress:


passive-dependent: stress leads to helplessness and dependency


passive-aggressive: stress leads to resistance and obstruction


aggressive: stress leads to overt irritation and destructive tendencies


The model underlying the “passive-aggressive personality” still assumes both an immature dependency or frustrated hostility. The notion of treated disorders as “reactions” came out of the work of Adolf Meyer at Johns Hopkins University and Sigmund Freud, using the contemporary notion within psychoanalysis that psychiatric symptoms were the result of emotional disturbances related to childhood development. This framework claimed that stress can lead to the ego being disorganized and anxiety to overwhelm the individual, with the repressed impulses leading to the behaviors described as “passive-aggressive.”
DSM-II
The DSM-II was established in 1968, led by Ernest Gruenberg. By this point, the 8th edition of the WHO’s ICD was also being released, so there was an ambition to align the new DSM with the ICD for consistency’s sake. The “reactions” within the “passive-aggressive personality” were consolidated as a single personality disorder characterized by indirect resistance and hostility. It still drew from psychoanalytic theories, but less explicitly so, partly because the late 1960s had major breakthroughs in psychopharmacology that reinforced the brain’s biological involvement in psychiatric disorders. While psychodynamic perspectives were still strong, there was a growing understanding that the DSM-I’s categorization wasn’t as stable as previously assumed. The ability to treat disorders pharmacologically opened the door to using treatment information to shape diagnoses and criteria.
DSM-III
The DSM-III was completed in 1980 after psychiatrists had been exploring the use of operational or diagnostic criteria.
Samuel Guze relates the story of meeting William Menninger’s brother Karl at an APA meeting delivering a talk. Karl
Links

jamanetwork.com/journals/archneurpsyc/article-abstract/651868
onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/1097-4679%28200007%2956%3A7%3C935%3A%3AAID-JCLP11%3E3.0.CO%3B2-8

wiki/pathologize.title: Pathologize
wiki/pathologize.content:
Overview
To pathologize means to identify some human behavior or emotion as abnormal, such that it’s worth addressing medically or psychologically.
The term often carries a negative connotation because of recent criticisms that normal human patterns are labeled as diseases or symptoms by the medical establishment, whether that’s by neurodivergent advocates who want society to accept differences rather than label them as sick or by mental health skeptics who believe diagnoses are handed out to those who don’t have severe enough impairments to warrant them. After all, some of the worst examples of pathologizing include drapetomania to describe the urge of slaves to flee, homosexuality as a type of “Sociopathic Personality Disturbance”, and hysteria to describe women whose behavior didn’t align with gender roles or patriarchal expectations. Institutions in power have a pattern of pathologizing behaviors or cultural patterns for groups they seek to use.
At the same time, pathologizing addiction meant a shift in framing the problem as a moral-religious issue into a medical and public health issue. “Substance use disorder (SUD)” frames addictive behaviors as a chronic brain disease with relapses and remissions, rather than an issue of willpower. Complex Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (C-PTSD) isn’t acknowledged by the DSM-5, but advocates for its incorporation argue that pathologizing the aftermath of prolonged chronic trauma is validating to those who struggle with symptoms that are reduced to personality flaws or miscategorized as personality disorders. The same applies to adult ADHD and helping people realize that the messaging they may have internalized around being “lazy” or “unmotivated” actually comes from issues in dopamine regulation due to structural differences in the prefrontal cortex. There are many kids who burnout or whose symptoms go overlooked because their grades are fine and they don’t have obvious behavioral issues, but then struggle later in life with basic executive function skills.

wiki/pearson.title: Pearson
wiki/pearson.content:
Overview
Based in London, England, Pearson is an international company that publishes educational and assessment materials. If you have been in an American school in the last two decades or had a child who was, you have almost certainly seen Pearson slapped on your materials.

wiki/peer-recovery.title: Peer Recovery
wiki/peer-recovery.content:
Overview
Peer recovery describes frameworks for mutual support among those who share lived experiences or shared identity, particularly in mental health and substance use recovery contexts. Public stigma, scientific limitations, and abuses of formal institutions have all been major factors in the growth of peer-led recovery groups and services all over the world. Evidence shows that including peer support into a treatment plan increases engagement in treatment, reduces the risk of readmission, decreases substance use and overdoses, and improves feelings of self-sufficiency.
Peer recovery specialists are jobs where lived experience with recovery is actually a useful qualification, and they usually involve formal certification with a training program and exams. These are distinct roles from addiction counselors and therapists.

wiki/peergalaxy.title: PeerGalaxy
wiki/peergalaxy.content:
Overview
Peer Galaxy is a platform that aggregates peer-led recovery services and events across the world with a focus on Oregon. From their main page, they maintain peer support, recovery and wellness activities, webinars, consumer input, and special events. They also focus on addressing barriers to participation through accessibility and translation options that are commonly a secondary consideration for both online and offline groups.
Links

www.peergalaxy.com/

wiki/peerpocalypse.title: Peerpocalypse | The Peer Company
wiki/peerpocalypse.content:
Overview
Hosted by The Peer Company (formerly the Mental Health & Addiction Association of Oregon), the national conference focuses on fostering collaboration that advances the peer recovery movement.
In 2026, the event took place in Seaside, Oregon from May 4-7 with the theme “Rooted & Rising.” From their main page:
“This theme honors where we’ve come from, our grassroots beginnings and the deep roots that ground the peer movement. Our history is one of resilience, truth, and connection. As we continue to grow, we carry those roots with us, and use them to shape the future of peer support with the wisdom of lived experience. Rooted & Rising invites us to celebrate how far we’ve come and to reach higher together, guided by the values that make our community strong.”
Attendees



Links

www.mhaoforegon.org/peerpocalypse-main-page

wiki/people-engaged-in-recovery.title: People Engaged in Recovery
wiki/people-engaged-in-recovery.content:
Overview
People Engaged in Recovery (PEIR) is a peer-led nonprofit in Alabama for individuals and families impacted by substance use disorders. They offer services like peer counseling, relapse prevention planning, support groups, and wellness activities. They also hosted a 100-mile “Enduring Their Legacies” walk that ended at the Alabama State Capitol in honor of those who overdosed and the families impacted by them.
Links

peopleengagedinrecovery.org/

wiki/people-pleasing.title: People-Pleasing
wiki/people-pleasing.content:
Overview
People-pleasing is a pattern where someone prioritizes the desires and emotional states of others over their own, usually as a result of fearing conflict or rejection. This isn’t the same as kindness or empathy though. People-pleasing instincts are often a coping mechanism or trauma response like fawning driven by a need to have a stable environment or to secure external approval. The term is not a formal diagnosis in the DSM-5, although Dependent Personality Disorder (DPD) describes patterns of people-pleasing in its criteria of symptoms.
Within recovery circles, people-pleasing is one of the most common patterns that gets addressed, especially when it involves waiving boundaries in the short-term that comes out as resentment in the long-term or codependent relationships with people whose behavior presents risks to sobriety.

wiki/peptides.title: Peptides
wiki/peptides.content:
Overview
Peptides are chains of amino acids that serve as the building blocks of proteins, and there are over 100 peptide medications approved by the FDA. Common examples include:


insulin: for diabetes


GLP-1 receptor agonist: for diabetes and weight management, like semaglitude and tirzepatide


teriparatide: for osteoporosis


In wellness and fitness spaces, there are trends of people taking unregulated peptides that are sold under legal loopholes, like claiming to be “research chemicals:”


Body Protection Compound-157 (BPC-157): despite the lack of evidence supporting its efficacy and a ban from the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA), it’s used with the belief that it speeds up healing in the muscle and tendons


Thymosin Beta-4 fragment (TB-500): often paired with BPC-157 under similarly unsubstantiated claims about its ability to improve healing and flexibility


CJC-1295 & Ipamorelin: together they trigger the secretion of more growth hormone and are taken with the goal of lowering body fact and building lean muscle mass


The risk of consuming these unregulated compounds goes beyond just a lack of scientific evidence about how they impact the body; because they’re bought off a gray market that bypasses traditional regulations and testing, they can be contaminated with bacteria, heavy metals, other substances, or simply incorrect dosing information.

wiki/perfectionism.title: Perfectionism
wiki/perfectionism.content:
Overview
Perfectionism is a personality trait of holding high expectations of oneself and/or others and applying critical evaluations when they are not met.
Models
Frost Multidimensional Perfectionism Scale (FMPS)
The Frost Multidimensional Perfectionism Scale (FMPS) was developed in 1990 by Randy O. Frost and models perfectionism through six dimensions:


Concern over mistakes: interpreting mistakes as failure that will cost respect from others


Personal standards: high expectations of oneself that have huge impacts on self-esteem and self-worth


Parental expectations: the perception that one’s parents have or had high expectations of them


Parental criticism: the perception that one’s parents were overly critical of mistakes or failures to meet expectations


Doubts about actions: a constant sense that daily activities or tasks are not being done well enough


Organization: a strong emphasis on order and precision


Hewitt & Flett Multidimensional Perfectionism Scale (HF-MPS)
Paul Hewitt and Gordon Flett proposed this model in 1991 to categorize perfectionism based on its interpersonal direction:


Self-Oriented perfectionism: an individual demands perfectionism from themselves


Other-Oriented perfectionism: an individual expects perfectionism from others


Socially prescribed perfectionism: an individual believes others expect perfectionism from them in order to be validated

wiki/permanent-supportive-housing-psh.title: Permanent Supportive Housing (PSH)
wiki/permanent-supportive-housing-psh.content:
Overview
Permanent Supportive Housing (PSH) is a housing intervention that follows a Housing-First to provide someone with a permanent lease without preconditions like treatment compliance. The target demographic includes chronically homeless individuals or households with a disability, serious mental illness, or chronic health condition.
PSH programs are one of the most effective ways to address homelessness, as up to 85% of chronically homeless individuals remain housed after one year following a PSH program. Individuals in PSH are also more likely to reduce their substance use voluntarily and participate in outpatient care for mental health. It also provides a stable place for treatment providers to reach an individual and seek care before a crisis happens, which studies show has led to a 40% reduction in visits to emergency departments, psychiatric hospitals, and shelters. It also decreases interactions with law enforcement, with a decrease in jail stays and citations.

wiki/person-first-language.title: Person-First Language
wiki/person-first-language.content:
Overview
Person-first language, or people-first language, is a way of phrasing language in a way that emphasizes the individual rather than a condition or a trait. One of the most common examples of that you’ll find on this site is the use of “person  struggling with substance use disorder” rather than “addict.”
Medical and research communities tend to use person-first language to maximize inclusivity, especially as studies have shown that language choices do make a difference in the subjective margins of even professional judgment. Clinicians and researchers who encounter the label “substance abuser” are more likely to have punitive attitudes than those who encounter the label “person with a substance use disorder.” There’s always a fuss any time people are asked to update their language outside of organic trends, but the evidence shows that there’s more than just theoretical or ideological harm being done with language.

wiki/personal-inventory.title: Personal Inventory
wiki/personal-inventory.content:
Overview
“Personal inventory” is a term popularized by 12-step programs that refers to the practice of examining yourself to build awareness over what you can change.
Twelve-Step
There are two steps that discuss personal inventories.
Step 4 says: “Made a searching and fearless moral inventory of ourselves”
This step is meant to catalog the moral and psychological baggage one has accumulated throughout one’s life, generally structured into a split between Resentments, Fears, Sexual Conduct, Harms, etc. This is then shared with a trusted person, commonly a sponsor.
Step 10 says: “Continued to take personal inventory and when we were wrong promptly admitted it.”
This step is an aspect of regular maintenance in which one examines their behavior to see what they could have done differently and plans to make amends if possible. It serves to diffuse the Resentments, Fears, Sexual Conduct, and Harms of Step 4 before they become bigger issues.

wiki/personal-responsibility-and-word-re.title: Personal Responsibility and Word Reauthorization Act of 1996

wiki/peyote.title: Peyote
wiki/peyote.content:
Overview
Peyote is a small cactus that contains over 50 alkaloids including mescaline, which produces psychedelic effects. It has been used for thousands of years by indigenous tribes throughout North America and continues to be used by the Native American Church. Outside of the Church’s exemption for religious purposes, peyote is a Schedule I controlled substance in the United States.

wiki/pharmacodynamics.title: Pharmacodynamics
wiki/pharmacodynamics.content:
Overview
Pharmacodynamics (PD) is the study of a drug’s effects on the body. Most drugs act on cellular receptors that activate () or block (antagonist) them to produce a desired reaction.

wiki/pharmacogenetics.title: Pharmacogenetics
wiki/pharmacogenetics.content:
Overview
Pharmacogenetics is the study of how a person’s genes influence the way a drug is metabolized. It’s considered a more narrow term than pharmacogenomics, but both are often used interchangeably.
For any particular substance consumed, someone might be considered a poor metabolizer, an intermediate metabolizer, or an ultra-rapid metabolizer. Poor metabolizers might break down a drug too slowly and suffer from side effects because it lingers in higher levels in their system. Ultra-rapid metabolizers might break down a drug too quickly and limit its effectiveness. Genetic testing can reveal whether someone has predispositions that might make a particular medication more or less effective. This is true across antidepressants, pain medications, blood thinners, antiplatelet drugs, cancer drugs, antivirals, antibiotics, and allergic reaction.

wiki/pharmacogenomics.title: Pharmacogenomics
wiki/pharmacogenomics.content:
Overview
Pharmacogenomics is the study of how one’s total genetic profile impacts the interactions a drug has in their body. The term is used almost interchangeably with pharmacogenetics, which has a slightly more narrow definition.

wiki/pharmacokinetics.title: Pharmacokinetics
wiki/pharmacokinetics.content:
Overview
Pharmacokinetics describes the changes a body makes to a drug after consumption, as the drug goes through absorption, distribution, metabolism, and elimination (ADME). It’s a central topic in psychopharmacology.

wiki/phencyclidine.title: Phencyclidine (PCP)
wiki/phencyclidine.content:
Overview
Phencyclidine, also called angel dust or PCP, is an addictive drug that causes dissociation, euphoria, mood swings, hallucinations, and paranoia. It was originally used as an anesthetic until it was noted to have severe side effects that persisted after operations. It’s now classified as a Schedule II controlled substance in the United States, though illicit recreational use continues; PCP can be snorted, swallowed, injected, or smoked, sometimes by dipping products like cigarettes or joints in them.
Short-Term Effects
The short-term effects of PCP include:


Dissociation


Sensory Distortions


Ataxia (loss of coordination)


Hypertension (elevated blood pressure)


Tachycardia (increased heart rate)


Shallow Breathing


Sweating


Nystagmus (rapid and involuntary eye movements)


Delirium


Paranoia


Hallucinations


Agitation


Analgesic painkilling


Muscle rigidity


Seizures


Catatonia


Hyperthermia (increase in body temperature)


Respiratory Depression


Coma


Death


Long-Term Effects


Memory Loss


Stuttering


Slurred Speech


Difficulty Concentrating


Persistent Psychosis


Depression


Anxiety


Suicidal Ideation


Toxic Encephalopathy


Kidney Damage

wiki/philopotes.title: Philopotes
wiki/philopotes.content:
Overview
Philopotes is an ancient Greek term that translates literally to “lover of drinking.” It didn’t have a negative connotation the way we might associate with “drunk” or “heavy drinker”; “partygoer” is a more fair comparison, since it might have been used to describe someone attending a party called a symposia. In some ancient Greek theater, a philopotes might have referred to an archetypal character whose drinking provides comic relief.

wiki/phobia.title: Phobia
wiki/phobia.content:
Overview
The National Institute of Mental Health defines a phobia as:
an intense fear of—or aversion to—a specific object or situation. While anxiety is natural under some circumstances, people with phobias feel fear that is out of proportion to the actual danger presented by the situation or object.
The DSM-5 offers three categories for phobias: Specific Phobias, Social Anxiety Disorder (Social Phobia), and Agoraphobia.
Links

wiki/phoenix-house-foundation.title: Phoenix House Foundation
wiki/phoenix-house-foundation.content:
Overview
From 1967 to 2019, the Phoenix House Foundation was a nonprofit that offered alcohol rehabilitation throughout the United States. It adopted several methods from Synanon, a very controversial group that became something of a cult. The documentary Born in Synanon goes into detailed interviews with its members, including children born and raised according to the program’s leaders. The Phoenix House itself was not affiliated with the cult aspects of Synanon; Dr. Mitchell Rosenthal had observed early Synanon group practices and brought them with him when founding Phoenix House.
In 2005, the United States Department of Justice labeled it a “model program.” In 2019, the Foundation dissolved into stand-alone regional organizations.

wiki/physician-health-program-php.title: Physician Health Program (PHP)
wiki/physician-health-program-php.content:
Overview
Physician Health Programs (PHPs) are organizations that support doctors and other healthcare professionals with mental health conditions, including substance use. The Federation of State Physician Health Programs (FSPHP) supports PHPs in almost every state; California is a notable exception in its lack of state-run PHPs. Substance use disorders (SUDs) suffer from a lot of stigma, but medical professionals are under especially heavy pressure to not report health issues. There’s often an idealized expectation that health professionals are free of any health condition themselves.

wiki/picoeconomics.title: Picoeconomics
wiki/picoeconomics.content:
Overview
Picoeconomics is a branch of behavioral economics that studies internal motivations within individuals using the principles of microeconomics.
Instead of viewing addiction as a failure of logic or a disease, picoeconomics explains addiction as a series of successive selves bargaining beween immediately gratifying rewards and long-term rewards. When both types of rewards are far away, an individual might express a preference for long-term rewards like health, relationships, and career success. However, when the immediate gratification option comes closer to being available, our brains place a massive spike on its value. This is called hyperbolic discounting and explains why those struggling with substance use can be sincerely trying to change yet end up in cycles anyways.

wiki/pink-cloud-syndrome.title: Pink Cloud Syndrome
wiki/pink-cloud-syndrome.content:
Overview
Pink cloud syndrome is a term that was coined in Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) circles that describes the optimism and even euphoria that one can feel during the early stages of sobriety. It’s often called a “honeymoon phase” in the context of a recovery timeline. It can be a trend that increases motivation and resilience, but it also risks overconfidence that leads one to drop their coping mechanism or support groups. Many who have a pink cloud phase end up relapsing because a sober life ends up being more mundane or disappointing than they initially felt.

wiki/pinney-associates.title: Pinney Associates
wiki/pinney-associates.content: A health consultancy which promotes tobacco harm reduction

wiki/place-based-policies-for-shared-eco.title: Place-Based Policies for Shared Economic Growth

wiki/pleasure-principle.title: Pleasure Principle
wiki/pleasure-principle.content:
Overview
The pleasure principle is a psychoanalytic concept used to describe the human instinct to seek immediate gratification while avoiding pain or stress.
The American Psychological Association’s Dictionary of Psychology defines it as:
the view that human beings are governed by the desire for gratification, or pleasure, and for the discharge of tension that builds up as pain or “unpleasure” when gratification is lacking.
In the classical psychoanalytic theory of Sigmund Freud, the pleasure principle is the psychic force that motivates people to seek immediate gratification of instinctual, or libidinal, impulses, such as sex, hunger, thirst, and elimination. It dominates the id and operates most strongly during childhood. Later, in adulthood, it is opposed by the reality principle of the ego. Also called pleasure–pain principle. 1
Links



Footnotes


APA Dictionary of Psychology ↩

wiki/police-assisted-addiction-and-recov.title: Police Assisted Addiction and Recovery Initiative (PAARI)
wiki/police-assisted-addiction-and-recov.content:
Overview
The Police Assisted Addiction and Recovery Initiative (PAARI) is a national non-profit that helps law enforcement develop diversionary pathways to treatment and recovery without involving arrest. PAARI now has over 800 partners in law enforcement across 46 states. They provide training and technical assistance (TTA), like the 2026 “Essential Deflection and Diversion Certification Program” to standardize diversion practices among law enforcement.
Historical Context
PAARI was founded in 2015 in Gloucester, Massachusetts as part of the “Angel Program” run by local law enforcement that allowed anyone to walk into a police station to turn over drugs without fear of arrest and receive placement into a recovery program.

wiki/polysubstance.title: Polysubstance
wiki/polysubstance.content:
Overview
Polysubstance use refers to using more than one substance within a short window of time. This can happen intentionally when users try to enhance or neutralize the effects of one substance with another, but it can also happen unintentionally when substances have been contaminated or cut with other substances.
Some categories of drug interactions include:


Depressant + Depressant: Combining opioids, alcohol, benzodiazepines, and muscle relaxants can compound the central nervous system and respiratory depression in ways that dramatically increase the risk of hypoxia, sedation, coma, and respiratory failure.


Stimulant + Depressant: Stimulants are sometimes used to mask the sedative effects of a depressant, or vice versa, but stimulants are often short-acting. This means that the depressive effects of higher doses can suddenly kick in when the stimulants wear off, which can cause cardiac dysrhythmia and strokes. Some combinations like cocaine and alcohol cause the liver to produce uniquely toxic metabolites like cocaethylene.


Stimulant + Stimulant: Stacking stimulants can over-activate the systems of neurotransmitters like dopamine, serotonin, and norepinephrine. This can lead to hypertension, hyperthermia, tachyarrhythmias, and seizures.


Serotoneregic Combinations: This combination can lead to serotonin syndrome, which presents with hyperreflexia, autonomic instability, muscle rigidity, high fever, and delirium.


Dissociative/Psychedelic + Cannabis: Cannabis changes the way other substances are processed, which increases the chances of panic attacks, paranoia, depersonalization, or psychosis

wiki/pope-urban-vii.title: Pope Urban VII
wiki/pope-urban-vii.content: In 1590, Pope Urban VII issued perhaps the first ban on smoking, threatening anyone with excommunication for using tobacco in or near a church. It covered smoking, chewing, or sniffing snuff. He died of malaria and holds the record for the shortest papacy in history: 12 days.

wiki/pope-urban-viii.title: Pope Urban VIII
wiki/pope-urban-viii.content: Unlike his predecessor who held the papacy for 12 days, Pope Urban VIII reigned for 21 years. He prohibited the use of tobacco in holy places under the threat of excommunication in a 1624 decree. Supposedly, the excessive sneezing and grime from chewing tobacco felt disruptive and disrespectful.

wiki/poppers.title: Poppers
wiki/poppers.content:
Overview
Poppers are inhalants made from alkyl nitrites, which produce a minutes-long euphoric sensation when consumed. They’re associated with relaxing muscles and widening blood vessels, so they’re often associated with party and casual sex scenes. They’re commercially available under labels like leather cleaners or nail polish removers.
The side effects of poppers includes:


Methemoglobinemia: a reduction in oxygen delivery throughout the body which can be potentially fatal


Vision and eye damage


Severe headaches


Fainting

wiki/pornography.title: Pornography
wiki/pornography.content:
Overview
Pornography refers to sexually explicit material that is intended to be sexually provocative or arousing.
Whether pornography is addictive or otherwise harmful for mental health remains controversial, but the medical establishment does not, as a consensus, recognize porn addiction as a disease or disorder itself. Neither the DSM-5 nor the ICD-11 mention a specific “pornography addiction,” though the ICD-11 does include Compulsive Sexual Behavior Disorder (CSBD) as an impulse-control disorder. Researchers often argue that porn use that interferes with daily life should be seen as a maladaptive coping mechanism for stress rather than a specific disorder, and they also argue that much of the psychological distress surrounding pornography use comes from internalized religious or moral conflicts. Still, there are Porn Addicts Anonymous (PAA) groups for those who wish to have peer support in maintaining abstinence from any and all usage of porn. 1
Links



Footnotes


“Home | Porn Addicts Anonymous” ↩

wiki/portraits-of-recovery.title: Portraits of Recovery
wiki/portraits-of-recovery.content:
Overview
Portraits of Recovery is a Manchester-based charity that works with contemporary artists in recovery from substance use, who the organization calls “Recoverists.”
Links

portraitsofrecovery.org.uk/

wiki/positive-reinforcement.title: Positive Reinforcement
wiki/positive-reinforcement.content:
Overview
Positive reinforcement is the process through which the likelihood of a behavior is increased by adding a reward right afterward. It contrasts with negative reinforcement, in which a behavior is incentivized through removing or stopping a consequence.
Substance use disorders are initially the result of positive reinforcement, where someone’s brain associates using a substance with dopamine spikes that signal it to be highly rewarding behavior. Eventually, when someone’s neurochemical baselines for feeling rewarded have changed, they feel the need to use substances to feel normal. Negative reinforcement drives many people away from sobriety more than positive reinforcement drives people towards substances.

wiki/post-exposure-prophylaxis.title: Post-exposure Prophylaxis (PEP)
wiki/post-exposure-prophylaxis.content:
Overview
Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is a treatment started after exposure to an infection, most commonly in the context of HIV, Hepatitis B, and bacterial STIs.
Populations that struggle with substance use disorders (SUDs) might engage in risky behaviors like sharing needles, syringes, and water or having unprotected sex. PEP can be delivered within 72 hours of someone’s exposure to one of these risk factors. For bacterial STIs, a single dose of Doxycycline STI Postexposure Prophylaxis (Doxy PEP) suffices. For HIV, a 28-day course of antiretrovirals is needed.
If someone is routinely exposed to the risks mentioned above rather than as an isolated emergency event, they might transition to Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) right after their PEP dose completes. PrEP is recognized as a highly effective, evidence-backed harm reduction tool.

wiki/potency.title: Potency
wiki/potency.content:
Overview
Potency generally refers to something’s capacity to act or strength of its effects. In pharmacology, potency can be measured in a few ways:


Half-maximal Effective Concentration: the concentration of a substance that creates a response that’s halfway between a baseline response and the maximum possible response


Half-maximal Effective Dose: the dose of a substance that produces a particular intensity of effect in 50% of a test population.


Half-maximal Inhibitory Concentration: the concentration of a substance that inhibits a biological process by 50%

wiki/potentiation.title: Potentiation
wiki/potentiation.content:
Overview
Potentiation refers to a process of making something more effective through synergy.
When using substances, the brain experiences Long-Term Potentiation (LTP), which means synapses are strengthened as they experience activity. The cues surrounding substances become associated with the intense reward of the substance, and the brain’s expectations lead to strong cravings. LTP describes the physiological mechanisms through which positive reinforcement is encoded in the brain. Recovery from substance use disorders involves sustained sobriety in order to weaken the potentiated pathways associated with using substances and strengthening those associated with new coping skills or experiences. Contingency Management offers immediate positive reinforcement to incentivize the potentiation of drug-free habits while the brain is still healing from a “hijacked” reward system.

wiki/power-of-attorney.title: Power of Attorney
wiki/power-of-attorney.content:
Overview
The power of attorney (POA) is a legal document that gives someone the authority to act on another person’s behalf. In legal terms, the principal grants authority to an agent or attorney-in-fact.
Individuals with substance use disorders can designate a medical POA to make decisions for them in case they get incapacitated as a result of severe intoxication, withdrawal, overdose, or coma. The proxy who holds the POA might be given an advance directive that specifies preferences beforehand around facilities, programs, and medications. They would also have the authorization to obtain records and coordinate with medical staff, which can be vital in emergency situations. However, POAs in the United States cannot be used to force someone into substance use treatment if they are conscious and able to protest; involuntary commitment laws and guardianship/conservatorship processes are separate from POAs and differ by jurisdiction.
There are other kinds of POAs too. A financial POA allows someone to make financial decisions on another person’s behalf, such as paying bills, managing mortgages, and handling banking. Someone who enters long-term treatment or fears they might be otherwise incapacitated can designate a proxy through a financial POA to ensure continuity in their financial commitments.

wiki/pre-exposure-prophylaxis.title: Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP)
wiki/pre-exposure-prophylaxis.content:
Overview
Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is a prescription medication taken to prevent the recipience of HIV from sex or injection drug use. It can come in the form of daily pills and long-acting injections to be taken twice a year. If someone has recently been exposed to a risk factor for HIV or bacterial STIs, they may first undergo a post-exposure prophylactic (PEP) treatment designed for short-term recent exposure before undergoing PrEP for long-term prevention.

wiki/prefrontal-cortex.title: Prefrontal Cortex
wiki/prefrontal-cortex.content:
Overview
The prefrontal cortex is part of the brain’s frontal lobe and plays a central role in complex behavior and higher-order thinking.
Key Functions


Executive Function


Impulse Control


Self-Regulation


Working Memory


Social Cognition


Subregions


Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex (dlPFC)


Ventromedial Prefrontal Cortex (vmPFC)


Orbitofrontal Cortex (OFC)


Anterior Cingulate Cortex (ACC)

wiki/prescription-drug-use-disorder-pdud.title: Prescription Drug Use Disorder (PDUD)
wiki/prescription-drug-use-disorder-pdud.content:
Overview
Prescription drug use disorder (PDUD) isn’t an official diagnosis itself, but the term can be found in research literature and surveys when estimating how many people struggle with substance use disorders that specifically stem from prescription drugs. The exact chemical nature and bodily effects of prescription drugs vary a lot from one to another, so it’s not very useful from a medical perspective to have a subcategory of SUD based solely on the method that the substances were obtained through. However, from policymaking and public health perspectives, that distinction can be useful in understanding the process through which pharmaceutials approved by medical professionals end up misused.

wiki/presidents-advisory-commission-on-n.title: President's Advisory Commission on Narcotics and Drug Abuse (the Prettyman Commission) of 1962

wiki/presidents-frontier-award.title: President's Frontier Award | Johns Hopkins University
wiki/presidents-frontier-award.content:
Overview
The John Hopkins University President’s Frontier Award is given to a faculty member poised to make a defining contribution. It was established in 2015 as a $300,000 funding award for potential breakthroughs backed by a donation from Louis J. Forster, a university trustee. Its multi-tiered nomination process goes through the Office of the Vice Provost for Research.
Past Winners


Jamie Spangler (2025): for molecular immunoengineering proteins that rewire the immune system for advanced therapies and regeneration


Joseph Sakran (2024)


Melissa Walls (2023)


Alexis Battle and Sarah Horst (2022)


Andrew Holland (2021)


Emily Riehl (2020)


Brice Menard (2019)


Deidra Crews (2018)


Michael Hersch (2017)


Scott Bailey (2016)


Sharon Gerecht (2015)

wiki/prevalence.title: Prevalence
wiki/prevalence.content:
Overview
Prevalence refers to how often something happens.
Key metrics about the prevalence of various phenomena around substance use:


over 58% of people aged 12 and older have used a substance in the past month


up to 20% of American adults experience substance use disorder


alcohol is the most common single substance use disorder


young adults aged 18-25 have the highest rate of drug use at 39%


males have a higher prevalence of SUD than females (20% vs 14.3%)

wiki/primary-care-physician-pcp.title: Primary Care Physician (PCP)
wiki/primary-care-physician-pcp.content:
Overview
A primary care physician (PCP) is a doctor who serves as the first professional point for coordinating general medical care. They can diagnose and treat everday illnesses, perform preventative care like checkups and screenings, assist in the management of chronic diseases, and provide referrals to specialists as needed. In the United Kingdom, they’re called General Practitioners (GPs).

wiki/prior-authorization.title: Prior Authorization
wiki/prior-authorization.content:
Overview
Prior authorization is a process where health insurance providers review and approve a medical service or medication before you receive it to confirm that it is medically essential and covered by your plan. Planned surgeries, hospital admissions, imaging scans, portable oxygen tanks, IV infusion pumps, expensive or habit-forming medications, and other areas usually require prior authorization.

wiki/pro-vapeo-mexico.title: Pro-Vapeo Mexico
wiki/pro-vapeo-mexico.content:
Overview
Pro-Vapeo Mexico is a civil advocacy group that represents vaporizer/e-cigarette companies and consumers that argue for harm-reduction over bans on nicotine products.
Context
Mexico has some of the strictest anti-tobacco laws in the world. Cigarettes can be legally bought and possessed, but smoking is banned in all public places including outdoor patios and individual private rooms in hotels.
In 2008, the General Tobacco Law banned the production and distribution of any product that resembled a tobacco product, including vapes, though the Mexican Supreme Court ruled in 2015 that it was unconstitutional to ban vapes while traditional cigarettes were still legal. President Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador (AMLO) issued multiple decrees from 2020-2022 attempting to ban the importation and commercialization of any electronic nicotine products, though the Supreme Court pushed back again in 2021. Eventually, in 2024 under President Claudia Sheinbaum, the Mexican Congress approved a constitutional amendment that included a vaping ban, placing vapes into the same legal category as fentanyl. In 2026, Sheinbaum proposed criminal penalties to enforce the ban since vaping companies were still selling their products.
Organizations like Pro-Vapeo Mexico argues that this repeats the same mistakes that the United States made with its own Prohibition amendment on alcohol. Businesses that were willing to comply with regulations were replaced with organized crime that use violence and distribute products that can’t be monitored for safety.

wiki/proceedings-of-the-society-for-the-.title: Proceedings of the Society for the Study of Inebriety (1900)

wiki/prognosis.title: Prognosis
wiki/prognosis.content:
Overview
A prognosis is a prediction about the likely course a health condition will take and the outcomes a patient might have.
With substance use disorders, the general prognosis is that it’s a chronic brain disease that involves relapses and remissions with many treatment options, and success is generally predicted based on recovery capital, co-occurring health conditions, severity of use patterns, and number of recovery attempts. Once someone has been able to maintain sobriety for 5 years, the likelihood of remaining sober is over 85%.

wiki/prohibition.title: Prohibition
wiki/prohibition.content:
Prohibition was a disaster. You can find lots of analysis from people far smarter and more experienced than me attesting to that. What’s most interesting to me though is how Prohibition was effectively a culture war.
The science of addiction, recovery, and treatment has always been very underdeveloped compared to other aspects of health. We can see that it’s in the nature of something as complex as addiction that it takes longer to discover patterns, assemble theories, and test solutions than other issues tied to a physiological function. That being said, Benjamin Rush, who signed the Declaration of Independence and held close relationships with a few US Presidents, wrote a very substantial argument in defense of treating alcoholism (“habitual drunkenness”) as a disease back in the 18th century. He argued that immoral behavior tied to drinking should be seen as a symptom of a disease that has afflicted one’s will and sanity. He added that Christians have an obligation to try and help all sinners, including someone lost to a substance.
So it’s interesting that the temperance movements which later praised Rush also abandoned the disease model for something between a moral model and a temperance model, blaming either the drinker or the drink at various points rather than assuming a public health perspective with a generous touch of communal spirituality. A ton of interests were at play that didn’t make the cut for Boardwalk Empire. There were saloons looking out for their bottom line, women’s groups fighting against domestic violence and family neglect, churches of different denominations that ventured into politics, politicians who were going to drink no matter what but needed to ride an issue into office, organized crime taking over the manufacture and distribution of alcohol, urban workers seeking a cleaner and safer environment as cities began to hold most of the American population, rural workers and labor unions seeking to disadvantage immigrants (especially Catholics) with a strong saloon culture, African-American coalitions seeking to prove their legitimacy as free Americans by holding up higher moral standards and allying with white church networks, and many others.
Before Prohibition and in the run-up to the Civil War, temperance movements were gaining steam but lost the moment when the sociopolitical framework for the institutions of slavery were challenged. The (im)morality of slavery and racism took priority over temperance, especially when it was leaned on heavily to cope with the brutal traumas they experienced. It wasn’t until the post-Civil War and post-WWI concerns about excessive drinking among soldiers and the struggles veterans had in reintegrating into daily life (which is actually the basis for America’s legal concept of disability) that temperance movements carried out a culture war.
One of the consequences of temperance movements having such a huge influence on the culture was a decline in institutions that researched alcoholism. After all, if the policies worked, millions of people who depend on that science would be completely liberated from that concern. Fewer hospitals, more factories and churches for the good sober Christian get-back-to-work mindset they would now have instead of cravings for drinking. Obviously, no such miracles happened, but the scientific, medical, and philanthropic communities had braced themselves for a massive decline in drinking that didn’t ever materialize.
Wartime Prohibition Act

wiki/prohibitionism.title: Prohibitionism
wiki/prohibitionism.content:
Overview
Prohibitionism describes the movements and ideology that argue that people avoid behaviors if an authority enforces rules against them with strict penalties.
It’s used commonly in the context of the Prohibition Era of the United States (1920-1933) when the Eighteenth Amendment and Volstead Act banned the sale of alcoholic beverages. The attempts to prohibit alcohol have historically been considered a disaster, especially in the way it led to bootlegging in black markets that incentivized organized crime to make deals with corrupt law enforcement.

wiki/prolonged-grief-disorder-pgd.title: Prolonged Grief Disorder (PGD)
wiki/prolonged-grief-disorder-pgd.content:
Overview
Prolonged grief disorder (PFD) is a condition defined by intense grief that interferes with daily life that extends past standard grieving periods for that society. The DSM-5-TR uses 12 months after a substantial loss for adults and 6 months for children. The ICD-11 sets the threshold at 6 months.

wiki/promoting-research-initiatives-in-s.title: Promoting Research Initiatives in Substance Use and Mental Health (PRISM)

wiki/prophylactic.title: Prophylactic
wiki/prophylactic.content:
Overview
A prophylactic is a medical treatment that prevents a condition from occurring. Examples include vaccines, pre-surgery antibiotics, PEP, PrEP, and preventative mastectomies and hysterectomies.
Within treatment for substance use, prophylactics include:


Antagonists: medications like Naltrexone block opioid receptors and the euphoric feeling that accompanies the use of opioids or alcohol; Naloxone can reverse overdoses that cause fatal respiratory depression


Anti-Craving Medication: medications like Acamprosate can help rebalance the disrupted glutamate and GABA systems caused by chronic alcohol use.


Relapse Prevention: coping skills and self-maintenance principles, usually based on Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy

wiki/prostitution.title: Prostitution
wiki/prostitution.content:
Overview
Prostitution refers to the exchange of sexual services for some type of compensation. Throughout most of the United States, prostitution is illegal, except for a few licensed institutions in Nevada. That doesn’t stop a black market from thriving though.
84% of street-based sex workers report issues with substance use. 50% of women and 18.5% of men in clinical treatment for substance use disorders (SUDs) have engaged in prostitution at some point in their life. These rates are driven by two patterns: prostitution is a way to pay for substances for those with SUD, and those who engage in prostitution are more likely to develop SUD when trying to cope with the traumas of sex work. In cases of human trafficking, victims are often coerced into substance use so that a dependency can be used against them as a method of compliance.

wiki/protective-factors.title: Protective Factors
wiki/protective-factors.content:
Overview
Protective factors are attributes that promote resilience and well-being, reducing the impact of risk factors.
The Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) uses the Socio-Ecological Model (SEM) to assess risk and protect factors across four levels:


Individual: biological and psychological traits


Relationship: closest social circles like family and peers


Community: settings where social relationships can start and develop


Societal: cultural, economic, and political factors

wiki/psilocybin.title: Psilocybin
wiki/psilocybin.content:
Overview
Psilocybin is a natural psychedelic found in over 200 fungi, or magic mushrooms.” Like alcohol and marijuana, it has a history going back thousands of years in cultures across the world.
Short-term effects of psilocybin include:


Sensory Distortion: enhanced visual perception with vivid colors and moving patterns, synesthesia, shifts in perception of space and time


Emotional Amplification: euphoria (good trip), paranoia and anxiety (bad trip)


Autonomic Stimulation: increase in heart rate and blood pressure


Mydriasis (Dilated Pupils)


Gastrointestinal Distress: nausea, upset stomach, vomiting


Motor Changes: Muscle weakness, tremors, chills, heaviness, sweating, shivering


Long-term effects include:


Increased Neuroplasticity: breaking repetitive thinking patterns by increasing neuroplasticity in the brain’s Default Mode Network (DMN)


Improved Mood: evidence shows that clinical delivery of psilocybin can improve the symptoms of Major Depressive Disorder, treatment-resistant depression, and anxiety


Reduction in Compulsive Behaviors: reduc


Increased Openness


Hallucinogen Persisting Perception Disorder (HPPD): a rare condition where someone experiences visual distortions for months or years after use


Psychotic Episode: individuals who have a history of or vulnerability to psychotic disorders might have an episode triggered as a result of use

wiki/psychedelic.title: Psychedelic
wiki/psychedelic.content:
Overview
Psychedelics are a class of psychoactive substances that act as agonists or partial agonists at the brain’s serotonin receptors.
The most common examples include:


Lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD): a synthetic derivative of ergot fungi


Psilocybin: a natural compound found in magic mushrooms


Mescaline: a natural compound derived from cacti like peyote and San Pedro


Dimethyltryptamine (DMT): a compound found in plants and brewed as ayahuasca

wiki/psychiatry.title: Psychiatry
wiki/psychiatry.content:
Overview
The term “psychiatry” was coined by Johann Christian Reil in 1808 to describe a medical approach to addressing mental disorders that was distinct from the field of psychology, which at the time separated the mind from the body as two different systems. Today, psychiatrists are medical doctors with MDs or DOs who address mental, emotional, and behavioral disorders. Although the profession is most commonly associated with psychopharmacology, the field includes psychotherapy, electroconvulsive therapy, and lifestyle interventions. They generally follow the DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 for diagnostic standards.

wiki/psychoanalytic.title: Psychoanalysis
wiki/psychoanalytic.content:
Overview
Psychoanalytic therapy brings unconscious thoughts and feelings into conscious awareness for examination and integration, usually relying on Freudian ideas of id, ego, and superego.
In classic psychoanalysis, a client will free associate their thoughts out loud and the therapist listens for unconscious patterns in their transference. Once the therapist brings them to the client’s attention, they are able to process the repressed emotions that were causing them to compulsively repeat an unhealthy pattern. A premise behind this approach is that gaining more insight will help a client exercise their conscious mind to gain control over their unconscious patterns.

wiki/psychodynamic.title: Psychodynamic
wiki/psychodynamic.content:
Overview
Psychodynamic therapy explores the patterns in someone’s internalized scripts in terms of an internal object, an internal self, and their affective link.
In a classic psychodynamic approach, a client and therapist engage in a collaborative conversation to find the unconscious scripts a client repeats in their daily life that drives unhealthy patterns in their behaviors and relationships. Once the client begins to use a script with the therapist and identifies the past memories associated with it, they can use the therapist to experience a validating relationship that challenges the old script.

wiki/psychogenic.title: Psychogenic
wiki/psychogenic.content:
Overview
A psychogenic disease refers to a medical condition that originates in the mind, as a more specific type of psychosomatic disease.
Psychogenic Disease used to be a diagnosis in the DSM-IV. It referred to a condition in which mental stress can lead to physical symptoms, often those of an existing disorder. It was also called “conversion disorder,” though the term was phased out for the DSM-5. There’s an binary implication in psychogenic that splits factors purely between physical and mental realms, when a better analogy is that the brain’s software and hardware are miscommunicating. Instead, the DSM-5-TR offers Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder (FND) and Somatic Symptom Disorder (SSD), and the ICD-11 offers Dissociative Neurological Symptom Disorder and Bodily Distress Disorder (BDD).

wiki/psychology.title: Psychology
wiki/psychology.content:
Overview
Psychology is the study of the human mind and the mental processes that shape outward behavior.
Major Schools


Behaviorism


Cognitivism


Psychoanalytic/Psychodynamic


Humanistic/Existential


Major Subields


Psychoneuroendocrinology


Psychoneuropharmacology


Psychoneuroimmunology


Behavioral Genetics & epigenetics


Neuropsychology


Industrial-Organizational (I-O) Psychology

wiki/psychoneuroendicronology.title: Psychoneuroendicronology
wiki/psychoneuroendicronology.content:
Overview
Psychoneuroendocrinology is the study of the interactions between mental processes, the nervous system, and the endocrine system that regulates hormones.
Allostasis is the process through which the body adjusts itself to maintain stability. Allostatic load refers to the impacts on the body over time when stress responses are chronically triggered, which involves the endocrine system releasing stress hormones for a cascade of bodily reactions.
Three major axes of the neuroendocrine system that intersect with psychology include the:


Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Adrenal (HPA) Axis: the feedback loops for stress, trauma, and depression, with cortisol being especially significant


Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal (HPG) Axis: the circuits for mood disorders, aggression, and reproductive behaviors driven by sex hormones (testosterone, estrogen, and progesterone)


Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Thyroid (HPT) Axis: the axis for metabolic speed and the thyroid hormones that influence mood, energy, and cognition

wiki/psychoneuroimmunology.title: Psychoneuroimmunology
wiki/psychoneuroimmunology.content:
Overview
Psychoneuroimmunology (PNI), also called psychoendoneuroimmunology (PNEI), is the study of the intersection of psychological processes, the nervous system, the endocrine system, and the immune system. In simple terms, the brain and the immune system influence each other through hormones.
One of the biggest problems being researched in the field is the role of inflammation in mental health. The cytokine hypothesis of depression proposes that systemic inflammation across the blood-brain barrier changes the metabolism of neurotransmitters. Cytokines that provoke inflammation reduce serotonin and contribute to Major Depressive Disorder (MDD). Chronic stress can cause neuroinflammation in the brain’s immune cells, called microglia, which can interfere with neuroplasticity in the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus. Decreased neuroplasticity can result in more rigid thought patterns that are difficult to change, a hallmark of clinical depression. Inflammation can form a vicious cycle too; chronic stress means the body is constantly being flooded with cortisol that desensitizes the immune system to its own brakes.

wiki/psychoneuropharmacology.title: Psychoneuropharmacology (Neuropsychopharmacology)
wiki/psychoneuropharmacology.content:
Overview
Psychoneuropharmacology (alternatively, neuropsychopharmacology), is a study of the way chemical reactions alter the brain’s functions and mental processes. It’s a specific subset of psychopharmacology.
Medications for the central nervous system (CNS) used to be organized by the Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) classification system proposed by the World Health Organization (WHO), but a major shift began in 2014 through the Neuroscience-based Nomenclature (NbN) proposed by the European College of Neuropsychopharmacology’s (ECNP) Nomenclature Task Force. Clinical practitioners and bureaucratic systems might still be using ATC due to the way it was built into early medical technology systems, but scientific standards recommend NbN systems.

wiki/psychopathy.title: Psychopathy
wiki/psychopathy.content:
Overview
Psychopathy isn’t an official medical or clinical diagnosis, but it carries weight as a personality construct explored by researchers of various fields. In general, psychopathy refers to a lack of empathy, a lack of inhibition, and a charming external appearance that compensates for lacking genuine emotional reactions. Antisocial personality disorder (ASPD) is often used instead, since many of the conventional traits of psychopathy are difficult to measure.
Researchers out of the field of criminology and criminal justice have often relied on the label in constructing the idea of a criminal personality or assessing the likelihood of someone with a conviction to reoffend. While certain assessments for psychopathy have predictive power in that regard, there are also controversies about the label and the automatic associations that go with it. Someone can score highly on an assessment as the result of other personality disorders or manic episodes, while some infamous serial killers don’t trigger the thresholds on assessments that we set for psychopathy. And of course, there’s always controversy around how objective any evaluator can be when they have their own biases going into an interview.
History and Context
Hare Psychopathy Checklist-Revised (PCL-R)
One of the tools considered a gold standard for psychopathy screenings is the Hare Psychopathy Checklist-Revised (PCL-R) which measures two factors: emotional detachment (measured by interpersonal traits and affective traits) and antisocial behavior (measured by lifestyle traits and antisocial traits). There are 20 items rated on a three-point scale:


Glibness/superficial charm


Grandiose sense of self worth


Need for stimulation/proneness to boredom


Pathological lying


Cunning/manipulative


Lack of remose or guilt


Shallow affect


Callous/lack of empathy


Parasitic lifestyle


Poor behavioral controls


Promiscuous sexual behavior


Early behavior problems


Lack of realistic, long-term goals


Impulsivity


Irresponsibility


Failure to accept responsibility for own actions


Many short-term marital relationships


Juvenile delinquency


Revocation of conditional release


Criminal versatility


Ted Bundy was evaluated to have a 39/40, Jeffrey Dahmer a 23/40, and John Wayne Gacy a 27/40. A 30 is considered the threshold for psychopathy in most North American settings.

wiki/psychopharmacology.title: Psychopharmacology
wiki/psychopharmacology.content:
Overview
Psychopharmacology is the study of the interactions between substances and the one’s thinking and behavior. Two of the dominant approaches include pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics.

wiki/psychosis.title: Psychosis
wiki/psychosis.content:
Overview
Psychosis is a state of mind involved with a detachment from reality through hallucinations, delusions, disorganized thinking, and abnormal motor behavior.
Psychosis and substance use have a bidirectional relationship. Substances like marijuana, cocaine, methamphetamine, alcohol, and others can trigger hallucinations, paranoia, and delusions. Some people who have an underlying mental health disorder, or a predisposition for one, might have an episode triggered by substance use. At the same time, those who feel distress as a result of psychosis from another mental disorder may end up using substances to cope with it. 50% of those diagnosed with schizophrenia also report struggling with substance use.

wiki/psychoterratic.title: Psychoterratic
wiki/psychoterratic.content:
Overview
Psychoterratic refers to mental and emotional states experienced in connection with the state of the environment and Earth as a whole. This includes:


anxiety and grief caused from the threats to ecological stability


solastalgia, or the distress experienced when someone feels a familiar home environment being altered around them.


terrafurie, or the state of anger directed at systems perceived to be threatening the environment


topophilia, or a positive bond someone has to a place


soliphilia, or the political solidarity needed to protect a shared environment

wiki/psychotropics.title: Psychotropic
wiki/psychotropics.content:
Overview
Psychotropics are substances that alter the central nervous system’s perception, mood, consciousness, and behavior. These include:


Antidepressants: these treat depression and anxiety by adjusting the levels of neurotransmitters like serotonin and norepinephrine in the brain. Ex: SSRIs, SNRIs.


Antipsychotics: these manage the symptoms of psychosis, schizophrenia, and bipolar disorder


Anxiolytics (anti-anxiety): these provide relief for panic, phobia, and anxiety. Ex: Benzodiazepines


Mood stabilizers: these balance extreme mood swings associated with bipolar disorder. Ex: Lithium


Stimulants: these increase dopamine and norepinephrine activity

wiki/public-health-and-public-order-outc.title: Public Health and Public Order Outcomes Associated with Supervised Drug Consumption Facilities - a Systemic Review
wiki/public-health-and-public-order-outc.content:
Abstract
“Consistent evidence demonstrates that SCFs mitigate overdose-related harms and unsafe drug use behaviours, as well as facilitate uptake of addiction treatment and other health services among people who use drugs (PWUD). Further, SCFs have been associated with improvements in public order without increasing drug-related crime. SCFs have also been shown to be cost-effective. This systematic review suggests that SCFs are effectively meeting their primary public health and order objectives and therefore supports their role within a continuum of services for PWUD.”
Links

pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28875422/

wiki/public-health-emergency.title: Public Health Emergency (PHE)
wiki/public-health-emergency.content:
Overview
A Public Health Emergency (PHE) is an event that threatens or challenges a community’s health or health systems. The exact definition depends on the organization or source being referenced. Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center writes that a PHE is:
“a complex or difficult situation that affects health systems in one or more geographic areas or from a single locality that has spread globally. It can result from disease (Covid-19, HIV/AIDS), natural disaster (earthquakes, extreme weather), industry (oil spills, lead paint), or policy (housing, war).” 1
A paper by researchers from the RAND corporation that was published in the American Journal of Public Health in 2007 notes that:
“Public health emergencies are defined as much by their health consequences as by their causes and precipitating events. A situation becomes emergent when its health consequences have the potential to overwhelm routine community capabilities to address them. Thus, the proposed definition focuses on situations “whose scale, timing, or unpredictability threatens to overwhelm routine capabilities.””
This definition is a little more expansive because of its emphasis on identifying emergencies the moment it becomes clear that treatment resources or capacities might be overwhelmed. In other words, if we don’t have enough medical hygiene products ready in case of a pandemic, we have a PHE right now, not when that pandemic happens.
Links

wiki/quaaludes.title: Quaaludes
wiki/quaaludes.content:
Overview
Quaaludes are synthetic central nervous system (CNS) depressants that were once prescribed for insomnia and anxiety. Because of its high potential for dependence and fatal respiratory depression, especially when mixed with alcohol, it was eventually moved to a Schedule II controlled substance in 1973 and a Schedule I drug in 1984. They’re also associated with enabling sexual assault through their amnesiac and sleep-inducing properties when slipped into a drink.
