wiki/qualifier.title: Qualifier
wiki/qualifier.content:
Overview
In Al-Anon circles, “Qualifier” or “Q” refers to a person in someone’s life whose drinking or substance use patterns have led them to (“qualified” them for) attendance at an Al-Anon meeting.

wiki/qualitative.title: Qualitative
wiki/qualitative.content:
Overview
Qualitative refers to properties of something that aren’t numerical, often with the goal of obtaining the data from subjective experiences. Qualitative research instruments include surveys, interviews, and ethnographies.

wiki/quality-adjusted-life-year.title: Quality Adjusted Life Year (QALY)
wiki/quality-adjusted-life-year.content:
Overview
A Quality-Adjusted Life Year (QALY) is a health-economics metrics that combines the length of life and quality of life to measure the value of some intervention.
A 1.0 QALY represents one year lived in perfect health. 0.0 represents death. Negative scores can result if someone enters a state considered worse than death. It allows for rough calculations when making decisions in environments with scarce resources. For instance, someone might live a year in perfect health (1 QALY) without a surgical intervention, or they might live two years with a 0.75 quality-of-life score with the intervention. 2 x .75 = 1.5, so according to QALY, the greater value is found in doing the surgical intervention. Obviously, individual preferences may differ enormously. The QALY unit just allows policymakers and administrators to look at the relative effectiveness or rough outcomes of a set of decision-making criteria.

wiki/quantitative.title: Quantitative
wiki/quantitative.content:
Overview
Quantitative refers to properties that can be measured or expressed with standardized units and measurable quantities.

wiki/quinine.title: Quinine
wiki/quinine.content:
Overview
Quinine is a naturally occurring alkaloid found in the cinchona tree, and it’s primarily used as a prescription medication that treats malaria. Although quinine isn’t a controlled substance itself, it’s commonly used as a “cutting agent” that contaminates street drugs like heroin and cocaine due to its similar texture and bitter flavor profile. It also tends to compound the stimulant effects of cocaine to make the effects feel more potent, or cause a rapid drop in blood pressure when injected alongside heroin that can feel like a rush.

wiki/radical-self-acceptance.title: Radical Self-Acceptance
wiki/radical-self-acceptance.content:
Overview
Radical self-acceptance is the acknowledgement and embrace of your entire self with all your experiences without judging yourself or denying reality.
Historical Context
Radical self-acceptance emerged after the ideas of unconditional positive regard in an era that focused on the pathologies caused by the repressed unconscious. Marsha Linehan, a Zen practitioner as well as a psychologist, introduced the idea of radical acceptance to Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT), in which someone accepts reality as it is without judging it or fighting it. That includes acknowledging that pain is a part of life and must be endured, which makes it a relevant tool when building distress tolerance skills and capacities. In 2003, Tara Brach derived “radical self-acceptance” from Linehan’s “radical acceptance” in order to describe a complete acceptance of oneself to remedy the feeling that one is fundamentally broken or flawed.

wiki/radically-open-dialectical-behavior.title: Radically Open Dialectical Behavior Therapy (RO-DBT)
wiki/radically-open-dialectical-behavior.content:
Overview
Radically Open Dialectical Behavior Therapy (RO-DBT) is an approach to disorders of emotional overcontrol (OC) that departs from traditional DBT, which targets dysregulation in the form of undercontrol. This means focusing on excessive self-control, perfectionism, rigidity, risk aversion, low receptivity, inhibited emotional expression, social-signaling deficits, vulnerability, and openness through disconfirming experiences. It can help in cases of anorexia nervosa, treatment-resistant depression, obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (OCPD), autism spectrum disorders, and other personality disorders involving avoidance and paranoia.

wiki/ranchi-institute-of-neuro-psychiatr.title: Ranchi Institute of Neuro-Psychiatry and Allied Sciences (RINPAS)
wiki/ranchi-institute-of-neuro-psychiatr.content:
Once established as a “lunatic asylum” for Indian soldiers in 1795, this was technically the first mental hospital established by the British dedicated to Indian patients, and the second oldest mental hospital in India still functioning. During the tenure of superintendent and notable physician Dr. J.E. Dhunjibhoy in the 1930s, it achieved one of the lowest mortality rates among Indian mental hospitals and began affiliations with the University of London and University of Edinburgh.
Links

pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5836339/

wiki/randomized-controlled-trials.title: Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs)
wiki/randomized-controlled-trials.content:
Overview
A randomized controlled trial (RCT) is a scientific experiment that randomly assigns targets to an experimental group and a control group without intervention to measure the effect of the intervention. RCTs are considered the gold standard for establishing cause-and-effect relationships in most fields of research compared to observational studies.

wiki/rational-choice-theory.title: Rational Choice Theory
wiki/rational-choice-theory.content:
Overview
Rational choice theory views individuals as calculating decision-makers, weighing costs and benefits to maximize their self-interest or satisfaction.
Historical Context
The premise that humans are rational actors driven by self-interest was a staple of conceptual frameworks for Enlightenment thinkers like Adam Smith and David Hume. Early on in the Cold War, there was a push to invest in new methods in social science that were more quantitative and enabled manipulable models to guide policy, and so rational choice theory and methodological individualism were used as premises. Economics, criminology, political science, sociology, and other fields began adopting frameworks based on the theory, and generally it was received controversially. Critics would argue that humans are limited in their time and cognitive faculties to find the choice that maximizes self-interest and that humans often make decisions based on impulses, emotions, and cognitive shortcuts instead of a strict logical analysis. In the early 2000s, as a result of progress in cognitive science and neuroeconomics, researchers like Daniel Kahneman proved that humans consistently use cognitive biases rather than rational optimization procedures.

wiki/re-narcotization.title: Re-Narcotization
wiki/re-narcotization.content:
Overview
Re-narcotization is the unfortunate result of naloxone (Narcan) staying in the body for less time than the fentanyl it seeks to neutralize in the case of an overdose, which can lead someone to slip back into an overdose after naloxone wears off.

wiki/reconsolidation.title: Reconsolidation
wiki/reconsolidation.content:
Overview
Reconsolidation in the context of psychology refers to the process in which a long-term memory is retrieved, updated, and restabilized.
The process first involves reactivation, in which a past memory or unconscious schema is invoked. If one experiences something that contradicts the prediction suggested by the past memory, the nervous system can process the new data and update the pattern of the old memory. However, if the nervous system is not calm enough to begin reconsolidation, it can trigger defense mechanisms or panic at the distress of reality being out of sync with one’s expectations. Modalities like EMDR rely on reconsolidation of past trauma in orer to weaken their influence on someone’s actions and reactions to triggers.

wiki/recovery-advocacy-project.title: Recovery Advocacy Project (RAP)
wiki/recovery-advocacy-project.content:
Overview
The Recovery Advocacy Project (RAP) is a national non-profit that gives grassroots organizing tools to people in recovery and their families, based around the idea that those in recovery should have a direct voice in political decisions and legislation that addresses their mental health condition. They intentionally court bipartisan support for harm-reduction tools like Naloxone (Narcan) or expanding funding for sober living environments (SLEs) and transitional housing.
Links

recoveryvoices.com/

wiki/recovery-capital.title: Recovery Capital
wiki/recovery-capital.content:
Overview
Recovery capital (RC) refers to the sum of resources a person has to sustain recovery for mental health conditions and substance use disorders in particular. The most commonly used domains of RC include:


Human capital: personal characteristics and qualities, including health, education, coping mechanisms, resilience, a sense of hope, etc.


Social capital: supportive relationships, like friends, family, peer-support networks, and community ties


Financial capital: money or assets that can be used to procure goods and services, from basic needs to specialized treatment


Cultural capital: values, beliefs, or organizational structures of particular faith-based or ethnic backgrounds that play a role in one’s identity


Community capital: systemic and local assets, including accessible facilities, recovery community organizations (RCOs), recovery-friendly policies like diversion programs, etc.


RC frameworks allow us to identify variables and construct factors with strong predictive power. One of the leading indicators of decreased chances of someone relapsing is the increase in recovery capital over the 90-days following sobriety. That ends up being a more reliable indicator than toxicology patterns or the past frequency of use.
Tests
Brief Assessment of Recovery Capital (BARC-10)
The Brief Assessment of Recovery Capital (BARC-10) is a 10-item survey that uses a 6-point Likert scale and is commonly used in clinical settings for tracking patient outcomes longitudinally. Studies show it successfully predicts sustained remission at 6 and 12 month windows.
Recovery Capital Index (RCI)
The Recovery Capital Index (RCI) contains 68 items and yields a score from 1-100.
Recovery Capital Assessment (REC-CAP)
The Recovery Capital Assessment (REC-CAP) contains 73 items as a result of combining 4 other scales.

wiki/recovery-oriented-care.title: Recovery-Oriented Care (ROC)
wiki/recovery-oriented-care.content:
Overview
Recovery-oriented care (ROC) is a framework for mental health and substance use treatment that focuses on an individual’s overall quality of life and integration into a community rather than just symptom reduction.
The Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) proposes four dimensions to recovery under the Recovery Support Strategic Initiative: health, home, purpose, and community. It also identifies ten guiding principles of recovery: hope, person-driven, many pathways, holistic, peer support, relational, culture, addresses trauma, strengths/responsibility, and respect. SAMHSA serves as one of the central institutions in the United States that promotes ROCs by incentivizing the creation of Recovery-Oriented Systems of Care (ROSC). 1

wiki/recovery-oriented-systems-of-care.title: Recovery-Oriented Systems of Care (ROSC)
wiki/recovery-oriented-systems-of-care.content:
Overview
Recovery-Oriented Systems of Care (ROSC) are networks of health and community services that wrap around individuals with mental health conditions in their regular environment, which goes beyond treatments for symptom reduction. They implement the frameworks of Recovery-Oriented Care (ROC) through infrastructure for the full range of problems related to substance use disorders. According to the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration’s (SAMHSA) 2010 Recovery-Oriented Systems of Care (ROSC) Resource Guide:
“The central focus of a ROSC is to create an infrastructure or “system of care” with the resources to effectively address the full range of substance use problems within communities. The specialty SUD field provides the full continuum of care (prevention, early intervention, treatment, continuing care, and recovery) in partnership with other disciplines, such as mental health and primary care, in a ROSC. A ROSC encompasses a menu of individualized, person-centered, and strength-based services within a self-defined network. By design, a ROSC provides individuals and families with more options with which to make informed decisions regarding their care. Services are designed to be accessible, welcoming, and easy to navigate. A fundamental value of a ROSC is the involvement of people in recovery, their families, and the community to continually improve access to and quality of services.” 1
Examples of ROSC services include:


Peer Recovery Support Services: peer coaching, mentoring, support groups


Housing Support: transitional housing, sober living environments, recovery residences


Employment and Education Assistance:, job training, vocational support, GED classes


Alternative Therapies: acupuncture, meditation, art therapy


Case management: care coordination across detox, residential treatment centers, inpatient care, outpatient care, primary care, local support programs, and community groups


Links

wiki/recovery-research-institute.title: Recovery Research Institute (RRI)
wiki/recovery-research-institute.content:
Overview
The Recovery Research Institute is a nonprofit research institute of Massachusetts General Hospital, which is affiliated with Harvard Medical School. Their projects include:


The Recovery Bulletin, a free monthly publication that summarizes global research in addiction science to over 20,000 professionals and policymakers


The Addictionary, a glossary that describes a unified scientific language


National Recovery Study, providing data on 22 million Americans who have had some definition of success in recovery from Substance Use Disorders (SUDs)


The institute’s data has been cited by the U.S. Surgeon General.
Links

giving.massgeneral.org/stories/the-recovery-research-institute-a-trusted-resource-on-addiction-issues

wiki/recovery.title: Recovery
wiki/recovery.content:
Overview
Recovery is a widely used term to mean the opposite of active addiction, but what exactly recovery means varies based on the context.
Definitions
Definitions of recovery generally fall into one of two categories: abstinence or harm-reduction. Literature and institutions derived from 12-step groups like Alcoholics Anonymous are more likely to declare abstinence from all recreational use of substances to be a necessary, but not sufficient, component to recovery. Other groups like SMART Recovery or medical institutions are more likely to adopt a harm-reduction perspective that encourages any change in substance use patterns towards a person’s health goals, however incremental the progress may be.
Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA)
The Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), in full self-awareness about the complex nuances to addiction treatment, published a paper called the Working Definition of Recovery:
“A process of change through which individuals improve their health and wellness, live a self-directed life, and strive to reach their full potential.” 1
Betty Ford Institute Consensus Panel
In 2007, the Betty Ford Institute Consensus Panel defined recovery as:
“a voluntarily maintained lifestyle characterized by sobriety, personal health, and citizenship”
Recovery Science Research Collaborative
In 2017, the Recovery Science Research Collaborative arrived at the definition:
“Recovery is an individualized, intentional, dynamic, and relational process involving sustained efforts to improve wellness.”
Links

wiki/redlining.title: Redlining
wiki/redlining.content:
Overview
Redlining refers to the historic practice in the United States of grading neighborhoods as hazardous for the purpose of withholding resources, which generally maintained segregated neighborhoods by guiding banks to deny loans in communities of color.
Studies show that neighborhoods that experienced redlining also experience some of the highest drug overdose rates. They’re also more likely to have liquor stores and bodegas that sell alcohol, lack safe recreational spaces, face scarcities of resources for mental health care, and have limited access to healthy food options.

wiki/reefer-madness.title: Reefer Madness (Tell Your Children)
wiki/reefer-madness.content:
Overview
Reefer Madness, originally titled Tell Your Children, is a hilariously outdated PSA about the dangers of marijuana. In fact, it’s somewhat of a cult hit as a stoner movie itself. The original release reflects the drug hysteria of a post-Prohibition America in which the public had tired of big institutional interventions into the problems of addiction and instead sought to foster a local culture of parents seeking direct, personal interventions into their children’s lives. After a while, it was edited and re-released as a way to depict scandalous content that was otherwise prohibited under the guise of being a cautionary set of warnings.
Live Commentary
“The motion picture you are about to witness may startle you. It would not have been possible, otherwise, to sufficiently emphasize the frightful toll of the new drug menace which is destroying the youth of America in alarmingly-increasing numbers.”
“Marihuana is that drug - a violent narcotic - an unspeakable scourge - The Real Public Enemy Number One!”
“Its first effect is sudden, violent, uncontrollable laughter; then come dangerous hallucinations - space expands - time slows down, almost stands still … fixed ideas come next, conjuring up monstrous extravagances - followed by emotional disturbances, the total inability to direct thoughts, the lost of all power to resist physical emotions… leading finally to acts of shocking violence … ending often in incurable insanity.”
“In picturing its soul-destroying effects no attempt was made to equivocate. The scenes and incidents, while fictionized for the purposes of this story, are based upon actual research into the results of Marihuana addiction. If their stark reality will make you think, will make you aware that something must be done to wipe out this ghastly menace, then the picture will not have failed in its purpose… Because the dread Marihuana may be reaching forth next for your son or daughter … or yours … or YOURS!”
This is the text that opens up the movie. Keep in mind this movie was released in the same era where the following substances were available over-the-counter:


Benzedrine Inhalers, loaded with amphetamine


paregoric (camphorated opium tincture) was accessible in liquid form for infants at any corner drug store


donnagel which contained opium extracts and belladonna alkaloids


terpin hydrate with codeine


bromo-seltzer as a hangover remedy that contained sodium bromide, a sedative toxin


Barbital and Veronal as early barbiturates


Hadacol and Geritol, which contained 12 to 15% alcohol while being marketed as “vitamin tonics” appropriate for families with children


Acetanilide as painkillers


But beware, the Real Public Enemy Number One is the Dread Marihuana! Hide your kids! Hide your wives!
Commentary
I’ll be honest, I really wish I was high while seeing this. What a missed opportunity.
Live Reactions
“Out of the traffic in these drugs, a lawlessness that we can scarcely estimate has grown and is now flourishing. It exists in almost every city and hamlet in the country… The weed marihuana is grown in every state in the Union.”
Interestingly, modern studies into D.A.R.E have suggested that Public Service Announcements (PSAs) and educational programs that frame substances as being an ever-present threat around them has the opposite effect of deterrence and marginalization of substance use. People, especially children, are more likely to walk away from these messages with the conclusion that substance use is normalized in society. If every city has marijuana, then it no longer seems to be some distant dangerous drug demolishing domestic order, but a fabric of that very domestic order itself that is practiced discreetly as a sign of maturity and respectability.
“It might be interesting and important for you to know some of the methods use in bringing these drugs into the country and the work of the forces of law and order, which are daily combating the traffic, always at the risk of life by their agents. This ceaseless fight against the drug traffic is directed by the Department of Narcotics, Washington.”
While there is appropriately a lot of blame placed on American Presidents Richard Nixon and Ronald Reagan for concocting and perpetuating the disastrous War on Drugs, we can see that the notion of a battle or a war against the presence of drugs through the state has older roots. This film was produced only a few years after Prohibition was repealed and black market organized crime groups that sold bootleg alcohol were addressed, so there was some recent precedence for expecting violence when regulating substances that are highly in-demand.
“At the outset of this letter, there is one vital fact I would like to submit. There is a powerful agency. I speak of the school-parent associations of this country, which can be invaluable in stamping out this scourge. Their help, their eternal vigilance, could be the deciding factor in our fight against it.”
As a rule of thumb, whenever a product of the culture of Protestant moral-psychology discusses “eternal vigilance” or “constant spiritual warfare” or some similar term referring to the need to be on constant guard from some external temptation or threat, I hear a comparison to Satan being set up.
“They are hidden in fake jewelry cases, in the heels of shoes, women’s shoes especially, because the drugs can be secreted in false heels. Hollowed shaving brushes are another medium. Books with false centers are often used. Watch cases are convenient hiding places. The value of drugs thus seized is enormous.”
I’m sorry, this is a PSA that’s supposed to discourage the use of drugs? They just told us that everyone everywhere is doing them, there are tons of effective hiding places in everyday objects, and selling drugs is very lucrative.
“Oh why don’t you button up your lips? You’re always squawking about something. You got more static than a radio.”
Unfortunately, Jack’s embrace of weed does not by any stretch of the imagination make him oriented towards progressive values about the opinions of women.
Mary: “Why, don’t you know him? That’s Hot Fingers Pirelli!”
Bill: “Boy, he really swings out hot with a mess of jive!”
Perfect. No notes.
Mary: “It’s sweet of you to help me, Bill.”
Bill: “I’ll show you anything except domestic science.”
Mary: “I see, don’t you want to learn anything about running your own home?”
Bill: “The answer is no. You know, after that session we had yesterday, I went home and told Mother that the trouble with her pot roast gravy was she hadn’t added three heaping teaspoonfuls of olive oil.”
Mary: “What did she say?”
Bill: “She didn’t say anything. She just threw me out of the kitchen.”
Mary: “I don’t wonder.”
Setting aside Bill’s bitch of a mother (that’s sarcasm, don’t @ me), my ears perked up at the phrase “domestic science,” which at first impression sounds like a lip-service concession to feminist activists who sought to eliminate disparities between men and women in terms of involvement in public life outside the domestic sphere. The actual history is more nuanced, and I intend to dig into it at some point. For now though, if I were being generous, I might say Bill’s disinterest in domestic science is potential foreshadowing for the corruption of the values and structures that preserved the middle-class white American lifestyle. If only Bill’s mother allowed his son to cook.
Bill: “Mary, before we do that math, how about reading some of this? It’s swell!”
Mary: “Romeo and Juliet?”
Bill: “You know, when I study this, I kinda think of you.”
If only this wasn’t a black-and-white movie, Mary might see this as a red flag.
Also, the average person in this movie dresses better in their daily life than I have in my entire life. What’s the point of all this post-WWII American exceptionalism when we don’t even wear suits and vests to school anymore?
Dr. Carroll: “There is no doubt that there is an organized gang distributing the narcotic to students, not only in my school, but all over the city. You government men have got to find some way to put an end to it!”
Mr. Wyatt: “Of course, I agree with you, Dr. Carroll. But do you realize that marihuana is not like other forms of dope? You see, it grows wild in almost every state of the Union. There’s practically no interstate commerce in the drug. As a result, the government’s hands are tied. And frankly, the only sure cure is a widespread campaign in education.”
Dr. Carroll: “Oh, it’s all right to talk about education, Mr. Wyatt? But we educators can’t do anything until the public is sufficiently aroused.”
There’s actually a lot more being reflected here than a simple plea for parents to be more involved in guiding the youth away from substance use. Early temperance movements have many of their roots in the Second Great Awakening, which most historians mark between the 1790s and 1840s, just a couple decades before the Civil War. These revival movements attempted to move past the Calvinist notions of predestination that predetermined who would go to Heaven or Hell before they were even born with a message about achieving salvation through personal choices. Many staunch religious activists advocated for the end of slavery and ban of alcohol, which culminated in Prohibition from 1920 to 1933. The rising “democratized” view on spiritual connections that claimed any individual could be saved through personal revelation rather than adhering to the strict practices and logic of institutional authorities. Gender stereotypes framed women as inherently more emotional, so feminists of the era were able to push back on traditional narratives that used the story of Eve and the Garden of Eden to undermine the moral character of women. Without access to suffrage or political office, the masses of women joining moral movements argued that the community was an extension of the home as part of the domestic sphere. As such, their moral and spiritual authority ought to guide social reforms while men dealt with the dirty aspects of politics, law enforcement, and war.
So, insofar as substance use could be framed as a moral failing, the local infrastructure set up by temperance activists and early feminists was particularly significant. Movies like Reefer Madness, originally titled Tell Your Children if you recall, were made and distributed by groups steeped in this culture. After the failures of Prohibition, in which the black market for alcohol thrived and led to widespread local corruption, there was a strong distaste from the American public for more solutions that involved government intervention. It’s no coincidence that Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) was started in the 1930s as well as a social and cultural movement that explicitly embraced anarchist ideas about mutual aid and voluntary association while eschewing institutional authorities.
The movie avoids condemning the government, instead framing federal law enforcement agencies as limited by their legal jurisdiction (via the interstate commerce clause) but supportive of efforts from the public to rise to the moral occasion and act against the dread marihuana. In fact, many officials like Harry J. Anslinger, first commissioner of the Federal Bureau of Narcotics (FBN), leaned into the hysteria promoted by the film to build momentum for crackdowns on drug use. Rather than attempting to change the moral character of the nation with a ban on a substance as widely integrated into daily life as alcohol, anti-drug coalitions reframed their project as preserving and protecting the public from a new intrusive threat to the order of society tied to immigrants and communities of color. Rhetoric from these anti-drug crusades shifted from standard morality plays derived from revivalist sermons to public service announcements concerning criminal and medical dangers coated in xenophobic and racism.
In the context of the movie, the contrast between the jazz being played in Jack and Mae’s apartment-turned-marihuana-den and the “swell” Shakespeare Billy and Mary recite at Mary’s middle-class home under the supervision of her mother is a completely unsubtle reference to “black” culture leaking into the lives of white communities.
“Bill, I’m going to ask you a straightforward question, and I’d like to have a straightforward answer… Isn’t it true that you have, perhaps unwillingly, acquired a certain harmful habit through an association with certain undesirable people?”
That’s not a straightforward question.
“Bill, are you a pothead?” is a straightforward question.

wiki/reel-recovery-film-festival-and-sym.title: REEL Recovery Film Festival & Symposium
wiki/reel-recovery-film-festival-and-sym.content:
Overview
The REEL Recovery Film Festival & Symposium is hosted by Writers in Treatment and features documentaries, short films, and feature-length movies that explore addiction and treatment with the goal of reducing stigma. It was co-founded in 2008 by Leonard Buschel and Robert Downey Sr.
Links

reelrecoveryfilmfestival.org/

wiki/regenerative-medicine-advanced-ther.title: Regenerative Medicine Advanced Therapies (RMAT)
wiki/regenerative-medicine-advanced-ther.content:
Overview
Regenerative Medicine Advanced Therapies (RMAT) are medical treatments that replace or repair damage in the human body that is the underlying cause of disease or injury.
For treating Substance Use Disorder (SUD), no RMAT therapy has been approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA), but there are experimental treatments that have progressed to human clinical trials. These include:
-The ALAUNUS Study: Allogeneic Human Mesenchymal Stem Cell (MSC) Infusions for comorbid Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD) and Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) are currently in a randomized clinical trial. Chronic drinking can cause

wiki/rehab-riviera.title: Rehab Riviera
wiki/rehab-riviera.content:
Overview
The term “Rehab Riviera” is a term to describe the massive concentration of rehabilitation centers and recovery resources in Southern California, especially around Orange County. It often has a negative implication due to widely-shared reporting about predatory business models and regulatory gaps in the network of private rehabilitation centers.

wiki/rehab.title: Rehab
wiki/rehab.content:
Overview
Rehab (rehabilitation) refers to a program or facility that restores something or someone to an improved condition.
In the context of treatment for substance use disorders, rehab can refer to a level of care between medical detoxification, residential treatment centers, inpatient facilities, partial hospitalization programs, and intensive outpatient programs.

wiki/relapse-prevention.title: Relapse Prevention
wiki/relapse-prevention.content:
Overview
Relapse prevention refers to coping skills developed to manage the triggers, risk factors, or warnings signs of a relapse.
Models
Marlatt and Gordon Relapse Prevention Model
The Marlatt and Gordon Relapse Prevention Model is a cognitive-behavioral framework developed by the same researchers who noted the Abstinence Violation Effect (AVE).
The CENAPS Model
The CENAPS Model proposes nine principles to sustain recovery:


Stabilization


Assessment


Relapse Education


Warning Sign Identification


Warning Sign Management


Recovery Planning


Inventory Training


Family Involvement


Follow-Up

wiki/relapse.title: Relapse
wiki/relapse.content:
Overview
A relapse is the return of a condition after a period of its absence or remission. In the context of substance use, it normally means using substances actively again after a period of sobriety or reduction in use.
In recovery circles, relapse is often considered a gradual process that involves emotional, mental, and physical dimensions. Some failure in routine or external stressor might trigger emotions that lead to mentally rationalizing or glamorizing using a substance again which leads to physically consuming substances again.

wiki/release-of-information-roi.title: Release of Information (ROI)
wiki/release-of-information-roi.content:
Overview
A Release of Information (ROI) is a document that allows a healthcare provider to share Protected Health Information (PHI) with another entity.
When entering a treatment program, it’s common to sign ROIs that allow the provider or facility to share information across your care network, including therapists, psychiatrists, case managers, insurance providers, reporting agencies, family members, and peer recovery.

wiki/remission.title: Remission
wiki/remission.content:
Overview
Remission describes a state when symptoms of a disease decrease or disappear. It’s a narrower concept than recovery, which describes the entire process of healing towards an improved quality of life.
In the DSM-5-TR, remission for substance use disorder (SUD) means that someone who used to meet its diagnostic criteria no longer meets any except cravings. Early remission is considered the period between 3 months and 12 months without meeting any SUD criteria, while sustained remission is used to describe the period of time after 12 months.

wiki/rescuing.title: Rescuing
wiki/rescuing.content:
Overview
In psychology, rescuing refers to the dynamic of trying to intervene on someone’s behalf to meet their needs or solve their problems. It’s often discussed in the context of codependent relationships and people-pleasing, where someone might try to compulsively rescue someone else as a way of feeling needed and useful in their relationships.

wiki/resentment.title: Resentment
wiki/resentment.content:
Overview
Resentment is the emotion associated with feeling mistreated or subject to injustice that cannot or was not addressed.
In recovery circles of all types, resentment is considered one of the most common triggers or signs of a relapse that can exist. The idea behind reciting the Serenity Prayer in Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) or embracing impermanence in Recovery Dharma (RD) or Refuge Recovery (RR) is to let go of attachments to events in life that produce resentment. There’s also an element of radical acceptance there about accepting that life is going to be unfair and one will suffer for it, and all one can control is the reaction to it. Carrying resentment, in and of itself, only adds distress and triggers to one’s life rather than creating a peaceful state of mind.

wiki/residential-treatment.title: Residential Treatment
wiki/residential-treatment.content:
Overview
Residential treatment refers to a live-in program at a specialized facility for mental health and substance use disorders. Usually, it means 24/7 supervision, individual and group therapy, and medication management across 30 to 90 days for longer-term recovery. It is considered a Level 3 operational tier according to the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM), which is a step down from inpatient hospitalization and a step up from partial hospitalization programs (PHPs). An increasing number of programs describe themselves as dual diagnosis facilities, meaning they address other mental health disorders alongside substance use disorders, like depression, anxiety, eating disorders, and PTSD.

wiki/resilience.title: Psychological Resilience
wiki/resilience.content:
Overview
The American Psychological Association (APA) defines resilience as
“the process and outcome of successfully adapting to difficult or challenging life experiences, especially through mental, emotional, and behavioral flexibility and adjustment to external and internal demands. A number of factors contribute to how well people adapt to adversities, predominant among them (a) the ways in which individuals view and engage with the world, (b) the availability and quality of social resources, and (c) specific coping strategies. Psychological research demonstrates that the resources and skills associated with more positive adaptation (i.e., greater resilience) can be cultivated and practiced.”
Resilience is an incredibly common topic in mental health and SUD recovery circles, since recovery is a non-linear challenging process that involves adapting to a lot of change. For many people who have struggled with coping skills and distress tolerance, resilience is a key trait in handling the stages before success. However, this emphasis on individual traits is sometimes criticized for ignoring the systemic and environmental factors that influence the situations individuals are put into, which is accounted for in recovery capital frameworks.

wiki/responsible-beverage-service.title: Responsible Beverage Service (RBS)
wiki/responsible-beverage-service.content:
Overview
Responsible Beverage Service (RBS) refers to a training and certification program for handling alcohol on-premises at a business. It focuses on checking IDs, recognizing intoxication, overservice prevention, and other regulations around the responsibilities and liabilities of a business serving alcohol.

wiki/ressentiment.title: Ressentiment
wiki/ressentiment.content:
Overview
“Ressentiment” describes feelings of resentment towards the perceived source of one’s powerlessness.
History and Context
Friedrich Nietzsche used “ressentiment” to lay the groundwork for his concept of “slave morality” as a psychological defense against the implication of one’s inferiority. Specifically, Nietzsche argued that those without power resent those who do have power, and they react by creating a system of morality that elevates their weaknesses into virtues while condemning the strength and success of others as vices. For instance, a worker may resent the financial successes of their company’s CEO, so the narrative that wealthy people are made unhappy by their own corruption and greed while workers can find happiness in honest, simple labor can be appealing. It allows someone to operate within an alternative hierarchy to attain and demonstrate value when feeling rejected by another hierarchy.
Commentary
I would argue that many therapeutic modalities are focused on dismantling ressentiment at the level of the individual’s mindset rather than examining ways for the individual to compete into a position of power. The “radical acceptance” that is spoken of in Dialectical Behavioral Therapy (DBT) and Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) is positioned towards the end of accepting reality as it is without the judgment that prompts a reactive rationalization that becomes ressentiment. One is encouraged to make peace with the inequalities that cause them suffering to move out of a reactive state defined by craving something one lacks, which is why the ascetic ideals derived from Buddhist frameworks were inspirational in the development of DBT and other recent modalities.
The argument could be made that Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy, DBT, ACT, etc. enable clients to actively pursue their values and goals without being bound to their immediate emotional reactions, harmful schemas, and negative core beliefs, and I could agree with that. The issue lies in the limitations of what therapy is: an institutional authority in a room whose limits of intervention are helping a patient unpack their internal relationship to their perception of reality through psychological mechanisms while retaining a normative set of beliefs about what healthy mechanisms ought to be. A therapist is highly limited in their ability to assess the external system a client operates within, so the model of reality that has to be constructed within a therapeutic setting is necessarily going to diverge from the model of reality outside the room.
Consider a client presenting with the belief “the world is fundamentally unsafe, so kill-or-be-killed is the mindset it takes to survive.” This client, in a pre-ressentiment phase, might have constructed a worldview in which their adaptation to the kill-or-be-killed mindset is virtuous.
A CBT practitioner might directly tackle this as a cognitive distortion or maladaptive coping mechanism. They might encourage the client to find evidence that contradicts the idea the world is always unsafe, such as examining their past for interactions or relationships that did feel safe to the client. This doesn’t actually engage with the client’s reality as much as it attempts to tune their model of reality towards one that, within the clinician’s assumptions of rational and helpful thinking, would produce less suffering. The clinician might reason that being able to identify safety would produce relief or restore executive functioning capacity for a client who might be facing chronic stress produced from a hypervigilant affect of a maladaptive defense mechanism, but what if the world truly is unsafe in the lived material reality that the client exists within? After all, even the relationship between the clinician and the client is generally contingent on the client’s capacity to pay for the clinician’s services, which are themselves regulated and formulated through institutional incentives unrelated to the client. The clinician’s model of reality necessarily diverges from the client’s actual reality under the Stoic premise that thoughts about events drive suffering rather than the events themselves. Rather than coming up with solutions that work through a “kill-or-be-killed” mindset and derive motivation to change reality out of rage or envy, the cognitive flexibility and emotional regulation it takes to not act are elevated as ideals, with the assumption that the client can make healthier decisions from this position. However, the metrics of a successful CBT intervention remain located in the client’s internal homeostasis rather than a true relationship to external reality. In this case, the metric becomes the client’s ability to challenge a belief in an unsafe world, even if validated by their external reality, in order to manufacture comfort by constructing evidence of safety. So long as the clinician and client are operating in the model of reality constructed within a room meant to exist outside of the client’s usual material reality, only the client’s self-reported interpretation of the world can be examined to determine whether there’s a pathological level of suffering and adjusted to reduce it. Within these bounds, we’re effectively rearranging deck chairs on the ship of ressentiment, guided by the clinician’s subjective assessment of the combination of “rational beliefs” that dispel the “cognitive distortions” until a reduction in pathological suffering is achieved.

wiki/risk-factors.title: Risk Factors
wiki/risk-factors.content:
Overview
Risk factors are any attributes or conditions that increase the probability of an adverse outcome happening, particularly developing a new condition or disease. The opposite of risk factors are protective factors, which are gaining more attention in strengths-based therapeutic modalities and recovery capital frameworks.
The largest risk factors for the global disease burden include:


High Blood Pressure: the single largest risk factor that contributes to strokes and heart attacks


High Fasting Blood Sugar: increases the risks for developing Type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease


High Body Mass Index: although BMI has received plenty of deserved pushback for painting an incomplete picture of health, it still points to a very real trend in obesity, which contributes to cardiovascular disease and a whole host of other health issues.


Tobacco Use: Smoking is the leading preventable cause of death in the world, given that it can lead to cancers, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and other conditions.


Alcohol and Substance Use: Substance use is the primary risk factor for individuals ages 15-49, with alcohol in particular being widely used and leading to liver cirrhosis, mental health crises, accidents, and cardiovascular stress.


Dietary Risks: Diets high in sodium or low in whole grains and fruits are more likely to lead to health issues


Inactivity: Many more jobs and lifestyles now are sedentary, which has a lot of negative consequences for one’s healthspan and metabolic health


Air Pollution: Both outdoor pollution and indoor smoke can increase the chance of developing lower respiratory infections and systemic inflammation


Chemical and Heavy Metal Exposure: This is especially salient with lead pollution, which has been highly damaging and continues to be an issue in developing and developed countries alike.

wiki/robert-deforde.title: Robert DeForde
wiki/robert-deforde.content:
Robert DeForde works with an organization called Shatterproof which works to convince medical professionals that addiction is worth treating through online and in-person trainings.
Links

www.npr.org/2026/08/06/nx-s1-5845162/addiction-treatment-overdose-deaths

wiki/rock-bottom.title: Rock Bottom
wiki/rock-bottom.content:
Overview
The idiom “rock bottom” refers to the lowest possible condition something or someone can be in. It comes from 19th-century mining industries as a phrase that referred to the hardest layers they could hit when digging down, and it was often adapted for slogans like “rock-bottom prices.” It was popularized by Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) in reference to a low point someone encounters in active addiction from which they might derive a gift of desperation that motivates drastic and lasting change.

wiki/rodrigo-de-jerez.title: Rodrigo de Jerez
wiki/rodrigo-de-jerez.content:
Wikipedia said it best: “He is credited with being the first European smoker.”
Jerez started smoking tobacco after a Taino settlement in Cuba introduced the practice to him. He attempted to introduce it in Europe, but he was accused of sinful consortations with the Devil when the sight of exhaling smoke frightened his home town. He was arrested and detained for seven years. By the time he was released, smoking tobacco had become a trend, and it would soon be a cash crop.
Links

static.abc.es/media/historia/2018/03/19/fumador-obra-kVNC—1240x698@abc.jpg

wiki/rorschach-test.title: Rorschach Test
wiki/rorschach-test.content:
Overview
The Rorschach test is a widely known yet controversial assessment that asks clients to interpret inkblot cards to examine their personality, thoughts, and feelings. Today, though it’s far less commonly used than before, a standard modern version exists called the Rorschach Performance Assessment System (R-PAS). Studies show that certain aspects of the Rorschach test can help identify schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, though the risk of “false positives” from healthy individuals with subjectively varied interpretations is also high. There also hasn’t been much evidence to support the theoretical premise of the test, which is that encountering ambiguous stimuli forces a projection from the unconscious.

wiki/roy-a-wise.title: Roy A. Wise
wiki/roy-a-wise.content:
“if I knew that my daughter was going to try either heroin or crack, I’d prefer that she try heroin.”
Wise words from Roy Wise

wiki/rudy-giuliani.title: Rudy Giuliani
wiki/rudy-giuliani.content: When he was the US attorney for the Southern District of New York, he purchased crack on camera to show how easy it is to buy drugs.

wiki/rumination.title: Rumination
wiki/rumination.content:
Overview
Rumination is the process of repeatedly replaying negative events or possibilities in ways that don’t productively drive at a solution. It’s a major symptom in depression, anxiety, Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD), and Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD). Developing the coping skills and structures to reduce isolation and prevent rumination is a common theme in recovery circles and literature. Rumination-Focused Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (RF-CBT) is dedicated CBT modality to address the process and function of rumination.

wiki/rural-addiction-prevention.title: Rural Addiction Prevention
wiki/rural-addiction-prevention.content:
Overview
Rural Addiction Prevention (RAP) is a nonprofit dedicated to preventing and treating Substance Use Disorder (SUD) in rural Alabama. Their spaces provide services like community education and free Naloxone (Narcan) as harm reduction.
Link

www.rapnow.org/

wiki/safe-sex.title: Safe Sex
wiki/safe-sex.content:
Overview
Safe sex refers to sexual practices that reduce the risk of spreading sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) and having unplanned pregnancies.
With substance use comes impaired judgment and impulsive decision-making, which means it’s more likely someone will fail to take the precautions of ensuring sex is safe. That significantly increases the chances of transmitting diseases like HIV or Hepatitis B and C. For a subset of the population with substance use disorders, sex work and transactional sex are likely to facilitate unsafe sex.

wiki/saito-satoru.title: Saito Satoru
wiki/saito-satoru.content: In a 1985 book, Satoru argued that a person with alcoholism was in some sense reborn as part of an underlying family problem, and the stress of a birth that isn’t seen as a family affair can exacerbate problems. This included addressing family dynamics that could be dysfunctional, since an alcoholic simply resuming their past role while being sober could lead to someone else developing a mental illness because of the stress.

wiki/saloon.title: Saloon
wiki/saloon.content:
Overview
A saloon is an older term for a bar or tavern where people socialize while drinking and watching entertainment.
Historical Context
In America, saloons emerged in the early 19th century to serve traders, miners, and cattle ranchers in small towns, and they were mostly designed to serve men. They became important local institutions that also acted as community centers, post offices, and voting stations. Saloons even gained political power themselves and lobbied for favorable regulations and policies. The temperance movement that brought on Prohibition in the early 20th century led to the widespread destruction of saloon culture in America. Sometimes, it also meant the literal destruction of saloons. Activists like Carry Nation conducted “hatchetations” during the movement for Prohibition, which meant tearing down saloons with hatches.

wiki/salvia.title: Salvia
wiki/salvia.content:
Overview
Salvia is a psychoactive plant from the mint family with hallucinogenic properties through the compound salvinorin A. While hallucinogens like LSD or the psilocybin found in magic mushrooms target serotonin, salvinorin A binds to kappa-opioid receptors. It causes intense psychedelic experiences and dissociations that can last up to an hour depending on whether it’s smoked or chewed. In the United States, it is not federally an illicit substance, though some states and other countries have restricted it.

wiki/san-francisco-opium-den-ordinance-o.title: San Francisco Opium Den Ordinance of 1875
wiki/san-francisco-opium-den-ordinance-o.content:
Summary
The San Francisco Opium Den Ordinance of 1875 was the first law in America that banned a non-alcoholic drug by making it a misdemeanor to visit places where people smoked opium.
It was driven largely over xenophobic fears about growing Chinese communities in the city, as well as concerns that it played a role in attracting white residents to Chinatown establishments away from white-owned ones. In doing so, law enforcement had the legal cover to selectively disrupt Chinese communities under suspicions of being an opium den while white neighborhoods continued using liquid opium as medicine.
Context
The 1870s were an economically rough time for California. The Long Depression of 1873 lasted until 1879 as the longest period of economic contraction recognized by the National Bureau of Economic Research.
Paradoxically, historians mark the beginning of the Second Industrial Revolution around the same time. Factories were adopting new technologies in steel, chemical manufacturing, and electrical grids. This meant goods could be cheaply mass manufactured which drove down their prices globally and cut down the profit margins businesses were expecting. Massive speculation in railroad companies after the Civil War proved to outpace actual returns. The collapse of banking house Jay Cooke & Company triggered panic that led to the temporary closure of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE). An estimated 18,000 businesses and 89 railroads went bankrupt in the US in the initial years, with a peak unemployment of 14% by 1878. Layoffs and wage cuts were met with violent backlash like the Great Railroad Strike of 1877.
However, finance and economics are hard concepts. Instead of blaming the rampant financial speculation or lack of policies to help workers transition during periods of massive change in the labor market, they blamed immigrants for dragging down wages and using underhanded tactics to undermine white businesses. White saloons and gambling houses viewed Chinatown opium dens as competitors for working-class white men seeking recreational substances. Factory owners and labor leaders alike claimed that opium addiction, though not alcoholism, was affecting the productivity of white workers. The Workingmen’s Party of California demanded a boycott of Chinese-made goods and Chinese-owned businesses.
Some of the claims bordered on hysteria and conspiratorial paranoia. Labor organizations practically alleged a nefarious plan to trap white workers in drug dependency in order for Chinese communities to get ahead. Yellow journalism companies ran stories that claimed Chinese men used opium to lure, seduce, and traffick young white women into “white slavery.” They would fabricate narratives painting Chinatown as a seedy underbelly and pay locals to pose in ways that fit the story they were trying to write. For politicians, anti-Chinese hysteria became a platform that could unite upper-class business owners fearing labor unrest and working-class European immigrants who feared job competition.
Thus, America’s first anti-drug law was born out of a desire to dismantle a minority community that was growing into an economic hub. White residents could still buy laudanum, or liquid opium, sold at pharmacies and high-end hotels in white neighborhoods. Opium itself wasn’t being restricted; only the methods and locations used by Chinese communities, namely smoking opium and dens. Local law enforcement had the pretext to raid businesses through Chinatown, which disrupted commerce, devalued real estate, and drove customers to other shops.
For a while, Chinatown businesses and operators relocated from San Francisco to Oakland or further inland to the Central Valley. And the same hysteria eventually relocated with them as rural laborers echoed the complaints about opium dens being established near their farms and railroad camps. In 1881, a statewide expansion of the San Francisco ordinance gave local law enforcement in every jurisdiction the ability to disrupt and segregate Chinese communities.
If all this sounds eerily familiar, whether you’re thinking about the War on Drugs or the fentanyl crisis being blamed on China in recent years despite the finding that most manufacturing happens in illicit labs in Mexico, you’re not alone.
Outcomes
A San Francisco Chronicle interview clipping preserved by a Dr. Harry Hubbell Kane in his 1882 book Opium-Smoking in American and China gives us some insight into how law enforcement at the time experienced the crackdown. When asked if driving the white opium smokers out of Chinatown would decrease the general prevalence of the habit, Officer James Mahoney replies,
“Not much. It will rapidly increase. The habit in past years, so far as whites were concerned, was confined to hoodlums and prostitutes mostly. Few decent men or women would care to come into Chinatown and smoke in the filthy dens here. Now that there are scores of places where the habit can be contracted in clean rooms and in respectable portions of the city, the practice will gradually extend up the social grade. Schoolboys and clerks who would never have gone into a Chinese den are already finding out the respectable places and learning to like the habit…  The anti-opium-smoking ordinance drove the white smokers out of Chinatown, but the vice came along and scattered the smokers, planting them, in fact, in every portion of the city.”
By forcing dens closed, opium was simply smoked in more discrete private locations like one’s own room. It’s difficult to classify a bedroom as an opium den, and small-scale paraphernalia can easily be hidden or disposed of in case of a raid. Mahoney claims even search dogs are ineffective, which he guesses could be a result of an opium-smoker being too repulsive for a dog to seek.
A Note About Selective Enforcement
When I see someone fanning the flames of division between local communities through bigotry and prejudice, I instinctively look for the money trail. I am personally of the belief that we as humans default to diversity, trade, and forgiveness until someone thinks they build a monopoly by dividing and conquering. The history of drug regulations makes it really easy to see how arbitrary the line is between “choice available to an informed consenting consumer” and “contagious threat to the entire community that must be eliminated.” It’s depressingly simple to map that line onto the preexisting ones around race, ethnicity, culture, religion, etc.

wiki/sangha.title: Sangha
wiki/sangha.content:
Overview
Sangha is a Sanskrit word that means “company” or “community.” In Buddhist contexts, including recovery networks like Refuge Recovery (RR) and Recovery Dharma (RD), the Sangha refers to a monastic community or fellowship. In modern practice, it generally means a fourfold community of monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen. It’s one of the Three Jewels alongside the Buddha and the Dharma.
For RD/RR, the Sangha functions analogously to the concept of meetings in Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) in terms of fellowship.

wiki/sanitarium.title: Sanitarium
wiki/sanitarium.content:
Overview
A sanitarium (or sanatorium) is a term for a medical facility designed for long-term treatment and rest.
Historical Context
In America, sanitariums are most commonly associated with tuberculosis and mental asylums. Historically, working-class individuals who struggled with substance use were institutionalized either in prisons or state asylums without real programs or treatment. Wealthier individuals often chose private sanitariums to avoid the discomfort and public embarassment of psychiatric institutionalization. Although the facilities represented a shift towards seeing addiction as a medical problem rather than just a moral or spiritual failing, their solutions were experimental and often dangerous. Among the most notable of these networks was the Keeley Institutes.

wiki/sapros.title: SAPROs (Social Aspects Public Relations Organizations)
wiki/sapros.content:
Overview
Social Aspects Public Relations Organizations (SAPRO) are interest groups funded by industries to facilitate corporate social responsibility (CSR) obligations and favorable public relations. They tend to argue for personal responsibility over industry accountability, lobby on public health measures in ways that favor industry self-regulation, and promote narratives that often promote industry-friendly media campaigns and criticize policies that threaten their profits. While traditional trade associations engage heavily with commercial lobbying, SAPROs refer specifically to organizations that target medical discourse and public health circles.

wiki/sarah-e-wakeman.title: Sarah E. Wakeman
wiki/sarah-e-wakeman.content:
Summary
Wakeman created the Matthew Perry Addiction Medicine Fellowship at Mass General Hospital.

wiki/saw.content:

The Saw franchise actually has a whole page for “Drug Addicts”: sawfilms.fandom.com/wiki/Category:Drug_Addicts. There are 24 total including the video games. Yes, there are Saw video games. No, I do not recommend you play them.
