wiki/scampi-lab.title: Social, Cognitive, Affective, and Moral Process Imaging (SCAMPI) Research Lab
wiki/scampi-lab.content:
Overview
The SCAMPI Lab uses neuroimaging techniques to investigate how neural networks relate to social decisions and Substance Use Disorders (SUDs).
Links

scampi.auburn.edu/currently-recruiting-studies/

wiki/schema.title: Schema
wiki/schema.content:
Overview
In psychology, schema refers to a pattern stored in long-term memory that’s actively used to interpret information from the world. People can resist updating their schemas even in the face of clear evidence, so a common goal of therapy is helping people become aware of their schemas and change them.
The American Psychological Association offers three definitions for schema, since the concept is used commonly in different contexts within psychology and its related fields:


“a collection of basic knowledge about a concept or entity that serves as a guide to perception, interpretation, imagination, or problem solving.”


“a cognitive structure representing a person’s knowledge about some entity or situation, including its qualities and the relationships between these. Schemas are usually abstractions that simplify a person’s world.”


“an outlook or assumption that an individual has of the self, others, or the world that endures despite objective reality. For example, “I am a damaged person” and “Anyone I trust will eventually hurt me” are negative schemas that may result from negative experiences in early childhood.”


Early Maladaptive Schemas (EMS) are those schemas that were internalized early in life but have become maladaptive over time.
Links

wiki/scorekeeping.title: Scorekeeping
wiki/scorekeeping.content:
Overview
Scorekeeping is a term that refers to tracking contributions, sacrifices, and offenses made in a relationship, usually to either gain the upper hand in an argument or track reciprocation.
In recovery circles, scorekeeping is a habit associated with building resentment over time, and one of the alternative habits people in recovery often cultivate is giving without expectation of return. Many people who have the habit of scorekeeping grew up in critical environments where love seemed to be conditional and earned, and they may carry that forward into new relationships by viewing them as fundamentally transactional. This type of insecurity in attachments can interfere with conflict resolution since scorekeeping requires tracking who is right or wrong rather than just solving the conflict.

wiki/screen-affect.title: Screen Affect
wiki/screen-affect.content:
Overview
In psychology, a screen affect is a defense mechanism where a more manageable emotion is substituted for a deeper one that becomes repressed. For instance, someone might romanticize the past as a screen affect to block out an early trauma, or someone might act angry to mask the fear of being abandoned.

wiki/screening-and-brief-intervention.title: Screening and Brief Intervention (SBI)
wiki/screening-and-brief-intervention.content:
Overview
Screening and Brief Intervention (SBI) is an abridged version of the Screening, Brief Intervention, and Referral to Treatment (SBIRT) framework that identifies problematic substance use patterns. SBI focuses on individuals with mild-to-moderate risk of developing chronic substance use disorders and can make meaningful improvements from simple conversations, usually with motivational interviewing techniques rather than referral to specialized treatment. For facilities or programs that lack the resources for warm-handoffs to specialized treatment, SBI is a viable alternative to settle for compared to SBIRT to still assist early detection and harm-reduction efforts.

wiki/screening.title: Screening
wiki/screening.content:
Overview
A screening is a brief structured process to identify risk factors or progression of a condition and its symptoms. In clinical psychology, these can consist of short questionnaires or self-report forms that warrant follow-up assessments that are more thorough. Common screenings in mental health treatment include:


Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9): evaluates the symptom severity of depression


Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7): evaluates chronic stress and anxiety


PCL-5: evaluates the symptoms of Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD)


AUDIT/DAST-10: evaluates the risks around alcohol and substance use

wiki/scrip-doctors.title: Scrip Doctors
wiki/scrip-doctors.content:
Overview
“Scrip doctors” is a term for doctors who illegally or irresponsibly write large numbers of prescriptions, which often end up being resold for recreational use. They might work out of a facility or center called a “pill mill,” and the most common substances acquired through them include opioids like hydrocodone, muscle relaxants like Soma, and benzodiazepines like Xanax.

wiki/sea-of-poppies-by-amitav-ghosh-2008.title: Sea of Poppies by Amitav Ghosh (2008)

wiki/secondary-victims.title: Secondary Victims
wiki/secondary-victims.content:
Overview
A secondary victim is someone who suffers harm as a result of witnessing or being otherwise influenced by a traumatic event that harmed a primary victim. These harms can include depression, anxiety, and Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD). In healthcare settings, this can extend to healthcare workers who suffer trauma or depression after harm befalls a patient. The term is distinct from secondary victimization, which refers to the additional harm caused to someone as a result of mistreatment from emergency, healthcare, or accountability systems.

wiki/section-307-of-the-california-penal.title: Section 307 of the California Penal Code (1881)
wiki/section-307-of-the-california-penal.content:
Summary
The statute’s official title is “An Act to add a new section to the Penal Code, to be known as section three hundred and seven, relating to opium smoking.” I will refer to it as Section 307 of the California Penal Code (1881), or Section 307 for short on this page.
Broadly, it expanded an 1875 local ordinance in San Francisco that outlawed opium smoking and opium dens with the intention of giving law enforcement the ability to disrupt Chinese communities that were seen as a threat by both white business owners and white labor groups. Liquid opium was still available over-the-counter at pharmacies in white neighborhoods. The real competition was over white working-class men and youth who seemed to prefer smoking opium in dens, and as a result frequenting Chinatown establishments generally, over the alcoholic drinks sold in white saloons run by European immigrants.
Context
The San Francisco Opium-Smoking Ordinance of 1875 caused a flight of opium dens and operators out of Chinatown to Oakland across the bay and inland towards the rural Central Valley.
The Workingmen’s Party of California (WPC) was an anti-Chinese labor coalition that had called for a boycott of all Chinese businesses and Chinese-made goods. The WPC echoed a growing public sentiment that Chinese communities were responsible for a rough labor economy that was actually the result of a contraction from excess speculation in railroad companies and a Second Industrial Revolution that was driving down the cost of goods internationally. Instead, labor organizations claimed Chinese workers were driving down wages and trapping white workers into drug dependencies, even “white slavery,” where young white women were supposedly lured by Chinese men into opium dens to be trafficked.
Much of the anti-Chinese sentiment resulted in violence. In July 1877, San Francisco white workers broke into more than twenty Chinese-owned laundries and set fire to company docks across a riot that lasted two days. The local police had been overpowered, and an impromptu army of 4000 volunteers was formed under William T. Coleman to restore order.
During the California Constitutional Convention of 1878-1879 to update the 1849 Constitution that oversaw the initial Gold Rush, the WPC won massive support through two main planks: anti-Chinese and anti-monopoly sentiment. The anti-immigrant xenophobia became such a strong part of the political culture that it became a defining schism between Western and Eastern faction of labor organizations, including the Workingmen’s Party of the United States (WPUS) that followed traditional Marxist theory into universal working-class solditary. Unfortunately for the WPC, this nativist populism was short-lived.
Their most prominent leader, Denis Kearney, was routinely ignored by Eastern labor and socialist groups who saw his emphasis on nativist racial divisions to be a non-starter. This meant a national coalition for the WPC was impossible, and the most radical voices openly called for clauses that would violate the U.S. Constitution and federal treaties. They reportedly claimed to want a federal crisis over “the Chinese question”, as they put it, in a revolutionary style.
Frank Roney led another faction of the WPC which was more traditionally Marxist and comprised of experienced trade unionists, like the WPUS, but still held anti-Chinese sentiment. The notable distinction is that Roney’s faction blamed capitalist monopolies for importing cheap Chinese laborers to exploit. The members believed that focusing on racial exclusion and targeting individual workers would only divide the labor factions in the face of corporate monopolies.
The issue was resolved through brute force. Kearney accused Roney’s faction of trafficking in overly intellectual European theory for the problems of American working-class labor, of being corporate spies undermining the labor movement, of being in league with Chinese interests, etc. His faction voted to expel Roney and other socialist organizers from the convention and systematically shut down local clubs that supported Roney. The Eastern WPUS had made official statements condemning Kearney as an “unprincipled demagogue” hijacking labor solidarity movements. Nevertheless, in the short-term, the WPC won 51 seats and had the power to write anti-Chinese exclusion legislation.
In 1881, Assemblyman Thomas Frewen, a WPC delegate from San Francisco, introduced Assembly Bill No. 181 (A.B. 181), which would be Section 307. The strength of the nativist populist movements gave it virtually unanimous support from the legislature and policymakers. There was hardly any pretense that opium itself was a public health issue that just happened to involve trade relations with China or Chinese-owned businesses. Governor George C. Perkins signed it into law, giving every sheriff the power to raid opium dens and arrest smokers.

wiki/sedative-hypnotic.title: Sedative-Hypnotic
wiki/sedative-hypnotic.content:
Overview
Sedative-hypnotics are central nervous system (CNS) depressants that relieve anxiety or aid sleep by olwing down brain activity. Sedatives on their own generally just reduce anxiety and excitement, but hypnotics specifically target the start of sleep cycles. Many medications actually act on a spectrum between them, with lower doses having a sedative effect while higher doses produces a hypnotic effect. Benzodiazepines, barbiturates, and melatonin agonists are all examples.

wiki/selective-attention.title: Selective Attention
wiki/selective-attention.content:
Overview
Selective attention is the process of focusing on specific stimuli while filtering out background information. The brain has a limited capacity to focus on information, so it has to select what it pays attention to. This can be done consciously through intentional focus or unconsciously through reactions to surrounding cues.

wiki/self-control.title: Self-Control
wiki/self-control.content:
Overview
In an everyday context, self-control refers to the ability to control one’s thoughts, feelings, impulses, and behaviors. It’s used interchangeably with terms like self-regulation, but in academic and psychological contexts, these terms have distinct meanings. Yet, there’s also a variety of definitions instead of a standard operationalized one:
“One of the narrower definitions of self-control equates the concept with inhibitory control. In this definition, self-control includes, and is limited to, the effortful inhibition of impulses. This inhibition is the key self-control component in many self-control theories and models, including those based on delay of gratification” 1
“Self-control has also been defined as the ability to delay immediate gratification of a smaller reward for a larger reward later in time (Ainslie, 1975; Mischel et al., 1989; Kirby and Herrnstein, 1995). This definition includes the effortful inhibition notion, but is extended in the sense that it emphasizes the self-control dilemma or conflict between a short-term, immediately gratifying option (that needs to be inhibited) and a long-term option with a larger reward value. The ability to forego the immediate reward reflects self-control.”
The strength model is one of the most prominent, heavily debated models of self-control, and refers to self-control as ‘… an act of self-control by which the self alters its own behavioral patterns so as to prevent or inhibit its dominant response’ (Muraven and Baumeister, 2000, p. 247). The most significant proposition from this model entails the ‘ego depletion’ phenomenon. 1
Generally, the definitions for self-control rely on some idea of effort and inhibition as components. They also might separate initiatory self-control, for initiating desirable change, and inhibitory self-control, for inhibiting undesirable impulses. For instance, eating healthy requires both initiating the habit of eating diverse whole foods and inhibiting the impulse to eat processed snacks. Doing just one helps and demonstrates self-control, but doing both helps more.
Within recovery from substance use, self-control is one of the core traits that programs seek to empower to prevent relapses and build the skills needed to pursue long-term goals with delayed gratification.
Links



Footnotes


The ‘Operational’ Definition of Self-Control ↩ ↩2

wiki/self-deception.title: Self-Deception
wiki/self-deception.content:
Overview
Self-deception is the act of denying reality consciously or unconsciously, usually as a defense mechanism for the ego and one’s capacity to tolerate anxiety. Common mechanisms of self-deception include:


Denial: refusal to acknowledge reality


Repression: blocking out intolerable thoughts and feelings


Rationalization: creating convenient or comfortable explanations or excuses


Projection: attributing one’s thoughts and feelings to others


Emotional reasoning


Selective attention


Overgeneralization


Self-Serving Bias: the tendency to attribute one’s success to skill and choices while attributing failures to bad luck

wiki/self-determination.title: Self-Determination
wiki/self-determination.content:
Overview
Self-determination is the ability to make choices without being coerced or compelled by external factors. In political science, it often refers to the ability of a group of people to decide how they want to structure their communities and political structures. In psychology, self-determination is applied to an individual’s ability to make choices about their own life.
Self-Determination Theory argues that humans have three psychological needs underlying their motivation: autonomy, competence, and relatedness. Intrinsic motivation means doing something because the action is personally engaging or meaningful. Extrinsic motivation means doing something for external rewards or to avoid external consequences. Intrinsic motivation is the result of having those three needs met, otherwise extrinsic motivation becomes the driver of our behavior.

wiki/self-esteem.title: Self-Esteem
wiki/self-esteem.content:
Overview
Self-esteem is an individual’s evaluation of their own value.
Despite the societal bias towards having an independent sense of self-esteem that remains immune to the judgment of others, researchers have proposed multiple evolutionary paradigms based on the functions of self-esteem:


Sociometer Theory: self-esteem functions as an internal metric for how much someone is included or excluded socially, so fluctuations in self-esteem that drive one to seek validation from others promote social bonding and maintaining relationships.


Terror Management Theory (TMT): self-esteem is a psychological shield from the terror of contemplating our mortality because it compels us to integrate into cultural and institutional structures to feel lasting significance in.


Identity Theory Integration: self-esteem is the result of processing external feedback for internalized standards about one’s identity


Historical Context
Leading up to the 1980s, self-esteem was framed as a single score describing how much someone generally liked themselves, In 1982, Viktor Gecas proposed two dimensions to self-esteem: efficacy-based, describing someone’s perception of their own capacity and effectiveness, and worth-based, describing someone’s perception that others value and respect them. In 2014, Peter Burke proposed a three-part mapping for self-esteem from identity that includes authenticity: social/group identity that generates worth-based esteem, role identity that generates efficacy-based esteem, and person identity which generates authenticity-based esteem. The authenticity dimension helps explain why someone can feel highly capable in their skills, highly valued by others, but still dislike themselves for not being who they feel they should be.

wiki/self-image.title: Self-Image
wiki/self-image.content:
Overview
Self-image refers to someone’s beliefs or internal model of themselves. It’s related to but distinct from self-esteem; self-image refers to how someone sees themselves while self-esteem refers to how someone feels about themselves, which includes how their self-image makes them feel.
Models
Self-Schema Theory
In Hazel Markus’s Self-Schema Theory, the self-image is a network of cognitive schemas stored in long-term memory. Each person holds schemas for different parts of their life that form part of the overall self-image, like a “shy” schema when at the grocery store, a “silent anger” schema when in conflict with a family member, or a “trustworthy confidante” schema when hearing a friend vent about their relationship. When we encounter information from the world, we apply selective attention towards information and cues related to self-schemas that validate them while filtering out contradictory evidence.
Self-Discrepancy Theory
E. Tory Higgins proposed a system of the self into three states:


The Actual Self: this is the self-image, which is the representation of the qualities you believe you actually have


The Ideal Self: this is the representation of the qualities you or someone else wants you to have


The Ought Self: this is the representation of the qualities you or someone believes you have an obligation to have


When people experience a discrepancy between their Actual Self and Ideal Self, they’re more likely to experience depression and disappointment. When people experience a discrepancy between their Actual Self and Ought Self, they’re more likely to experience emotions like anxiety and guilt.
Schema Therapy
Jeffrey Young derived Schema Therapy for Early Maladaptive Schemas (EMS), which are frameworks internalized during childhood that might be dysfunctional or warped in ways that produce distress, including somatic symptoms. If a child experiences unmet needs like a lack of compassion from caregivers, they might adopt maladaptive schemas for their self-image, like a “defective” schema that says one is fundamentally broken and unlovable.
Internal Working Models
John Bowlby and Kim Bartholomew proposed Internal Working Models as an approach to the development of mental representations rooted in attachment theory. Early relationships lead individuals to create the Model of Self (self-image) and the Model of Other, and four paths result out of that:


Positive Model of Self + Positive Model of Other = Secure


Negative Model of Self + Positive Model of Other = Preoccupied, Anxious-Ambivalent


Positive Model of Self + Negative Model of Other = Dismissing-Avoidant


Negative Model of Self + Negative Model of Other = Fearful-Avoidant, Disorganized


Looking-Glass Self
Charles Cooley’s model is a sociological framework rather than one driven by clinical psychology, but it has remained influential in both fields. There are three steps:


Imagination: you imagine the way your appearance and actions appear to others


Interpretation: you imagine how others judge your imagined appearance


Internalization: you develop a self-image based on the perceived judgment from others

wiki/self-injurious-thoughts-or-behavior.title: Self-Injurious Thoughts and Behaviors (SITBs)
wiki/self-injurious-thoughts-or-behavior.content:
Overview
Self-injurious thoughts and behaviors (SITBs) refer to any thoughts and behaviors that involve the intent to harm oneself, with suicidal intent being possible but not required.
Suicidal ideation refers specifically to thoughts about ending one’s life, and it can be either passive (wishing to go to sleep and not wake up) or active (making specific plans that include a method and date).
Intentional damage without suicidal intent is called non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI), which commonly includes cutting, scratching, burning, hitting, or banging oneself. It’s considered a maladaptive way to cope with overwhelming negative emotions.

wiki/self-regulation.title: Self-Regulation
wiki/self-regulation.content:
Overview
Self-regulation refers to one’s ability to observe oneself, judge the behavior, and adjust their responses.
Historical Context
The earliest foundations of the term self-regulation come from the idea of homeostasis with the body physically adjusting itself to maintain baseline functions, which Walter Bradford described as “regulation.”
America in the mid-20th century was dominated by behaviorist perspectives that argued human behavior was shaped entirely by external rewards and punishment. Albert Bandura introduced Social Learning Theory, which instead argued that humans create internal representations of feedback loops rather than purely reacting to environmental cues. Bandura described “self-regulation” as a three-step process consisting of self-observation, judgment, and self-response. Charles Carver and Michael Scheier introduced the TOTE loop as a framework of the human mind that uses positive reinforcement and negative reinforcement feedback loops: Test, Operate, Test, Exit. Self-control is considered a more narrow subset of self-regulation that emphasizes the ability to control impulses and initiate efforts.
Different specializations within psychology built on the concept of self-regulation in different ways. Social psychologists like Roy Baumeister explored the Strength Model that centers self-control in the efforts of self-regulation. Barry Zimmerman developed Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) as an educational framework that focused on how students step through forethought, performance, and self-reflection. Researchers in psychophysiology like Stuart Shanker tied self-regulation to the ability for the central nervous system to manage stress and excitement.

wiki/self-sabotage.title: Self-Sabotage
wiki/self-sabotage.content:
Overview
Self-sabotage is the act of undermining one’s own goals, consciously or unconsciously.
In recovery, self-sabotage is an extremely common topic that’s addressed when examining patterns of relapsing. Sometimes it stems from a fear of failure, where someone might relapse in advance of an opportunity, because that way they don’t have to confront the possibility of not being good enough. Other times, self-sabotage can stem from a fear of success because it’s unfamiliar and the brain doesn’t have strong schemas to handle a change in self-image. Like many maladaptive coping mechanisms, self-sabotage was likely at one point a successful survival strategy for times when a child learned that standing out through success could attract criticism, jealousy, or unwanted attention.
Historical Context
Within psychology, the patterns of self-sabotage date back to Sigmund Freud and the death drive, also called Thanatos. Freud proposed that humans have an innate drive towards self-destruction in order to achieve the peace of inorganic existence, so they unconsciously recreate painful patterns that feel familiar and therefore safe. Carl Jung argued that repressed parts of our selves form the Shadow that operates outside of our conscious awareness, which means we might have unconscious parts of ourselves that we’ve repressed work against our conscious desires.
In 1978, Edward Jones and Steven Berglas introduced the idea of “self-handicapping” to describe the pattern of people deliberately creating obstacles for themselves when they’re anxious about an upcoming event. If someone is anxious about a test, they may stay up all night so that they have a reason to point to for potential failure that isn’t their own skill or ability.

wiki/self-worth.title: Self-Worth
wiki/self-worth.content:
Overview
Self-worth is someone’s sense of being good enough to be deserving of respect as a human being. It’s distinct from self-esteem in that self-worth is about the belief in one’s inherent value as a human being while self-esteem is about the feelings someone has towards themselves. For instance, someone’s self-esteem about their skills might fluctuate based on their recent performance, but that may not impact their self-worth that says they still deserve to be treated like an equal human being.

wiki/self.title: Self
wiki/self.content:
Overview
The self is one of the most fundamental concepts in psychology and philosophy, and the theory of the self one uses can shape everything about the ideas, lifestyle, and treatment that work best for an individual.
“Western” ideas of the self tend to be individualistic, in that each person is viewed as an autonomous unit defined by intrinsic desires and personal attributes who bears ultimate responsibility over their own outcomes. In other cultures, the self is seen as a component of their community and is necessarily defined by the social roles they occupy. For instance, Buddhist worldviews argue that all things are impermanent and interconnected, which means that one’s self is constantly in a state of change influenced by the environment.
The relevance of this distinction becomes apparent in a lot of exercises and activities found in Western therapy. Many exercises geared towards finding an “authentic self” are necessarily using a particular idea of the self isolated from the environment that conditions “inauthentic” behavior. One might believe that there is no such thing as a “true self,” that the “self” is a construct under constant change that has to be accepted in its current state rather than dissected to separate authentic and inauthentic patterns.

wiki/selva-pascuala-mural.title: Selva Pascuala Mural
wiki/selva-pascuala-mural.content:
Overview
The Selva Pascuala mural is a rock painting in Villar del Humo, Spain that contains one of the earliest possible depictions of magic mushrooms in Europe. There are two bulls painted, one above the other, with the alleged mushrooms in a line of 13 umbrella-like figures between them.
A 2011 study published in Economic Botany, Brian Akers and Gaston Guzman proposed that the mural depicted Psilocybe hispanica, a psychoactive species that often grows on bull dung and could explain the relevance of the bulls to the mushrooms. The leading theory about the paintings is that they represent shamanistic rituals involving the consumption of mushrooms that were interpreted as providing access to different states of consciousness or visions. Two of the 13 figures have split bases resembling legs, which might suggest a psychological transformation that one experiences while using the mushrooms.
Historical Context
The artwork was first discovered by archaeologists in 1918. By the 1960s, researchers commonly described the painting as a series of geometric symbols, though modern researchers reevaluated this interpretation given contemporary perspectives that acknowledge the integration of psychoactive substances into daily life. Still, there are arguments made by scholars that the painting represents something other than shrooms, including the bull and the symbols having been painted at different occasions and by different groups rather than as a single scene. These alternatives include abstract markers for territorial or social boundaries that may not have any particular significance except for their practical use.

wiki/sequential-multiple-assignment-rand.title: Sequential Multiple Assignment Randomized Trial (SMART)
wiki/sequential-multiple-assignment-rand.content:
Overview
A Sequential, Multiple Assignment, Randomized Trial (SMART) is a type of clinical trial used for adaptive interventions that change treatment plans based on how patients respond. This allows researchers to evaluate options for first-line treatment, alternatives for non-responders, and maintenance for responders. For conditions like substance use disorder that involve chronic and complex needs with constant adjustments in levels of care, SMART can be especially helpful.

wiki/serenity.title: Serenity
wiki/serenity.content:
Overview
Serenity is a popular concept in recovery circles that describes the inner peace and emotional stability that comes from letting go of the desire to control things outside of oneself.
The Serenity Prayer is one of the most commonly repeated prayers in 12-step groups like Alcoholics Anonymous:
“God, grant me the serenity to accept the things I cannot change, the courage to change the things I can, and the wisdom to know the difference.”
The original prayer was written by Reinhold Niebuhr, who wrote it in the context of enduring hardships and setbacks for those participating in social justice movements.

wiki/serge-h-ahmed.title: Serge H. Ahmed
wiki/serge-h-ahmed.content:
Overview
Currently at the University of Bordeaux in France, Serge Ahmend is a neuroscientist with expertise in animal experiments.
Work
Papers

Imbalance between drug and non-drug reward availability: A major risk factor for addiction (2005) www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0014299905009659

“I review evidence showing that this apparent vulnerability results in large part from the lack of positive (i.e., alternative non-drug rewards) and negative (i.e., costs) incentives capable of turning animals away from the pursuit of drugs. In particular, most animals seem to take drugs and eventually become addicted, not because drugs are intrinsically addictive, but more likely because drugs are the only significant sources of reward available in the laboratory.”

wiki/serotonin.title: Serotonin
wiki/serotonin.content:
Overview
Serotonin is a neurotransmitter produced by the gut to regulate happiness, anxiety, sleep-wake cycles, digestion and nausea, bone density, libido, and other bodily functions.
Low serotonin levels have been linked to depression, anxiety, disrupted sleep, and digestion problems. Excessive serotonin levels can cause serotonin syndrome, which can happen as the result of mixing medications and substances.

wiki/severance.title: Severance
wiki/severance.content:
I almost forgot that Mark is actually a functioning alcoholic in this show.
One of the things that caught me off-guard was how Mark at work didn’t seem to struggle with compulsive urges at all. It’s not particularly unusual for functional alcoholics to make it through the workday without a drink or withdrawal symptoms. Mark at work definitely carries the physical effects of drinking from the night before, but his attitude and behaviors at work are still entirely distinct from his depressed self at home, which is the self that has the source of his self-medicating. This actually lends itself to a really good demonstration of the psychosocial aspects of substance use disorders.
The chip in his brain has not altered the neural pathways into “curing” his drinking habits. It only changes his memories concerning his identity to be reestablished in a new environment. We’re forced to examine Mark as a character whose transformation between different states of mental health can’t be attributed to something like a chemical imbalance or “hijacked” reward pathways. The chip erases the trauma of losing a loved one, gives him a new stable environment with clear objectives and incentives, and sustains social reinforcement through cooperative peers and feedback from authorities.

wiki/sexually-transmitted-infections.title: Sexually Transmitted Infection (STI)
wiki/sexually-transmitted-infections.content:
Overview
Sexually transmitted infections (STIs)  are infections that are commonly transmitted through sexual activity. The term is used interchangeably with sexually transmitted disease (STD) in everyday life, but technically they have different uses. STI is used when something has entered the body even if there are no symptoms, as is the case much of the time. STD is used when an infection has caused health issues or symptoms.
Common STIs include:


Chlamydia


Gonorrhea


Syphilis


Trichomoniasis


Human papillomavirus (HPV)


Genital Herpes (HSV)


Hepatitis B


HIV

wiki/seyyed-nassir-ghaemi.title: Seyyed Nassir Ghaemi
wiki/seyyed-nassir-ghaemi.content:
“In the past few decades, the biopsychosocial model served as a cease-fire between the biological and psychoanalytic extremism that characterized much of the 19th and 20th century history of psychiatry. Despite being broad and fostering an “anything goes” mentality, it fails to produce much guidance as a model… Critics tend toward dogmatism themselves, usually of postmodernist or libertarian varieties. Three alternative approaches include pragmatism, integrationism, and pluralism.”
Links

pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/847460/

wiki/shadow-work.title: Shadow Work
wiki/shadow-work.content:
Overview
Shadow work refers to psychological practices that explore repressed or unconscious parts of the self.
Historical Context
The term originates with Carl Jung’s work about the “shadow” that represents repressed traits. The term “shadow work” was coined by Connie Zweig and Jeremiah Abrams in 1991. Since then, the term became widely adopted in self-help and recovery circles through literature like shadow work journals that have structured prompts for self-reflection. Clinical therapy has also adopted ideas from shadow work, like in Internal Family Systems (IFS).

wiki/shame.title: Shame
wiki/shame.content:
Overview
Defining shame is complicated because the term is widely used and we think (and hope) that we’re pointing at the same feeling, but actual definitions can be contradictory or mutually exclusive.
The conventional ideas about guilt vs. shame in recovery circles is that guilt refers to the feeling that one has done something wrong while shame refers to the feeling that one’s being is fundamentally wrong. The implication then is that guilt might be useful, but shame is not.
Jean-Paul Sartre argued that shame is fundamentally a social experience that is felt not when someone does something wrong, but when someone realizes they are vulnerable to judgment in someone else’s worldview. If you were completely alone and could trust that you were, shame would be impossible to experience. Bernard Williams argued that even when someone experiences shame in private, it’s because they’re viewing themselves through the eyes of an imaginary audience.
Paul Gilbert explicitly separated the concept into external shame, or the vulnerability to being seen as bad, and internal shame, the feeling that one is bad. Plenty of people might not believe they’re bad, but might be highly concerned about the consequences of being treated as bad for justifiable reasons. The difference is significant, as it determines whether the problem comes from an internal issue like cognitive distortions or a genuinely hostile external environment.

wiki/shameless.content: I have a pretty big stomach for watching depictions of suffering, but this show is really fucking relentless. I stuck with it until Fiona left, it just got less interesting without her.

wiki/sharps.title: Sharps
wiki/sharps.content:
Overview
“Sharps” is an informal term for sharp objects that are generally disallowed from inpatient treatment centers.

wiki/shatterproof-calendar.title: Shatterproof Calendar
wiki/shatterproof-calendar.content:
Overview
Shatterproof started as a nonprofit in 2013 by Gary Mendell following the passing of his son, who took his own life after a struggle with Substance Use Disorder (SUD) and its social stigma. The Shatterproof Walk to End Addiction was launched in 2017, and, as of 2026, mobilizes across six cities in the United States with over 5000 annual participants and $1.5 million raised each year. Shatterproof continues to host regular events across the United States to raise awareness and funds for addiction initiatives, including webinars, workshops, trainings, and campaigns.
Attendees


Gary Mendell, Founder and CEO of Shatterproof


Stephanie Szostak, an actress who played a role in The Devil Wears Prada


Anthony Capuano, CEO of Marriott International


Links

shatterproof.galaxydigital.com/calendar/
fundraise.shatterproof.org/shatterproof-walk

wiki/shatterproof-treatment-atlas.title: Shatterproof Treatment Atlas
wiki/shatterproof-treatment-atlas.content:
Overview
Shatterproof is a nonprofit founded by Gary Mendell in 2013 to bridge the gap between the latest medical science and community treatment practices for Substance Use Disorders (SUDs). From 2017 to 2019, the organization collaborated with medical experts, state governments, and healthcare payers to develop a data-driven system that monitored facilities for compliance with the National Principles of Care. These principles include routine screenings, personalized treatment plans, long-term disease management, medications, external non-clinical support connections, etc.
In 2020, ATLAS (Addiction Treatment Locator, Assessment, and Standards) was launched as America’s first non-profit quality measurement tool for addiction and recovery services, allowing users to compare treatment providers and services anonymously. It was supported by Arnold Ventures, the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, and major insurers like Aetna, Anthem, Cigna, United Health, Blue Cross Blue Shield of North Carolina, Beacon Health Options, and Magellan Health.
As of August 2026, the Treatment Atlas platform serves 14 states with plans to expand. They also have a fair amount of engagement with the press, especially when evidence-backed interventions like harm reduction and MOUD are challenged.
Links

treatmentatlas.org/
www.fiercehealthcare.com/tech/shatterproof-launches-free-addiction-treatment-locator-tool-backing-from-aetna-anthem-cigna
www.shatterproof.org/shatterproof-national-principles-care

wiki/shatterproof.title: Shatterproof
wiki/shatterproof.content:
Overview
Shatterproof is a national non-profit that addresses Substance Use Disorders (SUDs) by promoting access to treatment and diffusing public stigma. They maintain a Treatment Atlas as an online platform to discover evidence-based SUD treatment facilities, run a National Stigma Initiative that involves educational modules for schools and workplaces, and host events like the Shatterproof Walk to End Addiction Stigma.
Links

fundraise.shatterproof.org/shatterproof-walk

wiki/shi-jiu.title: Shi Jiu
wiki/shi-jiu.content:
Overview
Edwin Van Bibber-Orr translates “shi jiu” from Song dynasty literature as “love of alcohol.”

wiki/sigmund-freud.title: Sigmund Freud
wiki/sigmund-freud.content:
“I need a lot of cocaine…”
Sigmund Freud is a character. It’s hard to find someone else who occupies the space in our culture that he does. Highly influential, incredibly wrong, amusingly absurd.
Freud loved coke. He tried treating his friend’s morphine addiction with it, who unsurprisingly said taking coke allowed him to take less morphine. His first major scientific publication was “Uber Coca”, which translates to “On Cocaine”, which begs us to ask whether he was on cocaine when he wrote On cocaine. The answer seems to be yes.
Freud recommended that cocaine be considered for treating digestive disorders, asthma, loss of sexual potency, melancholy, hysteria, and morphine addiction. This was met with strong condemnation from the German medical community. Also, his friend was now addicted to both coke and morphone.
To quote Freud, “I need a lot of cocaine… The torment, most of the time, is superhuman”

wiki/slip.title: Slip
wiki/slip.content:
Overview
A slip, also called a lapse, refers to a minor break in sobriety or temporary return to the behavior of active addiction. Although it’s a matter of some subjectivity, a slip implies a single moment or day that’s followed by an immediate return to routine. Maybe someone accidentally has an alcoholic drink at a party without realizing it, or maybe someone used a friend’s joint one evening at a party and has continued to be sober for weeks afterward. These slips or lapses are not considered a huge deal as long as they’re quickly corrected and normal routines are sustained, though it does add pressure for those who count the number of consecutive days they’ve been sober.

wiki/smart-approaches-to-marijuana.title: Smart Approaches to Marijuana

Smart Approaches to Marijuana (SAM) is a non-profit that campaigns for the legalization and commercialization of cannabis. It was founded by Patrick J. Kennedy and Kevin Sabet as a nonpartisan “third-way” option between the mass-incarceration of the disastrous War on Drugs and making weed available over-the-counter (OTC) by corporate giants. A core motto guiding their mission is “preventing another big tobacco,” which is a reference to how much strongly tobacco companies have lobbied governments around the world for favorable policies. 1

wiki/snuff.title: Snuff
wiki/snuff.content:
Overview
Snuff is a type of tobacco made from finely ground tobacco leaves that is then inhaled through the nose or placed inside the mouth. More than 80% of smokeless tobacco users live in South and Southeast Asia, particularly India and Bangladesh.
Short-term effects of snuff are similar to those of other tobacco products:


Elevated heart rate and blood pressure


Tissue inflammation and irritation


Anxiety and irritability, between doses


Nausea and stomach irritation


Dizziness


The same applies to long-term effects:


Increased risk of cancers of the oral cavity, tongue, gum, cheek, esophagus, pancreas, and other organs


Receding gums and bone loss around dental roots


Increased risk of coronary heart disease, atherosclerosis, and ischemic stroke


Increased risk of stillbirth or premature delivery

wiki/sober-living-environment.title: Sober Living Environment (SLE)
wiki/sober-living-environment.content:
Overview
Sober living environments (SLEs), also known as sober living houses or recovery residences, are shared housing arrangements that enforce substance-free policies while facilitating recovery meetings and treatments. It’s common for clients who complete inpatient or residential treatment programs to eventually stay in SLEs while completing a partial hospitalization program (PHP), an intensive outpatient program (IOP), or working before having the means to live independently. As a point of clarification, residential treatment centers are considered clinical environments that provide on-site treatment and therapy while SLEs are generally peer-based housing.

wiki/sobriety.title: Sobriety
wiki/sobriety.content:
Summary
From the README file uploaded to the GitHub repository:
“I mostly designed this out of spite for I Am Sober, which monetizes addiction recovery. This started as something I just wrote in the time I had between classes for a friend who was struggling with addiction and couldn’t get an I Am Sober subscription to track all the things he was struggling with, and I really just decided to publish it because I didn’t see a reason not to”
“I’m only half joking when I say I hate I Am Sober. It has several trackers and requires far more permissions than is reasonable for the features it provides, and the fact that a subscription is required to track more than two individual addictions is just horrific to me. Displaying the time since a given date, and allowing that date to be reset to the current time, are such simple features to implement that I genuinely cannot fathom how they can in good conscience monetize them, especially when their target audience is people struggling with addiction.”
“I just find the whole concept somewhat upsetting. For that reason, Sobriety will never have any trackers or anything of the sort, and will always be completely free. I want to help people, not profit off of their struggles.”
The project appears to have been started by Katherine Isabella Del Toro, going by the handle seaglade on GitHub, while a student at the Rochester Institute of Technology. The most recent update appears to have been in 2024.
Notes
I love this README.
That’s more or less the rationale I had before launching this site. It started out of spite for The Four Agreements, and in the process I ended up putting together notes that could pass for articles. I couldn’t think of a reason not to share it with others who have a deep-seated disgust for the way the New Age self-help and happiness industries monetize addiction recovery while discouraging collective action and systemic reforms. Also, I am not joking in the slightest when I say I think the world be on balance better off if every copy of The Four Agreements was burned.
So, I’m biased, but I like the cut of this dev’s jib. Fight the power, my friends.

wiki/social-determinants-of-health-sdoh.title: Social Determinants of Health (SDOH)
wiki/social-determinants-of-health-sdoh.content:
Overview
Social determinants of health (SDOH) are the environmental factors that affect health outcomes and quality of life. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) organizes five domains for these factors:


Economic Stability: employment, income, housing stability, affording healthcare


Education Access and Quality: early childhood education, high school graduation, higher education


Healthcare Access and Quality: nearby health services, health insurance, access to culturally-informed care


Neighborhood and Built Environment: access to safe hosuing, clean air and water, walkability, crime rates, transportation


Social and Community Context: support from community organizations, discrimination, exposure to violence


Studies have argued that medical care accounts for only 20% of a person’s overall health outcomes while environmental and social factors drive the majority of our health status.

wiki/solastalgia.title: Solastalgia
wiki/solastalgia.content:
Overview
Solastalgia is the distress caused when someone’s home environment changes while they’re still inhabiting it.
It was coined in 2003 by Glenn Albrecht in the context of environmental philosophy and natural disasters spurred on by climate change. Farmers, ranchers, indigenous populations, and rural communities in particular have strong personal, emotional, or religious ties to specific landscapes and can’t just relocate an entire network of people and cultural institutions easily.

wiki/soma.title: Soma
wiki/soma.content:
Overview
In the Rig Veda, soma refers to a sacred ritual drink offered to the gods. Consuming it was believed to grant divine vision, greater awareness of the universe, immense strength, and even immortality. Some researchers have proposed that soma historically might have referred to Amanita muscaria mushrooms, cannabis, ephedra, or other flowers and herbs.

wiki/somatism.title: Somatism
wiki/somatism.content:
Overview
Somatism is the framework that all mental illnesses and psychological processes have physiological origins. Humorism was a dominant somatist framework in Western and Islamic medicine for over a thousand years, and it argued that imbalances in bodily fluids were responsible for mental disturbances and disordered behavior.
Historical Context
The term “somatism” arose in early 19th-century Europe as opposition to psychicism, which argued that people had a soul or psyche, independent of a material body, that could become sick or disordered from moral failures or excessive passion. Somatists responded that souls are immortal and intangible, while diseases by definition occur in the disorder of tangible, temporary mortal bodies. The somatic view gained traction through the work of Emil Kraepelin, which catalogued patterns of symptoms with shared progression in the hopes of isolating biological foundations for diseases. The discovery of chlorpromazine in the 1950s, the first effective antipsychotic medication, facilitated a paradigm shift that saw psychiatric disorders as neurochemical imbalances. With the development of neuroimaging techniques like PET and fMRI, disorders have been mapped to the brain’s structures, activity levels, and neural pathways. However, the modern medical establishment has also shifted to acknowledge that social and interpersonal factors in people’s daily lives influence their symptoms and quality of life, so it’s common for clinicians to use a biopsychosocial model.

wiki/sons-of-temperance.title: Sons of Temperance
wiki/sons-of-temperance.content:
Overview
The Sons of Temperance were a fraternal mutual aid society founded to support total abstinence from alcohol. At its peak in 1855, it had over 134,000 members and thousands of chapters, but the US Civil War disrupted national networks and local chapters mostly merged into other temperance or Prohibition era organizations, like the Women’s Christian Temperance Union (WCTU) and the Anti-Saloon League. The branches in the United Kingdom and Australia eventually became a life insurance provider. The Order of the Sons of the Temperance Friendly Society in Britain survived until 2012.

wiki/special-action-office-for-drug-abus.title: Special Action Office for Drug Abuse Prevention (SAODAP)
wiki/special-action-office-for-drug-abus.content:
Overview
The Special Action Office for Drug Abuse Prevention (SAODAP) was a temporary agency established under the Executive Office of the President in 1971 to centralize substance use prevention, education, and treatment policies. Although it was scheduled to be terminated in 1975, some of its functions were transferred to the National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA) while others were recreated in the Office of National Drug Control Policy (ONDCP) in 1988.

wiki/specialist-supportive-clinical-mana.title: Specialist Supportive Clinical Management (SSCM)
wiki/specialist-supportive-clinical-mana.content:
Overview
Specialist Supportive Clinical Management (SSCM) is a treatment framework designed for anorexia nervosa that combines clinical management with supportive psychotherapy. Rather than challenging the irrational beliefs that prevent healthy eating with personal experimental evidence, as Enhanced Cognitive-Behavior Therapy (CBT-E) would, SSCM treats eating as a medical prescription while providing a validating space to discuss the coping skills needed to maintain progress. A premise of SSCM is that a brain that has undergone an anorexic period is malnourished and needs to be physically restored before it can effectively update its beliefs. Studies show that SSCM’s effectiveness is comparable to or even greater than CBT-E.

wiki/spirits.title: Spirits
wiki/spirits.content:
Overview
“Spirits” is a term for hard alcoholic liquors.
Historical Context
Middle Age alchemists used distillation to heat fermented beverages like wine or beer and extract concentrated alcohol. Scientists and physicians believed they were extracting an essence or “soul” out of the beverages through this process. By the 1670s, “spirits” came to mean strong alcoholic beverages.

wiki/spiritual-awakening.title: Spiritual Awakening
wiki/spiritual-awakening.content:
Overview
The idea of a “spiritual awakening” has existed in some form in virtually every culture to describe a deep change in someone’s perspectives that results from a new understanding of the world or the self.
In recovery circles, the term was popularized by 12-step groups like Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) to discuss the psychological and spiritual changes someone might experience as a result of doing the steps and losing their obsession with continuing past patterns of substance use. For the vast majority of those in 12-step programs, spiritual awakenings will be gradual changes over time rather than sudden transformations.

wiki/spiritual-but-not-religious-beyond-.title: Spiritual But Not Religious? Beyond Binary Choices in the Study of Religion (2014) by Nancy T. Ammerman

wiki/spiritual-but-not-religious.title: Spiritual But Not Religious (SBNR)
wiki/spiritual-but-not-religious.content:
Overview
Spiritual But Not Religious (SBNR) is a term used by those who engage in personal practices and hold sincere beliefs that relate to something deeper or more meaningful than everyday life without following an organized religion or religious sect. About 22% of adults in the United States identify as SBNR. Most who identify as SBNR still believe in God, a universal consciousness, or a spiritual interconnectedness between all things. Many will adopt ideas or concepts from many different religious or spiritual frameworks, and much of the modern landscape is shaped by the influence and legacy of New Age movements.

wiki/spiritual-bypassing.title: Spiritual Bypassing
wiki/spiritual-bypassing.content:
Overview
Spiritual bypassing is the practice of using spiritual ideas to avoid emotional or mental pain.
“Good vibes only” encapsulates the concept well, as do other slogans that use toxic positivity, where something might be dismissed purely because it’s uncomfortable. Ideas like enlightenment or non-attachment aren’t meant to eliminate grief, anger, or fear through dissociation, but to accept them as parts of the human experience and allow them to be processed. Other examples include “everything happens for a reason,” “nothing really matters,” and “failure always comes before success.” That’s not to say these platitudes can’t be used appropriately as part of healthy coping mechanisms or advice, but they can also just be used to dismiss someone having a normal spectrum of human emotions.
Commentary
Anecdotally, I’ve noticed a lot of people in recovery at some point began to believe that anger and grief are “bad” emotions that are the result of character defects, like attempting to control things outside of oneself. Spiritual bypassing can be a coping mechanism people use to avoid feeling “bad” emotions and repress them instead. In some cultures, even expressing hate for God is seen as a meditative activity that still explores the relationship between one and the universe.

wiki/split.title: Split
wiki/split.content:
Overview
This is one of the many movies and shows that I find repugnant for a sensationalized use of mental health disorders as a plot point, so before discussing any details of the movie, I want to just put a few facts out there.
First, individuals who have dissociative disorders are far more likely to be victims of violence or cause harm to themselves than commit violence against anyone else, which makes sense since dissociative disorders are generally the result of a prolonged history of trauma. 90% of those with a diagnosis of Dissociative Identity Disorder (DID) have documented histories of chronic child abuse or neglect. Keep in mind that the prevalence of DID is around 1%, meaning that if you’ve met 100 people, it’s plausible that you’ve met someone who has it, and you likely had no clue.
Second, post-traumatic growth (PTG) is the concept that an individual who undergoes trauma doesn’t just return to their previous baselines prior to the trauma, but instead develops more psychological resilience, empathy, and purposeful direction than before. It is not the background of a supervillain origin story where someone develops new abilities from some hidden ocean of human potential. It is the result of someone overcoming significant challenges, both internal and external, with the resources available within humans in general. Hollywood tends to think it’s doing something clever by inverting the public perception of trauma as something that breaks someone into a dysfunctional mess and instead deriving the antithesis to be some kind of sudden transformation with upsides and downsides, dramaticized in a movie’s narrative as entertainment with a moral lesson about perseverance and potential. In truth, healing oneself after trauma is a long process that comes with no singular triumphant moment or immunity to the things that were once troubling; it’s an arduous process of developing the resilience and coping skills to handle a grueling emotional spectrum, and it often involves healing through new environments and processes than just defeating a villain that stands as a metaphor for past issues.
Third, dissociative mechanisms are survival adaptations, meaning that individuals who have DID are just ordinary people who often go to great lengths to try and hide symptoms, and only a very small minority exhibit any kind of obvious switches in their identity. This is standard for anyone who might be neurodivergent and learns to “mask” their internal functions to avoid standing out, which can even extend to denying the existence of symptoms to themselves. This means that those who do switch between alters are more likely to make up excuses for why they seem different than just openly acknowledge other personalities to someone. To an outside observer, a switch can just look like someone spacing out before snapping back to the present moment, which one might easily attribute to being tired or preoccupied.
Fourth, because the brain is not literally a compartmentalized space or set of functions, switches don’t commonly manifest as distinct personalities checking in and out of control of a body. Instead, someone might experience strong passive influence from an alter or multiple alters simultaneously asserting influence at once, which can lead to dissociation, sometimes described specifically as depersonalization or derealization. Actual switches between alters aren’t conscious planned events any more than flashbacks resulting from PTSD are. Certain stimuli can serve as triggering events, especially if they’re associated with threats or major stressor, but someone might even experience a switch just in encountering a safe friend. Internally, switches can be heavily disorienting, meaning that headaches, nausea, dizziness, blurred vision, shivers, muscle twitches, and other somatic symptoms can emerge. Amnesia in DID, similar to flashbacks, can result in someone losing time and having no idea how they got somewhere, which means the idea of personalities somehow coordinating an elaborate conspiracy with each other an extremely far-fetched fantastical notion.
Fifth, while different alters in DID can be associated with bodily changes like different baseline heart rates and even different allergy profiles, the idea of one alter being able to climb on walls in a way no human can, having the skin strength to resist knives and shotguns, or curing their diabetes is science-fiction.
James McAvoy plays his parts well, and I’d by lying if I said there wasn’t well-executed entertainment behind the premise or that I disapprove of the general idea of being inspired by mental health struggles to produce artistic entertainment, but this movie very explicitly embraces DID as a plot device in ways that go beyond trauma demons. It courts integration with modern psychology and therapy over an actual diagnosis people receive and battle social stigma about. M. Night Shyamalan is low-hanging fruit as far as film criticism goes, so I’m going to be fair: Psycho suffers from these same problems, and I’m not necessarily willing to give it a pass just because it’s a product of the 1960s.

wiki/splitting.title: Splitting
wiki/splitting.content:
Overview
In psychology, splitting is a defense mechanism in which someone views somethings in black-and-white terms: either they’re entirely good or entirely bad. It protects the ego from experiencing the distress of ambivalence, and it’s commonly associated with Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD).
For instance, someone might have a pleasant dream that leaves them with an “all-good” version of their partner in mind when they wake up: “they’re my favorite sight to see when I wake up.” If they then realize their partner hasn’t done the dishes as promised, they might quickly switch to an “all-bad” version: “they’re so irresponsible, it’s immature and disgusting.” The ambivalent state of “I love my partner but I feel irritated when they forget to do what they promised.” is too difficult to hold. The same person might then switch to the “all-good” version if they fear that their partner might abandon them, and they might switch back to the “all-bad” version of their partner sets an actual boundary that makes distance that hurts to accept.

wiki/stand-up-for-mental-health.title: Stand Up for Mental Health (SMH)
wiki/stand-up-for-mental-health.content:
Overview
Stand Up for Mental Health (SMH) is a comedy therapy program that trains people with mental health diagnoses to practice stand-up comedy and build confidence in public, founded by David Granirer in 2004. Participants write stand-up routines about their personal experiences and perform shows for mental health organizations, military bases, colleges, universities, corporations, and general audiences.  One of the goals is to challenge stigma by presenting individuals with mental health conditions as funny and resilient rather than volatile or weird, as stereotypes might show. They operate in over 50 cities across Canada, the United States, and Australia. The documentaries “Cracking Up” and “Crack Up” have focused on the organization’s work to combat stigma in Canada and Australia, respectively. 1

wiki/stanton-peele.title: Stanton Peele
wiki/stanton-peele.content:
“exclusively biological concepts of addiction (or drug dependence) are ad hoc and superfluous and that addictive behavior is no different from all other human feeling and action in being subject to social and cognitive influences… In this reformulation, addiction is seen not to depend on the effects of specific drugs. Moreover, it is not limited to drug use at all. Rather, addiction is best understood as an individual’s adjustment, albeit a self-defeating one, to his or her environment. It represents an habitual style of coping, albeit one that the individual is capable of modifying with changing psychological and life circumstances. While in some cases addiction achieves a devastating pathological extremity, it actually represents a continuum of feeling and behavior more than it does a distinct disease state.”

wiki/state-unintentional-drug-overdose-r.title: State Unintentional Drug Overdose Reporting System (SUDORS)
wiki/state-unintentional-drug-overdose-r.content:
Overview
The State Unintentional Drug Overdose Reporting System (SUDORS) is a public health system designed to track overdoses, run by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) as part of the Overdose Data to Action (OD2A) program. It collects information on deaths caused by drug poisoning or overdose, such as demographics, substances involved, delivery method, place of death, death scene investigation reports, and a medical history that includes prior overdoses. Some states run their own surveillance extensions, like the California State Unintentional Drug Overdose Reporting System (CA SUDORS) managed by the California Department of Public Health.

wiki/sterilization.title: Sterilization
wiki/sterilization.content:
Overview
Sterilization has two main definitions:


the process of cleansing something of undesirable compounds or organisms


the process of removing an organism’s reproductive abilities


In the United States, eugenics laws of the 20th century led to forced sterilization of thousands of people with disabilities, including those who struggled with substance use disorder and were labeled “habitual drunkards,” “inebriates,” and “mentally unfit.”

wiki/steroids.title: Steroids
wiki/steroids.content:
Overview
In chemistry, steroids are a class of organic compounds necessary for the body’s functions. The two main categories include corticosteroids and anabolic-androgenic steroids.
Corticosteroids, also called glucocorticoids, are hormones similar to cortisol that manage stress response, immune response, and inflammation. They’re prescribed as pills, syrups, inhalers, nasal sprays, skin creams, and injections in order to address conditions resulting from inflammation or overactive immune system responses. That includes asthma, arthritis, lupus, inflammatory bowel disease, and allergies. Side effects involve high blood sugar, weight gain, insomnia, osteoporosis, weakened immune system, and skin thinning.
Anabolic-androgenic steroids are variants of testosterone whose medical uses involve delaying puberty or addressing muscle-wasting diseases. These are the steroids that are used by those attempting to enhance their workouts for more muscle or faster gains, often in doses that are up to 100 times higher than those in medical treatments. Side effects include high blood pressure, elevated LDL cholesterol, lowered HDL cholesterol, thickening of heart muscles, increased risk of heart attacks and strokes, testicular shrinkage, reduced sperm count, infertility, deepening voice, facial hair growth, menstrual irregularities, stunted height, liver damage, tumors, severe mood swings, mania, and clinical depression.

wiki/stigma.title: Stigma
wiki/stigma.content:
Overview
Stigma refers to negative beliefs, like stereotypes, that a society or collective group of people hold towards others based on their personal characteristics or circumstances.
Mental health conditions and especially Substance Use Disorder (SUD) have been the recipients of stigma for as long as the concept of a disorder has existed in virtually every culture on Earth. Because identifying a physiological cause behind mental health disorders has required advance neuroimaging techniques we’ve only developed over the last century, mental disorders were often seen as the result of a weak moral character, lack of willpower, personal defects, inability to handle trauma, and vulnerability to spiritual or supernatural disturbances. The stigma might appear to be a deterrent to undesirable behavior, but humans are flawed and will do an undesirable behavior anyways, so stigma can also have the effect of stopping those in trouble from coming forward. This is a known issue in medical professions like physicians who are worried about jeopardizing their career if they receive a mental health diagnosis or need time off to receive extended treatment at a rehabilitation center, since they feel expected to show ideal outcomes in personal health as a reflection of their professional competence.

wiki/stimulant.title: Stimulant
wiki/stimulant.content:
Overview
Stimulants are a class of psychoactive substances that speed up activity in the central nervous system (CNS).
Commercially available stimulants include:


Caffeine


Nicotine


Prescription stimulants include:


Adderall


Ritalin (Methylphenidate)


Concerta


Dexamphetamines


Illicit stimulants used recreationally include:


Cocaine


Methamphetamine


Synthetic cathinones (bath salts)

wiki/stop-the-addiction-fatality-epidemi.title: Stop the Addiction Fatality Epidemic (SAFE)
wiki/stop-the-addiction-fatality-epidemi.content:
Overview
The Stop the Addiction Fatality Epidemic (SAFE) Project is a national non-profit founded in 2017 to support community programs that address substance use, including education, destigmatization, expanding access to treatment and recovery resources, and distributing harm-reduction tools like Naloxone (Narcan) to reverse overdoses. Its programs are tailored for communities like college campuses, workplaces, and military families. It was created by James and Mary Winnefeld to honor their late son who passed away from an accidental opioid overdose.

wiki/strange-loops.title: Strange Loops
wiki/strange-loops.content:
Overview
Strange loops are circular paths found in hierarchies where moving in any direction eventually leads back to the same starting point. These hierarchies are then referred to as “tangled hierarchies.” I find that it’s easiest to explain the concept through examples:


Say you enter a store to return an item at the front-desk. The clerk says he can’t initiate a review for the item’s return without approval from the manager. The manager says she can’t approve the clerk’s request for a review without approval from the director. The director says she doesn’t review items until one of her subordinates has flagged it, sending you back to the front-desk clerk. This makes it so that escalating the issue up the hierarchy eventually takes you right back to the bottom.


A logo for a product in which someone is holding up the product, which features a smaller version of the logo for that product, leads to loop where zooming in on each layer of the logo just reproduces the image you were already looking at.


In the book Catch-22, the protagonist Yossarian attempts to get out of flying dangerous combat missions. He is told that to be grounded, one must be declared insane. In order to be evaluated, you must request to be grounded for being insane, since anyone who wants to fly more dangerous missions must be irrational and insane. Requesting to be grounded for being insane reflects a rational and sane desire to stop flying missions for your own safety. Therefore, you are sane if you request an evaluation for insanity, and you must keep flying dangerous missions regardless.


The acronym PHP in a software context stands for “PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor”, so each time you attempt to write out the acronym completely, you arrive at the same phrase that contains another acronym.


Our brains build a symbol called “I” through thoughts; the “I” feels like it’s the thing that controls what the brain thinks about. Any attempt to understand our own consciousness is arguably an approximation of our own approximation.



History and Etymology
The term “strange loop” was popularized by Douglas Hofstadter in Godel, Escher, Bach and I Am a Strange Loop.

wiki/stress.title: Stress
wiki/stress.content:
Overview
The American Psychological Association’s Dictionary of Psychology defines stress as:
“the physiological or psychological response to internal or external stressors. Stress involves changes affecting nearly every system of the body, influencing how people feel and behave. For example, it may be manifested by palpitations, sweating, dry mouth, shortness of breath, fidgeting, accelerated speech, augmentation of negative emotions (if already being experienced), and longer duration of stress fatigue.”
Models
Conservation of Resources (COR) Model
Stevan Hobfoll developed a framework called the Conservation of Resources model that begins with the premise that individuals generally try to gain and preserve resources in a given environment. Stress occurs when resources are threatened, when there’s a net loss in resources, or when investments in gaining resources fail to pan out.

wiki/student-recovery-group.title: Student Recovery Group
wiki/student-recovery-group.content:
Overview
The UChicago Student Wellness Center hosts a peer-led Student Recovery Group that offers weekly discussion groups, free meals, and sober networking events.
Links

wellness.uchicago.edu/healthy-living/wellness-programming/university-of-chicago-student-recovery-group/

wiki/student-wellness-services-caltech.title: Student Wellness Services (SWS) - Caltech
wiki/student-wellness-services-caltech.content:
Overview
The California Institute of Technology’s Student Wellness Services (SWS) was established in 2016 after the university merged its standalone health and counseling clinics. Their services include primary medical care, preventative medicine, STI testing, laboratory services, psychotherapy, crisis intervention, group sessions, occupational therapy, suicide prevention training, and substance use education. They apply a framework based on BASICS that considers harm-reduction rather than abstinence-only and consider common co-occurring disorders as part of their care, like anxiety and depression. If students have severe symptoms of Substance Use Disorders (SUDs), the clinicians at SWS can make external referrals confidentially.
Links

wellness.caltech.edu/counseling

wiki/students-against-destructive-decisi.title: Students Against Destructive Decisions
wiki/students-against-destructive-decisi.content:
Overview
Students Against Destructive Decisions, which used to be known as Students Against Driving Drunk, is a national youth health and safety organization that addresses violence, mental health, and substance use. They have thousands of chapters in middle schools up through colleges in the United States, delivering their messages through a pledge called the “Contract for Life,” peer-led events like National Youth Traffic Safety Month, corporate partnerships like State Farm for drunk driving simulators, and supporting youth leadership through a National Student Board of Directors.

wiki/sublingual.title: Sublingual
wiki/sublingual.content:
Overview
Sublingual refers to the place in the mouth under the tongue. Many medications are taking sublingually to bypass the digestive tract and liver metabolism to be absorbed directly into the bloodstream. This means they can begin working just a few minutes after they’ve been taken.
Examples of medications taken sublingually include:


Nitroglycerin: chest pain


Buprenorphine: Opioid Use Disorder (OUD)


Allergy medication


Vitamin supplements

wiki/substance-abuse-and-mental-health-s.title: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration

wiki/substance-abuse.title: Substance Abuse
wiki/substance-abuse.content:
Overview
“Substance abuse” is another term for “substance misuse” or “substance use disorder.” It was constructed relatively recently in the history of modern psychiatry, but it’s already being phased out by medical institutions, regulatory agencies, and research communities.
Historical Context
The term “substance abuse” was introduced in the DSM-III in 1980 and replaced “addiction,” since alcohol problems were viewed as a part of “Sociopathic Personality Disturbances” in earlier editions of the DSM that drew on Freudian psychodynamics. In the third edition, there was a new category called “Substance Use Disorders” that contained both Substance Dependence (for those showing physiological symptoms) and Substance Abuse (for those who had a pattern of usage that interfered with life without necessarily a dependence).
By the time the DSM-IV was published in 1994, substance abuse was seen as a milder form or early-stage version of substance dependence, which was the result of chronic substance abuse. Institutions like the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) have adopted the term into their brand and articulation of their mission.
In 2013, with the publication of the DSM-5, “substance abuse” was eliminated as a label, and the diagnosis was merged into a single continuum called Substance Use Disorder (SUD). Organizations like the National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA) have mandated terms like “substance misuse” or “SUD” over “substance abuse.” Researchers found evidence that the inclusion of the term “abuse” triggered negative biases even among medical professionals due to its association with contexts like abusive relationships.

wiki/substance-misuse.title: Substance Misuse
wiki/substance-misuse.content:
Overview
“Substance misuse” refers to the use of medications or legal substances in ways that don’t follow standard guidelines. It was proposed as an alternative to “substance abuse,” whose negative connotations impacted the way medical professionals and the public perceived those who struggle with Substance Use Disorders (SUDs) or suffered health consequences from their substance use patterns. This includes cases like elderly patients accidentally taking multiple doses of their medications due to forgetfulness or use someone else’s prescription in the case of an untreated injury.

wiki/substance-use-disorder.title: Substance Use Disorder (SUD)
wiki/substance-use-disorder.content:
Overview
Substance Use Disorder (SUD) was proposed as an official diagnosis in the DSM-5 in 2013, which eliminated the distinction between Substance Abuse and Substance Dependence from the DSM-IV. According to the DSM-5-TR:
“The essential feature of a substance use disorder is a cluster of cognitive, behavioral, and physiological symptoms indicating that the individual continues using the substance despite significant substance-related problems.”
“An important characteristic of substance use disorders is an underlying change in brain circuits that may persist beyond detoxification, particularly in individuals with severe disorders. The behavioral effects of these brain changes may be exhibited in the repeated relapses and intense drug craving when the individuals are exposed to drug-related stimuli.”
There are 11 criteria for SUD:


Substance is taken in larger amounts over a longer period of time than intended


Repeated attempts to control substance use that were unsuccessful


A large amount of time is spent obtaining, using, and recovering from substances


A strong desire or craving to use substances


Failure to meet major obligations at work, school, or home


Social/interpersonal problems that have been caused or made worse by using the substance


Giving up important activities for substance use


Use in physically dangerous situations


Continued use despite awareness of physical or psychological health issues


Increasing tolerance


Experiencing withdrawals or using substances to avoid withdrawals


Meeting 2 to 3 of these criteria in a 12-month period leads to a mild SUD diagnosis. Meeting 4 to 5 leads to a moderate diagnosis, and meeting 6 or more leads to a severe diagnosis.

wiki/substance-use-navigators.title: Substance Use Navigators
wiki/substance-use-navigators.content:
Overview
Substance use navigators (SUNs) are peer counselors or social workers that help stabilized patients with substance use disorders from facilities like Emergency Rooms (ERs) enter outpatient clinic or rehabilitation programs for long-term treatment.

wiki/sud-business-summit.title: SUD Business Summit
wiki/sud-business-summit.content:
Overview
The SUD Business Summit is hosted by the media platform Behavioral Health Business (BHB), designed for corporations to discuss the economics and investment landscape of the addiction and recovery industry.
Attendees


David Gomel, CEO of Rosecrance Behavioral Health


Jaime Vinck, President of Meadows Behavioral Health


Doug Leech, Founder and CEO of Ascension Recovery Services


Michael Garafalo, Directory of Behavioral Health at Fallon Health


Chuck Steiner, Senior Executive at Bradford Health Services
