wiki/the-lighthouse.title: The Lighthouse
wiki/the-lighthouse.content:
Commentary
Surreal Talk
Disclaimer: I love surrealism, which isn’t surreal at all. There’s nothing that tickles my interest like characters spiraling into insanity until we get a break from reality to parse through and interpret. So a 19th-century lighthouse ghost story casting Willem Dafoe as an old sea captain on a bender with the glittery vampire boy from Twilight? I’m locked in, chief. I went into The Lighthouse (2019) convinced I was going to love it, and I did. It’s absurd, it’s atmospheric, it’s tragic, it’s funny, it’s beautiful.
As far as depicting substance abuse, I view it as one cog in the movie’s psychological machine that gains significance from the the larger whole. Drinking accelerates other character dynamics instead of being a central theme itself, so the best way to interpret the depiction of addiction is to start with the movie’s broader ideas and see how substances operate within them.
The movie builds on a minimalist core structure that permits us to use its many references to earlier artists when seeding the development of our interpretations. The characters explicitly mention the mythology of Greek gods and Captain Ahab from Moby Dick. More subtly, the symbols and dialect reference poets such as Samuel Taylor Coleridge, Edgar Allan Poe, and Sarah Orne Jewet. In interviews about production, the cast mentions finding influence from H.P. Lovecraft and Robert Louis Stevenson. Robert and Max Eggers, the brothers who wrote and directed the movie, were raised by a professor who taught Shakespeare and introduced them to a revolving array of colleagues like Hyman Bloom. Robert describes having wanted to make a movie that Sigmund Freud and Carl Jung, giants of modern psychoanalysis, would enjoy together over popcorn.
Eggers Can’t Be Choosers
“My brother was working on a script called Burnt Island that was a ghost story in a lighthouse, and that’s all I knew about it at the time. I thought it was such a good idea, and a couple of months later, he said it wasn’t really working out, and I asked if I could take a crack at the concept. My version, of course, became a period movie and I called it The Lighthouse.”
— Robert Eggers
The movie stems from the interest of the creators, Robert and Max Eggers, in using New England Protestant ghost folklore to tell a tragedy about a dualistic identity crisis. We see dichotomies between old settler and young wanderer, head of the household and domestic subservience, maritime sailor and urban worker, task manager and grunt worker, static fulfillment and unmet craving, enlightened mystic and mystified skeptic, have and have-not, strict father and rebellious son, fart-maker and fart-sniffer, etc. It’s even shot in black-and-white.
When thinking about the intergenerational tension in the film, I wondered about the frame of influence that the directors themselves are acting within. In interviews, they’re open about their story’s references to Greek mythology like Proteus and Prometheus, classic American writers like Thomas Melville and HP Lovecraft, and psychoanalysts like Sigmund Freud and Carl Jung. They compare their approach to directing with Martin Scorcese and Guillermo del Toro’s approaches. Robert never knew his biological dad but when he was young, his mom married a professor who taught Shakespeare and introduced him to notable artists of their day like Hyman Bloom, and Robert would attend the same art conservatory in New York as Christopher Jackson who played George Washington in Hamilton.
“New England is where white European culture has been around for the longest, so if you’re going to be exploring these kinds of old-timey stories, you want a place that’s been around long enough to have ghosts, so to speak. I think, clearly, both of these movies are me trying to commune with the European non-indigenous folk culture of my region… we would drive up north to Maine to settings like The Lighthouse for vacations…”
Robert’s interest in the historical accuracy of his project is rooted in part from his own interest in the subject as part of his heritage.
“The idea of a fable or a myth is definitely at the forefront of our process… As we’re doing all this work, we start to see a story take place. And then we’re saying, ‘Okay, what fairy tales or folktales or myths is this starting to line up with?’ Then we realized, ‘Well, Prometheus and Proteus never hung out in any Greek myths before, but that seems to be what is kind of happening here,’ and Prometheus might be taking on some characteristics that he hasn’t in the past. But you know what? The classical authors did that all the time.”
“I think we’re all derivative in the beginning… I think you can identify influences in The Lighthouse for sure, but I feel like collectively I think I’m starting to become myself a little more, which hopefully I’ll continue to do.”
Armchair psychoanalysts might guess that Robert Eggers projects his idea of a tragedy about identity through the tensions between Young and Old in the movie’s plot from the perspective of a young filmmaker on his second project with a background learning from classical works. He’s self-aware about the tendency for artists to be noticeably derivative of older works before finding their own style. For Robert, the artists of these classical works he references might themselves be figures like Old, representing an older generation who hold their secrets to success in some metaphorical lighthouse. His dad being a professor is the cherry on top to guess the existence of some paternalistic character within the legacy of the classics to be honored.
Eggers had positive and encouraging experiences from other artists growing up, like Hyman Bloom who gave him a book on Northern European engravings that ignited a passion for visual arts.
“…my dad taught at the University of New Hampshire, and there was an art show by this Latvian immigrant, Hyman Bloom, and he was a New England painter who had this retrospective that was really amazing. And he had all these hellish imagery of demons and astral planes and stuff, huge scale. My dad met him, and my parents got along with he and his wife, and he would come over a lot. I was just enamored of this artist because, at the time, I wanted to be a visual artist.”
Unlike Old who tightly controls access to the lighthouse for himself, the mentors in Eggers’ life gave him some of their inspirational light that fueled his passion, encouraging his growth instead of controlling his direction. Consequently, Eggers seems comfortable adopting the aesthetics of classic authors while telling his own story, knowing full well that artists were constantly reconstructing myths and stories to fit new narratives, although he does lean heavily on researching historical authenticity while conscious about his credibility. The Lighthouse as a tragedy is a foil to his journey: Eggers feels integrated into the tradition of classic story themes through his welcoming experiences while Young feels excluded by the supervisory position that Old flaunts to discourage and discipline him.
With this theory in mind, let’s look at The Lighthouse as a young director’s idea of a tragic fable that involves losing one’s identity in order to be free enough to satisfy one’s desires.
The Lighthouse started as an idea called Burnt Island from his brother Max Eggers who wanted to adapt Edgar Allan Poe’s unfinished The Light-House about a lonely lighthouse keeper whose diary entries depict him hearing things in the walls and questioning his sanity. When I say unfinished, I mean it was about 800 words long, so it’s understandable that Max struggled to adapt and launch the project.
“…it really happened, in Wales, in the early part of the 19th century. The way the story is told and ends is like a folk tale, so how much truth there is to this “true” story, who knows. Very little of that story aside from the fact they’re both named Thomas came into The Lighthouse, but the idea that they were both named Thomas struck a chord. I was like, ‘Okay, this is a movie about identity, and can devolve into some weird, obscure places.’
Eventually, the brothers found the Smalls Lighthouse Tragedy, a 19th-century Welsh legend about two lighthouse keepers working together named Thomas who were known to fight all the time. One Thomas dies in an accident, and so the other Thomas, worried that he would be accused of murder if he just pushed dead Thomas into the sea, put the corpse into a coffin. As a result of the wind, dead Thomas’ arms come out from behind the coffin and sway as if beckoning living Thomas. The experience of keeping the lighthouse lit with the dead Thomas calling him was so stressful that living Thomas wasn’t recognizable to anyone who knew him before. This inspired Robert Eggers to craft a movie about identity in isolation.
“And then when we would go on family trips to colonial Williamsburg, and Plimouth Plantation, things that a lot of people thought maybe were boring, I fucking loved it. I was like, “Yeah. I want to be a blacksmith. This is great,” and I loved talking to the living history nerds. I thought it was the coolest thing.”
The Eggers brothers grew up in New Hampshire, so they have a personal attachment to the New England region and its history. Robert’s style is heavily focused on research and authenticity to construct an atmosphere, with the story building on top of the setting’s time, place, and idiosyncracies. In order to add their regional flavor to the story of an isolated lighthouse, they dug into writers of the 19th century who discussed maritime living. In terms of the dynamic between the directors and their older inspirations, their admiration for their home’s historic culture extends to the historic writers as well.
“It was a tremendous amount of research. Being that we’re setting the film in New England, [Herman] Melville seems like the first place to go take a look. [Samuel Taylor] Coleridge and [Robert Louis] Stevenson, on the other side of the pond, are some other usual suspects. We began trying to write both characters in dialect from the beginning… we both find that thinking in dialect, even if you’re still trying to sort it out, keeps you better in line with the thought process of the character.”
The brothers seem to take a process that starts by researching the outer world before building the inner one. Within their premise of a lighthouse ghost story, they focused on making the setting appear as authentic as possible to the time periods it was modeled after. The 19th century had plenty of photographs they could use to reconstruct sets from, including the entire lighthouse that was built from tools of the same period. As for the characters, their actions in the story come after the context of their life is assembled. For instance, when writing dialogue, knowing the specific dialect they articulate their thoughts in is important and defines the context they’ve lived in where that language is used. Their sources include Thomas Melville who wrote Moby Dick, Samuel Coleridge who wrote The Rime of an Ancient Mariner, and Robert Louis Stevenson who wrote Treasure Island.
“Robert Eggers is like a freak with research, so he made a lot of that available to me… I find the accent, I match it with a tone. Then that helps transport you to feel like another person and helps you be the text. Be the text because it’s a beautiful text pieced together from all these references, but it doesn’t necessarily feel like that. I only know that because he said, we liberally stole from Melville and Milton, this Maine writer Sarah Orne Jewett that’s where a lot of stuff comes from.”
— Willem Dafoe
Willem Dafoe, who acts as Old, reflects this sentiment in his approach to the character. The accent allows him to hear the tone, which then helps him better feel that he channels the character out of the text. He knows secondhand from Eggers that they used Melville, John Milton who wrote Paradise Lost, and a Maine poet who interviewed lighthouse captains named Sarah Orne Jewett.
“The most helpful source became the work of the writer from the good old state of Maine, Sarah Orne Jewett, who was writing in this period. She was interviewing sea captains and sailors and farmers, and writing her Maine stories in phonetic dialect. So that was like a jackpot. And then my wife came across a thesis on dialect and Sarah Orne Jewett by a woman named Evelyn Starr Cutler, and she broke down the different dialects and provided rules, so that we were able to double check that what we were doing worked.”
— Willem Dafoe
Jewett especially was influential as the source of the dialects for Young and Old. Her stories often reflect characters living outside of the framework of traditional marriage, such as widows, single women, or sea captains (like her grandfather) who lived in isolation.
“It’s the end of the 19th century where a Fresnel lens is commonplace in the top of a lighthouse beacon and you can have a bellowing foghorn. That steamship is a bit dilapidated. We happily say that it’s Maine, but it is somewhat ‘once upon a time,’ and certainly ‘the most remote lighthouse station at the end of the earth’ is also very much the intention.”
As an extension of that process, the story’s themes and characters are built out of the setting of the lighthouse itself as one of isolated repetition for its inhabitants, welcome beacons for wandering travelers, and liminality between ocean and land. Lighthouses are markers of transition for those on a journey who may be lost to, literally, continue traveling on more firm footing. Young is a wanderer adrift in his life who comes to the island to work at the lighthouse and find salvation for his shady past. They also feature a lot of monotonous isolated work by nature of many being positioned awkwardly away from dense living environments. As Old warns Young to encourage him to drink, one of the biggest dangers sailors encounter is boredom which can drive them insane. By nature, lighthouses are found along borders between sea and land on islands or coastal regions. Young himself is on the threshold of change, having just changed his name to start fresh.
Eggers reveals that he’s aware of how much creative liberty past authors took towards adapting older stories and how he doesn’t feel bound to mythological canon as much as he does to the actual historicity of the time period. Although he enjoys the aesthetics and representations of fables as vehicles to tell a story, he doesn’t see these stories as reflecting some universal psychological truth— or at least doesn’t feel the need to repeat them as he gives his own interpretation. Prometheus is historically depicted as a trickster-god who stole fire from Zeus to give to humanity out of compassion, although sometimes he is portrayed as simply rebellious since Prometheus was part of the Titans who Zeus overthrew to establish the rule of the Olympians. Proteus is historically depicted as a wide old man who possesses knowledge of the past, present, and future but is constantly changing shape to avoid being captured and forced to share it. Prometheus and Proteus don’t have any shared stories in traditional myths, but they still represent contrary archetypes that Eggers chooses to write about as part of his depiction of an identity crisis. Prometheus seeks knowledge and Proteus guards it, mimicking the dynamic between Young and Old.
“You got these guys that are put in this situation that’s like a purgatory and then the little personality, the little sense of self that they’ve created for themselves starts to get stripped away. You see what their real nature is and that points them into a kind of desperation that leads them to the liquor and the fantasy and all this stuff going on and it turns murderous and destructive because of the male toxicity of it all and it doesn’t work out for either of them.”
— Willem Dafoe
Dafoe offers the comparison to “purgatory” where the identities that Young and Old have made for themselves are stripped back because of their indefinite isolation together, which exposes certain dysfunctional ideas of masculinity fueling their egos in conflict.

wiki/the-lost-weekend.title: The Lost Weekend (1945)
wiki/the-lost-weekend.content:
“Nat, are you ever scared when you wake up? So scared, the sweat starts out of you, huh? No, not you. With you, it’s simple. The alarm clock goes off, you open your eyes, brush your teeth, and ready the Daily Mirror. That’s all. You ever lie in your bed, looking at the window? A little daylight’s coming through, and you start to wonder. Is it getting lighter? Is it getting darker? Is it dawn or is it dusk? That’s a terrifying problem, Nat. Because if it’s dawn, you’re dead. The bars are closed, the liquor stores don’t open until 9:00. And you can’t last until 9:00! Or it may be Sunday. That’s the worst. No liquor stores at all, and you guys wouldn’t open a bar until 1:00. Why?”
“Because we gotta go to church once in a while. That’s why.”
“Yeah, when a guy needs it most.”
Replace 9:00 AM with 6:00 AM and a bar with a food delivery app, and you could hear this exact sentiment from alcoholics in 2026.
Overview
The Lost Weekend is one of the earliest films ever made to treat alcoholism as a sickness rather than a pure moral failing or a punchline. As an adaptation of the novel [[fiction/the-lost-weekend|The Lost Weekend]], it features Don Birman as an out-of-work self-proclaimed writer who struggles with alcoholism.
After years of scraping by with a stagnant career and brotherly benefactor, and a stay at a mental hospital of some kind following episodes of suicidal intentions, Don attempts to straighten himself out for the sake of a budding romance with one Helen St. James. By the time we meet Don, he claims to have been sober for ten days but is anxious to find a way to keep drinking for a weekend trip with his brother, only to end up drinking before it even begins and losing the weekend to a bender. Yet, even after his brother, the bartender at his local haunt, and his landlady have all written him off as better off dead, Helen persists in her faith that Don can recover.
(Note: I’ve mentioned elsewhere that the language of “the alcoholic” and “the disease of alcoholism” have been phased out of scientific literature and serious scholarship in favor of terms like “substance use disorder,” but it feels distractingly anachronistic to not use the terms that the movie thinks in.)
Commentary
I watched this movie shortly after seeing Spider-Man: Brand New Day (2026) in theatres, and I found myself unexpectedly but pleasantly engaged with a movie that had no access to the digital tools and artistry that captured the scale of New York City from a spider’s-eye view. Instead, we get an almost claustrophobic series of encounters with Don and the dark shadows of his life, whose encroachment into brighter beacons is depicted through chiaroscuro typical of the time. Whether Don is at the bar begging for drinks or writhing between pleasure and pain while the shadows of iron bars are cast over him in other scenes, we get to feel trapped in them alongside him.
The movie remains grounded as a character study for an archetypal alcoholic going through the familiar beats of a bender: just wanting a bottle around as mental relief that a drink isn’t impossible, planning a few drinks around obligations, drinking far more than a few drinks, giving up on the idea of sobriety, stealing and lying and cheating once the money runs out, commitment to a medical institution, delirium tremens, the rock bottom of suicidal despair, and a decision to stay alive and attempt sobriety again after a loved one refuses to believe that they are condemned to a life of useless selfishness.
In many modern addiction and recovery media, seeking medical help and peer recovery groups like Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) is interpreted as a substantial turning point or even resolution in the narrative arc. Given the explosive growth of AA and their media campaigns in the decades following this movie’s release, Don’s story is one that has no such third party to intervene as authorities with a remedy. In fact, the movie affords almost no attention to institutional actors except to quickly write off the marketed cures and frame “alcoholic wards” as little more than an overgrown drunk tank managed by apathetic and condescending staff. The slices of the historical institutional attitudes toward alcoholism and addiction are unambiguously depressing and gritty. Where this makes the story more compelling to me is that it leaves us entirely with the non-professional connections of loved ones, and in that, I include the conventional wisdom that only an addict can reach another addict. In a genuinely touching moment, realizing that Don has begun planning his suicide after contemplating a life of delirious drinking, Helen breaks from the pattern of everyone else who gave up on Don to announce: “I’d rather have you drunk than dead.”
Granted, Helen is written almost entirely as a prop for Don to mistreat as evidence of the depravity of his addiction, and the other prominent female side character Gloria is almost entirely a prop to represent the tempting allures of the city’s passionate nightlife. Together, they represent an externalized Madonna-Whore duality for Don that corresponds to his internalized duality in the style of Jekyll-and-Hyde, which he terms Don the Writer and Don the Drunk. As such, when Don’s self-image collapses entirely into Don the Drunk, Helen serves as a corrective force to coax him back to Don the Writer. Still, the acting conveys a sincere sentiment felt by many whose loved ones have been in the throes of dysfunctional alcoholism and addiction: that even the messiest, most self-destructive version of them is preferable to the idea of their death. I for one was touched, which I found surprising given how fucking annoying a lot of addicts are and how often “I hope you relapse” crosses my mind.
I don’t find Bojack Horseman to be that interesting of a show to discuss from the perspective of alcoholism, but I couldn’t help but think about the artistic rendering of the visions and hallucinations of benders in the show as intense and existentially crippling. This isn’t to say that people don’t see equivalently insane experiences in real life after chronic drug use. However, The Lost Weekend comes from an era that seemed less driven towards absurdity to convey its impact, so the DTs we see are “simple” agonies rather than extravagant catastrophes that unpack a cascade of new layers of meaning from the subconscious. Don’s visions are limited to seeing a rat chew its way out of the walls only to be preyed on immediately by a bat; obviously, symbolizing Don the Drunk devouring Don the Writer after an attempt to break free of a life of quiet desperation.
Also, I was a little disappointed when I couldn’t find any evidence of an homage to Don Birman in the character of Don Draper Mad Men.
Also, they could’ve dialed it back on the theremin. Maybe it’s a side effect of living in 2026 after the theremin been a meme for decades, but it still adds a cartoonishly spooky dimension to some of the ridiculous faces Don makes in drunken stupors. Upon a cursory search for movie’s contemporary critics, I found a 1945 review in The Nation from James Agee that touches on the sound design:
“A few minutes of dead-silent pantomime (without music, please!) of deadly weakness, in hangover, for instance, might have made definitive a good deal that is here only sketched; it should be the kind of weakness in which it is virtually unbearable to lift a hand, and for some reason necessary to do much more than that. Much of the wrestling of minds and moods too, I suspect, could have been registered from outside, through lines, business, mere close-up, and posture: Chaplin, after all, has made incredibly complicated things articulate in pantomime… Sound and light peculiarities could have been impacted in the film and track by appropriate, dry exaggerations. A knocking radiator, an abrupt auto horn, coupled with the right kind of playing, might have told the audience as much in an instant as an hour of pure objectivity could”
And, amusingly, he takes a parting shot at the liquor industry who were not necessarily fans of movies that warned about the dangers of consuming their products:
“I undershtand that liquor interesh: innerish intereshtsh are rather worried about thish film. Thash tough.”
For context, Allied Liquor Industries, an American trade organization for the liquor industry, had formally launched a campaign to suppress the film and invoked the specter of Prohibition as a political enemy who would use the film as propaganda. The Schenley Distiller’s Corporation had offered Paramount 5 million to buy the film's negative and burn it to prevent distribution. Yes, the same Paramount that's now being driven into the ground by the Ellison failson. When the pressure campaigns failed and the movie became a hit, House of Seagram attempted to pivot their strategy by praising the movie with a new slogan: "some men shouldn't drink!" Billy Wilder supposedly joked that if he had been offered the 5 million directly, he would’ve taken it.
Verdict
Overall, I really like this movie. It holds up better than a lot of older films, and I feel good about recommending it to anyone who appreciates the historical significance of their content beyond the content itself.
Notable Quotes
“Love is the hardest thing in the world to write about. It’s so simple, you gotta catch it through details. Like the early morning sunlight hitting the grey tin of the rain spout in front of her house. The ringing of a telephone that sounds like Beethoven’s ‘Pastoral.’ A letter scribbled on her office stationery you carry in your pocket because it smells like all the lilacs in Ohio.”
“And out there in that great, big concrete jungle, I wonder how many others there are like me. Poor, bedevilled guys on fire with thirst, such comical figures to the rest of the world as they stagger blindly towards another binge, another bender, another spree.”
“We’re both trying, Don. You’re trying not to drink, and I’m trying not to love you.”

wiki/the-making-of-buddhist-modernism.title: The Making of Buddhist Modernism (2009) by David L. McMahan
wiki/the-making-of-buddhist-modernism.content:
Abstract
“Buddhism modernism is not just Buddhism that happens to exist in the modern world but a distinct form of Buddhism constituted by cross-fertilization with western ideas and practices.”
“The book creates a lineage of Buddhist modernism that includes liberal borrowing from scientific vocabulary in reformulations of Buddhist concepts of causality, interdependence, and meditation. It also draws upon Romantic and Transcendentalist conceptions of cosmology, creativity, spontaneity, and the interior depths of the human being. Additionally, Buddhist modernism reconfigures Buddhism as a kind of psychology or interior science, drawing both upon analytic psychology and current trends in neurobiology.”
“In its novel approaches to meditation and mindfulness, as well as political activism, it draws heavily from western individualism, distinctively modern modes of world-affirmation, liberal political sensibilities, and modernist literary sources. The book also examines this uniquely modern Buddhism as it moves into postmodern iterations and enters the currents of global communication, media, and commerce.”
Introduction
The abstract for this book can sound technical and dense. I appreciate that the author relays an anecdote that conveys their thesis:
“I asked my students in an introductory class on Asian religions - our first day dealing with Buddhism - to relate some of their ideas and images of the tradition. After the various impressions from popular films and magazine articles, someone faithfully conveyed that semester’s version of what has become a standard view: that Buddhism is a religion in which you don’t really have to believe anything in particular or follow any strict rules; you simply exercise compassion and maintain a peaceful state of mind through meditation. Buddhism values creativity and intuition and is basically compatible with a modern, scientific worldview. It is democratic, encourages freedom of thought, and is more of a ‘spirituality’ than a religion.”
“What many Americans and Europeans often understand by the term ‘Buddhism,’ however, is actually a modern hybrid tradition with roots in the European Enlightenment no less than the Buddha’s enlightenment, in Romanticism and transcendentalism as much as the Pali canon, and in the clash of Asian cultures and colonial powers as much as in mindfulness and meditation. Most non-Asian Americans tend to see Buddhism as a religion whose most importamt elements are meditation, rigorous philosophical analysis, and an ethic of compassion combined with a highly empirical psychological science that encourages reliance on individual experience. It discourages blindly following authority and dogma, has little place for superstition, magic, image worship, and gods, and is largely compatible with the findings of modern science and liberal democratic values. While this picture draws on elements of traditional forms of Buddhism that have existed in Asia for centuries, it is in many respects quite distinct from what Buddhism has meant to Asian Buddhists throughout its long and varied history…”
I’m not a Buddhist, but I am technically Asian American. I would largely agree with everything listed here. The student’s description of Buddhism is almost verbatim what I’ve heard many times over as a description of it by non-Buddhists in America. I’ve distilled Buddhism down in those ways too, especially if I have to quickly explain the concepts to someone who is just looking for a functional idea of what it is. I admit though, if I had known earlier that AA also calls itself “spiritual” rather than religious, I probably would’ve started referring to Buddhism as a religion more assertively.
Don’t mistake my derision for his though. I’m jaded from being bombarded with New Age literature within contemporary spiritual and recovery-oriented circles. I don’t doubt McMahan has a far more balanced set of experiences on the adoption of Buddhism and South Asian beliefs in America than me. I appreciate the perspective he gives in the place of my own hesitation to acknowledge the fusion of beliefs:
“It is, rather, an actual new form of Buddhism that is the result of a process of modernization, westernization, reinterpretation, image-making, revitalization, and reform that has been taking place not only in the West but also in Asian countries for over a century.”
This is a completely fair point, and I concede that I can reconcile my hesitation with it. If we accept that belief systems are constantly being shaped by the circumstances of life, then it stands to reason that religions are always in a state of change. Impermanent, if you will. Where I specifically feel friction is when the modernization of these concepts isn’t part of the narrative presented to us, leading to the impression that we’re receiving universal truths from long-lost ancient sources. McMahan calls out a pitfall I nearly stepped into moments before writing this sentence:
“It is tempting to think of the various modernizing forms of Buddhism as ‘Western Buddhism,’ given the influence of western science, philosophy, and psychology on modern variations of the dharma, as well as the visibility of American and European authors on the subject… The modernization of Buddhism, however, has in no way been an exclusively western project or simply a representation of the eastern Other; many figures essential to this process have been Asian reformers educated in both western and Buddhist thought. Nor can the motivations of major Asian figures in this process, such asn Anagarika Dharmapala, Daisetz T. Suzuki, and of late, the Fourteenth Dalai Lama, be reduced to the simple accommodation of Buddhism to western forms of modernity… Buddhist modernism- has been, therefore, a cocreation of Asians, Europeans, and American.”
I nearly used that exact term, in part because I was just reviewing Unsubscribed by Josh Korda where he describes a rationale for his own translation of the Pali Canon, but in ways that appear to inject more of a “Western” existentialist idea of an incomplete self yearning for wholeness. That makes it suitable for a lot of Western therapeutic concepts that discuss a narrative about the self, but misses the emphasis on interrogating the mental constructs that produce cravings for worldly attachments in the first place.
To be continued.

wiki/the-man-with-the-golden-arm-1955.title: The Man with the Golden Arm (1955)

wiki/the-man-with-the-golden-arm-by-nels.title: The Man with the Golden Arm
wiki/the-man-with-the-golden-arm-by-nels.content:
Overview
The Man with the Golden Arm is one of the first post-WWII era novels to document the difficulties soldiers experienced when readjusting to civilian life. Nelson Algren, the author, himself served in WWII as a medical corpsan, and he intended to write novels about experiences he had on the battlefield. After coming back to Chicago and observing how his fellow soldiers had trouble integrating into a corporate careers, he grew upset at the narratives he saw promoted by government and media figures that depicted soldiers adjusting just fine to daily life. Rather than homes in the suburbs, many lived in poverty and fell into a cycle of substance use, whether it was drinking or heroin. Algren decided to explore the rough low-income neighborhoods himself to document, with as much accuracy as possible, the lives of those veterans caught in a cycle of drinking.
Commentary
The book has a sharp vaudeville wit to its banter that speaks to Algren’s dedication to capturing the authentic conversational styles and mannerisms of the 40s Chicago neighborhoods he explored. There’s a lot of playfulness under the dark humor and cynicism. I haven’t yet finished it, but I intend to update this once I do.
Notable Quotes


“That night, while the little twenty-watt bulbs burned on in a single unwinking fury down the whitewashed tier, Frankie Machine was touched by an old wound fever and dreamed, for the second time in his life, of the man with the thirty-five-pound monkey on his back.”


“Man, I wasn’t hooked, I was crucified. The monkey got so big he was carryin’ me. ‘Cause the way it starts is like this, students: you let the habit feed you first’n one mornin’ you wake up ‘n you’re feedin’ the habit.”


“A monkey on the back” is an English idiom that refers to a hard and stubborn problem or burden. Algren popularized the euphemism in the context of drugs as a habit that was hard to kick.

“The great, secret and special American guilt of owning nothing, nothing at all, in the one land where ownership and virtue are one. Guilt that lay crouched behind every billboard which gave each man his commandments; for each man here has failed the billboards all down the line. No Ford in this one’s future nor ever any place all his own.”

Algren was deeply skeptical of America’s orientation towards consumerist materialism as a value and marker of goodness. The postwar boom oversaw a shift in production towards household commodities, associating peace and victory with wealth and consumption under a Puritan moral-psychology. State, media, and corporate institutions were all running high on this prosperity narrative while the reality of many soldiers who served was abject poverty and a revolving door with criminal justice systems. Algren specifically calls out billboards as a transmission vector for this narrative, with an advertisement depicting success and victory that induced guilt if you didn’t have what was being sold. Were you not working hard enough to be prosperous enough to buy the American Dream?
Billboards grew in this era as more Americans adopted cars as a center of their lifestyle amidst the growth of the Interstate Highway System. Owning a Ford represents the progressive nature of this consumerist process; you drive down the road in a car that shows you all the other things you have yet to buy to achieve the Dream when you get to where you’re going. After that, you drive some more to find more things to buy at the next place you’re going. Eventually you buy a new Ford to replace the old one, and you keep going until you don’t.

wiki/the-moonstone-a-romance-by-wilkie-c.content:
Overview
The Moonstone: A Romance is one of the earliest modern detective novels and strikes a little close to home. The namesake jewel in the novel is associated explicitly with Chandra, the god representing the Moon in Hinduism, which is also what my name translates to. It also helped popularize the trope of jewels being taken from a colonized and oppressed peoples before being taken again through an elaborate conspiracy.
While writing the book, Wilkie Collins was struggling with both gout and the recent death of his mother. He found relief in laudanum, a drink that mixed alcohol and opium. After the publication of the novel, he claimed to have taken so much laudanum at some point that he didn’t recall writing many passages, though characters in the novel suffer from memory distortion as a result of their own drug usage.
Notable Quotes

“The progress of the disease has gradually forced me from the use of opium to the abuse of it.”

wiki/the-simple-secret-of-being-happier.title: The Simple Secret of Being Happy
wiki/the-simple-secret-of-being-happier.content:
Foreword
Anyone who says they have a “simple secret” to anything immediately flags my snake oil detector. I think there are as many “get-happy-quick” schemes as “get-rich-quick” schemes.
Introduction
“When I was 10 years old, things started shifting between my parents and not for the better. One day, they called a family meeting… they told us that we’d be moving from our little log cabin in northern British Columbia, Canada to the southern part of the province. And that they would be divorcing… my father, Peter, had always been this happy-go-lucky guy. The divorce was extremely hard on him, and he was becoming more and more withdrawn. He was less engaged with my sisters and I, he had less energy, and I barely recognized him anymore. I remember thinking to myself, ‘is this my new dad?‘”
This sounds like depression, but I’m no doctor and good doctors don’t diagnose people over secondhand anecdotes from the Internet. Still, the Mayo Clinic has a page about signs you can observe among friends if you suspect depression, which includes “sadness, tearfulness, emptiness, or hopelessness… loss of interest of pleasure in most or all normal activities… tiredness and lack of energy… slowed thinking, speaking or body movements…” Divorce can certainly be a trigger for depression, and men demonstrate a higher risk for the first-onset of major depression after divorce than women. So, I assume this is going to be a story about the choices someone can make to combat depression in the face of tragedy that brings about the true definition of well-being according to Graham, which is resilience. Right?
“One day I woke up at his hosue… and I could hear music playing downstairs, which was very unusual… and there was my dad, Peter, dancing and making pancakes… I said ‘Wow Dad, you seem really happy today…‘”
“You know, Tia, I have had three of the worst years of my entire life, and I woke up this morning and I thought to myself, ‘I’m not going to have another bad year’.”
“I saw my dad choose happiness.”
Oh. Scrap the depression to delight story. That’s on me for being presumptuous.
People suffering from depression can end up in a vicious cycle where they lose interest and pleasure in activities they used to do, so they become less active, so there are fewer activity-reward pairings for the brain to experience, which lowers their mood further. Behavioral Activation (BA) has been one of the most evidence-backed treatments for addressing depressive symptoms. It breaks the cycle by assuming action precedes motivation and that the brain needs to regain momentum towards positive reinforcement through tiny manageable steps that grow over time.
For instance, if cleaning the house feels impossible, try putting dishes from the sink into the dishwasher, and allow yourself to celebrate that as a success. If going to the gym feels impossible, try a short walk. If your personal hygiene feels like it’s slipped out of control, just aim to put your toothbrush in your mouth or wash your face. Commit to it ahead of time like an appointment or deadline so that you’re prepared to do it regardless of your mood.
“One day at a time” and “just for today” are cliches in recovery circles that build on this concept: don’t think about never having a drink again, just focus on not having a drink for today. Reward yourself for that, and it gets easier each day to imagine staying sober.
In other words, recovering from anything, depression or addiction, tends to be a gradual progress. One does not wake up and simply choose to be happy. One can choose to try a small step towards giving your brain a little reward, which is going to be hard even as it gets a little easier each day. With a good support system, consistency towards rebuilding the systems that produce pleasure is possible. Having a good therapist can make all the difference in clarifying your values and monitoring your activities.
Remember that depression has a high rate of comorbiditiwa, and a therapist can flag something to look into with a psychiatrist. For instance, 60% of people with Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) also meet the criteria for an anxiety disorder, 14% for substance use disorder, and 72% with a chronic physical condition like diabetes, high cholesterol, hypertension, COPD, back pain, etc. Anecdotally, this isn’t surprising at all. I’ve known at least one person for each of those conditions mentioned who has also struggled with depression. They can even be the reason someone is restricted from the usual activities that bring them pleasure, which can start the negative reinforcement cycle.
I say all this now because depression is never actually mentioned in this video, so there won’t be a discussion about the author challenging their thesis with a condition that impacts 1 in 10 US adults and 1 in 5 young adults 18-25. I imagine those are the people most likely to click on a YouTube video about achieving happiness. In fact, I find it a little concerning that Graham begins with a very realistic premise for someone suffering from depression - years of low moods and energy following the fracture of a family dynamic - but pivots into happiness simply being a choice.
“So what did he do exactly? He started doing things that he enjoyed doing. So he played upbeat music all the time. He went back to school and changed careers. He exercised outside, spent time with his horses, and he spent a lot of time with his friends.”
So, he didn’t choose to be happy. He chose a series of rather major risky life changes that resulted in happiness rather than despair because they fortunately worked out. There’s a very big difference between making a playlist of good vibes for yourself and changing careers as an older worker when you have several young children dependent on you. The first could be a reasonable starting step for BA, but the second is a major step not everyone can or should take. Only 52% of adults over the age of 25 complete a degree in 6 years, of which three-quarters achieve the initial career goals they set out for. Obviously doable, but still a risk not everyone can make. Remember that these statistics don’t include people who want to make a career change but can’t afford the risk.
“at age 18 and 19, I was really struggling, and I was not happy… I knew there had to be more to life, and I knew that I had to choose happiness for myself. This decision took me from living in Calgary, Alberta to Hilton Head Island, South Carolina, where I worked with children one summer…it exposed me to the travel and hospitality industries. This experience led me to a 15-year career in the hospitality industry that I was passionate about and successful in…
I don’t understand this example. I understand that Graham made a major career change just like her dad which paid off. I understand that this career was international and lucrative. I’m missing the part that connects her decision to be happy to the professional success she attained later. Notice that her language attributes agency to the decision to choose happiness for herself rather than explaining the rationale of how the move lines up with her values: “The decision took me… it exposed me…”
“Remember, I’m from a little log cabin in northern Canada.”
This is technically true, but not honest. Set aside the fact that her dad owns horses and could return to school for a career change, or that her mom returned to school prior to the divorce after being let go from her old job. According to Graham’s podcast:
“my mom and dad were living in Northern British Columbia Canada, and they were running a ski area together called Powder King Ski Resort… my grandfather, my dad’s dad was a very large investor in this company… he made an executive decision that they were going to hire a professional marketing company… my mom was no longer needed at the ski area… She is instantly thrust into survival mode and she is not okay. She decides to take us down to the southern part of British Columbia where we have a little lake house and where we’d spend some time in the summer to get away from everything.”
It’s a little disingenuous to say you’re just from a little log cabin in rural British Columbia when your family actually runs a ski resort profitable enough to afford a summer lake house. In fact, the resort has a Wikipedia page and was listed for over $8 million in 2022: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Powder_King_Mountain_Resort
“In 1983, Peter Graham Jr., president and majority shareholder in the family-owned that had operated Azu Village for the previous four years, and Peter’s then-wife Claudia, presented a $7.7 million expansion plan… A real estate development at the base of the mountain would comprise 47 single-family lots and 106 multi-family units.”
So not just running a ski resort, but planning multi-million dollar expansions to develop the real estate to hold hundreds of people. This isn’t exactly a mom-and-pop shop. It’s totally possible that the real details reveal something like a land rich, cash poor family or an heir who threw away a fortune, but “little log cabin” is implying some rags-to-riches story based on the decision to be happy.
“A happy life is not about feeling happy all the time. This is a huge misconception.”
Is it? Are people going around expecting to be happy all the time?
“Here is the simple secret of being happier: spend time doing things you really enjoy doing. Society tells us what happiness is, what happiness looks like, but what really matters is how you feel. So many people struggle with happiness… Whether it’s kids, work, finances, politics, non-stop technology, social media, family, or the never-ending 24/7 negative news cycle.”
Surveys show that at least 40% of American households do not earn enough to cover basic necessities like housing, utilities, and child care. 62% of employed professionals report feeling financially unstable or struggling to pay their bills. 83% of individuals report significant financial stress from inflation on top of the high cost of living. Some studies suggest that over 75% of doctor’s office visits are directly linked to chronic stress and related ailments like chronic inflammation. 51% of adults report regular exhaustion without explanation, 48% report lying awake at night because of racing thoughts or excessive worry, 44% suffer from tension headaches or migraines, 34% experience stomach distress related to anxiety.
36% of young adults aged 18 to 25 meet the criteria for at least one mental illness, with an unstable job market and debt as their top stressors. 66% of teens report feeling overwhelmed by the issues of climate change, economic volatility, and political polarization. 27% of adults under 30 report a lifetime depression diagnosis which has doubled since 2017. These numbers get worse in some subgroups: high school girls are twice as likely as boys to present with severe depression, over 40% of LGBTQ+ youth report feeling seriously suicidal, and over 60% of young adults of color experience at least moderate anxiety and/or depression.
My guess is that far more people are barely treading water while worrying about existential challenges to the future of human society than expecting happiness all the time in an untroubled life.
If we were being charitable, we might think this is rhetoric aligned with the critiques of positive psychology and a “happiness industry” that promotes unrealistic standards of happiness.
For context, studies show that:


people with negative beliefs about emotions in general tend to present with more symptoms of anxiety and depression


people tend to predict that events, positive or negative, will impact them more severely and for a longer duration than they actually do


people who strongly value being happy tend to feel less happy when in a positive mood compared to others, which can be interpreted as the result of monitoring your own happiness excessively


I would agree with the idea of treating episodes of negative experiences as normal instead of always a problem to be solved until happiness is achieved. Good listening can just mean letting someone vent while asking questions from another perspective, rather than trying to categorize and change their emotional state. The latter can come across as invalidating their reaction and proposing they should have another.
Ironically though, that’s what saying “a happy life isn’t always going to be happy” does. Imagine the depressed young adult stumbling upon this video who worries about an unstable job market and polarization in communities, only to see that massive life changes were necessary for this immensely privileged speaker to be happy even some of the time.
This is exactly why I feel it’s necessary to call out the systemic context behind the “mindset is everything”, “happiness is a choice”, “the real prison is in your mind” types of mantras. Graham had a summer lake house to process “survival mode” while most Americans are chronically stressed about paying rent or mortgages. Of course someone like Graham has to make better choices to be happy: that’s the only way their life can get better since they have all the material advantages required to not have the chronic problems most unhappy people do.
“A happy life has meaning and purpose, and a happy life has different experiences that make you psychologically rich. You think happiness comes from meeting other people and society’s expectations, but really, it comes from creating your own.”
Note that neither Graham, her dad, nor her mom were struggling with meeting social expectations before. That’s not mentioned in the TED talk, though admittedly I haven’t gone through her entire podcast to see if she elaborates elsewhere. Either way, within this video, she only mentions her father’s divorce and her own vague unhappiness that led to partying and dropping out of college. There is no elaboration on how this connects with social expectations as a driver of unhappiness. It’s just shoehorned in as a truism.
Also, it’s not a very true truism. People do tend to report greater well-being when they pursue goals that are personally meaningful rather than imposed externally, which is rather obvious: you feel better doing things you want to do than things others make you do. However, people don’t find their values or idea of meaning independently of other people and broader society. That’s yet another example of hyperindividualism that attempts to assert that there is a self or an ego that can exist in a vacuum with complete control of itself.
A 2023 study of almost 38,000 adults found that the top predictors of well-being were loneliness, satisfaction with social activities, self-rated health, financial security and success, and personality (mainly neuroticism). This is a pretty consistent finding across time. A 2004 study by Martin Seligman found that the strongest correlates of well-being are social relationships, employment, health, freedom, and trust. A 2026 study of over 148,000 adults across natinos found that an internal locus of control (belief that one has control over their life) and state of health were the most important predictors. After that, household income, marital status, in-group trust, acceptance of homosexuality, and age.
Hardly any of that is related to creating your own expectations while shunning other people and society’s expectations. The two are in an inseparable loop with each other. You can’t have meaningful relationships, social engagements, or community participation without aligning yourself with the environment around you. That also means having the courage and responsibility to accept your agency over the environment and act on it.
But there’s no simple secret to addressing loneliness or financial insecurity. That requires social reform, which is hard and controversial, unlike TED talks which explicitly seek simple ideas to spread in 10-minute presentations. We’ll see what kind of literature she does end up referencing instead pretty shortly.
“I personally struggle to feed my family three times a day, seven days a week, every single week. I am not a good cook, and I don’t like cooking. Obviously, I would never make it on Top Chef. Bottom Chef called and said ‘don’t even bother.‘”
First of all, meal prepping isn’t hard. It’s a habit to learn like anything else. You can freeze some meals for months and they’ll still taste great when you reheat them. There are countless guides to do this online. My college had workshops to teach students about budget meal prepping. This is a solved problem.
Second of all, notice how “struggle” here went from “kids, work, finances, politics, non-stop technology, social media, family, or the never-ending 24/7 negative news cycle” to finding it inconvenient to assign yourself the task of making fresh meals from scratch three times a day for a family? We went from external threats to your peace and security to what I assume is an attempt to come across as relatable to unhappy middle-class moms, which is kind of her whole brand.
“Gallup’s research showed that 79% of people, globally, are disengaged while they’re working. That’s almost 80% of people. Many people are doing work that they don’t like or that’s not meaningful to them. Also, according to Gallup’s global research, 41% of people have a lot of stress and worry on a regular basis. The World Health Organization said one in four are not getting enough execise, and the term ‘work-life balance’ has over 2.8 billion search results on Google. And your brain, my brain, all of our brains have a negativity bias, which is really unfortunate. We have to work extra hard to be positive and optimistic.”
Notice that being disengaged with work is considered a proxy for unhappiness or lack of purpose. Why? You’ve never had a job you did just for a paycheck so you could enjoy the rest of your life or at least try to achieve basic security?
For those who don’t know, TED Talks have a reputation for being the kind of content that managers show employees when they want to avoid making any systemic changes in the workplace if boosting morale and positivity can fix it. Spoilers: it can’t. As Demings said, a bad system beats a good person every time. If you want people to be engaged in the workplace, give them engaging incentives. That’s as obvious a principle as “do things you enjoy in order to enjoy life more” or “do esteemable things if you want self-esteem.”
Also, our negativity bias isn’t necessarily “unfortunate.” It likely developed because paying more attention to threats and losses than rewards can be a good strategy for survival. You can run out of food and starve to death, but you can’t somehow eat more food now to avoid eating later, so loss can have more significance than gain. We might say that a bird in hand is worth two in the bush. Optimism is not in and of itself something desirable, it’s just a proxy that can tell us something about your general mental state.
“I’m going to share with you four things that many people really enjoy doing. I’m going to connect them to the science of happiness. And I want you to think about these for yourself.”
Happiness Choice Number One
“Happiness choice number one- Spend a lot of quality time with your friends and your family…The Harvard Grant Study of Adult Development, an over-80-year study, proved that our relationships and how happy we are in our relationships directly affect our health and our happiness.”
Setting aside the technical issues with the word “proved”, we see that Graham does in fact use the same literature I referenced above, with seemingly no awareness of how it contradicts the idea of creating expectations from within yourself instead of meeting those of other people and society.
You cannot have a happy marriage if you disregard your spouse’s expectations of you. You cannot be a good parent if you disregard your children’s expectations of you. You cannot keep a job if you disregard your employer’s expectations of you. You cannot sell to customers if you disregard the customers’ expectations of you. Simply put, you can either have relationships or you can be be a lone wolf, but you can’t be both. You can absolutely negotiate expectations within a relationship to align yours with another’s, but the fact they exist is an inescapable fact of life.
A 2022 study examined the 2003-2020 American Time Use Survey and found that nationally, social isolation increased while social engagement and companionship decreased. The COVID quarantines only accelerated consistent trends we observed. The study specifically highlights that “Hours worked per week emerged as a structural constraint to social connectedness.” So people who have to work more to make ends meet are less likely to spend time with their friends; remember that 40% of Americans don’t make enough to afford basic needs. That hardly seems like a choice someone can change.
Here’s a quick thought experiment: imagine that no one in the world had to work for a living at all, and basic needs are completely provided through a magic wand. How many people do you think would choose to keep doing exactly what they’re doing now, and how many people would quit to spend time with loved ones and/or traveling the world to meet new people?
Happiness Choice Number Two
“Happiness choice number two is getting a good night’s sleep. This means sleeping seven to nine hours a night, every single night. Research shows that sleep increases our happiness, improves our brain functioning, and improves our overall quality of life. So even though those streaming shows are so good or even though you could stay up just one more hour, just answer a few more emails, go to bed and leave your phone in the kitchen.”
Remember above that we talked about a vicious cycle, and how half of Americans lose sleep because of racing thoughts and excessive worry about the future? There are two main ways to interpret the combination of these facts. Either the use of technology before bed causes racing thoughts and worry which then prompts more technology use as a distraction, or people stressed about their lives can’t sleep use screens while lying in bed awake.
One 2025 meta-analysis looked at 21 studies with almost 550,000 participants. Each hour of daily screen time was associated with 3-5 minutes less sleep and 13.2 minutes of delay in bedtime. In 2024, a review of 25 studies across 4652 participants found that “daily screen time has a small” correlation with delayed sleep time, and “short-term daily fluctuations in screen time appear to have minimal impact on sleep duration, efficiency, or quality. Screen time may delay bedtime but is not inherently detrimental to other aspects of sleep health in youth.”
Another 2025 meta-analysis that looked at about 4,200 adults across 42 randomized controlled trials found that sleep hygiene education (SHE) produces only weak to modest impacts on insomnia relative to other approaches. Partial Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I), exercise, and accupressure all outperform sleep hygiene as factors in alleviating insomnia.
So overall, evidence shows that if you want completely optimal sleep, then improving sleep hygiene and cutting down on screen time can help. However, the top predictors of physician-diagnosed insomnia, according to a 2023 analysis that examined 684 variables, seem to be depression symptoms, age, a physician recommendation to exercise, weight, and waist circumference. In fact, depression symptoms contribute four times as much as age and ten times as much as body weight.
Another study aimed at subjective sleep quality instead of diagnosed insomnia found that the 38 objective variables analyzed for over 1400 adults could only explain 11-17% of the variance. In other words, factors other than sleep efficiency (percent of time spent in bed asleep), total sleep time, and number of sleep stage transitions are primarily responsible for subjective sleep quality.
It seems that symptoms of depression, anxiety and stress, age, body composition, physical health, and dysfunctional beliefs about sleep are consistently the biggest predictors we find. Screen time does appear to have a modest effect on sleep quality, duration, and efficiency but sleep hygiene overall isn’t that impactful. Depression, on the other hand, has an incredibly massive impact.
The evidence suggests, at least to me, that people are struggling with sleep for reasons unrelated to their screen time and turn to technology for something to do in bed. Once you notice how often communicators leap from loose associations to strong prescriptions, it’s hard to unsee.
Happiness Choice Number 3
“Happiness choice number three - Moving at least four times a week. Exercise increases our happiness, increases our brain functioning, and decreases stress and anxiety. Do not exercise to look good; exercise to be happier. And I know you’re busy. You don’t need to do an hour workout class. Even if you move 15, 20 minutes, you will get the benefit.”
Exercise is definitely associated with increased happiness and decreased stress and anxiety, particularly in individuals who have more of both. The encouragement to move even 15 or 20 minutes is largely in line with the tiny steps I mentioned above as part of Behavioral Activation. This is probably the most defensible recommendation in the talk.
It should be noted though that the relationship between depression and exercise is bidirectional. Depression is associated with becoming physically inactive over time, and people with higher physical activity are less likely to develop depression. 40% of respondents to the CDC Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS) cite a lack of time as their primary issue, and as many as 25% cite health problems or disabilities as an obstacle. Remember that over half of American adults report exhaustion without a clear explanation.
Also, I haven’t been pointing out how interconnected these issues are. Someone worried about making ends meet is more likely to pick up more hours, which means anxiety and a higher workload will both be contributing to less sleep. They might also have to cut out social engagement activities that doubled as physical activity. That can lead to more health complications like an increase in the symptoms of anxiety and depression or aggravation of another underlying health condition like hypertension. It’s easy to see someone spiral into that vicious cycle we mentioned before.
The gap between the highest-income adults and lowest-income adults in terms of meeting aerobic activity recommendations is about 20%, strongly suggesting that more financial security enables healthier lifestyle choices. Is that really surprising to anyone? Keep in mind these statistics include the fact that lower-income groups have more physical activity at work while higher-income groups incorporate more recreational exercise. Someone who works over 40 hours a week in a warehouse is probably not going to have the energy to hit the gym after or in the middle of the workday. For contrast, I’ve had a lot of meetings with at least one coder walking on a treadmill placed under their standing desk or squeezing in a home gym routine around lunch.
Happiness Choice Number 4
“Research shows that meaningful work makes us happier and way more motivated while we’re working and makes us happier in our personal life. And if you don’t have the opportunity right now to change jobs or change careers, just spend more time helping people, and your work will be more meaningful.”
From a Pew Research Center survey, 55% of American workers considering job changes were concerned about losing income, and 45% were concerned about losing benefits like healthcare. 50% of adults involved in some type of education or training report a lack of time due to work and family obligations as a barrier to their advancement. 20-30% of adults considering further education and training also have caregiving responsibilities. Women on average spent roughly twice as much time on caregiving for children than men, while men on average spend more hours working to support a household financially. As I said before, this type of career change is certainly doable, but definitely not equitably distributed.
As for helping people, there have been studies on something called “task significance” which tracks the belief that one’s work has an impact on others, but studies show it accounts for 14% of the variation in job satisfaction. In other words, it can definitely help yourself feel better to help others feel better, but you are heavily constrained in this by the parameters of your workplace. Also, if you have ever worked anything even closely resembling customer service, you’re probably laughing a little bit at the idea that you would be happier if only you tried to be more helpful.
Note that the solution being proposed is asking you to do more work with a positive attitude to feel better. It’s almost like positivity propaganda, and it’s not hard to see why managers might share this with their employees.
Conclusion
“There are many other happiness choices, such as spending time in nature, meditating, volunteering, journaling when you’re going through pain. It’s about you.”
There’s a rhetorical sleight of hand here where self-care that’s central to your health is being conflated with a “happiness choice.” These are entirely different things. There’s a really big distinction between reducing negative moods, increasing positive moods, increasing life satisfaction, and increasing a sense of meaning or purpose.
Also, the literature shows that all of these have small to moderate impacts on well-being on average. There seems to be an assumption that happiness is a linear combination of the “happiness choices” listed above. If you add up all the small changes, a big change must necessarily happen that puts you into the “happy life” category, right?
No. In fact, I was pleasantly surprised to see that there has been substantial criticism from scholars lately about this exact framing. Nicholas J.L. Brown & Julia M. Rohrer provide an incredibly comprehensive breakdown of the assumptions behind the “happiness pie” model that proposed 40% of our happiness can be attributed to individual actions in our control. I couldn’t possibly add anything in the way of commentary to the substance of the work, so I’ll shamelessly cite them directly:
“Consequently, there is little reason to believe that 40% is a reliable estimate of the variance in chronic happiness attributable to intentional activity—for example, if Lyubomirsky et al. had chosen a different (but, in our view, at least equally plausible) set of estimates, they might just as easily have concluded that as little as (100% − 80% − 15% = 5%) of variance in chronic happiness can be attributed to volitional activities. Of course, because of the conceptual issues that we have discussed, we do not believe that such an estimate would necessarily be more reasonable or more interpretable.”
They also include a sharper critique of the point about privilege I made before:
“Likewise, researchers should carefully reconsider the usage of terms such as “volitional activities”. What might be a matter of choice for some people can be a question of circumstances for others.”
“For example, middle-class Western parents with a comfortable household income can exercise a wide range of choice over the diet that they and their children consume; they can choose to drive their car to the farmer’s market instead of taking the bus to the discount grocery store, and afford to place organic blueberries rather than canned, syrup-laden fruit cocktail in their shopping cart. They can also enjoy a wide range of recreational activities, such as vacations to awe-inspiring or culturally important destinations, enabling them to enjoy the benefits of feeling that they are part of a meaningful world (Gilovich and Kumar 2015).”
“Indeed, Lyubomirsky et al. (2005) themselves described the types of volitional activities that they were considering in decidedly middle-class terms: “rather than running on a track, a fitness-seeking wilderness lover might instead choose to run on a trail through the woods… rather than learning classical pieces, a jazz-loving piano student might instead choose to work on jazz standards” (p. 122).”
Just like I said above, Graham’s examples also seem to be marketed at the middle-class moms (though these days we might say upper-middle class) whose idea of “struggle” might mean making three fresh meals everyday rather than affording subsistence-level meal prepping. Graham, like many get-happy-quick gurus, is just marketing “happiness circumstances” as “happiness choices” for the particular demographic whose circumstances allow them to make those choices.
“A subsistence farmer working from dawn to dusk in a developing nation, a worker who spends 14 h per day assembling electronic devices in a south-east Asian factory, or a single Western parent living in less fortunate circumstances than the family just mentioned, may not be in a position to make such choices. As with many phenomena studied by primarily Western psychologists (cf. Henrich et al. 2010), the list of volitional activities that are available to improve one’s well-being may be less than universal, not just for cultural reasons but also precisely because of one’s life circumstances.”
Anecdotally, if you ever want to make it really awkward in a room where someone is promoting a viewpoint from positive psychology, just bring up racism or sexism or another -ism. Ask what kind of self-care or volitional activities you need to offset the circumstances of systemic bigotry to your wellbeing. I have never once seen this point handled gracefully or tactfully, because the premise of this worldview is that you have freedom through consumer choice and the civil rights afforded by a liberal democracy. In practice, your freedom is limited by your access to capital, whether financial or political.
As someone from an Indian and Hindu background, my grandparents were alive to witness the liberation of Goa from Portuguese rule, a struggle that lasted from the 1490s to the 1960s. A huge misconception about Indian independence is that Gandhi and friends held peaceful hunger strikes with his best friend Martin Luther King Jr. that made the British and Americans feel silly enough to stop being racist and give rights. In practice, European powers stayed long after the 1947 deal for independence was struck. For 14 years, nonviolent and diplomatic attempts to negotiate the freedom of Goa from a Portguese dictatorship continued. It became an international affair that involved the UN, US, UK, Brazil, Mexico, and other parties with a stake in either India or Portugal.
In November of 1961, Portguese troops shot at a passenger boat and killed one while injuring the chief engineer. This was far from the only death that had happened since 1947 among unarmed nonviolent Indians in proximity to Goa, but it became an inflection point where enough was enough. By December, Prime Minister Nehru declared that the era of peaceful negotiation and adaptation to the occupying forces was over: “Continuance of Goa under Portguese rule is an impossibility.”
Prime Minister Salazar of the Portuguese had ordered “there will be no surrender rendered because I feel that our soldiers and sailors can be either victorious or dead.” Governor General Manuel Vassalo e Silva told the press “If necessary, we wil die here.” The Portguese President had ordered a scorched earth policy, so that Goa was to be destroyed before being conceded to India. This is the kind of detail that’s important to remember when discussing the conditions of developing nations and formerly colonialized territories.
The United States, both outside and inside the forum of the United Nations, was critical of India’s use of force for independence, which is rather ironic considering how the US obtained independence. Go listen to Hamilton if you’ve forgotten. On the other hand, the USSR had vetoed a UN Security Council resolution that would have condemned India’s liberation of Goa. Brezhnev criticized the response of Western institutions as coming “from those who are accustomed to strangle the peoples striving for independence… and from those who enrich themselves from colonialist plunder.”
Operation Vijay took 36 hours to force the Portuguese to surrender. 14 years of diplomatic resolution and adaptation was nowhere near as effective as just acting decisively and collectively against an obvious injustice.
My ancestors did not improve their lives by incorporating more exercise or turning off the TV sooner before bedtime when they didn’t even have the consistent electricity to have a fridge. They organized collectively to challenge institutions and force changes that they were told they would never be able to make. That created political and financial capital by recognizing community rather than the individual ego as the fundamental unit of human society. Individuals repeatedly made sacrifices to benefit the collective with the understanding that they were investing in the future prosperity of those who would one day call them ancestors. That gives meaning, purpose, and a place in the world. You cannot know what you can or cannot change until you try your absolute best to change it, and your absolute best only comes out when you’re working with people who empower each other.
All this to say, I have a very different frame of reference for what counts as “struggle” or “survival mode” than no longer having a job in a lucrative family business or wanting to cook three fresh meals every day. Perhaps the radically individualist positive psychology of “happiness choices” works for those who have reaped the benefits of colonialism to give themselves that choice. It doesn’t seem to work as well for those on the receiving end of it.

wiki/the-ten-kraters-of-eubulus.title: The Ten Kraters of Eubulus
wiki/the-ten-kraters-of-eubulus.content: Eubulus was a 4th century BCE Athenian poet to whom a fragment of a play is ascribed that we might call “The Ten Kraters of Eubulus.” The god Dionysus, associated with intoxication and transcendental experiences, outlined the progressive stages of drunkenness. It starts with love and pleasure, then shouting and violence, then engagement with law enforcement or other authorities, and finally some kind of physical sickness and mental madness. Dionysus advises drinkers to moderate and go home right as it begins to invoke feelings of sleepiness past love and pleasure.
