wiki/tobacco-containing-tobacco-products.title: Tobacco-containing tobacco product (TCTP)
wiki/tobacco-containing-tobacco-products.content:
Overview
Tobacco-containing tobacco product (TCTP) is a term that arose because of a quirk in the way that definitions are used in regulations in the United States. Under the Family Smoking Prevention and Tobacco Control Act, the Food and Drugs Administration defines a “tobacco product” as anything derived from tobacco, including synthetic nicotine. This means that e-cigarettes and tobacco-free nicotine pouches are still legally classified as “tobacco products.” The separate term TCTP arose to differentiate products that contained nicotine from products that contained raw plant matter (cigarettes, cigars, snus, pipe tobacco, etc.)

wiki/tobacco-control-research-group.title: Tobacco Control Research Group
wiki/tobacco-control-research-group.content:
Overview
The Tobacco Control Research Group (TCRG) at the University of Bath was established in 2007. In 2012, they launched a public knowledge exchange platform to monitor academic research findings and developments from the global tobacco industry.
Links

wiki/tobacco.title: Tobacco
wiki/tobacco.content:
Overview
Tobacco is a plant containing nicotine, an addictive stimulant, and it’s consumed when its leaves are smoked, chewed, sniffed, or vaped.
Combustible tobacco are products that are burned and inhaled, like cigarettes, cigars, cigarillos, and pipe tobacco.

wiki/tolerance.title: Tolerance
wiki/tolerance.content:
Overview
Tolerance is the pattern of a body adapting to chronic substance use such that larger doses are required over time to achieve the same effect. With repeated consumption of a substance, the liver and other organs become more efficient at clearing it from the bloodstream. Neurons adjust their sensitivity to chemical spikes by increasing or decreasing the number of receptors influenced by substance use. If someone stops using a substance for a period of time, their tolerance will likely drop rapidly. Unfortunately, in a relapse, many people will attempt to use the amount they last used despite the low tolerance, which means they might trigger an overdose.

wiki/tough-love.title: Tough Love
wiki/tough-love.content:
Overview
The idea of “tough love” is to use firm discipline, boundaries, and consequences to promote growth. There’s a lot of variation in both how people define “tough love” and how people feel about “tough love.”
In the best-case scenario, tough love involves applying consistent rules fairly but firmly. The tendency to take shortcuts by bending rules or skipping self-discipline is curbed by enforcement with consequences. Someone who uses tough love should ideally have the same compassionate intentions as someone who prioritizes forgiveness and harm reduction; they just have a different idea of what is most effective in helping others.
In the worst-case scenario, tough love can just be a euphemism for toxic dynamics or outright abuse under the belief that suffering builds character. Stigma around mental health issues, or at least patterns that Western psychiatry would recognize as pathologies, can be found in virtually every culture in the world. People in recovery often need a validating, supportive, and collaborative environment in order to safely work through the root causes behind their maladaptive coping mechanisms. Experiencing harm in environments that should be safe and reward vulnerability can alienate someone from seeking help from medical institutions.

wiki/towards-a-syndrome-model-of-addicti.title: Towards a Syndrome Model of Addiction - Multiple Expressions, Common Etiology (2004)
wiki/towards-a-syndrome-model-of-addicti.content:
“It is common for clinicians, researchers, and public pol-
icymakers to describe certain drugs or objects (e.g., games
of chance) as “addictive,” tacitly implying that the cause of
addiction resides in the properties of drugs or other objects.
Conventional wisdom encourages this view by treating dif-
ferent excessive behaviors, such as alcohol dependence and
pathological gambling, as distinct disorders.”
“Evidence supporting a broader conceptualization of addiction is emerging. For example, neurobiological research suggests that addictive disorders might not be independent: each outwardly unique addiction disorder might be a distinctive expression of the same underlying addiction syndrome.”

wiki/toxicology.title: Toxicology
wiki/toxicology.content:
Overview
Toxicology is the study of the effects of external agents on living things and ecosystems. That includes recreational substances, prescription medicines, poisons, pollutants, pesticides, and food additives.

wiki/training-and-technical-assistance.title: Training and Technical Assistance (TTA)
wiki/training-and-technical-assistance.content:
Overview
Training and technical assistance (TTA) describes specialized support services that teach individuals and organizations to implement new evidence-based practices, increase operational efficiency, and improve strategic planning.
In substance use recovery and treatment, TTA is a vital part of translating evidence from the latest research and trials into practice. There’s actually an entire field for this process called implementation science. One of the biggest examples of TTA infrastructure in the United States is the Addiction Technology Transfer Center (ATTC) Network, which provides TTA to professionals for SUD treatment. The Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) manages the ATTC, as well as the Prevention Techology Transfer Centers (PTTC) and Mental Health Technology Transfer Centers (MHTTC) for co-occurring mental health disorders. More recently, TTA from these centers has involved training emergency responders and clincians to handle high-potency substances like fentanyl and severe withdrawals.
Historical Context
In the United States, the federal government began using the term “Training and Technical Assistance” as part of the Economic Opportunity Act under the War on Poverty in 1965. Policymakers had realized that giving grant money to local communities and leaving them to figure out the operational details was highly ineffective, leading to duplicated efforts in siloed bureaucracies. TTA networks emerged to help local agencies and programs meet federal standards by providing training and operational support on top of grants.

wiki/transitional-housing.title: Transitional Housing
wiki/transitional-housing.content:
Overview
Transitional housing programs provide temporary housing to vulnerable individuals, typically coupled with specialized social and medical services. Vulnerable groups include those who had been homeless, experienced injuries and disabilities, or had mental health conditions. Stays generally last up to 2 years based on guidelines from the United States Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). Specialized services include case management, vocational counseling, job placement, recovery programs, and mental health services.

wiki/trauma-bonding.title: Trauma Bonding
wiki/trauma-bonding.content:
Overview
In clinical psychology, “trauma bonds” refer to attachments that form between an abuser and their victim. In an abusive relationship, an abuser alternates between intense kindness and love bombing before demonstrating cruelty and manipulation. The cycle can be unpredictable and release neurotransmitters, dopamine and oxytocin, in a way that can feel addictive. Breaking the cycle comes with the anxiety of the unknown and, for many, complications to their financial and housing security.
In everyday conversation, people might use “trauma bonding” to mean bonding with someone over shared hardship, but the definitions in the field of psychology concern abusive relationships.

wiki/trauma-informed.title: Trauma-Informed
wiki/trauma-informed.content:
Overview
Trauma-informed care (TIC) is an approach to care that recognizes the widespread nature of trauma in influencing people’s well-being, particularly in the sphere of mental health. The Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) offer six principles of TIC:


Safety


Trustworthiness and Transparency


Peer Support


Collaboration and Mutuality


Empowerment, Voice, and Choice


Cultural, Historical, and Gender Issues

wiki/trauma.title: Trauma
wiki/trauma.content:
Overview
The American Psychological Association’s Dictionary of Psychology defines trauma as:
“any disturbing experience that results in significant fear, helplessness, dissociation, confusion, or other disruptive feelings intense enough to have a long-lasting negative effect on a person’s attitudes, behavior, and other aspects of functioning.” 1
This definition is flexible about the details of the event and relies more on the emotional impact that one personally experiences. The DSM-5 is more specific in its criteria:
A. Exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence in one (or more) of the following ways… Directly experiencing the traumatic event(s)… Witnessing, in person, the event(s) as it occurred to others… Learning that the traumatic event(s) occurred to a close family member or a close friend… Experiencing repeated or extreme exposure to aversive details of the traumatic event(s)

wiki/travis-rieder.title: Travis Rieder
wiki/travis-rieder.content:
An associate professor at Johns Hopkins University focusing on bioethics.
Articles

www.cbsnews.com/news/nyc-drug-addiction-onpoint-harm-reduction/

“Johns Hopkins bioethicist Travis Rieder argues that support for places like OnPoint will never be decided solely by the empirical data. ‘I don’t actually think it’s why anyone believes what they believe… They have a view about what we should actually be helping people to do or not do, and then they find the evidence that best supports their view… Here’s what an overdose prevention site does: It says, ‘You are welcome here, and I will watch over you so that you don’t die today, and you’re worth that. You deserve that because you’re a human being and you have dignity.’ And I think that’s a really beautiful thing.‘”

wiki/trigger.title: Trigger
wiki/trigger.content:
Overview
In psychology, a trigger is any stimulus, internal or external, that activates a strong reaction based in a prior traumatic event.
Models
Diathesis-Stress Model
The Diathesis-Stress Model, also called Vulnerability Stress Model, proposes that a condition is triggered when an underlying vulnerability (diathesis) intersects with environmental factors (stressors). That vulnerability can be the result of genetic predispositions, past trauma, or unhealthy patterns from early childhood environments. Someone with high vulnerability
ABC Model (Cognitive Behavioral Therapy)
Within Cognitive Behavioral Therapy, the ABC Model tracks the emotional process initiated by triggers: Activating Event, Beliefs, Consequences.
Dual-Representation Theory
This model takes a neurocognitive approach and states that trauma is stored in two memory systems: Verbally Accessible Memories (VAM) and Situationally Accessible Memories (SAM). VAM are the conscious narratives processed by the brain’s hippocampus with chronological cause-and-effect. SAM are processed by the amygdala and include sensory and emotional experiences. Triggers force the brain to replay SAM without the context of time, which leads to re-experiencing parts or the whole of the trauma as if it is happening now. Some of these episodes of re-experiencing are called flashbacks or emotional flashbacks.
ABC Method (Applied Behavioral Analysis)
The ABC Method is an alternative framing to the ABC Model, though both accomplish a similar breakdown: Antecedent, Behavior, Consequence.

wiki/truism.title: Truism
wiki/truism.content:
Overview
Truisms are statements that are so obviously true that it’s often implied they’re not worth mentioning.
Recovery spaces have a lot of phrases that many consider to be truisms:


“Everything happens for a reason”: whether it does or it doesn’t, someone still has to process their emotions and suffering related to it, so this can push someone into intellectualizing events while repressing their emotions or systemic challenges


“It is what it is”: this phrase might intend to encourage acceptance of a situation, but it can also be used dismissively towards problem-solving or objections to toxic behaviors that cross boundaries


“Your best thinking got you here”: while it might be true that someone’s existing pattern of behaviors has to change and this phrase calls out denial, someone also uses their best thinking when they decide to follow other people’s advice. Their best thinking also gets them out. However, the implication of this phrase is that someone should let go of their own rational judgment and comply with something despite their skepticism.

wiki/turn-2-foundation.title: Turn 2 Foundation
wiki/turn-2-foundation.content: Founded by Derek Jeter, the Turn 2 Foundation funds programs that help adolescents progress into a healthy adulthood.

wiki/tuzk-e-jahangiri-by-jahangir.title: Tuzk-e-Jahangiri by Jahangir
wiki/tuzk-e-jahangiri-by-jahangir.content:
Summary
The Muslim Emperor Jahangir, the fourth ruler of the Mughal Empire, held an interesting contradiction. He was open about his own struggles with opium and alcohol dependence, leading to his wife Empress Nur Jahan running much of the empire while he was incapacitated. Both of his brothers also struggled with alcohol and opium. At the same time, he was adamant about banning the sale of drugs, rice-spirits, and especially tobacco.

wiki/twelve-step-facilitation.title: Twelve Step Facilitation (TSF)
wiki/twelve-step-facilitation.content:
Overview
Twelve-Step Facilitation (TSF) is a psychotherapy designed to promote abstinence through connection with 12-step fellowships like Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) and Narcotics Anonymous (NA). Unlike Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (CBT) which emphasizes self-empowerment through internal autonomy and coping skills, TSF explicitly aims to hand off a client into a fellowship that provides external resources to support a client’s internal work through the Steps. TSF builds on AA/NA concepts of a Higher Power as a remedy to personal powerlessness over a substance.

wiki/twelve-steps.title: Twelve Steps
wiki/twelve-steps.content:
Overview
The Twelve Steps are a guide to practicing recovery principles created by Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) and replicated by other anonymous mutual-aid societies built around the idea of peer fellowship, like Narcotics Anonymous (NA) and Gamblers Anonymous (GA). About half of all rehabilitation centers in the United States use 12-step programs in their baseline approach to treatment. Specialized therapeutic approaches have also been designed around 12-step fellowship, like Twelve-Step Facilitation.

wiki/uab-medicine-addiction-recovery-pro.title: UAB Medicine Addiction Recovery Program (ARP)
wiki/uab-medicine-addiction-recovery-pro.content:
Overview
The University of Alabama at Birmingham established the UAB Medicine Addiction Recovery Program in 1994, which runs out of the UAB Hospital and includes inpatient detoxification, intensive outpatient programs (IOP), specialized counseling with modalities like Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR), and structured aftercare for two years for long-term recovery.

wiki/uconn-recovery-community.content:
Overview
The University of Connecticut Recovery Community (URC) supports students who struggle with mental health issues, including Substance Use Disorders (SUDs). They arrange peer-led services for individual coaching, diverse recovery meetings including yoga, substance-free study and housing spaces, and sober recreational activities.

wiki/uehiro-oxford-institute.title: Uehiro Oxford Institute
wiki/uehiro-oxford-institute.content:
Overview
The Uehiro Oxford Institute (UOI) is a research center that replaced the Oxford Uehiro Centre for Practical Ethics as of 2024 at the University of Oxford. It’s funded by the Uehiro Foundation on Ethics and Education.
Researchers have explored topics related to Substance Use Disorder (SUD) like the debate between “judgment-shifts” or failure of self-control under free will, or the disruption of the cognitive link between wanting something and liking it that is often conflated when discussing dopamine as a “pleasure molecule” rather than a reward molecule. They manage a project called Ethics of Behavioural Influence and Prediction (EBIP) which explores the ethics of using neuroscientific interventions to manage crime related to substance use. They also discuss the idea of “cognitive enhancement,” where something like caffeine is celebrated as a daily ritualized stimulant that enhances performance while using other substances is heavily penalized.

wiki/uf-health-florida-recovery-center.title: UF Health Florida Recovery Center
wiki/uf-health-florida-recovery-center.content:
Overview
The University of Florida Health’s Florida Recovery Center is a specialized mental health treatment facility that addresses Substance Use Disorder (SUD) alongside other disorders. Their treatment options include psychotherapy like Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (CBT), detoxification, a partial hospitalization program (PHP), an intensive outpatient program (IOP), group sessions, and family therapy.

wiki/uncut-gems.title: Uncut Gems
wiki/uncut-gems.content:
Overview
Commentary
Pacing
Uncut Gems starts off chaotic and tense, and each scene only compounds the pacing. It begins with a mining accident to a crew of Ethiopian Jews, a zoom-in through multicolored black opals, a zoom-out from Adam Sandler’s colonoscopy, and Kevin Garnett playing himself with a celebrity personality. That’s the quietest the movie gets, because Howard and his friends speak at 100 decibels all the time, and always over each other. The emphasis on overlapping dialogue in the film, as if every person is impatiently rushing to get their personal needs met or their point of view out without waiting to hear what anyone else is expressing. Ironically, this only makes it take longer for anyone to actually communicate their point, leaving plenty of space in conversations to feel the tension of their escalation.
Howard’s Gambling Addiction
Howard is a hustler, and if there’s any sympathy to be found for him for the audience, it’s in the way he always markets himself as a well-meaning expressive underdog on the cusp of a big break, if only people would cut him a little bit of slack to work his entrepreneurial side. But underneath that, he’s decidedly greedy and self-centered, not just a gambling addict. The two are important to separate. He doesn’t just suffer from a compulsion to throw money out on bets as soon as some lands in his hands. Early on in the film, he’s neglectful to his kids, manipulative to his wife (who he’s replaced with a younger girlfriend from his store prior to finalizing a divorce), pads everything he says with a couple lazy lies to wear others down, and is always single-mindedly focused on chasing the next big deal for himself - or running from the next biggest threat, usually his loan shark of a brother-in-law. There are plenty of scenes where he’s around his family but almost entirely uninterested in how they are because he wants to see the outcome of a game on which he placed bets or work on one of his schemes.
These are not, in and of themselves, characteristic of gambling addictions, but moreso the result of a gambling addiction growing in a pathological liar who justifies selfish behavior without a second thought. After all, you can’t really make a thriller movie based on a single young man who spends their paycheck on fantasy football instead of paying off credit card debt or a working-class mother who keeps throwing grocery money into lottery tickets. For many, addictions develop as the result of choosing the addictive process or substance as a means of relief or self-medication from other problems in their life, like a caregiver for a family member who drinks to handle the stress of being always needed and isolated from a life outside their responsibilities. They may be conscious of their habit being unhealthy, but their brains are struggling with a divergence in what feels rewarding and what they consciously value. For others like Howard, they may have always been selfish in prioritizing their needs over others, so resisting a compulsion isn’t something they struggle with for long once the regret of failure wears off. When their brain says to chase the reward, they don’t attempt to push back. These distinctions are critical to draw in the way addiction is portrayed to delineate the moments to sympathize with a disease of compulsions from the moments to criticize someone refusing to take accountability for their actions.
Narratively, Howard doubles down again and again on the same responses to consequences that escalate while the tension rises towards an explosive culmination of his decisions. It’s neither a cautionary tale of addiction like The Lost Weekend nor a belated coming-of-age growth story like 28 days, both of which dig into someone with good intentions who struggles with a deep internal conflict. Instead the movie puts together a perfect storm around someone with little remorse, self-reflection, and impulse control.
The plot, through Howard’s character, is driven by one of the differences between addiction to substances and addiction to gambling. Studies have shown that while substances induce spikes in dopamine through guaranteed chemimcal reactions, gamblers experience dopamine spikes in the anticipation before a result, when the brain needs to pay attention in order to secure a reward. A 100% guaranteed reward doesn’t engage the brain because there’s nothing to pay attention to, but the anticipation of a 50% chance of winning lures the brain into seeking any possible way to tilt the scales into its favor. While someone who doesn’t struggle with gambling can feel demotivated by a loss from trying again, a gambling addict’s brain interprets losses as near-misses, with the actual reward being imminent if they just keep betting. That’s often why you’ll hear gamblers talk about the losses being more satisfying than the wins, because the loss builds more anticipation for how great the next win will feel that makes it all back. In Howard’s case, he’s not chasing the reward of the money itself, but the reward of the anticipation from making crazy bets and pawning insanely valuable items to make more bets. His internal method of calculating risks is a rewarding end in and of itself because it continually engages his brain in ways that the winnings themselves do not. The final scene where Howard locks his brother-in-law in his jewelry store’s security system and forces them all to watch the game he bet six figures on is perfectly illustrative of how his high works and divorces him from reality. He’s essentially guaranteed his death by refusing to pay his due to violent criminals and trapping them in a box, but he’s entirely obsessed with seeing the gamble he made play out on the screen, as if they’re all friends in a living room: “This is the beauty of betting. This is the beauty of betting, you know?” As the audience members, there’s even a part of us that might root for him to win the bet and survive, showing the gangsters that it was all worth it in the end because there was a method to his madness. But reality hits, and he and Arno are both shot dead. The movie ends with a zoom into Howard’s body through the bullet wound, paralleling both our zoom out from his colonoscopy and the black opal that one could supposedly see the universe inside.
Jewish Culture
The show features Howard as an Ashkenazi Jew, Howard’s wife’s family are Sephardic or Mizrahi Jews, the miners at the start of the film are Ethiopian, and there are a sprinkling of Russian Jews surrounding our main characters. The stereotypical association between Jews and African diamonds comes after the 1867 discovery of the jewels in South Africa. In the following rush, the visibility of Jews as financiers and merchants in the trade fed antisemitic tropes about greedy and shady business practices and international conspiracies. The movie 25th Hour (2002) directly references trading in “apartheid diamonds” when comedically reviewing stereotypes of the Orthodox Jewish communities in New York City. There has been a lot of discussion about whether Uncut Gems is reclaiming certain associations by casting Howard as an impulsive chaotic gambler rather than a financial mastermind. From an article about the movie published in Jewish Currents:
In The End of Jewish Modernity, Enzo Traverso argues that there are two paths for contemporary Judaism, represented by two archetypes: Leon Trotsky and Henry Kissinger. But Ratner is neither Trotsky nor Kissinger. This film is not remarking on the mid-20th-century Jewish position as the archetype of history. Ratner is nowhere near that. He’s a shlimazel trying to make money, which to me represents a closer, more intimate critique of how many Jews actually are—which is to say, pretty normal, average, shitty people.
Wait, that makes it sound like Ratner’s been deracinated by his shittiness. But there are plenty of stories about Ratner-like Jews. It’s the whole history of European antisemitism—Fagin and Shylock. And now here are the Safdie brothers—who are Jewish—telling this story, and a lot of Jews who watched it are like, “Maybe this is antisemitic?”, but also, “I know that guy.” Which is a really uncomfortable feeling to have.
I think part of what’s interesting about what the film is doing is the way it transforms the caricature that Arielle’s talking about into the modern literary archetype that Jacob’s talking about. Because it’s not just like a flatly realistic depiction of this Jewish asshole. It makes a whole world out of him. The film is sort of parable-like—it has a metaphysical undertone. The fact that we enter and exit Ratner, through the opal and through his body—speaking of assholes, through his colon—does make him a kind of archetypal figure.

Overview
The Unite to Face Addiction rally was held on 2015, which led to the formation of the nonprofit Facing Addiction, which merged with Partnership for Drug-Free Kids to form the Partnership to End Addiction. The group was part of a coalition of organizations lobbying for the passage of the Comprehensive Addiction and Recovery Act (CARA) in 2016. Local offshoots like Unite to Face Addiction Michigan (UFAM), continues to host annual rallies at the Michigan State Capitol.

wiki/valence-allocation.title: Valence Allocation
wiki/valence-allocation.content:
Overview
Valence allocation refers to the way positive or negative value, or valence is assigned to choices or experiences.
In the context of substance use, the brain experiences a massive flood of dopamine to signal a positive reward as a result of using substances that causes the brain to move positive valence away from natural rewards from the activities of everyday life. Instead, positive valence is assigned to the substance and the environmental cues around it. This happens through specialized neural circuits, namely the dopaminergic reward circuit in the ventral tegmental area (VTA), the amygdala, and the nucleus accumbens.

wiki/valence.title: Valence
wiki/valence.content:
Overview
Valence is the attractiveness of an object or event. Positive valence makes something desirable while negative valence means that something should be avoided. Valence allocation describes the process of assigning valence to the stimuli that one experiences. Evolutionary theorists argue that valence is a shortcut that gives organisms a instant gut-level calculation of whether something is beneficial or harmful rather than a slow logical calculation that freezes a system until it’s completed.

wiki/ventral-tegmental-area.title: Ventral Tegmental Area (VTA)
wiki/ventral-tegmental-area.content:
Overview
The ventral tegmental area (VTA) is a group of neurons in the midbrain where the brain’s dopamine pathways originate. Studies show that about 60% of the neurons are dopaminergic, 35% are GABAergic, and 5% are glutamatergic. The mesolimbic pathway signals from the VTA to the nucleus accumbens and limbic structures for the experiences of reward and pleasure. The mesocortical pathways signals to the prefrontal cortex and are involved in cognition, motivation, and executive function.

wiki/ventrolateral-prefrontal-cortex.title: Ventrolateral Prefrontal Cortex (VLPFC)
wiki/ventrolateral-prefrontal-cortex.content:
Overview
The ventrolateral prefrontal cortext (VLPFC) is a region of the frontal lobe of the brain. The left VLPFC maintains information in working memory and cognitive control; the right VLPFC plays a major role in motor inhibition, or stopping physical actions.
Chronic substance use is associated with reduced gray matter and hypoactivation in the right VLPFC, which means the physical act of holding oneself back from using substances again is more difficult to do. When exposed to triggers or cues for cravings, the VLPFC can become hyperactive and attribute high salience to the triggers, so one’s working memory can become focused on obtaining the substance through intense cravings instead of holding long-term benefits of sobriety in mind.

wiki/viagra.title: Viagra
wiki/viagra.content:
Overview
According to current medical consensus, Viagra is not physically addictive, but it is possible to develop a psychological dependence on it such that lacking it can contribute to anxiety and performance issues. Stopping the medication does not cause physical sickness, and sildenafil, the active ingredient, doesn’t activate the same pathways in the brain’s reward center as substances associated with addiction normally do.
Viagra is commonly used for case studies in public health and health economic content for a few reasons. First, sex sells. Second, sex medication sells; because sex has a high and constant demand from people, viagra is a medication that is in constant production and distribution.

wiki/vicarious-trial-and-error.title: Vicarious Trial and Error
wiki/vicarious-trial-and-error.content:
Overview
Vicarious trial and error (VTE) is a pattern where an organism pauses to examine alternative options before making a decision. That can include a rat in a maze or a student on a multiple-choice exam. VTE appears most often in the early stages of learning or when facing high-stakes or complex decisions. The more a pattern becomes learned as a habit, the less VTE is observed.
Chronic substance use affects the VTE in different waits depending on the type of substance used. Those with a history of chronic cocaine use showed lowered VTE behavior when looking at high-cost low-reward options, meaning their ability to deliberate before making a choice is disrupted. Those with a history of chronic morphine use showed the same VTE as non-users, but they struggle to change their minds and re-evaluate if the cost turns out to be unacceptably high.

wiki/victim-mentality.title: Victim Mentality
wiki/victim-mentality.content:
Overview
Victim mentality is a term that has two related but distinct uses. In a neutral sense, it can refer to a mindset or tendency for someone to perceive themselves as the victim of circumstances in their life, but it can be used negatively to describe someone constantly deflecting responsibility or neutrally to describe someone articulating traumatic experiences.
There was an attempt by some researchers to create the construct of a “Tendency for Interpersonal Victimhood (TIV)”, which measures four traits:

a need for recognition
moral elitism
lack of empathy
rumination

“The relationship between seeing oneself as a victim and a history of actual trauma was unclear in this research.”
Historical Context
“Victimology” was a term coined in 1947 by Benjamin Mendelsohn to describe the study of crime victims within the broader umbrella of criminology.
Early on, this meant a focus on “victim precipitation,” or the extent to which a victim is responsible for their victimization. In the context of a nation-state that imposes a system of laws on its populace, breaking the law is first an offense against state authority to maintain law and order, with the actual victim being a secondary consideration in the course of justice. Determining the victim’s role in the crime was thus driven by the goal of having a full accounting of people’s actions leading up to a law being broken.
The idea of “victim facilitation” qualified this by limiting the scope to unintentional actions that increased the risk of becoming the target of a crime. A woman whose drink is spiked with drugs at a bar is not blameworthy, but a victimologist might argue that leaving her drink unattended unintentionally raised the risk of being drugged and assaulted. On the flip side, “victim provocation” explicitly considers what the victim had done that might have incited another person to violence.
Notably, Mendelsohn was a lawyer who studied rape victims, and his victim typology that arose closely connected ignorance and voluntary participation in events preceding a crime with guilt. The category “victim with minor guilt” referred to victims who were either ignorant or unintentionally increased the risk of harm.
In 1948, Hans von Hentig published The Criminal and His Victim: Studies in the Sociobiology of Crime which sought to identify the characteristics of victims that made it more likely they would end up in a criminal-victim dynamic. He identified 13 types of characteristics that he reasoned were inherently associated with being victimized:

young
female
old
immigrant
depressed
mentally defective/deranged
acquisitive
dull normal
minority
wanton
lonesome
tormentor
blocked, exempted, and fighting

Von Hentig posited that whether someone with these qualities ends up becoming a victim depends on the actions they take given those characteristics. For young women, it might be taking risks that attract the attention of criminals. For immigrants and minorities, it may be a failure to assimilate to a “civilized” culture while retaining their “primitive” ways. For the depressed and lonesome, they may fail to recognize danger or somehow seek it because of their mental state. Tormentors maintain a constant aggressive disposition that incites others into harboring ill will towards them that can escalate into violence.
Marvin Wolfgang in 1957 was the first person to look at empirical data in regards to victimization, identifying 26% of all homicides in Philadelphia as “victim precipitated.” His student Menachem Amir would claim 1 in 5 rapes in Philadelphia were “victim precipitated” through either wearing revealing clothing, using risky language, or having a reputation for promiscuity or deviance.
In 1968, some time after the victim typology trend started among victimologists, Stephen Schafer wrote The Victim and His Criminal: A Study in Functional Responsibility. He proposed seven categories.

wiki/vital-alabama.title: VitAL Alabama
wiki/vital-alabama.content:
Overview
VitAL Alabama is a public health initiative based out of the University of Alabama that works to improve mental health and Substance Use Disorder (SUD) care across the state. Their projects include Connect Alabama as a mobile resource funded by federal CDC grants, suicide prevention screenings in rural counties, and the VitAL Annual Conference as a behavioral health summit. They also host other circuits, like the “Stop Judging, Start Healing” Stigma Summits and the Justice and Substance Use Alabama Summit.

wiki/vivitrol.title: Vivitrol
wiki/vivitrol.content:
Overview
Vivitrol is a prescription medication that contains naltrexone and is used to treat Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD) and Opioid Use Disorder (OUD). It’s administered as an intramuscular injection once a month to block the receptors in the brain that produce the rewarding effects of alcohol and opioids.

wiki/voices-for-non-opioid-choices.title: Voices for Non-Opioid Choices
wiki/voices-for-non-opioid-choices.content:
Overview
Voices for Non-Opioid Choices is a bipartisan national organizations dedicated to preventing Opioid Use Disorder (OUD) by advocating for alternative pain treatments to opioid medications or devices. The organization lobbied Congress for the passage of the Non-Opioids Prevent Addiction in the Nation (NOPAIN) Act, which allowed Medicare reimbursement on non-opioid pain management options for outpatient surgery.

wiki/volatile-organic-compound.title: Volatile Organic Compound (VOC)
wiki/volatile-organic-compound.content:
Overview
Volatile organic compounds (VOCs) are carbon-based chemicals with a high vapor pressure that easily evaporate into the air.
Many VOCs are part of inhalants that are targeted for recreational substance use. These include:


Toluene: spray paint, model glue, rubber cement, and industrial solvents


Nitrous oxide (“whippets”): whipped cream, chargers, medical anesthetics, automotive booster gas


Aklyl nitries (“poppers”): leather cleaners, industrial solvents, video head cleaners


Butane and Propane: lighter fluid, camping stove fuel, aerosol propellants


Acetone: nail polish remover, industrial adhesives, paint strippers


Tricholoroethylene: dry cleaning gluids, industrial degreasers, historical correction fluids

wiki/walden-two.title: Walden Two
wiki/walden-two.content:
Walden Two: Electric Boogaloo
There’s a very justifiable stereotype about academics that they live in elitist ivory towers, turning the rest of the world into variables to be studied and eventually controlled.
However, some of the most influential academics are often motivated by manifesting a worldview rather than just building a successful career. Francis Bacon was motivated to study the laws of the natural world as the laws of God, meant to be unpacked to be appreciated. Einstein presented defenses of socialist projects with critiques of the evidence generated by economics researchers. In his novels, Stephen Hawking would describe the Theory of Everything with an almost spiritual commitment to finding answers from the universe.
BF Skinner wrote Walden Two in the context to describe a world in which operant conditioning was accepted as a basic building block for the design of social systems. He argues through a fictional utopia that, with the right combination of incentives, a community could be fundamentally cooperative, peaceful, and leisurely. The society would be decentralized

Historical Context
“The Nixon campaign in 1968, and the Nixon White House after that, had two enemies: the antiwar left and black people. You understand what I’m saying? We knew we couldn’t make it illegal to be either against the war or black, but by getting the public to associate the hippies with marijuana and blacks with heroin, and then criminalizing both heavily, we could disrupt those communities. John Ehrlichman, President Nixon’s chief domestic policy adviser

wiki/washingtonian-temperance-society.title: Washingtonian Temperance Society
wiki/washingtonian-temperance-society.content:
Overview
The Washingtonian Temperance Society was founded in 1840 by six recovering alcoholics who practiced abstinence pledges, delivered “experience speeches” about their past, and actively recruited drunk men in their community. Their structure was focused on mutual aid and public confessions while generally minimizing the role of sectarian religious and politics in their meetings.
At one point, more than a tenth of Baltimore’s population and seven percent of New York City’s population were part of the Washington Temperance Society, or the Washingtonians. By 1845, most of the societies had collapsed and become inactive. Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) co-founder William Wilson (Bill W.) explicitly notes that the Washingtonians were an early mutual aid group for struggling alcoholics that fell apart because their involvement in outside issues drove them away from a primary purpose. Tradition Ten of AA is a rule derived from that historical lesson.

wiki/well-defined.title: Well-Defined
wiki/well-defined.content:
Overview
In science and math, a “well-defined” concept is something that has a clear meaning so that it can be interpreted the same way by everyone.
Historical Context
In the past, terms like “habitual drunkenness” existed, but there was no scientific or medical consensus about when that label should be applied. Legal cases based on someone’s intoxication, whether divorce or criminal cases, often applied local heuristics about what constituted occasional drunkenness vs habitual drunkenness. In the DSM-I and DSM-II, alcohol problems were classified under “Sociopathic Personality Disturbance;” the psychoanalytic approach essentially forced addiction to be seen as a structural personality problem.
As the field of psychiatry underwent a Kraepelinian paradigm shift, disorders were diagnosed through patterns of specific criteria believed to come from distinct physiological causes. This allowed disorders to have well-defined labels and criteria. In the DSM-3, published in 1980, this led to the creation of “Substance Abuse” and “Substance Dependence” as distinct labels. The DSM-5 now has a single Substance Use Disorder label that checks for 11 criteria and categorizes someone’s substance use pattern into Mild, Moderate, or Severe SUD.

wiki/what-would-you-do-alone-in-a-cage-w.title: What Would You Do Alone in a Cage with Nothing but Cocaine? (2026) by Hanna Pickard
wiki/what-would-you-do-alone-in-a-cage-w.content:
“Do the cocaine” is the obvious answer, but the book has a lot more to say than that.
Introduction
Commentary
It took me a while to appreciate the critical perspective philosophers of science provide about our research institutions. We take our instruments and traditions of knowledge for granted out of a very common human impulse to respect the legacy of the humans who came before us, so that those who inherit the legacy also inherit the legitimacy. Pickard summarizes the situation succinctly:
“In 1997, Alan L. Leshner, then directory of the US National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA), published his seminal article ‘Addiction is a Brain Disease, and It Matters,’ cementing a broken brain model of addiction as scientific orthodoxy. Since then, the brain disease model has grabbed the spotlight, claiming by far the lion’s share of funding and credibility, and putting neuroscience and animal models at the center of addiction research. Dissent is heresy. Junior scientists would be foolish to question the paradigm, while senior scientists have built their labs and legacies within it.”
This is a hurdle that, once recognized in research, pops the illusion of objectivity that holds academia beyond the reproach of institutional criticism, especially when the dominant paradigms for those modes of analysis are developed in those same academic institutions.
It’s especially easy to see this with AI research in 2026. Corporate labs completely outpace academic labs in funding and infrastructure, so academic talent is often forced to accept partnerships to do certain cutting-edge research projects at all. That’s assuming they don’t outright quit academic to work full-time for corporate labs or use their lab as a pipeline to startups they have a hand in. This means a lot of breakthroughs happen behind closed doors without independent auditing or peer-review. Even researchers have to consider the attention economy when hype and marketing are directly related to the interests of corporations, and therefore the probability of receiving research funding and opportunities for career advancement. Ethics researchers who study algorithmic bias or safety vulnerabilities are ignored if not harassed or blacklisted.
Addiction and recovery research struggles under a different set of pressures, but they impact the field nonetheless. The stigma and expense of any treatment or program make it difficult to get funding from sources outside of federal agencies, which are slow to pivot in response to new research and subject to sociopolitical headwinds. Policies like harm reduction that have strong empirical support are characterized by non-experts as proposals from morality or empathy rather than scientific rigor. Groups like Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) have been enormously successful in spreading their approach to recovery, but they developed prior to modern science and relied heavily on PR campaigns that treated mental health issues and addiction as “diseases like any other.” So to protest against the brain disease model isn’t just brushing up against established scientists with careers, but also against the conventional wisdom that the public has been made aware of through the education efforts of philanthropic and mutual aid societies. I couldn’t agree more with Pickard’s framing, but I think she sells her own point short by marking the 1997 Leshner paper as a singular event that cemented the brain disease model as orthodoxy in science. Or, as Pickard says, the “broken brain” model. There was a long history of AA collaborating with doctors and researchers behind it too.
I’ve said a lot without actually describing the broken brain model as Pickard frames it:
“The core idea of the model is as gripping as it is familiar. After prolonged drug use, ‘a metaphorical switch in the brain’ is flicked and the brain is ‘hijacked’ by drugs… the brain disease model treats addiction as occurring when the kind of freedom of will that we normally take for granted is lost: The ordinary, voluntary behavior of a rat or a person - pressing a lever, downing a drink, swallowing a pill, injecting, inhaling, or snorting a substance - becomes compulsive, transformed into a passive, involuntary symptom of a brain disease.”
“Hijacking” is one of the most common ways that the relationship between drugs and the brain’s dopmaine system are explained within recovery spaces, and I’m including psychoeducation classes in this. As a quick test, I spat “do drugs hijack the dopamine system” into Google, and received the following answer:
“Yes, addictive drugs completely hijack the brain’s natural dopamine reward system. They flood pathways with massive chemical surges—up to 10 times higher than natural rewards like food or social connection—rewiring how the brain processes motivation, pleasure, and control. You can review detailed scientific breakdowns of this process via the National Institute on Drug Abuse.”
Upon following the link to the NIDA page here nida.nih.gov/publications/drugs-brains-behavior-science-addiction/drugs-brain (published July 2020) and we see:
“Simple activities in everyday life can produce small bursts of neurotransmitters in the brain bringing pleasurable feelings. Drugs can hijack that process.”
“It was once thought that surges of the neurotransmitter dopamine produced by drugs directly caused the euphoria, but scientists now think dopamine has more to do with getting us to repeat pleasurable activities (reinforcement) than with producing pleasure directly.”
Clark Fisher, author of The Urge, has mentioned that it’s not necessarily a coincidence that “hijack” was produced as a term following the crime hysteria of the late 1990s, following carjacking being coined and popularized by national media like Nightline. The notion of a hostile invader suddenly seizing control of the path someone takes was already embedded in the public imagination. The notion of hijacking was intuitive and utilized as an attempt to combat stigma, though it had a lot of unintended consequences as well, such as increasing the risk of some patients developing a sense of learned helplessness from feeling they have no agency. It has remained controversial, though the ease of delivering the explanation has remained a factor in its popularity.
Also, Pickard makes an excellent shout-out to contingency management as “the most effective treatment for cocaine and some polydrug addictions… not pharmacological but behavioral… It is based on operant conditioning principles… elaborated by B.F. Skinner in the 1930s and 1940s” - well before the brain disease model and hijacking metaphor were commonly accepted. I truly love to highlight contingency management whenever it comes up. It’s the easiest counterargument to the idea that addiction can be understood and managed solely through the lens of an individual being internally disordered. In fact, from the studies we’ve done on animals since 1985, Pickard notes that 90% of rats would forego cocaine for sweetened water, and nearly 100% of rats would choose one minute of playtime with another rat over cocaine:
“So much for the idea that rats are compelled by their cocaine-broken brains to keep pressing the lever for more, when all it takes to lure them away is a drink of saccharin water, a minute of playtime, or the whiff of a buddy… Why then did they take so much cocaine in Bozarth and Wise’s 1985 experiment, when they were alone in a cage with nothing but cocaine? Presumably, because they were alone in a cage with nothing but cocaine. The currenly dominant scientific paradigm is broken. It is time for heresy.”
I reveal my own bias when I say this, but I can’t hide my love of writing that delivers the catharsis of cutting through a Gordion Knot that’s been sitting in my stomach. One of the best things about standing on the shoulders of giants is that there’s so much to see from the heights they’ve reached and depths they’ve traversed. But to step down and find a new vantage point, perhaps slaying the giant in the process, becomes more difficult too. The bigger they are, the harder they fall, and the harder it is to fell them. Pickard’s sword comes in the form of a paradigm which,
“can be distilled into two core and connected characteristics: humanism and heterogeneity.”
Humanism
Admittedly, the very first time I heard of the term humanism, I chalked it up as a feel-good garnish on top of a “real” substantive theory that was driven empiricism and rationality. I have since repented for my STEM bro ways.
Humanism historically has referred to a distinct approach within the umbrellas of psychology and philosophy that rejected Freudian psychoanalysis that treated unconscious drives as deterministic while also rejecting Watson’s behaviorsm that reduced human complexity to conditioning. Instead, humanism posits that each person exists within the center of their own subjective interpretation of reality shaped by their unique capacity for processing experiences. To the extent that fundamental biological drives for humans can exist in this framework, it is to reproduce the experience of itself with growth, differentiation, and fulfillment. A lack of congruence, or alignment, between an ideal self and a real self is seen as the source of pathological suffering. Cognitive distortions or denial supported by rationalizations are defense mechanisms against the tension of incongruence. Rather than external institutions or social expectations determining the success of an individual’s function, humanists tend to trust an individual in their own interpretation of reality to evaluate the feedback provided by their own subconscious processes. In fact, external imposition of the conditions of worth is considered one of the main reasons individuals are deterred from actualizing themselves according to their own feedback.
Pickard explains incongruence without using the term, sparing readers from jargon in a way I refuse to do myself:
“people with addiction tend to speak of when and why they first started using; where they use; who they use with; what makes them want to use; what drugs do for them; what drugs mean to them; how they crave them, love them, need them, hate them; how they feel when they use; how they feel when they don’t use; how they feel about the fact that they use; and even, for some people, how their use is part of their identity - their sense of who they are. Often, although not always, they also express uncertaintly about the brain disease model, which sits uneasily with their own experience of addiction.”
To some extent, duh. People rarely experience their life as random spiritual possession that actually hijacks the direction of their life. Isn’t that how we get the most boring horror movies too? Alien (1979) is the top rated horror movie on IMDB, and it’s not because the details concerning the biological process of the Xenomorph reproduction cycle was of intense interest to anyone except maybe hard sci-fi fans. There are countless nature documentaries about parasitic insects that scratch that itch far better. Alien shows us an apex biological predator indifferent to human suffering paralleled closely with a manmade corporation’s indifference, explicitly inspired by the cosmic apathy found in Lovecraftian horror. The android programmed to fulfill the corporation’s mission admires the alien as a “perfect organism” compared to the “expendable” working-class crew who are simply trying to earn paychecks for survival.
It’s similarly of little interest to us to consider addiction just a mechanistic process in which a substance has altered our biology. The term “hijack” is loaded with narrative implications that shape a subjective construction of one’s experience with a substance. It suggests an independent force or agent at work that overrides one’s autonomy and identity, not unlike a malevolent spirit or parasitic alien that hijacks one’s body. Before the instruments of modern medicine that allowed us to explain the world through material mechanisms and physical laws, lots of cultures built their systems of knowledge on the premise of spiritual laws. For instance, many in Ancient Greece thought that drinking invited the consciousness of the god Dionysus to inhabit one’s body, but this is arguably a deeply humanist perspective rather than a mechanical explanation. Dionysus as a concept served as a way to discuss an altered state of consciousness in which repressed desires and thoughts can emerge to drive action. The dissolution of ego, felt internally and perceived externally, in the process of Dionysus taking over introduces a liminality through which social and personal transgressions are negotiated. The word “enthusiasm” has its roots in exactly this type of possession referred to as enthousiasmos.
Not to wax nostalgic about an era I was never born in, but it feels often that in replacing supernatural explanations with mechanistic materialist ones vetted by rationality and empiricism, we pathologized common expressions of our experiences so that they could be mapped onto standardizable measures. Dionysus no longer possesses us when we drink; the GABA receptors responsible for inhibitory neurotransmitters are obstructed while our prefrontal cortex downregulates. Both Jung and Nietzsche used the myth of Dionysus to critique the hyper-rational and hyper-material paradigms that defined the trajectory of “Western” civilization. From a humanist perspective, Jung calls out the repression of the self that results from the conditioning of worth imposed by external social mechanisms. Nietzsche argued that the passions of life had been stifled and sterilized through the worship of reason and logic, thereby leading to a nihilism that reason cannot address.

wiki/white-knuckling.title: White-Knuckling
wiki/white-knuckling.content:
Overview
White-knuckling refers to enduring a stressful or painful situation with willpower alone. In the context of substance use, it refers to starting and maintaining sobriety without support of any kind, including handling withdrawals alone. For substances like alcohol and benzodiazepines, withdrawals can be potentially fatal. It also typically means foregoing detoxification, tapering, therapy, peer support groups like Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) or Recovery Dharma (RD), medication, and rehabilitation centers.
The term comes from gripping something so tightly that one’s knuckles turn white, which represents the result of relying on withstanding tension through willpower alone instead of seeking relief.

wiki/whole-person-care.title: Whole-Person Care
wiki/whole-person-care.content:
Overview
Whole-person care is a holistic approach to healthcare that addresses the entire individual with physical, mental, emotional, social, and spiritual dimensions of their well-being.
The National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH) proposed the Whole Person Health Index (WPHI) as a 9-item self-reporting instrument to screen someone’s general health.

wiki/wilhelm-wundt.title: Wilhelm Maximilian Wundt
wiki/wilhelm-wundt.content:
Overview
Willhelm Wundt was a German professor who was the first to distinguish psychology from philosophy and biology, call himself a psychologist, establish a formal laboratory for psychology, and start the first academic journal covering research in psychology.
Connections
Students

James McKeen Cattell, first American professor of psychology, 1895 President of the American Psychology Association

wiki/william-f-bill-callahan-leadership-.title: William F. "Bill" Callahan Leadership Award | NAADAC
wiki/william-f-bill-callahan-leadership-.content:
Overview
William F. Callahan was a detective and councilman who maintained a career in public service until retirement in 1971, after which he pivoted into addressing substance use disorders. He was appointed to the Connecticut Alcohol and Drug Abuse Council and was co-founer of PACES Counseling Associates of East Harford and Avon. He founded the Connecticut Federation of Alcohol and Drug Abuse counselors and helped to introduce the first counselor certification in the state.
To be eligible for the award, one must have had 15 years of addiction counseling experience, demonstrate leadership and activism in awareness projects, demonstrate support for other addiction counselors, and be a NAADAC member in good standing and compliance with the NAADAC Code of Ethics.

wiki/william-f-bynum.title: William F. Bynum
wiki/william-f-bynum.content: William Bynum (also referred to often as W.F. Bynum) is a notable historian whose 1968 paper pointed out the way acute impacts of alcoholism or heavy drinking were acknowledged by medicinal authorities, but the concept of “chronic alcoholism” still seemed ill-defined and elusive. He collaborated with another notable historian of medicine, Roy Porter, on the Companion Encyclopedia of the History of Medicine (1994)

wiki/william-howard-taft.title: William Howard Taft
wiki/william-howard-taft.content:
Taft said in a speech to Congress that cocaine was leading to the most serious drug crisis America had ever seen, at least by the year 1910.
When Taft was the governor general of the Philippines, he wanted to bring back a monopoly on opium to have a regulated supply in the place of foreign imports that emerged during the Spanish-American War. Religious leaders like Bishop Charles Henry Brent lobbied Taft until he agreed to declare a prohibition on opium instead.

wiki/wings-across-alabama.title: Wings Across Alabama
wiki/wings-across-alabama.content:
Overview
Wings Across Alabama is the largest peer-run mental health organization in Alabama. Their services include the Alabama Warm Line, peer-led support groups, and educational programs like Action Planning for Prevention and Recovery (APPR).
Links

wingsacrossal.org/about-us/

wiki/withdrawal-2025.title: Withdrawal (2025)
wiki/withdrawal-2025.content: A story of a young couple going through withdrawals together, shaped by Aaron Strand’s own experience with substance use.

wiki/withdrawal.title: Withdrawal
wiki/withdrawal.content:
Overview
Withdrawal is the process of suddenly stopping or reducing a substance that the body has adapted to over time, which is usually accompanied by many unpleasant symptoms. Withdrawal from alcohol and benzodiazepines are especially at-risk of being fatal. Withdrawal from common recreational substances includes:


Alcohol: High blood pressure, nausea, vomiting, dehydration, tremors, confusion, sweating, insomnia, seizures, delirium tremens (DTs)


Opioids: flu-like symptoms, nausea, vomiting, sweating, cravings


Stimulants: exhaustion, sleep disturbances, depressive episodes


Nicotine: Irritability, headaches, brain fog, restlessness

wiki/woodstock.title: Woodstock
wiki/woodstock.content:
Overview
“Woodstock” refers to the Woodstock Music and Art Fair held from August 15 to 18, 1969 in Bethel, New York. The event attracted up to an estimated 500,000 people and became cemented in the history of 1960s counterculture. It was known for having a culture of open air substance use among both the attendees and the performers. The fair’s medical director William Abruzzi adopted some early harm-reduction ideas to manage those having bad trips from psychedelics, like “freakout tents” to safely experience volunteers comfort and guide them through hallucinations.

wiki/workaholism.title: Workaholism
wiki/workaholism.content:
Overview
Workaholism is a compulsive need to work or inability to disengage from work for reasons other than financial or job requirements. It’s not classified as an official disease or disorder in the DSM-5-TR or the ICD-11, but it still describes a pattern of behavior that clinicians and treatment providers take seriously. It can be a marker of Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder (OCPD), depression, anxiety, and ADHD.

wiki/wraparound-services.title: Wraparound Services
wiki/wraparound-services.content:
Overview
Wraparound services are the non-clinical community resources that complement clinical approaches to treating those with behavioral and mental health issues. These include housing services, transportation coordination, vocational training, job placement, educational advocacy, court liaison services, benefits navigation, Medication-Assisted Treatment (MAT) care coordination, nutritional counseling, childcare services, and peer recovery support specialists.

wiki/writing-the-big-book-the-creation-o.title: Writing the Big Book - The Creation of AA (2019) by William H. Schaberg
wiki/writing-the-big-book-the-creation-o.content:
Chapter 1
“While these real-time documents provide the most unassailable evidence for what happened in Alcoholics Anonymous between late 1934 and early 1939, that history is further embellished by the later writings and statements of four early participants in the story: Bill Wilson (A.A.’s founder), Ebby Thatcher (the man who first exposed Bill to the ideas that led to the creation of A.A.), Jim Burwell (an early atheistic member of A.A.), and Ruth Hock (A.A.’s first secretary). The word ‘embellished’ is used here deliberately to emphasize the fact that each of these four major eyewitnesses has proven to be unreliable, to one degree or another, once their testimony is critically compared with the available archived materials.”
Schaberg’s tone feels a little coy here. “Embellished” is not a term used to convey the normal inaccuracy that goes with a flawed human memory, but instead the exaggeration and elaboration that comes with a generally intentional distortion of the truth.
He elaborates though that it’s “not meant to impugn everything that was said at some distance from the actual events, but knowing how defective and creative memory can be demands that we check and, if possible, correct those errors by comparing them with the more reliable, more believable evidence provided by contemporary documentation.”
It sounds like a focus on fact-checking, but we also get some narrativizing to preface that right away:
“Bill Wilson, the man who contributed more ‘factual’ information than anyone else to the traditional story of A.A., was by far the worst offender when it came to accuracy regarding their early history. This may sound harsh to Wilson’s many worshipful admirers in the Fellowship of Alcoholics Anonymous, but it is an undeniable fact… Wilson’s divergence from the truth was so common and so pervasive that it can only be compared to a dark cloud looming over any attempt to write an accurate history of A.A.’s early years, obscuring and even falsifying what happened at several key points in the story.”
“Wilson became increasingly aware of the need to curb his natural tendencies toward grandiosity… Bill regularly sidestepped these ego traps by modifying the facts, changing the story in ways that deflected attention away from himself.”
Embellished, indeed. Bill isn’t around to defend himself anymore, and while I know many AA members certainly are, I’ll still keep that in mind. I’m a little wary of works that begin by rhetorically priming the reader for a position before laying out something concrete to interpret. Schaberg explicitly points to Pass It On for corroboration, citing that Wilson was “never reluctant to stretch a fact for the sake of emphasis” and “was never likely to pass up the opportunity to deliver a parable where he thought it could do some good.” These do feel a little euphemistic to me.
“Finally, many aspects of the true stories just did not make for comfortable retelling once Alcoholics Anonymous became a successful national institution. This was the case, for instance, concerning A.A.’s early partnership with the Oxford Group”
While I don’t agree with everything about A.A. and have expressed that openly, I will repeatedly give it credit for providing a genuinely accessible fellowship network of people pursuing recovery and a fulfilling sober life.
The Oxford Group has no such distinction. Frank Buchman, its founder, thought a utopia on Earth would be possible through Christian dictatorships and wanted to convert Hitler. Wilson has credited the Oxford Group for being the primary source of the spiritual principles behind the Steps. I had assumed that this only meant that there was some overlap in membership before Wilson tried to create a space exclusively for alcoholics. “Partnership” implies something deeper than that, which piques my interest.

wiki/yage-vine.title: Yage Vine (Banisteriopsis Caapi)
wiki/yage-vine.content:
Overview
The yage vine has been used by the indigenous Amazonian nations for thousands of years, particularly to make drinks like ayahuasca. Over 70 different groups, including the Tukano, Siona, Inga, and Shipibo, have their own names and preparation styles of the vine. In generall, it was consumed by shamans and healers as part of ritual practices rather than ordinary people as a recreational substance. Studies have shown that the alkaloids in yage stimulate neuroplasticity, or the creation of new neural pathways. When brewed by itself instead of a companion plant with DMT, it’s not a psychedelic and behaves more like a sedative.

wiki/yale-program-in-addiction-medicine.title: Yale Program in Addiction Medicine
wiki/yale-program-in-addiction-medicine.content:
Overview
The Yale Program in Addiction Medicine (YPAM) operates as an interdisciplinary research initiative across the Yale School of Medicine. It manages an Addiction Recovery Clinic (ARC), consult services, specialized care like M|Medication for Opioid Use Disorder (MOUD) through the New London Buprenorphine Clinic and the Opioid Reassessment Clinic. It also leads the National Methadone Access and Quality Commission (NMAQC), funded by the Foundation for Opioid Response Efforts (FORE), which advocates for policy reform that standardizes patient experiences with and access to methadone.

wiki/yavin-shaham.title: Yavin Shahan
wiki/yavin-shaham.content:
Yavin Shaham is a neuroscientist at the National Institute on Drug Abuse Intramural Research Program.
Works

Volitional social interaction prevents drug addiction in rat models (2018)

“Addiction treatment has not been appreciably improved by neuroscientific research. One problem is that mechanistic studies using rodent models do not incorporate volitional social factors, which play a critical role in human addiction. Here, using rats, we introduce an operant model of choice between drugs and social interaction. Independent of sex, drug class, drug dose, training conditions, abstinence duration, social housing, or addiction score in Diagnostic & Statistical Manual IV-based and intermittent access models, operant social reward prevented drug self-administration. ”

wiki/young-schema-questionnaire-revised.title: Young Schema Questionnaire-Revised (YSQ-R)
wiki/young-schema-questionnaire-revised.content:
Overview
The Young Schema Questionnaire-Revised (YSQ-R) is a 116-item self-report questionnaire that measures Early Maladaptive Schemas (EMS). It was developed in 2022 as a refinement of Jeffrey Young’s YSQ-L3 using Rasch analysis.

wiki/z-drugs.title: Z-Drugs
wiki/z-drugs.content:
Overview
Z-drugs are a class of sedative-hypnotic medications mainly used for insomnia. These include:


Zolpidem (Ambien)


Eszopiclone (Lunesta)


Zaleplon (Sonata)


Zopiclone (Zimovane, Immovane)


They act as non-benzodiazepine benzodiazepine receptor agonists (NBBRAs) and bind to GABA receptors in the brain, which slows brain activity and causes sleepiness. Although designed to be less habit-forming than conventional benzodiazepines, they still come with a risk of dependence and withdrawals if used repeatedly or in excess.

wiki/zen-nihon-danshu-renmei.title: Zen Nihon Danshu Renmei
wiki/zen-nihon-danshu-renmei.content:
Overview
Zen Nihon Danshu Renmei, known in English as All Nippon Abstinence Association, is the largest network of self-help groups for those struggling with alcohol dependence in Japan outside of Alcoholics Anonymous (AA). They provide peer support networks, recovery group meetings, and rehabilitation programs.
Historical Context
The organization was formed in 1963 after consolidating local Danshukai groups that formed in Tokyo in 1958.

wiki/zero-limits-the-secret-hawaiian-sys.title: Zero Limits - the Secret Hawaiian System for Wealth, Health, Power, and More
wiki/zero-limits-the-secret-hawaiian-sys.content: There’s something about “the secret Hawaiian system” that tickles the same part of my brain that “ancient Toltec wisdom” does.

wiki/zohran-mamdani.title: Zohran Mamdani
wiki/zohran-mamdani.content:
In 2025, Zohran Mamdani was elected Mayor of New York City after being elected to the New York State Assembly in 2020.
Articles

www.cbsnews.com/news/nyc-drug-addiction-onpoint-harm-reduction/

“Just two months after taking office, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani visited OnPoint to show support for the program. ‘This weekend, the team at OnPoint NYC kept their doors open 24/7 so vulnerable New Yorkers had somewhere safe to go,’ Mamdani posted on X  in March, alongside photos of himself with Rivera and other staff.”

wiki/zoopharmacognosy.title: Zoopharmacognosy
wiki/zoopharmacognosy.content:
Overview
Zoopharmacognosy is the study of how animals self-medicate to address their illnesses.
As examples:


Chimpanzees swallow leaves to purge stomach parasites


Capuchin monkeys use limes and onions to repel insects


Crows flatten themselves over anthills to let ants climb through their feathers, since the ants release formic acid which destroys mites, lice, and fungi


Dolphins rub their skin against corals and sea sponges that release antimicrobial mucus and protects against infections through the skin

wiki/zyklon-b.title: Zyklon B
wiki/zyklon-b.content:
Overview
Zyklon B was the name for a cyanide-based pesticide developed in 1920s Germany. It was also one of the main chemicals used by the Nazis in gas chambers during the Holocaust for mass extermination. After WWII ended, executives and directors of the companies that supplied Zyklon B were tried and executed for war crimes.
